0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The message. John tells us who Jesus is, so that we may trust him and live: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (20:31). Belief here is not only agreeing that facts are true, but trusting a person; and life is not mere existence, but knowing God: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (17:3). Matthew shows Jesus as Israel’s King, Mark as the suffering Servant, Luke as the Saviour of the lost; John begins before creation and shows him as the eternal Word who was God and who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (1:14).

Background: the writer. The Gospel calls its author only the disciple whom Jesus loved, who reclined next to Jesus at the Last Supper (13:23), stood at the cross (19:26) and ran to the empty tomb (20:2–8): “This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things” (21:24; compare 19:35). He never names himself or his brother James. From the second century, beginning with Irenaeus, who had known Polycarp, a hearer of John, the church identified him as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. The same tradition says he wrote in old age at Ephesus, the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, probably about AD 85–95, the last of the four Gospels.

The first readers. John explains Aramaic words (Rabbi, Messiah, 1:38, 41) and Jewish customs such as the water jars “for the Jewish rites of purification” (2:6), so he expected readers who were not Jews, or Jews far from the land. Yet he assumes they can follow the Old Testament, and he writes for believers who had paid a price: the warning that those who confessed Jesus would be put out of the synagogue (9:22; 16:2) would have struck home. By then Rome had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, the church had spread across the empire, and false ideas about who Jesus was were in the air.

The world of the story. Much of the story is set in Judea and Jerusalem, around the pilgrim feasts: at least three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2) and the Feast of Dedication (10:22). The powers are the chief priests and the Pharisees, and above them Rome’s governor, Pontius Pilate. When John speaks of “the Jews” opposing Jesus he means chiefly the leaders in Jerusalem; John, Jesus and all the first disciples were Jews.

Why is it so different? John has no parables, fewer miracles and long discourses, and the great “I am” sayings are his alone. He was not correcting Matthew, Mark and Luke but completing them, choosing his material deliberately (20:30–31) and leaving out far more than he included (21:25). Where the others mostly give the Galilean ministry, John adds much from Jerusalem. The account of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is missing from the earliest manuscripts; this commentary holds that it was not part of John’s original Gospel, though it may record a true event.

Did John really write it? Many modern scholars think the beloved disciple was a Jerusalem follower of Jesus outside the Twelve, or that the Gospel grew within a community of his followers and was finished by others; some date it before AD 70. But the book claims an eyewitness behind it, it knows Jerusalem before its fall closely, the beloved disciple is paired with Peter just as John is in Acts, and the church’s testimony is early and consistent. The more likely conclusion is that John the son of Zebedee is the beloved disciple and the writer of the Gospel.

How the book makes its case. The prologue (1:1–18) gives the whole story in brief: the Word who was God came into the world he made, “his own people did not receive him” (1:11), but those who received him became children of God. Chapters 1:19–12:50, often called the Book of Signs, begin with John the Baptist pointing to “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (1:29). Then seven signs rise in power and publicity: water into wine (chapter 2), the official’s son healed at a distance (chapter 4), the invalid healed on the Sabbath (chapter 5), the five thousand fed and the walk on the water (chapter 6), the man born blind (chapter 9), and Lazarus raised after four days in the tomb (chapter 11). Each is a window onto who Jesus is, and each divides its witnesses. Around them come conversations (chapters 3–4) and mounting controversy (chapters 5–10). Again and again “My hour has not yet come” (2:4), until chapter 12: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23). Chapters 13–21 are the Book of Glory. In the upper room Jesus washes his disciples’ feet and teaches them (chapters 13–16) about the Father’s house, “another Helper” (14:16), the call to “abide in me” (15:4), the world’s hatred and the coming joy; then he prays for them and for all who will believe through their word (chapter 17). Chapters 18–19 tell of the arrest, the trials and the cross, where he says, “It is finished” (19:30); chapter 20 of the empty tomb, ending in Thomas’s “My Lord and my God!” (20:28). Chapter 21 ends not with a commission on a mountain but with a question on a beach, and Peter restored to feed Christ’s sheep.

Where it leads: to Christ. Seven times Jesus joins “I am” to a picture of what he is for us: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, and the true vine. These echo the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14), and when Jesus says, “before Abraham was, I am” (8:58), his hearers take up stones: they know he is claiming to be God. He fulfils Israel’s worship: he is the tabernacle where God’s glory dwells (1:14), the temple destroyed and raised in three days (2:19–21), the true bread of which the manna was a sign (chapter 6), the living water and the light of the Feast of Tabernacles (7:37–39; 8:12), and the Passover Lamb, of whom “Not one of his bones will be broken” (19:36). The signs point beyond themselves to his death and rising: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (3:14). In John the cross is not a defeat later reversed; it is where his glory is seen.

For us. John was written so that you may believe, and believing have life now, not only one day. It shows a Saviour fully God and truly man: weary at a well, weeping at a grave, yet raising the dead. It gives deep assurance: no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (10:28), and “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (13:1). And it asks every reader what Jesus asked Peter on the shore: “Do you love me?” (21:17). Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The eternal Word, who was with God and was God, has become flesh and made the Father known. Verses 1–5 tell who he was before anything existed: with God, himself God, the maker of all things, and the source of life and of a light the darkness cannot put out. Verses 6–8 bring in John, a man sent to bear witness to that light. Verses 9–13 tell the tragedy and the gift: the world he made did not know him and his own people did not receive him, yet all who receive him are made children of God, born of God. Verses 14–18 reach the summit: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth, and the only Son has made God known.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word is not an abstract principle but the personal Son of God, through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. Jesus is fully God, eternal with the Father, the one through whom all was created and the source of life, and becoming man did not make him any less God (see the note on vv. 13–14). On the switch of verbs from was to became, see the note on vv. 1–2.

A place among God’s children is given, not earned: the new birth has one source, God (see the note on vv. 13–14), and the right of verse 12 is a standing he grants, while the Son is kept for Jesus alone (see the note on vv. 11–12).

Grace and truth (vv. 14, 17) echo the name God proclaimed to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6): what Moses was shown in part has now come in person (see the notes on vv. 13–14 and vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Whoever grasps from the prologue who Jesus is will read every later sign rightly. The Word was God, not a god, is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s full deity in Scripture.

The darkness has not overcome it is the sentence a reader in a dark season needs (see the note on vv. 5–6).

Because nothing in the new birth was contributed by the one born, there is nothing in it he can later fail to keep up. For the Christian who cannot locate a moment of conversion, see the note on vv. 13–14.

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anything existed, the Word already was: face to face with God, and himself God. These two verses take us further back than any other page of the Bible, to the Son before the world, in eternal fellowship with the Father, sharing all that the Father is without being the Father.

In the beginning. The words deliberately echo Genesis 1:1: John begins a new Genesis, a new creation. But he goes further back. Genesis says what happened in the beginning; John says what already existed in the beginning.

Was the Word. Not “came to be”, but “was”. The tense (imperfect) means continuous existence: there was never a moment when the Word was not.

Why the Word? Because a word is what comes out of a person and tells you what is inside him. You can watch a man for a year and learn very little; he says one sentence and you know something you could never have worked out by looking. God is not visible. But God has an eternal Word, not a sound he makes but a Person, his own Son, and that Person has now walked into a room and spoken to people who could hear him. A word expresses what is in the mind; Jesus expresses who God is.

A word for Jews and Greeks. A Jewish reader hears Genesis, a world that exists because God spoke (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6), and the prophets, where the word of the LORD does what it was sent to do (Isaiah 55:11). A Greek reader hears logos, the reason holding the universe together, which his philosophers had been reaching for. He does not say the Word is a principle. He says the Word had a face, and we ate with him.

And the Word was with God. “With” (pros) means face to face with, turned towards. The Word is distinct from God the Father, in eternal fellowship with him: two persons, and between them not distance but communion. So love did not begin when God made someone to love. Before the world was made the Father loved the Son (17:24); love is not something God learned from his creatures but what he has always been (1 John 4:8).

And the Word was God. Not a god, not divine in some lesser sense, but fully God, God by nature. In Greek “God” comes first for emphasis (theos ēn ho logos). John needs to say two things at once: the Word is not the same person as the Father (“the Word was with God”), and the Word is nonetheless all that the Father is (“the Word was God”). Had he written “the God”, with the article, he would have said the Word was the Father. And the next verse closes the door: “All things were made through him”, so the Word cannot be among the things that were made. He stands on the Creator’s side of the line. Here is the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity: not yet named, but already present.

Watch the verbs. In these two verses the Word simply “was”, four times, in a tense with no starting point in view. From verse 3 the verb for everything else changes: all things “came to be”; there “came to be” a man sent from God (v. 6). In verse 14 that second verb is at last used of the Word himself: “the Word became flesh”. He never became God. He became man.

He was in the beginning with God. Verse 2 is not padding but a guard. “The Word was God”, standing alone, could be heard as saying the Word simply is the Father under a second name. So John says once more that he was with God, so that neither truth cancels the other: there is one God, and the Son is not the Father.

The alternative is silence. The alternative to this sentence is not a neutral universe but a silent one. If the beginning was matter alone, the deepest thing about reality is force: impersonal, uninterested and very old, and everything warm arrives late and by accident, and will go out. Many thoughtful people honestly hold that view. John says the deepest thing about reality is a conversation. Before anything existed that could hear him, God was speaking, and what he was saying was a Son.

In everyday life. Ask what you picture God doing before he made anything. If the honest answer is waiting, then you are praying to someone who needed you, and you will never quite shake the suspicion that you are a disappointing return on his loneliness. The God of this verse was not lonely. He made you out of a fullness already complete without you: a Father who had a Son to love before there was a universe, and who has decided to bring you into that love. Pray to him like that today.

Does this mean there are three Gods? No. Christians believe in one God, as firmly as any Jew (Deuteronomy 6:4). But this one God exists eternally as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three persons who share one and the same divine being. The Son is not a part of God, or a third of God, or a junior God; he is wholly God, as the Father is, and he is not the Father. No picture from creation captures it, and most attempts (water, ice and steam; one man as father, son and husband) end up teaching an old error: that God is one person wearing three masks. We do not believe it because we can picture it, but because God has said it, and because only a Saviour who is truly God can bring us to God.

If Jesus is God, who was he praying to? To his Father. Prayer between the Son and the Father is not God talking to himself; it is the eternal conversation of verse 1, overheard on earth. Before the world existed, the Father and the Son were face to face in love (17:5, 24). When the Son became man, that relationship was carried into a human life, so that he prayed, depended and obeyed as a man. The prayers in the Gospels are not a problem for the doctrine of the Trinity; they are one of the clearest windows onto it.

Where Christians differ, and beyond. Jehovah’s Witnesses translate “the Word was a god”, arguing from the absence of the article before theos. This commentary’s view: this is grammatically mistaken. In Greek, a noun placed before the verb without the article usually stresses the nature or quality of the subject; here it does not mean “a god”. John means the Word was fully divine, all that God is, without being the same person as the Father. A “god” alongside God would be polytheism, which John, a Jew, utterly rejected. The church confessed it at Nicaea (325): true God from true God, of one substance with the Father.
verseByVerse.note: “In the beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. “The Word” (Greek logos) was a term both Jews and Greeks understood: God’s self-expression, through which he created and revealed himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything that exists was made through the Word, and the life in him is his own, the life that is the light of men. He is the Creator, not a creature, and the source of all life, natural and eternal.

All things were made through him. The Father created all things through the Son (Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2; 1 Corinthians 8:6). The scope is total: there is no eternal matter independent of God, and the Word is not one creative force among many. If all things were made through him, he himself was not made.

And without him was not any thing made that was made. John says it twice, forward and backward, and the second clause is a fence. There is no back door into existence: no raw material lying about, no dark thing that got in by another route. It also refutes the ancient heresy (Arianism) that the Son was the first and highest created being.

Everything that was used against him. Follow “all things” into the story this Gospel is about to tell. He made the wood the cross was cut from, the ore that became the nails, the hands that drove them, and the breath in the lungs of the men swinging the hammers. Nothing was ever used against him that he had not first supplied.

In him was life. John’s word is zōē, 36 times in this Gospel. He does not mean simply being alive, which plants and animals share with us, but the life that belongs to God himself: “as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (5:26). Everything else that lives has life the way a room has light at four in the afternoon: on loan, from elsewhere, and shortly to be withdrawn. In the Word life is not on loan. It is his own, and he gives it.

What John means by eternal life. When John speaks of “eternal life”, he means this same life, God’s own life, shared with us (see also Eternal Life in the Theological Dictionary). It is a quality before it is a length. Jesus defines it himself: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (17:3). Not facts about God, but the knowing of a child with a father, a friend with a friend: knowing God, being loved by him and loving him back, life at its fullest (10:10).

It begins now and never ends. John keeps saying “has”: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (3:36; compare 5:24). It starts the moment a person trusts Christ, it is not cut off by the death of the body, and it reaches its fullness at the resurrection, when Jesus will “raise him up on the last day” (6:40).

Where this life is found. In one place only: “this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:11–12). It is not a substance Christ hands out and then leaves us to keep going on our own; it is himself, shared with us as we are joined to him by faith. Its opposite in John is not ceasing to exist but perishing (3:16): being cut off from God, the source of all life.

The light of men. In this Gospel light is the revelation of God, truth and salvation, set against the darkness of sin, ignorance and death. By chapter 8 Jesus will say it outright: “I am the light of the world” (8:12). The light is not a body of teaching he brought with him but the overflow of the life he is. Nobody is illuminated by studying him from across the room; people are illuminated by being near him.

The spring of life went down into death. The only one in the universe who has life in himself chose to die. The spring of all life went down into death, and on the third day came up out of it still the spring; and the life that is the light of men now shines on graves, because he has been in one and come out.

What do you have that you did not receive? Nothing, not even your next breath (1 Corinthians 4:7). Whether that is terrifying or restful depends on what the giver is like, and John has twenty-one chapters to show you.

For the one sitting with a diagnosis. Say this carefully to the reader who has been given bad news, or who is watching someone thin out in a bed. The Christian hope is not that life is generally stronger than death; it plainly is not, and pretending otherwise is cruelty dressed up as comfort. It is that there is one place in the universe where life was never borrowed and so cannot be called back in, and that he has come within reach. He does not offer to extend the loan. He offers himself (11:25).

If he made everything, did he make evil? No. He made all things good (Genesis 1:31). Evil is not a thing God created but the ruin of good things he did create: a creature turning its God-given powers against him. Darkness is not a rival substance; it is what results when creatures turn from the light. Nothing the Word made is evil in itself, not the body, food, sex, work or the material world, and nothing evil is outside his rule. He who made all things is able to remake them, and this Gospel is about to show him beginning to do it.

Textual note. The oldest manuscripts carry no punctuation, and some early readers ran the sentence on: “without him was not any thing made. That which has been made was life in him.” On either reading the Word is the Creator and the life is in him. It is a question of where the full stop goes, not of what is being claimed.

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light of God has always been shining into the world’s darkness, and the darkness has never put it out; and now God sends a man, with a name, to point to it.

The light shines. The verbs so far have been past: “was”, “was made”. This one is present, the first present tense in the passage, slipped in at the exact point where the darkness enters. Whatever else has finished happening, this has not; it is going on while you read. It shone in the garden after the fall, in the promise of a serpent-crusher (Genesis 3:15), and through the long night of Egypt, the exile and the silent centuries. It walked into the darkest Friday the world has known and let the dark close over it, and on the third morning the dark gave it back.

And the darkness has not overcome it. The darkness in this Gospel tries to put the light out, and that is what Good Friday is, and it fails. The verb looks back on something settled: the dark is real and present, but it has already had its verdict handed down. And the darkness also fails to understand what it is looking at: a teacher of Israel who cannot follow a sentence about birth (3:10), Pharisees asking whether he means them (9:40).

A man sent from God. With no warning we are out of eternity and in a wilderness with a man who has a name. This Gospel never calls him the Baptist; it has no need to, since he is the only John it names, and the author never names himself. “Sent from God” marks a true prophet; “a man” sets him against the Word who was God. And the verb changes: “there came to be a man”. He has a start date. The Word does not.

The eternal with an address. Christianity’s strangest claim is not that God is eternal but that the eternal turned up in a particular decade, at a particular stretch of river, and that a man with a job and a diet was sent from God to point at him. After centuries of prophetic quiet, the first voice God sends in this Gospel is a man saying: look over there.

What it does not mean. A sentence this confident can be turned into a cruel demand that sufferers feel victorious. It does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated. It says the dark did not put it out. If you are in a season where God seems to have gone quiet and the light appears to be one candle in a very large room, you are not failing to believe the verse. You are living inside its first clause: “The light shines in the darkness”. It asks you only to notice that the light is still lit, and has been through much worse than yours.

If the light has won, why is there still so much darkness? Because the victory is decisive but not yet complete. At the cross and the empty tomb the darkness did its worst and lost. But God in patience has not yet ended the age, so that the light may go on shining into the dark and drawing people out of it (2 Peter 3:9). We live between the decisive battle and the final day, when there will be no night at all (Revelation 22:5). So the Christian is neither naive about evil nor despairing before it: the darkness is real, still dangerous, and already beaten.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood”. The Greek (katelaben) means to seize, to lay hold of: it is used of an enemy overtaking a man on the road, and of a mind finally getting hold of an idea. So the King James read “comprehended” and most modern versions “overcame”, and both are honest translations. John very likely means both, since his Gospel shows the darkness failing to grasp the light as well as failing to put it out; the opposition between light and darkness in the sentence makes “overcome” the leading sense.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood.” The John of verse 6 is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John came for one purpose, to bear witness to the light so that people would believe; he was not the light himself.

He came as a witness. “Witness” is one of the load-bearing beams of this Gospel, turning up with its related words nearly fifty times: John the Baptist, the Father, the Scriptures, Jesus’ works, the Spirit and the disciples all bear witness to Jesus (5:31–39). John is writing something shaped like a trial, and the reader is addressed not as an audience but as a jury. The Greek word gives us martyr, because of what testimony so often cost; the man in this verse would lose his head for it (Mark 6:27).

That all might believe through him. “Believe” (pisteuō) occurs about 98 times in John, but the noun faith never. For John faith is an action: believing, trusting, coming, receiving. The goal of all witness is belief (20:31), and every sign, discourse and encounter in this book is designed to produce it.

Through him. God could have brought people to faith without an intermediary, and he did not. He appointed a man with a strange diet and a rough manner, standing in a river, and routed faith through him (Romans 10:14). Almost certainly you can name the person it came through for you, and almost certainly they were not impressive.

He was not the light. Why say so? Because John’s influence outlived him by decades: Paul met about twelve men at Ephesus who knew only John’s baptism (Acts 19:1–7). This flat denial very probably corrects a movement the author knew was still alive (compare v. 20; 3:28–30). His whole identity here is stated in negatives: not the light, and soon not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet. That is no diminishment. A signpost that people admire and stop at has failed; a signpost they walk straight past, on their way to where it pointed, has done the whole of its job.

A lamp and the Light. Jesus will later call John a burning and shining lamp (5:35): lit from somewhere else, burning itself down. The light in this prologue has no source behind it. The Baptist lost his head testifying to Christ; Christ gave his life testifying to the Father (18:37), and his death did what no witness’s death could do. He is the faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), and the truth he bore witness to was himself (14:6).

I am no John the Baptist: can I still be a witness? Yes. A witness is not someone with special training but someone who tells what he knows to be true. You may not be able to explain the Trinity or answer every objection, but you can say who Jesus is, what he has done, and what he has done for you. The man born blind did it with almost no theology at all: “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see” (9:25). Witness happens over a kitchen table, or in an honest answer when someone asks why you still go to church. And the results are not yours to produce. A witness is responsible for the truth of his testimony, not for the verdict of the jury.

parallels.desc: he was a burning and shining lamp

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true light, of which every other light is a reflection, came into the world he had made, and the world did not recognise him.

The true light. “True” (alēthinon) means genuine, real, as opposed to imitations and shadows: a favourite word in John, as in the true bread (6:32) and the true vine (15:1). Jesus is the reality to which all other lights point, and every human experience of light, beauty, reason and goodness is a dim reflection of him.

Which gives light to everyone. Every human being receives some light from the Word: reason, conscience, and the knowledge of God through creation (Romans 1:19–20; 2:14–15). Not that everyone is saved, but that everyone is accountable. Theologians call this common grace: God’s kindness to all, which does not save but holds back evil and makes life bearable; he “sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). So no human being is simply outside the reach of this light. Every flicker of conscience, every ache after beauty, every stubborn refusal to believe that cruelty is merely a preference is light, and it is his, falling on people who have never heard his name.

World three times. He came into the world he had made, and John says “world” three times in a single sentence, each time turning the knife.

Did not know him. “The world” (kosmos, about 78 times in John) here means humanity in rebellion against God. Isaiah had found the image: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib, but Israel does not know” (Isaiah 1:3). And this comes before any hostility begins: the first thing said about the world’s response to God arriving in it is not that it fought him, but that it did not notice. The Maker walked into his workshop and the tools did not know his hand. He came anyway, knowing he would be unrecognised, for the very people who would look straight at him and see nothing.

What it does not mean. “Gives light to everyone” has been made to carry a great deal: that all people are already savingly enlightened, that every religion is a road up the same mountain. John settles it in the next breath: the light shone on the world, and the world did not know him. The sun rising over a city is not the same thing as the city waking up.

Would I have known him? Almost certainly not. The people best equipped to recognise him are the ones this Gospel shows missing him (vv. 11–12). If recognising God depended on being religious, well taught or sincere, the record of the first century is against you. So John does not urge the reader to look harder. He says something else entirely, in verse 13: those who did receive him were born of God. Recognition was never going to come from the side of those who could not see. It had to be given.

So what about people who have never heard of Jesus? They are not without light: creation and conscience speak to them of God, and they are accountable for what they know (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). But that light by itself has never saved anyone, because the human heart suppresses it. Salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, for there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). That is not a reason for despair but for mission. God has sent his gospel to the ends of the earth and saves people in every nation through it. The right response to this question is to pray, to give, and to go.

Uncertain wording. “Was coming into the world” can belong to the light, as the ESV takes it (the true light was coming into the world), or to “everyone”, as the older versions read it: “the light that lights every man that comes into the world”. The Greek allows both. The ESV’s reading fits John’s stress on the light’s arrival (3:19; 12:46), and the difference is not doctrinally serious.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Word came home to his own people and was shut out, but everyone who receives him, whoever they are, is given the standing of a child of God.

He came to his own. John changes the gender of a word halfway through the sentence, and the tragedy is in the change. The first “his own” is neuter and plural in Greek: his own things, his own home, Israel, to whom he had given the law, the prophets and the promises. The second is masculine: his own folk, the household. And “receive” is the verb for welcoming somebody in off the road. He was not turned away at a border by strangers; he was left standing at his own door by people who knew the address because it was theirs too.

They were not badly prepared. They had the Scriptures, the temple, the calendar and a national hope built around his arrival. A Messiah who came to rule them, and not to approve them as they were, threatened what they already had: their standing, their righteousness, their control of the temple (11:48). Religion can be the best hiding place from God there is, and the first to shut the door on him were the people most at home in his house.

But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name. Then “but”, and the sentence turns. Some did receive him, and “all” means whoever they are, Jew or Gentile, from anywhere. To receive him is to believe in him: the same act described from two angles. To believe in his name is to rest your whole weight on Jesus as the one he says he is (20:31), not admiring him from a distance but trusting him with yourself.

The right. Not power or ability but authority, legal standing (exousia). God does not merely make it possible for people to be his children; he confers the standing, and it holds because of who conferred it. That is worth having on a day when you do not feel like anybody’s child: your standing was not issued by your feelings and is not withdrawn by them.

To become children of God. Across this Gospel, Son of God is Jesus’ title alone; believers are called children of God. Jesus is Son by eternal right; we are children by gift, by adoption through faith in Christ (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:14–17). And “become” means something happened that had not happened before. In one sense God is Father of all, since he made and sustains everyone (Acts 17:28); but by creation everyone is God’s creature, and only by a new birth does anyone become his child.

What it means to be a child of God. A change of family, with everything that comes with it. A child has access: through Christ “we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). A child has provision: “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). A child receives discipline, a mark of belonging, not of rejection: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). A child has an inheritance: believers are “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). And a child has brothers and sisters, the whole household of faith.

My Father and your Father. All of it comes through the Son. He did not cling to his place at the Father’s side; he came home and was shut out, so that strangers could be let in. And on the morning he rose, the Son who alone is Son by right sent word: “go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God’” (20:17).

In everyday life. Ask what word rises first when you think of God: Judge, Employer, Landlord keeping an eye on the property, distant relative, or Father. Not the word you can defend, but the one your stomach reaches for at four in the morning when something has gone wrong. When you pray today, begin with Father: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your heart to cry it (Galatians 4:6). Bring him the small things, take his correction without despair, and treat the believers you find hardest as family, because they are.

When your own family will not receive him. Some who follow Christ pay for it at home: a father who stopped speaking, a family who treat the faith as an embarrassment, a husband or wife who did not sign up for this. He knows what it is to be the odd one in his own house, from further in than you do, because his own people eventually killed him. Keep loving them, keep praying, and keep the door open from your side (1 Peter 3:1–2).

If my own father failed me. If your own father was absent, or frightening, or simply never much interested, you are not disqualified from this verse; you are its natural audience. The word Father is not being defined for you by the man who taught you to flinch at it. It is being defined by the Son who spends twenty chapters showing you what his own Father is like.

Is believing then my contribution? If the right is given to those who receive and believe, has believing not become the qualifying act, the one contribution that is finally mine? Verse 13 shuts that door before anyone can get a foot in it: those who believe were born, not of the will of man, but of God. Faith is truly yours: you believe, and you are commanded to. But it is never a payment you hand over. It is the empty hand of a child who has already been given life.
verseByVerse.note: “His own” is Israel, God’s own people.

parallels.desc: sons of God through faith

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new birth that makes us God’s children comes from God alone; and God himself has come to us, for the eternal Word became a real man and lived among us, and in him we see God’s glory, full of grace and truth. This is the heart of the prologue, and of the Christian faith.

Not of blood. John names three closed doors before the open one, each one a door people have actually tried. “Not of blood” (the Greek is plural, bloods, from the thought that a child came from the mingled blood of both parents): not descent. Being born a Jew, or into a Christian family, does not make you a child of God. A godly mother is one of the great mercies of God, and she is not a birth certificate. Grace does not travel down a bloodline.

Nor of the will of the flesh. Not natural desire, the bodily desire by which children are conceived. Nothing we have by being human can produce this birth.

Nor of the will of man. Here the word is the specific one for a male, a husband, a father. In the Greek and Roman world the head of the house decided whether a newborn was acknowledged into the family at all. John says: not that either. No one can decide you into God’s family: not your father, not a minister, not a church roll, and, hardest to hear, not you. The decisive vote is not yours to cast.

But of God. Becoming God’s child is a new birth, and its source is God alone (3:3–8; James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:3).

Then why should I preach, or call anyone to believe? Because God gives the new birth through his word (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). The same Jesus who says no one can come unless the Father draws him (6:44) cries out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (7:37). The call is sincere and it is for everyone. We do not know whom God is bringing to life; we only know that he does it as the gospel is spoken. A sovereign new birth is not a reason to keep quiet. It is the only reason to expect anything when we speak, because we are talking to people who cannot raise themselves, and we know who can.

When you cannot find the moment. Some Christians go cold at this verse, because being born again makes them look for a date, and there is none. They have believed as long as they can remember, and fear that what happened to others has not happened to them. But nobody remembers being born, and nobody treats that as grounds for doubting it happened. You establish your birth not by memory but by breathing. John gives the present-tense evidence in his first letter: “we know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers” (1 John 3:14), and “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God” (1 John 5:1). The birth is behind the faith as its cause, not in front of it as its reward.

A pulse, not a feeling. Run the honest test. Do you want things you did not use to want? Has sin you once enjoyed gone quietly sour on you? Do you pray when nobody would know if you did not? Have you had every reason to walk away from Christ and found that you could not? None of those is a feeling; all of them are a pulse. But this must not become a false comfort. If nothing in that list is true of you, the news is not that you should look harder for a memory. It is that God gives new birth, and that you may ask him for it.

And the Word became flesh. The verb of beginning, used until now only of created things, is at last used of him. The eternal Word became a real human being, with a human body and soul. He did not merely appear to be human, as the Docetists taught, an early group who thought matter beneath God (1 John 4:2–3). Nor was he changed into a man, ceasing to be God. He took human nature to himself while remaining what he was. He did not visit flesh, or wear it like a coat and take it off again. He became it.

Flesh. John does not write that the Word became a man, though that is true, or that he took a body. He writes sarx, flesh, the crudest, weakest, most mortal word available to him: what a man is when you consider that he gets tired, hungry and thirsty, bleeds when cut, and dies. Having climbed thirteen verses to the highest claim in the New Testament, John sets the two words side by side without a cushion between them: the Word, and flesh. Many of the great errors about Christ in the next four hundred years were attempts to soften that collision, and John’s own letters show him already fighting them.

Make it concrete. He had to be taught to walk and fell over doing it. There were teeth coming through, splinters in a carpenter’s hands, sweat, and the kind of tiredness where you fall asleep in a boat in a storm. At some point somebody changed God’s nappies. God did not send a message, a projection or an appearance. He arrived in a body that could be hurt. God became what we are, so that we could become what he made us to be.

And dwelt among us. “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent” (eskēnōsen), tabernacled, and John reaches back to Exodus. Israel in the wilderness builds a tent to God’s specification, and the glory of the LORD fills it so completely that Moses cannot go in (Exodus 25:8; 40:34–35). God chose to live in a portable structure of goat hair and dyed skins in the middle of the camp, moved when they moved. From outside it was the least impressive dwelling imaginable; inside it was unbearable with glory. This time the tent was a body: a plain exterior that nobody in Nazareth found worth a second look, and inside, the glory. He is the true tabernacle, the place where God meets his people.

And we have seen his glory. “We”: John and the apostles, eyewitnesses who kept looking (1 John 1:1–3). “Glory” (doxa) is the visible radiance of God’s presence that filled the tabernacle. They saw it in his signs (2:11), and supremely at the cross, which John calls his glorification (12:23; 17:1). John does not even narrate the transfiguration. The glory these men saw was chiefly a man dying a shameful death in public, so do not look for God’s glory only in whatever is going well.

The only Son. “Only Son” (older versions, “only begotten”) means unique: he is the Father’s Son as no one else is, sharing his nature (see v. 18).

Full of grace and truth. At Sinai Moses asks, “Please show me your glory” (Exodus 33:18), and is put in a cleft of the rock while God passes by proclaiming his name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The last two words in the Hebrew are hesed and emet: covenant love and covenant faithfulness, the two things you most need to be true of anyone you stake your life on. What Moses was given a glimpse of, from behind, through a crack in a rock, these men watched cook breakfast on a beach (21:9–13).

A tent pitched to be taken down. The tent he pitched among us was meant to be taken down: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (2:19, 21). The Son took flesh so that it could be torn for us, and then raised, and it is flesh still, at the right hand of the Father. The Bible ends with the same word coming back: “the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). The tent was temporary; God’s living among us is not. God has a human face now, and he will keep it for ever.

Did he stop being God when he became man? No. He did not exchange one nature for the other, or blend them into something in between. He is one person, truly God and truly man, the two natures joined without confusion and without separation (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). As man he grew tired, wept and died; as God he upheld the universe throughout (Hebrews 1:3). He laid aside the display of his glory, not his deity. That is why his death can save: it is the death of a real man, in our place, and the life of the one who dies is the life of God.

Why does grace come before truth? Because that is how God revealed himself at Sinai: steadfast love first, then faithfulness. In Jesus they are never separated. His grace is not soft on sin, and his truth is not hard on sinners. He tells the woman caught in adultery that he does not condemn her, and then that she must go and sin no more (8:11, in a passage missing from the earliest manuscripts, as most modern Bibles note). Grace without truth would be sentiment that leaves us as we are; truth without grace would be a sentence we could not survive. In him we receive both whole, and we are meant to carry both into how we treat one another.

Where Christians differ: faith and new birth. Arminians teach that a person, enabled by grace, chooses to believe and is then born again; on that view “not of the will of man” rules out only natural descent and human effort as the source of life, not a free human decision to believe. This commentary’s view: Reformed theology reads verses 12–13 together: those who believe are those born of God, not of the will of man. The new birth is God’s sovereign work, which produces faith (1 John 5:1, where “everyone who believes … has been born of God”, perfect tense). We believe because we have been born of God, not the reverse. Yet we truly believe, and are commanded to.
verseByVerse.note: “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent”: God’s presence among his people, as in the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: that I may dwell in their midst
abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
born of the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist testifies that Jesus, though he came after him, existed before him, and from Jesus’ inexhaustible fullness all his people receive grace after grace.

Cried out. Loudly, publicly, like a herald. Twice now the poem about the eternal Word has been interrupted by a man with a name and a location: this Gospel refuses to let the Word float free of history. And the Baptist had probably been dead some sixty years when this was written, and his testimony is still ringing.

He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me. One sentence, three time-words: later in arrival, ahead in rank, earlier in existence. The third, which explains the second, could be said of no one else in Israel. Jesus came after John in time, but ranks above him, because he existed before him, eternally (8:58). And John was born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:26, 36), an older relative. A man pointing at a younger relative and saying “he was before me” is either making the claim of the prologue or talking madness, and the man saying it staked his life on it.

His fullness. Everything that is in him, nothing held back (plērōma; Colossians 1:19; 2:9). And the word that governs it is “all”. The oldest saint you know and the person converted last Tuesday draw from the same supply, and neither is drawing on a smaller tap.

Grace upon grace. The picture is not a heap but a succession: grace giving way to grace, the way waves arrive. Nobody is on their last grace: there is another behind it, and behind that a fullness that has not been touched. Wave after wave it comes, and the sea is not lowered.

What it does not mean. Grace that keeps arriving can be misheard as grace that does not mind. A wave is not a shrug. The supply outlasts your failures; it is not indifferent to them. The man who concludes he may now sin comfortably has missed whose fullness it is coming out of (Romans 6:1–2).

Am I running out of grace? Many of us, somewhere in the middle years, quietly start doing arithmetic: I have confessed this same sin so many times, I have had my share, whatever I was given at the beginning must be wearing thin. That is the arithmetic of a fixed quantity, and it is wrong. The grace you are living on this morning is not the grace of your conversion, stretched and rationed and going grey at the edges. It is a new one, and a new one has come every day since.

How do I actually receive grace? By coming to Christ himself, again and again, with empty hands. Grace is not a substance stored up in sacraments or earned by effort; it is the favour and help of God given to us in his Son. We receive it as we trust him, and God has given ordinary means by which he keeps feeding that trust: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, baptism, and the fellowship of his people. None of them is magic, and none of them is optional for a hungry soul. Go to them not to earn anything but to receive, the way a child goes to the table.

Uncertain wording. “Grace upon grace” is literally “grace in place of grace” (charin anti charitos), a compressed phrase. Many take it, as above, as grace continually replacing grace, one gift following another. Others read it as the grace of the new covenant in place of the grace of the old, since verse 17 at once sets Moses beside Jesus Christ. Either way, the verse speaks of endless grace from Christ’s fullness.
verseByVerse.note: John was born about six months before Jesus; “he was before me” points to Jesus’ existence before his birth.

parallels.desc: in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law came as God’s gift through Moses, but grace and truth arrived in person in Jesus Christ, and he, the only God, has made the invisible God fully known.

Given through Moses. The law was a gift of God, good and holy (Romans 7:12), revealing his will and exposing sin. It was “given”: God was the giver, and Moses the one through whom it came.

Came through Jesus Christ. Here is the prologue’s verb of arrival, used when the Word became flesh. The law was handed over; grace and truth walked in. Not that there was no grace in the law, but that the fullness of grace and truth came in Jesus. The law could command but not give the power to obey.

Moses is not the villain. Jesus in this very Gospel forbids setting the two men against each other: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (5:46). And “grace and truth” echoes what God called himself at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), so the sentence is not saying Moses got the rules and we got the kindness. The same grace and truth have now come up the road on two feet. Moses had the account; we have the person the account was about.

Jesus Christ. This is the first time the full name appears in the Gospel, and one of only two places John writes it (17:3). At the moment the eternal meets the historical, he puts down a man’s name and title, as if to say: this one, the one you have heard of.

No one has ever seen God. God in his essence is invisible (Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16). Yet Moses and the elders saw the God of Israel and ate and drank (Exodus 24:9–11), and Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1). John means that nobody has seen God as he is in himself, unveiled. And he says more later: Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him”, meaning Christ (12:41). The Old Testament sightings of God were not exceptions to this verse. They were early appearances of the one this verse is about.

The only God. The Greek monogenēs (older versions, “only begotten”) does not mean Jesus had a beginning. It means one of a kind; Isaac is called by it in Hebrews 11:17, though Abraham had another son. It speaks of uniqueness of relationship, not origin in time, which is why the Nicene Creed insists on “begotten, not made”: he was not created. He is, and always was, the Father’s own. So the prologue ends as it began: the Word is God.

Who is at the Father’s side. Literally “in the bosom of the Father”, the place of closest intimacy. John uses the word once more: at the last supper one disciple is reclining at Jesus’ side, the same word, kolpos (13:23). The place the Son eternally holds with the Father is the place John found himself given with the Son.

He has made him known. “Made known” (exēgēsato) gives us exegesis, the explaining of a text: to draw out into the open, to tell in full. In Greek the verb has no object; the sentence ends, “he has explained”. He himself is the explanation. The one person who has never been anywhere but the Father’s side has come out and told us, and the telling was a life: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:9).

In everyday life. Most of us carry a picture of God assembled out of odds and ends: what our father was like, our temperament, the last sermon that frightened us. Take one thing on that picture you are fairly sure of: that he is disappointed in you, say, or reluctant, or hard to get hold of. Now ask where you would find that in Jesus Christ. If it is not in him, it is not in God, because he is God’s own explanation of himself, and there is no other.

Does this mean Christians can ignore the Old Testament law? No, but we read it through Christ. The law still shows us God’s holy character and our sin, and its moral heart, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still describes how love for God and neighbour behaves (Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 13:8–10). What has changed is our relation to it. We are not justified by keeping it, because Christ kept it for us and bore its curse (Galatians 3:13). The ceremonial laws of sacrifice and cleanness were shadows, and Christ is the substance (Hebrews 10:1). And now the Spirit writes the law on our hearts, so that we obey from love rather than fear (Jeremiah 31:33).

If Jesus shows us God, what about the hard parts of the Old Testament? They are not a different God. The same Lord who drowned Pharaoh’s army wept over Jerusalem; the same Jesus who welcomed sinners overturned tables in the temple and warned of hell more than anyone in Scripture. Jesus does not cancel God’s holiness and judgment; he reveals them at their most intense at the cross, where God’s wrath against sin fell on his own Son, and there God’s justice and his mercy meet. Read the hard passages in the light of Christ, and where they puzzle you, trust the character of the God you have seen in Jesus while you keep studying.

Textual note. The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son”. The best manuscripts read monogenēs theos, “the only God”. Either way the sentence teaches the same thing, and the older evidence points to the reading that calls him God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son.” “At the Father’s side” is literally “in the bosom of the Father”, the place of closest intimacy.

parallels.desc: no one may see me and live
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The week of witness begins, and every voice in it points away from itself to Jesus. John the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem what he is not, not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet, and calls himself only a voice preparing the Lord’s way (vv. 19–28). The next day he points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, on whom he saw the Spirit come down and remain (vv. 29–34). Then the witness bears fruit: two of his disciples follow Jesus, Andrew brings Simon, Jesus finds Philip, and Philip brings Nathanael, the sceptic who confesses Jesus as Son of God and King of Israel (vv. 35–49). Jesus promises greater things: heaven opened over the Son of Man (vv. 50–51).
verseByVerse.theology:
This section shows how testimony works: John testifies to Jesus, Andrew to Simon, Philip to Nathanael, and each one who meets Jesus points another to him. The titles accumulate (Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man), each true, each partial, each pointing to the one who exceeds them all. Faith begins with testimony and ends in meeting him: Come and see.

Two cautions belong here. The Jews, first used in this section, usually means the Jerusalem authorities, not a people (see the note on vv. 19–20). And the Lamb should not be tied to one background (see the note on vv. 29–30).

The call by the Sea of Galilee in Matthew and Mark is not a rival version of this meeting but a later summons: here men meet Jesus and begin to believe, and later they leave their nets for good. Faith by stages is the normal pattern (see the note on vv. 49–50).
verseByVerse.examples:
Behold, the Lamb of God gathers the lambs of the Old Testament into one person (see the note on vv. 29–30).

Nobody in this section recruits by argument. Andrew fetches his brother with a five-word sentence. Philip’s testimony is incomplete twice over, and Nathanael came anyway (see the note on v. 45).

Two cautions. Andrew won his brother the same day, but that is the exception, and this chapter does not rebuke anyone who has prayed for a relative for decades (see the note on vv. 40–41). And I saw you under the fig tree both comforts and exposes (see the note on v. 48).

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the authorities ask John who he is, his first answer is who he is not: he is not the Christ. The narrative opens with a week of testimony (1:19–2:11), ending at the wedding in Cana, and it begins with John the Baptist under interrogation, asked the question of the whole Gospel: “Who are you?”

The Jews. This phrase turns up some seventy times in this Gospel, and because it has been put to appalling use it is worth stopping over at its first occurrence. In John “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus: the men who send delegations, convene meetings and eventually take a case to Pilate. Sometimes it simply means Jewish people or customs (2:6; 4:9), but it is never a verdict on a whole people. John was a Jew. Every disciple in this book is a Jew. Its central figure is a Jew who keeps the feasts and says that “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22).

Sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem. An official delegation, perhaps from the Sanhedrin, the ruling council, to establish by what authority an unlicensed man is conducting a religious rite in the open country. Levites assisted the priests and also served as temple police.

He confessed. Emphatic and freely given, though the moment offered him a real opportunity. People were questioning in their hearts whether he might be the Christ (Luke 3:15); the delegation had come to him, and a career was available. He puts it down in the first sentence he speaks in this Gospel. The word is the one used elsewhere for confessing Christ publicly when it costs you; here what he confesses is what he is not. And “I” is emphatic: I am not; someone else is.

The question comes back to Jesus. The same men will put the same question to the right man: “Who are you?” (8:25); “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (10:24). John answers by stepping out of the question. Jesus answers by saying openly who he is, often to people who had not asked: “I who speak to you am he” (4:26). And in the end it is his claim about himself that they will take to Pilate (19:7).

What it does not mean. What John describes is an argument inside a family about the family’s own hope, the sharpest kind of argument there is, and the moment it is read as one people’s verdict on another it has been turned inside out. Christians have done that, at scale, with results that do not bear describing. The term must never be used to justify hatred of Jewish people. Read the phrase as the Gospel uses it: the authorities in Jerusalem, and not your neighbour.

In everyday life. This temptation usually arrives as an offer: somebody credits you with more wisdom or spirituality than is true, and the correction would be awkward. John corrected his in front of an official delegation, at the height of his influence. You are already accepted in Christ and need no one’s overestimate, so when someone leans on you this week as if you were more than you are, say so, and point them to him.
verseByVerse.note: In John’s Gospel “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: whether he might be the Christ

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John refuses every title the delegation offers him, Elijah and the Prophet as well as the Christ, because they all belong to the one who comes after him.

Are you Elijah? Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah. Malachi, the last of the prophets in our Old Testament, closes with God’s promise to send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5): the last word of the prophets before some four centuries of silence, and so the thing everyone was still waiting for when the silence broke. John even dressed like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6).

I am not. Watch the three answers shrink. “I am not the Christ”: a full sentence. “I am not”: three words. “No”: one. By the next verse he will not claim to be a person at all, only a voice. And John has said egō ouk eimi, “I am not” (v. 20); Jesus will use the formula again and again without the negative: egō eimi, “I am” the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd. Before Jesus says “I am”, the greatest of the prophets says “I am not”, and so leaves the phrase free for him.

Are you the Prophet? The prophet like Moses whom God would raise up, to whom Israel must listen (Deuteronomy 18:15–18); Peter later identified him with Jesus (Acts 3:22).

Every crown he set down. All the titles John refused belong to another, and that other wears them all: the true Prophet like Moses, the Lord whose day Elijah heralded, the Christ. Every crown John set down, Jesus picks up, and they fit.

So was John Elijah or not? Yes in role, no in person. The angel told his father that he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), which is exactly what Jesus later says he did (Matthew 11:14; 17:12–13). Jesus is describing a role; John is refusing a reputation: the returned prophet as a figure in his own right, with his own following, around whom a movement could be built. His denial is not a contradiction but humility. He will not let the crowds build an identity around him that would compete with the one coming after.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah; “the Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah
a prophet like me
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressed for an answer, John calls himself only a voice, the one Isaiah foretold, clearing the road because the LORD himself is coming.

We need to give an answer. The pressure in the question is very human: they have to file a report. Somebody in Jerusalem is expecting a finding, and this man keeps saying what he is not.

The voice. What he gives them is barely anything at all (Isaiah 40:3): not a person with a title, but a voice. A voice exists only while it is being used, and then the words it carried go on without it. Jesus is the Word; John is only the voice.

Isaiah 40, the turn to comfort. Isaiah 40 is the great turn in that book from judgment to comfort, addressed to exiles who had concluded that God had lost interest. “Comfort, comfort my people”, it opens, and then a voice: “prepare the way of the LORD”. The picture behind it is a road gang. When a king was coming, the road was made ready, hollows filled and rocks cleared, because a monarch does not pick his way over broken ground. John is not the king or the escort. He is the man out in front with the news that someone is coming and the road is in no condition for it.

The LORD himself is coming. In Isaiah the one announced is the LORD himself, and John applies it to a man who will walk up to him next morning: like the prologue, he is saying that this man is the LORD. And the comfort was spoken to people who had waited so long they had stopped expecting anything.

Make straight the way of the Lord. Prepare the road by repentance, and preparing the way is not decoration but demolition and haulage. In the sermons John actually preached it was quite specific: what you do with your coat and your food, how you handle money, whether you use your position to squeeze people (Luke 3:10–14). He did not tell them to feel differently. He gave them roadworks.

What does making straight the way look like for me? Clearing out of the way whatever you know Christ would have to step over to reach you. The grudge you are nursing, the money you are handling dishonestly, the habit you keep hidden, the relationship you know is wrong, the apology you owe. Confess it to God, and where it involves others, put it right. You do not do this to earn his coming; he is coming anyway, and he comes to sinners. You do it because a heart busy defending its rubble cannot welcome a king.

parallels.desc: the voice in the wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind the questioners stand the Pharisees, the most earnest religious people of the day, and the scene quietly shows that sincerity and Bible knowledge are not enough to recognise the Christ.

Sent from the Pharisees. The first delegation was the temple’s clergy; this note names a group behind the sending whom we will meet throughout the Gospel.

Who the Pharisees actually were. They were not the temple establishment, which was the wealthy priestly families, mostly of the rival Sadducee party. The Pharisees were a lay movement: a few thousand men, many of them tradesmen and teachers, who took the law of God with complete seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. They tithed their herbs, knew the Scriptures by heart, and believed in the resurrection and the coming Messiah. Ordinary people admired them enormously. If sincerity had been enough, or knowledge of the Bible, or moral effort, they would have been first at the river.

The righteousness they were missing. What the Pharisees wanted was right: a people fit to stand before God when he came. Every tithed herb was reaching after a righteousness that would at last be enough, and the only righteousness that ever was enough was about to be lived out a few yards away by a man from Nazareth, and then counted to sinners who trust him. A Pharisee of the strictest kind said so later: “not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:9).

What it does not mean. When a Christian says Pharisee he almost always means someone stricter than himself, and that is nearly the opposite of the truth. The Pharisee problem is not strictness. It is being so certain you are on God’s side that nothing God could do would surprise you, and therefore nothing he did would you recognise. That condition is available at every point on the scale of strictness, and most available to those who have been right about something for a long time.

Should I then distrust every careful, serious Christian? No. Taking God’s word seriously in the details of life is good, and the New Testament commands it. Nicodemus, a Pharisee, came to Jesus (3:1), and Paul was one before Christ found him (Philippians 3:5). The danger is not seriousness but self-trust: relying on our own record to stand before God, and refusing to be corrected by him. The cure is humility: keep your Bible open in front of you rather than behind you, and keep asking God to show you where you are wrong.

Uncertain wording. The Greek can be read in two ways: that the delegation of verse 19 had been sent by the Pharisees, as the ESV takes it, or that some Pharisees had been sent as well, a second group among the questioners. On either reading the Pharisees stand behind the inquiry; the first is the more usual reading.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked by what right he baptises, John points away from himself to the one already standing among them, unrecognised.

Then why are you baptizing? Washing was associated with the cleansing God promised for the messianic age (Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 13:1). Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism, but one washing marked entry into the covenant people from outside: later Jewish sources describe Gentile converts being circumcised and immersed, washed clean of their paganism. Whether that practice was already established in John’s day is debated, but the offence was felt either way. John was baptising Jews: sons of Abraham wading into a river to be washed as though they needed to come in from outside. It was a sermon preached without a word: your ancestry will not do it; you need cleansing, in public.

I baptize with water. Only water, an outward sign. His answer does not defend his credentials at all. He changes the subject to the only subject.

Among you stands one you do not know. “Among you”: in this crowd, not somewhere else. “Stands”: present and settled; he has been here while you were asking your questions. The best-informed religious men in the country are standing within yards of him, investigating the wrong man. The Lord of glory stands among ordinary people, unannounced, unhurried, waiting to be known.

Was John’s baptism the same as Christian baptism? Not quite. John’s was a baptism of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming one; Christian baptism is into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, a sign of union with the Christ who has now died and risen (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3–4). That is why the disciples Paul met at Ephesus, who knew only John’s baptism, were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:1–7). What the two share is the sign of cleansing and the call to turn. Like John, this commentary holds that baptism belongs to those who repent and believe (Acts 2:38; 8:36–38), as the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches, because in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith. Many faithful Christians baptise their children, seeing baptism as the covenant sign given to believers’ children as circumcision once was, and we honour them as brothers and sisters who do so in good conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John counts himself unfit for even a slave’s lowest task towards the one coming after him, and the King he announces will one day stoop to that very task himself.

The strap of whose sandal. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. A later rabbinic saying gives the sentence its edge: a disciple served his teacher in almost every way a slave would, except the one duty with the feet, untying and carrying the sandals. So John does not say he is unworthy to be the man’s disciple. He says he is unworthy to do the one job a slave’s list contained and a disciple’s did not.

In Bethany across the Jordan. East of the Jordan, not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived, and its location is uncertain. If, as many think, it lay near the crossing opposite Jericho, this is where the nation came out of the wilderness into the land, and where Elijah went up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:8–13). John is standing at Israel’s front door, on the outside, telling the covenant people they need to come in again.

The King with a towel. Twelve chapters later, the one whose sandal strap John was not fit to loosen ties a towel round his waist, kneels, and washes the feet of men who will every one of them fail him before morning (13:4–5). The task too low for the herald is the task the King performs. Those feet walked to Calvary and were nailed there. Years later, on Patmos, the apostle who wrote this verse saw them again, like burnished bronze, and fell at them as though dead; and the Lord laid his right hand on him and said, “Fear not” (Revelation 1:15–17). This is our Lord: majesty that kneels, and glory that lifts the fallen to their feet.

In everyday life. Consider the lowest job in your church, the one nobody puts on a rota: stacking the chairs, the bins after the meal, the lift home for the person who talks too long. Would you be glad to be known as the person who does that and nothing else? Then go and do it, for the one who washed your feet.

Is it healthy to think of myself as unworthy? It depends what you mean. John’s unworthiness is not self-hatred or low self-esteem; he spoke with great boldness and never doubted his calling. It is simply an accurate measurement of himself against Christ: next to him, the greatest of men is not fit to touch his feet. But the gospel does not leave us there. The same Christ who is infinitely above us kneels to wash us and calls us friends (15:15). Humility is not thinking badly of yourself; it is thinking truly of Christ, and then receiving gladly what he gives to the unworthy.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read Bethabara, but the earliest read Bethany.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan, not the Bethany near Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: where John had been baptizing at first

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John points to Jesus as the sacrifice God himself provides, the one who lifts the sin of the world onto himself and carries it away. This title is the key to the whole Gospel.

The next day. John is marking off the days of this first week (vv. 29, 35, 43; 2:1); see the note on vv. 43–44.

Behold, the Lamb of God. Four lambs were available to a Jewish imagination, and they are not interchangeable.

The lamb of Genesis 22. Isaac carries the wood for his own sacrifice and asks, “where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” “God will provide for himself the lamb” (Genesis 22:7–8). Then a ram is caught in a thicket, and the promise of a lamb is left standing, unfulfilled, for two thousand years.

The daily lamb. A lamb every morning and evening in the temple, for centuries (Exodus 29:38–42): its own testimony that a sacrifice you have to repeat tomorrow has not dealt with anything permanently (Hebrews 10:11–12).

The Passover lamb. A year-old male without blemish, killed at twilight, its blood on the doorposts, and the destroyer passing over that house (Exodus 12). The Passover lamb was not, strictly, a sin offering. It marked a house as belonging to God and turned aside the judgment falling everywhere else.

The lamb of Isaiah 53. “Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter”, he opened not his mouth; and this is the only one of the four in which a lamb bears sin: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all”; “he bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:6–7, 12).

Let John decide it. Two things in his own account are decisive. He alone dates the crucifixion so that Jesus is condemned on the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14), when the Passover lambs were being killed. (How this fits the other Gospels, where the Last Supper is a Passover meal, is long debated; careful harmonisations exist.) And he alone tells you which Scripture was fulfilled when the soldiers did not break his legs: “Not one of his bones will be broken” (19:36), the Passover rule of Exodus 12:46. So John’s frame is Passover. But “who takes away the sin of the world” echoes Isaiah’s sin-bearing servant. The Baptist has put the Passover lamb and the sin-bearing servant into one person and pointed at him.

The whole doctrine in one lamb. Isaiah tells you how it works: the iniquity is laid on him and he carries it in our place. Passover tells you what it does for you: judgment is real, and it does not come into the house marked with blood. Genesis supplies the question, and the daily lamb explains why there had to be a last one.

Who takes away the sin of the world. “Takes away” (airōn) means to lift up and to carry away: he takes sin up onto himself in order to take it away (Isaiah 53:4, 11–12; 1 Peter 2:24). Then “the sin”, singular, the whole mass of human guilt treated as one load that can be picked up. And “of the world”: not of Israel only, but of people from every nation (11:51–52; 1 John 2:2). The men listening had come from Jerusalem with the categories Israel and everyone else. John says “world”, the word that breaks the fence, and the rest of this Gospel keeps breaking it: a Samaritan woman, a royal official’s household, some Greeks who ask to see him (10:16).

He was before me. The Baptist repeats the riddle of verse 15. The man walking towards him is still the one who existed before him: becoming man did not make him less than God.

He did not have to be caught. Every morning and every evening, century after century, a lamb died in Israel, and not one of them chose to. This one walks down the riverbank of his own accord to become the last. The one who put the ram in the thicket is walking toward the altar himself. All that blood was rehearsal. And the title is not a stage he passed through.
