On Patmos John looks for the Lion of the tribe of Judah and turns to see a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, and the whole of heaven falls down before it (Revelation 5:5–6). It is what he is called in glory.

In everyday life. The first word is an imperative: “Behold”. Look. Not understand it, or feel it, or resolve to do better: the one instruction a man carrying something too heavy can still obey. When guilt comes back today, do not argue with it from your own record. Look at the Lamb, and say: he took that away.

Even my sin? People rarely doubt that Christ takes away sin in general. They doubt whether he takes away the particular thing they have never told anyone, the one that feels too shameful to sit beside ordinary sins. Had he said “sins”, you might wonder whether yours was on the list. He said “the sin”, the whole weight of it, lifted as one load. Whatever yours is, if you come to him it is not too heavy or too dark for the Lamb to carry; it was laid on him with all the rest (Isaiah 53:6), and none who come will be turned away (6:37).

Is the whole idea of sacrifice not primitive? It looks primitive only if sin is small. The sacrifices taught Israel two things a modern mind finds hard to hold together: God is holy, so sin cannot simply be waved away, and God is merciful, so he provides a way for the sinner to live. Every lamb said that sin is deadly serious and that a substitute could die in the sinner’s place (Leviticus 17:11). The animals could never actually pay (Hebrews 10:4); they were pictures. The Lamb of God is the reality: not a human gift bribing an angry God, but God himself providing, and in his Son becoming, the sacrifice. That is not less civilised than our ideas of forgiveness. It is the only kind that takes both justice and love seriously.

Where Christians differ: “the sin of the world”. Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s grace enables everyone to believe but leaves the decision with each person) take “the world” to mean that Christ died for every person equally, making salvation possible for all; they point to 3:16 and to 1 John 2:2, “for the sins of the whole world”. This commentary’s view: in John, “the world” usually means humanity in rebellion against God, not every individual, and the point is the scope of Christ’s work: not Jews only, but people from every nation (10:16; 11:52). Christ’s death actually takes away sin; it does not merely make removal possible. It takes away the sin of all who are his, from all over the world. This is often called definite atonement: Christ died to save his people for certain, because this Gospel speaks of a death that accomplishes what it sets out to do (6:37–39; 10:11, 15; 17:2). Faithful Christians read these verses differently, and they preach the same Lamb. The gospel is offered freely to everyone (3:16), and none who come will be turned away (6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Lambs were offered daily in the temple and at Passover; Isaiah’s servant goes “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.”

parallels.desc: the Passover lamb
God will provide the lamb

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even John, Jesus’ own relative, had to be shown by God who Jesus was, and his whole ministry existed so that Jesus might be revealed to Israel.

I myself did not know him. The two men were relatives (Luke 1:36), so this need not mean he knew nothing of him. He did not know him as the Messiah until God revealed it (v. 33). Knowing Jesus as a kinsman is not the same thing as knowing who he is.

For this purpose. The baptising was never the point, nor the crowds. The whole operation existed to create an occasion at which one person could be identified. It was scaffolding, and scaffolding is judged by the building. Every ministry exists for the unveiling of Christ, not the establishing of the minister.

That he might be revealed to Israel. To reveal is to make visible (phaneroō), and the verb becomes this Gospel’s word for what Jesus does: at Cana he manifested his glory (2:11), and by the Sea of Tiberias he revealed himself again (21:1, 14). No one stumbles on the Son of God merely by being near him. He makes himself known, to people who did not know him.

For the one raised in a Christian home. If you have heard it all since infancy and wonder whether familiarity has spoiled it: a prophet sent from God was in exactly that position and needed God to reveal it anyway, and God did.

For the one who distrusts his own certainty. John’s certainty did not come from inside him. God told him in advance what sign to watch for (v. 33), and he saw it, outside himself, on a particular day, in front of witnesses. That is where yours rests too. The events this book reports did not happen inside anybody’s feelings, and they do not stop having happened on the mornings when you cannot feel anything at all.

But in Matthew, did John not recognise him? In Matthew John protests, “I need to be baptized by you” (Matthew 3:14). The two fit together. John knew Jesus as a relative and a righteous man, and in Matthew he senses that Jesus is greater than he. What he did not know until the sign was given was that this was the one who baptises with the Spirit (v. 33). His protest came at the baptism itself; his certainty came with the descending Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave John a sign, the Spirit coming down and remaining on one man, and by it John knew that Jesus is the one who baptises with the Holy Spirit.

Like a dove. At Jesus’ baptism (Mark 1:10), which this Gospel does not describe, giving instead the Baptist’s testimony to it. The dove may evoke the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and the dove that returned to Noah (Genesis 8:11): new creation and peace.

It remained on him. “Remained” means abode, stayed. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on prophets and kings for particular tasks, and could depart (1 Samuel 16:14). On Jesus the Spirit rests permanently (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1); he has the Spirit without measure (3:34). And the word (menō, around forty times in this Gospel) is the one behind chapter 15: “Abide in me, and I in you” (15:4). Its first appearance is not about us at all but about the Spirit settling on the Son and not lifting off again.

He who sent me. God. John did not work it out or sense it. He was told in advance precisely what to watch for, and then he stood in the water and watched, perhaps for months. God gave him a sign specific enough to be checked, and then honoured it.

Baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Water is applied from outside; it goes on you, and it comes off. The Spirit is given, and he stays, because the giver is the one on whom he has been seen to stay (7:38–39; 20:22). Fulfilled at Pentecost, and in every believer’s new birth (3:5).

The Trinity at the river. Here is the whole Trinity without the later vocabulary: the Father who sends and speaks, the Spirit who descends and settles, the Son on whom he settles. The definitions came centuries later to protect the report. And our abiding does not begin with our effort to hold on to Christ. It begins with the Spirit resting on Christ permanently, and our abiding in him is a share in that: the Spirit who rested on Jesus without measure has been poured out from him on all his people, and he will not lift off from them either.

Have I been baptised with the Spirit? If you belong to Christ, yes. This phrase has been used to make Christians anxious about whether they have missed a second experience. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers, whose love for Christ is plain, speak of a later baptism in the Spirit, and we gladly own them as brothers; we read these texts as describing how every Christian begins. The New Testament is blunt about it: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9), and “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is no category of Christian still waiting for the Spirit. If you belong to Christ, what John announces here has already happened to you, whatever it felt like at the time. You may and should ask to be filled afresh, to walk in step with him and to know his power more (Ephesians 5:18), but that is growth in what you have, not a gate you have not yet passed.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John gives his settled, sworn testimony: Jesus is the Son of God. This is the climax of his witness, and the truth this Gospel was written to make known (20:31).

I have seen and have borne witness. Perfect tenses: a completed action whose result still stands. He is not describing a moment of enthusiasm but giving sworn evidence that cannot now be withdrawn, which is what a witness does in a Gospel shaped like a trial.

The Son of God. Jesus is the unique Son of God (v. 18). But it is worth knowing what the title would have meant to the men standing there, because it did not yet mean to them all that it means in the creed. In Israel’s Scriptures son of God could be said of the king: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). So the crowd would have heard a claim about the Messiah, the anointed king. John, writing decades later for readers who have now read his first chapter, means that and what verse 18 said as well. The title grows as the Gospel goes on. It does not change its mind.

He came, he pointed, he went. After one more pointing the next day (vv. 35–36), we hear from the Baptist only once more, in chapter 3: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). His arrest is mentioned in passing (3:24), and he gets no death scene.

What if my faithful service seems to have come to nothing? You are in good company. The greatest man ever born of women, on the Lord’s own assessment (Matthew 11:11), has a public career of perhaps a year, spends it telling people to look at somebody else, is imprisoned on a private grudge and, as Mark tells us, executed to keep a promise made at a birthday feast (Mark 6:21–28). From the inside it could have looked very like a wasted life. He had seen, and he had borne witness, and that turns out to be the whole job description. God does not measure faithfulness by visible results, and he forgets nothing done for his Son (Hebrews 6:10). Your testimony, too, once given, still stands.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God”. If so, John is echoing Isaiah 42:1: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him”, exactly what has just happened; and the servant of Isaiah 42 is the one who by Isaiah 53 is led to the slaughter.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God.”

parallels.desc: my Chosen One

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John points his own disciples to Jesus, knowing they will leave him, because the Lamb of God is worth leaving everything for.

Two of his disciples. Andrew (v. 40), and probably John, the author, who never names himself. These are not a crowd but his own men, who had attached themselves to him, fasted when he fasted and prayed the prayers he taught them (Luke 11:1). As Jesus walks by, the Baptist looks at him intently (emblepsas). That is what the two notice first: not the words, but where the man is looking.

Behold, the Lamb of God! Shorter, and repeated. He does not soften it or ask them to stay in touch, and the next verse is the two of them walking off after somebody else. It is the second day running he has said the same thing (vv. 29, 36). The pressure to say something not said before is very often vanity; the preacher’s task is not novelty but faithfulness. This man had one line and used it until it took his followers away.

The Lamb worth leaving for. Why would two men walk away from a prophet they loved on the strength of a handful of words? Because the day before John had said what this Lamb does, and nothing in John’s own ministry could do that: his baptism could call for repentance, but it could not lift anybody’s guilt. He is sending his disciples to the only person who can give them what he has spent his life telling them they need. He is not losing them to a rival; he is handing them to their Saviour. This is the glory of the Lamb: he is so worth following that the best of men counted it joy to lose his disciples to him.

The friend of the bridegroom. The cost is what makes it remarkable. He is at the height of his influence, dismantling it deliberately, one pair of disciples at a time. When people later complained that everyone was going over to Jesus, he gave them the picture of the best man at a wedding: “The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete” (3:29). The happiest man at the party is the one who is not the groom and never thought he was.

Is it wrong to want to be appreciated in ministry? Not in itself. Paul longed to see his converts and rejoiced in their love (Philippians 4:1), and wanting your work to bear fruit and your people to flourish is good. What John shows is where that desire must be held: under a greater joy in Christ himself. The test is not whether you ever enjoy being thanked, but whether you can rejoice when people outgrow you, leave for another church, or never mention you again, because they are following him. If that is hard, tell the Lord so honestly and ask him to make his glory sweeter to you than your own.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two disciples take one sentence seriously enough to move their feet, and everything that follows in this Gospel begins there.

Followed. The first use in this Gospel of the verb that will describe the Christian life to the last page: literally, walked after him. At this moment it means nothing more spiritual than walking behind a man on a road. They had settled nothing and had no question prepared, and it is Jesus who turns round and breaks the silence (v. 38).

So little to go on. No miracle had happened, and nothing had been explained. Everything in the next twenty chapters, the water into wine, the raising of Lazarus, the upper room, the empty tomb, follows from two men taking one sentence seriously enough to move their feet. Say it plainly to anyone whose beginnings were unimpressive: the first conversion in this Gospel was a sentence overheard, two men walking off after somebody without a plan, and an awkward silence broken from the other end.

The voice behind the voice. They heard John, and followed Jesus. Later Jesus explains what was happening on that road: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (10:27). They follow because they know the shepherd’s voice, and they know it because he knew them first.

What does following Jesus mean today? More than believing things about him: it means going where he goes. We follow him by trusting him for forgiveness, by listening to his words in Scripture and doing them, by taking up the life he gives us among his people, and by going his way when it costs us (Luke 9:23). It is a whole life, but it is lived one step at a time: the next obedience you know about, the next sin to turn from, the next act of love. You do not need to see the whole road; these two did not. You need to keep him in front of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' And they said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and you will see.' So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ first words in this Gospel are a question about what we want, and his answer to the disciples’ hesitant reply is an invitation to come and stay with him.

What are you seeking? The first thing the Word says once he has begun to speak is not a statement but a question, and a question about what you want. Not what they believe or have done, but what they are looking for. It is the same word (zēteō) he uses in the garden when the soldiers arrive: “Whom do you seek?” (18:4, 7). And on resurrection morning, to a woman crying at a tomb: “Whom are you seeking?” (20:15). Nobody in this Gospel gets to Jesus without being asked it.

We are not mainly thinkers but lovers. The modern West tends to picture a person as a mind making choices: give people the right information and they will do the sensible thing. Jesus does not begin there. He asks these two men not what they think but what they want, because the steering of a life lies in its desires. Augustine put it in four Latin words, usually rendered “my love is my weight”: as a stone is carried down by its weight, a person is carried wherever his love takes him. That is why our arguments so often lose to our longings. Few of us are seeking truth in the abstract. We are seeking to be someone, to be safe, to be admired, to be loved, and we quietly arrange our beliefs around getting it. The gospel does not only correct our ideas. It gives us a better love to be carried by: the Word who came looking for us before we thought of looking for him, and who turned round on the road to ask what we wanted.

Rabbi, where are you staying? John translates Rabbi, Teacher, for Greek readers. “Staying” (meneis) is the same word as “remained” (v. 32): abiding. They duck his question: asked what they are seeking, they answer with a question about an address, as people do when a question goes too deep too fast. He lets them. He does not force the deeper conversation; he answers the question they were able to ask.

Come and you will see. Not an argument, not a leaflet: an address and an afternoon. Philip will repeat it (v. 46). It is not a recommendation to stop thinking; this Gospel was written from evidence deliberately selected so that you might believe (20:30–31). “Come and see” is an invitation to examine the case from close up rather than from the road.

They stayed with him. The same verb again: abode. They asked where he abides, and the answer turned out to be that they could abide there too. The teaching of chapter 15, “Abide in me”, is already present in this conversation, and nobody in it knows (15:4). The eternal Word, who was with God in the beginning, opened his door to two strangers on an ordinary afternoon and let them stay.

About the tenth hour. About 4 p.m., as the ESV notes. Why is that in the Bible? Because the man writing it was very probably the unnamed one of the two, an old man now, and he still knows what time of day it was. He does not tell us what was said in that room. He remembers the hour, as you remember the afternoon that divided your life in two.

An afternoon, and then a room. They asked where he was staying, and he gave them an afternoon. Later he gave them the whole answer: “In my Father’s house are many rooms” (14:2), and the word for rooms is built from the very verb they had used. “Come and see” was the first word of an invitation that ends in a room prepared for us.

What if I came for the wrong reasons? Most people do. The question is aimed past the disciples at whoever is reading. Most people come to Christ seeking something other than Christ: relief from a fear, a way out of a mess, certainty, respectability, a marriage saved, a peace they remember having. Look at what he does with that. He asks the question, and then screens nobody out on the strength of the answer. He does not tell them to come back when their motives are pure. The question is not a filter but the beginning of an education, and this Gospel is largely the record of people arriving with a small want and being given something they had not known to ask for. Come as you are, and let him change what you want.

How do I come and see today, when Jesus is not physically here? Through the means he has given. He is present by his Spirit, and he speaks in his word. Read one of the Gospels slowly, from start to finish, asking at each page what it shows you of him. Pray, speaking to him as someone who is listening. Go where his people gather and his word is preached, and keep going. Ask honest questions and bring them to Scripture and to mature Christians. The disciples spent an afternoon in his company; you can spend your mornings there. The invitation has not been withdrawn.

Uncertain wording. Counting from sunrise, as Jews ordinarily did (see Hours of the day), “the tenth hour” is about four in the afternoon, which is why they stayed the rest of the day. Some think John counts hours from midnight, Roman style, which would make it ten in the morning. That question matters chiefly at 19:14; here the ESV’s reading is the natural one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m., late enough that they stayed the rest of the day.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Andrew’s first act as a disciple is to find his own brother and tell him that they have found the Messiah.

Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. Always known in relation to his more famous brother. This Gospel gives Andrew three scenes, and he does the same thing in every one. Here he brings his brother. In chapter 6, with five thousand people to feed, it is Andrew who says there is a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, and adds honestly, “but what are they for so many?” (6:8–9). In chapter 12, when some Greeks ask to see Jesus and Philip does not know what to do with the request, he takes it to Andrew, and Andrew takes them in (12:20–22). Every time he is bringing somebody to Jesus: his brother, a boy with a packed lunch, and foreigners nobody was sure were allowed.

He first found his own brother. His first act as a disciple is to tell his family, the nearest person and therefore the hardest: nobody is less impressed by your spiritual development than the person who watched you grow up. Andrew never preaches a sermon in the New Testament; every recorded saying of his is an introduction or a question. But the whole of Peter’s life, the denials, the restoration on the beach, the sermon that added three thousand in a morning, enters the story because his brother could not keep quiet for an afternoon.

We have found the Messiah. Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) are the same title; only John uses the Hebrew word in the New Testament (also 4:25). And there is an irony in that “we”. By themselves they found nothing. A prophet was sent to tell them where to look, Jesus turned round and spoke first, and in the next scene it is Jesus doing the finding (v. 43). Every person in this chapter who says they have found him was found.

The Anointed One. Israel’s kings and priests had oil poured on their heads; Isaiah promised one on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest (Isaiah 11:2; 61:1). The day before, the Baptist had seen the Spirit come down on Jesus and remain. Andrew’s word was exactly right: the one anointed with God’s own Spirit without measure, the King every earlier anointing had been waiting for, now sitting in a room by a river, being introduced to fishermen.

What if my family has not believed after years of prayer? This verse gets used to prod people who do not need prodding. Andrew found his brother the same day, and it worked. That is not the pattern but the exception, and the New Testament knows it. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him during his ministry (7:5); they came in later, after the resurrection, in God’s time. If you have been praying for a brother, a son or a husband for twenty years and nothing has moved, this verse is not a reproach. It is a reminder that Andrew’s job was to fetch him, not to convert him, and that the fetching is the only part any of us has ever been responsible for. Keep praying, keep loving, and leave the hour with God.
verseByVerse.note: “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “anointed one”, the promised king.

parallels.desc: Andrew and Simon called by the lake

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looks at Simon, knows him as he is, and gives him a new name that describes not what he is but what grace will make him.

Jesus looked at him. A penetrating gaze, seeing who he was and who he would become: the same verb used six verses earlier of the Baptist looking at Jesus. Simon is being examined, and what comes out of the examination is not a verdict but a name.

You are Simon the son of John. Jesus knows him already. “You are” is present: an accurate description of the man as he is, known without being told.

You shall be called Cephas. Future tense, and between the two tenses is the rest of Simon’s life. Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean rock, as the ESV notes. The name stuck so hard that Paul, writing to Greek-speaking churches twenty years later, still calls him Cephas by reflex (1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9).

A name before the evidence. At this moment Simon has confessed nothing, left nothing, promised nothing. The name is handed to him before there is a single piece of evidence for it, and when the evidence comes in it runs the other way: he will swear he is ready to lay down his life, and hours later deny three times that he is a disciple (13:37; 18:17, 25–27). The names God gives are declarations of intent, not descriptions of performance. Gideon is addressed as mighty man of valour while hiding in a winepress (Judges 6:11–12); Abram is renamed father of a multitude while Sarah is still barren (Genesis 17:5). The name arrives first and the man walks toward it, usually badly, and usually for years.

Called back by his old name. “Simon, son of John” is what Jesus called him on the first day, and what he called him again at the end, on the shore after the denials, three times over (21:15–17). The Lord who named him Rock before he had done anything did not withdraw the name when he had done the worst. He came back for him by his old name and gave him sheep to feed. The one who calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17) is faithful to his word about us, and he finishes the people he names.

In everyday life. You have been told you are a child of God, a saint, a new creation, and the daily evidence is someone who lost their temper before breakfast. The gap is not proof that the name is false; it is the normal condition of everyone God has ever renamed. So ask what name you would give yourself this morning from the evidence, and then which ones God has used of you: forgiven, child, saint, beloved. When you fail today, do not rename yourself by the failure. Confess it, and walk on toward the name.

Does naming Simon the rock make him the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads this with Matthew 16:18 as the founding of an office passed on to the bishops of Rome. The name is real and prophetic; Peter did become a foundation stone of the church. But Scripture says the church is built on the apostles and prophets together, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20); Peter calls himself a fellow elder (1 Peter 5:1); and nothing in the New Testament speaks of his office passing to successors. Peter’s foundation work was done once, through his preaching and his letters, and we stand on it whenever we believe the gospel he preached.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean “rock.”

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus himself finds Philip and calls him with two words, “Follow me”, the call that runs from the first page of the Christian life to the last.

The next day. John has been counting days since the delegation arrived: “the next day” (v. 29), “the next day again” (v. 35), and now “the next day” once more. Then, at the start of chapter 2, “On the third day there was a wedding at Cana”. Add them up and John has laid out something very close to a week, which is hard to read as an accident in a book that opened with the words “In the beginning”.

A new week of creation. The exact arithmetic is debated; commentators reach six days or seven. But the shape is unmistakable, and so is where it lands. A week that begins with a man announcing that the light has come into the world ends at a wedding, with water turned into wine and his glory manifested (2:11). Genesis brings its week to man and woman made in God’s image and joined as husband and wife; John’s week ends at a wedding. The one who made the world is now at work making it new.

He found Philip. Here the verb turns round. Everyone so far has been finding somebody: John points, Andrew finds Simon, and in a moment Philip will find Nathanael. Here, for the first time, Jesus himself does the finding; nobody fetched Philip. In the end it is always Jesus who finds us (Luke 19:10).

Follow me. The first “Follow me” in this Gospel: two words, no explanation, no terms offered, no indication of where. It is also the last thing he says to Peter on the last page, on a beach after breakfast: “You follow me!” (21:22; compare 21:19). Everything in between is what it looks like to obey it. The Creator who began the first week by speaking light has begun a new week by speaking to a man from Bethsaida, and the word that made the world is now making disciples.

From Bethsaida. A fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee (Mark says Peter and Andrew lived at Capernaum, Mark 1:29). It is also one of the towns Jesus later laments: “Woe to you, Bethsaida!” (Matthew 11:21). Three of the twelve came out of Bethsaida, and the town itself did not believe. That is a comfort and a warning. If you have come out of a family or a church or a town where the gospel was heard for years and did nothing, its unbelief is not a verdict on you. And if you have grown up with a great deal of exposure to Christ and have never actually moved, exposure is not the same thing as following, and being near where God is working is a more dangerous position than being far from it, not a safer one.

In everyday life. He found you before you followed, and no one follows him without stumbling; your standing rests on his perfect obedience, not on the straightness of your steps (Romans 5:19). So ask what following him would mean in the specific decisions in front of you this week, a conversation, a temptation, the use of an evening, and take the step.

If Jesus finds us, do I have any part to play? Yes, a real one, but it comes second. You respond: you hear his call, and you follow. Philip did not stay where he was and wait to be carried. Yet the order matters for your peace. You did not stumble on Christ by your own wisdom or hold on to him by your own strength; he came looking for you, and he will not lose what he has found (10:28). So follow him gladly, and when you feel your grip weakening, remember whose grip it really is.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip, a disciple for perhaps an hour, finds his friend and tells him that Jesus is the one the whole Old Testament was written about.

Philip found Nathanael. Philip was found by Jesus in one verse and is finding a friend in the next. Nobody has taught him to do this, and nobody has told him he is allowed to. Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in the lists of apostles (Matthew 10:3). He was from Cana in Galilee (21:2).

Of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote. Not a vague religious phrase but a claim that can be checked: the whole Old Testament points to Jesus (5:39, 46; Luke 24:27). Moses had written of a seed of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), of the offspring of Abraham in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), of a ruler from Judah to whom the obedience of the peoples belongs (Genesis 49:10), of a star coming out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), and of a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15). The prophets had written of a virgin’s son called God with us (Isaiah 7:14), a child on David’s throne called Mighty God and Everlasting Father (Isaiah 9:6–7), a servant pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), a ruler from Bethlehem whose origin is from of old (Micah 5:2), and a king coming humble and mounted on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus did exactly what Philip has just done, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27).

Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. How people knew him, and incomplete in two respects. He was not from Nazareth in the sense that mattered prophetically: he was born in Bethlehem, as Micah had specified, which the crowd will throw at each other in chapter 7 as a reason he cannot be the Christ (7:41–42). And he was not the son of Joseph by birth, as the Gospels insist (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:34–35). Philip may not yet have known of the virgin birth. John does not correct him. The mistakes stand on the page, Nathanael comes anyway, and by the end of the conversation he is confessing more than Philip knew how to say.

In everyday life. Read the Old Testament as Philip did: it is about Jesus. When you read it this week, ask of each passage what it promises, what pattern it sets up, or what longing it leaves open that Christ fulfils.

What if I get it wrong when I talk about Jesus? This is for you if you have ever kept quiet for fear of getting it wrong. The first missionary sentence in this Gospel is incomplete twice over, and God used it to bring in one of Jesus’ closest followers. Philip’s grasp of Christ was partial, second-hand, an hour old and inaccurately expressed. What he had was true enough to be worth passing on, and the passing on is what he was asked for. Accuracy grows; nobody is waiting for you to be finished. Say what you know, admit what you do not, and point the person to the Gospels, where Jesus can speak for himself.
verseByVerse.note: Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in their lists.

parallels.desc: Nathanael of Cana

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael’s scorn is met not with argument but with an invitation, and Jesus greets the sceptic as a true Israelite with no deceit in him.

Can anything good come out of Nazareth? The remark is funnier and smaller than it sounds. Nazareth was an obscure village, probably a hamlet of a few hundred people, up a hill off the main road. It is never named in the Old Testament, nor by Josephus, who lists dozens of Galilean towns and knew the region as a commander. No prophecy was attached to it, and the Messiah was expected to come from Bethlehem (7:41–42). And Nathanael was from Cana (21:2), a village a few miles off. This is not lofty prejudice from a man in Jerusalem. It is one small place being rude about another small place nearby, which is a thing small places have always done.

The ordinary form of unbelief. Some honest unbelievers have looked long and hard. But many people do not reject Christ after weighing the evidence. They decline to look, on the grounds that nothing worth having has ever come from that quarter: that sort of church, that kind of person, those people, that book. It is not an argument. It is a reason not to have to make one.

Come and see. Philip does not argue. He passes on Jesus’ own invitation (v. 39) exactly as he received it. He could have started a debate about origins, and he would have lost, because he had his facts slightly wrong. Instead he offers the man a look. The best answer to objections is often an encounter with Christ.

An Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit. A true Israelite, honest, without guile, and there is a wordplay in it that a Jewish ear would catch instantly. The word for deceit is dolos, used in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 27:35, when Isaac, shaking, tells Esau what has happened to his blessing: “Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing”. Jacob, whose name was heard as deceiver, got what he wanted by deception and spent twenty years running from the consequences (Genesis 27:35–36). So here is a true son of Israel, descended from Jacob, with none of Jacob in him: “Blessed is the man … in whose spirit there is no deceit” (Psalm 32:2). And having opened with Jacob, Jesus will close the conversation four verses later with the night Jacob slept on a stone.

Honest, not sinless. It does not mean Nathanael is sinless, or even nice. The last thing out of his mouth was an insult about Jesus’ home town, and in a sense it is for that very honesty that he is commended. He says what he actually thinks; there is no gap between what is in him and what comes out of him. He was rude, and he was honest, and Jesus prefers that to smoothness by a wide margin.

Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Good did come out of Nazareth: the best that ever came out of anywhere. The Lord of glory grew up in a village no one thought worth naming, and he kept its name to the end; over the cross Pilate wrote, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (19:19). The slight became part of the title of the King.

The Israelite with no deceit at all. The same word is used of Jesus himself: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22, quoting Isaiah 53:9). Nathanael is an honest son of Jacob. The man speaking to him is the one Israelite in whom there was no deceit at any depth, the faithful servant Isaiah saw, who would be numbered with the transgressors and bear their sin. Nathanael’s honesty brought him to Jesus; Jesus’ sinlessness is what makes it safe for a sinner to come. He is not ashamed of small places, or of the honest sceptics who come out of them.

For the awkward one. Say this to the Christian who has always felt himself the awkward one: too blunt, too doubtful, the person who asks the question everyone else is too polite to ask. It is not a smooth man that Jesus stops to praise here. It is the sceptic from the next village who said the wrong thing out loud.

So should I avoid giving reasons when people object? No. Peter tells us always to be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in us, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and Paul reasoned in synagogues and marketplaces. Learn what you can, and answer honest questions honestly. But arguments are not the goal: the aim of every answer is to bring the person to Christ himself. So when the objection is really a reason not to look, do not get stuck defending Nazareth. Invite them to read a Gospel with you, to come to church, to see for themselves.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was an obscure village; it is never named in the Old Testament. “No deceit” may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, the deceiver who became Israel.

parallels.desc: your brother came deceitfully
in whose spirit there is no deceit

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had seen and known Nathanael before anyone called him, and he uses what he knows not to shame but to welcome.

How do you know me? Nathanael’s surprised question is already halfway to a confession; they had never met, and he suspects something extraordinary. Jesus’ answer begins, “Before Philip called you”, stating the order deliberately. Before the human contact, before the invitation, before Nathanael had any idea that anything was happening, he was already the subject of attention. Everything Philip did was second. Christ knows his people before they ever turn to him.

I saw you. Whatever happened under that tree was private enough that being told “I saw you” turned a sceptic into a confessor inside a minute. A man who had been mocking Nazareth moments earlier now says, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God!” Something known to no one else had just been referred to by a stranger. Jesus saw him, supernaturally, and knew what was in his heart (2:25).

For the one who feels unseen. This verse comforts one reader and undoes another. To the one who feels unseen, the years of praying in a room nobody knows about, the caring for someone that nobody is counting, the faithfulness that has produced no visible result and no acknowledgement: this is the verse. He saw you: not deduced you, not was informed about you, but saw. He simply lets you know that the private place was never as private as it felt.

For the one with something to hide. To the one who has something under his own fig tree that he would rather were not seen, the same sentence lands as exposure. He saw that too. But look at what he does with what he saw. He mentions the tree and stops, and the whole weight of the encounter is not accusation but welcome. The one person with complete access to your private life is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he does not use what he knows to shame those who come to him. Whether being seen frightens or comforts depends on the face of the one who was watching, and we know that face now: it is the face of the Lamb of God, full of grace and truth.

Does Jesus know everything about me now? Yes. He knew what was in man (2:25), and as the risen Lord he searches minds and hearts (Revelation 2:23). He knows your thoughts before you speak them, the sins you have hidden, and the sorrows you have never voiced (Psalm 139:1–4). For an unbeliever that is a solemn truth, because nothing will be hidden at the judgment. For a believer it is the ground of deep rest: you never have to pretend before him, and you cannot surprise him into rejecting you. He took you knowing everything. Bring him the truth, because he has it already.

Uncertain wording. What Nathanael was doing under the fig tree is not told. Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace in the messianic age (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10), and later rabbinic stories picture teachers studying under one. Preachers have supplied the scene for centuries: that he was praying, or reading Genesis 28 about Jacob at Bethel, which would explain the answer Jesus gives three verses later. Any of these may be right, but the text says none of them. What is certain is the effect: Jesus knew something private that no stranger could have known.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security.

parallels.desc: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sceptic makes the fullest confession yet, Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus welcomes his small faith by promising him far greater things.

Rabbi, you are the Son of God! The fullest confession so far in the Gospel, and it comes from the sceptic. Son of God and King of Israel were both messianic titles (Psalm 2:6–7), and Nathanael may not yet understand all that the first one means. It is true in the fullest sense the prologue has already given: not only the anointed king, but the only Son who shares the Father’s very being and was at his side before the world began (1:1, 18).

You are the King of Israel! Not a devotional phrase but a political claim, and in an occupied country it gets people killed. A crowd will shout it with palm branches (12:13), and Pilate will have it written in three languages above his head and refuse to change the wording (19:19–22). The title Nathanael gives him in a field in Galilee ends up on his execution notice. He is right, he has no idea what he is saying, and the man he says it to knows exactly what it will cost. The King of Israel wore his title on a cross, and then rose to wear it on a throne.

Do you believe? This could be read as a mild reproach, that faith resting on one impressive moment is a thin foundation. But what follows is a promise. Jesus does not tell Nathanael his faith is inadequate, but that it is small compared with what is coming, which is a different thing and much kinder. Jesus in this Gospel is notably unfussy about where faith starts. He tells a royal official that people will not believe unless they see signs and wonders, and then heals his son anyway (4:48–50). He invites Thomas to put his finger in the wounds (20:27). He never turns away a small faith for being small. What he does, repeatedly, is refuse to let it stay that size.

Greater things than these. The signs of the Gospel, and the glory of the cross and resurrection: not different things, but greater. Whatever brought you in is the smallest thing that will ever happen to you. And the honest word on the other side: the greater things promised here were not more moments of being privately known. They were a cross and an empty tomb, and what Nathanael went on to see included the worst week of his life. Greater does not mean more pleasant. It means more of who this person is, and there are parts of who he is that can only be seen from somewhere painful.

What if my faith has gone flat since the beginning? Some Christians have a moment they have been living off for thirty years: a conversion, an answered prayer, a week when God seemed close, and everything since has felt like a slow decline from it. The moment has quietly become a museum rather than a beginning. This verse says it was never meant to be the peak. It was the fig tree, the thing that got you to look up. Jesus promises greater things, chiefly a deeper sight of himself, and he gives them through his word, through suffering, and through the long faithfulness of ordinary years. Ask him to show you more of himself, and go looking where he has promised to be found.

parallels.desc: my King, my Son
the King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth: in him the way between God and sinners stands open, as Jacob glimpsed in his dream.

Truly, truly. Amen, amen: a double truly found only in John (25 times), and this is the first. Amen is what you say to somebody else’s statement: yes, let it stand. Jesus puts it in front of his own sentences, twice. That is either extraordinary presumption or a claim about who is speaking. He never argues for his authority in this Gospel; he simply talks as though it is not in question.

You will see. The ESV notes that “you” is plural: he turns from the one man to the whole group, and by extension to everyone reading. The fig tree was for Nathanael. This is for all of us.

Heaven opened. This is Genesis 28:12, Jacob’s dream at Bethel: a ladder set up on the earth, reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it. And the circumstances are not respectable. Jacob is running, having cheated his brother out of the blessing by lying to his blind father’s face, with Esau intending to kill him. He sleeps on a stone in open country, alone and guilty, about as far from a holy place as a man can be, and there heaven opens over him, with the LORD standing above it, promising to be with him and bring him back.

Surely the LORD is in this place. Jacob wakes afraid and names the place: “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it. … How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Genesis 28:16–17). That fear was right. Where heaven opens the holy God is near, and no sinner stands there casually. Read it against verse 26 of this chapter, where the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem, “among you stands one you do not know”: the same discovery, centuries apart. God turns out to have been present in the place where nobody thought to look for him.

On the Son of Man. Jesus is the ladder: the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel, the house of God, the gate of heaven. The way between God and humanity is open through him alone (14:6). Nathanael, the true Israelite (Israel was Jacob’s new name), will see what Jacob saw, fulfilled in Jesus. Jesus may even be settling a translator’s question in Genesis: the Hebrew says the angels were ascending and descending on it, or on him, and the ancient rabbis discussed both. Jesus says: “on the Son of Man”. Jacob thought he had found a place; Jesus says the point of contact is a person. “Son of Man” is the title Jesus uses most often for himself, from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion.

Ascending first. The order is odd in Genesis and odd here: ascending first, then descending. You would expect angels, who live in heaven, to come down before they go up. They start at the bottom. Wherever the ladder’s foot is, that is where the traffic begins, and Jesus has just said where the foot is standing: on earth, where the Son of Man is.

The ladder has legs. That is the point, and the reason this verse is the right end to the chapter. Jacob stumbled on the gate of heaven by accident, in the dark, and marked it with a stone and called it Bethel, house of God, so that he could find it again. Many religions since have tried the same: locate the place, secure the access, mark it so it can be returned to, whether a shrine, a practice, or a state of mind you were in once. Jesus tells a man who has believed for a few minutes that the ladder has legs. The meeting point between heaven and earth is not a site you have to find or a condition you have to achieve. It is a person who walks about. Jacob was terrified of the gate he found. This one goes looking for men under fig trees, calls them by name before they have been introduced, and invites them to come and see. And what makes the open heaven good news is the one it opens over: in the Son of Man the holy God can be approached by guilty people, and they live.

In everyday life. Wherever you are today, the kitchen, the office, the hospital, the place you feel far from God, say what Jacob said and mean it: “Surely the LORD is in this place”. Then pray, not as someone trying to climb up to God, but as someone for whom the way has been opened in Christ. You do not need a holy place. You need the Son of Man, and you have him.

Does this mean I will see angels? Not necessarily, and you should not go looking for visions. Jesus is not promising the disciples a literal sighting of a stairway; he is telling them that in him the traffic between heaven and earth is now open, and that they will see it in what he does: the signs, the cross, the resurrection, the ascension. Angels do serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), usually unseen. But the wonder of the verse is not the angels. It is that you have access to the Father through the Son, now, in ordinary prayer, because heaven is open over him and you are in him.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “hereafter”; the earliest do not.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples. “Truly, truly” is a solemn formula found only in John.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s ladder, angels ascending and descending

1.title: The Word Made Flesh
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.<sup>2</sup>He was in the beginning with God.<sup>3</sup>All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.<sup>4</sup>In him was life, and the life was the light of men.<sup>5</sup>The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.<sup>6</sup>There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.<sup>7</sup>He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him.<sup>8</sup>He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.<sup>9</sup>The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.<sup>10</sup>He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.<sup>11</sup>He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him.<sup>12</sup>But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,<sup>13</sup>who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God.<sup>14</sup>And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.<sup>15</sup>(John bore witness about him, and cried out, “This was he of whom I said, ’He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.’”)<sup>16</sup>For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.<sup>17</sup>For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.<sup>19</sup>And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”<sup>20</sup>He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, “I am not the Christ.”<sup>21</sup>And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”<sup>22</sup>So they said to him, “Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”<sup>23</sup>He said, “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ’Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.”<sup>24</sup>(Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)<sup>25</sup>They asked him, “Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”<sup>26</sup>John answered them, “I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know,<sup>27</sup>even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.”<sup>28</sup>These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.<sup>29</sup>The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!<sup>30</sup>This is he of whom I said, ’After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.’<sup>31</sup>I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel.”<sup>32</sup>And John bore witness: “I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him.<sup>33</sup>I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ’He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’<sup>34</sup>And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”<sup>35</sup>The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples,<sup>36</sup>and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”<sup>37</sup>The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.<sup>38</sup>Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, “What are you seeking?” And they said to him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are you staying?”<sup>39</sup>He said to them, “Come and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour.<sup>40</sup>One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.<sup>41</sup>He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which means Christ).<sup>42</sup>He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas” (which means Peter).<sup>43</sup>The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>44</sup>Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.<sup>45</sup>Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”<sup>46</sup>Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”<sup>47</sup>Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”<sup>48</sup>Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”<sup>49</sup>Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”<sup>50</sup>Jesus answered him, “Because I said to you, ’I saw you under the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these.”<sup>51</sup>And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
1.overview:
Where we are. John 1 opens the Gospel further back than any other book, before creation itself. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole Gospel; then the story begins with a week of witness at the Jordan (vv. 19–51) that runs on to the wedding at Cana (2:1–11).

The message. The God no one has ever seen has made himself known, in person. The eternal Word, who was with God and was God, has become flesh and lived among us, so that in a man we see the Father’s glory, full of grace and truth. All who receive him become children of God, and the rest of the chapter shows what receiving him looks like: hearing a witness, following, coming to see, and finding that he found you first.

Why it was said. John wrote for believers who had paid a price for confessing Jesus and were hearing false ideas about him (see the introduction). This chapter tells them at once who he is, and that John the Baptist, whose movement still had followers, was only a witness to him.

How the chapter makes its case. The prologue moves from eternity into history: the Word, God and Creator, source of life and light (vv. 1–5); John, sent as a witness (vv. 6–8); the world that did not know him, and the gift of becoming God’s children by a birth from God (vv. 9–13); the Word made flesh, full of grace and truth, who has made the Father known (vv. 14–18). Then the narrative: John refuses every title and calls himself only a voice (vv. 19–28); he points to Jesus as the Lamb of God, on whom the Spirit came down and remained (vv. 29–34); his disciples follow Jesus, and each one found becomes a finder, Andrew bringing Simon and Philip bringing Nathanael (vv. 35–49); and Jesus promises heaven opened over the Son of Man (vv. 50–51).

Where it leads. The whole chapter is about Christ, and it piles up his titles: Word, light, only Son, Lamb of God, Son of God, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man. The Lamb points straight to the cross, where the sin of the world is carried away. He is the tabernacle where God’s glory dwells and the ladder between heaven and earth: God has come to us, and the way to God is open in him.

For us. You do not have to guess what God is like: look at Jesus. Come to him as these first disciples did, with half-formed questions and small faith, and he will take you in, name you and show you greater things. Then do what Andrew and Philip did, and bring someone else.

keyVerse.quote: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the summit of the prologue and the heart of the Christian faith. The eternal Word of verse 1 has become a real man and pitched his tent among us, so that the glory once hidden in the tabernacle is seen in a human life, full of the grace and truth God proclaimed to Moses. Everything else in the chapter, from the Lamb of God to heaven opened over the Son of Man, flows from this: God has come to us in person.

1.reflection:
John says the Word was with God and was God, and that the only Son has made the Father known (vv. 1, 18). What picture of God do you carry that does not match what you see in Jesus, and how would your prayers change if you took Jesus as God’s own explanation of himself?

His own people did not receive him, yet all who receive him are given the right to become God’s children, born not of human will but of God (vv. 11–13). What difference does it make that your standing as God’s child rests on his gift rather than on your feelings or your record?

John the Baptist refused every title and pointed even his own disciples away from himself to the Lamb of God (vv. 19–36). Where are you tempted to accept more credit or attention than is yours, and what would it look like to point people to Jesus instead?

Andrew brought his brother, and Philip answered a sceptical friend with nothing more than “Come and see” (vv. 41–46). Who is one person you could invite to look at Jesus, and what keeps you from doing it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus has come to bring the joy of God’s new age, and he does it quietly, in his own time, for those who trust his word. At a village wedding the wine runs out, and Mary brings the need to him (vv. 1–3). He tells her that his hour has not yet come, yet she sends the servants to do whatever he says (vv. 4–5). They fill six stone jars kept for Jewish purification, and the water becomes the best wine of the feast, though only the servants know where it came from (vv. 6–10). This first sign reveals his glory, his disciples believe in him, and he goes down to Capernaum with his family (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
John calls the miracles of Jesus signs: not mere wonders but pointers to who he is. This one shows him as the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom, turning the old into the new, scarcity into abundance. His hour, the hour of the cross and glorification, has not yet come, and every sign points toward it.

What Jesus uses for the sign is part of its meaning, and so is the abundance (see the note on vv. 6–7).

A sign is a signpost, and he manifested his glory is the first sight of the glory promised in 1:14 (see the note on vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus honours marriage by performing his first sign at a wedding (see the note on vv. 1–2).

The Son’s first miracle was done because somebody was going to be embarrassed, so no trouble is too small to bring to him (see the note on v. 3).

The world serves its best first; the gospel runs the other way (see the note on vv. 9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus begins his signs at a village wedding, sharing in human joy as the Maker who has come to make his creation new.

On the third day. John has been marking off the days (1:29, 35, 43), so a book that opened with “in the beginning” has laid out a week and arrived at its end (see the box below). Many have also heard in “the third day” a hint of the resurrection.

A wedding at Cana in Galilee. Cana was a village a few miles north of Nazareth, so small that no other book of the Bible mentions it. At the very end John notes that Nathanael was of Cana in Galilee (21:2). So the man who asked whether anything good could come out of Nazareth is very probably at a wedding in his own village, watching Nazareth’s carpenter make the best wine anyone there had tasted. He had been promised greater things (1:50). It did not take long.

What a wedding was. Weddings lasted up to a week, with the whole village invited, and the groom’s family had to feed and supply them all. Hospitality was not a courtesy but a duty, and failing in it brought public shame.

The mother of Jesus. Perhaps she was helping, as a relative or friend of the family. Jesus’ five or more disciples, as extra guests, may be part of the reason the wine ran out, though the text does not say so. John, who names Nathanael and Nicodemus and Lazarus and even Malchus the servant, never names her: she is always the mother of Jesus. Apart from a passing mention (2:12), she appears in only two scenes, the first sign and the cross, when his hour has come (19:25–27), and both times he calls her “Woman”.

Jesus also was invited. He honoured marriage by his presence (Hebrews 13:4). He was no ascetic; he came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34). The eternal Word who was with God before there was light spent one of his first recorded days as a man at a village party, and stayed long enough to notice the drink running out. He who would walk the road to Calvary first walked the road to Cana.

Where the week lands. Genesis runs six days of making, crowned by man and woman made in God’s image; John’s week ends at a wedding, with more wine than anyone could drink. The guest is the Word through whom all things were made (1:3). The Maker of the first week has come into his own creation to begin it again, and this time the week ends not with a garden but with a feast, where the one who brings the wine is himself the Bridegroom (3:29).

Are holiness and enjoyment at odds? Some have quietly come to believe that the serious Christian is the one who does not much like anything. But the first sign was done at a wedding, for a family about to be embarrassed, and it produced more than a hundred gallons beyond what the occasion required. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Food, friendship, music, marriage and laughter are his gifts, and receiving them with thanks is not worldliness but worship (1 Timothy 4:4–5). What turns a gift into an idol is not enjoying it but loving it more than the Giver.

What does this say about marriage? That God honours it. Marriage was his idea from the beginning (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus chose a wedding for the first display of his glory. Marriage between a man and a woman is a living picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and history ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9), so every Christian wedding is a small sign of the great one. And if you are single, widowed, or your marriage is hard, the deepest wedding is still yours: the Bridegroom has come for his bride, and you belong to her.

Uncertain wording. “On the third day” counts from the last day John mentioned (1:43), but not every earlier day is marked, so the total cannot be fixed: the wedding falls on about the sixth or seventh day of his sequence. What is clear is that John is counting deliberately, and the likely sense is a week of new beginnings brought to its close.
verseByVerse.note: Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth. A wedding feast could last a week.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A family faces public shame, and Mary brings the need to Jesus without telling him how to meet it. It is a small trouble, and that is the point.

The wine ran out. Nobody is ill or in danger. But in a culture built on honour and shame, with the whole village present, the shortfall would be talked about for years. Most of our troubles are of this kind, though most of our praying is not about them: the moment everyone saw you had run out. Jesus could have opened his ministry by raising a dead child. He opens it by rescuing a family’s reputation at a party.

They have no wine. Mary states the problem and stops: no request, no reminder of who she is, no proposed method. She brings the need and trusts him to act, a model of prayer. And this was the first of his signs (v. 11): she has thirty years of knowing him and no record of miracles. Her faith rests on who he is, not on any assurance that he will do what she asks.

The wine the prophets promised. In the prophets abundant wine is a sign of the messianic age: the mountains will drip sweet wine (Amos 9:13–14; Joel 3:18), and on Mount Zion the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of well-aged wine and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). A wedding where the wine has run out may picture the old order run dry; the Messiah arrives, and the first thing he does is supply the wine. Isaiah’s feast and Cana have the same host, and he will swallow up death by going into death himself.

A small shame lifted, a great one carried. The Lord of glory began his signs by lifting a small shame from a bridegroom in Cana, and finished his work by carrying the great one. He endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), mocked before a whole city, so that no one who trusts in him would ever be put to shame (Romans 10:11). The wine at Cana cost him a word; the covering for our disgrace cost him his blood. Nothing that troubles his people is beneath his notice, and nothing that shames them was beyond his bearing.

What it does not mean. Mary’s way is not a technique. There is nothing wrong with asking God for specific things; the Psalms are full of it, and Jesus told us to ask (Matthew 7:7). But much praying is really a plan presented for approval, anxious because it has already decided what the answer must look like. She leaves the method with him, which is wise, since what he does is not remotely what anyone would have asked for.

Is it really all right to pray about small things? Yes. Paul says, “in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6), and “everything” includes the small. The God who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30) is not bored by your car, your exam, or the awkward meeting on Thursday. It acknowledges that nothing in your life is outside his care, and it keeps you honest, because the person who prays only about emergencies has quietly decided he can manage everything else on his own.
verseByVerse.note: Running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gently tells his mother that his work runs on his Father’s timetable, not hers, and she answers by pointing everyone to him.

Woman. A respectful form of address, not a rude one, but not the word a son would usually use for his mother. It signals a gentle distance: he is still her son, and will care for her to the end (19:26–27), but in the work his Father has given him he answers to his Father alone.

What does this have to do with me? Literally ‘what to me and to you?’, a Hebrew idiom meaning, in effect, ‘this is not yours to direct’ (see the box below). Jesus acts on his Father’s timing, however well meant his mother’s (Luke 2:49). With “my hour has not yet come” it sounds like a refusal, after which, puzzlingly, he does exactly what the situation required. Did she change his mind?

Why does he refuse and then act? “My hour” everywhere in this Gospel means the hour of the cross and the glory that follows it, set by the Father (7:30; 8:20; 12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1). So “my hour has not yet come” does not mean ‘I will not act now’ but that the hour when he is fully revealed is still ahead. That is why the sign is so quiet that only the servants know. At Cana he gives a veiled foretaste of the messianic feast; at the hour he will give the thing itself, when his blood is poured out and the new covenant is made. The wine of Cana is real, but the feast it points to is bought at Calvary.

The two ends of his ministry. At the cross, when the hour has arrived, he says, “Woman, behold, your son” (19:26), and arranges her care with almost his last breath. But from this verse on she has to learn to know him as the one whose hour is coming, one of the hardest things a mother has ever been asked to do.

Do whatever he tells you. Mary’s last recorded words in the Gospels, and advice worth a lifetime. She does not take offence; she points others to him. And the sentence has a precedent. In the famine in Egypt Pharaoh says, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do” (Genesis 41:55). A shortage nobody can fix, and the answer is to go to the one man who has what is needed, Joseph then and a greater than Joseph now, and do what he says without asking how.

Honouring Mary rightly. Jesus’ answer is no snub: he honours her faith and meets the need. Scripture calls her blessed among women and favoured by God (Luke 1:28, 42, 48), and Protestants have often been too shy of saying so. But her best word points away from herself: not “do what I tell you”, but “whatever he tells you”. The way to honour her is to take her advice.

How do I know what he is telling me to do? Chiefly from Scripture. Most of what he asks is already plain: love God, love your neighbour, forgive, tell the truth, be faithful in marriage, give, pray, gather with his people, make disciples. Most of us have more than enough to obey before we need further guidance. In decisions Scripture does not settle directly, such as which job, which house, whom to marry among believers, ask for wisdom (James 1:5), take counsel from mature Christians, and choose what best serves Christ and others. You do not need a voice. You need to do what he has already said.

Where Christians differ: Mary’s intercession. Roman Catholic devotion has seen Cana as a picture of Mary’s power as intercessor, obtaining favours from her Son. This commentary’s view: the passage shows the opposite emphasis: Jesus gently declines her direction and acts in his own time, and Mary directs the servants to him: do whatever he tells you. She is a model of faith and of pointing to Christ, not a mediator between us and him. There is one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).

Uncertain wording. The idiom behind “what does this have to do with me?” is known from the Old Testament and the Gospels, but its force depends on tone, which writing cannot carry. It can be a sharp rebuke, as when demons cry it at Jesus (Mark 5:7), or a gentle ‘leave this to me’ from someone about to act in his own way and time. Paired with the courteous “Woman”, and followed by the sign itself, the gentler sense is very probably meant.
verseByVerse.note: “Woman” was a respectful form of address, not a rude one. Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

parallels.desc: “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do”

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes the jars that stood for Israel’s washing rites and has them filled to the brim, ready to turn the old order of cleansing into the overflowing joy of the kingdom.

Six stone water jars. Everything in this sign turns on what the water was for. Stone did not become ritually unclean as earthenware did, so stone jars held water for ceremonial washing (Mark 7:3–4): of hands, of vessels, of whatever defilement a person picked up in an ordinary week. Six is perhaps one short of seven, the Bible’s number of completeness, though John does not say so. The jars stood for the old order of ritual purification.

Each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Literally ‘two or three measures’: between 120 and 180 gallons (450 to 680 litres) in all, six to nine hundred bottles, for a village wedding late in the feast. The need was enough to avoid disgrace; what arrives is more than the family could drink in a month. In his kingdom God does not give just enough.

Fill the jars with water. “And they filled them up to the brim.” An ordinary command, unexplained, and obedience, as Mary had said. Full to the brim, so nothing could be added: what follows is no trick. The servants could not make wine; they could only fill jars, and they filled them to the rim.

The machinery of cleansing. Jesus makes the miracle not from a well or an empty wine jar, but from the equipment of a whole system for people not clean enough to come near God. He does not smash the jars; he fills them. The washing-water is not condemned but fulfilled and turned into joy, because the one who fills them will himself make the cleansing they could only point to. The long centuries of washing and sacrifice end not in a smaller religion but in a feast.

Was the Old Testament law then a bad thing? No. The purification rites were God’s own gift, teaching Israel that he is holy and that sinners need cleansing to come near him. They were good, and temporary, like a signpost meant to be passed: they could make the body ceremonially clean but never cleanse the conscience (Hebrews 9:9–14). What they pointed to, Christ provides: the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). So we do not despise the jars. We thank God for them, and drink what they were waiting for.

Does the size of the miracle mean God will always give me more than I need? Not in the sense of more money or easier circumstances: Paul knew hunger and need as well as plenty (Philippians 4:12). What the sign promises is the character of God’s grace, which is never measured out grudgingly. In Christ he gives forgiveness that covers every sin, a Spirit poured out without measure, an inheritance that cannot fade, and a love that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). Your circumstances may be thin; his grace to you is not, and it is always enough for what he calls you to bear (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In everyday life. Think of something you did only adequately: the visit kept short, the apology with a qualification attached, the giving calculated to be defensible. Not defiance; simply not to the brim. He has filled you from his own fullness, so obey him in the ordinary instructions, all the way, before you see how it helps. And where your obedience stops short of the rim, as all of ours does, his did not: his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19).
verseByVerse.note: Stone jars did not become ritually unclean, so they were used for purification water. The ESV notes that each held two or three measures, twenty to thirty gallons: well over a hundred gallons in all.
