parallels.desc: the washings of the Jews

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without a word over the water, Jesus changes it, and the servants carry it out trusting nothing but his instruction.

Now draw some out. No prayer, no touch. Somewhere in that sentence the water became wine, silently, by his will, and John does not describe it: he cares more about what a sign means than how it looked. The Word who spoke the world into being needs no ceremony; and out of sheer kindness he chooses to work through the hands of servants who trust him.

The master of the feast. Probably a trusted guest or senior servant in charge of the food and drink.

So they took it. More obedience, and a real risk. If nothing has happened, they are handing the master of the feast hand-washing water in front of the party. All they had was a sentence from a guest and a woman’s instruction to do whatever he said. They do not taste it first in the kitchen and then decide whether to carry it out. That is what trust is: acting on his word before seeing the result.

Does faith mean acting without any evidence at all? No. The servants were not leaping in the dark; they had a word from Jesus and the testimony of someone who knew him. Christian faith rests on solid grounds: the eyewitness record of his life, death and resurrection, the fulfilled Scriptures, changed lives. What it lacks is a guarantee of how each step of obedience will turn out. We trust the person, then act, and the confirmation often comes after, as in every relationship of trust.
verseByVerse.note: The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best wine comes last, and only the servants who obeyed know where it came from: so God keeps his best until the end, and his best is his Son.

The servants knew. The steward tastes it and cannot account for it; the bridegroom gets the credit and has no idea what for; the guests drink it and never learn that anything happened. The knowledge went not to the man with the office, nor to the one being honoured, but to the servants who carried the jars: they obeyed a strange instruction and therefore found out (7:17).

Where from? The word (pothen) will follow Jesus through the whole book. The crowd in Jerusalem will say they know where this man comes from (7:27); a healed blind man will marvel that the authorities do not (9:29–30); and at the end Pilate, out of his depth in his own judgment hall, will ask him, “Where are you from?”, and get no answer (19:9). The first person in this Gospel unable to account for what Jesus has done is a wine steward at a party, and he will not be the last.

The bridegroom praised by mistake. The bridegroom is praised for the one thing at his own wedding he had nothing to do with. Within a chapter John the Baptist will use that word of Jesus: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (3:29). The real bridegroom is standing in the room, and the compliment goes to the wrong man from one who does not know what he is saying, as when a high priest explains that it is better for one man to die for the people (11:49–52).

The good wine until now. The world puts its best first: the advertisement beats the product, and almost every pleasure is best at the start and then fades. God works the other way round. The old covenant was good, but the new is better (Hebrews 8:6), and Scripture ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). The steward’s compliment describes how God runs history: he keeps the best until last.

The good wine is the Son himself. Long ago God spoke by the prophets; he kept his best for these last days, when he spoke to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The one who made the wine at Cana would give his own blood for the new covenant, and every cup of grace since has come from that store.

In everyday life. If you suspect your best days are behind you, the years when you felt most alive and most in love with God, say the steward’s sentence over your life. Without Christ that fear would be right. For anyone in Christ the order is reversed: the best is still ahead.

What it does not mean. The best wine last is not an assurance that your circumstances will improve, and it must not be handed to someone as though it were. Plenty of Christian lives get harder; health goes, and the people you love are buried one at a time. What is promised is not a better stretch of road but a better end, and that end is not an ending but life with him for ever.

Not a killjoy. The steward’s remark about guests who have drunk freely makes no sense of grape juice. Nothing here licenses excess or shames the Christian who abstains, but the sign does say that the God who came among us was no killjoy: his first miracle was a wedding present, and an extravagant one.

What if alcohol has been a problem for me or my family? Then abstaining is not legalism but wisdom, and often love. Freedom to drink is not an obligation to drink, and Paul says it is good not to drink wine if it makes a brother stumble (Romans 14:21); the brother may be you. If drink has a hold on you, the gospel offers forgiveness and real help: confess it honestly to God and to a trusted Christian, get practical support, and remove it from your home. And if a parent’s or spouse’s drinking has wounded you, this passage does not ask you to celebrate wine. It shows you a Lord who brings joy without ruin, and who can heal what drink has broken.

Where Christians differ: wine and alcohol. Some Christians argue that biblical wine was unfermented grape juice, and that Christians should abstain completely. This commentary’s view: the wine Jesus made was real wine, as the master’s comment shows. Scripture praises wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15) while forbidding drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35). Christians are free to drink in moderation and free to abstain; they must never get drunk, and must be willing to abstain out of love for weaker brothers (Romans 14:21). Abstinence is a wise choice for many, but not a command.

parallels.desc: a feast of well-aged wine
the mountains shall drip sweet wine

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This first sign reveals Jesus’ glory, the glory of God’s own kindness, and his disciples’ faith grows. Then he goes down to Capernaum with his family and his followers.

The first of his signs. John calls Jesus’ miracles signs (sēmeia), pointers to who he is. Matthew, Mark and Luke commonly call them dynameis, mighty works; John never uses that word for them. A mighty work invites you to be impressed. A signpost points somewhere you have not yet reached, and a traveller who praises its carpentry has missed the point. That is what will go wrong with the crowds in chapter 6, who came looking for him not because they saw signs but because they ate their fill of the loaves (6:26).

Seven signs. John records seven signs before the resurrection: water into wine (2:1–11), the official’s son (4:46–54), the paralysed man (5:1–15), the five thousand (6:1–15), walking on water (6:16–21), the man born blind (9:1–41), and Lazarus (11:1–44). The counting is debated at the edges, but he tells us at the close what he was doing (20:30–31). And the word for “first” is the one that opened the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word”: this was the beginning of his signs.

And manifested his glory. His divine glory, hidden in his humanity, shone through: “we have seen his glory” (1:14), and here is the first instalment. Glory is the shining out of who God is. When Moses asked to see it, God made his goodness pass before him and proclaimed his name, merciful and gracious (Exodus 33:18–19; 34:6). At Cana that same goodness is seen in a man’s kindness to a bridegroom in trouble.

The glory in clay cups. The glory that filled the tent until Moses could not go in, that drove the priests from Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8:11), that left Isaiah crying out that he was undone, was in a back room in Cana, quietly seeing to it that a young couple were not humiliated on their wedding day. Nothing shook; nobody fell down. The steward went on doing his job, the bridegroom accepted a compliment he had not earned, and the glory of the eternal God went round that room in cups.

His disciples believed. That is the purpose of the signs (20:30–31). They had already believed (1:41–49); now their faith deepened. Faith is not a switch thrown once; it grows, is tested, and grows again. These same men will scatter on the night of his arrest. If your faith is larger or smaller than it was five years ago, that is not instability; it is the ordinary condition of everyone in this chapter.

His mother and his brothers. The first mention of his brothers in this Gospel, and John will tell us where they stood: “not even his brothers believed in him” (7:5). Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake shore, became Jesus’ base in Galilee (Matthew 4:13; Mark 2:1), and “went down” is literal, since Cana sits in the hills and the lake lies below sea level.

For the one praying for family. This is for you if you have been praying a long time for someone in your family. A flawless life lived in front of them for three decades did not convert his brothers, and neither did this wedding. Yet James is later found leading the church in Jerusalem, called a pillar by Paul, and writing a letter that is in your Bible (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9). What changed them was the resurrection: the risen Christ appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and did what thirty years under one roof had not. Keep praying.

Should I look for signs and miracles today? Look for what the signs were for. They were written so that you may believe (20:31), and Jesus blessed those who have not seen and yet have believed (20:29). God still answers prayer and can heal and provide in ways that astonish us; ask him freely. But the apostolic signs belonged to the founding of the church, and we need no fresh wonders to confirm a gospel already confirmed. That is the view called cessationism, held because the New Testament ties such signs to the apostles’ own witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, in Pentecostal and charismatic churches among others, believe these gifts continue, and we honour them as brothers; all agree that every sign points to Christ. A faith that keeps demanding new signs has missed the one they point to. You have the signs, in writing, and the Lord himself.

Nature hurried, not nature broken. Since David Hume, many have felt that a report of a miracle must be weighed against the uniform experience of humanity, and will always lose. C. S. Lewis observed in Miracles that this argues in a circle: we can know that experience against miracles is uniform only if we already know that every report of one is false. The real question is whether there is a Maker free to act in what he made. Augustine, preaching on this wedding, pointed out that the one who made wine at Cana makes it every year in the vineyards from the rain that falls on the vine, and we no longer wonder at it only because it happens every year. At Cana the Lord of the vineyard did quickly what he always does slowly: not an intruder vandalising nature, but the owner at work in his own house. And the story has a darker end: the one who gave the best wine at a wedding was given sour wine on a cross (19:29), so that we might sit down at the marriage supper of the Lamb.

Who were the brothers who went down to Capernaum? The natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brothers; Matthew names them (Matthew 13:55–56), and Paul met James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:19). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, take them as cousins or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. But Scripture never says so, and the plain reading is the more likely.
verseByVerse.note: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” — pointers to who he is. Capernaum was a fishing town on the lake shore.

parallels.desc: these are written so that you may believe

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the Lord of the temple and the true temple, the place where God now meets his people. At Passover he finds the temple court turned into a market and drives the traders out, forbidding them to make his Father’s house a house of trade (vv. 13–16). His disciples recall that zeal for God’s house will consume him, while the authorities demand a sign (vv. 17–18). He offers one: destroy this temple, and in three days he will raise it. John explains that he meant his body, as the disciples grasped after the resurrection (vv. 19–22). Many at the feast believe because of his signs, but he does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every heart (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Malachi 3:1). The zeal that consumes him is the Son’s passion for his Father’s honour, and my Father’s house is the claim that gives him authority there.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge (see the note on vv. 21–22).

Verses 23–25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader (see the note on vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.examples:
The buying and selling had filled the one court where the nations could pray (see the note on vv. 13–14).

The anger of this scene is not at odds with meekness, and it is no warrant for aggression on God’s behalf (see the note on vv. 15–16).

The chapter break hides a connection between verse 25 and Nicodemus (see the note on v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Passover the Lamb of God comes to his Father’s house and finds worship turned into a market, filling the one court where the nations could pray.

The Passover of the Jews was at hand. John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), the main reason the ministry is reckoned at about three years. Passover remembered the lamb whose blood turned judgment away from Israel’s houses (Exodus 12), and the man the Baptist has just called the Lamb of God (1:29) now walks into a court full of sheep for sale. The Lord has come to his temple, as Malachi said he would (Malachi 3:1), and the first thing he does there is turn over the furniture.

In the flow. At Cana he turned the water of purification into wine; here he confronts the centre of the system of sacrifice, and verse 21 will say that the true temple is his body. The scene opens the conflict with the Jerusalem leaders that ends at the cross.

In the temple. He found them: he is not told about it; he arrives and looks. The trade was not obviously a racket. A sacrifice had to be without blemish, and a lamb carried a hundred miles had a poor chance of passing inspection; buying one on site, already approved, was practical.

The money-changers. Every adult Jewish man owed an annual half-shekel temple tax. It had to be paid in the coinage of Tyre, whose silver was reliably pure, even though it carried the image of a pagan god. So pilgrims had to change their money. The changers took a commission, and the trade was probably controlled by, and profitable to, the high-priestly families; later Jewish writings remember them for exactly that.

The court of the nations. The temple’s courts grew more restricted as you went in: the Court of the Women, the court for Israelite men, the priests’ court. The outermost and largest was the Court of the Gentiles, the only place where a non-Jew could come and pray; beyond it a barrier warned any foreigner who passed that he would have himself to blame for his death, and inscribed stones from it have been dug up. The market was in that court. The one place where a Gentile could come near the God of Israel had been given over to livestock pens and currency tables.

A house of prayer for all the nations. So at the later cleansing Jesus cries out Isaiah’s words with the clause we usually leave off: “for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7; Mark 11:17). The offence is not only commerce in a holy place, but that the religious had shut the outsider out of prayer. The court they had filled with trade was the court he meant to fill with worshippers from every tribe and tongue.

Rot by convenience. Reasonable arrangements, each defensible, had together turned worship into a transaction, with nobody deciding it. Institutions do not usually rot by scandal; they rot by convenience. And the heart likes the arrangement. A God who can be dealt with at a counter asks for your money but not for you: pay the fee, perform the rite, and you are free to go. That is religion as a way of keeping God at a safe distance, the opposite of what the temple was built for.

In everyday life. The easy application is about churches selling things, which lets us think the passage is about somebody else. The harder question is the Court of the Gentiles one: does anything in the way your church operates, its vocabulary, its arrangements, the things everyone knows and nobody explains, make it hard for an outsider to get near God? Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations; they had simply needed the space. Christ made room for you when you were far off. Make room for one such person this Sunday.

Is it wrong for churches to sell things or handle money? Not in itself. Churches need money for ministers, the poor and missionaries, and Scripture commands generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7); a bookstall or a collection is not a temple market. The question is whether money and convenience have begun to shape worship and push people out: whether the gospel is ever made to look like something you buy, whether the poor feel unwelcome, whether leaders profit from the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Watch the purpose, not merely the transaction.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax. John places this cleansing early; the other Gospels record one in the last week.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus clears his Father’s house with deliberate, controlled zeal, acting as the Son with the owner’s authority, and careful even then of the poor.

Making a whip of cords. Some readers enjoy this scene too much; others are quietly embarrassed by it. The Greek is more restrained than the paintings: a whip improvised from cords, perhaps rushes or ropes lying about a place full of tethered livestock, most likely for driving the animals, not for beating people.

He drove them all out. Whoever “all” includes (see the box below), the authorities who arrive do not accuse him of assault; they ask for his credentials. Whatever happened, it was not a brawl.

The coins and the cages. The action is graded. The animals are driven out; the coins are poured across the floor and the tables turned over; but the pigeon-sellers are told to take their cages away. One likely reason is that pigeons were the offering of the poor, the sacrifice for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7), and released birds do not come back. Even in the middle of it, he will not wreck what the poorest worshippers depended on.

My Father’s house. Not “our Father’s house” but “my Father’s house”: Jesus claims a unique relationship with God, as he did at twelve in this same building (Luke 2:49), and that is what gives him the right to the whip. He is not a reformer with views on temple administration but the Son, dealing with what has been done to his family’s house. “A house of trade” perhaps echoes Zechariah 14:21: on the day of the LORD there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of hosts. That day has come, and it should sober us as well as thrill us. The one who came to Cana as a guest comes to the temple as its owner, and Malachi, who promised that the Lord would come suddenly to his temple, asked in the next breath who could endure the day of his coming (Malachi 3:1–2).

He held the whip, then bore the lash. In this chapter the Son holds the whip. Before the Gospel ends, Pilate has him flogged (19:1), and the one who drove the traders from his Father’s house stands silent under the lash, scourged to make a defiled people into a clean house for God. The zeal that would not let his Father be cheapened is the same love that let himself be beaten for those who had cheapened him.

Is this consistent with the gentle Jesus? It is, once we ask what anger is: what love does when what it loves is being damaged. A man who can watch his child be harmed and feel nothing is not gentle; he is absent. We have redefined gentleness as the absence of strong feeling, when in Scripture meekness is strength under command, and everything here is under command. He does not snatch up a weapon; he stops and makes a whip of cords. It was not a loss of temper but a decision. The Lamb of God has a holy wrath (Revelation 6:16), and it is the same love that weeps over Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. This passage has been used to justify much that has nothing to do with it. It is no warrant for Christians to be aggressive on God’s behalf, still less violent, and no cover for the man whose temper is a standing problem in his household and who has learned to call it righteous anger. Two things separate this from that. Every scrap of it is aimed at the abuse of God’s honour and the exclusion of the powerless, none at a slight to himself; when the injuries were personal he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; 1 Peter 2:23). And this is the Son acting in his own house with the owner’s authority. If your anger is regularly about your own treatment, this passage is not about you.

Then is anger always wrong for me? No. “Be angry and do not sin,” Paul writes (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real evil, cruelty, injustice, abuse, the dishonouring of God, can be right, and indifference to it is no virtue. But our anger is rarely pure, so Scripture fences it: be slow to anger (James 1:19–20), do not let the sun go down on it, never take revenge (Romans 12:19), and do not let it harden into bitterness. Ask whose honour your anger is defending. Then bring it to God, act through right channels, and leave vengeance to him.

One cleansing or two? John places a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry, the other Gospels one at the end; the details differ, and Jesus may well have done it twice, though John sometimes arranges true events by their meaning and not strictly by date. Either way the point of the scene is untouched.

Uncertain wording. “He drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen” can be read two ways. The Greek may mean ‘he drove them all out, both the sheep and the oxen’, so that “all” is the animals, or it may mean the traders together with their animals. Scholars divide. Either way the coins poured out and the tables overturned show that the traders were driven out of business, and no one is reported struck.

parallels.desc: no longer a trader in the house of the LORD
my Father’s house

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples see in Jesus the zeal of Psalm 69 that would consume him, while the authorities, without defending the market, demand to know who authorised him.

His disciples remembered. The verb comes twice in this chapter, and the two rememberings are not alike. Here the Scripture comes to mind at once, while the coins are still rolling. Later they will remember his saying about the temple of his body, and it will take three years and a resurrection to do it (v. 22).

Zeal for your house will consume me. Psalm 69:9, from a psalm of the righteous sufferer often applied to Jesus (15:25; Romans 15:3). “Consume” means devour. In the psalm the zeal has already consumed the psalmist; what the disciples remember is “will consume me”, a prediction: this will eat him. His zeal for his Father’s house will carry him to his death. John reaches for this psalm of a man hated without cause again at the cross, when they lift up the sour wine (19:28–29): the zeal and the vinegar come out of the same psalm.

What sign do you show us for doing these things? By what authority? Prove you are a prophet with a miracle. The irony grows as the book goes on: the question is asked in a Gospel built out of signs, by men who, as a body, will be shown sign after sign and refuse to believe.

Querying the credentials. Nobody says the market should stay, defends the money tables, or argues that the Court of the Gentiles was the right place for livestock. What is challenged is his standing to do anything about it: not “you are wrong”, but “who authorised you?” The safest way to avoid a charge is to query the credentials of whoever brought it.

The reproaches fell on him. The same verse of Psalm 69 goes on: “the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me”, and Paul says that was Christ (Romans 15:3). He was so jealous for his Father’s name that he let the abuse aimed at heaven land on his own head, and in being consumed he became the house where God and sinners meet.

In everyday life. Jesus’ zeal for his Father’s honour cost him his life, and it was spent for you. You are accepted because of him, so you have no reputation you need to protect. When you are rightly challenged about something wrong in you, resist the urge to query the credentials of the one who said it. Ask first whether it is true.

What is zeal, and why do I not seem to have it? Not a temperament. The naturally intense are not thereby more godly; much of what passes for zeal is a strong personality with a subject. What the disciples saw was a man who could not be indifferent to his Father’s honour because he loved his Father: zeal was the shape his love took when that honour was damaged. So do not ask whether you are zealous enough; no one has ever answered that helpfully. Ask what it takes to move you. Find the last thing you could not simply let pass, and you have located what you love. If it is not God’s honour, ask him to grow your love for him, and the zeal will follow.

parallels.desc: zeal for your house has consumed me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one sign Jesus offers is his resurrection: they will destroy the temple of his body, and in three days he will raise it. His hearers can think only of Herod’s stones.

Destroy this temple. “Destroy” is a command with the sense ‘if you destroy’. It sounds like a dare, though both sides know they will never pull down Herod’s stonework. But in about three years they will do precisely this to the temple he actually meant, his body (v. 21). “Raise up” (egeirō) is the word for resurrection.

Forty-six years. Herod began rebuilding around 20 BC, which puts this at about AD 27, one of the main fixed points for dating Jesus’ ministry. The work went on until about AD 63, and in AD 70 the Romans burned the temple. They held up to the Son of God a building that would stand complete for about seven years. They were not wrong about their temple; they were wrong about which temple was standing in front of them. He let them destroy the true temple, his body, and on the third day he raised it, never to fall again.

And will you raise it up in three days? They take him literally, and mock: the first instance of a pattern that runs through this Gospel. A teacher of Israel will hear “born again” and ask whether a grown man can enter his mother’s womb a second time (3:4); a woman at a well will hear “living water” and point out that he has nothing to draw with (4:11); a crowd will hear “bread from heaven” and ask for a permanent supply (6:34). Every time, the flattest reading is the one that spares the hearer from dealing with Jesus himself. The natural mind cannot perceive the things of the Spirit without new birth (1 Corinthians 2:14).

How testimony gets bent. At his trial witnesses say, “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands’” (Mark 14:58), and at the cross passers-by jeer at him for it (Mark 15:29). He said “you destroy”; they reported “I will destroy”. The pronoun was moved, and a prophecy about what they would do to him became a threat about what he would do to them. Little was invented. Something was shifted, and that was enough to hang a capital charge on.

Why did Jesus speak in riddles? Not to hide the truth from honest seekers, but to draw them in and expose hearts. A saying like this sticks in the memory and opens up later, as it did for the disciples (v. 22). It also sifts the hearers: those who want to understand him keep asking, while those who have already decided against him take the flattest reading and walk away. Jesus never plays games with people who truly want him. When Nicodemus asks, he explains at length; when the disciples ask, he tells them plainly. If something he says puzzles you, do what they did: stay near, keep reading, and ask.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years brings us to about AD 27. The work went on for decades more.

parallels.desc: the charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true temple, the place where God meets his people, is Jesus’ own body, and the disciples grasped it only after he rose.

The temple of his body. John’s explanation, and the key. The theme of God’s dwelling runs the length of the Bible, and this verse is its turning point. The Word “dwelt among us” (1:14), the language of the tabernacle where the glory came down; now the temple, the house where God could be met, is a body: not a building that contains the presence, but a person in whom God is present. In the old temple a worshipper met God by coming to a place, through a priest, with a sacrifice. Now we come to a person. When you pray in Jesus’ name and trust his sacrifice, you come as near to God as any high priest behind the curtain, for through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18).

After he was raised. They heard the words, and for nearly three years the words meant nothing to them. Then the resurrection made the sentence clear, as he had promised: the Holy Spirit will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (14:26). This verse is that promise at work, recorded by a man on the receiving end of it.

The Scripture and the word. They believed two things with one verb: a sentence Jesus spoke in a courtyard is placed beside the Old Testament as the same kind of word, with the same authority. John does not name the Scripture. Passages such as Psalm 16:10, “you will not abandon my soul to Sheol”, and Isaiah 53 were among those the apostles later preached, and Jesus himself opened the Scriptures to them after he rose (Luke 24:27): their faith was in the whole Old Testament witness to his death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

No temple in the city. For a thousand years God had consented to be met in a house of stone: the smoke, the blood, the curtain, the one room no one could enter but once a year and never without blood. Then a man stood in the middle of it and said the meeting place was himself; three years later they killed him outside the city, and the curtain was torn in two, from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). The house was never the point. The Son was the point, and the house had been saying so, in stone, for a thousand years. At the end of everything John sees “no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). There is no building at the end. There was never going to be.

We are his temple too. His people, united to him, become God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22), living stones built on the living cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4–5). Where Christ’s people gather in his name, God dwells; and each believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

For anyone in the middle of something they cannot read. Christians are often pressed to understand what God is doing while he is doing it: to have an account of the illness, the redundancy, the years that went nowhere, the prayer that was not answered. That pressure does not come from this book. The men closest to Jesus, watching the most important events in history from a few feet away, understood almost none of it until afterwards, and were not disqualified for it. What was asked of them was not comprehension. It was staying near enough to remember.

Then does it matter where or how we worship? Where, much less than before. True worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (4:21–24), and you can meet God in a kitchen as truly as in a cathedral. How, very much. We come to God only through Christ, the true temple, and must worship him as he has revealed himself, not as we invent. And because the church is his temple, gathering with his people is not optional decoration; it is where he has promised to dwell (Hebrews 10:25; Matthew 18:20).

parallels.desc: they remembered his words

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many believe because of the signs, but Jesus, who knows exactly what such faith is worth, does not entrust himself to them.

Many believed. Faith produced by spectacle: real, but shallow. Nothing has yet been asked of these people; they have been carried along by a movement that is going well. John is not saying their belief is fake, but untested.

Did not entrust himself. A play on words English cannot carry. They believed (episteusan) in him, but he did not believe (episteuen), entrust himself, to them: the same verb both times. He did not treat their excitement as a commitment, or open his heart to them as he would to friends (15:15).

Because he knew all people. This is not cynicism but knowledge. Not all who follow the miracle-worker will follow the crucified one, and many want his blessings without himself. In chapter 6 a crowd of the same kind is fed and follows him across a lake; then he says something they find intolerable, and “after this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (6:66). That is this kind of faith meeting the first thing it did not like.

Withholding, not withdrawing. He did not entrust himself to them, but he did not send them away either. The very next thing in this Gospel is that a member of the Jerusalem establishment comes at night with a compliment about signs, and receives the longest and tenderest explanation of the new birth in the Bible. Jesus refuses to be naive about them, but he does not dismiss them.

Same words, different outcome. John uses of these people the phrase he used of the saved: “believed in his name” (1:12). The difference lies not in the words but in what the faith does when it is tested. So Scripture does not ask whether your believing began with the right feeling, but whether you are still holding on to Christ. And those to whom God has truly given faith he will keep to the end (Philippians 1:6).

How do I know my faith is not like theirs? Handle this slowly, because it unsettles the already unsettled. If you have read it and started auditing your own conversion, see that the people described here were not troubled at all; they were delighted. Nobody in that crowd lay awake wondering whether their faith would hold. Anxiety about the reality of your faith is not a symptom of their condition; it is nearly always a symptom of caring whether it is real, the one thing this crowd did not do. Look away from your faith to its object: true faith rests on Christ himself, not on the excitement of signs, and he keeps those who are his (10:28–29).

parallels.desc: I the LORD search the heart

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knows every human heart as only God does, and that is both the worst news and the best, for he went to the cross knowing it all.

No one to bear witness. This Gospel is full of witness: the Baptist, the works, the Father and the Scriptures all bear witness to Jesus (5:31–39). About himself he was content to have others testify. About human beings he needed no one to bear witness, because he already had all the evidence.

He himself knew what was in man. He knows the human heart perfectly, as only God does (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Psalm 139:1–4). He knew Nathanael (1:47–48), and he will know the Samaritan woman’s past (4:18) and Judas’ betrayal (6:64).

The chapter break in the wrong place. Verse 25 ends with the word “man”, anthrōpos, and the next sentence John wrote begins: “Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus”. He knew what was in man, and here comes one: a good, learned, searching member of the ruling council who has understood nothing, and who will be told that what he needs is not more instruction but to be born. His first words, that no one can do these signs unless God is with him, are the sign-based faith of the Passover crowd in the mouth of one of the best-qualified men in Jerusalem.

The worst news and the best. That Christ knows what is in a man is either the worst news or the best. The worst, because you can never show him an edited version of yourself, not even the one you tell yourself at three in the morning. The best, for the same reason, once you see what he did after reading it.

Full-knowledge love. The man who knew what was in man went to Jerusalem anyway, into the hands of people whose hearts he had read in full, and died for them. Love based on a favourable report would be worth nothing, because the report would be wrong. There was no report. He looked. He knew what was in Judas on the night he dipped the morsel and handed it to him, and what was in Peter when he called him a rock. He knew what was in the men who would drive the nails, and he did not revise the plan. The cross is not love in ignorance of human sin; it is love offered in full knowledge of it.

In everyday life. A short question: is there anything you are hoping God has not noticed? Name it, silently, now. Naming it told him nothing he did not know. And the very next chapter contains the words “For God so loved the world”. Be honest with him today about what he already knows, and receive what he offers.

If he knows my heart, why should I confess? Because confession is not giving him information; it is agreeing with him. When you confess, you stop hiding and start walking in the light with him (1 John 1:7–9). He already knows; what changes is you. Confession breaks the power of secrecy, humbles pride, and opens you to receive the forgiveness he has promised. It is the difference between a child whose father knows what he did and a child who comes and says so. The father’s knowledge is the same. The relationship is not.

parallels.desc: you alone know the hearts of all

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.<sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”<sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.”<sup>5</sup>His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”<sup>6</sup>Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.<sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom<sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”<sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.<sup>12</sup>After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.<sup>13</sup>The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.<sup>15</sup>And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.<sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”<sup>17</sup>His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”<sup>18</sup>So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?”<sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”<sup>20</sup>The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?”<sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.<sup>22</sup>When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.<sup>23</sup>Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing.<sup>24</sup>But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people<sup>25</sup>and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 introduced Jesus as the Word made flesh and the Lamb of God, and promised his first disciples “greater things” (1:50). Now his public work begins, with a village wedding in Galilee and the temple in Jerusalem at Passover.

The message. With Jesus the new age God promised has arrived, and it is centred on him. He is the Bridegroom who brings the overflowing wine of the kingdom in place of the water of the old washings, and he is the true temple, the place where God and sinners meet, which will be destroyed and raised in three days. Because he knows every heart, the faith he looks for is not excitement at his signs but trust in himself.

Why it was said. John wrote so that his readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ and have life in his name (20:31). They lived after Rome had burned the temple, and some had been put out of the synagogue (see the introduction). This chapter tells them they have lost nothing: the true temple is the risen Christ.

How the chapter makes its case. At Cana (vv. 1–12) the wine runs out; Mary brings the need to Jesus, who answers that his hour has not yet come; at his word servants fill six purification jars, and the water becomes the best wine of the feast. This first sign reveals his glory, and his disciples believe. In Jerusalem (vv. 13–22) he drives the traders from the temple court as the Son in his Father’s house, and when asked for a sign points to the temple of his body, destroyed and raised in three days. Finally (vv. 23–25) many believe because of his signs, but he does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in man; and the stage is set for Nicodemus.

Where it leads. Both scenes look to the cross. The hour that has “not yet come” (v. 4) is the hour of his death and glory; the zeal that will “consume” him (v. 17) carries him there; and the body they destroy he raises on the third day (vv. 19–22). The wine of Cana is a foretaste of the feast his blood would buy, and the temple of his body becomes the meeting place of God and his people for ever (Revelation 21:22).

For us. Bring Jesus your needs, small as well as great, and do whatever he tells you. Come to God through him, not through rituals, places or payments, for he has opened the way himself. And let your faith rest not on spectacle but on the one who knows everything about you and gave himself for you anyway.

keyVerse.quote: This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.
keyVerse.note: This verse names what every sign in John is for: to show Jesus’ glory and to bring people to believe in him (20:30–31). At Cana the glory of the Word made flesh (1:14) is seen in kindness to a family in trouble, and the rest of the chapter shows where that glory will shine in full: in the temple of his body, destroyed and raised.

2.reflection:
At Cana Mary simply told Jesus, “They have no wine”, and then told the servants to do whatever he said (vv. 3–5). What small needs or embarrassments do you hesitate to bring to him, and what would it look like to leave the method with him?

Jesus turned water kept for purification rites into more of the best wine than anyone could drink (vv. 6–10). What does this sign show about the difference between religious ritual and the grace Christ brings? Where do you expect God to give only “just enough”?

In the temple Jesus found reasonable arrangements that had crowded out the one place where outsiders could pray (vv. 13–16). What in our church life, or in your own habits, might make it hard for an outsider to draw near to God?

Jesus did not entrust himself to those who believed because of the signs, for he knew what was in man (vv. 23–25). Why is it both sobering and comforting that he knows your heart completely and still went to the cross for you?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one enters God’s kingdom by religion or effort: he must be born from above, and God gives that life through his Son lifted up on the cross. Nicodemus, a leading Pharisee, comes by night and is told that without birth from above no one can see the kingdom (vv. 1–3). The birth is of water and the Spirit, as Ezekiel promised, and it is as free as the wind (vv. 4–8). Israel’s teacher has missed it, but the Son of Man from heaven must be lifted up like the bronze serpent so that whoever believes may have eternal life (vv. 9–15). God gave his Son to save the world, not to condemn it, and the light now divides those who come to it from those who love the dark (vv. 16–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills: no one can produce, control or predict it, and the Spirit gives it to those whom the Father has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God’s motive is love for a world set against him; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. And the light that has come shows each person’s verdict by whether he comes to it or runs from it.

The chapter rules out religious effort as a way in, not because effort is insincere but because flesh, which here means human nature even at its best, cannot give birth to spiritual life.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Born again”, or “born from above”, is one of the fullest descriptions of salvation in the New Testament: it names the kind of change (rebirth, not reform), its source (God), and its necessity (without it the kingdom cannot be seen).

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best that human religion can produce comes to Jesus by night, sure that he is a teacher from God, and still does not know who he is. Nicodemus is no hypocrite, and that is the point: if anyone could reach the kingdom by religion, he could.

The link. John has just said that Jesus knew what was in man (2:25), and the next sentence begins: “Now there was a man of the Pharisees”. Same word, back to back. Having told us that Jesus reads the human heart, John opens one up.

A man of the Pharisees. One of the Pharisees, the movement that took God’s law with total seriousness in the details of an ordinary week: devout, learned, moral. John has not chosen a tax collector. If a man could be got into the kingdom by conviction, learning, discipline or religious office, Nicodemus is already inside.

A ruler of the Jews. A member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council of seventy-one. Jesus will call him “the teacher of Israel” (v. 10).

By night. Perhaps for fear of being seen (12:42; 19:38) with the Galilean who had just overturned the temple tables; perhaps for a quiet talk, since later Jewish writings commend study of the law at night. But John rarely mentions night without meaning more. In this Gospel people love the darkness (v. 19), and the blackest moment is marked with the words “And it was night” (13:30). Nicodemus came out of the darkness towards the light, and where he goes from there is the whole of his story.

Three appearances. Each is further out into the open. Here he comes at night with a compliment. In chapter 7, as the authorities move against Jesus, he speaks up, not bravely, but he speaks, and is answered with a sneer (7:50–52). And when most of the Twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he helps bury the body at a Roman execution site, bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, in front of anyone who cared to look. He seems to have become a believer. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon. What began in this conversation did not finish that evening, and it does not seem to have failed.

A teacher come from God. Respectful, and true as far as it goes. The “we” suggests colleagues who think this and have not come. Calling Jesus a teacher leaves Nicodemus a student, a position he can hold with dignity. But Jesus has not come as prophets and rabbis come: he descended from heaven (v. 13), the Word who was God (1:1). The teacher of Israel has come to consult a promising colleague, and has in fact come to the one every Scripture he has studied is about (5:39). He does not need a better teacher. He needs to be born.

Unless God is with him. Every clause is true. It is also precisely the position of the Passover crowd who believed because they saw the signs, and to whom Jesus did not entrust himself (2:23–24). Nicodemus is that crowd with a doctorate.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus secretly or hesitantly? It is where many begin, and Jesus did not turn Nicodemus away: he gave a frightened, half-convinced man at night his fullest teaching on the new birth. If you are exploring the faith quietly, or are a believer still afraid of what others will think, come anyway. But do not stay in the dark, for whoever is ashamed of Christ and his words, of him he will be ashamed (Luke 9:26). Ask him for courage for the next step into the light.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. Coming by night may have been for secrecy or simply for quiet conversation.

parallels.desc: Nicodemus speaks up in the council
he brings spices for Jesus’ burial

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers not the compliment but the need: no one, however religious, can even see God’s kingdom unless God gives him a new birth from above.

Truly, truly. A doubled amen, which in this Gospel only Jesus uses. The prophets said “thus says the LORD”; he says “I say to you”, on his own authority.

Unless one is born again. The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above”. Both are intended: a second birth, and a birth from God. Nicodemus hears only the first, not from stupidity but because his mind has no place for what is being said. A second natural birth would change nothing; flesh would still produce flesh (v. 6).

What does born again mean? That the Holy Spirit gives a spiritually dead person new life: a new heart that loves God and is able to repent and believe (Ezekiel 36:26; Ephesians 2:4–5). Theologians call it regeneration. It is not turning over a new leaf, an emotional experience, or joining a particular kind of church, but something God does in a person, as hidden as conception and as real as birth, and its effects show in a changed life: faith in Christ, love for God and his people, hatred of sin (1 John 5:1; 3:14). Every true Christian is born again; there is no other kind.

He cannot see. Here the verb is “see”; in verse 5 it is “enter”. The kingdom is not a locked room he stands outside, rattling the handle, but a country he cannot even see, which is why argument alone never brings anyone in: he must first be given sight. The kingdom of God, the headline of Jesus’ preaching in Matthew, Mark and Luke, appears in John only here and in verse 5: once, in a night conversation with one man, to tell him that he cannot get in as he is.

The wrong category. Nicodemus has spent his life on a project of improvement, and by any available measure it has succeeded. He is not told that he did it badly or must try harder, but that it was the wrong category of thing altogether. You cannot educate your way into a family: a man may study a language for forty years and still not be French. Grace does not improve what we are by nature; it makes us new. It does not help a heart that is already willing; it gives a new heart.

The King across the room. Nicodemus cannot see the kingdom, and its King is a few feet away, speaking to him. The birth from above is not another way in beside Christ, but God opening blind eyes to see the King and receive him (1:12–13). The God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness”, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Seeing the kingdom is not a vision of a place but the sight of a face. No one climbed into his family; we were born into it from above, while we were still blind.

In everyday life. Ask what would have to change for God to be more pleased with you than he is today. If the honest answer is a list (pray more, lose the temper less, sort out the thing nobody knows about), this verse is aimed at exactly that instinct. Every item may be worth doing; not one of them is a birth. Bring the list to God, and ask him first for what only he can give.

Can anyone really start again? We have never had more ways to try: a new city, a new career, a new body, a new name. The philosopher Charles Taylor has called ours an age of authenticity, in which each of us is expected to fashion a way of being human that is our own. Nicodemus’ project was the older, religious version, but both rest on the conviction that I can be my own author, and Jesus offends both: the moralist’s record does not get him in, and nor does the free spirit’s self-creation. That is why it is good news. A self I have made has to be kept up and defended, and anyone who has lived on a reputation knows how tiring that is. A life given from above is not on loan against my performance, and the Father who gives it does not take it back after a bad year.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above.” Nicodemus hears one sense; Jesus means both.

parallels.desc: born of God
born again to a living hope

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can give birth to himself: the new birth is the cleansing and the new heart God promised through Ezekiel, and it is his work, not ours.

How can a man be born when he is old? Nicodemus takes it literally, or perhaps means: how can someone my age, after a whole life of religious habit, change completely? It is not a silly question but an honest man, baffled, facing something only God can do. And his own picture answers it: a person cannot cause his own birth. That is the point.

Water and the Spirit. Together they recall God’s promise through Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:25–27): water, cleansing from sin; Spirit, new life; one birth with two aspects. Israel was in exile, the temple rubble, the name of God dragged through the mud of the nations by the very people who carried it, and into that God said: “I will sprinkle clean water on you.” “I will give you a new heart.” “I will remove the heart of stone.” “I will put my Spirit within you.” God does every verb, and there is not one instruction in the passage: not what a beaten people must do about their condition, but what he will do about it, when they have nothing to bring. What Jesus presses on Nicodemus is not a rite he has missed but this work of God, promised six hundred years earlier to people who had proved beyond argument that they could not fix themselves. The teacher of Israel should have known it (v. 10), and he is one of the people it was made about.

The promise in person. The one telling him is the man on whom the Baptist saw the Spirit come down and remain, he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). The God who promised to put his Spirit within his people has come in person to keep his word.

Then what is baptism for? Baptism is the sign Christ commanded for those who have been born again and believe (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38, 41). It pictures what the Spirit has done, washing from sin, burial with Christ and rising to new life (Romans 6:3–4); it is the believer’s public confession of faith and the church’s welcome into its fellowship. So it matters greatly, but it is not a switch that produces new life: this Gospel says again and again that believing gives life (1:12; 3:15; 20:31). This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.1–2), that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, because in the New Testament it follows hearing and believing (Acts 2:41; 8:12). It honours paedobaptist brothers and sisters, who baptise the infants of believers as the covenant sign that replaced circumcision, and who agree that baptism does not of itself regenerate.

Where Christians differ: “born of water”. Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican teaching take the water to be baptism, and teach that baptism is the means of regeneration (baptismal regeneration). Others take water to mean physical birth, the water of the womb; others take it as John’s baptism of repentance. This commentary’s view: the best reading, in context, is Ezekiel 36: water and Spirit describe one spiritual birth, the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit. Nicodemus could not have understood a reference to Christian baptism, not yet instituted, and Jesus expected him to understand (v. 10). Baptism is the sign of this new birth, not its cause. The thief on the cross entered paradise without baptism (Luke 23:43).
verseByVerse.note: Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart.

parallels.desc: I will sprinkle clean water on you and put my Spirit within you
the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Human nature can only reproduce itself; spiritual life comes from the Spirit alone. Religion, morality and effort, however good, are still flesh.

Flesh is flesh. Human nature, mortal and fallen, working with its own resources. Like produces like: an apple tree does not, with any encouragement, produce a pear.

Spirit is spirit. New birth is not the improvement of the old nature but the creation of a new one (2 Corinthians 5:17), and we do not cooperate in our own birth: the initiative and the power belong to the Spirit. A Christian remains an ordinary human being, but there is now in him a life that comes from God and is alive to God: he can pray as a child to a Father, love what God loves and grieve over what grieves him, because the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16).

Spirit and life in his words. Jesus will tie it to himself: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all”, and his words are spirit and life (6:63). The Spirit brings the dead to life through the words of Christ, as Christ once called into a tomb and a dead man came out (11:43–44).

What it does not mean. Not an insult aimed at the body. This Gospel has just said “the Word became flesh” (1:14) as the highest news in the world. “Flesh” means everything a person is by birth, including the best of it: the intelligence, the moral seriousness, the religious instinct, the genuine longing after God that had a member of the Sanhedrin walking through Jerusalem after dark. All of that is real, none of it is spirit, and no quantity of it turns into spirit. If it could, the right advice to Nicodemus would be to produce more of it, and a great deal of religion gives exactly that advice.

For the one who has tried and failed. There is a hard comfort here. The effort did not fail because there was too little of it; effort was never the way spiritual life comes. Stop trying to manufacture it, and ask the Spirit to give it.

For the one raised in a Christian home. Spiritual life cannot be inherited or picked up from the family, the church, years under good teaching, or a Christian vocabulary used fluently. Flesh gives birth to flesh in a minister’s house as reliably as anywhere else. But if that worries you, take heart: a real love for Christ, however small, a grief over sin, a wish to be his, is not something flesh produces. It is a sign that the gift has come.

Does this mean nothing good can come from an unbeliever? Not in the ordinary sense. Unbelievers can be honest, generous, brave and kind, and we should thank God for this common grace (Matthew 5:45). But none of it can make a person right with God or produce love for him. The flesh can build hospitals and write symphonies; it cannot give birth to a child of God. That is why the gospel is not advice for decent people to try harder, but news for dead people that God gives life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone must be born again, and the new birth is the free, sovereign work of the Spirit: unseen like the wind, and known by what it does.

You must be born again. The “you” is plural: through Nicodemus Jesus addresses everyone who has assumed that being properly brought up, taught and serious would be enough. And “must”: no exceptions.

The wind blows. The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit”, as Hebrew ruach does, so this is more than an illustration: no one controls, commands or predicts the wind, or the Spirit. He is the wind that hovered over the first creation and breathed into the dry bones of Ezekiel’s valley, and he has never asked anyone’s permission to bring the dead to life.

You hear its sound. Wind is not vague. It takes roofs off and puts ships on rocks. What it is not is manageable: you never see it, only what it does. Nicodemus wants a method; Jesus points him to the wind, because there is none.

So it is. The new birth comes where the Spirit wills (1:13), and its effects are seen in a changed life. On this Reformed theology builds its teaching that God’s call is effectual: when God calls a person by his Spirit through the gospel, the call does not merely invite; it brings him, giving the very life that answers (6:44; Romans 8:30). No one is dragged in against his will: the Spirit so renews the will that the person comes freely and gladly, wanting Christ for the first time.

The breath of the risen Lord. On the evening of the resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (20:22). The wind that brings the new birth comes from the one who died and rose, and its first work is always to turn a dead heart towards him (16:14).

In everyday life. Pray today, by name, for someone you love who is not yet born again. You cannot make the wind blow, but you can ask the one who sends it.

So is there nothing I can do? There is no technique that produces the new birth, but that does not leave you idle. Sailors cannot make the wind blow, but they can put up a sail, and it makes all the difference whether they have. Reading Scripture, hearing it preached, praying, keeping company with God’s people: none of these produces the wind, but all are sails, the means through which God ordinarily gives new life (Romans 10:17; 1 Peter 1:23). Nor does it mean no one can know whether he has been born again; John wrote a whole letter to settle that question (1 John 5:13). If you want God, ask him; the wanting is itself the breeze.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit.”

parallels.desc: you do not know the way the spirit comes
come from the four winds, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s leading teacher cannot grasp the new birth, though his own Scriptures promised it, because he has never seen that his own heart is the problem.

How can these things be? Nicodemus’ last words in this conversation, and then he fades from view. His second “how” goes deeper than his first: not mocking disbelief but genuine confusion.

Are you the teacher of Israel. The word “the” is the sting: not “a teacher” but “the teacher”, the man other teachers consulted.

And yet you do not understand these things? The Old Testament had promised the new birth: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27; 11:19), the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), the new covenant written on hearts, so that all would know the LORD (Jeremiah 31:33–34), and the valley of dry bones brought to life by the Spirit (Ezekiel 37). All say the same thing: Israel’s problem is not information, and the solution will not be effort; God himself will have to act. A man who had spent a lifetime in those texts had every piece of the puzzle on the table in front of him.

Why he missed it. He knows the verses but has never applied them to himself, because the promise of a new heart is good news only to a man who has concluded that his own heart is the problem, and Nicodemus has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary.

The tone of the rebuke. Jesus asks a question and goes on talking, giving this bewildered official more teaching on the new birth than anyone else in the Gospels receives. The rebuke is real, and it is not a rejection. It is what it looks like when the light shines on someone it intends to keep.

How the new heart comes. Nicodemus asks how, and within a few sentences Jesus answers with the cross (vv. 14–15). The new covenant he knew from the prophets would be made in blood, and Jesus is its mediator (Hebrews 9:15). The “how” of the new birth is not a technique. It is a Person, lifted up for sinners.

I know my Bible well but feel nothing. What should I do? This is a real condition, and it deserves to be named rather than scolded. A person can hold correct positions on every disputed doctrine, spot a bad sermon inside two minutes, and have no living love for God behind any of it. Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to read less, but the skill that handles Scripture well can also hold it at arm’s length, as a subject rather than God calling you. So read it differently: slowly, prayerfully, asking what it says to you, and confessing what it shows you. Ask the Spirit to give you a heart that is moved (Psalm 119:18). And look to Christ, not to your feelings; warmth follows sight of him.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel”: a recognised authority who should have known the prophets’ promises.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks as an eyewitness of heaven, and unbelief is not a failure to understand his testimony but a refusal to receive it.

You do not receive. The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus now addresses the whole group Nicodemus represents. Not “cannot understand” but “do not receive”. Testimony is not something you solve. You either take it from the witness or refuse it, and refusing it is a decision about a person.

Earthly things. Not trivial things, but things that happen down here: a birth, a wind over a field, the Spirit at work in a man in Jerusalem.

Heavenly things. Truths about heaven itself, which only one from heaven could reveal (v. 13): a descent from heaven, a lifting up, a Son given, the love of God for the world. If they will not accept what God does on earth, where its effects can be seen, they will not accept what he says about heaven.

Should I settle the hard questions before I trust Christ? Not necessarily, and Jesus’ order here is wise. People often want to begin with the furthest questions: predestination and free will, those who never heard, the timetable of the last days, why there is suffering. They are real questions, and Scripture says much about them. But Jesus will not take a man to the mysteries of heaven who has not yet dealt with the mystery standing in the room: that he needs to be born and cannot arrange it. Settle the plain things first, your need and Christ’s sufficiency for it. Many hard questions look different from inside the family.

Uncertain wording. “We speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen”: the plural is not explained. It may include his disciples or the Baptist, or be Jesus speaking with the authority of heaven; some hear an answer to Nicodemus’ own “we know” (v. 2). What is certain is that this is eyewitness testimony, resting on what Jesus himself has seen (vv. 13, 32).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is addressing Nicodemus’s whole circle.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the Son of Man, who came down from heaven, can reveal heaven, and he must be lifted up on the cross, as the bronze serpent was, so that the dying may look and live.

No one has ascended. No human being has gone up to heaven to bring back knowledge of God (Deuteronomy 30:12; Proverbs 30:4). Jesus can speak of heavenly things because he has come from heaven (v. 31).

But were not Enoch and Elijah taken up to heaven? They were taken (Enoch, Genesis 5:24; Elijah, 2 Kings 2:11), but they did not go up and come back to tell what they had seen. In the setting of verses 11–12, Jesus’ point is that no one has ascended to bring down knowledge of heavenly things.

As Moses lifted up the serpent. Numbers 21:4–9. Near the end of forty years Israel complained about the food, the route, God and Moses in one breath. God sent poisonous snakes, and when the people repented and cried out, he did not remove the snakes. He had Moses set a bronze serpent on a pole where the whole camp could see it, and anyone bitten who looked at it lived.

A strange remedy. An image, made at the command of the God who had forbidden images for worship, of the very thing that was killing them, and it required the dying man to do nothing at all: no offering, no journey. A man face down in the sand with poison in him has one thing left that he can do, and it is to turn his head.

The serpent’s afterlife. Israel kept it, and centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it and broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). Even the instrument of God’s mercy will be turned into an idol if it is kept long enough. The look was never meant to stop at the bronze, but to reach the God who gave it.

So must the Son of Man. “Must” (dei): it has to happen, because God has planned it, and given what sin is, there was no other way. The cross is not a tragedy that overtook a good plan; it is the plan, and it was the plan before there was a wilderness or a serpent (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:19–20).

Lifted up. Used of the cross three times in John (here, 8:28 and 12:32–34), with a double meaning: raised off the ground, and exalted (hypsōthēnai). John explains it himself: “He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die” (12:33). The cross is his glory and his throne. He is never more visibly the King than when he is nailed up under a placard announcing it.

What hung on the pole. As the serpent, a symbol of the curse, was lifted up, so Jesus, made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), was lifted up on the cross. The sentence God’s law pronounces on lawbreakers fell on him, so that it would not fall on those who trust him (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:10–13). What hung on that Roman cross was our sin: not his own, for he had none, but all of it, laid on one body, in daylight, where the whole camp could see (2 Corinthians 5:21). He became, in our place, the curse that was killing us, so that looking at him would be the end of it.

What does it mean to look to Christ? To look is to trust: to turn away from every other hope and rest your whole weight on Christ crucified for you. It is not a feeling you must work up or a degree of understanding you must reach; the dying Israelite did not need to understand bronze, only to believe God’s word and turn his eyes. If you feel that your sin is killing you, you are not being melodramatic; it is what the passage says is happening. The instruction is not to fight the snake, or explain how you were bitten, or show improvement first, but to look: God deliberately made the remedy the one thing a dying man can still manage. Look when you first come to him, and keep looking: when guilt accuses, when temptation bites, when death comes near. “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven” after “the Son of Man”. The KJV and NKJV include the phrase; many of the earliest manuscripts lack it, so most modern Bibles put it in a footnote. If those words are original, they point to the Son’s unbroken communion with the Father even while on earth (1:18).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven.” In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: the bronze serpent on a pole
he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever looks to the lifted-up Son in faith receives eternal life: a life that begins now and can never be lost.

Whoever believes in him. “Whoever” means anyone: not whoever understands, for Nicodemus is proof that understanding is not the entrance, and not whoever qualifies. The dying Israelite did not have to comprehend the bronze; he had to trust that the God who told him to look meant it.

May have eternal life. The first appearance of the phrase that will become the Gospel’s whole purpose, and it arrives attached to a snake on a pole. Eternal life (zōē aiōnios) is the unending life of the age to come. But “life” matters more: zōē, the life that was in the Word from the beginning (1:4), his kind of life, shared with us: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (17:3). Given to dying sinners who looked, it cannot be lost, outlived or buried.

It begins now. “May have” is present: not will receive at death, not will be awarded at the judgment. This Gospel keeps saying it until there is no way to miss it: “whoever believes has eternal life” (6:47); whoever believes “has passed from death to life” (5:24). Passed. Already. For anyone in Christ, death is not the doorway into eternal life but an interruption in the middle of it.

Does eternal life mean I will float in the clouds for ever? No. Scripture pictures the age to come not as a ghostly existence but as resurrection life in a renewed creation: new heavens and a new earth, where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1–4). Believers who die go at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and they will be raised bodily when he returns (5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44). At the centre is not a place but a person: we will see him and know him and enjoy him for ever. That knowing begins today.

Uncertain wording. Where do Jesus’ words end? The ESV notes that some interpreters end them at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, so red-letter Bibles differ. Some reasons suggest John is now reflecting: the tense shifts to the past, God’s giving of his Son is spoken of as completed, and “only Son” is a phrase John uses in his own voice (1:14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Others reply that nothing signals a change of speaker. Nothing hangs on it: whether Jesus said it or the apostle who leaned on his chest wrote it, it is Scripture. The words are not more true in red ink.
