Textual note. The KJV adds “should not perish” here, borrowed from verse 16; the earliest manuscripts do not have it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God loved a world in rebellion against him, and showed it by giving his only Son, so that whoever believes in him is rescued from perishing and given eternal life. The Son came not to condemn the world but to save it.

The best-known verse in the Bible. Martin Luther is often credited with calling John 3:16 the gospel in miniature. Its danger is familiarity: a verse can be worn like a coin, still legal tender, with the face rubbed off. Take the words slowly.

For God so loved the world. The ESV notes that this can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world.” “So” (houtōs) means “in this way” more than “so much”. The verse does not merely tell us how great the love is; it points to the gift and says, that is how.

The world. The word we have quietly made sentimental. In John the world is humanity in rebellion against God: the world that did not know him (1:10), that cannot receive the Spirit (14:17), that hates Christ and his people (7:7; 15:18–19). The verse does not say God cared about a rather nice planet, but that he set his love on the very thing that was set against him. The wonder is not that the world is big, but that it is bad. Nothing in us was the reason for that love, and it has never needed anything in us to keep it going.

That he gave his only Son. “Gave”: in the incarnation, and supremely on the cross. To give a thing is to part with it, and the weight of the verse rests on the fact that the Giver did not keep what he gave. “His only Son”: unique, beloved, not created (1:14, 18; see the box below), eternally the Father’s delight before there was a world, and put into the hands of a race that did not know him or receive him. Abraham was told to take “your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love” (Genesis 22:2), and at the last moment his hand was stopped and a ram was provided. On Golgotha no hand stopped the Father’s. He did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32), because this time the Son was the Lamb.

Should not perish. “Perish” (apolētai) means be destroyed, be lost for ever, and it is stated without softening. This is not a verse about improving lives but a rescue verse, and rescue implies something to be rescued from.

Not to condemn. The purpose of his first coming was salvation, not judgment (12:47), and salvation through him alone (14:6; Acts 4:12). It is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgment exists, as the next sentence proves. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anybody; that the drowning is real is why it was launched.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. The Father gave the Son, and the Son gave himself. Paul, who had once hated his name, wrote it in the first person: “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). The love of John 3:16 is wide enough for the world and personal enough to have a single name on it.

In everyday life. Say the verse about yourself, out loud, with your own name where the world stands. It was written not to be agreed with as a general truth but to be believed by somebody. Then think of one person who needs to hear it, and pray for a chance to tell them.

Does perish mean simply ceasing to exist? No. Some have taught that the lost are finally annihilated, but Scripture speaks of the wicked going away into eternal punishment as the righteous go into eternal life, with the same word for both (Matthew 25:46), and of a destruction that is everlasting and conscious, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Revelation 14:11). To perish is to be lost: cut off from God, under his wrath for ever (v. 36). It is told here not to frighten us for its own sake but to show the size of the rescue.

Is it not cruel for a father to send his son to die? Only if the Son were an unwilling third party. Father and Son are one God, and the Son lays down his life of his own accord (10:18), while the Father gives what he loves most. The cross is not God making someone else pay so that he need not. It is God himself, in the person of his Son, bearing the judgment his own holiness requires, because he would rather suffer than lose us.

Can I tell anyone that God loves them? Yes, with care. God’s goodness and kindness extend to every person he has made (Psalm 145:9; Matthew 5:44–45), and his offer in the gospel is sincere to all: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but would rather they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). So you may say to anyone: God gave his Son; believe in him and you will not perish; come to him, and he will not turn you away (6:37). But do not tell anyone that God loves them in a way that makes no claim on them, or that they are safe without Christ. The love of John 3:16 calls rebels to believe.

Where Christians differ: God’s love and the extent of the atonement. Some take this verse to prove that Christ died equally for every individual, making salvation possible for all: this is the Arminian view, which holds that God’s choosing rests on faith he foresees, and many faithful Christians hold it or something near it. This commentary’s view: the verse teaches God’s love for a rebellious world, the gift of his Son, and the promise of life to everyone who believes. It is the foundation of the free offer of the gospel to all people: anyone who believes will be saved. It does not say Christ died in the same way for every individual. Elsewhere John shows that Christ lays down his life for his sheep (10:11, 15), and that those who believe are those the Father gives him (6:37, 44). Both truths stand: the gospel is offered to all, and those who believe are saved by a Saviour whose death secured their salvation. Reformed theology calls this definite (or particular) atonement: Christ died to save, and surely saves, those the Father gave him. Believers who read these verses differently are brothers to be heard, and all agree that whoever believes will not perish.

Uncertain wording. “Only Son” translates monogenēs. The KJV’s “only begotten” takes it from roots meaning “only” and “born”; most scholars now take it to mean unique, the only one of his kind. The word is used of Isaac (Hebrews 11:17), who was not Abraham’s only child but his unique son of promise. Both renderings confess a Son who is uniquely and eternally the Father’s.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world”; the stress is on the manner of his love.

parallels.desc: your son, your only son

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in Christ is free from condemnation, but whoever refuses him stays under the condemnation that already rests on him, because people love the darkness more than the light.

Not condemned. No condemnation, now or ever (5:24; Romans 8:1): the verdict is settled. The Light did not come to condemn a world that loved the dark, but to bear its condemnation.

Condemned already. The word that frightens people is “already”, and it is more merciful than it sounds. Unbelief is not their only sin; they are already condemned for their sin, and by refusing Christ they refuse the only rescue and remain where they are (v. 36). No sentence is passed the moment someone hears of Christ and declines; it was passed long before. Christ walked into a situation that was already lost, and nobody was standing in neutral territory waiting to see how they felt about him. So the gospel is not an examination a person might fail, which would make Christ’s coming add a danger, but a rescue a person might refuse. That is why not believing in the name of the only Son of God is the final sin: it refuses the only cure.

This is the judgment. “Judgment” (krisis) is the verdict, the dividing line: not a throne or a book opened, but a person arriving. The light is Jesus (1:9), and the judgment is what people do when he comes.

Loved the darkness. Jesus traces the deepest root of the world’s unbelief not to a lack of evidence but to what people love. The verb matters: not tolerated the darkness, not drifted into it, but loved it. So the judgment is already showing now, and God’s verdict at the end will make public what each person had already chosen to love; that is why the last day can be perfectly just, and no one will be surprised by it. This is not a verdict on every honest questioner; Nicodemus came with questions and Jesus welcomed him. It names the root of the world’s refusal, and each of us can recognise it in himself.

Because their works were evil. This puts the problem exactly where Nicodemus has been told it is. If unbelief were an information problem, teaching could solve it, and he of all people would be safe. It is a problem of what we love, and love cannot be argued into a person; a new heart has to be born.

How strong must my faith be? Some read “condemned already” and at once start checking whether they have believed hard enough, or sincerely enough, to cross the line. Read it again. The condemnation attaches to one thing only: not believing in the name of the only Son of God. The verse is not measuring the quality of anyone’s faith but distinguishing those who have come to him from those who have not. A weak hand on a strong rope is not the same as no hand at all, and this verse is about which rope, not the strength of the grip. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves.

What of those who have never heard of Christ? This verse describes everyone apart from him: no one is saved another way (14:6; Acts 4:12). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). That is why Paul asks how they are to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14): the answer is not speculation but mission. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), including with infants who die before they can hear: the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3), and many Reformed pastors, Spurgeon among them, have believed that every child who dies in infancy is among the elect. Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief with that Judge, whose tenderness to children Jesus showed when he took them in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who cling to their sin keep away from Christ’s light for fear of being exposed, but those who are true come to it, and the light shows that what is good in them is God’s work.

Hates the light. “Exposed” (elenchthē) means convicted, shown for what one is. The instinct needs no teaching: a child who has broken something goes quiet and moves towards the door. The edited self we give at dinner parties, the friendships kept carefully shallow: it is the same reflex, grown up. Stay where the lighting is kind.

Avoidance feels like busyness. Avoiding the light rarely feels like avoiding it. It feels like having no time to pray, finding a book of the Bible dull, preferring to read about the faith than sit still before God. The man in this verse is not shaking his fist; he simply does not come. Not every dry season is avoidance, though: tiredness, grief and depression can make prayer heavy for people who love the light dearly. The mark of this verse is unwillingness, not difficulty, and anyone grieved by his own coldness is already turned towards the lamp.

Whoever does what is true. Literally “whoever does the truth”. In Scripture truth is something a person can do: integrity, really being what you appear to be. So the two groups are not the clever and the stupid, or the religious and the irreligious, but those who will come out into the open and those who will not.

Carried out in God. His works were done by God’s grace and in union with him, and the light shows it. Perhaps there is a word here for Nicodemus, who had come by night: come into the light.

Exposed and not ashamed. The next chapter shows what coming to this light looks like. A Samaritan woman with five husbands behind her is told the whole of it, and runs into her town saying, “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did” (4:29). The light is not a searchlight hunting criminals but the face of the Saviour, who exposes in order to heal.

He was exposed for us. At the cross the soldiers divided his garments (19:23–24), and the Light of the world hung stripped in the open, bearing the shame our hiding had earned. He clothes with his own righteousness those who come out of the dark (Isaiah 61:10). The Lord was uncovered in the light so that we could stand in it clothed.

What it does not mean. Not that good people come to Christ and bad people avoid him, which would undo the whole chapter. “His works have been carried out in God”: whatever is found in the light was put there by the one holding the lamp. Even then it is never flawless; it is accepted because the Son obeyed perfectly in his people’s place, and his obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19). This is not salvation by works. It shows which way real faith moves: towards the light.

How do I come into the light in practice? By refusing to hide from God or from his people. Confess to God, naming what you have done rather than speaking vaguely (1 John 1:9). Read Scripture in a way that lets it search you, not only inform you (Hebrews 4:12). Where a sin has a grip on you, tell a mature, trusted Christian, and let them pray with you and ask you about it (James 5:16). Put right what can be put right. None of this earns forgiveness; Christ has done that. It is simply what it looks like to live as a forgiven person who no longer needs the dark.

parallels.desc: expose the works of darkness

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ must increase, because he comes from heaven and holds all things in his hand. Jesus’ disciples baptise in Judea while John, not yet in prison, baptises at Aenon (vv. 22–24). When John’s disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus, John answers that no one receives anything unless heaven gives it; he is only the bridegroom’s friend, his joy is complete when he hears the bridegroom’s voice, and Jesus must increase while he decreases (vv. 25–30). The closing verses give the reason: the one from above speaks the words of God, has the Spirit without measure and has received all things from the Father, so whoever believes in the Son has eternal life, and on whoever refuses him the wrath of God remains (vv. 31–36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Baptist’s last words in this Gospel (if the closing verses are his) sum up its theology: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God’s wrath. There is no middle ground. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

The wrath remains: it does not arrive but stays where it already was, and what remains can be lifted (see the note on v. 36).
verseByVerse.examples:
“He must increase, but I must decrease” is the mark of all genuine ministry: a minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ’s has misunderstood the calling.

The words were not sentimental, and this is the passage for anyone being replaced (see the note on v. 30).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a time Jesus’ disciples and John the Baptist baptise side by side in Judea: two ministries, and no rivalry between the men who lead them.

Into the Judean countryside. An early Judean ministry, recorded only in John. Jesus leaves the centre, where a member of the Sanhedrin sought him out, for the fields, where the water is.

Baptizing. Jesus himself did not baptise, but his disciples did (4:2). They handled the water, the sign; the Lord kept for himself the giving of what it signifies, the new birth by the Spirit (1:33).

Water was plentiful. First a practical remark: crowds need water. It may also suggest immersion, though it is not conclusive.

Two ministries, no rivalry. Neither man treats the other as competition. The only people in this passage worried about the arrangement are the followers, which is how it usually goes.

How should I think about other churches in my town? As fellow workers, where they preach the same gospel. Christ has one church in many congregations, and the success of a faithful church down the road is a gain for the kingdom, not a loss for yours. Pray for them by name, speak well of them, and rejoice when people are converted there. Where the gospel itself is denied, love must speak plainly. But most of our rivalries are not about the gospel at all. They are about numbers, style and pride, and those are not worth one moment of the Spirit’s grief.

Uncertain wording. Where Aenon (“springs”) near Salim lay is uncertain: perhaps in the Jordan valley, or in Samaria. Its name at least fits John’s remark that water was plentiful there.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
John notes that the Baptist was still free: this Judean ministry came before the Galilean ministry the other Gospels describe, and a shadow already falls across the Baptist’s next words.

Not yet put in prison. The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest (Mark 1:14). John explains that this Judean ministry came earlier, overlapping with the Baptist’s. The aside reads like the remark of someone who knows the order of events, which fits this Gospel’s claim to rest on an eyewitness (21:24).

A shadow across the parenthesis. The reader is told in passing how this ends. The man about to say “He must increase, but I must decrease” is a few months from a cell and not long from an executioner. He spoke those words not from a settled retirement but on a downward slope.

Forerunner to the end. John went before Jesus in birth, preaching and baptising, and in suffering too: Elijah had already come, Jesus said, and they did to him whatever they pleased, and so also the Son of Man would suffer (Matthew 17:12–13). The King who followed would go further into the dark than John ever went: under the wrath of God for sinners.

Do the Gospels contradict each other on the order of events? No; they complement one another. Each writer selected and arranged true events for his purpose, and John, probably writing last, often fills in what the others pass over, and here even shows where his account joins theirs. Apparent differences in order usually arise because one writer groups events by theme while another follows the calendar. Not every question of order has a certain answer, and believers can say so honestly while trusting the accounts. Read together, the four give a fuller picture of one Lord, from four angles, resting on eyewitness testimony.
verseByVerse.note: The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest; John fills in an earlier period.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A quarrel about washing turns into jealousy, as John’s disciples complain that the one their master pointed to is now drawing everyone away.

A discussion arose … over purification. Perhaps about John’s baptism compared with Jesus’, or with Jewish washings; John does not say. This Gospel has kept returning to cleansing since the six stone jars at Cana (2:6), and the New Testament’s great statement about humility began as a dispute about whose water counted. The answer is not a better rite but a person, the Son who would himself make purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3).

He who was with you. They do not name Jesus. Every word is the language of a threatened camp: “he who was with you” treats him as a junior member of John’s movement, and “to whom you bore witness” implies that he owes his success to John’s recommendation.

All are going to him. “All” is not true, since John is still baptising crowds; it is what anxiety says, the arithmetic of a man watching numbers move the wrong way. And “look”, the smallest word in the sentence, gives it away: they are pointing, the way you do when someone is not nearly as alarmed as you think he should be.

Loyal and wrong. The saddest thing is that they are being loyal, out of real affection. That is how the ugliest instincts in church life often come dressed: as concern, about standards, about a church down the road that seems to be doing rather well. John is not comparing at all, because he settled who Jesus is at the Jordan. While his disciples counted heads, John looked at the Lamb, and there was nothing left to count. Christ is the end of all our comparisons.

How do I deal with jealousy of other Christians? Name it honestly as sin, not as concern, and confess it to God. Then fight it with truth: their gifts and fruit were given from heaven (v. 27), so envying them is a complaint against God; and you are one body, so their gain is yours (1 Corinthians 12:26). Thank God for them specifically, out loud, and pray for their further blessing; envy rarely survives sincere intercession. And look again at Christ, because jealousy grows where we have stopped being satisfied in him.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything anyone has, from a ministry to its success to the faith that receives Christ, is a gift from heaven, so there is no room for envy or for pride.

Not even one thing. John’s ministry, Jesus’ ministry, every gift, every success. The sentence is absolute, and the temptation is to hear it as modesty and move on. Not most things. Not the important things. Not one (1 Corinthians 4:7).

It cuts both ways. If Jesus is drawing the crowds, heaven gave him them, so envying him is a complaint against God. If John’s numbers are falling, heaven arranged that too, and he can accept it as God’s assignment. And if John ever had a crowd, that was given as well, so it was never his to lose. Envy always needs a sense of ownership: this was mine, or it ought to have been. Take away the ownership and there is nothing for envy to attach to; a man cannot be robbed of what he was only ever handed. The same truth cuts against taking credit: the intelligence, the temperament, even the capacity to work hard, were all given.

The Gift from heaven. The greatest thing ever received from heaven was a few miles away: God gave his only Son, the true bread from heaven (6:32). Even the Son, as the one sent, lives as one who receives from the Father (5:26; v. 35). And the Father who gave the Son gives also the empty hands that take him: “No one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father” (6:65). We have nothing we did not receive, and so nothing to boast of except the Giver.

If everything is given, does my effort not matter? It matters greatly, and it too is given. Paul says he worked harder than any of the apostles, and in the same breath, “though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). God gives gifts so that we will use them diligently, and he holds us accountable for what we do with them (Matthew 25:14–30). The point is not passivity but humble contentment: working hard with what we have been given, without pride when it prospers or envy when others prosper more.

parallels.desc: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is glad to be only the friend of the bridegroom, because Jesus is the Bridegroom, the LORD come to claim his bride, and John’s joy is to see her given to him.

I am not the Christ. John has said it since chapter 1 (1:20, 23), and it has never once sounded like a disappointment. He can watch the crowd leave without panic because he never mistook himself for the reason they came.

The bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20); in the New, Jesus is the bridegroom and his people are the bride (Mark 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7; 21:2). John is quietly giving Jesus the role that belongs to the LORD himself. The LORD who betrothed Israel to himself in faithfulness has come in flesh to claim his bride from every nation at the cost of his own blood.

The friend of the bridegroom. Like a best man, he often helped arrange the wedding and brought the bride to the groom. His joy was to see the marriage happen, not to take the bride for himself, and the moment the bridegroom’s voice was heard, his work was over.

Rejoices greatly. “He rejoices with joy”: the Greek doubles it. This is not resignation in disguise but the gladness of a man whose work has succeeded, and for him success means no longer being needed. And “complete” speaks, in the Greek tense, of joy brought to fullness and staying full, said at the very moment the crowds are moving to Jesus. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life.

In everyday life. If you teach, lead, parent or befriend people in the faith, ask whose voice they are learning to love, yours or the bridegroom’s. Your task is to bring them to him and step back. When someone you have helped grows close to Christ in a way that no longer needs you, let it complete your joy rather than diminish it.

What does it mean that the church is Christ’s bride? If Jesus is the bridegroom, there is a bride, and the people baptised in that river, with all who would follow for two thousand years, are not the crowd at the wedding but the one being married. Christ loves his people with the faithful, exclusive, self-giving love of a husband, bound to them by covenant for ever; he gave himself up for her, to make her holy and present her to himself in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27). The church belongs to him, not to its leaders; ministers are at most the friends of the bridegroom. And our story ends with a wedding, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9). If you are in Christ, you are not merely a guest at that feast. You are part of the bride.
verseByVerse.note: The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought bride and groom together; his joy was the groom’s joy.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s rise and John’s fading belong to one plan of God, and John embraces it gladly, because what matters is that Christ is honoured.

He must increase. On most readings, the Baptist’s last recorded words in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36). “Must” (dei) is the word used of the Son of Man who must be lifted up (v. 14): the rise of one and the shrinking of the other belong to one plan of God, which John has no say over. The first clause is the one that matters, and Christ is increasing still, his glory filling more of the earth until it covers it as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14).

But I must decrease. Not reluctantly but gladly: the motto of every true servant of Christ. John is like the moon, which has no light of its own: when it fades, that is not a tragedy but the arrival of morning.

What “I must decrease” came to. He said it, and then it happened, and not gently. Herod arrested him for telling the truth about a marriage. From a cell he sent to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, or whether they should look for another (Matthew 11:2–3), not the question of a man serenely fulfilled. And he was beheaded without trial, to keep a promise made in front of dinner guests. Yet Jesus’ verdict came while he was in that cell, doubting: “among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11). The man who arranged his whole existence around becoming unnecessary seems to have wobbled at the end, and was called the greatest anyway.

In everyday life. This is the verse for anyone being replaced: by the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the children who no longer ring, the body doing less than it did. The world has no account of these except loss. Make John’s words your prayer, “Lord, may you increase, and may I decrease”, and remember that the one who must increase went lower for you than any slope can take you.

Does decreasing mean I must think nothing of myself? No. John did not despise himself; he knew exactly who he was, the voice, the friend of the bridegroom, and he did that work with courage. Decreasing is not self-hatred or false modesty but the gladness of seeing Christ honoured more than yourself, and the willingness to be forgotten if he is remembered. Nobody in Scripture is asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking; the decrease is a completed joy solely because of who is filling the space. You are asked to make room for him, and in him you will find yourself more truly than you ever could by holding on (Matthew 16:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus must increase because he alone has come from heaven: he is above every earthly teacher and speaks of what he has seen, though most will not receive it.

Above all. Here is the principle underneath everything in this chapter: where a person comes from decides the authority he speaks with, and Jesus, from heaven, is supreme over all.

He who is of the earth. John the Baptist, and every human teacher. If it is the Baptist speaking, the man Jesus would call the greatest born of women places himself among those of the earth without complaint. He is being accurate about the one distinction that matters: not between a great man and a small one, but between everyone born here and the one who came from somewhere else. The best teacher in Israel and the last of the prophets are both of the earth. Only one person in the passage came down.

What he has seen and heard. Jesus speaks from direct knowledge of heaven (v. 11), as no other teacher can. He came down from that height to tell us what he had seen, and all truth is safe in his mouth.

No one receives. A general rejection (1:11), not literally no one, as the next verse shows: not a statistic but a lament. The testimony is perfect; the evidence was never the problem.

If Jesus is above all, how should I weigh other voices? Every other voice is of the earth, however wise, and must be tested by his: teachers you admire, traditions you love, experts, your own feelings, the spirit of the age. Many say true and useful things, and we should listen humbly. But when they contradict what Christ has said in his word, he wins, every time (Galatians 1:8). That is what sola Scriptura means in practice: not that only the Bible is useful, but that only the Bible, as the word of the one from above, has the final say.

Uncertain wording. Who is speaking? Verses 31–36 may continue the Baptist’s words or be the Gospel writer’s reflection; as with Jesus’ words to Nicodemus (see the note on v. 15), the Greek has no quotation marks. John often moves from reporting a voice to adding his own without announcement, because the two say the same thing. Either way the words explain why Jesus must increase, and their authority is unaffected.

parallels.desc: you are from below, I am from above

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To believe Jesus’ testimony is to put your signature to the truth that God does not lie.

Sets his seal. Some do receive it. A seal pressed into wax by a signet ring was the ancient equivalent of a signature on a contract: this is mine, I stand behind it. Setting a seal was not an opinion but a commitment.

That God is true. Jesus speaks God’s words (v. 34), so to believe him is to affirm that God is truthful. Faith here is not first a feeling, or even a benefit received, but a signature, put to the claim that God tells the truth in advance of much of the evidence, since much of what he has said has not happened yet. And to refuse it is to call God a liar (1 John 5:10): if God has testified about his Son and a man declines the testimony, there is no third position. So unbelief is not always the humble position it can seem; it is a verdict about someone’s character. That does not make every doubter dishonest. It means the question is finally personal: whether God can be trusted.

The Son the Father sealed. On Jesus God the Father has set his seal (6:27), certifying the Son by the Spirit who came down and remained on him at the Jordan (1:32–33), by the works he gave him to do, and finally by raising him. So the believer’s seal is a countersignature beneath the Father’s own. And a seal works both ways, for believers are themselves sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). The one who signs his name to God’s truthfulness discovers that God has already signed his name to him.

What if I believe but still have doubts? Then you are like many in Scripture: the father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), the psalmists who asked how long, John the Baptist in his cell. Doubt is not the opposite of faith; unbelief is. Faith is trusting God’s word while questions remain. So bring your doubts to God honestly, take them to his word, talk to mature believers, and keep doing what faith does: praying, gathering, obeying. Your seal is not on the strength of your feelings but on the truthfulness of God, and he does not change when you waver (2 Timothy 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true.

parallels.desc: let God be true

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks the very words of God, has the Spirit without limit, and has received all things from the Father who loves him.

The words of God. Jesus’ words are God’s words (7:16; 12:49–50; 14:10): not in the partial, occasional manner of the prophets, but fully.

Without measure. Prophets received the Spirit in measure, for particular tasks. On the Son the Spirit rests in fullness, and out of that fullness the Son gives, so that what reaches the believer is not a diluted portion (see the box below).

The Father loves the Son. The eternal love within the Trinity (5:20; 17:24), before anything was made: the oldest fact in existence, and everything in this chapter flows from it. In the upper room the Son asked that this very love might be in his people: “that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them” (17:26). The oldest love there is has been opened, and there is room inside.

All things into his hand. All authority (13:3; Matthew 28:18), including salvation and judgment: the Father withholds nothing from the Son. And it is the same hand out of which no one is able to snatch his sheep (10:28–29). What has been put into that hand includes people, and nothing has ever been taken out of it.

Can I be sure I am safe in his hand? If you belong to Christ, yes: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (10:28). Your security rests not on the strength of your grip but on his. You will still stumble and doubt, but it is the Father’s will that the Son should lose nothing of all that he has been given (6:39), and the Son always does it. That is not a licence to drift. It is the ground on which a trembling believer can stand.

Uncertain wording. “He gives the Spirit without measure”: the Greek does not say who gives. It may be the Father giving the Spirit to the Son, as at the Jordan (1:32–33; Isaiah 11:2), or the Son giving the Spirit, as the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (1:33). Both are true, and in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything comes down to the Son: whoever believes in him has eternal life now, and whoever refuses him stays under the wrath of God. The chapter that began with the new birth ends with the sharpest possible alternative.

Whoever does not obey the Son. The two halves deliberately do not match. We expect “believes” and “does not believe”; John writes “believes” and “does not obey” (apeitheō, refuses to be persuaded). He is not smuggling works into salvation. Faith in Christ is obedience to God’s command (1 John 3:23), and the unbelief here is not an opinion politely held but a refusal of someone who has every right to be obeyed.

The wrath of God remains. “Wrath” (orgē) is God’s settled, holy opposition to sin, and this is its only appearance in John’s Gospel. All people are already under it because of sin (Ephesians 2:3), and it remains on those who refuse the only one who can remove it. Nothing arrives; the wrath remains, the same truth as “condemned already” (v. 18).

The abiding word. The verb is to abide (menō). It first appeared when the Spirit came down and remained on Jesus (1:32–33), and it will run to the vine: “Abide in me, and I in you” (15:4). Something abides on everyone. On Christ, the Spirit rests. On those who are his, he himself abides. And on the one who refuses him, the wrath he was born under simply stays where it was.

Not a drop is left. Christ bore God’s wrath for those who believe (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). As they came to arrest him, Jesus said to Peter, “shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (18:11). It was the cup of the wrath that remains on the unbelieving, and he drank it to the bottom, so that for those who believe in the Son not a drop is left. Between the man who came in the dark and the wrath of God stand the Son given and the Son lifted up. Worthy is the Lamb who drank the cup so that it would never be ours.

What it does not mean. This verse frightens people, and some of them are the wrong people. It is not addressed to the Christian who has bad days, or doubts, or a faith that feels thinner than he wishes. The one described here is not struggling with the Son; he is declining him. And the present tenses, “has eternal life” and “remains”, describe the two states people are in this evening. If wrath remains rather than arrives, it can be lifted rather than merely postponed, and this chapter has said how: the way the poison was lifted in the desert, not by the dying man’s exertion but by his looking at something raised up on his behalf.

How can a God of love have wrath? Because his love is holy. Wrath in God is not a mood that flares and fades but his steady, just opposition to evil, the right response of perfect goodness to what destroys his creatures and defies his glory. A God who felt nothing about cruelty, abuse and lies would not be loving but indifferent. And the cross shows the two together: God’s love provided what his justice required, when Christ bore the wrath we deserved as our substitute (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The chapter that speaks of wrath speaks of a love that gave its only Son. The love is the way out of the wrath.

parallels.desc: the wrath of God is revealed

3.title: You Must Be Born Again

Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”<sup>5</sup>Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.<sup>6</sup>That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.<sup>7</sup>Do not marvel that I said to you, ’You must be born again.’<sup>8</sup>The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. ’I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’<sup>29</sup>The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all.<sup>32</sup>He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.<sup>33</sup>Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.<sup>34</sup>For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.<sup>35</sup>The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.<sup>36</sup>Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with Jesus not entrusting himself to those who believed because of his signs, “for he himself knew what was in man” (2:25). Chapter 3 opens one such man: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, the best that Israel’s religion could produce. Then John the Baptist gives his last testimony.

The message. No one, however devout, can see God’s kingdom as he is: he must be born again, from above, by the Spirit of God. That life is not achieved but given, and God gives it through his Son, lifted up on the cross so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. Everything now turns on what each person does with the Son.

Why it was said. John’s first readers lived among people proud of their religious heritage, and some had paid a price for confessing Christ (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that ancestry, learning and religious seriousness never brought anyone into the kingdom; the new birth and faith in the Son do. Acts finds disciples of John the Baptist still in Ephesus years later (Acts 19:1–7), and the Baptist’s own words here answer anyone tempted to put him first.

How the chapter makes its case. Nicodemus comes by night with a compliment, and Jesus answers with his need: without birth from above no one sees the kingdom (vv. 1–3). That birth is of water and the Spirit, Ezekiel’s promised cleansing and new heart, as free as the wind (vv. 4–8). Only the one who came down from heaven can tell heavenly things, and he must be lifted up like the bronze serpent so that whoever believes may live (vv. 9–15). Behind it all is God’s love, giving his only Son to save, though the light divides those who come to it from those who love the dark (vv. 16–21). Then John’s disciples complain that all are going to Jesus, and John rejoices as the bridegroom’s friend (vv. 22–30), because the one from above is above all and holds all things in his hand (vv. 31–36).

Where it leads. The new birth the prophets promised comes through the Son of Man who descended from heaven and was lifted up, made a curse in our place like the serpent on the pole. God’s love is measured by the gift of his only Son, and the wrath that remains on unbelievers is the cup he drank for all who believe (18:11). The chapter ends with the Bridegroom come for his bride, and all things in his hand.

For us. Being religious, decent or well taught is not enough: you must be born again, and only God can do it. So stop trying to make yourself a new life, and look to Christ lifted up, as a dying man looked at the serpent. And if you belong to him, let him increase while you gladly decrease.

keyVerse.quote: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s gospel in one sentence. Everything Jesus has told Nicodemus about the new birth and the Son lifted up flows from it: the love of God for a world set against him, measured by the gift of his only Son and offered to whoever believes. It also stands between the rescue the chapter promises and the judgment it warns of (vv. 18, 36).

3.reflection:
Nicodemus was devout, learned and respected, yet Jesus told him he must be born again (vv. 1–7). Why is it so hard for religious, decent people to hear that they need a new birth rather than improvement? Where are you tempted to rely on your own record?

Jesus compares the new birth to the wind: no one controls it, but its effects are seen (v. 8). What does that mean for how we pray for, and speak to, friends who do not yet believe? What “sails” can we help them put up?

Jesus likened himself to the bronze serpent, which the dying had only to look at to live (vv. 14–15). What does it mean to look to Christ in everyday life, especially when guilt or temptation bites?

John the Baptist rejoiced as the crowds left him for Jesus: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (v. 30). Where do you find it hardest to decrease, in your work, ministry, family or reputation, and how does seeing Jesus as the Bridegroom change that?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes looking for worshippers and finds them where no one expected: a Samaritan woman with a broken past, and then her whole town. Resting at noon by Jacob’s well, he asks her for a drink, crossing the barriers of sex, race and religion (vv. 1–9). He offers her living water that becomes a spring of eternal life (vv. 10–15), brings her history gently into the light (vv. 16–18), answers her question about the right mountain with the news that the Father seeks worshippers in spirit and truth (vv. 19–24), and tells her plainly that he is the Messiah (vv. 25–26). She leaves her jar and brings her town, while he tells his puzzled disciples that the harvest is ready (vv. 27–38). Many believe, first through her word and then through his (vv. 39–42).
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious programme or a moral reform; it is the life that is in himself. He does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source (see the note on v. 10).

Worship in spirit and truth does not mean heartfelt worship as opposed to formal worship (see the note on v. 24). And the decisive clause is that the Father is seeking such worshippers, which is what the chapter has been showing since verse 4 (see the note on vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.examples: The five husbands need more care than they often get (see the note on v. 18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus leaves Judea because the Pharisees are now watching his growing following, and his hour has not yet come.

The Pharisees had heard. Just before, John’s disciples complained to him that “all are going to him” (3:26). Now the same report reaches the Pharisees, who had already sent men to investigate John (1:24). The news made John’s disciples jealous, though John himself refused their jealousy; it makes the Pharisees start watching Jesus.

Making and baptising more disciples than John. The news was a count of disciples, not doctrine or a healing. When religious authorities measure ministries by headcount, they are already treating the kingdom of God as one organisation competing with others. John had given the right response to the same figures: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30).

Jesus himself did not baptise. John makes 3:22 more exact: the disciples did the baptising. There is no record of Jesus baptising anyone with his own hands, so no group of Christians could ever claim a superior baptism from him; Paul was glad for the same reason to have baptised almost nobody at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:13–17).

Why did he leave? Not in fear: he had recently cleared the temple courts in front of these same authorities. A clash now would come too soon. Everything in this Gospel moves towards his hour, the time the Father has set for his death, and it has not yet come (2:4; 7:30). There is a courage that walks away from a fight it could win, at a time of its own choosing, because the fight is not the point.

Does it matter who baptises me? No. The power of baptism lies not in the minister, however gifted or famous, but in Christ, who commanded it, and in the faith of the one baptised into him. Jesus left the water to his disciples so that no one would treasure a baptism for the hand that gave it. If you were baptised as a believer by an ordinary pastor in an ordinary church, you were baptised into exactly the same name as those baptised on the Jordan. Thank God for the one who baptised you, but do not boast in him.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had to go through Samaria, not because the map required it, but because his Father had an appointment for him there.

He had to pass through Samaria. Strict Jews are often said to have gone round Samaria by the Jordan valley, though Josephus says Galilean pilgrims usually took the direct route, about three days. The road through Samaria was the quicker one, not the only one, so John’s “had to” says more than a fact about maps.

The word of divine necessity. The word (edei) is the one this Gospel uses for things settled in heaven: “You must be born again” (3:7); “so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (3:14). The necessity that put him on that road is the necessity that put him on the cross. The Father had prepared a woman, and a town, to hear him.

Who were the Samaritans? Their Jewish neighbours called them half-breeds and heretics, an enemy’s description rather than a fair one. When Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC, it deported the leading families and resettled foreigners in the land, leaving a population mixed in blood and religion (2 Kings 17:24–41). By Jesus’ day the Samaritans held to the five books of Moses alone and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. The hostility had recent history in it: late in the second century BC the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple on Gerizim, and its ruins stood on the mountain above the well.

Her name on his Son’s road. The Son did not drift into Samaria; the love that sent him into the world sent him there. Long before the woman set out on an errand she had run a thousand times, the Father had set her name on his Son’s road, so that a tired man would be sitting on the wall of the well when she arrived; and the Son walked that road gladly, though his own people avoided it. Our God does not wait behind a wall for the clean and the qualified; he must go through Samaria, because he will not leave his sheep in enemy country.

Does every detour in my life have a purpose like this? This verse does not promise that every closed door hides a well and a waiting woman, or that you will be told the reason. It does show that the God who arranges routes is not confined to the sensible ones, and that at least once in history the pointless-looking detour was the whole plan; and God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Hold your detours with open hands. You may never see the reason this side of glory, but you are not on the road by accident.
verseByVerse.note: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it by the Jordan valley; the direct route went through it.

parallels.desc: Philip preaches in Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eternal Word, through whom all things were made, sits down worn out by a well in enemy country, on ground thick with Israel’s history.

A town of Samaria called Sychar. Probably near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim, close to the modern city of Nablus.

Jacob’s field. John names Jacob twice in two verses. This is the field Jacob bought outside Shechem, one of the few pieces of the promised land a patriarch ever owned outright (Genesis 33:18–20). He willed it to Joseph (Genesis 48:22), whose bones were buried there after being carried out of Egypt and through forty years of wilderness (Joshua 24:32). Here Israel swore to serve the LORD (Joshua 24), and here the kingdom tore in half a few generations later (1 Kings 12). Hardly a square yard of Israel is more layered with promise, oath and failure, and it lies in Samaria, in enemy country.

Jacob’s well was there. One of the most certainly identified sites in the Gospels, it goes down more than a hundred feet through rock.

Wearied. The word means worn out by labour, the exhaustion of work rather than lack of sleep. He is truly human: tired here, thirsty in verse 7, and hungry, as the disciples’ errand implies (v. 8). The Gospel opened by saying that all things were made through him (1:3); now the Word made flesh (1:14) is too worn out to walk on. John sets the two facts side by side and explains neither away, and any picture of Jesus that drops one of them has stopped listening to John. The one who made the stars sat down because his legs ached, and the tired man on the well is the Lord who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who upholds the universe by the word of his power.

Beside the well. Literally “on the well”, on the low stone wall around its mouth, with nothing to draw with.

The sixth hour. Counting the hours of the day from sunrise, about noon, the worst time to walk or to fetch water. Women usually drew water together, in the cool of morning or evening, so a woman coming alone at noon was probably avoiding the others; but John does not say so, and the guess should be held lightly.

From this well to the cross. The man sitting here with no bucket is about to offer a stranger water that ends thirst for ever. Fifteen chapters later, almost the last thing he says before it is finished is “I thirst” (19:28). He ended thirsty: the living water he offers her freely cost him the cross.

Was Jesus really tired, if he was God? Yes. The eternal Son took to himself a true body and a reasonable soul (the Westminster Shorter Catechism, Q. 22), with the common weaknesses of our nature, yet without sin (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2), and in that nature he truly grew weary, hungry and thirsty. His divine nature did not tire or become less than God, but the person who sat on the well was the Son of God, and the weariness was his own. That is the glory of the gospel, not its weakness: a Saviour who only seemed human could neither stand in our place nor sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

In everyday life. A word to the reader who is simply tired: not spiritually dry, just tired, with the day still eight hours long. There is no rebuke here and no call to push through. The Son of God sat down on a wall because he could not go on, and the most important conversation in the chapter happened while he was in that state. Exhaustion is not a lapse in discipleship. Sit down if you must, and let him use you there.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon, the heat of the day.

parallels.desc: Jacob buys land at Shechem
Joseph buried there

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God begins his rescue of this woman by asking her for help, and in four words crosses the barriers of sex, race and religion.

A woman from Samaria. Alone, at noon, and unnamed; yet she has become one of the most remembered people in the Bible.

Give me a drink. By the standards of the day, much is wrong with this scene. A man, alone, speaks to a woman, alone, in an isolated place, when some teachers held that a man should not even greet a woman in public. A Jew asks a Samaritan for water, raising a question of ritual cleanness she will name herself, since the vessel is hers. And he asks a favour of somebody with nothing, which is not how benefactors behave. He crosses all three barriers at once, and explains none of it.

He begins by asking. Not with her history, which he knew in full, her defective theology or her nationality: every one of those comes up later, and none is the doorway. Nor is it a technique; a favour asked to open a conversation is a manoeuvre, and people can smell it. He was genuinely thirsty. She is approached not as a case or a project but as the person by the well with the rope. He who owns the cattle on a thousand hills asked a sinner for a cup, and made himself dependent: here on a woman with a rope, later on borrowed boats, borrowed rooms and a borrowed tomb. He could have commanded the water to rise. He asked her for it instead, because he had come for her, and not for the water.

How do I start a conversation about Christ without it feeling artificial? Begin where Jesus began: with honesty and ordinary common ground. Most of our awkwardness comes from arriving as the one with all the answers, which sets up a transaction where one party is deficient and both know it. The deepest common ground between two people is not that one is right but that both have needs. Be genuinely interested in the person, accept their help when you need it, and let real questions come. Do not hide that you are a Christian, and do not force the subject; pray for the moment and take it when it comes, as Jesus does in verse 10.
verseByVerse.note: A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, still less a Samaritan.

parallels.desc: meetings at a well

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her astonishment that a Jewish man would ask her for a drink opens the door to everything that follows.

The disciples had gone. So the conversation was private; and a party of Jewish men buying food in a Samaritan town was already looser about boundaries than custom allowed.

How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? Not a rebuff, and not bitterness, but astonishment. In one breath she names everything that stands between them. She has spent her life on the wrong side of a line she did not draw, and somebody from the other side of it is asking her for a drink.

No dealings. Hatred ran deep on both sides: a Samaritan village would later refuse Jesus, and James and John wanted to call down fire on it (Luke 9:52–54).

The crack through which grace enters. Contempt she could have handled; she knows how to brace herself against it. She has no defence against a Jewish man asking her a favour, so she is off balance and talking. Many outside the faith have braced themselves for contempt from Christians. The most disarming thing we can offer is not a better argument, but the absence of the contempt they expected.

It began at a well, with a cup. Christ “is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). He went to the cross to make one new people out of enemies, and every church where former enemies share the Lord’s Table is a monument to what he began beside Jacob’s well.

Does this mean Christ does not care about truth, only about kindness? No. In a few verses he will tell her plainly that the Samaritans worship what they do not know (v. 22). He crosses the barrier of contempt, not the barrier of truth: he refuses the hatred, the ritual separation and the assumption that she is beneath him, but never gives up the truth about God or about her life. The church needs both. Love that hides the truth is not love, and truth spoken with contempt is rarely heard.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “have no dealings with” (synchrōntai) occurs only here in the New Testament, and it may mean more narrowly that Jews did not use vessels in common with Samaritans, as the ESV footnote allows. That fits the scene exactly: her surprise is not only that a Jew has spoken to her, but that he proposes to drink from her jar. Either way the point stands: Jews kept apart from Samaritans, and Jesus does not.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and settlers brought in by Assyria; Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility. The ESV notes that the last sentence may mean Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans.

parallels.desc: the settling of Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She knows neither the gift nor the giver; if she did, she would ask, and he would give her living water.

If you knew the gift of God. The gift is eternal life, given by the Spirit and found in Christ himself (3:16; Romans 6:23). It is free: it cannot be earned or bought.

Who it is. This matters most, because a promised gift is worth only as much as the giver’s power to give it, and she is looking at a tired man with no bucket. The one asking for water is the one who gives it.

You would have asked him. Not qualified, or made amends, or got the mountain question right. On Jesus’ own account only one thing stands between her and living water: it had not occurred to her to ask, because she did not know who she was talking to. Her history is about to be laid out, and it changes nothing; her being a Samaritan is a barrier already crossed. Ignorance, not unworthiness, keeps her poor, and he does not lecture her for it. He tells her, in stages, until she asks.

Living water. “Living water” (hudōr zōn) ordinarily meant running water, a spring, as against the still water of a cistern or well. So she thinks he is offering her running water from some spring, just as Nicodemus took “born again” to mean a second physical birth.

What is the living water? In the Old Testament God himself is “the fountain of living waters”, whom his people forsook for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13), and living water pictures the life and the Spirit that God pours out on his people (Isaiah 44:3; 55:1; Ezekiel 47; Zechariah 14:8). John tells us plainly what Jesus means: at the feast Jesus promises rivers of living water to whoever believes, and John adds that he said this about the Spirit (7:37–39). The gift at the well is the Spirit of God dwelling in a person, the new birth Nicodemus could not grasp, now pictured as a spring: God himself coming to live in you, and giving from within a new love for him, an understanding of his word and the power to turn from sin (Ezekiel 36:27; Galatians 5:22–23). And Jesus is the giver: he is the fountain.

Then why do so few people ask? Because they do not know the gift or the giver. Many who stay away from Christ think they are refusing a set of rules, a dull institution or a moral lecture, not living water. So Christian witness must keep pointing to who Jesus is and what he gives. When people truly see him, the asking follows.
verseByVerse.note: “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern.

parallels.desc: the fountain of living waters

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She takes him literally and asks, not seeing the irony, whether he is greater than Jacob; he is.

Nothing to draw water with. Travellers carried a leather bucket and a rope; Jesus had neither, and the well is deep. Hers are the sensible objections of a competent person, taking him literally, as Nicodemus did (3:4).

Our father Jacob. The Samaritans claimed the patriarchs as their own, which Jews disputed. In one phrase she has half crossed the boundary she raised: they share a forefather, and she is standing on his land.

Are you greater than our father Jacob? The question expects the answer no. The answer is yes. Jacob gave a well; Jesus gives living water. Jacob dreamed of a ladder between heaven and earth; Jesus is the ladder (1:51). The crowd will ask the same kind of question about Abraham, and Jesus will answer, “before Abraham was, I am” (8:53–58): John keeps putting the true answer in the mouths of people who mean it as an impossibility. Jacob’s well served his descendants for nearly two thousand years. The man she is talking to made the water.

Her literalism is the staircase. He does not correct her about the bucket. He takes the difficulty she has raised and uses it as the next step up.

What do I do with objections that seem to miss the point? Take them seriously, as Jesus does. A question that sounds naive or off-target is very often the real question, held at the only end the person can reach. Do not mock it or brush past it; answer what can be answered, and use it to lift the conversation toward who he is. Patient, respectful answers to plain questions have led more people to Christ than clever arguments.
verseByVerse.note: The well is deep, said to be over 100 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing drawn from this world’s wells satisfies for long, because we were made for God. It is a strange thing to say to a woman with a jar in her hand, and it covers everything: Jacob’s water is not bad, but no drink of it lasts.

It is simply true. Every good thing works on the same cycle: it satisfies, the satisfaction wears off, and the need returns at full strength, slightly sooner than last time. The meal, the holiday, the promotion, the applause, the relationship: none of them fails. They work exactly as advertised and then stop, and the stopping is not their fault. “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing” (Ecclesiastes 1:8).

He came himself to the well. God did not make us small enough to be filled by the world. He made us for himself, as Augustine confessed, and nothing less than himself will ever fill us. When we had forsaken the fountain for cisterns that hold no water, he came himself to the well and offered us the fountain again.

Thirst is not the sin. Say it plainly to the reader who keeps going back to the same well and hates himself for it, whether the well is a bottle, a screen, a person he should have stopped calling, or the approval of someone he cannot get out from under. The verse does not rebuke the thirst; God made us to thirst. It says that the well you keep returning to has never once promised what you keep hoping it will give. It gives what it has, every time, and the interval between drinks gets shorter, which is the mechanism of every addiction. If your well has become an addiction, do not fight it alone: tell your pastor, and get skilled help.

He does not despise the well. He asked for a drink from it. The problem was never that people love good things too much, but that they ask of them what they were never built to carry.

If I am a Christian, should earthly pleasures stop satisfying me? They should satisfy you more truly, because you no longer need them to be God. A Christian can enjoy a meal, a friendship or a holiday as the Father’s gift, give thanks, and let it go when it ends, because his soul is not hanging on it. The gifts keep their taste; their running out is simply no longer a disaster. The danger comes when we ask a gift to do what only the Giver can do.

In everyday life. Take the thing you were once most sure would settle you. Suppose you got it. Did the wanting stop, or did it change address? That is not cynicism about good gifts but evidence of what kind of creature you are. Name the well you keep going back to, and bring that thirst to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The water Jesus gives does not merely refill a thirsty person; it becomes a spring within, rising to eternal life.

Never be thirsty. A strong double negative in the Greek: never, ever. A door closes on the whole cycle of drinking and thirsting again.

A spring of water. Then the image stops being about drinking at all. He does not promise to keep her topped up; the water becomes in him a spring, and the one who drinks becomes a source. A well is a hole where water is stored: it has to be gone to and hauled out of, and it is finite. A spring is water arriving from underneath, under its own pressure, and it will not stay down. He does not hand out cups; he opens springs.

Welling up. The word means leaping, springing up (hallomenou), and is used of the lame man leaping in the temple (Acts 3:8). This is the life of the Holy Spirit within the believer (7:38–39), a source that never runs dry, rising toward its goal: eternal life.

Sir, give me this water. She still misunderstands, wanting to be spared the daily trip, and perhaps the shame of coming alone at noon. But she has asked, which is more than Nicodemus managed, and in this Gospel to misunderstand and hold out your hand is better than to understand and not ask. He does not correct her yet; he lets her ask for the right thing for the wrong reason, and goes on. No one comes to him with perfectly pure motives, and he has never yet sent anyone away until their motives were right.

Why, then, do believers still thirst for God? The Psalms are full of it: “As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God” (Psalm 42:1). The thirst that ends is the thirst of emptiness, the restless search for something to fill the soul. The Christian has found the spring; but a spring is drawn on every day, and Jesus goes on inviting his own: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (7:37). This longing is the appetite of those who have tasted and want more, and it will be fully satisfied when we see him face to face (Revelation 7:16–17).

What if I feel dry, not like a spring at all? Feelings rise and fall, but the spring is the Spirit himself, and he does not leave the believer (14:16). Dry seasons come to all God’s children, through tiredness, sorrow, sin or God’s wise testing. In them, keep to the means by which the Spirit refreshes his people: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. Confess any sin you know of, and keep asking; the promise rests on the faithfulness of the one who gave it, not on how full you feel today. If the dryness has become a lasting darkness, with sleep, appetite or hope failing, talk to your pastor and see your doctor too; medicine is no failure of faith.

In everyday life. If you belong to Christ, the source is already inside you. Begin the day not by hauling up your own resources but by asking the Spirit to rise in you, for patience with the children or joy in a dull task.

parallels.desc: like a spring of water whose waters do not fail

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns from thirst in general to her own life, because no one can receive living water without facing their own thirst and sin.

Go, call your husband. The turn is abrupt: she has just asked for the gift, and he tells her to fetch her husband. It is not a change of subject but the moment the conversation stops being about a topic and becomes about her. Thirst in general and life in general can be kept at a safe distance; her husband cannot. Jesus goes straight to the wound.

Where the difficulty lies. Many people find Christianity beautiful and are never once cornered by it, because they only ever discuss it as something about people in general. What changes everything is a sentence like “go, call your husband”: a sentence about you.

I have no husband. Four true words, used to hide something: not a lie, but an accurate sentence built into a wall to close the subject.

You are right. He does not knock the wall down. He agrees with it, and then says what it was built to keep out. People who expose us usually start with what we got wrong; Jesus starts with what she got right. It is the difference between being caught out and being told the truth by somebody plainly on your side.

Why does Christ bring up my sin if salvation is a free gift? Because the gift is for sinners, and no one drinks who will not admit they are thirsty. Jesus raises her history not to make her earn the water but so that she will know it is offered to her, the real woman, and not to an idealised version of her. A gospel that never touches your actual life cannot save your actual life. Repentance is not a price paid for grace; it is the hand opening to receive it. When Christ puts his finger on something, he means to heal it.

In everyday life. Is there a subject you steer around in prayer, the way she steered around her household? Name it to him today; he raises it only to heal it.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shows that he knows her whole history and names its one present wrong, yet he goes on speaking to her, without contempt.

You have had five husbands. He had never met her, and he knows every year. In that culture a woman could not ordinarily divorce her husband, while a husband could dismiss a wife for very little. So five marriages may mean five times widowed, or five times sent away: a life of things done to her at least as much as by her.

Not your husband. She is living with a man without marriage. This is the one irregularity Jesus names outright, and it is real: the present arrangement is not a marriage in God’s sight. That may be why she came to the well alone at noon.

What you have said is true. The gentleness is not softness about sin: the one speaking is the holy God in human flesh, whose eyes are too pure to look on evil (Habakkuk 1:13), and the wonder is that holiness so pure came close enough to ask her for a cup.

How much do we actually know? A great deal has been built on very little. John never calls her immoral, and Jesus never tells her, as he tells the man at the pool, to sin no more (5:14). The town comes out at her word (vv. 29–30, 39), which is not how a town treats a woman it has entirely cast out. Women divorced against their will, widowed young or long ago abandoned have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. What it does say is this: Jesus knew every year of her history before she said a word, asked her for a drink anyway, told her plainly who he was, and sent her back to tell her town.

Are the five husbands a symbol? Some have read them as an allegory: Assyria resettled Samaria with people from five foreign cities, each bringing their own gods (2 Kings 17:24–31), so the five husbands stand for false worships and the sixth for corrupt Samaritan religion. It is ingenious, but John gives no hint of it, the numbers do not work cleanly, and it dissolves a real woman into a symbol, the very thing this passage refuses to do. She is not a diagram of Samaria. She is a woman with five marriages behind her and a man in the house now, standing in the heat with a jar.

She met the Bridegroom. Five marriages had ended, and the man in the house had not married her. Then, at a well, the kind of place where Isaac’s bride was found and Jacob met Rachel, she met the Bridegroom (3:29), who came to give, not to take. He knew the whole history before she spoke, and it did not alter the offer by a drop. The Lord who searches the heart is the Lord who died for what he finds there.

What if I am living in a situation like hers? Then hear both halves of this verse. Christ knows your situation completely, and he does not pretend it is right: living together outside marriage is not what God designed, and he calls you out of it, into marriage or into chastity. But he says it while offering you living water, not while slamming a door. Come to him as you are; he will not send you away, and talk honestly with a pastor about the steps to take. And if your story is one of being left, widowed or divorced against your will, this verse lays at your feet no shame that belongs to others.

parallels.desc: he knew what was in man

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing that he is a prophet, she raises the great dispute between their peoples, where God should be worshipped, and Jesus takes up her question.

A prophet. Only a prophet could know such things. Her understanding is growing: from “a Jew” (v. 9), to “sir” (v. 11), to “a prophet”, and soon to the Christ (v. 29).

This mountain. Mount Gerizim rose directly above the well; she could have pointed at it. Israel was told to pronounce the blessings there (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12), the Samaritan copy of the law even named it as the place for the altar, and on its summit lay the rubble of their temple (see the note on vv. 3–4). The dispute she raises is a ruin she can see, and the people who made it are this man’s people.
