But you say Jerusalem. Is she changing the subject to avoid her sin, or asking sincerely? Both are possible, and the honest thing is to hold them together. It may be deflection: a man has just named the most painful arrangement in her life, and within a sentence she is discussing which religion is right. Religion is uncommonly good for this, because arguing is far easier than being known. Or it may be entirely genuine: before somebody who has just proved he can see, she asks where a sinner should go to find God, and takes the only chance she may ever get.

Jesus does not force a verdict. He answers with the fullest teaching on worship in the Gospels, which is what he would do if the question were sincere, and the only thing that would help if it were not. He is after the person, and he will follow her down any road she takes until she finds herself in front of him. And the argument, he is about to say, is over, and neither side won it.

What should I do when someone turns a personal conversation into a religious debate? Answer the question briefly and honestly, as Jesus does, and then bring it back to the person and to Christ. Do not be drawn into a long argument about church history, other religions or the hypocrisy of Christians while the real matter waits. You might say: “That is a fair question, and here is a short answer; but can I ask what you make of Jesus himself?” Winning a debate of this kind rarely wins the person.
verseByVerse.note: “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped; a Samaritan temple had stood there until the Jews destroyed it more than a century before.

parallels.desc: the blessing on Mount Gerizim
the place the LORD will choose

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Jesus the hour is coming when the Father will be worshipped everywhere, and no holy mountain, Samaritan or Jewish, will matter any more.

Woman, believe me. The courteous address he used to his mother (2:4; 19:26); and “believe me” asks for trust before he says the thing that will cost her her side of the argument.

The hour is coming. The new age Jesus is bringing through his death and resurrection. In John “the hour” is always tied to his glorification (12:23; 17:1) and to the gift of the Spirit.

Neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. “Neither”: not “your mountain is wrong and ours is right”, which was the whole dispute. The argument is not settled but made obsolete. Jesus himself is the new temple (2:19–21), and after his resurrection God can be worshipped anywhere, through him. Within about forty years the Jerusalem temple would be rubble too, as the one on Gerizim already was.

The Father. The first time in this conversation he uses the name. She asked where; he answers who, with the family name. Worship in the new age is the worship of children.

The end of holy places. What is dismantled here is the instinct, deep in most religions, that God is more available in some places than others, and that reaching the spot is most of the work. It survives in people who would deny holding it: the sense that prayer counts more in a church building than in a car, or before six in the morning than at eleven at night, and the low-grade grief of coming home from a place where God seemed close. The mountain has been closed, and everyone who cannot get to the holy place, the housebound, the shift worker, the mother of small children, the prisoner, has been kept away from nothing at all.

Does this mean church buildings and gathering on Sunday do not matter? Gathering matters; the place does not. Christ abolished holy geography, not the holy assembly. Believers are commanded not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), and the gathered church is where the word is preached and the Supper shared. But the building is a roof, not a temple: God is no more present in the sanctuary than in your kitchen, but is present with his people wherever they meet in Christ’s name. Love your church’s gathering because God’s people are there, not because the bricks are holy.

Is this not what people mean by spiritual but not religious? Only half. Jesus abolishes the holy place, but he does not make worship private or a matter of taste. In the next breath he says that the Samaritans worship what they do not know, that salvation is from the Jews, and that the Father must be worshipped in truth (vv. 22–24), and in this Gospel the truth is Jesus himself (14:6). He removed the location, not the object or the way. A spirituality that builds its own picture of God has only built a new mountain inside the self, and it can no more bring a sinner to the Father than the old one could.

parallels.desc: in every place incense will be offered to my name

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samaritan worship was in the dark, because God made himself known through Israel; but the hour of true worship has come, and the Father himself is seeking worshippers.

You worship what you do not know. This clause keeps the passage from becoming a mere lesson in tolerance: generous as he is, Jesus is not indifferent to the disagreement. Keeping only the five books of Moses, the Samaritans knew God in outline, incompletely and with distortion.

Salvation is from the Jews. He does not call Samaritan religion another route up the same mountain. God revealed himself to Israel, and the Messiah came from Israel according to the flesh (Romans 9:4–5). He does not flatter her; he tells her the truth.

From, not for. Salvation comes from the Jews; it was never for the Jews alone, so the same sentence removes any boasting. Israel’s privilege was something to pass on, not to keep. Israel was the well the water came through, and a well does not congratulate itself on the water.

And is now here. The new worship is beginning at this well, in this conversation, in the presence of Jesus.

In spirit and truth. By the Holy Spirit, and according to God’s revelation of himself in Jesus (see the note on v. 24).

The Father is seeking. This turns ordinary religious instinct upside down. We assume worship is what we do to find God; here God is the one out looking. She came to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there, who had come by a road his countrymen avoided: the verse is happening as he speaks it. God does not need our worship (Acts 17:25); he seeks us for our good and his glory. He sought Adam in the garden, Israel in Egypt, this woman at the well, and you. “We love because he first loved us”, and we worship because he first came looking.

Is it narrow to say other religions do not know God? It is honest, and it is what Jesus says. Many religions contain true things about right and wrong, and everyone has some knowledge of God from creation and conscience (Romans 1:19–20). But saving knowledge of God comes only through his own revelation, given to Israel and fulfilled in Christ, and no one comes to the Father except through him (14:6). To say otherwise would not be kind; it would leave people at a dry well. And notice the spirit in which Jesus says it: sitting with a Samaritan, asking her help, offering her the gift. Truth about other faiths should always come with that kind of love.

What if I do not feel like much of a worshipper? Take heart from the last clause. Perhaps for years the singing has not moved you, your prayers have felt dutiful, and others have plainly had something you lack. This verse does not tell you to try harder to find God. It says the Father is out looking for worshippers, and his search has a far better record than ours. True worship is measured not by the strength of your feelings but by whether you come to the Father through the Son, trusting what he has revealed.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses.

parallels.desc: out of Zion shall go the law

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God is spirit and bound to no place, true worship is not a matter of reaching the right spot but of coming to him by his Spirit and according to his truth, revealed in his Son.

God is spirit. One of the great definitions of God in John’s writings, with “God is light” (1 John 1:5) and “God is love” (1 John 4:8). It does not mean that God is “a spirit”, one ghostly being among others, nor a vague force or impersonal energy: the God described here talks, seeks, loves, and is called Father in the same breath.

What it does say. God has no body and is not in one place rather than another; no mountain or temple can contain him (1 Kings 8:27; Acts 17:24–25). A temple can be burned and a mountain captured, as Gerizim had been, without touching him, because he was never on it. He fills heaven and earth, dwells in unapproachable light, and is nearer to each of us than our own breath; and this God, who needs no house, has made his home in the hearts of those who believe.

Must worship in spirit and truth. Worship must match the nature of the one worshipped. If God were local, worship would be a matter of arriving. Since he is not, it is a matter of what kind of person you are before him, and everyone is before him all the time.

Not sincerity against ritual. The phrase is often read as heartfelt against formal, but that misses it. “Spirit” here is the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus described to Nicodemus as the agent of the new birth and has just pictured as a spring within. “Truth” is more than sincerity; in this Gospel truth is a person before it is a quality: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (14:6). So this is worship enabled by God’s own Spirit and shaped by his revelation in his Son: both gifts, neither a technique. And it cuts both ways. It rules out worship that is correct and dead, the right words in the right order with nobody home, and worship that is warm and invented, deeply felt and directed at a God assembled from preference. Truth without Spirit is a corpse; Spirit without truth is a mood.

If God is spirit, how could Jesus be God in a body? In his own being God is spirit and has no body. In the incarnation the eternal Son did not turn into matter or stop being spirit; he took a true human body and soul into union with himself (1:14), so that the invisible God is seen in Jesus (1:18; 14:9). This does not contradict “God is spirit”; it is the wonder of it. The God no mountain could contain chose to dwell among us in the flesh, so that we might know him and worship him in truth.

In everyday life. Ask what is left of your worship when the service is dull, the preacher poor and the room cold. That residue is the part that was in spirit and truth; the rest was the building.

Where Christians differ: how far does Scripture govern worship? Some traditions favour elaborate liturgy, ritual and visual symbols; others, free and spontaneous worship. Lutherans and Anglicans have generally held that churches may use what Scripture does not forbid; Reformed churches, that they should use only what it commands (the Westminster Confession 21.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.1). This commentary’s view: Reformed churches have drawn from this verse, among others, what is called the regulative principle: worship is shaped by what God has revealed in his word, not by human invention, and offered from the heart by the Spirit. External forms matter less than the heart, but the elements of worship must come from Scripture (the reading and preaching of the word, prayer, singing and the sacraments), while circumstances such as times, buildings and the order of service are arranged with wisdom, so a planned service or a written prayer is no breach of it. This is held charitably toward brothers who differ in practice.

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
She waits for a Messiah still to come, and Jesus tells her plainly that he is the one.

I know that Messiah is coming. With only the five books of Moses, the Samaritans had no royal prophecies of David’s line. They looked for the prophet like Moses into whose mouth God would put his words (Deuteronomy 18:15–18); later Samaritan writings call him the Taheb, the restorer.

He will tell us all things. They expected a teacher who would settle everything, the mountain included. Whether she is putting the matter off or simply longing, she leaves it all to someone still to come, while he is standing three feet from her.

I who speak to you am he. Literally, “I am, the one speaking to you” (egō eimi): an ordinary way of saying “that is me”, but also the first use of the weightiest phrase in this Gospel. “I am” echoes the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), and Jesus will use it of himself again and again (6:20; 8:58).

To her, first. He has spoken by night with Nicodemus, a member of the ruling council, without ever saying this, and his disciples have been with him for months. The first time Jesus plainly says he is the Messiah, he says it to a Samaritan woman with a broken past, alone, in the heat: not to the Sanhedrin, not to Nicodemus.

He had been waiting for her. A whole people had waited for a prophet like Moses who would one day tell them all things, and the waiting was answered in one sentence to one woman at a well. The voice that once spoke from a burning bush, where Moses hid his face, spoke now from the wall of a well, and she did not need to hide hers. The one she had been waiting for had been waiting for her.

Why does Jesus say so openly here what he hides elsewhere? The Samaritans expected a Messiah who would be a teacher and restorer, not a king leading a revolt. In Galilee and Judea the title would have brought crowds wanting to make him king by force (6:15). In Samaria the claim carried less political danger, and it could be said plainly.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses. Jesus’ “I who speak to you am he” is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples are shocked to find him talking with a woman but keep their questions to themselves, while she leaves her water jar and goes back to town.

They marveled. Not even that she was a Samaritan; simply a woman, when rabbis were expected to avoid talking with women in public. Their surprise is the instinct of every religious person who quietly ranks people into those worth Christ’s time and those not. Grace upsets the ranking, because none of us earned his time either (Romans 5:8).

The questions nobody asked. The first question the disciples did not ask, “What do you seek?”, is almost the question Jesus himself asked at the start of this Gospel: “What are you seeking?” (1:38). They do not put it to him, or to themselves. They have learned that he does things they would not have advised, and not yet learned to ask why. It is possible to follow Christ for years without bringing him the question that is actually there: the prayer not answered, the person not healed, the passage that troubles. This Gospel is full of people who asked him poor questions and got somewhere; bring him yours.

She left her water jar. She came for water and forgot it, because she had found living water. It is not a symbol she intended; people leave things behind when something has made the errand irrelevant. She would have to come back for it: the daily walk and the heat remained, but not her reason for coming alone. The jar on the wall of the well is a small monument to a soul that had found its spring.

Does this show that women may teach men in the church? Her witness was an invitation, “come, see a man”, and her neighbours then came to Christ himself and believed because of his word (vv. 39–42). Every believer, man or woman, is to bear witness to Christ like this. The authoritative teaching of the gathered church is a different thing, which Paul reserves for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). This commentary holds that view because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), though many faithful Christians read the passage differently and deserve a respectful hearing. On any view, Christ honoured this woman’s witness, and a town came to him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her testimony, one honest sentence about being known and a question, brings her whole town out to Jesus.

Come, see. The woman who came to the well alone runs to the people, with the words of Jesus and Philip on her lips (1:39, 46).

All that I ever did. By any standard we would apply, this is poor evangelism. She has one fact, it is about herself, and she overstates it, “all that I ever did”, when he had named her marriages and the man in her house. She cannot explain the living water, she has no doctrine of the incarnation, and she held the Samaritan view of the mountain that he had just set aside. And the town came out. She does not hide her past: the very thing that made her ashamed becomes her testimony. She does not need to add that he did not despise her; her whole manner says it. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted, and that is the entire content of her testimony.

Can this be the Christ? A tentative question, nearer to “this could not be the Christ, could it?”, as the Greek frames it. She does not preach; she invites them to decide for themselves, and that may be its strength. A woman with a finished doctrine would be easy to dismiss; a woman asking a question she plainly cannot answer, agitated and without her water jar, is harder to walk past. People argue with a conclusion; they find it harder to argue with somebody who has obviously been changed.

They were coming to him. She did not try to settle the question for them. She brought people to where Jesus was, and stepped aside.

What if I do not know enough to witness? Then you are in exactly her position, and look what God did with it. You do not need a theology degree; you need to know what Christ has done for you and where people can find him. Tell the truth about your own life, invite people to come and see, to read a Gospel, to come to church, and let him do the rest. Keep learning, so that you can give a reason for your hope (1 Peter 3:15), but do not wait until you know everything. She knew one sentence, and a town came out.

In everyday life. Write down in one sentence what Jesus has done for you, the plainest, truest sentence you can. Then ask God for one person to say it to this week, with an invitation added: “come and see”.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, "Rabbi, eat." But he said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While a town walks out to Jesus, his disciples press him to eat, and he speaks of food they know nothing about.

Rabbi, eat. A town is walking out across the fields toward Jesus because of something that happened while the disciples were shopping, and their contribution to the moment is to press him about lunch.

They are being kind. He had been too tired to walk, and they had fetched food: it is thoughtful, and completely blind. The largest thing that had happened all day was standing in front of them, and they saw a man who had not eaten. That describes a great deal of church life. The failure is rarely a failure to care. The caring is all practical, the rota, the building, the meal, and what God is doing in the room goes unremarked because nobody was looking for it there.

Food you do not know about. As with the water (v. 10), Jesus speaks of a spiritual reality and is misunderstood, the third time since Nicodemus heard “born again”. She said water, and he answered with water that was not water; they say eat, and he answers with food they do not know. He takes the ordinary object already in the conversation as a handle on something the hearer has no other way of reaching. Our words were made for the world we can see, so the unseen can be spoken of only by borrowing them, and that is why almost everyone in this Gospel misunderstands him at first. He pays that cost in nearly every conversation, and never once sounds impatient.

Is it wrong to care about practical things in church? Not at all. Someone has to buy the bread, and the disciples were right to look after their tired Master; practical service is honoured throughout Scripture (Acts 6:1–6). The danger is only that the practical becomes the whole of what we see. Do the rota and the catering gladly, as service to Christ, but lift your eyes while you do it, and ask: what is God doing here, and with whom?

parallels.desc: man shall not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples said to one another, "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What sustains Jesus most deeply is doing his Father’s will and finishing the work he was sent to do.

Has anyone brought him something to eat? Literal again, and the most human sentence in the chapter. They are not mocking; they have concluded, reasonably, that somebody must have got there first with a basket.

My food. He did need food; he had been too tired to walk. But something works in him the way food works, and he names it: his deepest satisfaction and sustenance is doing the Father’s will (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4). Talking to this woman had refreshed him more than food.

Obedience that feeds. That is not how obedience usually feels. We tend to think of doing God’s will as expenditure, drawn from a limited account to be topped up later by rest or pleasure; Jesus calls it food, something that fills him. Much of what drives us runs the other way: we work in order to be fed, by approval, success or the feeling of being needed, and when the praise stops we go hungry. Jesus was fed by the Father’s will itself, so no crowd could fill him up and no rejection could empty him.

To accomplish his work. “Accomplish” (teleiōsō) means to complete, from the same family of words as his cry from the cross, “It is finished” (tetelestai, 19:30). What he does at this well and at Calvary is one work (5:36; 17:4).

Glad obedience, all the way to the cross. The Son delighted to do his Father’s will all the way to the cross. His obedience was never grudging, and God counts that perfect, glad obedience as theirs for all who trust him (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). And because he finished the work, our obedience can be food too: not a wage we pay, but the joy of children doing the will of a Father who has already given us everything in his Son.

Does this mean I am doing ministry wrongly if it exhausts me? No. The verse has sometimes been used to flog tired people, and it should not be. The man who said it had sat down earlier that same day because he could not go on. Weariness in God’s work is normal and honourable, and rest is God’s gift, not a failure (Mark 6:31). What the verse says is that some work, whatever it takes out of the body, puts something back into the soul, and that this marks work done for the Father rather than merely about him.

In everyday life. Compare two things you do for God: one that leaves you flat, and one that tires you and yet you would not give up. The difference is often between a task you took on to be useful and a task the Father actually gave you. The first is a job. The second, in the words of this verse, is food.

parallels.desc: having accomplished the work

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, then comes the harvest'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The harvest the disciples think is months away is already walking toward them, and sower and reaper will rejoice together.

White for harvest. Picture what he is looking at: the town coming out across open country toward the well (v. 30), perhaps in white robes, through the fields. He is not offering an image; he is pointing. The harvest is walking toward them while they are asking about lunch, ripened in secret by the Spirit long before anyone noticed.

Already receiving wages. The reward of gospel work is handed over during the work, and the fruit is gathered for eternal life. This harvest does not rot.

Sower and reaper. In ordinary farming the reaper gets the visible result. Here somebody prayed for years and saw nothing, somebody else said one sentence and saw a town come out, and the two are paid at the same table.

His seeing fills the fields. The Lord of the harvest sees fields where we see empty roads. He lifted his eyes on a weary afternoon and saw a town coming; he saw you, too, long before you came to him. Fields that look empty to us are never empty to him, and his seeing, not our sharpness, is what fills them.

Does this mean everyone around me is about to believe? No. Jesus is speaking of what God was doing that day in Sychar; elsewhere he says the labourers are few and that many will reject the word. But people are usually nearer to believing than we suppose. God has his elect in every place (Acts 18:10), those whom he chose in Christ before the world began and will surely bring to himself (Ephesians 1:4; John 6:37), and the Spirit is often at work where we see nothing. So sow widely, pray boldly, and write no one off. The last people anyone expected were already on their way.

How do I lift up my eyes? The disciples had walked through Sychar to buy food and seen only a market; Jesus saw a harvest. Learning to see as he sees is mostly ordinary. Notice who is already in front of you: the neighbour, the colleague, the parent at the school gate are your fields, not the people you wish you knew. Pray for them by name, asking the Lord of the harvest (Matthew 9:38) to work in three or four of them, and watch for what he does. Ask, and listen: Jesus began with a request for water, and a real question about someone’s life opens more doors than a speech. Expect God to be ahead of you: he was at the well before the woman arrived, and he is at work in people you have written off.

Uncertain wording. Grain sown in winter was reaped in spring, but it is not certain whether “There are yet four months, then comes the harvest” is a proverb for the wait between sowing and reaping, or a plain remark that harvest was still four months off, which would set the scene in winter, with the grain still green. On the second reading “white for harvest” cannot describe the crops and must point to the townspeople coming out; on either reading, that is the main point.
verseByVerse.note: Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was roughly the gap between sowing and harvest, and the saying may have been proverbial.

parallels.desc: the ploughman shall overtake the reaper

verseByVerse.quote: "For here the saying holds true, 'One sows and another reaps.' I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples reap what others have sown, so no harvest is theirs to boast of, and no faithful sowing is wasted.

One sows and another reaps. A proverb, and here it holds true in a direction nobody expected: the disciples will reap a harvest prepared by others.

Others have labored. Who were the others? Some are very old: Jacob gave the well beside them, Joseph’s bones lie in the field, Moses sent Israel to that mountain to hear the blessings, and the prophets laboured for centuries. Some are recent: John the Baptist had been preaching not far away. And some are only hours old: Jesus himself, and a woman who had gone back to her town and done all the sowing there was time for. The disciples arrive with the shopping and walk into a harvest that centuries of history and one conversation had prepared. In Acts, Philip, and then Peter and John, would reap in Samaria what Jesus sowed here (Acts 8:4–25).

Somebody always got tired first. The word for laboured shares its root with “wearied” in verse 6. Every harvest anyone reaps was preceded by exhaustion the reaper did not feel and often never hears about.

Entered into their labor. Every gospel worker builds on others’ work, so there is no room for pride (1 Corinthians 3:6–9). The building was paid for by people now dead. The doctrine you preach was fought for by people who were burned for it. The person ready to believe in front of you was worked on for years by somebody whose name you will never learn, quite possibly a grandmother who prayed, saw nothing, and died thinking she had failed.

What about the sower who never sees fruit? This is the verse for the discouraged sower: the parent who has prayed for a child for thirty years, the Sunday school teacher who watched most of a generation drift, the missionary who came home with almost nothing to report. There is no promise that the sower sees it; there is a promise, one verse earlier, that when it is finally seen, he rejoices with the reaper. God forgets no seed sown in faith, and your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Keep sowing.

In everyday life. Name three people who sowed the gospel in you. If any are still alive, write to one of them this week and thank them. And sow faithfully today, even if others reap.

parallels.desc: cities you did not build
I planted, Apollos watered

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many Samaritans believe through her word and ask Jesus to stay, and he does, for two days, under Samaritan roofs.

Because of the woman’s testimony. John repeats her sentence rather than summarising it, so we know exactly what carried (see the note on vv. 28b–30). Everyone in that town had known the earlier version of her.

They asked him to stay. “Stay” (meinai) is John’s great word “abide”. It is one thing to be persuaded about a man, another to want him in the house for two days.

Two days. A Jewish rabbi ate Samaritan food, off their plates, under their roofs, for two days, each act carrying a ritual cost in the eyes of the men in Jerusalem. The text does not treat this as remarkable, and that says a great deal. The Son of God was not ashamed to lodge with Samaritans, because they asked him, and he loves to be asked.

In everyday life. Ask Christ to stay: in your home, your evenings, your plans. Faith that keeps Christ at the town gate is not yet the faith of Sychar.

Is the later giving of the Spirit in Samaria a pattern for us? In Acts the Samaritans receive the Spirit only after the apostles come. That was a later group, at a special moment in the spread of the church, when God showed that Samaritans were fully included in the one church of the apostles (Acts 8:14–17). These Samaritans in John truly believed, knowing Jesus as the Saviour of the world. Neither passage sets up a two-stage pattern for all believers: everyone who truly believes in Christ has the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

parallels.desc: Samaria receives the word

verseByVerse.quote: And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing Jesus for themselves, many more believe, and these Samaritans confess what Israel’s teachers had missed: he is the Saviour of the world.

Because of his word. Testimony brings people to Jesus; his word brings them to faith.

No longer because of what you said. No insult to her, but where every true witness hopes to lead: they no longer rely on her account, because they have heard him for themselves. Her task is done.

Saviour of the world. The summit of the episode: not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of all peoples, Samaritans included. A saviour rescues from something, and John has named it: from the judgment that rests on everyone who does not believe, into eternal life (3:16–18, 36). The title appears in the New Testament only here and in John’s first letter (1 John 4:14).

A title fit for Rome. Inscriptions across the empire honoured emperors as saviour and benefactor. Readers who knew that would hear a title fit for Rome given to a Jewish teacher in a Samaritan village, by Samaritans, outsiders to Israel’s hopes.

The ironies stacked in the sentence. The people who confess him are the people a Jew would not share a cup with, and they reach it in two days, when Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel with every advantage, could not follow what Jesus said about being born again. And in the chapter where Jesus has said that “salvation is from the Jews”, Samaritans are the first to confess a Jew as the Saviour of the world. Outsiders understood what insiders missed.

Caesar claimed the title and is dust. Christ bears it and reigns for ever. One day a great multitude that no one can number will stand before his throne and cry that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb, and among them will be a town from Samaria and a woman whose name we never learned.

Does Saviour of the world mean that everyone will be saved? No. It means that Jesus is the Saviour not of Jews only but of Samaritans and Gentiles too, of all who believe, as these Samaritans did. Paul calls God the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe (1 Timothy 4:10). The title speaks of the scope of the offer and the reach of his rule, not of universal salvation.

What if my faith is still borrowed? That is where this whole town started, and where most people start: a parent, a minister, a book. It is a good place to begin and a poor place to remain, because a second-hand faith is only as durable as the person it leans on, and people move away, disappoint and die. Do what the Samaritans did: hear him for yourself. Read the Gospels as his own words to you, pray to him directly, and sit under the preaching of his word asking him, not the preacher, to speak.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “the Christ, the Saviour of the world”; the earliest lack “the Christ”, so most modern Bibles omit it.

parallels.desc: the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 43–54 — The Official's Son: The Second Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith that rests on Jesus’ word, without a sign, is the faith he looks for, and this second sign at Cana shows it. Jesus goes on to Galilee, where his own people welcome him because of what they saw in Jerusalem, a welcome John shadows with a proverb about a prophet without honour (vv. 43–45). A royal official from Capernaum begs him to come and heal his dying son (vv. 46–47). Jesus exposes the hunger for signs, then sends the man home with only a promise: “Go; your son will live” (vv. 48–50). The man believes and goes, and his servants’ news shows that the fever left at the very hour Jesus spoke; he and his whole household believe (vv. 51–54).
verseByVerse.theology:
The second sign shows faith that believes the word of Jesus before any visible confirmation. In this Gospel faith grows from believing because of signs, to believing his word, to believing in the crucified and risen Lord himself, and each stage is a step deeper into trust in his person.

The two numbered Cana signs (2:11; 4:54) frame everything between them (see the note on v. 54).
verseByVerse.examples:
The official believed before he saw (see the note on vv. 49–50). That is the pattern of mature faith: not the absence of evidence, but trust in the word of the one who cannot lie, before the confirming experience comes.

His prayer was not eloquent, and the answer was not smaller than he asked (see the notes on vv. 46–47 and v. 48).

verseByVerse.quote: After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes on to Galilee, and John’s aside about a prophet without honour warns us not to mistake the welcome there for faith.

No honour in his own hometown. There is a genuine puzzle here: the proverb says a prophet has no honour in his own hometown, and John then reports that the Galileans welcomed him (see the uncertain wording below). Either way, the aside casts a shadow over the applause before it arrives, so that the reader does not mistake the noise in Galilee for something better than the silence in Judea.

Being liked and being believed. They are not the same, and the first can be an obstacle to the second. A church well thought of in its town is not a bad thing, but it does not prove that the town believes. The Galileans were delighted with him, and chapter 6 will show how long that lasted.

Should I expect rejection from those closest to me? Often, yes. Jesus’ own brothers did not believe in him for a long time (7:5), and he warned that a person’s enemies may be those of his own household (Matthew 10:36). Familiarity can breed a kind of deafness: they knew you before, and find it hard to take seriously what has changed. Keep living faithfully and lovingly among them, speak when there is opportunity, and pray. Jesus’ brothers were in the upper room after the resurrection (Acts 1:14).

Uncertain wording. Which is “his own hometown” here? It may be Judea, the land of his birth, with Jerusalem, where the authorities have just demanded his credentials and the Pharisees have been counting his disciples. The sentence then explains why he left Judea, and it fits John’s habit of using “his own” for those who should have received him and did not (1:11). Or it may be Galilee, where he grew up, and the welcome there was no real honour: the next verse says they welcomed him because of what they had seen him do in Jerusalem, which is enthusiasm for a performer, popularity rather than honour. The first is the more likely, since John has just shown Jesus rejected in Jerusalem and Galilee does in fact welcome him; but the verse does the same work either way.

verseByVerse.quote: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Galileans welcome Jesus for the signs they saw in Jerusalem, a warm welcome that falls far short of the Samaritans’ faith in his word.

The Galileans welcomed him. Because of his signs in Jerusalem at the Passover (2:23), not because of who he was. This is the sign-faith John introduced at 2:23–25: real as a beginning, insufficient as a foundation.

Set the two receptions side by side. John has arranged them to be compared, and the comparison is uncomfortable. The Samaritans had no signs, only a woman’s sentence about being known and two days of listening to him, and they arrived at the Saviour of the world, believing because of his word (v. 41). The Galileans had everything else: they were his own people, they had seen the signs with their own eyes, and they welcomed him warmly. What they had was an appetite for signs, which he names in a moment (v. 48) and which chapter 6 will test to destruction: after the bread and the fish, “many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (6:66). What separates the two is not information or privilege but what they were looking for when they came. Spiritual sight is not proportional to religious advantage.

Warm approval with nothing underneath. The Galileans are much the easier group to belong to. They were not sceptics or opponents but fans: pleased he had come, speaking well of him, turning out when he was in the area. The most dangerous position in this chapter is not hostility but warm approval with nothing underneath it. If you fear that describes you, take heart: fans do not lose sleep over whether they truly love him. The concern is itself a sign of life, and the remedy is not anxious self-examination but looking again at Christ.

Is it wrong to come to Jesus because of what he can do for me? It is not wrong to begin there; most of us did, and Jesus welcomed the sick, the hungry and the desperate. The problem is staying there, because faith that wants only his gifts will leave when the gifts seem to stop. Saving faith rests on Christ himself, as Lord and Saviour, and trusts him even when he gives nothing visible. If you came for help, keep coming, and ask him to show you himself, until you would want him even with nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A royal official whose son is dying walks a hard day’s journey to beg Jesus to come down and heal him.

Cana again. The site of the first sign, and this will be the second (v. 54): John frames these chapters between two signs at Cana. The Samaritan woman was not looking for Jesus, and he found her; this man comes looking for Jesus and will be given only a word.

An official. A royal official (basilikos), probably serving Herod Antipas: a court appointment, a household, standing. Antipas was officially only a tetrarch, but people commonly called him king (Mark 6:14). Capernaum lies on the lakeshore; Cana is up in the hills, about twenty miles away, a hard day’s walk and a climb.

He went to him. A courtier left a dying child and travelled all day into the hills on the strength of a report, to beg a travelling teacher to come. Nothing about it is dignified. When a man of standing goes in person rather than sending a servant, every door his rank could open has already been tried, and everything he normally relies on has failed.

Come down. He needs Jesus present. Everything he has seen work, physicians, officials, favours, requires the person to be in the room. He is not lacking faith; he is exercising the only kind he has.

Is it wrong to ask God to come and be present in my crisis? Not at all. Many people pray like this: “Lord, be in the room at the operation; come to my son.” It is what a frightened person asks for someone they love, and the psalms are full of such prayers. This story does not rebuke the request but enlarges it: the answer is the same, delivered without the twenty miles. Christ is not limited by where he is, and by his Spirit he is present with his people everywhere.

Is this the same as the centurion’s servant in Matthew and Luke? Probably not (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10). Here it is a royal official’s son, at Cana, and the man asks Jesus to come down; there it is a Gentile centurion’s servant, at Capernaum, and the centurion says he is not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof. The likeness is in the healing from a distance, which Jesus did more than once.
verseByVerse.note: The official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum lay down by the lake, about 20 miles from Cana.

parallels.desc: a similar healing of a centurion’s servant

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus exposes a faith that will believe only if it sees, and so sets the test the official is about to pass: will he trust a word alone?

Unless you see signs. The “you” is plural. Jesus is not turning on a frantic father but speaking over his head to the Galileans in general (v. 45), who came out to see whether there would be more signs. The rebuke is aimed mainly at them.

What was it for? It is a hard thing to hear when one’s child is dying, so why did Jesus say it? The clue is what happens next. Jesus does not, in the end, give this man a sign he can see. He gives him a sentence. The man is about to be asked to do what the crowd will not: take a word and go, with nothing in his hands. The apparent rebuke sets up the test, and the father passes it within two verses.

Then are miracles bad for faith? No. John records Jesus’ signs precisely so that we may believe (20:30–31), and Jesus appeals to his works as evidence (10:38; 14:11). Signs are good when they point us to Christ and lead us to trust his word. The weakness Jesus exposes is a faith that will believe only if it keeps seeing: faith in the spectacle rather than in the one who performs it. The signs were given once for all and are written down for us. We do not need fresh ones; we need to believe what has been written.

In everyday life. There is relief here for anyone who has prayed badly under pressure. When something is genuinely at stake, the words go, the composure goes, and what is left is a single sentence repeated. This chapter records such a prayer word for word (v. 49), and records that it was answered at once and generously. Jesus was not waiting for a better-formed request. He hears the stammered prayer of a frightened parent as clearly as the psalms of the saints.
verseByVerse.note: The “you” here is plural: Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general.

verseByVerse.quote: The official said to him, "Sir, come down before my child dies." Jesus said to him, "Go; your son will live." The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers the father’s plea with a word spoken from a distance, and the man believes it and goes home with nothing else: the faith Jesus looks for.

Before my child dies. Not an argument. He does not defend his motives or engage with the theology of signs; he says it again. And the word for his son is a diminutive, paidion: “my little boy”. The rank has fallen off the man entirely.

Go; your son will live. Five words: no journey, no touch, no prayer, no condition attached. The man asked him to come down, and Jesus declines and answers anyway, from twenty miles away.

The man believed the word and went on his way. He came to bring Jesus down to the house and is sent home without him, with only a sentence about a child who was dying when he left. He did not wait for proof, and that is the miracle in this verse, before the other is known. He had no evidence of any kind and no way of hearing anything until he arrived, which would take the rest of that day and into the next. The whole journey home was made on the strength of five words, and every hour of it the other explanations were open to him: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come. This is what it looks like when a promise is the only thing in a person’s hands: not the absence of fear, for there is no reason to think he was calm, but the willingness to act as though the word were true while everything visible is unchanged and the clock is running.

His word is enough. The Word who was in the beginning speaks, and it is done. A father turned his back on the healer he had come to fetch and went home with a sentence, and the sentence was worth more than the visit. The grass withers and the flower fades, but the word that sent a man down the hill from Cana stands for ever.

Is the official’s faith just wishful thinking? No. Wishful thinking trusts a feeling; this man trusted a person and a sentence, and the sentence could be checked, which is exactly what he did the next day when he asked the hour (v. 52). Biblical faith is not believing without reasons. It is resting on someone who has shown himself trustworthy, and staying on his word while the evidence is not yet in. Its strength lies in its object: a weak faith in a reliable Christ saves, and a strong faith in the wrong thing does not.

Does this mean that a parent with enough faith can secure healing for a sick child? No. This was a particular word from Jesus to this man, “your son will live”. We have no such word about every illness, and the faith he commends is trust in what Christ has said, not confidence that he will do what we ask. A parent whose child was not healed did not fail to believe enough. Nor are prayer and the doctor rivals: God usually heals through means, and taking a sick child for medical care is no failure of faith. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he loved (11:35), and his promise to his people is not that no child will die, but that whoever believes in him, though he die, yet shall he live (11:25).

What has Christ actually promised me, then? Far more than one healing. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37), that he will never leave nor forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), that nothing can separate them from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39), that he will raise them on the last day (6:40), and that he is preparing a place for them (14:2–3). These words are as certain as the one spoken at Cana. Faith takes them and walks home on them, often long before the evidence arrives.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the road home his servants meet him with the news that his son is alive and recovering.

His servants met him. On the road, the next day (v. 52): somebody in that household was so relieved they set off to shorten the wait.

Recovering. Literally, “was living”: the very word Jesus had used. They think they are reporting an ordinary recovery: the fever has turned.

How God’s answers usually arrive. Not with a label on them. The feared thing does not happen, and from outside it looks like an ordinary good outcome. The father is about to ask one question, a plain matter of fact, that turns a recovery into a revelation: when?

How can I tell whether something was an answer to prayer or just coincidence? Often you cannot prove it, and you do not need to. God governs all things, including the ordinary course of events (Matthew 10:29–30), so the recovery that looks natural is still his gift. But it is worth doing what this father did: go back and check. Note what you prayed for and when, and notice what happened; over time a pattern of God’s faithfulness becomes plain. Give thanks for every mercy without needing to label it a miracle, for every good gift comes from above (James 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, "Your son will live." And he himself believed, and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fever left the boy at the very hour Jesus spoke, and the father, and then his whole household, believe.

He asked them the hour. The seventh hour was about one in the afternoon, counting the hours of the day from sunrise, as the ESV does.

That was the hour. The fever broke at the hour the words were spoken, twenty miles away. Nothing had touched the boy and nothing had been sent. It was not coincidence. The one through whom the fever, the boy and every mile between them had been made simply spoke, and the distance turned out not to matter, because it never had. He does not have to be near a thing to reach it; he is the reason it is there.

He himself believed. A second time. The first (v. 50) was trust in a promise about his son; now John says simply that he believed, and in this Gospel that means trusting Christ himself. Faith in a healer has become faith in his word, and then in him.

All his household. The first household conversion in John (compare Acts 16:15, 34): not a formula or a guarantee, but a family with a boy who was well and a father who could tell them the hour.

What if my household has not believed? Then this verse must not be used to reproach you. Many faithful people have households that have not followed, and Jesus warned that families would be divided over him (Luke 12:51–53). Salvation is God’s gift, and each person must believe for himself. What this verse gives is hope and a pattern: pray for your whole household by name, live the faith visibly before them, and tell them plainly what Christ has done. God delights to save families, and he is not finished with yours.

Does the household believing support baptising whole households, including infants? Here the household believed; John says so. That is the pattern this commentary sees throughout the New Testament: those who were baptised, or counted as believers, were those who heard and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers, read the household passages differently and see in them the covenant inclusion of children, and they hold that view with deep conviction and care for their children’s souls. We honour them as brothers. But this verse, at least, describes a household of believers.

Uncertain wording. One word is easy to read past: “yesterday”. Capernaum is more than an afternoon’s walk from Cana, so unless “yesterday” means after sunset, when a Jewish day began, the father spent a night on the way. Many see in that a quiet sign of faith, since a man still frightened for his son would hardly have stopped. It is a likely reading, not a certain one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

parallels.desc: he believed, with his entire household

verseByVerse.quote: This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John numbers this the second sign at Cana, closing the section that began with the first, and this time the sign rests on a word alone.

The second sign. John counts, and then stops; the numbering never resumes. The count ties the two Cana signs together: both at Cana, both after a journey north, both ending in belief (2:11; 4:53).

A frame around the chapters. Between Cana and Cana, Nicodemus, a member of the ruling council, cannot understand the plainest thing, and a Samaritan woman understands enough to fetch a town. Both needed exactly the same gift, and only she went home and told a town. The man with everything missed it, for now (19:39), the woman with nothing did not, and a royal official closes the section believing on a word alone.

What changes between the first sign and the second. At the wedding he was present and instructed the servants. Here he is twenty miles away and only speaks, and the voice works across a day’s journey as if it were not there.

A sickroom he never entered. Each of Jesus’ signs reveals who he is: the Lord of creation who turned water into wine, the Lord of life who drives out death with a word. The glory that shone at the wedding shone again in a sickroom he never entered. And the same voice will one day speak at every grave, and all who are in the tombs will hear it and come out (5:28–29). Blessed be the Word made flesh, whose glory is full of grace and truth.

Why does this matter for me? Because this is the position of everyone who follows Christ after the ascension. We are the man on the road home: no touch, no visible presence, no sign before our eyes, only his word, a distance and the walking. John says that he wrote these signs down so that people who were never in the room might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:30–31): so that there could go on being men and women who walk home on nothing but his sentence, and find that the fever went at the hour it was spoken.

parallels.desc: the first sign

4.title: The Woman at the Well
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John<sup>2</sup>(although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),<sup>3</sup>he left Judea and departed again for Galilee.<sup>4</sup>And he had to pass through Samaria.<sup>5</sup>So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.<sup>6</sup>Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.<sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”<sup>8</sup>(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)<sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ’Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”<sup>11</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?<sup>12</sup>Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.”<sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,<sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”<sup>15</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”<sup>17</sup>The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right in saying, ’I have no husband’;<sup>18</sup>for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.”<sup>19</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.<sup>20</sup>Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.<sup>22</sup>You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.<sup>23</sup>But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.<sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”<sup>25</sup>The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.”<sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”<sup>27</sup>Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, “What do you seek?” or, “Why are you talking with her?”<sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people,<sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”<sup>30</sup>They went out of the town and were coming to him.<sup>31</sup>Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”<sup>32</sup>But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”<sup>33</sup>So the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.<sup>35</sup>Do you not say, ’There are yet four months, then comes the harvest’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.<sup>36</sup>Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.<sup>37</sup>For here the saying holds true, ’One sows and another reaps.’<sup>38</sup>I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”<sup>39</sup>Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me all that I ever did.”<sup>40</sup>So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.<sup>41</sup>And many more believed because of his word.<sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”<sup>43</sup>After the two days he departed for Galilee.<sup>44</sup>(For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)<sup>45</sup>So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.<sup>46</sup>So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill.<sup>47</sup>When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.<sup>48</sup>So Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”<sup>49</sup>The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”<sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.<sup>51</sup>As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.<sup>52</sup>So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”<sup>53</sup>The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son will live.” And he himself believed, and all his household.<sup>54</sup>This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 closes the part of John’s Gospel that runs from Cana to Cana (2:1–4:54). Jesus has just talked by night with Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel (chapter 3), and John the Baptist has said of him, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). Now Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee, by way of Samaria.

The message. The Father is seeking true worshippers, and his Son goes looking for them across every barrier we put up. He offers living water, the life of God’s own Spirit, to anyone who will ask, however far outside or however broken; he is the Messiah and the Saviour of the world; and the faith he looks for takes him at his word.

Why it was said. John wrote for believers scattered across the empire, many of them not Jews, after the Jerusalem temple had fallen (see the introduction). This chapter told them that true worship never depended on a mountain or a temple, that a Samaritan town was among the first to confess Jesus, and that believing his word without seeing is not second-best faith but the very faith he commends.

How the chapter makes its case. Tired at Jacob’s well, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink (vv. 1–9) and offers her living water that becomes a spring within (vv. 10–15). He brings her history into the light without contempt (vv. 16–18), answers her question about the right mountain by announcing worship of the Father in spirit and truth (vv. 19–24), and tells her plainly that he is the Messiah (vv. 25–26). She brings her town, while he tells his disciples that his food is the Father’s will and the harvest is already ripe (vv. 27–38). The Samaritans believe because of his word and call him the Saviour of the world (vv. 39–42). Then in Galilee, where people want signs (vv. 43–48), a royal official believes a single sentence, and his son lives (vv. 49–54).

Where it leads. The man who sits thirsty at the well is himself the fountain: the Spirit he promises will be given once he is glorified (7:37–39), and the last thirst we hear of in this Gospel is his own, on the cross (19:28). The quarrel over the mountain ends because he is the true temple (2:19–21); the work he speaks of finishing here (v. 34) is finished at Calvary (19:30); and the word that heals across twenty miles is the voice that will one day call the dead from their tombs (5:28–29).

For us. No history is too tangled and no background too far outside for Christ to come looking: he knows everything about you and still offers living water, and you have only to ask. Then take him at his word, as the official did, and tell others in one honest sentence what he has done, as the woman did.

keyVerse.quote: but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter turns on this offer. What Jesus gives is not one more drink from the world’s wells but a spring inside a person, the life of God’s own Spirit (7:38–39), which no history disqualifies and no dry season exhausts. The woman asked for it before she understood it, and he did not withdraw the offer.

4.reflection:
Jesus begins with a request for water, not with the woman’s history or her theology (v. 7). What does that teach us about speaking of him to people who expect contempt from Christians? Where could you begin like that this week?

Jesus says that everyone who drinks Jacob’s water will be thirsty again (v. 13). Which wells do the people around you, and you yourself, keep going back to, and what would it mean to bring that thirst to Christ?

Jesus brings up the woman’s husbands only after offering her living water, and he exposes her without contempt (vv. 16–18). Why does he raise her history at all, and why is it good news that he knows everything about us?

The Samaritans believed “because of his word”, and the official “believed the word that Jesus spoke to him” (vv. 41, 50), while the Galileans wanted signs (v. 48). Which promises of Christ are you being asked to walk home on now, before you can see the outcome?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus does on the Sabbath what only God does, and so he is charged with making himself equal with God. At the pool of Bethesda he picks out a man who has lain there thirty-eight years with no one to help him, and heals him with a word, unasked (vv. 1–9). The authorities see only a man carrying his mat on the Sabbath (vv. 10–13). Jesus finds the man in the temple and warns him of something worse than paralysis, and the man reports him (vv. 14–15). When Jesus defends his work, saying that his Father is working and so is he, they understand him exactly, a claim to be equal with God, and begin to plan his death (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The opposition shows what Jesus was claiming. When he defends his Sabbath work by appeal to his Father’s, the leaders understand him to claim equality with God, and he does not correct them (see the notes on vv. 16–17 and v. 18).
verseByVerse.examples:
The healing shows how grace comes: the man did not ask, did not know who Jesus was, and showed no faith before he was healed.

Jesus’ question, whether he wants to be healed, speaks to anyone who long ago stopped asking God for something (see the note on vv. 5–6). On the mat carried through the city, see vv. 8–9.

verseByVerse.quote: After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for a feast and comes to a pool where the city’s sick lay waiting, beside the gate where the sacrificial sheep came in.

A feast of the Jews. If it was one of the three pilgrim feasts, Jesus was keeping the law that every Israelite man appear before the LORD at the place he chose (Deuteronomy 16:16). Each visit to Jerusalem in this Gospel brings conflict (v. 16).

By the Sheep Gate. The Sheep Gate, rebuilt in Nehemiah’s day (Nehemiah 3:1), was in the north wall near the temple, and its name suggests that sheep for sacrifice were brought in there. The healing happens beside the gate of the sacrificial lambs, in the presence of the Lamb of God (1:29).

A pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda. If the name means “house of mercy” (see the box below), here was a colonnade full of blind, lame and paralysed people waiting for water that mostly did not come: either the bitterest name in Jerusalem or a prophecy. On this day it proved to be the second, because the Lord of mercy himself had come to it.

Five roofed colonnades. For a long time this was treated as proof that the writer did not know Jerusalem: a four-sided pool needs four colonnades, not five. Then it was dug up. Excavations near the Church of St Anne uncovered a double pool north of the temple, with colonnades on the four outer sides and a fifth across the partition between them, though details of the layout are still debated. That does not prove the miracle, but it removes a confident objection: the writer knew a detail of the city that was later lost. “Has” is present tense, which may suggest John wrote before AD 70, or may simply describe the scene vividly.

Does archaeology prove the Bible true? It cannot prove the miracles or the gospel, which rest on the testimony of God in his word, received by faith through the Spirit. But it has again and again confirmed the Bible’s places, names and details, as here. That matters, because Christianity stands or falls on real events in real places, and a writer accurate in passing details is reasonably trusted on the larger things.

Uncertain wording. John usually names the feasts, but not this one, so it cannot be identified or the chapter dated precisely; Pentecost, Tabernacles and Purim have all been suggested. The manuscripts spell the pool’s name in other ways too (the ESV notes Bethsaida; many scholars prefer Bethzatha), and its meaning is not certain: “house of mercy” is a common explanation, but not the only one.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Bethsaida. Archaeologists have uncovered twin pools there with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle.

parallels.desc: the Sheep Gate

verseByVerse.quote: In these lay a multitude of invalids — blind, lame, and paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The colonnade is full of exactly the people the Messiah was promised to heal, and Jesus walks in among them.

A multitude of invalids. “Paralyzed” is literally withered. These are the conditions Isaiah promised would be reversed when God came, “then shall the lame man leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:5–6), and the ones Jesus listed for the Baptist: the blind see, the lame walk (Matthew 11:4–5). The colonnade is full of people still waiting. And in a city full of holy places, the Son of God spends part of a feast day here, where untreated suffering was most concentrated. Where suffering gathers, he does not withdraw.

A mercy for the quickest. Whatever was true about that water, the belief around it had a cruel shape: whoever gets in first is healed (v. 7). It was a mercy for the quickest, who needed it least, and closed to the man who had been there longest. Jesus does not touch the water, carry the man to it or make him first. He heals him where he lies. That is the difference between a mercy you have to qualify for and a mercy that comes to where you are.

In everyday life. Every town has its colonnade: the care home, the hospital ward, the street where people sleep. Its people are not a problem to be managed but the very ones Jesus walked towards, and his servants find, often to their surprise, that he is already there.

Does a missing verse mean the Bible is unreliable? No (see the textual note below). We have thousands of New Testament manuscripts, far more and far earlier than for any other ancient book, and comparing them shows clearly where a later copyist added a note. Modern Bibles are open about these places, as the ESV is here. No doctrine depends on a disputed verse, and the fact that we can identify such additions shows how well God has preserved his word.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add the end of verse 3 (“waiting for the moving of the water”) and verse 4, about an angel who stirred the water, so that the first person to step in was healed. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added to explain verse 7, reflecting popular belief. That is why the verse numbers jump from 3 to 5. Some think the pool was fed by an intermittent spring that bubbled up, which people believed had healing power. Nothing is lost by its absence: the man trusted the water and its legend; Jesus ignored the water entirely and healed with a word.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel stirring the water and the first one in being healed, a popular belief explaining why the sick waited there.

verseByVerse.quote: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, "Do you want to be healed?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the whole multitude Jesus chooses one man, long past hoping, and wakes him with a question.

An invalid for thirty-eight years. Longer than many people lived then. If he was struck down at twenty, he is nearly sixty, and he has spent his whole adult life on a mat beside a pool, watching other people get well. The number may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:14), but John does not say so, and the link is better held loosely.

When Jesus saw him. The man did not ask, and John does not explain why Jesus chose him. Grace is sovereign: God gives his kindness freely, as he chooses, not as a wage for anything he finds in us (Romans 9:16). And Jesus knew that he had been there a long time without being told (2:25).

Do you want to be healed? To a man who has lain beside a healing pool for thirty-eight years it sounds almost like an insult. Yet Jesus does not ask this of everyone he heals, so it is meant for this man and this history. A want disappointed for thirty-eight years does not stay clean and sharp. It goes quiet, gets managed and turns into a routine: the same spot, the same hours, the same near misses, until the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; it is what happens to human beings. So the question is not cruel but the most respectful thing in the passage. Jesus asks a man who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants, and wakes him to desire.

What if I have stopped hoping for something? The question is for you too: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the sin confessed so often the confessing has gone hollow, the prayer abandoned around the fifth year of praying it. It is not a rebuke but an invitation to say aloud what would be different if God moved, which is harder than it looks. He may answer as you ask, or differently, or in his own time; but he invites you to bring the desire to him honestly rather than bury it. Hope in God is never foolish, even when hope in the circumstance has worn thin.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering before entering the land (Deut 2:14), though John does not draw the link.

parallels.desc: thirty-eight years until that generation perished

verseByVerse.quote: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked whether he wants to be well, the man can only explain why he never will be: he has no one.

Sir, I have no one. The loneliest words in the chapter. What he names as his problem is not his legs but that in thirty-eight years, in a colonnade full of people, nobody had stayed close enough to put him in the water. The Greek is bare: ‘a man I do not have’. The paralytic in Mark had four friends (Mark 2:3); this man had none. He is surrounded by people and alone, a common kind of alone.

Another steps down before me. Every time, someone quicker got in first: thirty-eight years of nearly.

He does not answer the question. He describes the system and his place at the bottom of it. Not one word is untrue and not one is an answer. Not knowing who is speaking to him (v. 13), he is talking to the answer while explaining why there isn’t one.

The friend of the friendless. When there was no man to help, the Son of Man came, the one who stays when everyone else has stepped down before us. He was himself forsaken by all his friends, so that no one who trusts him need ever say again, “I have no one”.

Why does Jesus heal someone who showed no faith? Because grace does not wait for us to be ready. This healing pictures how God saves: not because we reached the water first, or had the right friends, or even knew who he was, but because Christ came to us and spoke. Faith is the hand that receives Christ, and God gives that hand too (Ephesians 2:8); here the healing came first and the knowing later. So pray for people who seem to have no faith at all. Christ can begin where there is nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus heals with a word alone, at once and on the Sabbath, and sends the man out carrying the evidence.

Get up, take up your bed, and walk. Three commands, all impossible, given before there is any evidence that he can obey. The bed is a krabattos, a poor man’s mat, the pallet a beggar rolls under his arm. No pool, no stirring, no helper: the word that commands gives the power to obey.

At once. After thirty-eight years, instantly, with no touch and no prayer: grace arriving unrequested, which is why Bethesda has so often been read as a picture of the gospel.

The mat. A healed man walking away is a private mercy. A healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. Jesus tells him to carry it on the Sabbath, in Jerusalem, at a feast, past the authorities. That is deliberate, and the rest of the chapter follows from it.

Now that day was the Sabbath. John mentions the Sabbath only after the healing, so that the reader feels the joy first and the objection second. Jesus knew what day it was, and his answer in verse 17 shows he chose it: the word that called the world out of nothing called a withered man off his mat on the day of God’s rest, and gave him the first true rest he had known in thirty-eight years.
