In everyday life. It is possible to be genuinely helped by Christ and entirely discreet about it, to leave the mat at the pool. He told this man to pick it up. Is there some evidence of his grace in your life that you have kept out of sight?

Where Christians differ: must Christians keep the Sabbath? Both views are held by faithful believers. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that the fourth commandment still binds, the day of rest now kept with joy on the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, as a day for worship and works of mercy. Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ, the true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so that no day binds the conscience (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5–6), while still gathering gladly on the first day, the day of resurrection. This commentary’s view: the second fits the New Testament best: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not the fourth commandment moved to Sunday, and no one may bind another’s conscience over it. The first view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree with what this passage plainly teaches: the day was never meant to forbid mercy, and Jesus is Lord of it.
verseByVerse.note: The bed was a light mat. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by tradition, drawing on the prophets.

parallels.desc: a similar command to a paralytic
bear no burden on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with a man walking for the first time in thirty-eight years, the authorities see only a broken rule. They have a real text behind them, but they apply it where it was never meant to go.

So the Jews said. In John, “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole (see the introduction). Jesus, his disciples and the healed man were all Jews.

Not lawful. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200 but preserving older tradition, lists carrying an object from one domain to another among the thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2).

Be fair to them first. They were not inventing a rule out of nothing. Jeremiah had said, “do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 17:21–22), naming the very city and gates. He was forbidding the traffic of trade, loads carried in to be bought and sold (compare Nehemiah 13:15–19); a healed man carrying his own mat home was never what he had in view. So this is not religious people making things up, but something more uncomfortable and far more common: applying a real command of God in a situation it was never written for, and being badly wrong while sounding entirely correct.

Seeing only the rule. A paralysed man is walking through Jerusalem carrying his own bed, and they have not one question about how, not one word to him about what has happened. They see the mat, the mat is against the rules, and the man holding it is invisible: a miracle processed as an infringement. And the heart has a reason to prefer the rule. Rules you can keep give a sense of control and of standing before God. A grace that comes unasked to a man who had kept nothing threatens that whole arrangement, because it says that God’s best gift cannot be earned.

Lord of the day they were guarding. The Sabbath was God’s sign of the rest he would give his people, and the giver of that rest had just given it. The one load the man lifts that day is proof that his real burden has been taken away. The men at the gate see the Sabbath command broken; they are looking at what it pointed to, walking past them on two healed legs.

In everyday life. Think of the last time something happened in a Christian setting outside your expectations: a convert with a chaotic life, someone doing good work with theology you would want to correct. What was your first reaction? Discernment is a duty. But these men’s first reaction was a rule, and the second, joy at what God had done, never came.

Does this mean rules do not matter? No. God’s commands are good, and Jesus never broke the law of God. What he exposed was a way of handling it that loses sight of its purpose: love for God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–40). “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). These men cared about their reading of a rule more than about the man in front of them and the God who had just healed him. Keep God’s commands, but never let your system of applying them blind you to his mercy.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: But he answered them, "The man who healed me, that man said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healed man points to the one who healed him; his questioners cut out the healing and ask only who gave the order.

The man who healed me. His logic is sound: someone with the power to end thirty-eight years of paralysis with a word plainly has standing to say what may be carried and when. That is not an evasion but an argument. What he lacks is a name.

Who is the man who said to you? He says, “The man who healed me”. They say, “the man who said to you”. They repeat his sentence with the healing surgically removed: not who healed you, but who told you to break the rule. That is how an inconvenient fact gets edited out of a discussion.

The right question for the wrong reason. Yet “Who is the man?” is the question every page of this Gospel answers: the Word made flesh, the Lamb of God, the Lord who heals. His enemies asked it to name a suspect, and at the last answered it themselves without knowing, with a title fixed above his head on a cross: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (19:19).

Be gentle with the healed man. He has had his legs for perhaps an hour, and is questioned by the most powerful men in the city about a rule he broke because he was told to (on his later naming of Jesus, see vv. 14–15).

What do I say when I am challenged about my faith and do not know much yet? Say what you know, as this man did: what has happened to you and who did it. The man born blind said, “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see” (9:25). That is enough to begin with. Then go and learn more, and do not be ashamed to say, “I do not know the answer to that yet, but I will find out.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man was healed without knowing who healed him, because Jesus slipped away rather than draw a crowd.

Jesus had withdrawn. He was gone before a crowd could gather around the miracle, as he will be again (6:15), the opposite of what anyone building a following would do. He does good to those who do not know his name, content to be unrecognised; but in the next verse he comes looking.

Set him beside the man born blind. The contrast is deliberate. That man is interrogated by the same authorities, grows sharper with every round, is thrown out of the synagogue, and then, found by Jesus, worships (9:38). This man is asked one question and produces a name. One received his sight, lost his standing and gained Christ; this one received his legs and told the authorities who had done it.

Can someone receive God’s blessings and still not be saved? Yes, sadly. The healing did not, as far as we are told, save this man. A marriage restored, a diagnosis reversed, a job that came in time: each may be a genuine gift from God and leave the recipient where they were. God sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and many received healing from Jesus without following him (Luke 17:17–18). Blessings are meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), but they do not save; only faith unites us to Christ. So do not measure your standing with God by your circumstances, good or bad. Ask instead: do I know him, trust him and follow him?

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, 'See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.' The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes looking for the man he healed, to warn him that there is something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat.

Jesus found him. The man had gone to the temple, perhaps to give thanks, walking where for years he could only have been carried. And Jesus goes looking for a man who does not know his face: the healing was the beginning of the errand, not the end. He comes back for people, for the blind man after he is thrown out (9:35), and for Peter on a beach after the denials (21:15).

See, you are well! Sin no more. The order matters. He is not told to stop sinning so that he may be helped; he has been helped, and now he must turn from sin. Jesus does not say that all illness is punishment for sin, or that this man’s thirty-eight years were a sentence served (see the question below). He warns him that sin has worse consequences than paralysis: eternal judgment. That is what any of us most needs to hear on the far side of a mercy. Sin is worth abandoning not because it made you ill, but because judgment is real, and the body you have just got back will not last for ever. He loves us too well to heal our bodies and leave our souls in danger: his warnings are as much mercy as his miracles.

He told the Jews. Why? Perhaps naively, perhaps to protect himself, perhaps as testimony; John does not say, and it is wise not to judge him harshly. But from then on the authorities pursued Jesus (v. 16).

Am I ill because of something I did? John settles the general question four chapters on: shown a man born blind, the disciples ask who sinned, and Jesus rejects the premise (9:3). Illness is not a scoreboard. In a world under the curse bodies fail, and you cannot read a person’s sins off their illness. Job’s friends built a theology on the opposite assumption, and God said they had not spoken rightly of him (Job 42:7). Sometimes a particular sin brings particular harm, and then repentance is the path. But do not assume your suffering is punishment. If you are in Christ, the punishment for your sin was borne at the cross, and whatever you suffer now comes from a Father’s hand.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin, but warns that sin leads to worse than illness.

parallels.desc: go, and from now on sin no more

verseByVerse.quote: And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus defends his Sabbath work by claiming to work as God works: his Father has never stopped working, and neither does he.

Persecuting Jesus. The tense means they kept on persecuting, and the cause was a pattern, “these things”, not one incident.

My Father is working until now. The claim lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3), but Jewish teachers, as rabbinic writings later record, knew that God does not down tools on the Sabbath: children are born and people die on it, and giving life and judging the dead were the standard examples of divine work that never stops. One recorded answer was that God is exempt: the whole universe is his house, so he may work in his own home on his own day. Jesus takes that exact exemption and applies it to himself. He does not merely argue that mercy is allowed on the Sabbath; he claims the freedom that belongs to God alone, because his work is God’s work. And he says “my Father”, not “our Father”: a unique relationship.

The rest of God and the work of God. God rested on the seventh day from making the world, not from upholding it; there has not been an hour since when he was not holding it in being. And Jesus does what the Father does: he holds the stars in their places and a healed man on his feet with the same hand.

Who actually kept the Sabbath that day? A man who had spent every seventh day of nearly four decades on a mat beside a pool walked home on this one. If anyone in Jerusalem entered into rest that day, it was him. The one accused of breaking the Sabbath is the only person in the story who gave anyone a Sabbath, and the men defending the day spent it drawing up charges. The day was made as a mercy; to use it to stop a healed man carrying his bedding is not strictness but a misreading of what the day was for.

Is God really working all the time, even in the boring parts of my life? Yes, in the dull Tuesday as much as in the dramatic answer to prayer, upholding all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), working all things for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and completing the good work he began in you (Philippians 1:6). You may not see it, but you are never in a moment that God has left unattended.

Textual note. In verse 16 some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add that they sought to kill him; the earliest do not, and John says it in verse 18 anyway.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath, sustaining the world; Jesus claims the same right.

parallels.desc: lord even of the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The authorities understand Jesus exactly: in calling God his own Father, he is making himself equal with God, and for that they resolve to kill him. John agrees with their reading of his words, though not with what they did about it.

Seeking all the more to kill him. The first time John mentions the plot, and the thread runs on through the Gospel (7:1, 19; 8:37; 11:53). He healed a man who had been on the ground for thirty-eight years, and they began to plan his death.

His own Father. “His own” (idion): personally, in a way no one else could. Jews called God Father collectively, the Father of the nation. To call God one’s own Father, in a way that made one’s working and God’s working the same working, was a different kind of sentence altogether.

Making himself equal with God. Either Jesus was a blasphemer, or he is God. Their charges were wrong only in how they put them. He was not breaking the Sabbath, only their reading of it; he never once broke the law of God. And he was not making himself equal with God, but stating what was already the case, a larger claim altogether.

In the flow. The whole chapter turns on this verse: everything after it is Jesus’ answer to this one charge, which he does not deny but unfolds. John opened by saying that the Word was God (1:1) and will close with Thomas saying, “My Lord and my God!” (20:28); here, halfway between, Jesus’ enemies state the same truth as an accusation.

The people who understood him best. The idea that he was a teacher of ethics whose followers later made him divine cannot survive this verse: the people who wanted him dead understood him best. Nobody organises an execution over the golden rule; they killed him for who he said he was. If John wrote late, did he put the claim in Jesus’ mouth? The earliest Gospel tells the same story: Mark has the scribes call him a blasphemer for forgiving sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:7), and the high priest condemn him for blasphemy at his trial (Mark 14:61–64).

The only true charge against him. When the charge was finally brought to Pilate, it was that he made himself the Son of God (19:7): the only accusation ever brought against him that was true, and true in a sense the prosecution never suspected, since he had not made himself anything. He had come from his Father’s side, and was on his way back to it by the cross they were preparing. He claimed equality with God and died for the claim, and the empty tomb was the Father’s verdict that every word of it was true.

If Jesus is equal with God, why does he pray to the Father and obey him? Because within the one God there are three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal in power and glory and distinct in how they relate to one another (Westminster Confession 2.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3). From all eternity the Son shares one life, one will and one love with the Father. And in the work of salvation he became man, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6–8). So his prayers and obedience do not make him less than God. They show us God the Son living out, in our nature, the love and unity he has always shared with the Father.

parallels.desc: you, being a man, make yourself God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–47 — The Son's Authority: Witness and Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son is equal with the Father, and life and judgment are in his hands, so the only safe place is with him. Jesus answers the charge of verse 18 by unfolding it. The Son does whatever the Father does (vv. 19–20); he gives life to whom he will and holds all judgment, so that all may honour him as they honour the Father (vv. 21–23). Whoever hears and believes has already passed from death to life, and at the last day all the dead will hear his voice (vv. 24–29). Then he calls four witnesses: John, his works, the Father and the Scriptures (vv. 30–40). At the end the trial turns on his accusers, who love human praise more than God (vv. 41–47).
verseByVerse.theology:
The discourse claims for the Son the two works that belong to God alone, giving life and judging, and the honour that belongs to God alone. No one can honour God while declining Christ. The four witnesses are not offered as proofs that force belief; that the leaders reject them shows the state of their hearts.

The Son has life in himself as the Father does (see the note on vv. 26–27). And verse 29 does not teach salvation by works (see the note on vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.examples:
The claims of this discourse leave no middle ground: a man who says he will raise the dead and judge the world is either deluded or who he says he is. And the judgment of the last day is already being decided in each person’s response to him now (vv. 24, 28–29).

The chapter also names three ways of being religious without coming to Christ: enjoying a faithful preacher for a while without following where he points (v. 35); studying Scripture as if life were found in the text rather than in the one it points to (v. 39); and living for the approval of one’s own circle rather than the glory that comes from the only God (v. 44).

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son never acts on his own, because he and the Father work as one: whatever the Father does, the Son does, and the Father in love shows him everything. Jesus answers the charge of verse 18 not by denying it but by explaining it.

Nothing of his own accord. It sounds like a limitation, but it is the strongest claim in the paragraph. Anyone can act independently of God; every one of us does it hourly, and that is what sin is. Only one person can say that he never has, and that everything he does is what he sees the Father doing, continuously and without deviation. No prophet ever said that. And “whatever the Father does”: everything, not approximately but exactly, which only one who is God can do.

The workshop. There may be a picture underneath this. In that world a trade passed from father to son by watching: a boy stood in his father’s shop and learned by seeing it done. The picture is homely and the claim enormous, for what is made in this workshop is raising the dead and judging the world.

The Father loves the Son. The verb here is philei; in 3:35 the same love is agapa, and John uses the two interchangeably. This love shows the Son everything and holds nothing back. The Father loved the Son before the world was made (17:24), and into that eternal love, by grace, God brings his people, loving them even as he loved the Son (17:23). And he will show him greater works than healing a paralysed man: giving life and judging (vv. 21–22).

God has always been love. We tend to picture God before creation as alone, perhaps a little lonely, so that he made us for company or applause. This verse will not allow it. Before anyone else existed, a Father was loving a Son and showing him everything. Timothy Keller often pointed out, taking up C. S. Lewis’s picture of a dance, that each person of the Trinity delights in the others and turns attention to them, so that the life of God is not self-centred but self-giving. We were made to join that dance; instead we stand still and expect everyone to circle us, the hunger for “glory from one another” that verse 44 exposes. God did not make us to get a love he lacked, but to share a joy he already had. The Son left that embrace and was forsaken on the cross, so that those who trust him are loved, in his own words, “even as you loved me” (17:23). See also Trinity in the Theological Dictionary.

In everyday life. In the Son his Father is your Father, and his Spirit is in you. Before the main decisions of today, ask: what is my Father doing here? Do your work as a child learning in your Father’s workshop. And when you catch yourself wanting the room to revolve around you, turn it outward: praise someone else’s work, and let the praise go unreturned.

How can I explain the Trinity simply? Start with what the Bible says, not with an illustration. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. The three are not the same person: the Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father, the Spirit is sent by both. So God is one in being and three in persons. Most illustrations, water and ice and steam, or one man as father, son and husband, end up teaching an old error, that God is one person wearing three masks. Better to say plainly: this is beyond us, it is what God has shown us about himself, and it is the most beautiful truth there is, because it means God has always been love.

Where Christians differ: the Son and the Father. Arians (named after a fourth-century teacher who held that the Son was the first and highest creature) and today Jehovah’s Witnesses read “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” as proof that the Son is inferior to the Father. This commentary’s view: the passage teaches that the Son is equal with the Father in nature and power (he does whatever the Father does, gives life, judges and receives equal honour), while distinct in person and relationship (the Father sends; the Son is sent and obeys). This is the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, three persons, equal in power and glory, distinct in relations (Westminster Shorter Catechism 6).

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son does the two works that belong to God alone: he gives life to whom he will, and the Father has handed all judgment to him.

The Father raises the dead. In the Old Testament only God gives life to the dead (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Kings 5:7). Jesus now names the two works that Jewish teachers said God never stops doing, giving life and judging (see the note on vv. 16–17), and claims both.

To whom he will. By his sovereign choice: spiritual life now (v. 24) and resurrection life at the last day (v. 29). Not to whoever qualifies or reaches the stirred water first. The first half of the chapter demonstrates the clause. Jesus walked into a colonnade of sick people, healed one and left, and John offers no account of why that man. A Christ who healed everyone at the pool would be easier to admire and would tell us nothing about how mercy actually comes to anyone. What we have is a man who was not first in the queue, had nobody, and got up and walked. Christians differ over whether that choice rests on faith God foresees (the debate is set out at 6:37); all agree that no one is saved by merit.

All judgment to the Son. The final judgment, which belongs to God alone (Genesis 18:25), is given to the Son (Acts 17:31). Every human being will be judged, and the judge is the one who was crucified, no stranger to human life. The hands that were pierced will hold the scales of the last day, and the voice that told a paralysed man to stand will summon the nations.

In everyday life. If you are praying for someone who seems far from God, take heart: the Son gives life to whom he will, and no one is too far gone for his voice.

But Jesus also says he did not come to judge the world. He says it in 3:17 and 12:47, and in 8:15, “I judge no one”. He came the first time to save, not to condemn; the condemnation already rests on those who reject him (3:18). At the end all judgment is committed to him, and he will judge (v. 27). And in 8:15 he means that he does not judge as they do, by outward appearance and merely human standards.

If the Son gives life to whom he will, is it unfair to those he passes by? No one has a claim on God’s mercy; if we did, it would not be mercy. All of us deserve judgment, and God would be just to leave us to it. That he saves any is pure grace, and that he saves a great multitude is amazing grace (Romans 9:14–16). And the same Christ freely invites all: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37). No one who wants to come is turned away. If you want Christ, that wanting is itself the sign that he is giving you life.

parallels.desc: I kill and I make alive

verseByVerse.quote: "that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father has given life and judgment to the Son so that all may honour the Son exactly as they honour the Father, and to refuse the Son that honour is to refuse the Father.

Just as they honor the Father. “Just as” fixes the measure: not honour above every other teacher, but the same kind and degree of honour as the Father receives, which is worship. God will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). If the Son is to be honoured just as the Father, the Son is God.

The Father wants his Son honoured. We might assume that honour paid to the Son is a detour from the Father. The verse says the reverse: the Father gave life and judgment to the Son precisely so that all may honour him. Holding back honour from the Son does not protect the Father’s.

Whoever does not honor the Son. This closes every exit. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ (1 John 2:23). Many believe in God, admire Jesus as a moral teacher, and regard his divinity as a later addition. This verse says that arrangement does not exist, not because Christians are narrow, but because the Son himself refuses to be admired as anything less than God. It is better stated than hedged.

Owed the worship of the universe. The Father has decreed that every knee shall bow to the Son, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). No praise of Christ needs holding back in case it overshoots. The man who stood bound before a council and was mocked by soldiers is owed the worship of the universe, and one day he will have it.

In everyday life. Listen to how you speak about Jesus outside church: with colleagues, with family, in an argument. It is easy to slide into speaking of him as a figure of great importance rather than a person to be worshipped. Speak of him today as your Lord.

Is it right to pray to Jesus and sing to him, or only to the Father? Both. Ordinarily Christians pray to the Father through the Son by the Spirit, since through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18). But Stephen prayed to the Lord Jesus as he died (Acts 7:59), the first Christians called on his name (1 Corinthians 1:2), and all heaven sings to the Lamb (Revelation 5:12–13). Worship offered to the Son is not misdirected; it is exactly what the Father wants.

parallels.desc: no one who denies the Son has the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever hears Christ’s word and believes the Father who sent him already has eternal life: he will never be condemned, because he has already crossed from death to life.

Has eternal life. Hearing and believing is the way life is received, and the tense is present: already.

He does not come into judgment. No condemnation (3:18; Romans 8:1). This is the strongest assurance in the chapter: not will be acquitted at the judgment, but will not come into it. The verdict was settled at the cross, where Christ took the condemnation in the believer’s place (Romans 8:3). No accusation can reopen the case, because the Judge has given his verdict, at the cost of his own life.

Passed from death to life. Perfect tense: has crossed over and remains on the other side, from spiritual death (Ephesians 2:1) to eternal life. Not is crossing, nor will cross when the accounts are settled. The believer is not a candidate for life awaiting a verdict, but someone who has already emigrated.

An hour is coming, and is now here. These dead are not in graves but walking around Jerusalem, spiritually dead and unaware of it, and some are about to hear a voice and start living. In verse 28 he will not add “and is now here”, and that hour will involve tombs. Two kinds of rising, one spiritual and now, one bodily and still ahead; the same voice does both.

The dead will hear. As Lazarus would hear his voice and come out of the tomb (11:43), so the spiritually dead hear his voice in the gospel and are made alive (Ephesians 2:4–5). This is regeneration, the new birth of 3:3–8: God giving life to someone dead toward him, so that he now hears, believes and loves what he once ignored. The dead do not cooperate in being raised.

In everyday life. When you share the gospel, remember whose voice gives life. Your task is to speak his word faithfully; his is to raise the dead.

But Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. How can believers not come into judgment? Both are true (2 Corinthians 5:10). The believer does not come into judgment in the sense of condemnation (Romans 8:1); that verdict has been given. But his life and work will be reviewed for reward, and some will suffer loss though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

What if I am frightened of the last day? Then hear this verse as Jesus meant it. This verse rules out a faith in which everything is provisional, a hope that the balance will come out right with a private suspicion that it may not. If you have heard Christ’s word and believe the Father who sent him, the passing has happened. You will stand before Christ as one already acquitted, your sins carried away by him: not a hearing but a homecoming. Your assurance rests not on the strength of your feelings but on the word of the Judge himself.

parallels.desc: dead in trespasses, made alive

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son has life in himself, as the Father does, and as the Son of Man he has authority to judge.

Life in himself. God depends on nothing; life is his by nature. Put plainly: everything that lives has life on loan. A tree has it from the soil and the light, an animal from what it eats, a man from his food and breath and a heart that has not yet stopped, and every one of those supplies can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself is to be the one exception: to hold life not as a supply but as his own being, underived, with nothing behind it that could fail. Theologians call this aseity, from the Latin a se, from himself, and it belongs to God alone.

Granted to the Son. The Son too has life in himself, not borrowed but his own (1:4). “Granted” does not mean the Son once lacked it; it is not an event in time. The eternal Son receives life eternally from the Father, as he eternally comes from the Father. Theologians call this eternal generation: the Father has always been the Father and the Son has always been the Son. There was never a time when the Son was not (1:1–2); he is not a creature given life at some point, and what the Father is, the Son is. And having become man, he has this life as a man too, to give to others.

Because he is the Son of Man. As a man he can judge humanity fairly, having lived as one of us (Hebrews 4:15). The one who will judge the human race was tired at a well, wept at a grave, and knows from the inside what it costs to be one of the accused. The one who holds life in himself took a body that could be killed, gave his life away, took it up again, and now gives it to whoever hears his voice.

What difference does it make that God has life in himself? Because God depends on nothing, he cannot be worn out, run out or used up. He does not need you, so his love for you is pure gift, not a deal. And because the Son has life in himself, the life he gives is not a borrowed supply that might run dry but his own inexhaustible life. Whoever is joined to him by faith is joined to the one source of life that can never fail: “because I live, you also will live” (14:19).

Uncertain wording. We might expect ‘because he is the Son of God’, and in the Greek there is no “the”, simply ‘a son of man’. The phrase may stress his true humanity, or recall Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man who receives an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). Most likely both are meant: he judges as a true man, and as the man to whom Daniel’s kingdom is given.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man given dominion

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A greater hour is coming: at Christ’s voice all the dead will rise bodily, those who have done good to life and those who have done evil to judgment.

Do not marvel at this. The spiritually dead living at his voice is the smaller wonder; wait until the graves. This time he says only that an hour is coming, not that it is now here: it is the last day.

All who are in the tombs. Everyone who has ever been buried, righteous and wicked, in every unmarked place, in the sea and under the ash, raised in the body, the one to eternal life, the other to condemnation. And the summons is a voice, the voice of the man who told someone in a Jerusalem colonnade to pick up his mat, a man who has been in a tomb himself, and came out, and knows the way.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by good works. In John the “good” is above all believing in Jesus (6:29), and life comes to whoever hears his word and believes (v. 24). The deeds are evidence, not payment: they show whether a life had crossed from death to life (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Nobody is raised to life because their record was good enough, but this Gospel will not let faith be a word said once with nothing following.

In everyday life. Verse 29 asks whether the crossing has left any tracks: what would your life look like to someone who watched it for a year without hearing you say anything about God? If you see little, do not despair: the tracks are often plainer to others than to ourselves, and life is received by hearing and believing (v. 24), not by the size of the tracks.

How can a loving God raise anyone to judgment? Because he is holy as well as loving. A judge who shrugged at cruelty, betrayal and the abuse of the weak would not be loving but indifferent, and every victim would know it. God takes evil seriously because he takes people seriously. And he takes mercy as seriously: the Judge who will speak at the graves came first to be judged in our place (v. 24), and those who come to him will find that the Judge is their Saviour.

What will the resurrection body be like? Your own body, raised, not a different one, just as Jesus’ risen body bore the marks of the nails (20:27). For believers it will be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), like Christ’s glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The unbelieving dead will also be raised bodily, to face judgment and conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). So the body matters: what you do with it now is done with something God intends to raise.

Where Christians differ: one resurrection or two? This verse speaks of one hour in which all who are in the tombs come out, the righteous and the wicked together (compare Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15). Premillennial Christians (who expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth) read Revelation 20 as teaching two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart, the first for believers and the second for the rest. Many faithful Christians read it so, and the hope all share is the same: Christ will return, raise the dead and judge the world. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is the one this verse gives: a single general resurrection at Christ’s return, with Revelation’s first resurrection referring to the new life believers already share with Christ. This is the amillennial view, which takes the thousand years as a picture of the present age between Christ’s two comings.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son’s judgment is just because he judges only as he hears from the Father, and he accepts the law’s demand for more than one witness.

As I hear, I judge. The Son never acts apart from the Father (v. 19), so his judgment is perfectly just, because it is the Father’s.

Not my own will. Perfect submission (4:34; 6:38). That is the qualification for a judge: not superior intelligence but the total absence of self-interest.

If I alone bear witness. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Witness has run through this Gospel since the Baptist (1:7–8); now the case is formally opened. “Not true” means it would not count as evidence in court, not that it would be false. He is under no obligation to argue, yet the Son who claims to raise the dead builds a case like a defendant, because the men in front of him will move only on evidence, and he will give them evidence rather than stand on his dignity.

In everyday life. Only one man has ever sought the Father’s will and never his own, and his perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Because your standing with God rests on his obedience and not on being right, you can be honest about your motives: before you form an opinion of someone today, ask what you stand to gain from it. A judgment with self-interest in it is already bent.

But in 8:14 Jesus says his testimony about himself is true. Is that a contradiction? No; each answers a different question. Here he meets them on their own ground: you require corroboration, and here are the witnesses. In chapter 8 he answers a challenge to his knowledge: he alone knows where he came from and where he is going, so his testimony, whatever a court makes of it, is accurate. One statement is about legal standing, the other about truthfulness. He does not need corroboration to be right; he offers it because they need it to be persuaded.
verseByVerse.note: The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself did not count as valid evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not stand alone: another witness, the Father himself, testifies for him, and that testimony is true.

The other witness. Some take it to be John the Baptist (v. 33), but it is most likely the Father, since “the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me” (v. 37). Both point the same way: John spoke because the Father sent him (1:6, 33). And the Father cannot lie.

The witnesses. Jesus now calls four witnesses, as in a trial: John the Baptist (vv. 33–35), his works (v. 36), the Father (vv. 37–38), and the Scriptures, including Moses (vv. 39–47).

There is another. He is standing alone in a hostile room: the disciples are not mentioned in this chapter, and the healed man has just named him to the authorities. The corroboration comes from outside the building, from the one who sent him, and does not depend on anyone present being persuaded.

In everyday life. If you have to hold a position alone today, in a family, at work, in a church that has gone somewhere you cannot follow, remember: “There is another”. It is not an encouragement to be stubborn, but a statement about where the verdict actually comes from.

How should I argue for the faith with someone who wants proof? From knowledge, not anxiety. This Gospel is itself a gathering of evidence, and says so (20:30–31). So give reasons gladly: the eyewitness testimony, the empty tomb, fulfilled prophecy, changed lives. But arguing with fear underneath communicates the fear rather than the case, and Jesus never once sounds worried about the verdict. The truth does not depend on your winning the argument. Speak calmly, honestly and kindly, and leave the persuading to God.
verseByVerse.note: The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it as John the Baptist (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: "You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus points to John the Baptist, a witness his accusers had investigated themselves, not because he needs a man’s word, but so that they may be saved.

You sent to John. The delegation of 1:19. They cannot dispute his standing, because they investigated him themselves, and John told them on the record who he was. Jesus is producing the transcript of their own enquiry.

He has borne witness. He testified that Jesus is the Lamb of God and the Son of God (1:29, 34). The tense matters: the testimony stands, still doing its work in a hearing he is not present at. “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30), and by now the decreasing has gone a long way. He is not in the room; his witness is.

Not from man. Having called John, Jesus says at once that his case does not rest on him. Even the greatest man born of women is still a man, and a man’s word is too weak a foundation for who Jesus is.

So that you may be saved. He mentions John for their sake, because they respected him. Under investigation by men already working out how to kill him (v. 18), he says that his reason is not to win his own acquittal but to win them. While they plotted his death, he argued for their life.

In everyday life. When you have to say something hard to someone this week, check your motive first: are you speaking so that they may be saved, or so that you may be right?

Does my witness matter if I never see results? Yes. Faithful testimony goes on working after the one who gave it is silent, in rooms they never entered, long after everyone but God has forgotten them. John was probably in prison, perhaps already dead, when Jesus cited him. Your words to a child, a friend or a colleague may be called as evidence by the Spirit years from now. Speak truly, and leave the timing to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John was a lamp, truly alight, and they enjoyed his light for a while, but never followed it to the daylight it was lit for.

A burning and shining lamp. A lamp, not the light itself (1:8). The word is lychnos, the ordinary oil lamp you carry into a room after dark: burning with zeal, shining to give light, but still only the thing you use until morning. The tense is past: by now John was probably in prison.

For a while. Literally ‘for an hour’. The whole country went out to the Jordan (Matthew 3:5), and it lasted about as long as such things last. They did not follow where he pointed: enthusiasm without repentance. Now the daylight it was lit for stands before them, and they are working out how to kill him.

The lamps pass. Christ is the light; every faithful preacher is only a lamp lit by him, burning for a while and then put out. The lamps pass, but the light of the world shines on, and the city to come has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23).

Enjoying is not following. There is a way of consuming preaching as an experience: hearing a man who is genuinely alight, feeling something, discussing it warmly, and being at the end of the season exactly where you started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous. It feels like following, and it is only enjoying.

Is it wrong to have a favourite preacher? Not in itself; it is right to thank God for preachers who help you. But the Corinthians turned admiration into parties, “I follow Paul”, “I follow Apollos”, and Paul rebuked them (1 Corinthians 3:4–7). A good preacher, like John, is a finger aimed at Christ, and a good hearer follows where the finger points. If you would stop going to church when your favourite preacher leaves, it may be the lamp you love and not the light.

parallels.desc: I have prepared a lamp for my anointed

verseByVerse.quote: "But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ works, given him by the Father to finish, are a greater witness than John’s, and through them the Father himself testifies that he sent his Son.

Greater than that of John. First, the works the Father has given him to accomplish, culminating in the cross (17:4; 19:30): not demonstrations he chose, but an assignment to be finished, the same word as in 4:34. The healing at the pool was not an improvisation but an item on a schedule, as was every other sign in this book, and the last one.

The works bear witness. The works show who he is (10:25, 37–38; 14:11), and they outrank the Baptist for a simple reason. John’s testimony was a man’s word, and men have been wrong. A man who had been on the ground for most of his life is walking through Jerusalem carrying his bed, and that fact depends on no one’s credibility. Either it happened or it did not.

The Father has borne witness. Perfect tense: a lasting testimony. When? The Gospel offers several answers: the Spirit descending and remaining at the Jordan, which the Baptist saw and reported (1:32–34); the Scriptures, which he is about to name; and most simply the works themselves, since it is the Father who gives them. Each witness alone could be argued with. Together they make a strong case, and in this room the problem was not a shortage of evidence, which is why the next words turn from the evidence to the men.

Where can I see Jesus’ works today? In the written record first, given for this very purpose (20:31). But also in what he goes on doing by his Spirit through his church: sinners converted, drunkards made sober, enemies reconciled, the dying unafraid, the gospel spreading through every nation as he said it would. These do not replace Scripture, but they are the living fruit of the finished work, and they bear witness too. Look for them, and tell others what you have seen.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: "His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all their religion, Jesus’ accusers have never truly heard God or seen him, and his word does not live in them; the proof is that they do not believe the one he sent.

Never heard, never seen. Here the discourse turns, and it should be felt as an insult before it is understood as a diagnosis. The most religiously accomplished men in the nation are told that they have never heard God’s voice, never seen his form, and do not have his word living in them. At Sinai Israel heard God’s voice and saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12). The invisible Father, whose voice no sinner could bear and whose form no eye has seen, has shown his face in Jesus Christ (14:9).

His word abiding in you. The phrase looks ahead to the vine (15:4, 7). What they lack is not information about God, which they had in quantity, but God’s word taking up residence. It is possible to know the whole text and never have it live in you.

You do not believe. The proof: when the Word of God stood in front of them, they did not recognise him. The Father makes himself known through the Son, so trying to know God while bypassing Jesus is not another road to God. It does not reach him. The trial has changed sides: it opened with Jesus in the dock, and now the men who convened the hearing are being examined. The finding is not that they weighed the evidence wrongly. The evidence was never the problem.

But Israel heard God’s voice at Sinai, and Moses saw his glory. Jesus is not denying that, but saying that these hearers have not truly heard or seen, since God’s word does not abide in them (v. 38). And no one has seen the Father as he is (1:18; Exodus 33:20); the appearances of God in the Old Testament were real but partial, and many believe they were appearances of the Son himself.

Why do good arguments sometimes change nothing? Because the difficulty is not always in the evidence. Anyone who has argued about the faith with someone they love has watched a good case land on nothing. Sometimes the argument is worth improving, but this verse describes a condition in which no quantity of evidence will be enough, because the problem lies in the heart. Knowing that keeps us praying for someone, not merely preparing for the next conversation. Only God can open the heart (Acts 16:14).

parallels.desc: you heard the sound of words, but saw no form

verseByVerse.quote: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They searched the Scriptures for life, but would not come to the one the Scriptures point to, who alone gives that life.

You search the Scriptures. They studied the Old Testament with great diligence; later Jewish tradition remembers scribes counting its letters. They were serious Bible students.

In them. A saying attributed to Hillel runs: “the more study of the law, the more life” (Mishnah Avot 2:7). The sentence turns on a preposition they got wrong. The life was thought to be located in the text, obtainable by handling it. Jesus does not deny that the Scriptures give life; he denies that the life is in the text itself, and not in the one it points to.

They bear witness about me. The purpose of Scripture is to point to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). The Scriptures are the fourth witness in his case, and no one calls a witness so that the court may admire the witness.

You refuse to come. The problem was their will: not ‘you cannot’, not ‘you have not understood’, but “you refuse”. Men had bent over scrolls for a lifetime, tracing every promise of the one who was to come, and he stands in the room, having just healed a man. The distance between the text and the person was a few feet, and they would not cross it.

The search that never wants to arrive. Our culture admires the seeker more than the finder. The German writer Gotthold Lessing gave the mood its classic form in the eighteenth century: if God held all truth in his right hand and, in his left, the endless striving after truth, he wrote, he would humbly choose the left. There is something noble in that, and something evasive. A search that never ends never has to ask anything of me; a destination would. These men were devoted searchers, and their searching had become a place to stay, a way of being busy about God without ever coming to him. Jesus is not hostile to questions; he is what the questions were for. And arriving does not end the adventure: whoever comes to him finds the seeking turn into knowing a person, and a person, unlike an open question, is never used up. Eternity will not be long enough to finish knowing him.

Am I in danger of reading the Bible like this? This is aimed at people who read their Bibles, so it is better felt than pointed at someone else. A person can study Scripture seriously as a closed system, enjoying the tracing of themes and the satisfaction of a passage finally coming clear, and the exercise can end in itself. It feels like devotion, and it can go on for years without once arriving at a person. The remedy is not to study less but to study prayerfully, asking at every passage what it shows of Christ and how you will come to him because of it. After the last passage you studied, did you end up knowing something, or wanting him? Only one is what the text was for.

How does “you refuse to come” fit with “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (6:44)? The inability is not that people want to come and are prevented, but that their wills are bound by love of themselves and their own glory (v. 44). They cannot because they will not, and that is why they are responsible. Only the Father’s drawing changes the will.

Uncertain wording. The Greek for “you search” has the same form as the command ‘Search’, and the King James Version reads it so; searching is rightly commended elsewhere (Acts 17:11). But the context favours a statement: they were searching, and missing the one the Scriptures spoke of.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus needs no one’s praise, and so he can tell these men the truth: for all their religion, they do not love God.

I do not receive glory from people. He seeks his Father’s glory (7:18; 8:50). With no stake in their good opinion, his assessment of them is not coloured by what he needs from them, and a man who wants nothing from you is the only one who can tell you the truth about yourself.

The love of God within you. Despite their religiousness they did not love God; if they did, they would love the one he sent (8:42). They are failing not mainly a logic test but a love test. To have the love of God within you is for God himself to have become your joy, so that you are glad when he is honoured and grieved when he is not (Matthew 22:37), the one thing no religious activity can counterfeit.

Why this sentence is frightening. These men would have passed every other test: attendance, orthodoxy, knowledge of the text, moral seriousness, faithful keeping of the feasts. And it explains the whole chapter. They watched a man paralysed for decades get up and walk, and their only response was a rule about carrying. Nothing in them leapt. A person who loves God cannot watch God act and feel only procedural concern; the loving gets in the way. Their reaction was not a failure of information. It showed accurately what was in them.

What if I fear this describes me? Then take comfort: the men in this passage were entirely untroubled by the question, and your anxiety shows that you care about loving God. And the remedy is not to work up an affection, for love for God is not manufactured by an effort of will. It is what happens when a person actually sees him, which is what Jesus spent this chapter offering. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Look at his love for you in Christ, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5).

Uncertain wording. “The love of God” can mean love for God or God’s love; the Greek permits both, and in this Gospel the two are never far apart. The context, which asks whether these men love the God they claim to serve, points chiefly to love for God.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The root of their unbelief is that they live for one another’s praise, so they reject the one who comes in God’s name and would welcome anyone who flattered them.

In my Father’s name. He comes with his Father’s authority, representing him, and he is rejected: “his own people did not receive him” (1:11).

Another in his own name. False messiahs who came on their own authority were often welcomed; in AD 132 Simon bar Kokhba led a disastrous revolt, and Rabbi Akiba is said to have hailed him as Messiah. A man sent by God, pointing away from himself, asks us to submit to God’s choice. A man who comes on his own authority lets his followers feel they have picked their own leader, and that flatters them.

Glory from one another. The root of their unbelief is love of human praise (12:42–43). “Glory” here means reputation, the opinion others hold of you. These men held a currency they issued to each other: standing, deference, the seat at the front, the title in the street. It could only be earned from those inside the system, so it could only be kept by not leaving. Belief in Jesus would have cost each of them everything the system paid. A man cannot pursue two kinds of honour that exclude each other; he will take the one he is nearer to.

The glory that comes from the only God. The way out is in the same verse. He does not tell them to want no approval at all, but that they are seeking it from people who have nothing lasting to give. God’s approval is the honour that matters, and Christ will one day say to his servants, “well done”. He refused the glory men offered and received the glory the Father gave, and now shares it with those who trust him: “The glory that you have given me I have given to them” (17:22).

In everyday life. Think of the decisions you would make differently if nobody you respected ever found out: what you would say in a meeting, which opinion you would voice, whether you would mention Christ in a particular room. That gap shows how much you live for “glory from one another”. But in Christ the only God has already given you his approval, and it is not withdrawn when you fail.

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely: a good name is valued (Proverbs 22:1), but people’s opinion must not decide what you say and do about Christ (Proverbs 29:25).

How do I seek the glory that comes from God? Not by trying harder to stop caring what people think. The hunger for honour does not die by being starved; it is displaced by a better meal. Start from what you already have. In Christ the Father’s delight rests on you before you have done anything, because it rests on his Son (Matthew 3:17; Ephesians 1:6). Name the audience. When you catch yourself rehearsing what someone will think, ask quietly whose verdict you are working for, and turn the answer into prayer. Do some good in secret. Jesus told us to give and pray “in secret”, trusting the Father “who sees in secret” (Matthew 6:4, 6). Say the costly true thing. Once this week, mention Christ or take a stand where it may cost you a little standing, and notice that you survive it. Look at the one who went without it. Jesus was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3), and he did not need their glory, because he had his Father’s. Joined to him, neither do you.

parallels.desc: Theudas and Judas the Galilean

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will not need to accuse them: Moses, the one they trust, already does, because he wrote about Christ and they will not believe him.

I will not accuse you. The reversal is complete. They convened this hearing and have been the prosecution throughout; now the defendant says he will not prosecute. For one second it sounds like mercy, and then the sentence finishes.

One who accuses you. Moses, the giver of the law they trusted, the name that gave them standing, will be their prosecutor. The law they thought would save them will condemn them (Romans 3:19–20). Yet the curse Moses pronounced on all who break the law, Christ bore himself, becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

He wrote of me. Moses wrote of Christ: the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the offspring of Abraham (Genesis 22:18), the ruler from Judah (Genesis 49:10), the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14), and above all the prophet like Moses: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me” (Deuteronomy 18:15–18). And the claim is larger than a few predictions: the whole body of his writing was about him, the tabernacle and the glory that filled it, the priest who went in with blood once a year, the rock that gave water, each written by a man who saw only part of what he was describing. So the disagreement in this room is not between a Jewish teacher and a Christian innovation, but about what Moses was for. Jesus claims him as his own witness and tells the men holding the scrolls that they have misread the author they built their lives on.

Did Moses really write the first five books? Jesus treats it as settled that Moses wrote (compare Mark 12:26; Luke 24:27, 44), and he means the books of the law. That need not mean Moses wrote every line: the account of his death (Deuteronomy 34) was plainly added by another hand, and many believing scholars allow for some later editing; but Jesus treats the law as Moses’ own testimony.

parallels.desc: a witness against you

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If they will not believe what Moses wrote, they will not believe what Jesus says, for faith in Scripture and faith in Christ stand or fall together.

His writings … my words. They claimed to honour Moses but did not truly believe him, and Jesus places his own words alongside Moses’ writings. The logic is simple. Moses wrote of Christ. They do not believe Christ. Therefore they do not, in any sense that matters, believe Moses, whatever they think they are doing when they read him. The chapter ends on a question left unanswered, which is the point: the answer would have to come from the men it was asked of.

The problem is not the medium. People unpersuaded by Scripture are not waiting for a better delivery. These men had the writings, the works, the Baptist, the Father’s testimony, and the man himself, available for questions.

Stand back and see the whole chapter. It opened with a man who could not get himself to the water, who had nobody, and he was made whole. It closes with the most scripturally literate men in the nation, who had every witness heaven could produce, and would not come. The man on the mat had no friends, no theology, and a voice telling him to stand up, and he got up; the men with all the evidence stayed sitting down. Between the two lies the sentence that explains both: the Son gives life to whom he will.

Should I trust the Old Testament as much as the words of Jesus? Yes. Jesus puts Moses’ writings and his own words side by side, and treats doubting one as the road to doubting the other. He quoted the Old Testament as settling arguments and said, “Scripture cannot be broken” (10:35). The whole Bible is one book with one Author and one subject, and the Old Testament is not a lesser Bible to be outgrown but the testimony to Christ that Jesus himself used. Read both Testaments with the same trust, because the Lord you love trusted both.

5.title: The Son Has Life in Himself
5.text: <sup>1</sup>After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.<sup>3</sup>In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.<sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?”<sup>7</sup>The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.”<sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.<sup>10</sup>So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.”<sup>11</sup>But he answered them, “The man who healed me, that man said to me, ’Take up your bed, and walk.’”<sup>12</sup>They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ’Take up your bed and walk’?”<sup>13</sup>Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.<sup>14</sup>Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.”<sup>15</sup>The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.<sup>16</sup>And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”<sup>18</sup>This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.<sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise.<sup>20</sup>For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.<sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.<sup>22</sup>For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,<sup>23</sup>that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.<sup>25</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.<sup>26</sup>For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.<sup>27</sup>And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.<sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice<sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.<sup>30</sup>“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>31</sup>If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.<sup>32</sup>There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.<sup>33</sup>You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth.<sup>34</sup>Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.<sup>35</sup>He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.<sup>36</sup>But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.<sup>37</sup>And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen,<sup>38</sup>and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.<sup>39</sup>You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,<sup>40</sup>yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.<sup>41</sup>I do not receive glory from people.<sup>42</sup>But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.<sup>43</sup>I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.<sup>44</sup>How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?<sup>45</sup>Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.<sup>46</sup>For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.<sup>47</sup>But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”
5.overview:
Where we are. After welcome in Samaria and Galilee (chapter 4), Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for a feast. The third sign, a healing at the pool of Bethesda, sets off the first plot against his life, and from here the controversy rises through chapters 5–10.

The message. Jesus is not merely a healer sent from God; he is the Son who does everything the Father does. He gives life to whom he will, all judgment is in his hands, and he is to be honoured just as the Father is honoured. Whoever hears his word and comes to him has already passed from death to life; whoever refuses has rejected the Father too, however devoutly he reads his Bible.

Why it was said. John wrote so that his readers might believe and have life (20:31). Many had paid a price for confessing Jesus, some put out of the synagogue (see the introduction), and the question between them and their accusers was the question of verse 18: is Jesus equal with God? Here Jesus answers it himself.

How the chapter makes its case. At the pool (vv. 1–9) Jesus heals with a word a man who has lain there thirty-eight years with no one to help him, on the Sabbath. The authorities see only a man carrying his mat (vv. 10–16), and when Jesus answers, “My Father is working until now, and I am working”, they rightly hear a claim to equality with God, and seek to kill him (vv. 17–18). He unfolds the claim (vv. 19–29): the Son does what the Father does, gives life now to the spiritually dead who hear his voice, and will raise and judge all the dead. Then he calls his witnesses: John, his works, the Father and the Scriptures (vv. 30–40). Finally the trial turns on its judges, who do not love God, live for one another’s praise, and will be accused by Moses himself (vv. 41–47).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to the cross and the empty tomb. The plot that begins here (v. 18) ends with the charge that “he has made himself the Son of God” (19:7). The one who has life in himself laid it down and bore the judgment, so that whoever believes “does not come into judgment” (v. 24), and his own opened tomb is the pledge that “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice” (v. 28).

For us. We cannot get ourselves to the water; Christ comes to us where we lie and speaks. Yet we can read the Bible for years without coming to him. Hear his word, believe the Father who sent him, and rest in the verdict already given: whoever believes has passed from death to life.

keyVerse.quote: Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on the claim that life and judgment belong to the Son, and this verse tells us what that means for anyone who hears him. The healed man stood up at his word, and the scholars who would not come to him stayed where they were; here Jesus says how the dead come to life: by hearing his word and believing the Father who sent him. The verdict on such a person is not pending but given, because the Judge himself bore the judgment.

5.reflection:
Jesus asked a man who had waited thirty-eight years, “Do you want to be healed?” (v. 6), and the man answered by explaining why nothing could change (v. 7). Is there something you have stopped hoping or praying for? What would it mean to bring that desire honestly to Christ again?

The authorities saw a man walking for the first time in thirty-eight years and could only say that he was breaking a rule (v. 10). How can sincere Christians come to see rules more clearly than people? Where might you be in danger of it?

Jesus says that whoever hears his word and believes “does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (v. 24). How should this shape the way you think about your failures and about the last day?

The men who searched the Scriptures most carefully would not come to Jesus, and he traced their unbelief to seeking “glory from one another” (vv. 39–44). How can we read the Bible so that it brings us to Christ? Where does the wish for others’ approval hold you back from following him openly?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus gives the hungry more than they need from almost nothing, and then shows his frightened disciples who he is. On a hillside at Passover he sees the crowd’s need before anyone asks, tests Philip, takes a boy’s five barley loaves and feeds five thousand until they are full, with twelve baskets left over (vv. 1–13). The crowd hails him as the Prophet and tries to make him king by force, but he refuses a throne of bread and withdraws alone (vv. 14–15). That night the disciples row against the wind without him, until he comes walking on the sea, speaks the words “It is I; do not be afraid”, and brings them at once to land (vv. 16–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Together the two signs show Jesus as Lord of provision and Lord of the sea. On his words on the water, “It is I”, see the note on vv. 19–20; on the crowd that wants to crown him, see vv. 14–15.
verseByVerse.examples: Philip’s sum was correct, but he answered the wrong question (see vv. 6–7). And walking on the sea is the most revealing of the nature miracles (see vv. 19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great crowd follows Jesus across the lake, drawn by what he does for the sick rather than by who he is. By the end of the chapter it will have thinned to a handful (vv. 66–67).

The Sea of Tiberias. Another name for the Sea of Galilee, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore around AD 20 and named after the emperor Tiberius.

Because they saw the signs. They followed for the miracles, not for who he was (v. 26): understandable, but not yet faith. In this Gospel a sign is never an end in itself (20:30–31). The healings were the old promises coming true (Isaiah 35:5–6), each a finger pointing at the healer. The crowd was right to follow the signs and wrong to stop at them, and this chapter is the day he tells them what the finger was pointing at.

In the flow. Jesus had just told the leaders in Jerusalem that Moses wrote of him (5:46), and chapter 6 is full of Moses: Passover, a mountain, bread in the wilderness, a crossing of the sea, a grumbling people and a demand for manna. At every point Jesus is shown to be not the one who passes on bread from heaven, but the bread himself. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus recorded in all four Gospels.

He fed them anyway. They were following for the wrong reason, and he did not begin by correcting their motives; he began by giving them lunch. He is kind to the ungrateful and generous to the half-hearted. The rebuke comes the next morning.

Is it wrong if I first came to Christ for what I needed from him? No; almost nobody arrives for adequate reasons. People come because a marriage is failing, a child is ill, or the fear of dying has become concrete, and each is a version of wanting the loaves. This chapter does not despise that beginning: Jesus received the crowd and fed them. What he will not do is leave anyone there. The question is not why you first came, but whether you are now coming to him for himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named after the emperor Tiberius.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sits on the hillside as a teacher, but what he gives there is first a meal, and only afterwards its meaning. The crowd delighted by the bread will be offended by the explanation: it is possible to enjoy what Christ does and find what he says intolerable.

Jesus went up on the mountain. The hills east of the lake, and an echo of Moses going up the mountain (Exodus 19; 24). He goes up before the crowd arrives, and again by himself after they have gone (v. 15), Mark tells us to pray (Mark 6:46).

Greater than Moses on the mountain. Moses went up to receive what God gave and came down to pass it on, faithful as a servant in God’s house (Hebrews 3:5). Jesus goes up and sits, the posture of a teacher (Matthew 5:1) with authority of his own, and what follows comes from his own hands: “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (1:17). Moses could only tell Israel where the manna came from. This teacher will feed them himself, and then tell them that he is the bread.

The same Lord sat down in the grass. When God came down on Sinai, the mountain was fenced and the people begged not to hear his voice again (Exodus 19:12; 20:19).
