On a Galilean hill the same Lord sat down in the grass with fishermen around him. His people have not come to a mountain that burns but to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 12:18–24).

How can I find time to be alone with God when life is so full? Jesus’ days were fuller than yours, and he still withdrew, as a habit. Begin small and regular: a set time, a set place, a Bible and a few minutes of prayer, even in the car before work or after the children are asleep. Protect it as you would a meeting with someone you love. The aim is not a perfect routine but real fellowship with the Father, which feeds everything else you do.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, "Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Passover time Jesus sees the hungry crowd before anyone asks, and draws Philip into the question of how to feed them.

Now the Passover was at hand. The second of the three Passovers John mentions (2:13; 11:55), and it colours the whole chapter: unleavened bread, a lamb killed, and behind them the memory of bread that came down morning by morning for forty years. At the next Passover Jesus would give his flesh for the life of the world (v. 51), dying as the Passover lamb (19:36).

A large crowd coming. Jesus sees the need and moves first; in Matthew and Mark the disciples even suggest sending everyone away. Before we know we are hungry, he has planned the meal.

Jesus said to Philip. Philip was from nearby Bethsaida (1:44) and might be expected to know where food could be bought.

Where are we to buy bread? An echo of Moses: “Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?” (Numbers 11:13). Note the pronoun: “we”, not “they”. Jesus includes Philip in a responsibility Philip has not accepted and could not discharge. That is how the test is set: by quietly making the crowd’s hunger his problem too.

Does Jesus expect me to meet needs I cannot possibly meet? He expects you to care about them and bring them to him, not to supply what only he can; “we” means you are included in the work, not left to do it alone. When a need is too big for you, the hungry, the lonely, the lost, do not look away and do not despair. Bring it to Christ in prayer, offer what you have, and do the part he gives you. He knows what he will do.
verseByVerse.note: This is the second Passover John mentions; the Passover setting prepares for Jesus’ words about bread and his flesh and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ question was a test for Philip’s sake: he already knew what he would do, and Philip answered with a correct sum and no hope.

He said this to test him. To stretch Philip’s faith: would he look to his own resources, or to Jesus?

He himself knew. One of the kindest asides in the Gospel. The crowd’s dinner did not depend on Philip passing the test: the question came from someone who had already decided, so that the man being asked might find out what was in him.

Two hundred denarii. A denarius was a day’s wage (as the ESV notes), so this was about eight months’ wages. Philip’s sum is correct; his problem is not his arithmetic. He was asked where the bread would come from, and answered how much it would cost. Whoever turns every question about God’s provision into a question about available resources will always arrive at the same answer: always right, and always beside the point.

In everyday life. Is there a situation you have been treating as a budget problem rather than a question about God? Do the sums, by all means; then ask where the bread will come from.

Why does God test us if he already knows what is in us? Not to inform himself, but to show us and strengthen us. His tests are not entrance examinations with the result pending. They let us discover where our own arithmetic runs out, which we need to know and can learn no other way, and they prove and refine faith as gold is refined by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). God never tests in order to make his children fall (James 1:13); he tests to make them stand.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: where am I to get meat?

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, said to him, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Andrew brings the little that is there, a poor boy’s lunch, and says honestly that it is nothing for so many; it is all Jesus needs.

Five barley loaves. Only John mentions the boy and the barley. Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor, a child’s packed lunch of the plainest kind; the fish were probably small, dried or pickled.

But what are they for so many? Andrew is again bringing someone to Jesus, as he brought his brother (1:41) and will bring the Greeks (12:22). It is easy to look down on him for this half of his sentence, but he alone has gone and looked. Philip did the sum; Andrew found out what was actually there, and brings it, saying out loud that it is absurd and bringing it anyway. That is not weak faith. It is the posture the chapter requires: hands out, holding something insufficient, with no idea what will happen.

The Elisha story underneath. Elisha once had twenty barley loaves, a servant who objected, “How can I set this before a hundred men?”, a command to give, and food left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Andrew’s sentence is almost the servant’s. What differs is the scale, and the source. Elisha fed a hundred from twenty loaves, speaking as a messenger: “for thus says the LORD, ‘They shall eat and have some left’” (2 Kings 4:43). Jesus feeds five thousand from five, and quotes no one. He gives thanks, and the bread multiplies in his own hands. The prophet passed on the word of God; this man is the Word, and the bread is his to give.

What if what I have to offer seems ridiculously small? Then you are in good company: a boy with five cheap loaves. Jesus does not ask for enough; he asks for what you have. Put your few hours, weak prayers and stumbling words in his hands, and let him decide what they are for. The miracle began not with abundance but with an offering. Nothing suggests Jesus wanted the disciples to feel confident. He wanted the loaves.
verseByVerse.note: Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Have the people sit down." Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus seats the crowd like guests at a banquet, gives thanks to his Father, and from his own hands feeds every one of them until they want no more.

Have the people sit down. The word means recline, as guests did at a banquet. About five thousand men sat, and with women and children many more (Matthew 14:21).

Much grass. Spring, at Passover, turning a hillside into a dining room: “green pastures” (Psalm 23:2). Mark says Jesus had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34); four chapters later Jesus will say, “I am the good shepherd.”

When he had given thanks. Having given thanks (eucharistēsas): the word the church would take for its central meal. John mentions only the thanksgiving, perhaps pointing to the Lord’s Supper, which he never describes. Jesus probably said a blessing like the one Jewish households still say before eating, whose core is recorded in the Mishnah (Berakhot 6:1): “blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.” Said over five loaves before five thousand people, one of the most ordinary sentences in Jewish life turned out to be true as never before.

He distributed them. The other Gospels tell us the disciples carried the food to the crowd, but John keeps every eye on Jesus: the bread came from his hands, a picture the chapter will explain when he says the bread he gives is his flesh (v. 51).

As much as they wanted. Not the little piece each that Philip had calculated could not be managed, but everyone eating until they stopped wanting more. He is the host who never rations his grace.

Should Christians still give thanks before meals? Yes, and this verse is one reason why. Jesus gave thanks before he gave the bread, and everything created by God is good and is made holy by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). A short prayer at the table confesses that every meal comes from the Father’s hand, and keeps us from eating like the crowd, who enjoyed the bread and never looked up at the giver.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add here that the disciples carried the food to the people, but the earliest copies of John do not.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost." So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all had eaten their fill, Jesus had the leftovers gathered so that nothing would be lost, a first glimpse of how he keeps his people.

That nothing may be lost. Only John records this command. The man who made the meal could make another, and the first thing he says after five thousand have eaten is: pick up the bits. In him extravagance and carefulness are not opposites; his abundance is never wasteful.

Twelve baskets. More left over than at the start: perhaps one for each apostle, perhaps a hint of the twelve tribes. What is handed over to him comes back larger.

The word lost. To be destroyed or lost (apollymi): the verb runs through the rest of the chapter and on into the Gospel. Jesus will soon say that the Father’s will is that he should lose nothing of all the Father has given him (v. 39), and when the soldiers come, John says this fulfilled the word: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one” (18:9). So the barley crusts in the grass are the first instalment of a promise about people. The one who sends men round a hillside so that a scrap of a poor child’s lunch is not wasted will not lose a single person the Father has given him.

What if I feel like a scrap, not worth keeping? Then this verse was written for you. He sent his disciples after crumbs anyone else would have let lie in the grass; if he cares for crusts, he cares far more for the people the Father has given him. Your worth to him rests not on how whole or impressive you feel, but on his love and his promise. He does not lose what is his.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd rightly sees in Jesus the Prophet like Moses but tries to make him a bread-king by force, and he refuses.

The Prophet. The prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15). Right about who Jesus is and wrong about what he is for, five thousand people went up a hill with a crown.

To make him king. A political Messiah to lead a revolt against Rome, at the feast of liberation. The verb is violent: harpazein, to seize, used of a wolf carrying off a sheep (10:12). The danger here comes not from the authorities but from an adoring mob who have decided what he is for.

Jesus withdrew again. His kingdom is not of this world (18:36), and this was the temptation Satan offered in the wilderness (Matthew 4:8–10): a crown without a cross. He does not refuse the kingship; he is the King, and will say so to Pilate. He refuses a kingship on their terms: a bread-king, crowned by popular demand, who solves the food problem and then the Roman problem and never goes near a cross. So he walked away up a hill in the dark to talk with his Father.

He refused the throne of bread. He would not be crowned by a crowd, because he had come to be crowned with thorns. He refused the throne of bread so that he could take the throne of the cross, and from there the throne of heaven.

Is it wrong to want Jesus to solve my problems? It is not wrong to bring him your problems; he invites it. It is wrong to try to make him king on your terms, a Saviour who exists to deliver your agenda. The crowd wanted bread, political freedom and no cross. He gives far more, in his way: through his death, by his Spirit, for eternity. When he does not do what you want, it is not because he cannot, but because he is King, and his plans are better.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised. Many hoped for a Messiah who would lead a revolt against Rome.

parallels.desc: my kingdom is not of this world

verseByVerse.quote: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples obey and set out across the lake, and night falls with Jesus not yet with them: obedience did not keep them out of the dark, but his absence had an end.

His disciples went down to the sea. Mark says Jesus made them go (Mark 6:45), perhaps to remove them from the crowd’s political excitement. After the best day of their lives, five thousand fed and a crowd trying to crown their master, by evening they are alone on black water. Anyone who has had a high Sunday followed by a Monday will recognise the pattern.

It was now dark. In John, darkness often carries more than the time of day (3:2; 13:30). The weather is real, not an allegory, but a reader cannot hear that it was dark and Jesus had not yet come without remembering its first page: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (1:5); and later, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness” (8:12). The disciples’ darkness is measured by his absence, and it will end not at sunrise, but when he reaches them.

Jesus had not yet come. Two facts sit side by side, and John softens neither: they are exactly where they should be, doing what they were told; and it is dark, and he is not there. But writing decades later, knowing how the night ended, he puts in the word “yet”, and it is the only comfort in the sentence: not that the darkness is short, or that it means something, but that his absence has an end. He sends his people out across black water, and he is never not coming.

Why does God sometimes seem absent when I am trying to obey him? Seeming absent is not being absent. The disciples were in the boat by his command, he had gone up the mountain to pray, and he saw them in the dark (Mark 6:46–48). Scripture is honest that believers pass through seasons when God feels far away (Psalm 13:1; 88). In them, keep rowing in the direction he sent you, keep to his word and prayer, and remember the “yet”. He has not forgotten you, and he will come.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A storm blows up on the lake: ordinary weather, not a punishment, striking men who were doing exactly what Jesus had told them.

The sea became rough. One sentence, with no dramatics. The lake lies about seven hundred feet below sea level in a bowl of hills, and cold air spilling down the ravines brings squalls with little warning. It is weather, not a supernatural assault, and the men rowing into it were fishermen who knew the lake.

The wind he made. All things were made through the Word (1:3), that night’s wind among them, and soon he would walk on top of the water it was stirring.

Sometimes the wind is simply the wind. John does not say the storm came because they had done wrong, or to teach them a lesson. Much harm is done by treating every hardship as a message. In a world under the curse boats get caught out on lakes, and being in the middle of obeying God when it happens is not evidence of anything.

Is every hardship a sign that God is displeased with me? No. God does discipline his children in love (Hebrews 12:6), and sometimes trouble is the fruit of our own sin. But many hardships are simply part of life in a fallen world, and God uses them for our good without their being punishments (Romans 8:28). The disciples were in the storm because they obeyed. Do not torment yourself decoding every trial. Confess any sin you know of, trust your Father’s love, and look for the Lord who comes across the water.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds are common.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes to his terrified disciples walking on the sea, doing what only God does, and calms them with the words of God’s own name: “It is I; do not be afraid.”

Three or four miles. Literally twenty-five or thirty stadia (as the ESV notes): roughly halfway across. Mark says the wind was against them (Mark 6:48).

Walking on the sea. In the Old Testament God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19), and the sea pictures chaos; Jesus walks on it as its master. Mark adds, “He meant to pass by them” (Mark 6:48), which sounds like indifference until you know that passing by is the language of God showing himself, as he passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:22) and Elijah at the cave (1 Kings 19:11). The waves Job says God tramples were under a pair of ordinary feet with the dust of a Galilean hillside still on them.

And they were frightened. The right response, recorded without embarrassment. When the holy God draws near, the right first response of sinful creatures is fear (Isaiah 6:5), and the comfort that follows means something only because the fear was real.

It is I. Literally “I am” (egō eimi): an ordinary way of saying “it is me”, rightly translated so, and also the divine name (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10–11), the two words behind the burning bush on which this Gospel will build seven declarations.

Do not be afraid. God’s word to his people throughout Scripture (Isaiah 43:1–2). They are not told there is nothing to fear, but who it is: the one on the water is the one whose sea it is.

The first thing he said was his name. The voice that said “It is I” over the black water will say “I am he” in a garden at night, and armed men will draw back and fall to the ground (18:5–6). The same words flatten those who come against him and quieten those he comes to save. He walked across a storm to reach tired men who had not asked him to come, and the first thing he said was not a rebuke but his name, and he made it their peace.

In everyday life. Name the thing you are most afraid of this week, then say to yourself the words he said on the lake. He does not promise the thing will not happen. He tells you who is coming toward you across it.

Did Jesus really walk on water, or is this a story with a spiritual meaning? He really did. John presents it as something that happened, seen by the disciples on a particular night at a measured distance from shore, and the meaning depends on the event: it shows who Jesus is precisely because he did what only God does. If the Word made flesh could make bread out of five loaves and raise the dead, walking on the water he created is no difficulty. To make it a mere symbol is to lose the very thing it reveals.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear turns to gladness as they take Jesus into the boat, and at once they arrive: his presence, not their rowing, finished the journey.

Immediately at the land. Perhaps a further miracle. Psalm 107 describes men at sea whose courage melts; they cry to the LORD, he makes the storm be still, and he brings them to their desired haven (Psalm 107:23–30). John does not quote the psalm, but a reader who knows it will hear it.

The shape, not the mechanics. They had rowed for hours and covered half a lake. He steps in, and the journey is over. What they achieved by straining was real and was not enough; what finished it was his presence in the boat.

Does this mean my troubles will disappear if I have enough faith? No, and the passage itself guards against that. This crossing had a storm, hours of rowing and real fear; but the arrival did not finally depend on the rowing. Christ does not promise that faith will make difficulties evaporate. He promises to be with his people in them, and to bring them home at last.

Uncertain wording. The Greek behind “glad to take him” can also mean that they wanted to take him into the boat, leaving open whether he actually stepped in before they landed; either way, fear has turned to gladness.

parallels.desc: he brought them to their desired haven

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–71 — The Bread of Life Discourse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus himself is the bread from heaven, given in death and received by faith, and only those the Father draws will come. The crowd finds him at Capernaum wanting more loaves, and he tells them the one work God requires is to believe in the one he has sent (vv. 22–29). When they demand manna, he answers that he is the bread of life, and none who come will be cast out (vv. 30–40). Their grumbling meets the teaching that no one comes unless drawn, and their quarrel the call to eat his flesh and drink his blood (vv. 41–59). Many disciples leave; Peter confesses that there is no one else to go to, though one of the Twelve will betray him (vv. 60–71).
verseByVerse.theology: The key to the eating language is Jesus’ own explanation in v. 63 (see the notes on vv. 52–53 and 63–64). Alongside it the chapter sets the sovereignty of grace (vv. 37–40, 44–45, 65). Grace and the call to believe are held together throughout.
verseByVerse.examples: The departure of many disciples (v. 66) shows that following Jesus for his gifts is not the same as believing in him. Peter’s answer is the model for anyone facing a hard saying (see the note on v. 68).

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd works out that Jesus cannot have crossed by boat, yet never asks how he did: close attention to Jesus with no curiosity about who he is.

Only one boat. They had counted the boats: he cannot have crossed the lake. Then they cross it themselves and find him on the other side, and instead of wondering how he got there, they only ask when he arrived (v. 25). It is possible to be extremely observant about Jesus and entirely incurious.

Other boats from Tiberias. Perhaps blown across by the storm.

After the Lord had given thanks. John’s own aside calls Jesus “the Lord”, a title he rarely uses of him during the ministry, and stresses the thanksgiving: he writes as one who has since watched the same action again and again at the Lord’s Table, among churches that gave thanks over bread every week.

The Lord who gave thanks. In this Gospel “the Lord” is what Mary Magdalene calls the risen Jesus (20:18) and what Thomas confesses (20:28). The man who bowed his head over five loaves and thanked his Father, as any son of Israel would, is the Lord whom the church worships. He gave thanks as a man, and he receives thanks as God.

Can I be interested in Jesus without really knowing him? Very easily: this crowd worked out the clues and travelled to find him, and all of it stayed on the surface. Many people today read about Jesus, discuss him, even admire him, without asking the question his actions force: who is this, that he does what only God does? The cure is to stop treating him as a puzzle and come to him as a person, asking him to show you himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd crosses the lake to find Jesus, a costly search aimed at the wrong thing, and he lets himself be found.

Seeking Jesus. Diligently, but for the wrong reason (v. 26). Give them their due: it is several miles across that lake. They find him at Capernaum, the town of the synagogue (v. 59), and the search still fails, because finding Jesus and receiving him are two different things (1:11).

Effort is not evidence. It is possible to work hard at religion, to travel, give, attend and serve, in pursuit of something other than God. The energy proves the wanting; it says nothing about what is wanted.

He let himself be found. The one who slipped away from a crown the night before stands in the open next morning, ready to be questioned by the same people, because he has come to give himself and means them to hear it. Though we seek him for poor reasons, he seeks us for his own, and does not stop until he has given us himself.

How do I know if I am seeking Jesus for the right reasons? Ask what you would do if the benefits were removed: the community, the sense of purpose, the moral order, the hope of things going well. Suppose only Christ were left. Would you still cross the lake? No one answers that perfectly; mixed motives are normal, and even the apostles had them. The question is which way you are moving: toward wanting him more than his gifts. Ask him to make it so.

verseByVerse.quote: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sets aside their curiosity about when he came and tells them why they came: for the loaves, not for the one the loaves pointed to.

Rabbi, when did you come here? A polite title (Rabbi, teacher) and an idle question. They want to know when he arrived; he tells them why they came.

Not because you saw signs. They had watched the miracle but not seen it as a sign. A sign is a signpost: it points beyond itself. They had eaten the signpost and never looked where it pointed, for the bread on the grass was saying that the one who gave it is himself the bread of life (v. 35).

You ate your fill. The verb (echortasthēte) once belonged to the feeding of animals, but by this time simply meant to eat your fill (compare Matthew 5:6). Being filled up was the whole of what had happened to them: they want what he gives, not who he is.

The danger of every good gift. Nobody decides to want the gift more than the giver. It happens by ordinary appetite: we enjoy the gift, want more, and go round again, for years, without once looking at where the bread came from.

He wanted them to have him. He fed them with his own hands and now speaks hard words with the same love; a lesser benefactor would have kept the loaves coming. His bread and his rebuke come from one heart, and the rebuke is the larger gift.

Does Jesus mind that I pray for practical things? No. He taught us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11), and fed this crowd gladly. The problem is not asking for bread, but wanting only bread. Pray for your needs freely and specifically, then let every answered prayer turn your eyes to the Father who gave it and the Son who is himself the bread of life. A prayer life that is all requests and no worship has begun to eat the signpost.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not spend your life on bread that goes stale, but seek the food that lasts for ever, which the Son of Man gives and the Father guarantees.

The food that perishes. Physical food is necessary but temporary (Isaiah 55:2). “Perishes” is the verb translated “lost” in v. 12; the loaves of the day before were already going stale. Most of what we labour for is not wrong in itself. The trouble comes when we ask it to bear more than bread can bear: a career asked to give us our worth, a family asked to give us our meaning, comfort asked to give us peace. Bread asked to be God always goes stale in the hand.

The food that endures. They are to work for it, yet it is a gift. The working is not the purchasing: a man may labour hard to get to where something is being given out without having earned it. What is forbidden is not effort but effort aimed at the wrong provision.

The Father has set his seal. A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. At the baptism and through the signs the Father has stamped his Son: this one is mine, this one is true, this one I stand behind. Every promise of the gospel carries that stamp, and there is no higher guarantee to ask for.

Does this mean I should not work hard at my job? No. Scripture commands honest work and says that if anyone will not work, neither should he eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Jesus warns not against daily labour but against making it the goal of your life. Work hard for your bread, as service to Christ (Colossians 3:23), but give your deepest hope to the food that endures, and even your daily work will be changed by it.

How do I work for the food that endures? Not by earning it, for the Son of Man “will give” it, and the work turns out to be believing in him (v. 29). It means putting yourself, again and again, where he gives it out. Feed before you hurry: hear his word before the day’s demands reach you, even one Gospel paragraph read slowly. Notice what you are asking bread to do: when you are anxious about money, praise or results, tell Christ you have been asking a perishing thing for what only he can give. Come to his table and his people each Lord’s Day, where the word is preached and the Supper is set before you. Spend some of your strength where it lasts: a neighbour helped, a child taught to pray, the gospel sent further. And do it all as someone already fed, because the Father has set his seal on the Son, not on your effort.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity.

parallels.desc: why do you labour for that which does not satisfy?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they said to him, 'What must we do, to be doing the works of God?' Jesus answered them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked for the works that please God, Jesus names one: believe in the one God has sent.

What must we do, to be doing the works of God? They take “work” literally: tell us the deeds, the rules, that will earn this food. They ask about works, plural: a programme, a list. There is real sincerity in it, for a list can be worked at, progress measured, and a person can know where he stands.

This is the work of God. The plural becomes singular: not works but one work, believe. It is “the work of God” in a double sense: the work God requires, and the work God does in us (vv. 44, 65; Philippians 1:29). Salvation is not by doing but by believing in Jesus.

The easiest and the hardest answer. Easiest, because a man on his deathbed with no strength for a list can do it. Hardest, because it offers nothing to measure. A list lets a person keep control of the transaction; faith hands it over. They asked for a list, and God answered with a Person.

Him whom he has sent. Faith is not a technique or a mood; it is trust in the one God has sent, standing in front of them as he says it. Faith saves because of the one it rests on. The work that saves was done by another, on a cross, and finished, so a weak faith in a strong Saviour saves, because the strength is his.

In everyday life. If a sermon that ends without steps to take leaves you mildly frustrated, that instinct is the one in this verse. Before you do anything for God today, rest in what he has done for you.

If faith is not a work, why does Jesus call it the work of God? Because he answers their question in their own words and turns it inside out: the only work is to believe, which is to stop working for acceptance and receive it. Faith is not a contribution that earns a reward but the empty hand that takes Christ, and even that hand is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8–9). We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and the good works that follow are the fruit of salvation, never its price.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A day after eating a miracle, the crowd demands a sign to match Moses’ forty years of manna: they want a supply, and they appoint themselves judges of the evidence.

Then what sign do you do? Yesterday they ate bread that came out of nothing; this morning they ask for a sign, as though he had done nothing yet. Gratitude is short-lived, whatever the size of the mercy: the generation that walked out of Egypt through a parted sea was complaining about the food within about a month (Exodus 16:1–3).

That we may see and believe you. They are proposing terms: produce the evidence and belief will follow, with themselves as judges. Jesus never accepts that arrangement from anyone (20:29).

Our fathers ate the manna. Exodus 16. Some Jewish writings from around the end of the first century expected the manna to fall again in the days of the Messiah (2 Baruch 29:8). Moses, they imply, gave bread daily for forty years; one hillside meal was a single afternoon. They are negotiating for a supply.

Bread from heaven. Psalm 78:24; Exodus 16:4. They quote Scripture correctly and use it as a weapon against the man in front of them. Jesus will take the sentence apart word by word and show they have misread its subject (5:46).

The sign they wanted was talking to them. The manna was always a picture of him. Jesus will not give them a bigger miracle. He will give them the explanation of every miracle: himself, come down from the Father.

Why doesn’t God give more signs to convince unbelievers? Because more signs do not produce faith in an unwilling heart; this crowd had just eaten a miracle and wanted another. In Jesus’ parable Abraham says that if people do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). God has given sufficient evidence in the signs written in the Gospels, the resurrection and his word. What the unbeliever needs is not more light outside but new sight within, which is the Spirit’s work. So pray for unbelievers, and keep showing them Christ.

parallels.desc: he gave them the grain of heaven
bread from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus corrects their reading of Scripture: the manna came from God, not Moses, and the Father is giving the true bread now, a person who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

Not Moses. He corrects their quotation in two places, both in the grammar. First the subject: God said, “I am about to rain bread from heaven for you” (Exodus 16:4). The manna was never Moses’ to give; he woke up to it on the ground like everybody else.

My Father gives you the true bread. Then the tense. They said God “gave”: past, finished. He says the Father “gives”: it is happening in the room. “True” (alēthinon) means the real thing, of which the manna was a shadow.

He who comes down from heaven. The Greek can also mean “that which comes down”. Until now every hearer has assumed the bread is a thing; now it turns out to be a person (3:13), and he gives life not only to Israel but to the world, the first time Jesus says how far the bread reaches.

The manna was always too small a picture. It kept a nation alive for forty years, but it had to be gathered again the next day, went rotten if hoarded, and did not keep the generation that ate it from dying (vv. 49–50). And it cost heaven nothing. The bread of God is heaven’s own Son: it cost the Father his Son and the Son his life (3:16), and the Spirit makes it our food.

In everyday life. Your soul needs daily bread as much as your body. Before you check your phone tomorrow morning, gather your manna: a passage of Scripture, read slowly, with a prayer that Christ would feed you by it.

How is the manna a picture of Christ? In several ways (Christians call such an Old Testament picture a type). It came down from heaven, as he did. It was given freely, by grace, to people who could not feed themselves in the wilderness. It had to be received and eaten, not merely looked at. It was enough for all who gathered it (Exodus 16:18), and Paul calls it “spiritual food” (1 Corinthians 10:3). But Christ surpasses the type: the manna sustained a life that ended; he gives life that never ends.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Sir, give us this bread always." Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not merely give the bread of life; he is it, and whoever comes to him and believes in him will never hunger or thirst.

Sir, give us this bread always. Like the Samaritan woman (4:15), they still think of physical bread: asking for the right thing and meaning the wrong one.

I am the bread of life. The first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John: the bread of life (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the door (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), the true vine (15:1). “I am” (egō eimi) echoes the divine name: the great I AM, who fed Israel in the desert, says that he himself is the food of the soul. Most of the seven take something ordinary and say: I am the thing itself, and every example you have met was the picture. And bread comes first, not the grander light: the plainest, most daily thing in the world, said to people in a district where a bad harvest meant a funeral.

Shall not hunger. Coming to Jesus is like eating; believing in him is like drinking (4:14). Coming and believing are the same thing: in this Gospel faith is not an inward opinion but a movement toward a person. Every human being is running an experiment on what will finally satisfy, and has found the answers temporary. He is not offering to improve the supply. He is saying the appetite ends in him.

In the flow. The whole chapter turns on verse 35. The sign, the night on the sea and the demand for manna lead to it, and the coming (vv. 37–40), the drawing (vv. 44–46) and the eating (vv. 51–58) unfold it. If a reader holds on to one sentence of John 6, it should be this one.

In everyday life. Pay attention to your hungers today: for approval, comfort, distraction, control. Each time you feel one, take it to Christ in a short prayer, and ask him to be what that hunger is really looking for.

What does it mean to feed on Christ day by day? To keep coming to him and believing in him, drawing your life from him as you draw strength from food: hearing and reading his word, for his words are spirit and life (v. 63); praying to him; trusting his death for you afresh when you are guilty; coming to his table; resting on his promises when you are afraid. Faith is not a single meal but a daily diet. You do not eat once and live for ever on the memory; you go back to the table.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: come, buy and eat

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd has seen Jesus himself and still does not believe: unbelief is not a lack of evidence. Faith takes something more, and Jesus names it next: the Father’s giving and drawing (vv. 37, 44).

You have seen me. Not “you have seen my works”, though they had, but “you have seen me”. They have had him in front of them for a whole day, with a meal in between. The disciples could say, “we have seen his glory” (1:14); this crowd looked at the same face and saw a man who might keep the bread coming.

If only we had been there. We may think we would have believed if we had been there. But the people who watched him make bread out of nothing are the people he calls unbelieving.

In everyday life. Pray for those who have seen and heard and still do not believe; only God can open their eyes. Choose one person you have been trying to convince, and this week spend more time praying for them than arguing with them.

Would I believe more easily if God gave me more evidence? Probably not. The crowd had more evidence than you will ever have, and it did not produce faith; not because evidence is worthless, but because the problem lies deeper than the mind. Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ, opened to the heart by the Spirit (Romans 10:17). If you struggle to believe, do not wait for a sign. Go to the Gospels, read what he said and did, and ask the Father to give you eyes to see. That is a prayer he delights to answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone the Father gives to the Son will certainly come to him, and everyone who comes, whoever they are, he will never turn away.

All that the Father gives me. The Father has given a people to the Son (17:2, 6, 9, 24), and they are given before they come. “All” of them will come: not might, but will. This is unconditional election and effectual calling: the Father chooses a people, gives them to the Son, and draws them so that they certainly come (v. 44). Unconditional means the choice rests on God’s free love, not on anything he foresaw in them (Ephesians 1:4–5); effectual means the call does what it says, and brings them. Jesus says this to a crowd that came for bread, with many of his disciples about to leave. He is not counting the room or measuring anyone’s grip on him; he simply says that everyone the Father has given him will arrive.

Whoever comes to me I will never cast out. “Never” (ou mē) is the strongest negative in Greek. “Cast out” is physical, used of the man born blind put out of the synagogue (9:34) and the traders driven from the temple (2:15). No one who came to him is ever put outside afterwards. The promise does not depend on how a person came, from conviction, desperation or sheer exhaustion, nor on what they have done since. The only condition is “whoever comes”, stated so broadly that no one can be excluded by a technicality. If you come, however unworthy, he will receive you.

Not to do my own will. His mission is to do the Father’s will, which is to save all the Father has given him. He did that will perfectly, as no one else ever has, and his obedience is counted to those who come to him (Romans 5:19), so their welcome never rests on how well they have done it themselves.

In everyday life. Ask yourself what you are secretly afraid would get you thrown out: not sin in general, but the particular thing. Now read verse 37 again. It has no exceptions clause, and the man who said it knew everything about you before you came and made the promise anyway.

How do I know if I am one of those the Father has given? By coming. Your name is not written in the secret counsel of God where you can read it, but its effect is written where you can see it: whoever comes to Christ was given by the Father. So do not wait for an answer to “Am I chosen?” before coming. Come to Christ now, as you are. That coming is the evidence of the Father’s giving, and the Son’s promise of welcome stands over you.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians (a broad family that includes many Methodists, Pentecostals and others) teach that God chooses those he foresees will freely believe. Many faithful Christians hold this view, and they too confess that salvation is all of grace. This commentary’s view: the text puts the Father’s giving first and the coming second, as its result: all that the Father gives will come. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (also 6:44, 65; 10:26; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). Yet human responsibility is real: everyone who comes is welcomed, and those who refuse are responsible (5:40). Both truths are taught together, and we hold them together.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father’s will is that the Son lose not one of those given to him, but raise every one up on the last day, and the Son will do it.

This is the will of him who sent me. He is quoting his job description. If a single person given to Christ were finally lost, the Son would have failed to do what the Father sent him to do, and that can never be (5:19).

Lose nothing. “All that he has given me” is literally “everything that” (pan ho): the whole company of the given seen as one gift. “Lose” (apollymi) is the word of the fragments in v. 12 (see the note on vv. 12–13). This is the perseverance of the saints: everyone God truly saves he keeps believing to the end, grounded not in the strength of the believer but in the will of the Father and the faithfulness of the Son (10:28–29; 17:12; 18:9).

Raise it up on the last day. Salvation is not complete until the body is raised; the phrase comes four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54). Everyone dies, and what is promised is a keeping that runs through the grave and out the other side. He does not say he will do his best. On the last day he will stand with every one of his people, saying, “Behold, I and the children God has given me” (Hebrews 2:13).

What it does not mean. Not that someone who professes faith and then abandons Christ for ever was one of the given (1 John 2:19). Nor that believers can live carelessly: those whom Christ keeps, he keeps believing and following (10:27).

What if I fall into serious sin? Have I lost my salvation? If you belong to Christ, no. Peter denied him three times and was restored (21:15–19); David fell into adultery and murder, and repented (Psalm 51). A true believer may fall grievously and for a time, bringing God’s fatherly displeasure and much grief on himself (Westminster Confession 17.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.3), but he will not fall finally, because Christ will not lose him. The proof that you belong to him is that you cannot rest in the sin: you are grieved, you return, you confess. Run back to him now. The door he promised never to shut is still open.

What about the warning passages, like John 15:6 and Hebrews 6? The promise here is not conditioned on our holding on. He warns his sheep so that they will not wander, and the warning itself is one of the ways his hand holds them (see the box below).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Many Arminians teach that a genuine believer may abandon faith and finally fall away, pointing to warnings such as 15:6 and Hebrews 6:4–6. This commentary’s view: this verse rules it out, since the Father’s will would fail; the warnings are one of the means by which Christ keeps his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same will, seen from the human side: everyone who looks to the Son and believes has eternal life now, and will be raised on the last day.

Everyone who looks on the Son. “Looks” (theōreō) means to gaze, to look with attention. The crowd had seen him without believing (v. 36); this is seeing that leads to faith. And “everyone” is wide open: no one who looks and believes is shut out.

Looking is the one thing required. It sends the reader back to the bronze serpent, where the dying were told to look and live (3:14–15), and forward to the cross: “They will look on him whom they have pierced” (19:37). Looking is the one thing a person with nothing left can still do.

The pastoral order. Held next to verse 44, these verses produce a tension that has divided the church, yet Jesus spoke them four verses apart with no sense of conflict. The door has “everyone” written over it, and no one is kept out by the doctrine of election. What the drawing explains is not who may come but why anyone does, a question asked afterwards, looking back, by people already inside.

In everyday life. When you feel guilty or afraid today, do not look inward first. Look at the Son, lifted up on the cross for you, and believe. Then tell someone else to look.

Can I freely offer the gospel to everyone if God has chosen only some? Yes, and you must; Jesus himself does both in the same breath. The offer is sincere: whoever looks and believes will live, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). You do not know who the elect are, and you are not asked to find out. You are asked to say to everyone: look to the Son and live. Election is not a reason to hold back the invitation; it is the guarantee that the invitation will not fall on deaf ears everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." They said, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, 'I have come down from heaven'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd grumbles as their fathers did in the wilderness, because they think they know exactly where Jesus comes from: how can Joseph’s son claim to have come down from heaven?

The Jews grumbled. “Grumbled” (gongyzō) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling in the wilderness, where the manna was given (Exodus 16:2, 7–8): they act out their fathers’ story while they talk about their fathers’ bread. “The Jews” here means people in the Galilean synagogue opposing Jesus, offended by his claim to heavenly origin.

Whose father and mother we know. They know his family, and could probably have named the street, so they think they know where he comes from. They know only half the truth. John’s readers know he came from the Father (1:14), and many would know he was born of a virgin. Familiarity breeds contempt (compare Mark 6:3), and from inside that information there is no way to reach the conclusion that the man came down from heaven.

How does he now say, I have come down from heaven? Their objection is the incarnation itself, and it is still the stumbling block. God did not arrive in a form that made the conclusion easy. He came as somebody’s son, in a known family, from a town people could point to, and the very facts that make the story checkable make it seem incredible.

In everyday life. The obstacle here is familiarity: the sense of already knowing all there is to know about him. Read a Gospel this week as if for the first time, and stop wherever the man of Nazareth does what only one from heaven could do.

How can Jesus have a human mother and come down from heaven? Because he is one person with two natures. As the eternal Son he came from the Father; as man he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). Joseph was his legal father, not his natural father. The crowd saw only the human side and thought it ruled out the divine. But the one who came down from heaven really did grow up in Nazareth, and the carpenter’s son really is the Word who was with God in the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws him, and everyone the Father draws comes and will be raised on the last day.

Do not grumble among yourselves. Jesus does not argue about his family. He goes to the root: why they cannot believe.

No one can come to me. “Can” (dynatai) is about ability, not permission. Fallen human beings, left to themselves, are unable to come to Christ (3:3; 8:43; Romans 8:7–8). The historic name for this is the bondage of the will: the will is not destroyed or forced but bound, so that it chooses freely and always chooses against God until it is set free.

Unless the Father who sent me draws him. “Draws” (helkō) is used of hauling a net full of fish to land (21:6, 11) and of drawing a sword (18:10): an effective pull, not a gentle suggestion. Yet it forces no one against their will; it changes the will, so that the sinner comes gladly, as v. 45 explains: the Father teaches, and the taught come.

I will raise him up. Drawn, comes, raised, and none drop out on the way. At the end of this Gospel the disciples haul a net to the shore where the risen Jesus stands with breakfast ready, and for all the fish the net is not torn (21:6–11). So the Father draws: every one he pulls is brought to his Son, and none is lost.

What this doctrine is for. It is often used as a weapon, and it is not one. Nobody has been given the list of the chosen, and Jesus is pleading with the very room he describes. It is an explanation for people who already believe, and it answers one question: why did I believe, when the man beside me heard the same message and did not? The only answer the chapter permits is that somebody came and got me. That removes the last possibility of taking credit, and with it the fear that a faith I produced could be one I might fail to keep.

What it does not mean. Not that people who want to come are turned away because they are not drawn: anyone who wants to come has already been drawn. Nor does it excuse unbelief: people do not come because they will not (5:40), and they are responsible for it.

Does this make us puppets? No. A puppet has no will; the sinner has one and uses it freely, and that is the problem: left to himself he prefers his own way to Christ (3:19). God’s drawing does not switch the will off but sets it free, so that for the first time the person wants Christ. No one in heaven will say, “I was dragged here against my will.” Everyone there will say, “He opened my eyes, and I came running.”

If no one can come unless drawn, why should I evangelise? Because the Father draws through means, chiefly the gospel spoken: he teaches (v. 45) through the word preached and shared, and faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:14–17). The doctrine makes your witness not pointless but hopeful. You are not trying to talk dead people into life by your own power; you are speaking the words the Father uses to raise the dead. Speak boldly, pray earnestly, and expect him to draw.

Where Christians differ: is the Father’s drawing resistible? Arminians teach that God draws everyone (citing 12:32) with a grace that can be resisted, so that some who are drawn do not come. Many earnest believers read it so, and both sides agree that whoever comes owes it to grace. This commentary’s view: in this verse the one who is drawn is the one who is raised up on the last day; if drawing could be resisted, the verse would promise resurrection to people who never come. The drawing is effectual. In 12:32 Jesus says he will draw “all people”, meaning all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews (the Greeks of 12:20 have just asked to see him), not every single person. This is effectual calling: the Spirit’s work by which God persuades and enables us to embrace Jesus Christ, freely offered in the gospel.

parallels.desc: I will draw all people to myself

verseByVerse.quote: "It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father draws by teaching, as the prophets promised, and everyone he teaches comes to Jesus, the only one who has seen the Father.

It is written in the Prophets. Isaiah 54:13, a promise about the restored people of God in the new covenant age (compare Jeremiah 31:33–34). “All” means all God’s people: in the new age God himself teaches every one of them, not just prophets and priests.

Heard and learned. This explains drawing: the Father draws by teaching, opening mind and heart to hear and learn, and everyone who learns comes. It is inward teaching that always succeeds, like the new birth (3:3–8) and the opening of Lydia’s heart (Acts 16:14).

He who is from God. Being taught by the Father does not mean having visions of God (1:18). He teaches by pointing to the Son, the only one who has seen him, so every lesson in the Father’s school ends at the same place.

How does God teach me today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He does not normally speak in private voices or visions. He teaches as the Scriptures are read and preached, the Spirit opening your mind to understand and your heart to love what you hear (Luke 24:45; 1 Corinthians 2:12). So put yourself under his word, with prayer, in the fellowship of his church. Every true insight into Christ you have ever had was a lesson from the Father.

Where Christians differ: does God still give private words today? Some believers expect him to. This commentary’s view: since the apostles, Scripture is his complete and sufficient word, while we gladly respect believers who expect more; and both agree that nothing heard elsewhere may add to Scripture or contradict it.

parallels.desc: all your children shall be taught by the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus states the promise at its simplest: whoever believes has eternal life, now, because he is the bread of life.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The doubled amen is peculiar to this Gospel. Amen normally comes afterwards, agreeing with someone else; Jesus puts it in front of his own words, vouching for them with God’s own authority. Here it introduces the simplest sentence in the chapter, so that the weakest believer may rest on it.

Whoever believes has eternal life. Not “whoever believes and does”, but “whoever believes”; and “has”, now. The sentence says nothing about how much is believed, or how well, or with what feelings, and nothing about understanding, in a chapter where hardly anyone understands anything.

I am the bread of life. The great “I am” saying repeated (v. 35): a preacher who has been interrupted, argued with and grumbled at, going back to the point.

In everyday life. If you believe, you have eternal life today. Live from it, not towards it: obey God not to gain life but because you already have it, by the Spirit who gives it (v. 63). Do one thing today that you would do only if you were sure you were safe in Christ.

I worry whether I am really one of the elect. What should I do? Stop auditing the secret counsel of God and look at the promise in front of you (see also the note on vv. 37–38): “whoever believes has eternal life”. If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, the promise is yours. Assurance grows as you look at him, not at yourself (Westminster Confession 18.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2).

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, read believes on me; the earliest have simply believes, with the same meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The manna kept people alive only for them to die; the bread from heaven is given so that whoever eats it will not die.

And they died. The crowd had held up the manna as the great sign (v. 31). It kept people alive for a day, and the whole generation that ate it died in the wilderness, many in unbelief (Numbers 14:29; 1 Corinthians 10:5): the part of the story they were not quoting.

The best of our arrangements. So the manna is not the standard Jesus has to match. Medicine, food, safety and all the ordinary mercies are real, but each extends a life rather than saves it. The best possible outcome of all our arrangements is a longer wait.

Eat of it and not die. Not “eat and live longer”, but “not die”: not escape from the body’s death, but death no longer the end (11:25–26). He is the Lord of life who went down into death himself and came out again, so that those who feed on him might pass through death into life.

But Christians still die. What does “not die” mean? That the death that is final, separation from God for ever, will never touch you. Your body will die, unless Christ returns first; this Gospel will soon show Jesus weeping at a friend’s tomb (11:35). But for the believer death is no longer the end of the sentence. At death the soul goes immediately to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1), and at the last day the body will be raised. The manna could not stop a single funeral. This bread does not stop them either. It stops them being the last word.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The living bread is Jesus’ own flesh, which he will give in death in the place of others for the life of the world, and whoever eats it, by faith, will live for ever.

If anyone eats of this bread. Living bread is bread that is alive and gives life. Eating is a picture of believing (compare v. 35 with v. 47): as food becomes part of you and keeps you alive, so receiving Christ by faith unites you to him and gives you life.

The bread that I will give ... is my flesh. Here the discourse turns. “I will give”: future, looking to the cross. “For” (hyper) means on behalf of, and in sayings like this one, in the place of (10:11, 15; 11:51–52): it is the preposition Caiaphas will use, “that one man should die for the people” (11:50). “My flesh” is his real human body (1:14), given up in death. To feed on Christ is to trust in his sacrifice.

For the life of the world. “The world” in John is humanity in its rebellion against God, Gentiles as well as Jews (11:51–52).

The bread is a dying man. The whole discourse has been walking toward this: not spiritual sustenance in general but a specific man, on a specific afternoon, dying in the place of others, who can feed anyone only because he was broken first. Nothing compelled it. He could have gone on making loaves for forty years, as the manna had come, and been crowned for it. He declined the crown, and came back to say that what he intended to give was his flesh.

In everyday life. When guilt rises today, do not argue with it from your record; answer it from his cross. Every time you trust his death for you, you are feeding on him.

Can I tell anyone that Christ died for sinners like them? Yes. The death of Christ is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and the gospel offers it freely to everyone: whoever eats of this bread will live for ever. You may say to anyone, “Christ died for sinners, and if you come to him, you will find that he died for you, and his death will not fail you.” Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the cross actually saves, rather than merely making salvation possible.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ died for everyone alike? Some take “for the life of the world” to mean that Christ died equally for every human being. This commentary’s view: in John, Christ lays down his life “for the sheep” (10:11, 15), for those the Father has given him (17:9, 19). “The world” here stresses the extent of his people, from every nation, and the greatness of the gift, not that every individual is saved. His death actually gives life, to everyone who feeds on him. This is definite atonement: the death that truly secures life for all who are his. Many faithful Christians believe Christ died in the same way for every person, and they preach the same free offer; the difference is over what the cross was designed to accomplish, and both sides glory in it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowd takes him crudely, Jesus presses harder: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, receiving his death as your life by faith, you have no life in you.

The Jews then disputed among themselves. “Disputed” (machomai) means fought: the grumbling has become open argument, and the room has split.

How can this man give us his flesh to eat? They take him crudely and literally, as Nicodemus took the new birth (3:4) and the woman took living water (4:11). The misunderstanding is part of John’s method: it leads to deeper teaching.

Unless you eat. Jesus does not soften it; he adds the blood. Flesh and blood separated speak of a violent death: the body broken and the blood poured out. To eat his flesh and drink his blood is to receive his death as your life, by faith, depending on it entirely.

How appalling this sounded. The prohibition on blood was absolute (Genesis 9:4): whoever ate any blood, God would set his face against him and cut him off from his people (Leviticus 17:10), for the blood was the life, and the life belonged to God. In a synagogue, Jesus names the one thing their law forbade on pain of being cut off, and says it is necessary.

You have no life in you. Without faith-union with the crucified Christ there is only death, for the respectable too: a person may be busy, moral and religious and still be dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). Life in this Gospel is knowing God (17:3).

What no Israelite was allowed to take. The law kept the blood for the altar, given to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11). What no Israelite was ever allowed to take, the Son of God gives: his own life, poured out in death, received by faith, so that sinners condemned to die might live by his.

What it does not mean. Not literal eating of Jesus’ physical body; the crowd thought that, and Jesus corrects it in v. 63: “the flesh is no help at all”. Nor that everyone who takes the Lord’s Supper has eternal life, or that no one who has not taken it can be saved. The thief on the cross never took it, and was with Christ that day.

Why does Jesus use such shocking language? Because nothing less would describe a union with a dying man so complete that the nearest picture is taking him into yourself and living on him. The picture offends because the reality is so total. Faith is not admiring Christ from a distance or agreeing with his teaching; it is depending on his death as your only life, as completely as your body depends on food.

Where Christians differ: John 6 and the Lord’s Supper. Roman Catholics read these verses as teaching transubstantiation, the bread and wine becoming Christ’s actual body and blood; Lutherans see Christ’s body present in, with and under the elements; some see here only a symbol of faith. This commentary’s view: the Supper had not yet been instituted, and Jesus speaks to the crowd of something they must do now, on pain of having no life. Feeding on Christ is believing in him (vv. 35, 40, 47). John 6 is about faith, not first about the sacrament. Yet the same feeding is what happens at the Supper: there, as Calvin taught, believers by the Spirit truly feed on Christ’s body and blood, not by a change in the bread, but by being lifted up in faith to the living Christ, who nourishes them with himself. The Supper is a visible, sealing form of what John 6 describes.
verseByVerse.note: Drinking blood was forbidden by the law, which made these words shocking.

parallels.desc: the life is in the blood

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps feeding on Christ by faith has eternal life now and will be raised on the last day.

Whoever feeds on my flesh. The verb changes from the usual word for eat to trōgō, to chew or munch. Some take it as deliberately vivid; others note that it simply serves as the present tense of eating in later Greek. Either way the present tense matters: the ongoing feeding of a life of faith, on bread that never runs out because the one who is the bread is infinite.

Has eternal life, and I will raise him up. The positive side of v. 53, and the last of the four appearances of the refrain. It repeats v. 40 almost word for word, with “feeds on my flesh” where v. 40 had “looks on the Son and believes”: the parallel shows that feeding means believing.

In everyday life. Next time you come to the Lord’s Supper, prepare for it the day before: confess your sins, give thanks for the cross, and come hungry.

Does the realism of this language support the Roman Catholic view? The reading deserves to be stated at its strongest. The crowd plainly took Jesus literally, and instead of correcting them he pressed harder, moving to the more vivid word “feeds on”; he says his flesh is true food and his blood true drink; and when disciples walked away he did not call them back to say he had meant a figure.

The answer in verse 63. That is a serious argument, and the passage answers it nine verses later. When his own disciples call the saying hard, Jesus tells them what it was: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all”, and his words are spirit and life (see the note on vv. 63–64). And whoever feeds on him abides in him (v. 56), and abiding is John’s word for a relationship held by faith, not by digestion. On the Supper not yet having been instituted, see the box “Where Christians differ: John 6 and the Lord’s Supper” at the end of the note on vv. 52–53. Whatever this chapter describes, it is how a crucified Saviour is received: by believing in him, as he said outright in verse 35.

Then is the Lord’s Supper only a memorial? No, nor an optional extra. The Reformed churches have taught that Christ is truly given to his people at his table and truly received, really and spiritually, by faith, through the Spirit, so that the feeding is no mere metaphor even though his flesh is not chewed (1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; Westminster 29.7). The disagreement with Rome is not about whether Christ gives himself to us there, but how, and whether the once-for-all sacrifice can be offered again. It cannot (Hebrews 10:10–14). So come to the table expecting to meet him: not in the bread, but by the Spirit, through faith, the risen Christ feeding you with himself.

parallels.desc: a participation in the blood of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s flesh and blood are the real food and drink of which all others are copies, and whoever feeds on him lives in him, and he in them.

True food. “True” (alēthēs): real, as the true light (1:9) and the true bread (v. 32); not genuine as opposed to fake, but the real thing of which every other example is a copy.

Abides in me, and I in him. “Abides” (menō), remains, dwells: one of John’s great words (15:4–10; 1 John 2:24, 27). Feeding leads to union with Christ. The word was used when the Spirit came down on Jesus and remained (1:32), but here for the first time the abiding runs both ways. Ordinary bread goes into the man and is changed into him. Here the one fed ends up inside the food: two persons who come to be in each other.

What does union with Christ mean in everyday life? It means that everything Christ is and has done is yours, and that your life is now bound up with his. His death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness is credited to you, his Spirit lives in you, and his resurrection guarantees yours (Romans 6:4–11; Galatians 2:20). You are never alone, never facing temptation in your own strength; when you work, suffer, love or die, you do it in him. Learn to say, with Paul, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”

parallels.desc: abide in me

verseByVerse.quote: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Son lives because of the Father, so whoever feeds on the Son will live because of him, for ever, as the manna’s eaters never did.

The living Father. The Son’s life comes from the Father (5:26), the living one, the fountain of life, who has never had life handed to him.

Whoever feeds on me. Now not flesh and blood but simply “me”: the person of Christ received. The believer lives because of Christ as Christ lives because of the Father. The two are not the same in kind: the Son’s life from the Father is eternal, and ours is a gift to creatures. But the pattern is the same, and so is the source. Life flows down from the heart of God into the hearts of sinners and will never run dry.

Not like the bread the fathers ate. The discourse ends where it began, with the manna (vv. 31–32). The manna was a substance, and substances sustain and then stop. What is offered here is a place in a chain that begins in the life of God and has no end.

Hard to want. He has said it four ways in twenty verses. The disciples will call it a hard saying, and they are right, though not for their reason: it is not hard to follow, but hard to want.

Does “live forever” just mean existing for ever? No. Everyone will exist for ever, the lost as well as the saved (5:29). Eternal life is not mere endless existence but a quality of life: knowing the Father and the Son (17:3), sharing in the very life of God, with joy, holiness and love that never fade. It begins when you first believe, and will be complete in the resurrection, in a new creation without sin or death.

parallels.desc: Christ who lives in me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus preached all this in the synagogue at Capernaum, and many who had followed him found it not hard to understand but hard to accept.

In the synagogue. The whole discourse was given in the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus’ base in Galilee. The remains of a later white limestone synagogue stand there on the dark basalt foundations of an earlier one, possibly the one Jesus taught in, which a Gentile centurion had built (Luke 7:5).

Many of his disciples. Not the Twelve, nor the Jews who have grumbled since verse 41, but a wider circle who had travelled with him and called him teacher; being called a disciple did not mean being a true believer (v. 64). The crowd’s objection was hostility; this is desertion forming in the ranks.

This is a hard saying; who can listen to it? “Hard” (sklēros) means harsh, offensive, used of a stiff wind or a harsh master, and “listen” means accept, obey. Not “who can understand it?”, but “who can go on sitting here while this is said?” Genuine intellectual difficulty deserves patient work, but this is the other kind of objection: the thing is understood perfectly well and found intolerable. Jesus’ reply does not soften the content; it points them to his ascension and to the Spirit.

Truth that will not bend. The man in the synagogue is the Word made flesh (1:14), and he cannot make the saying easier: to soften it would be to say something less true about himself, and he will not do that even to keep the people who have followed him longest. What makes the saying hard is that it is about a cross: a Messiah whose flesh is given and whose blood is poured out, and a salvation that leaves the sinner nothing to bring but hunger.

The Jesus with the hard sayings cut out. Thomas Jefferson admired Jesus enough to make his own edition of the Gospels. With a blade and several copies of the New Testament, he cut out the teaching he thought worthy, pasted it into a book, and left the rest on the floor: the miracles, the claims to be one with the Father, the resurrection. His version ends with the stone rolled against the tomb. Many do the same more quietly today, keeping the Sermon on the Mount and leaving John 6 on the floor. But the saying that emptied the synagogue was not a hard command. It was the claim that we have no life in us unless we receive his flesh given for us. The moralist cannot bear that, because he hoped to contribute something; the modern person cannot bear it, because he did not know he was starving. The ethics we keep can only show us how far short we fall. The saying we cut out is the only one that feeds.

What should I do with a teaching of Jesus I find hard to accept? First, make sure it is what he actually teaches, read in context. Then ask honestly whether you do not understand it, or do not like it. If the first, study and ask for help. If the second, bring the struggle to Christ himself, as you would to a friend whose judgment you trust more than your own. Many believers have found that the sayings they once resisted became the ones they love most. Faith does not mean pretending something is easy; it means trusting the one who said it.
verseByVerse.note: The remains of a later synagogue at Capernaum stand on the foundations of an earlier one, perhaps the one where Jesus taught.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knows his followers are offended, and points them to his return to where he was before, which will prove that he came down from heaven.
