Knowing in himself. Jesus knows what is in people (2:24–25); nobody reported it. The knowledge that read the woman at the well now reads his followers as they quietly decide to leave.

Do you take offense at this? “Offense” (skandalizō): to trip, to stumble. The cross is the great stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Ascending to where he was before. In John, his going up includes the cross, resurrection and ascension together (3:13–14; 12:32–34). His ascent proves his claim that he came down from heaven (vv. 38, 42), and shows that his flesh would not stay on earth to be literally eaten. “Where he was before” carries the weight: it is the very thing the objectors of verse 42 denied, and he answers by naming, without argument, the place he came from and is going back to.

Why does the ascension matter to me? Because the one who ascended is now reigning, praying and preparing. He sits at the Father’s right hand as King over all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–23), always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), has sent the Spirit (16:7), and is preparing a place for you, and will come again (14:2–3). The ascension means you have a friend at the very centre of all power, wearing your nature, and your life is hidden with him there (Colossians 3:1–3).

Uncertain wording. The sentence is left unfinished in Greek (“Then what if you were to see …?”), so the hearer must supply its end. It could mean: if this offends you, how much more will his ascent, the full revelation of his heavenly origin, overwhelm you? Or: when you see him ascend, you will understand that he truly came from heaven, and that his words about his flesh were not about literal eating. Both readings fit the context, and either way the ascension vindicates his claim.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life comes by the Spirit through Jesus’ words, not by physical eating; yet some of those nearest him do not believe, as he has known from the start.

It is the Spirit who gives life. As in the new birth (3:5–8). This is the key to the chapter: Jesus tells his own disciples what the previous twenty verses were about.

The flesh is no help at all. “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit, not Jesus’ own flesh given for the world (v. 51). Having just told them to eat his flesh, he says flesh is no help at all: not a contradiction but a signal that they have been thinking in physical, literal terms, the wrong way to take him.

Spirit and life. His words do not merely describe spirit and life; they are spirit and life. The saying they have just called intolerable is itself what carries the life, so the way to eat him is to receive what he has said: eating means believing. That explanation comes from Jesus himself, long before any church had a doctrine of the Supper to defend.

Some of you who do not believe. Said to their faces, to the people standing closest. John adds that Jesus knew “from the beginning”, probably from the start of his ministry: he chose the Twelve knowing what Judas would do (v. 70; 13:18). It is the first mention of the betrayal in this Gospel.

Not ink but breath. On the evening of his resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (20:22). His words are not ink but breath: the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live (5:25). He knew every unbelieving heart in the room, and spoke life into it anyway.

In everyday life. Without the Spirit, even the Bible is read and not heard. Before you open Scripture today, pray in one sentence: “Holy Spirit, make these words life to me.”

Did Jesus’ knowing make Judas betray him? No. Foreknowledge is not compulsion. God’s eternal purpose does include even the sins of men, so that the cross came by his definite plan and foreknowledge (Acts 2:23), yet God is not the author of sin, and Judas acted freely and wickedly, and was fully responsible (Westminster Confession 3.1; 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; 5.4). The terrible thing in this sentence is not what it does to Judas’s freedom but what it shows of Christ’s patience. He kept a man beside him for years, giving him everything he gave the others, knowing.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coming to Jesus is the Father’s gift, so no believer can boast, and none need fear that his own resolve will fail.

This is why I told you. He quotes himself (v. 44) at the very moment the teaching is being proved true, as disciples walk away.

Granted by the Father. “Granted” (dedomenon): given as a gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29). Three times in this chapter the Father gives (v. 37), draws (v. 44) and grants (v. 65): drawing stressed the power required; granting stresses the gift. Unbelief is human refusal; faith is God’s gift.

No room for pride. What separates those who stay from those leaving is not insight, loyalty or a better grasp of the argument: it was granted them. Every believer will say on the last day, not “I chose well”, but “he chose me”; not “I held on”, but “I was held”.

The comfort in it. If staying were a matter of resolve, every Christian would be one bad season away from the door. The eleven did not out-endure the others; they were given something, and the giving did not depend on their performance that evening or any evening afterward. Within a year every one of them would run away and one would deny knowing him. They came back, because the one who received them kept them: “While I was with them,” he would pray, “I kept them in your name ... and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction” (17:12).

In everyday life. The person you find hardest to be patient with looks different once you remember that your faith was granted, not earned.

Are those to whom coming is not granted still responsible? Yes. The inability is not a prison door shut on someone trying to get out; it is a will that does not want to come (5:40). No one is turned away who comes, and no one stays away against his will. God’s gift is mercy, owed to no one; its absence is justice, not cruelty.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many followers walk away, not over a scandal but over a sermon, and Jesus, without softening a word, offers even the Twelve the door.

Many turned back. The turning point of Jesus’ Galilean ministry: the day before, a crowd wanted to make him king (v. 15). “Turned back” is literally went away to the things behind. They had followed for bread and a political Messiah. There was no scandal and no miracle gone wrong; he preached a sermon, and it emptied the room. This is where the faith based on signs at 2:24 and the Galilean welcome of 4:45 were always going to end.

No longer walked with him. They stopped travelling in the same direction. Falling away often looks less like a decision than like a road no longer taken.

Do you want to go away as well? The first mention of “the twelve” in John, and a question framed in Greek to expect a no. Jesus does not beg them to stay, soften his teaching or chase the crowd. He offers his closest circle the door, testing them and inviting a confession: a real question, from a man who has just watched a room empty and has nothing left to hold anyone with except himself.

He would not be less than he is. The message was himself, and he would not be less than he is to be more popular. He stood in an emptying synagogue and did not flinch, and the same faithfulness took him to a garden at night, where he said of his friends, “let these men go” (18:8).

Were these disciples true believers who lost their salvation? Some read them so. But John has already shown that a shallow following and believing is not the same as being born again (2:23–25), and Jesus says plainly that some of them did not believe (v. 64). More likely they had followed without being given saving faith: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

What if someone I love has walked away from Christ? Then this chapter is for you. It happened to Jesus, in his own town, in numbers, after his own preaching, and it was no evidence that anything had gone wrong in him; nor is it necessarily evidence that you failed. Keep loving them, keep the door open, and keep praying: some who seem to have walked away are wandering believers whom the Shepherd will bring back, like Peter, and the Father who draws can still draw. Leave the final judgment with God, who knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter answers for the Twelve that there is no one else to go to, because Jesus alone has the words of eternal life.

Simon Peter answered him. Peter speaks for the Twelve, as he does in the other Gospels (Matthew 16:16).

Lord, to whom shall we go? A confession made in a hard hour: not a compliment or a declaration of loyalty but a question, and the question is the point. Peter does not claim to understand everything; nothing suggests the Twelve grasped the discourse better than the people walking out. He says that after all they have seen and heard with Jesus, no other teacher is a real alternative.

You have the words of eternal life. Peter has heard v. 63 and believed it. The men leaving called the words a hard saying; he calls them life. The difference is not that he found the saying easier, but what he concluded about the speaker. Christ alone speaks words that raise the dead and feed the soul for ever.

In the flow. John 5 ended with men who had every witness and would not come (5:40); John 6 ends with a few who have not understood everything and will not leave. The difference is the one the chapter has explained: the Father gives, draws and grants (vv. 37, 44, 65).

Stronger than enthusiasm. A faith held in bewilderment is not a poor one. Some holding on survives precisely because it no longer depends on full comprehension: not “I understand and therefore I stay”, but “I have nowhere else to take this, and the words that give life are here.”

What should I do when I have doubts? Do what Peter did: take them to Jesus, not away from him. Doubt is not the same as unbelief; it is often faith struggling. Be honest with God about your questions (the psalms are full of honest complaint), and ask, “Where else would I go?” Every alternative has its own hard sayings, and none offers what Christ does: words of eternal life from one who rose from the dead. Stay close to his word and his people, talk to a mature Christian, and keep coming. Many of the strongest believers have known seasons when all they could say was Peter’s question.

parallels.desc: all the words of this Life

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter confesses that Jesus is the Holy One of God, and Jesus replies that he chose all twelve, yet one of them is a devil.

We have believed, and have come to know. Both verbs are perfect tense: a settled conviction. And the order is the one this Gospel keeps insisting on: believing first, knowing second. The servants filled the jars before they saw the wine; the official walked home before he had news; these men believed and then came to know.

The Holy One of God. Set apart, consecrated and sent by the Father (10:36). “Holy” is the word God uses of himself (Leviticus 11:44): this man stands wholly on God’s side of that line, pure where we are stained (compare Luke 5:8), and his holiness did not keep him from us but brought him to us. A demon cried the same title in a synagogue in this same town (Mark 1:24); Peter says in faith what the demon cried out in fear. Orthodox words can mean two different things depending on who says them and why.

Did I not choose you, the twelve? Encouragement and warning together. He chose them, not they him (15:16). Peter has just said the finest thing anyone says in the chapter, for all of them, at the lowest point of the ministry so far, and the reply must have been hard to hear. Jesus does not correct what Peter said about him, only the assumption that Peter spoke for every one of them. Eleven of them meant it.

One of you is a devil. “Devil” (diabolos): an adversary. Not that Judas was a demon, but that he was the devil’s tool (13:2, 27). Choosing Judas to be an apostle is not the same as God’s choosing a person for salvation (17:12). And Jesus says it of a man who had as yet done nothing publicly wrong, and who had just stayed when others left.

Can a church contain people who are not truly Christians? Yes. The visible church has always included some who are not born again, as the Twelve included Judas, and as Simon the magician was baptised while still bound by sin (Acts 8:13, 20–23). Only God sees the heart perfectly. So churches must preach the gospel to their own members as well as outsiders and practise loving discipline, and every believer should examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5). But it is no reason to suspect everyone. Love believes all things, and we leave the final sorting to Christ.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, borrowed from Matthew 16:16; the earliest and best read “the Holy One of God”, and the ESV rightly follows them.

parallels.desc: Peter’s confession

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John names the traitor: Judas, one of the Twelve, who stayed when others left and yet was going to betray him.

Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. “Iscariot” probably means man of Kerioth, a town in Judea (Joshua 15:25), which would make Judas the only Judean among the Twelve (see the box below). Nobody in the room worked out who was meant; at the last supper they will still be asking. John names him for readers who know how it ends.

One of the twelve. The betrayer was an insider. Jesus knew, kept him close, and washed his feet (13:5, 26). The betrayal fulfilled Scripture (13:18; Psalm 41:9), yet Judas was fully responsible for it (Mark 14:21).

Judas stayed. The crowd leaves, the wider circle leaves, and Judas stays. He heard the hard saying and did not walk out; he stood there when Peter said, “to whom shall we go?” He remained among the twelve for about another year, was trusted with the money, and had his feet washed by the man he sold. Nearness guarantees nothing: three years inside the smallest circle with the Son of God did not produce faith in one man of twelve. The chapter has told us what does: “no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father”.

From the very hands that made it. He knew which of the twelve would sell him, and kept him close: such is the patience of the Son of God with sinners. The chapter ends where it began, with bread. Five thousand ate it and were hungry again next morning. One of the twelve ate from the very hands that made it, and starved. But all who come to the living bread are fed for ever.

Could I be a Judas without knowing it? If you are asking the question in fear, almost certainly not. Until after the betrayal Judas is never once recorded as troubled about his own state. Anxiety about your own heart, sorrow over sin, longing to love Christ more: these are not the marks being described. The mark of Judas is a man entirely at ease while he loves something more than Christ (12:6). So examine yourself honestly, confess what you find, and then look away from yourself to the Saviour who never casts out anyone who comes. Fear that drives you to Christ is grace, not a sign of reprobation (God’s passing someone by).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of “Iscariot” is not certain. “Man of Kerioth” is the most common explanation, and fits John’s calling his father “Simon Iscariot” too. Other suggestions link it to a word for a dagger-carrying assassin or to an Aramaic word for a false man, but neither has won wide agreement, and nothing in the passage depends on it.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.<sup>2</sup>And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.<sup>3</sup>Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.<sup>4</sup>Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.<sup>5</sup>Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?”<sup>6</sup>He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.<sup>7</sup>Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”<sup>8</sup>One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,<sup>9</sup>“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.<sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.<sup>12</sup>And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost.”<sup>13</sup>So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.<sup>14</sup>When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!”<sup>15</sup>Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.<sup>16</sup>When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,<sup>17</sup>got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.<sup>18</sup>The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.<sup>19</sup>When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened.<sup>20</sup>But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”<sup>21</sup>Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.<sup>22</sup>On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.<sup>23</sup>Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.<sup>24</sup>So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.<sup>25</sup>When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.<sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”<sup>28</sup>Then they said to him, “What must we do, to be doing the works of God?”<sup>29</sup>Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”<sup>30</sup>So they said to him, “Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?<sup>31</sup>Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ’He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”<sup>32</sup>Jesus then said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.<sup>33</sup>For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”<sup>34</sup>They said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.<sup>36</sup>But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.<sup>37</sup>All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.<sup>38</sup>For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>39</sup>And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.<sup>40</sup>For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”<sup>41</sup>So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”<sup>42</sup>They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ’I have come down from heaven’?”<sup>43</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves.<sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>45</sup>It is written in the Prophets, ’And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me—<sup>46</sup>not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.<sup>47</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.<sup>48</sup>I am the bread of life.<sup>49</sup>Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.<sup>50</sup>This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.<sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”<sup>53</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.<sup>54</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>55</sup>For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.<sup>56</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.<sup>57</sup>As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.<sup>58</sup>This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.”<sup>59</sup>Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum.<sup>60</sup>When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”<sup>61</sup>But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this?<sup>62</sup>Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?<sup>63</sup>It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.<sup>64</sup>But there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)<sup>65</sup>And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”<sup>66</sup>After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.<sup>67</sup>So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”<sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life,<sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”<sup>70</sup>Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”<sup>71</sup>He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 ended in Jerusalem with Jesus telling the authorities that Moses wrote of him (5:46). Now, in Galilee near Passover, the feeding of the five thousand and one of Jesus’ longest discourses bring his Galilean ministry to its turning point: the largest crowd he ever drew dwindles to the Twelve.

The message. Jesus does not merely give bread; he is the bread from heaven, to be received, not just admired. Whoever comes to him and believes, feeding on his flesh given in death, has eternal life now and will be raised on the last day. No one comes unless the Father draws him, and no one the Father gives will be lost.

Why it was said. John’s readers knew the cost of confessing Jesus and the pain of seeing others fall away (see the introduction). The chapter shows that enjoying Jesus’ gifts or following for a season is not feeding on him, and that those who stay, stay because the Father holds them.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus feeds five thousand from a boy’s lunch and refuses a bread-king’s crown (vv. 1–15), then comes to his disciples across the stormy lake: “It is I” (vv. 16–21). The crowd that came for loaves demands manna; he answers that the work God requires is to believe, and that the Father gives the true bread (vv. 22–34). Then the centre: “I am the bread of life”; all the Father gives will come, and none who come will be cast out (vv. 35–40). The grumblers hear that no one comes unless drawn, and that the bread is his flesh given for the world (vv. 41–51); the quarrellers, that without eating his flesh and drinking his blood they have no life (vv. 52–59). Many disciples leave; Peter confesses there is no one else to go to, though one of the Twelve is a devil (vv. 60–71).

Where it leads. At the next Passover the bread was broken: Jesus refused a crown of bread on this hillside so that he could give his flesh on a cross for the life of the world (v. 51). The manna was the picture; he is the reality. And the one who would not let a crust be lost (v. 12) loses none of those the Father has given him (v. 39; 18:9).

For us. Ask whether you come to Jesus for his loaves or for himself. Feed on him day by day, in his word and at his table, and rest on his promise that whoever comes will never be cast out. And when others walk away, say with Peter, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

keyVerse.quote: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this sentence. The sign on the hillside, the night on the lake and the demand for manna all lead to it, and the coming, the drawing and the eating that follow unfold it. Jesus does not merely give what we need; he is what we need, and the promise is open to whoever comes.

6.reflection:
The crowd followed Jesus for the loaves, and he fed them anyway before he challenged them (vv. 2, 26). What first drew you to Christ, and how have your reasons for following him changed? Which of his gifts are you most tempted to want more than him?

Philip did the sums, while Andrew brought a boy’s lunch knowing it was not enough (vv. 7–9). What need in front of you seems too big? What small thing could you put in Jesus’ hands this week?

Jesus says that all the Father gives him will come, that he will never cast out anyone who comes, and that no one can come unless the Father draws him (vv. 37, 44). How do these truths humble you and comfort you, and how should they shape the way we share the gospel?

When many walked away, Peter said, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (v. 68). When have you been tempted to walk away? What has kept you, and how can we help someone who is struggling to stay?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole chapter asks where Jesus comes from, and answers: from the Father, so he can give what the feast only pictured. He refuses to go up as his brothers urge, as a public campaign, and goes in his Father’s time (vv. 1–13). In the temple he teaches that his words are the Father’s and exposes leaders who keep Moses’ law in name while plotting murder (vv. 14–24). The crowd’s confused objections about his origin meet his claim to come from the God they do not know, and an arrest is ordered (vv. 25–36). On the last day he offers rivers of living water, the Spirit (vv. 37–39), and the chapter ends in division, failed arrests and a council that will not give him a hearing (vv. 40–52).
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on where Jesus comes from and by whose authority he speaks. Asked how he knows the Scriptures without a rabbi, he answers that his teaching is the Father’s (see vv. 16–17). The two questions, where he is from and who gave him authority, are really one: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: The Feast of Booths looked back to the wilderness and forward to living waters from Jerusalem, and Jesus stands up at its climax and says that the river flows from him (see the note on vv. 37–38). On the officers who came back empty-handed, see vv. 45–46.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Booths was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will not walk into the hands of men who want him dead before his Father’s time, and the feast now approaching is the one that celebrated God living among his people in a tent.

After this. About six months, from Passover (6:4) in spring to the Feast of Booths in autumn. The hillside crowd of chapter 6 has melted away and many disciples have stopped walking with him (6:66). John passes over the summer and moves straight to the next confrontation.

Seeking to kill him. Since the Sabbath healing in Jerusalem (5:18) the authorities had wanted him dead, and the whole chapter happens under that threat. Yet he is no coward: in the spring he will walk into Jerusalem in the open, knowing what waits for him. He is refusing to die at a time of other people’s choosing. His hour has not yet come (v. 30); he moves when the Father says, and his moves are never reactions.

The Feast of Booths. The Feast of Booths, or Tabernacles (skēnopēgia, pitching of tents), was the third of the great pilgrim festivals, with Passover and Pentecost (Deuteronomy 16:16). It came in September or October, at the end of the harvest, and lasted seven days, with an eighth day of solemn assembly (Leviticus 23:33–43). Families slept for the week in shelters of branches on courtyards and flat roofs, remembering the wilderness years when they had nothing and God provided everything. It was the most joyful feast of the year.

The water and the light. By Jesus’ day two ceremonies had been added. Every morning water was poured out at the altar, with songs of joy (Isaiah 12:3; see the note on vv. 37–38). At night great lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, and the sources say there was not a courtyard in Jerusalem that did not glow with their light. Zechariah 14, with its living waters from Jerusalem, was read at this feast and names Booths as the festival all the nations will one day keep (Zechariah 14:16). Against this background Jesus will say “come to me and drink” (v. 37) and “I am the light of the world” (8:12): he stands in front of the ceremony and says that it was about him.

The God they were remembering. Israel had kept this feast for more than a thousand years, and that year the God they were remembering was walking the roads of Galilee in a body, deciding when to go up to his own festival. He who had led them by cloud and fire now walked by his Father’s word, unhurried and unafraid, towards the feast, and beyond it towards the cross, where the true tabernacle, his body, would be torn down, to be raised again in three days.

Was Jesus wrong to avoid danger? No. Trusting God has never meant walking carelessly into harm. Jesus refused to throw himself from the temple to prove that God would catch him (Matthew 4:5–7), and here he refuses to throw himself into the hands of men who had already decided to kill him; Paul was let down over the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). The question is not whether we take sensible steps to stay safe, but why. Fear says, “I must save my life at any cost.” Faith says, “My life is in the Father’s hands, so I will neither waste it nor cling to it.” When the hour came, the same Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him back.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was the joyful autumn harvest festival. For a week people lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel’s years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His brothers urge him to win a following in Judea by a public show, the world’s way of doing things. It sounds like sensible advice, and that is exactly what is wrong with it.

His brothers. James, Joses, Judas and Simon (Mark 6:3), and Mark mentions sisters as well. They appear again and again with Mary as her family (Mark 3:31; Acts 1:14).

Your disciples. Perhaps the followers in Judea, or those who had turned away (6:66). The phrase is spoken at arm’s length: your disciples, not ours.

No one works in secret. If you want to be known, go public: any modern adviser would say the same. But his kingdom does not advance by staged displays for the largest possible audience.

Show yourself to the world. “If” reveals their doubt: they do not deny the miracles, but they do not trust him. It is Satan’s temptation again (Matthew 4:5–7). He had shared the Father’s glory before the world existed (17:5), and laid it aside so completely that his own brothers thought he needed a publicity campaign. And he will show himself to the world: in this Gospel that is the cross, the lifting up, its title written in three languages for every passer-by (19:20). They have named the right event and the wrong method, with no idea that the showing will kill him.

In everyday life. Be wary of advice that measures faithfulness by publicity: grow the following, build the brand. Some visibility is simply the cost of telling the truth. But ask of any plan, in your church or your own heart: is this aimed at making Christ known, or at making me known? From the outside the two can look identical for a long time.

Where Christians differ: who were Jesus’ brothers? Roman Catholic teaching takes them as cousins, and Eastern Orthodox teaching as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, to preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity. This commentary’s view: the natural reading is that they were Mary’s later sons (Matthew 1:25; Luke 2:7). It is not the centre of the gospel, but the Gospels plainly suggest that Jesus grew up in a crowded house with brothers and sisters, and Mary is honoured as the mother of our Lord without needing a perpetual virginity.
verseByVerse.note: His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the brothers who grew up with Jesus did not believe in him, and yet that was not the end of their story. John’s aside is among the most useful in the New Testament for a particular kind of grief.

Not even his brothers. Compare Mark 3:21. They had shared a small house with him for most of their lives, watched him work, eat, sleep and pray, and did not believe. If moral excellence at close range were enough to produce faith, they would have been the first converts in history. Familiarity is the enemy of awe: they knew Jesus the man too well to recognise Jesus the Lord.

But that is not the end of the story. After the resurrection Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the brothers were among the believers praying in the upper room (Acts 1:14). James later led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9) and is generally held to have written the letter of James, as Judas (Jude) is held to have written Jude. Unbelief like theirs was overcome only by resurrection: the power that raised Jesus from the grave raised James from his unbelief.

The eternal Son, judged ordinary. For thirty years the eternal Son let his brothers judge him ordinary, and never forced their faith. When it came, it came as worship. James, who could have signed himself the brother of the Lord, wrote “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1); Jude called himself “a servant of Jesus Christ”, and only then a brother of James (Jude 1). The brothers who told him to show himself to the world spent their lives showing him to it. His patience with those closest to him wins.

The case was not closed. Take the person you have most nearly given up on. Had this chapter been the last word about James, every reasonable observer would have closed the case: a lifetime of evidence, no result. It was six months from being reopened, and nothing in between looked like progress. The worst week of all, the week his brother was crucified, was, as far as we can tell, the week that led to his conversion. Bring that person’s name back to God today. And if you grew up around Christianity, take the warning: it is possible to grow up in the very house and still not believe.

My family has watched my life for years and still does not believe. Have I failed them? Not necessarily. The most compelling life ever lived was on display in one household for thirty years and did not persuade the people in it, so unbelief proves neither that your witness was poor nor that the case for Christ is weak. Faith is not produced by example alone; it is the gift of God, who opens blind eyes when he chooses (6:44). Your example still matters: make the gospel credible, apologise when you fail, keep loving them. But converting them was never your burden. Keep praying, and leave the timing with the one who went to see James.
verseByVerse.note: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the brothers were among the believers after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: with Mary and his brothers
he appeared to James

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus lives by his Father’s timetable, not his brothers’; the world leaves them alone because they belong to it, and hates him because he tells it the truth about its evil.

My time has not yet come. “Time” here means the right moment for a thing (kairos). John’s usual word is the hour (hōra), the fixed appointment of his death and glorification (see the note on vv. 30–31).

But your time is always here. Any time suits them: they have no mission, no appointment and no threat over them. It is not a compliment.

The world cannot hate you. “The world” in John is humanity organised in rebellion against God. Not “does not” but “cannot”: they belong to it, speak its language and want what it wants. Their safety is a bad sign; the world leaves them alone because they are no threat to it. Later he tells his disciples the same truth from the other side: “If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own” (15:19).

Its works are evil. Light shows up the darkness (3:19–20). People do not object to Jesus as a teacher of kindness, but when he says their works are evil. The world tolerates many kinds of religion and moral teaching; it cannot tolerate the claim that its basic direction is sinful and that only grace can save it. The cross is its answer to that testimony.

Too loving to flatter. He could have been loved by the world: he had only to stop saying that its works were evil. He loved the world too much to flatter it, and let it hate him to death, so that the people who hated him could be forgiven. The light did not dim itself to be welcome in the dark.

What it does not mean. Being disliked is not proof of faithfulness. Christians are often disliked for being rude, harsh or politically obnoxious, which has nothing to do with Christ. The verse names the cause exactly: having the truth told about oneself by someone who loves you enough to tell it. So the test is not, “am I disliked?” but, “is there anything in my life that would make the world uncomfortable if it were paying attention?” A faith with no friction may have quietly stopped saying the thing that causes it; and the one who bore the world’s hatred for us gives his Spirit for both courage and love.

Is it not arrogant for Jesus to call the world’s works evil? Only if he spoke from a safe height and exempted himself and his friends. He says it to his own brothers here and to the leaders of the temple in the same chapter, and he says it as the one who has come to carry that evil away. A doctor who tells you the truth about the tumour is not arrogant; the one who hides it to keep you comfortable is cruel. And this doctor pays for the cure with his own life. A teacher who never names evil can never save anyone from it.

But does God not love the world (3:16)? Both are true, and John holds them together. The world is humanity in rebellion against God, and God loves it anyway, not because it is lovable but because he is love, enough to send his Son into it knowing it would hate him. So the world that hates Jesus is not a world God has given up on, but the world he came to save. Christians are called to the same double stance: not loving the world’s rebellion (1 John 2:15), and loving the people caught in it enough to tell them the truth.

parallels.desc: if the world hates you

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses to go up to the feast in the way his brothers mean, as a public bid for recognition, because his Father’s time has not yet fully come.

You go up to the feast. One always went up to Jerusalem, high in the hills; the pilgrim psalms are the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134). Some see a play on the word: the same verb is used of his going up to the Father (20:17), which will not happen at this feast.

I am not going up to this feast. Yet he does go (v. 10), and the sentence has been used for centuries, as by the third-century critic Porphyry, to accuse Jesus of lying. It can be answered well, because the whole exchange is about how he goes, not whether he travels. His brothers were urging a campaign: “show yourself to the world” (v. 4), go up publicly, with the crowds, and stake your claim. That is the going up he refuses, and John supplies the distinction in the very next sentence: he went “not publicly but in private” (v. 10). The man who would refuse to come down from a cross did not trim his words to make an afternoon easier.

For my time has not yet fully come. “Fully come” (peplērōtai, been fulfilled). He is not managing his image with a convenient untruth, but declining a schedule that was not his Father’s.

He remained in Galilee. Not passivity but restraint: the hour set from eternity cannot be rushed by family pressure or popular demand. And when it came, nothing could stop him going up: to Jerusalem, onto the cross, from the grave, and to the Father’s right hand, where he reigns over every timetable in the world, including yours.

If manuscripts differ, can I trust my Bible? Yes. Comparing the many early copies of the New Testament, far more than for any other ancient book, shows clearly where a copyist slipped or smoothed. Most differences are spelling, word order or small words like this “yet”, and none touches any teaching of the faith. The harder reading is kept precisely because it is harder, and the copyists’ attempts to ease it show how anxious they were about every word. Your Bible’s footnotes are a sign not that the text is shaky, but that it has been handled with great care.

Textual note. Many manuscripts, including two of the earliest papyri, read “I am not yet going up,” and the KJV and NKJV follow them. Other early manuscripts read “I am not going up,” and most modern Bibles judge this the original, since a scribe was more likely to add “yet” to ease the problem than to remove it. So the honest course is to answer the harder text rather than shelter behind the easier, and as we have seen, the harder text needs no shelter.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “yet”: “I am not yet going up.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes up to the feast quietly, on his own terms, while the whole city searches for him and argues about him.

Not publicly but in private. The Son of God goes up to his own people’s feast in a stream of pilgrims, unrecognised. The secrecy is brief: hidden in verse 10, he is teaching in the temple courts by verse 14. What he refused was his brothers’ method (see the note on vv. 8–9); days later he does the most public thing available to a man in Jerusalem, alone.

Looking for him. Two searches run through the chapter: the authorities look for him to end him, the crowd because they cannot stop talking about him. He walks through the middle of both.

Where is he? “Where” is a key word in John 7 and 8: where he comes from, and where he is going (vv. 27, 34–35; 8:14, 21). They will not use his name, like people discussing somebody they have already decided about. Yet beneath the question lies the deepest question there is: where is God? John’s answer across twenty-one chapters is that he is here, in this man, at this feast.

The man they cannot find is the tent. The word for the feast shares its root with John’s verb in 1:14: “the Word became flesh and dwelt”, literally pitched his tent, “among us”. The whole city is sleeping under branches to remember the time God travelled with them in a tent, and the man they are looking for is the tent. He who once filled the tabernacle with a glory so great that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35) came up the road dusty and anonymous, to stand among his people and call them to himself. He came close enough to be overlooked.

Is it ever right for a Christian to be secret? Sometimes discretion is wisdom, as here: believers in hostile countries meet quietly, and no one need announce every plan to people who mean him harm (Matthew 10:16–17). But discretion about our movements is not silence about our Lord. Jesus hid his journey for a few days; he never hid who he was. Hiding our faith because we are ashamed of Christ is not wisdom but fear (Mark 8:38). Prudence protects the mission; cowardice abandons it.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd is divided over Jesus, a good man or a deceiver, but fear of the authorities keeps even those who think well of him quiet.

Much muttering. The word used of the grumbling in 6:41 (gongysmos), and of Israel’s in the desert; here it means whispered debate, among admirers and accusers alike.

Some said, “He is a good man.” The kindly verdict, and the one most people still reach for, but it falls far short (see the question below).

Others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.” “Leading astray” (planaō) was a serious charge: the false prophet who leads Israel away from God was to be put to death (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Later Jewish writings describe Jesus as one who practised sorcery and led Israel astray, and misleading the nation is among the charges before Pilate (Luke 23:2). The one thing nobody says is that he might be telling the truth about himself.

For fear of the Jews. It is not his opponents who are silent, but the people who think well of him. The phrase becomes one of John’s refrains: it is why the blind man’s parents will not answer a straight question (9:22), and why Joseph of Arimathea kept his discipleship quiet (19:38). John will name the root: “they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God” (12:43). Yet the Lord mumbled about in the courts of his own temple will one day be confessed aloud by every tongue, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).

In everyday life. Recall a recent conversation in which you could have said something about him, and did not. What held you back was probably not persecution but the half-second of awkwardness: a far lighter pressure than theirs, but the same mechanism. He was not ashamed to die openly for you, and his Spirit gives the words: next time, say one true sentence about him.

Why can’t Jesus simply be a good man and a great teacher? Because of what he taught. A good man does not claim to be equal with God, to forgive sins against other people, to be the bread from heaven, or to be the judge of everyone. If those claims are false, he was either deceived about himself on a scale no sane good man could be, or deceiving others, the charge in this verse. The only verdicts that take him seriously are deceived, deceiver, or Lord. Some reply that the later church put the large claims in his mouth; but the earliest sources, Mark and the letters of Paul, written within a few decades, already present him forgiving sins and claiming to be the coming judge (Mark 2:5–10; 14:62), and already worship him as Lord (Philippians 2:9–11). The good teacher who claims nothing was invented later, to avoid having to decide.

Does John’s phrase “the Jews” make his Gospel anti-Jewish? No. John was a Jew, Jesus was a Jew, nearly every believer in this Gospel is a Jew, and Jesus says “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22). Here “the Jews” plainly means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed him, as the sentence itself shows: the Jewish crowd is afraid of the Jews. The Gospel gives no warrant for hatred of the Jewish people. Christians who have used it that way have sinned grievously, and contempt for Jews denies the Christ who was born a son of David and wept over Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: a prophet who leads you astray
that impostor

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Halfway through the feast Jesus teaches openly in the temple, and the experts are astonished that a man with no rabbi behind him knows the Scriptures so deeply.

About the middle of the feast. Around the fourth day of the seven. He let the festival fill up until the crowds were largest, then walked into the busiest place in Jerusalem and began to teach.

Into the temple. Malachi had promised, “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1). In the middle of a feast, without announcement, he does, and before long he is exposing the hearts of the men who ran it (v. 19).

How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied? “Learning” is literally “letters” (grammata), knowledge of the Scriptures and their interpretation. He was not illiterate; Luke shows him finding his place in a scroll in the synagogue (Luke 4:16–17). “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi, as Paul was under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). A teacher was expected to cite his teachers: “Rabbi So-and-so said, in the name of Rabbi So-and-so.” It was a sensible system, protecting a community from anyone with a private revelation. Jesus quoted no rabbi, yet knew the Scriptures more deeply than any of them. They are not quite sneering, but trying to account for something that does not fit their categories, as the council later is with the apostles (Acts 4:13).

The chain ended in him. They looked for a chain of teachers behind him and found none, because the chain ended in him. He is the Word who was with God in the beginning, and every true teacher who has ever opened the Scriptures has been borrowing from him. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and he gives them freely to fishermen.

Does this mean training does not matter for preachers? No. Asking where a teacher studied has saved the church from much nonsense. Paul was highly trained, and elders must be able to teach and hold firm to sound doctrine (Titus 1:9; 2 Timothy 2:15). Jesus is unique: his teacher was the Father. For everyone else, study is the ordinary way God makes faithful teachers. But the final test is not a certificate but whether a teacher’s words agree with Scripture and point to Christ. A trained man can be wrong and an untrained believer right, and both must be weighed by the Word.
verseByVerse.note: “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi.

parallels.desc: uneducated, common men

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ teaching comes from the Father who sent him, and anyone whose heart is set on doing God’s will will recognise it as God’s.

Not mine. He did have a teacher: the Father (5:19; 8:28; 12:49), a far greater authority than any line of rabbis. He who is God took the posture of one who listens, receives and passes on, so that what reaches us is nothing less than the Father’s own word.

If anyone’s will is to do God’s will. “Will” (thelē) means wants, desires. The condition for knowing the truth is not first intellectual but moral and spiritual: a will set on doing what God wants. How could I know whether this is true? Willingness first, knowledge second. A person who insists on staying uncommitted while he weighs the evidence keeps himself, however honestly, from the one kind of evidence that matters most here.

He will know. The problem with unbelief is not lack of evidence but an unwilling heart (5:40; 8:43–47). That is not a cheat. Some things can be known while remaining uninvolved, like the boiling point of water; others only from inside. Nobody learns whether a person is trustworthy by studying them at a distance; you find out by trusting them. To say God is known in the second way is a claim about what sort of being he is: not an object to be examined but a Lord to be obeyed. And the promise is wide: not “if anyone is clever or educated”. The condition is a willing heart, open to the least equipped person in the room.

What it does not mean. Not that we come to faith by our own good will, as if some people are naturally willing. No one can come unless the Father draws him (6:44), so the willing heart is itself God’s work: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God” (8:47). The verse shows how the Father’s drawing works: he gives a heart that wants to obey, and that heart recognises the Son’s teaching as God’s. But the person who genuinely wants God’s will will never be left in the dark.

In everyday life. Take the one thing you already suspect God wants of you: not a doctrine you are unsure of, but the plain duty you have been avoiding, the apology, the confession, the habit. Do it, in the strength of the Spirit who gave you the wanting. Sometimes doubt stands on top of disobedience and cannot survive its removal. You will not obey perfectly; the Son did his Father’s will perfectly for you, and your halting obedience is accepted in him.

I want to believe, but I still have doubts. Does that mean my will is not set on God? No. Doubt is not unwillingness. Many true believers carry questions for years, and Scripture is full of them (Psalm 73; Mark 9:24). This verse describes the person who keeps God at arm’s length so as not to have to obey him. If you want God’s will, even weakly, and are grieved by your doubts rather than comfortable with them, that wanting is itself his work in you. Bring your questions to him, keep reading his word, and keep obeying what you know. Light comes along the road of obedience, often slowly, but it comes.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A true teacher seeks the glory of the one who sent him, as Jesus does; then he turns on his accusers, who boast of Moses’ law while plotting murder.

Seeks his own glory. A test for any teacher: not his eloquence or success, but the direction his ambition points. Who is bigger at the end of the sermon?

No falsehood. Jesus seeks only the Father’s glory, and that is the proof of his truthfulness. “Falsehood” here is adikia, unrighteousness: not merely inaccuracy, but anything crooked at all, a bent motive under a straight sentence. The claim is either true or insufferable, and in him it is simply true.

Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. The tone changes abruptly: he has been reasoning, and now he accuses. They pride themselves on Moses, but do not keep his law.

Why do you seek to kill me? The law forbids murder, and they are planning one; they accuse him of breaking the Sabbath while they plan to break the sixth commandment. John told the reader at verse 1, but no one in the courts has admitted it, and Jesus says it aloud in the middle of an argument about Moses, the most pointed place it could go. Within months the men standing in front of him will do precisely that. He is reading their diary aloud, and leading into verses 21–24, where he defends the healing of chapter 5 from their own law: the accused becomes the judge.

He kept it for them. Only one teacher has ever had no falsehood in him at all. Every word he spoke aimed at his Father’s glory, and the Father answered by glorifying him (17:1). The men who held Moses in their hands and murder in their hearts stood before the only man who ever kept the law perfectly, and he kept it for them, all the way to the cross they were planning for him.

How can I tell whether a preacher is seeking his own glory? Watch over years, not a single sermon. A man seeking Christ’s glory makes Christ large and himself small, and opens the text rather than using it as a launch pad for himself. He is accountable to others and does not build a ministry that cannot survive without him. He is glad when someone else is preferred, slow to defend his reputation, quick to admit he is wrong. Be wary of the teacher whose stories are mostly about himself, who cannot take correction, or whose church seems to exist to display him. And turn the test on yourself: when you serve, whose name do you most want remembered?

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd calls Jesus mad for saying that people want to kill him, and he answers by going straight back to the one act of mercy that started it all.

You have a demon. A way of saying mad (10:20; compare 8:48, 52). On the crowd’s part it is alarm more than hostility: pilgrims who know nothing of the plot hear a teacher say people want to murder him, and conclude he is unwell. Whoever names what the room has agreed not to see is usually called mad, the cheapest response available. Here the man was entirely correct.

Who is seeking to kill you? They do not know; the leaders do (v. 25). John keeps the groups apart: the crowd here is the festival pilgrims, ignorant, volatile and mostly well disposed. “The Jews”, in John’s shorthand, generally means the Jerusalem leadership, the men of verse 1 who had already decided. The reader, told in the first sentence, knows what the crowd does not.

One work. The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath (5:1–9), which started the plot to kill him. “Marvel” here means they are disturbed and shocked by it, not admiring. Chapter 5 was at an unnamed feast, chapter 6 at Passover, and this is Tabernacles: many months on, they are still on it. “One” shows how far out of proportion the grievance is. A single kindness to a man ill for thirty-eight years has produced a settled determination to kill the one who did it, and has outlasted the memory of everything else he has done.

He did not answer evil for evil. His reply goes straight past the insult. The Holy One, on whom the Spirit rested without measure, heard his own people say he had a demon, and did not answer evil for evil.

In everyday life. Most of us carry a grievance like this somewhere: one act, by one person, still held against them months or years later, while everything else they have done is forgotten. Grudges grow in the dark. Brought to the God who has dropped every charge against you, they can be seen for the size they really are, and let go.

How should I respond when people think my faith is foolish or unhinged? Much as Jesus did: without panic and without retaliation. He went straight back to the real issue. Do not take the bait of defending your sanity or intelligence; gently bring the conversation back to Christ himself. Paul was told he was out of his mind and answered with courtesy and the truth (Acts 26:24–25). If they said it of the Master, they will say it of his servants (15:20). It is not a sign you have failed. It may be a sign you have been clear.
verseByVerse.note: The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus argues from their own practice: they already allow circumcision to go ahead on the Sabbath, so they already know that God’s day makes room for his work on a person.

Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers). Jesus argues from their own law, in a rabbinic form his opponents would have recognised instantly. Circumcision was given to Abraham (Genesis 17:10–12), centuries before Moses, and the law confirmed it (Leviticus 12:3). So the obligation they allow to override the Sabbath is older than Sinai, and they already know how to rank two commandments that seem to collide.

You circumcise a man. The law said a boy must be circumcised on the eighth day. If the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, circumcision went ahead, even though it was work; the rabbis agreed, and the Mishnah says everything needed for circumcision may be done on the Sabbath. Jesus takes their own ruling and asks why it stops where it does.

What kind of thing wins. Circumcision overrides the Sabbath because it marks a child as belonging to God. The rule they accept is not a technicality but mercy: when a rule and a person’s standing before God seem to collide, the person wins. Jesus is about to apply their own principle to a man who had lain on a mat for thirty-eight years.

He received the sign himself. The Lord who reasoned about the eighth-day sign had received it at eight days old (Luke 2:21), marked with the covenant he had made with Abraham. And what the sign promised, he gives: a circumcision made without hands, the putting off of the body of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11), so that people from every nation are marked as God’s own, not by a knife but by his death and rising.

Does this mean God’s commandments can be broken when they clash? No. God’s law does not contradict itself; the problem lay in how men had applied it. The Sabbath never forbade works of necessity and mercy, as even the confessions that keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath say (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Jesus shows that the command, rightly understood, always had room for love. When obeying God and loving people seem to conflict, look again at what God actually commanded.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when that day was a Sabbath. It began with Abraham, before Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the Sabbath allows circumcision, it allows far more the healing of a whole man, so they must stop judging by the surface and judge rightly.

Light and heavy. The argument goes from lesser to greater, a standard rabbinic method they called “light and heavy”: if it is right to perform circumcision, which affects one part of the body, on the Sabbath, how much more right is it to make a whole man well? Some rabbis argued the same way that saving a life overrides the Sabbath; Jesus goes further: healing fits the very purpose of the Sabbath, a day of rest and restoration.

Right judgment. “Appearances” (opsis) means what is seen on the surface: they see only that he worked on the Sabbath. Right judgment looks at what was really done, and why, as God looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). This verse is often quoted as if it said the opposite: it is a command to judge. Jesus’ complaint is not that they judged him but that they judged badly.

So am I allowed to judge people or not? Jesus’ two sayings fit together once you see what each is about. “Judge not, that you be not judged” (Matthew 7:1) forbids the judgment that sets itself up as final, condemns the person, and exempts the speaker from his own standard (the log in one’s own eye follows at once). This verse requires the judgment that looks past the surface to the substance. The first forbids condemning; the second commands discerning. A Christian must tell right from wrong, truth from error, and a wolf from a sheep. What he must never do is sit in God’s seat over another person’s soul, or judge by rumour, appearance or prejudice.

What does keeping the Lord’s Day look like in practice? Begin with what it is for: meeting the risen Christ with his people. So put gathered worship at the centre and arrange the day around it. Rest from ordinary work where you can, not to earn favour but as a gift that says your life does not depend on your labour. Make room for the word, prayer, family, hospitality, and visiting the lonely or the sick. Works of mercy and necessity are always in place: nurses, carers and parents of small children are not breaking anything. And do not make the day a burden for others; Jesus came to free the Sabbath from that.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Jesus never abolished the Sabbath in the Gospels, but showed its true purpose. Some Christians keep a strict Saturday or Sunday Sabbath; others see no special day at all. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day, the first day, when Christ rose, is a privilege for Christians, set apart gladly for worship, fellowship and rest, not as a binding law with rules about work, and with works of mercy always in place; no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). The view of the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

parallels.desc: judge righteously

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Local people who know of the plot are amazed to see the wanted man teaching freely, and wonder whether the rulers have secretly decided he is the Christ.

The people of Jerusalem. Locals, who know of the plot the pilgrims denied (v. 20).

Speaking openly. “Openly” (parrhēsia) means saying everything without holding back, the word used in verse 13: “no one spoke openly of him.” The people who admire him whisper; the man they want dead speaks freely in the temple.

Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ? The Greek form expects the answer no; they are half joking, half wondering. Their reasoning is not stupid: if the authorities wanted him, and he stands in public untouched, perhaps the rulers have quietly come round.

The restraint nobody can see. They are wrong, and John supplies the reason four verses later: “no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come” (v. 30). The inaction they are trying to explain is a restraint nobody in the story can see. That is the shape of much providence, God’s unseen hand governing great events and small, so that not even a sparrow falls “apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29). Things do not happen, and everyone constructs a reason; the real one is hidden from them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd rules Jesus out because they think they know where he comes from, and in fact they know neither his birthplace nor his true origin.

We know. They know he is from Nazareth. It is the deepest irony in the chapter, for John’s readers have known since the first verse that he comes from the Father’s side.

No one will know. Some Jewish writings speak of the Messiah hidden until God suddenly revealed him; others knew he would come from Bethlehem (v. 42). The crowd uses both against him within fifteen verses: here his origin is known, in verse 42 it is the wrong one. Any candidate who satisfied the second would fail the first.

The irony. They know neither his birthplace, Bethlehem, nor his true origin, the Father. Objections that cancel each other out are a human habit, not a peculiarly Jewish one: when a conclusion has been reached in advance, the reasons arrive afterwards and do not need to be consistent with each other, since their job is not to establish the conclusion but to protect it.

He made the hills Nazareth stood on. The one “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (Micah 5:2) consented to a hometown people could sneer at, and let men think they had him summed up. The man in front of them had made the hills Nazareth stood on.

So where did Jesus come from? Three answers, all true. As a man, he was born in Bethlehem, the town of David, as Micah foretold (Matthew 2:1–6), and grew up in Nazareth, which is why he was called a Nazarene. As the Son, he came from the Father, with whom he was before the world began (1:1; 17:5). And he came into the world by the Holy Spirit, conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary (Luke 1:35). His enemies knew only the town where he grew up; faith knows all three: the eternal Son, born of a woman, raised in a despised village, so that no one could say God had come too high for them to reach.
verseByVerse.note: Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus cries out that they know only the human facts about him: he was sent by the true God, whom they do not know and he does. Everything else in John 7 and 8 rests on this claim.

So Jesus proclaimed. “Proclaimed” (ekraxen, cried out): a loud, public, solemn declaration (v. 37; 12:44). He raises his voice in the temple courts.

You know me. Either a concession, “yes, you know the human facts, as far as they go”, or with an edge, as near to sarcasm as he comes: “so you know me, do you?” What follows tips it towards the second. What they know (v. 27) has left them ignorant of the half that matters: he was sent.

Him you do not know. “True” (alēthinos): genuine, real. To reject the Son is to show that you do not know the Father (8:19; 15:21). He tells a courtyard of devout people, at their own feast, that they do not know God, not imperfectly but at all, and that he does. This is the charge they will not forgive, and the attempt to arrest him in the next verse shows they understood how much he claimed.

I know him. The ground he gives is not experience but origin: he started with God, as God (1:1, 18). No prophet, priest or rabbi had ever stood in the Father’s presence and come out to tell us what he saw. He came out shouting it in the temple, and then he opened the way into the Father’s presence with his own blood, so that people who did not know God could be brought home to him.

In everyday life. Knowing God comes through knowing the Son. If God feels distant or unreal to you, look at Jesus: read a Gospel, slowly, and ask at each page, “so this is what God is like.” Then talk to him about what you see.

Can someone be sincerely religious and still not know God? Yes, and this verse is the proof. These men prayed, fasted, studied Scripture and kept the feasts, and Jesus says they did not know the one they worshipped. Knowing God is not the same as being religious. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3), and no one comes to the Father except through the Son (14:6). That is no reason to sneer at sincere people of other faiths or none, but it is a reason not to leave them where they are. And we should ask ourselves honestly: do I know God through Christ, or do I only know the religion?

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can arrest Jesus, because the hour the Father has set for his death has not yet come, and meanwhile, among the hostility, many begin to believe.

His hour had not yet come. Now the word John has been holding back returns: not kairos, the right moment of verse 6, but hōra, the appointment of his death, resurrection and return to the Father (2:4; 8:20; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). That hour is the cross, announced in chapter 12. What protects him is not a bodyguard but an appointment with his own execution that has not yet fallen due: he is safe because his death is fixed for another day.

Many believed. Belief in John can be shallow (2:23–25; 8:30–31), but here it is a start: amid hostility and arrest warrants, faith is quietly spreading.

When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done? Their reasoning is modest and mostly right: could anyone do more than this? It is not a complete confession, but it is not nothing.

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me until my work is done? Not quite. The verse does not say God’s servants are always preserved until they have done all we think they should; Stephen was stoned early in his ministry, and John the Baptist was beheaded on a whim at a party. It says something narrower and more solid: nothing whatever happens outside the Father’s timing, including what looks like defeat. The providence that keeps hands off Jesus here will hand him over in chapter 18, in the same loving work. Your days are written in his book (Psalm 139:16). No accident, no enemy and no illness can shorten them by an hour.

Is faith that starts from miracles real faith? It can be the beginning of real faith, and Jesus does not despise it; he does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20). John himself wrote down the signs so that we may believe (20:31). But faith that stops at what Jesus can do has not yet reached who he is. The crowd in chapter 6 wanted more bread and walked away when he offered himself. True faith moves from the works to the person: from what he did, to trusting, loving and following him when there are no signs at all. Whatever first drew you to Christ, the question is whether you have come to rest in him.

parallels.desc: his hour had come

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What finally moves the authorities to send for the temple police is not his teaching but the fact that ordinary people are starting to believe.

The crowd muttering. Not the teaching, nor the claim to have come from God (v. 29), but the muttering of verse 31 triggers the warrant. The Pharisees move when the numbers move, which tells you what they feared to lose: their grip on the people. When religion becomes a position to protect, the coming of God himself feels like a threat, and the people who should have been first to welcome him are the first to send for the police.

The chief priests and Pharisees. The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8); the Pharisees were the lay party of strict law-keeping. Together they made up much of the Sanhedrin, and in this Gospel they act together only to deal with him (11:47, 57; 18:3). Opposition to Christ unites people who cannot stand each other, as it will unite Herod and Pilate (Luke 23:12).

Officers to arrest him. The officers were the temple police, Levites who kept order in the temple under the chief priests. The rulers of the temple sent officers against the Lord of the temple. They will come back empty-handed (v. 46).
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with arrest, Jesus announces that he will soon go home to the Father who sent him, where those who reject him cannot follow.

I will be with you a little longer. About six months remained before the cross. He answers an arrest warrant by announcing his travel plans, and takes the confrontation out of their hands: they think they are deciding whether he stays, and he is leaving anyway, for somewhere they cannot follow.
