Going to him who sent me. Jesus speaks of his death, resurrection and ascension as a going home to the Father (13:1, 3; 16:5, 28). He is not driven out; he goes.

You will not find me. A solemn warning that a time will come when it is too late (Proverbs 1:28; Isaiah 55:6: “Seek the LORD while he may be found”). It is spoken to men holding an arrest warrant, who will one day want what he offered and find it withdrawn: not a threat aimed at the worried, but a fact aimed at the comfortable.

Where I am you cannot come. Not “where I will be” but “where I am”: he speaks as the one who already belongs to the Father’s presence. Unbelievers cannot follow him there (8:21). He says something similar to the disciples later (13:33), but with a promise: you will follow afterwards (13:36; 14:3).

That where I am you may be also. He went home by way of the cross, and not alone: where his enemies could not come, he has gone to prepare a place for his friends (14:2–3). To unbelief he says, “Where I am you cannot come”; to faith he says, “I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.” The same words that warn the proud are the hope of every believer.

In everyday life. If there is something you have been meaning to settle with God, a sin to confess, a step of obedience, a first prayer, do not leave it for a better week.

I am frightened that it may be too late for me. Is this verse about me? If it troubles you, that is evidence it is not describing you. The seeking that fails here is that of men who refused him to his face and would one day want rescue without wanting him. Scripture never shows a penitent sinner finding the door shut. This Gospel says the opposite: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37), said to a crowd that mostly walked away. While you are alive and can call on him, the door is open. Call on him now.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders mockingly guess that Jesus means to go off and teach the Greeks, and without knowing it they describe exactly what his gospel will do.

The Dispersion among the Greeks. The Dispersion (diaspora) means the Jews scattered outside the land, in the cities of the Greek-speaking world; probably more lived outside the land than in it. The leaders make his words sound absurd: he must mean going off to foreign cities to teach Gentiles, which no respectable Jerusalem teacher would do.

The irony. Their mocking guess was prophetic. Through his apostles Jesus did go to the Dispersion and teach the Greeks. The gospel went from Jerusalem to the synagogues of the Dispersion and then to the Gentiles (Acts 11:20; 13:46), carried above all by Paul, a Pharisee trained in Jerusalem, and the letters of James and 1 Peter are addressed to the Dispersion. John was probably writing for readers in those very cities; for them, a mocking question had turned into their own address.

Enemies who say more than they know. It will happen again at 11:50, when Caiaphas remarks that it is better for one man to die for the people, and John stops the story to point out that he was prophesying without the least idea of it. The Lord of history takes the sentences of those most determined to stop Jesus and makes them true in a sense they would have found intolerable. A taunt in the temple became a map of the mission, and the scattered nations heard the voice that Jerusalem refused.

What does he mean by saying...? They are thinking on the wrong level. Yet they quote his words back, both halves, in full, which men dismissing something rarely do. They are worrying at a sentence they cannot get out of their heads. They have no idea what it means, they are certain it is nonsense, and they cannot leave it alone.
verseByVerse.note: The Dispersion means the Jews living scattered outside the land among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the climax of the feast that remembered water from the rock, Jesus offers himself as the source: anyone who is thirsty may come to him and drink, and rivers of living water will flow. The argument gives way to an invitation; in 8:12 he takes up the feast’s other image, the light.

On the last day of the feast, the great day. Later Jewish writings describe water carried each morning from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured out beside the altar, while the people sang the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) and prayed for rain; on the seventh day the priests circled the altar seven times. The ceremony looked back to the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6) and forward to the promised day when living waters would flow out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8, read at this feast) and from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12). The rabbis said that whoever had not seen the joy of the water-drawing had never seen joy.

Jesus stood up and cried out. Teachers usually sat. Just as the water ceremony is ending for another year, into the silence after the last pouring, a man stands up in the temple courts and shouts. The ceremony remembered water from a rock for a nation that would otherwise have died in the desert; he offers, to anybody at all, what it had only ever pointed at.

If anyone thirsts. It echoes Isaiah 55:1: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters.” He is the rock that gives the water (1 Corinthians 10:4), and to come and drink is to believe (6:35). The terms are as wide as language permits: not “if anyone is worthy, or prepared, or knows enough”. The only qualification is an appetite, which nobody can manufacture or fake.

As the Scripture has said. “Heart” is literally “belly” (koilia), the innermost being. Jesus is summing up a theme (see the box below), from Isaiah 58:11 (a spring whose waters do not fail) to Ezekiel 47. Ezekiel saw that river come from under the temple threshold and deepen, ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, until no one could cross it, and everything it touched lived. The river of promise they had been singing about is standing in front of them.

Rivers of living water. Not a cup, not a well: rivers, more than anyone could ever use. A man of thirty-odd with no house, under an arrest warrant and dead by spring, offers at his people’s greatest festival to be the river. “Living water” was the everyday phrase for running water, from a spring or stream rather than a cistern, and God calls himself “the fountain of living waters” (Jeremiah 2:13): life that keeps flowing from God himself and never goes stale.

The true Rock was struck. The rock was struck in the wilderness and water gushed out for a rebellious people. The true Rock was struck on a hill outside Jerusalem, and from his pierced side came blood and water (19:34). The feast poured out one golden pitcher a morning; the river from him has run for two thousand years and never run low, and the offer has never been narrowed: “If anyone thirsts, let him come.”

In everyday life. Think where you go when you are dry: the screen, the fridge, the shop, the bottle, the approval of others. None of them is the river. When you feel that thirst, pray a single sentence: “Lord Jesus, I am thirsty; give me yourself.” Then let it flow on to others. Rivers are for giving away.

I do not feel thirsty for God. Is this invitation for me? Thirst does not always feel like longing for God. Often it feels like restlessness, boredom, or the dull ache after the thing you hoped would fill you has not. Augustine confessed that God made us for himself, so that we find no rest anywhere else, and most restlessness is that thirst in disguise. If you have ever wanted more than this life gives, the invitation is for you; and if you feel nothing at all, come anyway, and ask him to make you thirsty.

So how do I actually come and drink? To come and drink is to believe: to trust Jesus himself, and keep trusting him, for what only he can give. In practice it means turning to him in prayer as someone who needs him, listening to him in his word, and receiving him in the means he has given: the preaching of the gospel, the fellowship of his people and the Lord’s Supper. Drinking is not a single gulp at conversion but a daily return to the spring. When you are dry, do not first try harder; go back to him and drink.

Uncertain wording. Three things cannot be settled. Which day: “the great day” is probably the seventh, the climax of the water ceremony, though some think the eighth day of solemn assembly. Which Scripture: no single Old Testament verse says this, so Jesus is most likely gathering up the passages above. Whose heart: the Greek can be punctuated two ways, as the ESV notes. Most take it, with the ESV, of the believer’s heart: the one who drinks becomes a source of blessing to others (4:14). Others read: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him drink who believes in me. As the Scripture has said, out of his heart...”, so that the rivers flow from Christ’s heart. That reading fits a ceremony in which water flows from the temple, and Jesus is the new temple (2:19–21); but the ESV’s reading is natural, and most scholars think it likely. The difference is smaller than it looks, since the next verse explains that Jesus means the Spirit, who comes from Christ to the believer and then out through him. The spring is Christ either way; the question is only how far downstream the sentence is looking.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar each day of the feast. No single verse says these exact words; Jesus draws on several prophecies. The ESV notes a different punctuation that makes Jesus himself the source of the water.

parallels.desc: come to the waters
water flowing from the temple
living waters from Jerusalem

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rivers are the Holy Spirit, given to everyone who believes, once Jesus had been glorified through his cross, resurrection and return to the Father.

Now this he said about the Spirit. John stops the story to explain, as he does when a saying would otherwise be misread (2:21; 12:33). The Old Testament often pictures the Spirit as water poured out (Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). The rivers are the Spirit, not an influence but a person, and John writes from the other side of Pentecost, of what had since happened to him and his readers. “Those who believed” means every believer, not some special class (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2).

For as yet the Spirit had not been given. Literally “for the Spirit was not yet.” The Spirit was of course active in the Old Testament (Psalm 51:11) and in Jesus’ ministry (1:32), but he had not yet been given in the new covenant way, poured out on all God’s people to dwell in them for ever (14:16–17). Before Pentecost the Spirit came mostly upon prophets, kings and craftsmen for particular tasks; after it he made his home in fishermen, slaves, widows and children, all who believe. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation lives in ordinary believers, and will never leave.

Because Jesus was not yet glorified. To glorify is to show someone’s true greatness. In John that begins, astonishingly, at the cross, where the Son’s love and obedience are displayed most fully (12:23–24), and is completed when the Father welcomes him back to the glory he had before the world existed (13:31; 17:1, 5). The Spirit could not come until Jesus had finished his work and returned to the Father (16:7); then the exalted Christ poured him out (Acts 2:33). The river could not flow until the rock had been struck, so the invitation of verse 37 came from a man on his way to a cross.

In everyday life. If you believe in Christ, the Spirit lives in you; you are not waiting for him. Before the hard conversation, the temptation or the task beyond you, ask him to fill you and pray simply: “Holy Spirit, you live in me; help me now.”

How do I know I have the Spirit? Not first by a feeling, but by what he does. He brings you to confess that Jesus is Lord and mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3). He makes Christ precious to you (16:14). He teaches you to call God Father and to trust him as his child (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate sin and fight it, and slowly grows his fruit in you: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit lives in you, dramatic experience or not. Weak faith is still Spirit-given faith.

What does it mean to be filled with the Spirit? It means to be more and more under his influence, as a sail is filled by the wind. Paul commands it as a continuing thing, “be filled” (Ephesians 5:18), and shows its marks in the next verses: worship, thankfulness and humble service in home and church. You seek it by keeping in step with him: reading the word he inspired, praying, confessing sin quickly, obeying what he shows you, and asking. Jesus promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Where Christians differ: receiving the Spirit. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching often holds that the baptism of the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, marked by speaking in tongues. This commentary’s view: this verse says all who believe receive the Spirit, from the moment of faith (1 Corinthians 12:13). There may be many fresh fillings and deeper experiences of the Spirit, but no second class of Christians. The sign gifts of the apostolic age, such as tongues and prophecy, served to confirm the founding of the church and have ceased, while the Spirit himself remains with every believer for ever. Scripture ties those gifts to the apostles and the founding of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4), and the Scripture they served is now complete. Many faithful brothers and sisters in Pentecostal and charismatic churches read the evidence differently; they love the same Lord and seek the same Spirit, and they deserve to be heard with respect.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The invitation divides the crowd: some see in Jesus the Prophet like Moses, some the Christ, and some dismiss him because of where they think he comes from.

This really is the Prophet. “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15–18; compare 1:21; 6:14). Some Jews thought of the Prophet as distinct from the Messiah; Jesus is both (Acts 3:22).

Is the Christ to come from Galilee? The Greek expects the answer no. John lets the objection stand: all through this Gospel people reject Jesus on grounds that one honest question would have collapsed, and nobody asks it.

Moses gave water; Jesus gives the Spirit. Moses struck the rock and the people drank; then he died outside the land, promising another prophet. The crowd saw Moses in Jesus, rightly, and still fell short of the truth. Moses gave water; Jesus gives the Spirit. Moses spoke God’s words; Jesus is God’s Word. Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant, and Christ is faithful over it as a Son (Hebrews 3:5–6).

Why did people expect different figures, a prophet and a Christ? The Old Testament promises came in many strands, and few saw how they fitted together: some looked for the prophet like Moses, some for a king of David’s line, some for a priestly figure, or for several, arriving separately. Jesus is all of them in one person: the Prophet who speaks God’s word, the Priest who offers himself, the King who reigns. Hence the Reformers’ threefold office. The categories built to receive him were too small one by one, and too confusing together, until he filled them all.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objectors quote Scripture correctly, that the Christ comes from David’s line and from Bethlehem, and reject Jesus for not fulfilling the very prophecies he fulfils. So he divides the crowd.

The offspring of David, and from Bethlehem. They were right that the Messiah would be a son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), and right that he would come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; compare Matthew 2:5–6). They are not twisting the text; they reach a false conclusion because they have a fact wrong and never thought to test it.

The irony. They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem and was descended from David. John expects his readers to know the story (Matthew 1–2; Luke 2). It is possible to quote Scripture accurately and apply it validly, and still end up on the wrong side of God, through an unexamined assumption underneath: that he was from Galilee felt like common knowledge, so nobody checked.

A division. “Division” (schisma): Jesus divides people (9:16; 10:19), and no one can stay neutral about him. The tear runs through crowds, the council and his own family. He said himself that he had not come to bring peace but a sword, and that a man’s enemies would be those of his own household (Matthew 10:34–36). The division is not the goal and it is not the good. It is what happens when a claim this large meets people who are free to refuse it, and the alternative, a Christ small enough that nobody need decide about him, was never on offer.

Kept to the letter, in a manger. The one they said could not be the Christ was born in the very town they named, of the very line they demanded. God kept his word to David to the letter, in a manger, while the scholars of Jerusalem went on arguing, and the division over his Son is the sign that the Son has come.

What if following Christ is dividing my family? It hurts, and Jesus knew it from the inside: his own brothers did not believe. First, make sure the division is over Christ, not your harshness, pride or a quarrel dressed up as faith. Then stay loving, patient and honest, without withdrawing, retaliating or preaching at every meal. Honour your parents and keep your promises where you can do so without denying him (Ephesians 6:2). Keep bringing each of them to God in prayer. And take comfort that the division need not be the last word: the brothers who did not believe in John 7 were praying with the disciples in Acts 1.
verseByVerse.note: They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: from Bethlehem shall come a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some want to seize him, and no one does: the Father’s unseen restraint holds, because the hour has not come.

No one laid hands on him. Three attempts (vv. 30, 44, 45), three failures, and the reason given only once: “his hour had not yet come” (v. 30).

What providence looks like from inside. There is strikingly little to see: no lightning, no escape, no crowd parting. Some men felt like seizing a teacher and somehow did not; asked, they would probably have said the moment passed. The ordinary reasons a thing does not happen are the means God uses, not an alternative to him; here the restraint worked on a private impulse that never became an action.

The hand he let men seize. No hand could close on him that autumn, because the Father had not yet given him up. In the spring the Son of Man was delivered into the hands of men, as he had said he would be (Mark 9:31), and he went into them willingly, so that his people might be kept in his own. “No one will snatch them out of my hand,” he said (10:28), and the hand that holds them is the one he let men seize.

If God restrains evil, why does he not restrain all of it? Scripture gives not the whole answer, but enough to trust him. God restrains a great deal of evil we never see, and he permits some evil for purposes we cannot yet see, never approving it, and always turning it to good for those who love him (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28). The clearest example is this story: God held back these hands in the autumn, and in the spring let wicked hands crucify his Son, accomplishing through the greatest evil the greatest good. If he can do that with the cross, he can be trusted with what he permits in your life.

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers sent to arrest Jesus come back without him, arrested instead by his words.

The officers. The temple police sent in verse 32 return empty-handed, perhaps several days later, long enough to have heard the invitation of verse 37.

No one ever spoke like this man! An extraordinary admission from men trained to obey orders, who had heard many teachers in the temple (Matthew 7:28–29). An excuse would have been easy: the crowd was too thick. Instead they admire him openly before the men who ordered the arrest. They make no confession of faith; they simply could not do it, and said why.

The truest sentence in the chapter. The most honest testimony in the chapter comes from unbelievers with everything to lose by giving it. Nameless, they say it, are sneered at, and disappear. That is its own small comfort for anyone who has said the right thing once, at cost, and seen nothing come of it. It went into the record. Decades later John was still writing it down; it has outlasted the council that mocked them.

The voice of creation, in a Galilean accent. The voice that said “Let there be light” spoke in the temple courts in the accent of Galilee, and hardened men sent to bind him went back unable to do it. It called Lazarus out of a tomb; it will call all the dead from their graves (5:28–29); and in between it calls, through the plain reading of his word, sheep who know it and follow (10:27).

What was it about how he spoke? Not technique. Other teachers quoted authorities; he spoke with his own (Matthew 7:29). Other teachers explained God; he spoke as one who had come from him, and his words were spirit and life (6:63). He spoke with perfect truth and perfect love at once, which no one else has managed. He knew what was in a man (2:25), so his words went straight to the heart. And he spoke the Father’s own words (v. 16). When you read the Gospels and find a saying of his lodging in you and refusing to leave, you are feeling what the officers felt.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees answer the officers not with reasons but with scorn and the weight of authority: no one who matters believes in him. Even as they say it, one of their own is about to speak up.

Have you also been deceived? “Deceived” (planaō): led astray, the same word as verse 12. This is not a request for reasons but a warning shot, meant to make the officers feel foolish. Nobody so much as answers what they said, that no one ever spoke like this man.

Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him? The argument from authority, familiar to this day: none of the experts believe, so it must be false. Not that Jesus is wrong, but that no one who matters thinks he is right: policemen are asked whether they will set their judgment against the learned, and nothing more is heard from them. The irony: Nicodemus is sitting in that chamber and is about to speak (v. 50); Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, will be revealed as a secret disciple (19:38), and both men will carry the body of Jesus the following spring; and later many priests will believe (Acts 6:7).

Consensus is evidence about people. Consensus is not nothing; the church has generally been right to suspect the man who alone sees the truth. But what most people think tells you about the people, not about whether the thing is true, and its worth depends entirely on whether the people are free to say what they think. In this room they were not, and the proof is that the one sympathiser present could manage only a question about procedure.

Should I ignore scholars and experts when they reject Christianity? No. Listen to them, learn from them, and take their arguments seriously; many scholars are believers, and honest scholarship has served the church well. But ask what their actual reasons are, and weigh them. The consensus of one century is often the embarrassment of the next. The question is not who believes, but whether it is true. Look at Christ yourself, and read the evidence for the resurrection with your own eyes.

parallels.desc: many even of the authorities believed

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders dismiss the ordinary people as ignorant of the law and under its curse, and so pour contempt on the very people who had come closest to the truth.

This crowd that does not know the law. The leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the details of the law and its oral traditions, calling them the “people of the land” (am ha’aretz), and some rabbinic sayings warn against eating with them or marrying their daughters. The phrase came to mark something like a caste, people not trusted to tithe or keep the purity rules.

Is accursed. The law did pronounce a curse on those who did not keep it (Deuteronomy 27:26). The irony again: the leaders who know the law are breaking it, as Nicodemus will point out in the next verse. It is the class judgment of the educated on the uneducated, dressed as a theological verdict.

The people who got closest. Confused, divided and badly informed, the crowd is nonetheless asking whether this might be the Christ. It is the pattern of the whole Gospel: a Samaritan woman hears one of the plainest statements of his identity (4:26), fishermen stay when the theologians leave, a blind beggar will out-argue the council. And the men who know God’s law best say that nobody who matters believes in him and everybody else is cursed.

The people of his heart. The rulers called the crowd accursed; Christ became a curse for them, and for us, on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the people of the land and the Gentiles alike (Galatians 3:13–14). He did not curse the ignorant; he taught them, healed them and died for them. The despised people of the land turned out to be the people of his heart.

Does this mean knowledge is dangerous and I should not study? No. Knowledge of God’s word is a great gift, and Scripture urges us to grow in it (2 Peter 3:18). The problem in this verse is not knowledge but pride: knowledge without love puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1). The test is what learning does to the way you see other believers. If it makes you more humble, and delighted when an untrained Christian sees something true, it is doing its proper work. If it makes you contemptuous, it has become the thing in this verse. Study hard, and stay low.
verseByVerse.note: Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the finer points of the law.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, the one ruler who had met Jesus, appeals to the law the council boasts of: no one may be condemned without a hearing. It is a small step, but a costly one, on a long road to open faith.

Nicodemus, who had gone to him before. Nicodemus, a member of the council who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2), answers their question (v. 48) by his presence: here is one ruler at least open to Jesus.

Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? He does not defend Jesus outright, but appeals to justice. The law required a fair hearing (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 17:4), and the men who boast of knowing it are condemning a man without trial. It seems little, but he has just heard the room agree that anyone who believes in Jesus is deceived. Speaking at all marks him as a sympathiser, and the sneer shows he was heard that way and what going further would cost. And he is entirely right: the only legally correct sentence spoken in the chamber comes from the one man there who has actually met Jesus.

The shape of his story. Three appearances: by night with a question (3:1–2); here, with a cautious objection about procedure; and finally at the cross, in daylight, in public, carrying about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury a condemned man (19:39), a quantity fit for a king, at the moment when being associated with him could not have looked worse. The journey took perhaps two years. Grace was not in a hurry, and it did not let go.

In everyday life. Nicodemus said little here, but he said something. In the meeting where someone is being talked about unfairly, the one sentence may be simply: “should we not hear his side first?” It costs something to say it, and the Lord who bore so patiently with Nicodemus will strengthen you for it.

Is it all right to be a secret or cautious believer? A cautious beginning is not the same as settled secrecy. Nicodemus’ first steps were small, and many true believers begin quietly. But John does not leave him there, and we should not stay there. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and John says sadly of some rulers that they believed but did not confess him, because they loved human praise (12:42–43). If you are a quiet believer, ask what the next honest step is: telling one friend, joining a church, being baptised. Faith that is real grows towards the light.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: inquire diligently

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council answers Nicodemus with a sneer and a wrong fact about the prophets, and breaks up without a verdict.

Are you from Galilee too? Nobody answers his question about procedure; they mock him as one of the northern peasants. It is not a rebuttal but a way of putting a man in a category so that nothing he says needs weighing.

Search and see. “Search” means search the Scriptures. They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), only a few miles from Nazareth, and Isaiah had promised that a great light would shine in Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16). The men who dismissed the crowd as ignorant of the law (v. 49) get a fact about the prophets wrong, because they are angry, and never notice.

They went each to his own house. The council breaks up without decision. This sentence (v. 53) begins the passage about the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the ESV places in brackets. The earliest and most reliable manuscripts do not contain it, and some place it elsewhere (after Luke 21:38, for example). Its style is unlike John’s; the KJV prints it because it follows later manuscripts. It is very likely a true story about Jesus preserved in the church, but not originally part of John’s Gospel, and we comment on it in chapter 8 with that caution.

The flattest sentence in the chapter. No verdict, no arrest, no resolution, while the man they were discussing, as the bracketed story goes on to say, went out to the Mount of Olives. “They went each to his own house.” He had no house to go to. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58).

In everyday life. When you notice yourself answering a point by attacking the person who made it, stop, and ask whether what they said is true. Anger made these scholars forget their own Bibles; wait until you are calm before you answer.

Why does my Bible put brackets here, in the middle of a scene? Because the bracketed passage runs from this sentence to 8:11, opening at the last verse of a chapter. The brackets hide nothing; they tell you honestly what the manuscripts show. The story itself is very probably a true memory of Jesus, and it may be read and treasured as one, provided no doctrine is made to rest on it alone.

Textual note. One early papyrus reads “the Prophet” here, meaning the prophet like Moses would not arise from Galilee, which would make their claim less obviously false. The ESV follows the majority of manuscripts.
verseByVerse.note: They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee. The ESV notes that the earliest manuscripts do not include 7:53–8:11 and brackets the passage.

parallels.desc: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher
Galilee of the nations

7.title: Rivers of Living Water
7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.<sup>2</sup>Now the Jews’ Feast of Booths was at hand.<sup>3</sup>So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing.<sup>4</sup>For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world.”<sup>5</sup>For not even his brothers believed in him.<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always here.<sup>7</sup>The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil.<sup>8</sup>You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come.”<sup>9</sup>After saying this, he remained in Galilee.<sup>10</sup>But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private.<sup>11</sup>The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, “Where is he?”<sup>12</sup>And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, “He is a good man,” others said, “No, he is leading the people astray.”<sup>13</sup>Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.<sup>14</sup>About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching.<sup>15</sup>The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?”<sup>16</sup>So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.<sup>17</sup>If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.<sup>18</sup>The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood.<sup>19</sup>Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?”<sup>20</sup>The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”<sup>21</sup>Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you all marvel at it.<sup>22</sup>Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.<sup>23</sup>If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man’s whole body well?<sup>24</sup>Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”<sup>25</sup>Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, “Is not this the man whom they seek to kill?<sup>26</sup>And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?<sup>27</sup>But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from.”<sup>28</sup>So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know.<sup>29</sup>I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.”<sup>30</sup>So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.<sup>31</sup>Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, “When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?”<sup>32</sup>The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.<sup>33</sup>Jesus then said, “I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me.<sup>34</sup>You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come.”<sup>35</sup>The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?<sup>36</sup>What does he mean by saying, ’You will seek me and you will not find me,’ and, ’Where I am you cannot come’?”<sup>37</sup>On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.<sup>38</sup>Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ’Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”<sup>39</sup>Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.<sup>40</sup>When they heard these words, some of the people said, “This really is the Prophet.”<sup>41</sup>Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “Is the Christ to come from Galilee?<sup>42</sup>Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”<sup>43</sup>So there was a division among the people over him.<sup>44</sup>Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.<sup>45</sup>The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”<sup>46</sup>The officers answered, “No one ever spoke like this man!”<sup>47</sup>The Pharisees answered them, “Have you also been deceived?<sup>48</sup>Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?<sup>49</sup>But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed.”<sup>50</sup>Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them,<sup>51</sup>“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”<sup>52</sup>They replied, “Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”<sup>53</sup>[[They went each to his own house,
7.overview:
Where we are. About six months have passed since the feeding of the five thousand, when many disciples turned back (6:66). Now the autumn Feast of Booths arrives, and Jesus goes up to Jerusalem, where the authorities already want him dead (5:18). Chapters 7 and 8 both take place at this one feast.

The message. Everyone at the feast is asking where Jesus comes from, and he answers: from the Father, who sent him. So he can give what the festival only pointed to. The shelters of branches and the water poured at the altar remembered God living among his people and giving them water from the rock; now Jesus stands up and says that anyone who is thirsty may come to him and drink, and receive the Spirit.

Why it was said. John’s first readers had paid a price for confessing Jesus, and were surrounded by people who called him a deceiver (see the introduction). This chapter shows that the arguments against him were old and confused, that the honest witnesses were on his side, and that the river he promised had already reached them in the Spirit.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus refuses to go up on his unbelieving brothers’ terms, as a public show, and goes privately in his Father’s time (vv. 1–13). In the temple he teaches that his words are the Father’s, and exposes leaders who boast of Moses yet plot murder over a Sabbath healing (vv. 14–24). The crowd argues about his origin; he declares that he comes from the God they do not know, an arrest is ordered, and he warns that he will soon go where they cannot follow (vv. 25–36). On the last great day he cries out his invitation to the thirsty, and John explains that he meant the Spirit (vv. 37–39). It ends in division, failed arrests and Nicodemus mocked for asking a fair hearing (vv. 40–52).

Where it leads. To the cross, the hour that “had not yet come” (v. 30). The Spirit could not be given “because Jesus was not yet glorified” (v. 39), and in John that glory begins at the cross. The rock in the wilderness had to be struck before water flowed; the true Rock was struck, and from his pierced side came blood and water (19:34). Then the risen Christ poured out the river he had promised.

For us. The invitation has not been narrowed since it was shouted across the temple courts: the only qualification is thirst. Come to Christ and keep coming, and the Spirit he gives will flow on through you to others. And do not let fear keep you quiet about him, as it kept the crowd.

keyVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’”
keyVerse.note: This is the climax the whole chapter has been building towards. After days of argument about where Jesus comes from, he stops answering questions and offers himself as the water the feast had been celebrating, and John tells us that the water is the Spirit (v. 39). The only condition is thirst, and the gift is not a cup but rivers.

7.reflection:
Jesus’ brothers had lived with him for years and still did not believe (v. 5), yet later they were praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14). Who is the person you have most nearly given up praying for? What does this chapter give you to keep going?

The crowd thought well of Jesus, but “for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him” (v. 13). What makes you hesitate to speak about Christ, and what would one true sentence about him sound like in the conversations you have this week?

Jesus says that whoever wants to do God’s will “will know whether the teaching is from God” (v. 17). How have you found that obedience and understanding go together? Is there a plain duty you have been avoiding?

Jesus invites “anyone” who thirsts to come to him and drink, and promises rivers of the Spirit flowing out (vv. 37–39). Where do you tend to go when you feel dry, and what would it look like to come to him instead, and let what he gives flow on to others?

8.title: The Light of the World

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the light of the world, and the only way out of the darkness is to believe that he is who he says he is. The bracketed story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), probably not part of John’s original Gospel, shows that light at work: her accusers are exposed, and she is neither condemned nor excused. Then Jesus declares himself the light of the world (v. 12), answers the charge that he testifies only to himself by naming the Father as his second witness (vv. 13–20), and warns that unless they believe “I am” they will die in their sins (vv. 21–24). The cross will show who he is (vv. 25–29), and many believe (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is full of courtroom language and the bare words “I am”, the name of the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus says that he judges no one (v. 15), and also that his judgment is true (v. 16); how the two fit together is shown in the note on vv. 15–16.
verseByVerse.examples: She goes free because the one who alone had the right to condemn her would bear the penalty himself (see the note on vv. 9–11). Every Christian stands where she stood.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a night on the Mount of Olives, Jesus is back in the temple at dawn, teaching the ordinary people who come to him. The story that begins here was very probably not written by John, though it is very likely true (see the textual note that follows).

Textual note. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is printed in brackets in the ESV. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have it; the early church fathers who commented on John verse by verse pass straight from 7:52 to 8:12; and where the story does appear in later manuscripts, it wanders: after 7:36, after 7:44, at the end of John, or after Luke 21:38. Its style is more like Luke’s than John’s, and most scholars, conservative evangelicals included, conclude that it was not part of John’s original Gospel; the KJV, following later manuscripts, prints it without brackets. Yet many believe it records a true event from Jesus’ life, preserved in the church’s memory. Because Scripture is God’s word as originally given, the church should not build doctrine on this passage alone; but what it shows of Jesus is taught elsewhere in Scripture too.

How could such a thing happen? A passage that wanders like this has almost certainly been added rather than removed, and many manuscripts that include it mark it with the symbols scribes used for doubtful material. They knew. Yet almost nobody thinks the story was invented. It was known very early in the Latin-speaking churches, and Jerome says he found it in many manuscripts. Augustine suggested that some men of little faith had removed it, fearing it would give their wives licence to sin. It is the kind of story that would be uncomfortable to keep and hard to imagine anyone making up: very probably a true memory of Jesus that circulated on its own and was written into John’s Gospel where it fitted.

Should I be shaken by the brackets in my Bible? No. The brackets are the church showing its working, in public, about twelve verses out of some eight thousand in the New Testament. Nothing is hidden and nothing is lost: the Lord who says “neither do I condemn you” here says it in substance all through the Gospels, and everywhere calls sinners to leave their sin. So the passage may be read, treasured and preached as a faithful record of Jesus.

The Mount of Olives. While the council went “each to his own house” (7:53), Jesus spent his nights in Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:37), across the Kidron Valley, on the hillside where months later he would pray in agony and be arrested.

All the people came to him. While the leaders plot, ordinary people come, and at daybreak the temple becomes again a house of teaching.

He sat down. The posture of a teacher, and of authority: not a guest in the temple but its Lord, teaching in his Father’s house.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem. Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders drag a woman caught in adultery into the middle of the crowd, and the man is missing. She is not being brought to justice but used as bait.

The scribes and the Pharisees. The scribes were the experts in the law; John never uses the word elsewhere, another sign of the passage’s different origin.

Caught in adultery. Where is the man? Adultery is not committed alone, and the law required both to die (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). The men about to quote Moses have already broken the law they cite by leaving one of the guilty at home, choosing the defendant who is easier to drag in and whose life matters less to them. It is the oldest and most familiar pattern: a woman made to carry in public a shame that a man is quietly allowed to walk away from.

In the midst. In a ring of men, in the temple courts at dawn, she is brought not to a court but to a lesson, and made the visual aid. This is how every one of us stands before God’s judgment: no cover, no defence, fully seen.

Teacher. The title of respect, from men who have arranged the one situation in which they think any answer will destroy him.

In everyday life. You stand only because Christ refused to use your sin against you. So watch for the moment when someone else’s failure becomes useful to you: to win an argument, to look better, to settle a score. Put it down.

Why does Jesus never mention the missing man? He does not need to: everyone present could count. By refusing the part they had written for him, he will not complete a sentence that was never being passed honestly, or let God’s law be used as a stone in somebody else’s fight, and the missing man stands as a silent witness against the accusers. When a community is fierce about one person’s sin and silent about another’s, according to who is more convenient to blame, it is not defending holiness. It is using it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They quote half of Moses to set a trap, and Jesus answers first by stooping to write on the ground.

Moses commanded us. The law of Moses specified stoning for a betrothed woman (Deuteronomy 22:23–24), and the man was to die with her (see the note on vv. 3–4). They quote half the law.

So what do you say? The trap. If Jesus says, “Let her go,” he contradicts Moses and loses his standing as a teacher of the law. If he says, “Stone her,” he abandons his name as the friend of sinners and defies Rome, which did not allow the Jews to carry out death sentences (18:31). Either way they have a charge, and the woman is not a person to them but a prop.

He wrote on the ground. We are not told what, and guesses abound: the accusers’ sins, the law requiring both parties, a line from the prophets. One rests on where the scene sits rather than on imagination. Jeremiah says that those who turn away from the LORD “shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water” (Jeremiah 17:13), and the fountain of living water is what Jesus had cried out about on the last day of the feast (7:37–38). If that is what his finger traced, the accusers were watching their own verdict being written while they waited for his. It cannot be proved and should not be preached as certain; perhaps the point is simply that he refuses to be rushed.

The Lawgiver in the dust. What is certain is the posture. Asked to pronounce a death sentence, he first goes down into the dirt of the courtyard while a woman stands in a circle of men, and puts himself lower than everyone present, including her. The Lawgiver was crouched in the dust of his own temple, and the men quoting his law at him did not know it. He had come down to keep that law in every point for people who had broken it, and in the end he would be lifted up from the ground to bear its curse (Galatians 3:13).

In everyday life. When someone who has already decided what you should say presses you for an instant answer, you may pause. Stoop before you speak: pray, think, and let the heat go out of the moment.
verseByVerse.note: The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death; the man is missing. Rome did not allow the Jewish authorities to carry out executions, so the question was a trap either way.

parallels.desc: both of them shall die

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus upholds the law and turns it on the accusers: only an honest witness, clear of the same sin, may throw the first stone.

Without sin among you. Under the law the witnesses threw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7), and a false witness suffered the very penalty he had sought for another (Deuteronomy 19:16–19). Jesus does not deny the law, dispute the facts or make a speech about mercy. He hands them the stones and attaches the condition the law already contained: are you fit to carry out God’s judgment? No answer could keep closer to the law, and it empties the courtyard. To men who had brought the woman and not the man, it would have landed like a hand on the shoulder.

Once more he bent down. He goes back to the ground, leaving them with their consciences and free to leave without being stared at. Grace does not humiliate even the accusers; it invites them to look at themselves.

In everyday life. The last time you were quite certain somebody else was in the wrong, would your certainty have survived being asked, before witnesses, whether you were clear of the same thing? Remember the one who had every right to throw a stone at you and did not.

So does a church or a court have to be sinless to deal with sin? No. Otherwise no court could ever sit and no church could ever discipline anyone, and Scripture commands both. Judges and elders act as servants of God’s justice, not as people claiming to be better than the accused (Romans 13:4; Galatians 6:1). What this verse demands is honesty: that those who judge are not guilty of the same thing, are not using the process for their own ends, and know their own need of mercy. A pastor confronting sin, a parent correcting a child, a court sentencing a crime can all do right, with clean hands and a humble heart.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

parallels.desc: the hand of the witnesses first against him

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers leave one by one, and the only one with the right to condemn her does not, but sends her away from her sin. Mercy comes first, and the changed life follows from it.

Beginning with the older ones. The oldest have the longest memories of their own sins. Each came in sure he stood on the right side of the law, and left knowing, at least for a moment, that he stood where she stood: the hardest discovery a religious person can make, that his record has not made him safe and he needs the same mercy as the sinner he came to accuse.

Left alone with the woman. Augustine’s famous phrase: “two were left, misery and mercy.” The only one without sin, the only one with the right to throw the stone, remains.

Woman, where are they? “Woman” is a respectful address (2:4), and the question is gentle, almost wondering. The trap has collapsed; what remains is a woman, a silence, and mercy.

Neither do I condemn you. Not because her sin does not matter, but because he came not to condemn the world but to save it (3:17). He does not say the charge was false or the law harsh. The others had merely lost the right to throw; he had the right and declined to use it. This is mercy from the judge’s seat, and it costs him, for he himself would bear her condemnation on the cross (Romans 8:1–3). Within months he was under condemnation himself, outside the city. She walked out of that courtyard alive because somebody else did not.

Sin no more. Grace and holiness together: he calls it sin, and tells her to leave it. He does not say, “Sin no more, and then I won’t condemn you,” but, “I don’t condemn you; now go and sin no more.” Grace is the root of obedience, not its reward: the changed life follows the acquittal and does not purchase it. Yet grace does not leave people where it finds them; the command is real, addressed to a real situation she has to go home to.

A verdict that will never be reopened. Marched in by a ring of men, she walked out alone with no one holding her arm. So the Lord releases sinners: not on probation, not under watch, but sent home with a verdict that will never be reopened, because the one who spoke it was going to answer for it himself.

Who are you to judge? For many today this scene settles every moral question: nobody is without sin, so nobody may call anything sin. Yet the same culture is as quick as any scribe to pick up a stone, and someone’s worst moment can be passed round the world before lunch. Without forgiveness there are only two settings: excuse the wrong, or destroy the person. Jesus refuses both: he names the sin and sends her from it, and he will not throw the stone, though he alone had the right. The scribes had law without mercy; our age wants mercy without law, which turns out to be indifference dressed as kindness. She met a holiness that would not call her sin small and a love that would not let it crush her, and at the cross the two were joined: the sin judged in full, the sinner set free.

Was she forgiven if she had not repented? The story does not tell us what was in her heart, and we should not invent it. It shows the order of grace: Jesus speaks mercy and then calls for a changed life, and that call is itself a call to repent. Elsewhere Scripture is plain that forgiveness is received through repentance and faith (Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19). Repentance is necessary, but it is not the price. No one earns the verdict by changing first: we come as we are, receive his mercy, and his mercy sends us out to live differently.

What if I keep falling into the same sin after being forgiven? Then come back, as often as you need to. “Go, and from now on sin no more” is a real command, and Christ means it to be obeyed. But it comes from the one who has already said, “Neither do I condemn you”, and that verdict is not withdrawn when you stumble (1 John 1:9–2:1). Fight the sin seriously: cut off what feeds it, tell a trusted believer, ask for help. When you fall, do not hide from him, as shame always urges; run to him. The freedom to obey grows out of being forgiven, never out of the fear that he might stop forgiving you.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the light of the world, and whoever follows him will not be left in darkness; his testimony about himself is true because he alone knows where he comes from and where he is going.

Again Jesus spoke to them. John’s own narrative resumes from 7:52: still the Feast of Booths, still in the temple. On the last day of the feast Jesus offered living water (7:37–38); here he offers light. The rest of the chapter tests the claim, and chapter 9 acts it out: a man born blind receives his sight, while the men who claim to see remain in the dark (9:41).

I am the light of the world. The second great “I am” saying (after 6:35). The lamps of the feast recalled the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). Jesus is the true light, not just for Israel but for the world (1:4–9; Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Light in Scripture means God’s presence, truth, holiness and salvation (Psalm 27:1).

Beside the cold lamps. He was standing in the treasury (v. 20), in the Court of the Women, where the great lampstands of the feast had been lit every night: four enormous golden stands, the sources say, so tall that young priests climbed ladders to fill them, while men danced with torches through the night. Now the feast is probably over and the lamps are cold. As with the water, he waits until the ceremony is over and says that what it pointed to is standing in front of them, and does not go out: the light of the pillar of fire, the glory over the tabernacle, the radiance that filled Solomon’s temple, now in the temple in a body, offering himself to everyone.

Will not walk in darkness. Darkness in John means sin, ignorance and death (1:5; 3:19; 12:35). The verb is about walking, not seeing: the promise is not first that we will see everything, but that we will have him with us. Israel did not get a map in the wilderness; they got a pillar of fire that moved, and followed it one night at a time. And the follower will have “the light of life”, the light that gives life (1:4).

Its lamp is the Lamb. The lamps of the feast were put away for a year; this light has never been put away. The darkness tried to put him out on a cross and could not; “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (1:5). At the end the city of God will need no sun or moon, “for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

Your testimony is not true. A fair legal objection: self-testimony was not accepted, as Jesus himself had granted (5:31), and readers notice the apparent clash with chapter 5.

My testimony is true. The rule is meant for ordinary witnesses, and Jesus alone knows the truth about himself. Nor is he withdrawing what he said in chapter 5; he is denying that he is alone, as he says next: “it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father” (v. 16).

Where I came from and where I am going. He knows his origin and his destiny; they do not. No human can verify his testimony from outside; only God can, and he does (v. 18).

In everyday life. Name the area of your life that feels darkest at the moment: a decision, a grief, a secret. Bring it to him in prayer today, and take one step of obedience in it, however small. The light comes to the one who follows.

What does it mean in practice to follow the light? Trusting Jesus and going where he leads, one step at a time, by his word. You may not see far ahead, but you will not be left in the darkness of sin, confusion about God, or hopelessness about death. Read his words and do them; in a choice, ask what honours him; when you sin, bring it into the light quickly (1 John 1:7). Following the light is less like being given a floodlight than a lamp for your feet (Psalm 119:105).
verseByVerse.note: At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts. This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: a pillar of fire to give them light
a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They judge by appearances; Jesus did not come to condemn, yet when he does judge, his judgment is the Father’s and is true.

You judge according to the flesh. By human standards and appearances (7:24). They looked at a Galilean with no credentials and drew the obvious conclusion, which was wrong.

I judge no one. Not that Jesus never judges (5:22, 27), but that judging was not the purpose of his first coming (3:17; 12:47). Then, anyone who meets him meets him as Saviour; the judging is real, it is his, and it is kept for the last day. He who will sit on the throne at the last came the first time to stand in the dock. The judge of the living and the dead let men who judged according to the flesh judge him, so that his people could stand in the last judgment without fear.

My judgment is true. His judgment is God’s judgment, for the Father and the Son act together (5:30).

If Jesus will judge everyone, why does God seem to let things go now? Because the court has not yet sat, and the delay is grace. God is not relaxed about sin but patient, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). The interval is given for the unbeliever to turn, and for the believer to call others to turn. And it comforts anyone who has been wronged and seen no justice: nothing has been forgotten. The judge is Christ, and his judgment is true.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law asks for two witnesses, and Jesus has them: himself and the Father who sent him.

In your Law. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). “Your Law” does not distance Jesus from it but stresses that they are the ones who claim to live by it: very well, let us proceed by your own procedure. A prophet says, “thus says the LORD”; here the Lord of the law himself agrees to be tried by its rules.

The Father who sent me. On any ordinary reading it is an outrageous answer: he satisfies a rule meant to stop anyone’s account of himself being taken on trust by calling a witness nobody else can call or cross-examine. But that witness had already testified in public, three ways: in the works he gave Jesus to do (5:36), in the Scriptures (5:39), and at the Jordan (1:32–34).

Two witnesses, and both of them God. At the Jordan the Father’s voice owned him as his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17); at the empty tomb the Father spoke again, louder, by raising him from the dead. The God who cannot lie has told us who Jesus is, and in telling us has shown us what he is himself: a Father who delights in his Son, and gives him to the world.

But how can I believe a witness I cannot see? As these men were meant to: through the testimony he has given. It is in the works of Jesus, recorded so that you may believe (20:31); in the Scriptures, which from Moses onwards point to him (5:39, 46); and supremely in the resurrection, by which God declared him to be his Son (Romans 1:4). And the Spirit himself bears witness, opening our eyes to what is there (15:26; 1 John 5:6–10). You are not asked to believe without evidence, but to receive the evidence God has given rather than demand another kind on your own terms.

parallels.desc: two or three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can know the Father except by knowing Jesus, and these men, standing in God’s house, know neither.

Where is your Father? They want to see this second witness, a fair request in any human court; perhaps it is also a sneer at the rumours about his birth (v. 41).

You know neither me nor my Father. He does not produce the Father, offer a sign, or argue. The witness they want to examine cannot be summoned into the courtyard, and the only access to him is through the man they are cross-examining.

You would know my Father also. To know Jesus is to know the Father (14:7–9), and every other road to the Father is closed (14:6). It should be said without softening: there is no way to know God that goes around Jesus, not through sincerity, not through the law these men administered, not through the temple they were standing in. We need not climb up to heaven to find out what the Father is like; the Son came down, stood among the offering boxes, and said, know me and you will know him. Every glimpse of the Father we will ever have, in this age and the next, will be in the face of Jesus Christ.

In the treasury. Probably in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-shaped offering boxes stood: one of the busiest places in the temple, where he would later watch a widow put in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44). Where Israel brought its gifts to God, he tells them they do not know God, and though he speaks so boldly, to men who wanted him dead, no one can touch him, because his hour had not yet come.

In everyday life. When you catch yourself picturing God as harsh, distant or indifferent, set that picture beside the Jesus of the Gospels: crying out to the thirsty, touching the leper, weeping at a grave. Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9), so let the Son correct the picture.

What about people who love God but do not believe in Jesus? Jesus’ words are hard and clear: to know the Father you must know the Son, and to reject the Son is to show that you do not know the Father (5:23; 1 John 2:23). Many people are sincere, devout and morally serious without Christ, and we should respect their seriousness and treat them with love. But sincerity is not the same as knowing God, and there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12). That calls not for pride but for urgency and tenderness: the God they are looking for has come in Jesus, and they need to hear of him.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is going back to the Father, and those who refuse him will die unforgiven, unable to follow where he goes.

I am going away. As in 7:33–34, he is going to the Father, and where he is going they cannot come: heaven is closed to those who reject the one who opens it.

You will die in your sin. The most frightening sentence in the chapter: to die unforgiven, still carrying your guilt, and so to face God’s judgment with it. Isaiah saw the holy God and cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5); to come before that holiness with every sin still on your account is the most fearful thing that can happen to a human being (Hebrews 10:31).

One root, many fruits. “Sin” is singular here: the root sin of unbelief (16:9), which verse 24 names as not believing that he is who he says. There the word is plural: the sins that flow from that root. Every sin will be brought into the light at the judgment, but the decisive matter is a person’s relation to Christ, because he alone can take sins away. To refuse him is to keep every sin one has ever committed.

Will he kill himself? A worse misunderstanding than in 7:35. Suicide was thought to send a person to the lowest depths of Hades, so perhaps they mean he is going where they would never go. (That was a belief of the time, not the Bible’s teaching: Scripture treats suicide as a grave sin but never as an unforgivable one. If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today, and if you are in danger now, call the emergency services.) The irony is deep: Jesus will lay down his life of his own will (10:17–18), but they will be the ones who put him to death. Wrong about the manner and the motive, they are right about the fact; once again his enemies prophesy without knowing it.

In everyday life. Do not carry your sin to the grave. If there is anything you have never brought to Christ, bring it today.

Can a believer die in his sin? No. A believer dies in the Lord (Revelation 14:13), with every sin forgiven, because Christ has borne them. If you trust him, even weakly, even with sins you are still fighting, you will die forgiven and wake in his presence. The warning is for those who refuse him; for those who come, the promise of 6:37 stands: he will never cast them out.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes from above and is “I am”, the God of Israel in the flesh, and those who will not believe it will die in their sins.

You are from below; I am from above. Two realms, two origins (3:31). He is not insulting them but explaining why the conversation keeps failing: both sides use the same words, and one of them came from somewhere else.

That I am he. Literally “that I am” (egō eimi), with nothing added. This is the divine name. In Exodus 3:14 God revealed himself as “I am who I am,” and in Isaiah the Lord says again and again, “I am he” (Isaiah 41:4; 43:10, 13, 25; 46:4; 48:12), using in the Greek Old Testament the same words Jesus uses here. Jesus is claiming to be the God of Israel come in the flesh. Translators rightly supply the pronoun, but the bare form is what the hearers got, the form God used at the bush. It comes back at verse 28, and at verse 58 it nearly gets him stoned.

Unless you believe. The condition is as narrow as anything he ever said: not “unless you live well, or keep the law”, which these men did with great rigour, but unless you believe that he is. Salvation is not faith in faith or vague faith in God, but faith in Jesus as Lord and God (20:28). His identity is no optional extra on top of a decent life but the point on which everything turns, and the men listening understood him perfectly.

The name now has a face. The fire that burned and was not consumed, the voice that sent Moses to Pharaoh, the God who said through Isaiah that before him no god was formed (Isaiah 43:10), stood in the temple in a human body and spoke the same name. The name that made Moses hide his face now has a face of its own, and it is turned towards sinners.

In everyday life. When you say the creed, or sing that Jesus is Lord, do not let the words slide past. Jesus is God: the one who loves you is the I AM.

Does this warning fall on people who have never heard of Jesus? It falls first on those who, like these men, have heard the claim plainly and refuse it. But Scripture as a whole is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). That is why the church is sent to the nations. God is just: no one will be condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of, but for real sins against the light they had (Romans 1:20; 2:12). And the Reformed churches have held that elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit. The right response is not to speculate but to go, and send, and pray.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus God? Jehovah’s Witnesses, Unitarians and others teach that Jesus is a created being, a lesser god or a great prophet. This commentary’s view: Jesus here claims the divine name and makes faith in it necessary for salvation. With 1:1, 5:18, 8:58, 10:30 and 20:28, John teaches plainly that Jesus is God the Son, one with the Father. This is not a secondary doctrine: unless you believe, you die in your sins.
verseByVerse.note: “That I am he” is literally “that I am”: the divine name.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe me, that I am he

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked who he is, Jesus says he has been telling them all along: the problem is not his words but their hearts.

Who are you? The central question of the chapter and of the Gospel, perhaps asked as a sneer: who do you think you are? After the bread, the water, the light, and the claim made twice already in this conversation, they still ask it, and Pilate will ask where he is from and get no answer at all (19:9). This Gospel exists to answer it.

Much to judge. He knows a great deal about the men in front of him and says almost none of it: the restraint of one who could expose every heart and chooses not to, yet.

In everyday life. If you are waiting for God to say something new before you obey what he has already said, start with what he has said.

Why do some people hear the gospel many times and never seem to understand? Because the problem is rarely the explanation. These men heard the clearest teacher who ever lived and still asked who he was. Understanding the gospel needs not only information but a heart opened by God (6:44; 2 Corinthians 4:4–6). So do not imagine that cleverer words would make everyone believe, and do not give up on people who do not understand yet. Keep saying it plainly and lovingly, and pray that God will open their eyes.

Uncertain wording. The Greek behind “just what I have been telling you from the beginning” is notoriously difficult. The ESV reads it as an answer: I am what I have said all along. Others take it as an exclamation: why do I speak to you at all? The ESV’s reading suits the context, since Jesus has been telling them who he is from the start. Either way he offers them nothing new: he has said it, and the failure is not in the phrasing.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they lift Jesus up on the cross, they will see who he is: the I AM, saying only what the Father taught him. His execution will be his exaltation.

When you have lifted up the Son of Man. In John, “lifted up” (hypsoō) means both the cross and his exaltation (3:14; 12:32–33), the language of Isaiah 52:13 about the Servant who will be “lifted up.” “You” will do it: they are responsible for his death. This is the second of three such sayings, and John never lets the two meanings come apart: execution and enthronement are one event. As the bronze serpent was lifted on a pole and whoever looked lived, so whoever looks to the crucified Son in faith has eternal life.

Then you will know that I am he. Again “I am” (egō eimi). The cross will reveal who he is: to some for their salvation (the centurion, Mark 15:39; the thousands at Pentecost, Acts 2:36–41), to others for their judgment. Their understanding will come too late to stop the cross, and it will be the cross that brings it.

As the Father taught me. The cross will also show his perfect obedience. “Taught” is a domestic word: a son in a workshop, learning the trade by watching his father (5:19–20). The authority these men keep demanding an account of is not seized but received, as a trade is handed from father to son.

The throne was a cross. Those who lifted him up thought they were finishing him. But the hour when he looked most defeated, nailed up where everyone could see him, was the hour he won the victory and was shown to be King, as Pilate’s sign over the cross said, in three languages (19:19–20).
