In everyday life. When you want to know whether God loves you, do not look first at your circumstances. Look at the cross. It is where the I AM was lifted up for you, and what it says does not change with the weather.

Does this make the Son less than the Father? No. The Son is equal with the Father in being (10:30; 8:58). His being sent, obeying and doing nothing on his own belong to the work of salvation he freely took on for our sake, gladly taking the servant’s part (Philippians 2:6–8), not to any lesser godhood. He does nothing on his own because he and the Father act as one: a son who does exactly what his father does is not less than his father but his likeness. And the Son’s obedience is not a sign of inferiority but the glory of his love: he delights to do the Father’s will.

How is the cross a glory, when it looks like defeat? Because at the cross we see most clearly who God is: his justice satisfied, his love poured out, his wisdom displayed and his power at work, all at once, in one man dying for others (Romans 3:25–26; 5:8). What his enemies meant as his shame, God made his throne. That is why Christians speak of the glory of the cross, and why Paul would boast in nothing else (Galatians 6:14).
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him." As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father never leaves the Son alone, because the Son always does what pleases him; and even in this hostile crowd many believe.

He has not left me alone. The Father is always with the Son, even when the world rejects him (16:32). The crowd is hostile, the disciples are nowhere said to be present, and his brothers do not believe him; the ground of his calm is a person, the one who sent him and has not gone away.

Always. No one else could say this: it is a claim to sinlessness (v. 46; Hebrews 4:15). From anyone else it would be the remark of a man with no self-knowledge; nothing in the record suggests that of him. On the cross he would cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), not because he had displeased the Father, but because he bore our sin, and in that very act was most pleasing to him.

Forsaken so that we never will be. That perfect obedience, which we could never offer, he offered for us, and it is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). He was forsaken so that we never will be, and because he always pleased the Father, the Father is pleased with all who are in him.

Many believed in him. In the middle of the most hostile exchange so far, faith is being born, and the next verses will test what it was worth: not all who believe in some way are true disciples.

In everyday life. When you stand alone for what is right, at work, in the family, in a room where everyone else has gone along, remember that the Father is with you as he was with the Son.

Does this mean that when God feels absent, I must have displeased him? No; this verse must not become a formula that crushes people. Gethsemane and the cry from the cross forbid that reading: the one who always pleased the Father went into the dark anyway, so that those who have not always pleased him need not be abandoned. Believers may feel God’s absence through grief, illness, exhaustion, or a trial sent to deepen their faith (Psalm 88; Isaiah 50:10); sometimes sin is the cause, and then the remedy is confession. If the darkness lingers, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see your doctor as well: low mood can have bodily causes, and treating them is no failure of faith. Your feelings are not the measure of his presence. His promise is: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

parallels.desc: I am not alone, for the Father is with me

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–59 — The Children of Abraham and the Great I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: True faith stays in Jesus’ word, and what people do shows whose children they really are. Jesus tests those who had believed him: the truth sets free, but everyone who practises sin is a slave, and only the Son can make him free indeed (vv. 31–36). Descent from Abraham proves nothing without Abraham’s faith and works; plotting to kill the one who tells the truth shows the likeness of another father, the devil (vv. 37–47). Insulted as a Samaritan with a demon, Jesus promises that whoever keeps his word will never see death, and says that Abraham rejoiced to see his day (vv. 48–56). Then comes the climax, “before Abraham was, I am”, and the stones (vv. 57–59).
verseByVerse.theology: The passage sets two families side by side: Abraham’s children and the devil’s. The mark of each is not ancestry but likeness: Abraham’s children believe God, and the devil’s children lie and want to kill. This is a diagnosis of every unconverted heart, not a charge against one people (see the note on vv. 43–44). The truth that sets free (v. 32) is not an idea but the Son himself (v. 36), and the freedom he gives is release from slavery to sin.
verseByVerse.examples: The stones at the end of the chapter are the authorities’ answer to his claim that before Abraham was, he is: they were right about what he claimed, and wrong to reject it (see the note on vv. 57–58).

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mark of a real disciple is staying in Jesus’ word, and the truth found there, which is Jesus himself, sets people free.

To the Jews who had believed him. Believed “him”, what he said, rather than believed “in him” (v. 30). John may intend no difference, but the conversation shows that their faith had not reached the root, and by verse 59 they are picking up stones. That answers the question every reader asks: how can believers be told a few verses later that their father is the devil? They had accepted his claims; they had not given themselves to him.

If you abide in my word. “Abide” (menō): remain, continue, make your home in. The mark of a true disciple is not an initial response but continuing in Jesus’ word. Real faith lasts (15:4–10; Colossians 1:23; Hebrews 3:14); those who leave were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

The truth will set you free. “The truth” is not just correct ideas but the reality of God revealed in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6), and knowing him sets you free from sin (v. 34). Carved over university gates, the sentence is made to mean that information liberates; but it comes with a condition, “if you abide in my word”, and the truth it speaks of is a person. To know him is to be loosed from chains we did not even know we wore. He does not hand us a manual and wish us well; he invites us to make our home in his word, and he makes his home in us.

So what does abiding in his word look like day to day? Living in the Bible rather than visiting it. Read it to hear his voice, not to tick a box, and let it shape what you think about God, yourself, money, sex, work and death. Sit under faithful preaching with his people. When it says something you do not like, stay with it and ask for grace to obey. Memorise a verse and turn it over through the day. Abiding is less a technique than a home: the place you keep coming back to and living from.

Does abiding mean I can lose my salvation if I fail? No. Jesus is not describing a test you must pass to stay saved, but the mark that shows who is truly saved. Those whom the Father gives to the Son are kept by him, and no one can snatch them out of his hand (10:28–29). The grace that brings a person to Christ keeps him continuing in Christ (Philippians 1:6), so abiding is both a command and a gift: we are told to remain, and God works in us so that we do. A true believer may stumble badly, like Peter, but he is brought back. What this verse warns against is a faith that never put down roots and so falls away when the word becomes hard.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, 'You will become free'?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They insist they have never been slaves, but Jesus says that everyone who keeps on sinning is a slave to sin.

Never been enslaved. A remarkable claim from people under Roman rule, whose garrison stood beside the temple as they spoke, fresh from a festival remembering the exodus, in a nation whose Passover makes children ask why they were once slaves. They meant something narrower and prouder: that as Abraham’s offspring they had never lost their standing before God, whatever the politics. People will say almost anything rather than admit that they are not free.

A slave to sin. “Practices” (poiōn, present tense, keeps doing): habitual sin. “Slave” (doulos): sin is not just something we do but a master that owns us (Romans 6:16–20), and this slave has nothing to buy his freedom with. Jesus does not argue about the history; he names a bondage they cannot check by looking out of the window. We were slaves who called ourselves free, and Christ came to us not with a lecture but with a ransom. He took the form of a slave, and was sold for thirty pieces of silver, so that slaves of sin could be bought back.

In everyday life. Take the thing you would stop if you could: the temper, the drink, the screen, the way you talk about a particular person. You have decided to stop before, and meant it. Paul spent a chapter on that condition, willing a thing and not doing it (Romans 7:14–25), and ended it with thanks to God through Jesus Christ. So stop trying to free yourself, and ask the one who can; and if it has become an addiction, ask for help from your church and from those trained to give it.

Is a Christian who still struggles with a habitual sin a slave of sin? Not in the sense Jesus means. “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (v. 36): a believer’s standing has changed, and sin will have no dominion over him (Romans 6:14). He may still lose battles, and must keep fighting. But the slave in this verse serves sin as his master without wanting to be free; the believer hates the sin he struggles with and runs to Christ for help. The struggle itself is a sign that a new master has come.

But is freedom not simply being free to run my own life? That is what most people mean by it, and exactly what these men thought they had. But everyone serves something. Live for approval and you are ruled by other people’s opinions; live for success and you are driven by the next target; live for comfort and you cannot bear to lose it. Each master promises freedom and then demands more. Jesus does not offer independence, which no creature has ever had, but a new master who gave himself for his servants, whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30).
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; they meant they had never inwardly accepted slavery.

parallels.desc: slaves of sin

verseByVerse.quote: "The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slave has no lasting place in the house, but the Son does, and he can make slaves into free sons for ever.

The son remains forever. A slave had no permanent place in a household; he could be sold or sent away at any time, while a son belonged there for good. Perhaps there is an echo of Ishmael, son of the slave woman, who was sent away, while Isaac, the son of promise, remained (Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:30). Physical descent from Abraham does not secure a place in God’s house.

Free indeed. “Indeed” (ontōs): really, truly. The freedom he gives is real and permanent, freedom from sin’s guilt and power. The Son, permanently in the house, has authority to change a slave’s status, and what he gives is not parole but adoption into God’s family for ever (1:12; Romans 8:15): his name, his care, his Spirit in our hearts and a share in the inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7). The eternal Son, always at home with the Father, opened the door of that house to slaves and runaways and made them sons and daughters. He did not bring us in as servants to the kitchen but as children to the table.

Freedom that cannot be lost. Political freedom can be lost by a change of government, financial freedom in a market crash, and health fails. This freedom rests on the standing of someone who cannot be evicted from the house. It is given, not earned, so it cannot be forfeited by a failure, since it was never bought by success. The condition lies with the Son, not the slave: not whether the slave improves, but whether the Son acts.

In everyday life. Live like a son, not a slave. If you find yourself serving God anxiously, as though one more failure would get you evicted, tell yourself the truth: in Christ you are a son, and the son remains for ever.

What does it feel like to be free indeed? It may not feel dramatic. Often it begins quietly: a conscience no longer crushed by guilt; the first real ability to say no to a sin that used to rule you; a strange new desire to please God rather than merely avoid punishment; the settled sense that you belong in the Father’s house and will not be thrown out. It grows over a lifetime, and its full flowering is still to come, when the children of God are finally set free from all decay and sin (Romans 8:21). Freedom is not doing whatever you want. It is wanting, more and more, what you were made for.
verseByVerse.note: A slave had no permanent place in a household; a son did.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman and her son

verseByVerse.quote: "I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are Abraham’s descendants, but their plan to kill Jesus shows that his word has no room in them and that they take their orders from another father.

I know that you are offspring of Abraham. Physically, yes. The concession is generous: the descent is real, but it is not doing the work they think it does.

My word finds no place in you. “Finds no place” (ou chōrei): makes no progress, has no room in you. They have heard him for days, but there is nowhere in them for it to go: a house with every room occupied, where the word arrives, finds no space, and stands in the doorway. The evidence he gives is not their arguments but what they intend: to kill him. Whatever someone says about God, what he plans to do to God’s messenger tells the truth about him. There was no room for him in the inn at Bethlehem, and no room for his word in the men in the temple. Yet he did not close the door on us.

Two fathers. Jesus speaks from his Father; they act from theirs, whom he will soon name (v. 44). He speaks of what he has seen with his Father; they do what they have heard, at second hand, from a source they have never examined. That is how most evil spreads. Very few people have consciously met the father of lies; they have simply heard something, about a neighbour, a race, a rival, and acted on it without asking where it came from.

What fills the room where Christ’s word should be? Usually not one great rebellion but many ordinary things: busyness, entertainment, worry, the opinions of the people we most want to please, a settled idea of God we do not want disturbed. The parable of the sower names them: the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desire for other things choke the word (Mark 4:19). Making room is practical. Turn off what crowds out silence. Bring your fixed ideas to Scripture and let it correct them. Ask God to clear space in you, and he will.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Abraham is our father." Jesus said to them, "If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s true children share his faith and do his works, and Abraham never tried to kill a messenger from God.

Abraham is our father. They repeat it, sensing the insult.

The works Abraham did. True children resemble their father. Abraham believed God (Genesis 15:6), and his true children are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7). He welcomed strangers who came from God with a message, and set food before them under a tree (Genesis 18:1–8); these men are planning to kill one.

A man who has told you the truth. A deliberately small description. Not “the Son of God”, not “the light of the world”, though he has said both this week, but the least contestable account of himself, and he asks whether killing such a person is something Abraham would have done.

This is not what Abraham did. The whole argument in a sentence, and they answer it by changing the subject. Yet there is mercy in it: what is required is not a different ancestry, which nobody can acquire, but a different faith and life, which God can give.

He did not disown the family. Abraham set food before three strangers under the oaks of Mamre and found that the LORD had come to his tent (Genesis 18); his sons in the temple were planning the death of God’s messenger. Yet Abraham’s greatest Son did not disown the family. He died for it, and widened it, so that the promise of descendants as many as the stars is kept not by bloodline but by grace, in people from every nation who believe God as Abraham did.

Can I rely on my Christian family or background? No more than they could rely on Abraham. A Christian upbringing is a great gift, and God often works through families (Acts 16:31; 2 Timothy 1:5). But nobody is a child of God because his parents were: God has children, not grandchildren. Each person must come to Christ himself, by faith, and the evidence will be a family likeness: trusting God’s word, welcoming his Son, and doing the works of faith. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure the faith you were taught has become your own.

parallels.desc: Abraham welcomes the LORD’s messengers

verseByVerse.quote: "You are doing the works your father did." They said to him, "We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God." Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They claim God as their Father, but anyone whose Father is God loves the Son he sent.

You are doing the works your father did. Their father, he implies, is someone other than Abraham.

We were not born of sexual immorality. “We” may be emphatic, implying “unlike you”: a hint, perhaps, at rumours about Jesus’ birth, for later Jewish writings spread a story that he was illegitimate. Or they may mean that they are not spiritually illegitimate, not idolaters, whose unfaithfulness the prophets called adultery (Hosea 2:4). If the first, then cornered on Abraham they reach for a rumour about his mother, and he does not stoop to answer it: the eternal Son of the Father allowing himself to be called illegitimate, so that we who were not God’s children could be adopted into his family.

We have one Father, even God. They move from Abraham to God himself, the highest claim available to a Jew.

You would love me. The test of being God’s child is love for his Son; you cannot love the Father and hate the Son (1 John 5:1). Not “you would agree with me”, but “you would love me”: children recognise the family, often before they have worked out the theology. The test is about the heart and cannot be answered by argument, which is why the conversation is about to collapse into abuse.

I came from God. He came out from the Father’s side, and not of his own accord: he was sent by the very one they claim as Father.

In everyday life. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Tell him today, in your own words, why you love him, and if the words do not come easily, ask him to make you love him more.

How do I know whether I love Jesus? Love for Christ is not first a feeling, though it often includes feeling. Jesus gave its marks himself: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (14:15). Love wants to be with him, in prayer and in his word. It treasures what he has done and is grieved when he is dishonoured. It loves the people he loves, his church (1 John 4:20), and is sorry for sin because sin wounds him. If you find even a small and struggling version of these in yourself, that is the family likeness, and it is God’s work. If you find none, ask him to show you his Son, and keep looking at him in the Gospels, for that is where love for him is born.
verseByVerse.note: Their retort may hint at rumours about Jesus’ own birth.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cannot hear Jesus because they will not, and their wish to kill him and their refusal of the truth bear the likeness of the devil, the murderer and liar.

Why do you not understand what I say? “What I say” is his speech (lalia), the way he talks; “my word” (logos) is the message, and they cannot bear to hear it. The problem is not intellect but will: they are unable to hear because they will not (6:44; 7:17).

You are of your father the devil. The hardest words Jesus says in John end an argument begun at verse 37: Abraham’s children would act like Abraham (v. 39), God’s children would love God’s Son (v. 42); now he names the father whose likeness they do show. Not all Jews, but these men, who want to kill him, show by their actions whose children they are; spiritual parentage shows in behaviour (1 John 3:8–10). This is a moral diagnosis, not an ethnic slur, and not a permanent sentence. Nor is it a loss of temper: love that wants a man free must first tell him he is bound (v. 34), and the Jesus who speaks this hard word to men planning murder lays down his life for his sheep (10:11).

He was a murderer from the beginning. What the devil has always wanted is death. His lie led to death in Eden (Genesis 3:1–5; Romans 5:12), and Cain’s murder of his brother soon followed (Genesis 4:8; 1 John 3:12). The desire to kill Jesus is the family trait. The father of lies thought he had won when the Son of God was killed, but the Truth went to the cross and broke the liar’s power.

The father of lies. Lying is his native language. The two marks of the family are murder and lying, and both were in the courtyard: they intend to kill the one who tells them the truth, and they refuse the truth itself.

A family quarrel, from inside the family. No verse in this Gospel has been put to worse use: for centuries these words were used to stir up hatred against Jewish people, with terrible results. It is a straight inversion of the text. The speaker is a Jew, in the Jewish temple, at a Jewish feast, who has already said that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). The Evangelist is a Jew, and the audience is not a race but particular people in a particular courtyard (v. 31). A prophet of Israel rebuking the leaders of Israel is not an outsider attacking a people; it is the oldest and most Jewish thing in the Bible. Isaiah called them “rulers of Sodom” (Isaiah 1:10), and nobody thinks Isaiah anti-Jewish. Whoever takes these words as a weapon against Jewish people sides against the Jewish Messiah, whose charge here is that his hearers intend murder, and then goes out to commit it himself. The verse condemns him. Paul, who felt the whole weight of this, could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers according to the flesh (Romans 9:3), and insisted that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). That is the settled Christian mind.

In everyday life. You have been brought out of the liar’s family into the house of the God who cannot lie, and his Spirit lives in you, so refuse the old family likeness. Think of the small lies: the exaggeration, the excuse, the half-story that leaves you looking better. Speak the truth in love, even when it costs you.

Is everyone who is not a Christian a child of the devil? Scripture says that apart from Christ all of us were by nature children of wrath, following the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:1–3; 1 John 5:19). That describes the human condition, not a special insult for some, and it includes the person reading this, before grace found him. So it leaves no room for pride or contempt: the believer is a former member of that family, rescued by mercy. And it gives great hope: the Son came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8) and bring people out of that family into God’s. Treat unbelievers as people you once were, and whom God may yet adopt.
verseByVerse.note: The devil’s lie led to death in Eden; the first murder followed.

parallels.desc: “You will not surely die”

verseByVerse.quote: "But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They reject Jesus precisely because he tells the truth, and not one of them can convict him of a single sin.

Because I tell the truth. Not “although” but “because”. The children of the father of lies reject truth because it is truth: to a heart shaped by lies, truth is not neutral but repellent.

Which one of you convicts me of sin? “Convicts” (elenchei): proves guilty. No other human being could make this challenge, for he is the sinless Son (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). He stands before men who have watched him for months, sent officers and looked for a charge, with every motive to produce one, and invites them to name a single thing. John records no answer. That silence is the loudest thing in the chapter. And if he is sinless, he is no liar, and their unbelief has no excuse.

The saints move the other way. From the best person you have ever known the question would be unbearable, for the closer anyone gets to real goodness, the more sharply he sees his own failure. Yet the man nearest to God never once, in any record, confesses a sin. He teaches his disciples to pray, “forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), and does not join in. That is either a serious defect of self-knowledge, which nothing else about him supports, or it is simply true. For thirty-odd years in a fallen world he never thought an unclean thought, spoke a careless word, or failed to love God with all his heart. And then he who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus never sinned? Because our salvation depends on it. A sacrifice for sin had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5; 1 Peter 1:19). With a single sin of his own, Jesus would have had his own account to settle, and nothing left over for anyone else. Because he owed nothing, he could pay what we owed; because he was perfectly righteous, his righteousness can be counted to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). His sinlessness also makes him the perfect high priest: tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, and so able to help us when we are tempted (Hebrews 4:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God." The Jews answered him, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only those who belong to God hear God’s words; having lost the argument, his opponents call Jesus a Samaritan with a demon.

Whoever is of God hears the words of God. Belonging to God comes first, and hearing follows (10:26–27; 18:37). When Christ’s words are preached, something in such a person answers that this is true and for him, and he keeps coming back.

You are not of God. They do not hear because they are not of God, and their failure to hear is the evidence of where they stand: the truth of 6:44, that no one comes unless the Father draws him, seen from the other side.

A Samaritan and have a demon. Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult: Samaritans were considered heretics, of mixed race and false worship (4:9), so perhaps they meant he was a traitor to Israel or rejected the true tradition. “Have a demon” means mad or possessed. There is a nasty precision in it, answering his question about their parentage with one about his, and a rich irony, for the Samaritans called him the Saviour of the world after two days (4:42), which is more than Jerusalem has managed. The demon charge is the standard explanation for a man whose power is undeniable and whose claims are unacceptable: the works are real, so something is at work in him, so it must not be God. It needs no evidence, and it ends the conversation, which is its purpose.

In everyday life. When people run out of arguments, they often reach for insults. Do not be surprised when it happens to you, and do not answer in kind. And when you are losing an argument, do you reach for a label to stop having to listen?

If hearing depends on being of God, is it my fault if I do not believe? Yes, still. Scripture holds both truths together. No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (6:44), yet those who refuse him are fully responsible, because they refuse what they could see is true and love the darkness (3:19). These men are not described as longing to believe and prevented; they do not want to hear. And if you do want to hear, if something in you is drawn to Christ as you read this, that drawing is the Father at work. Do not wait to discover whether you are of God before you come. Come, and you will find that you are.
verseByVerse.note: Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calmly denies having a demon and leaves his reputation in his Father’s hands, for the Father will vindicate him.

I do not have a demon. He denies the second insult once, without heat, and leaves the first unanswered, for he is not ashamed to be thought a Samaritan (4:40). Then he moves straight back to the subject.

You dishonor me. To dishonour the Son is to dishonour the Father (5:23): their honour is the same currency, and slighting the Son is no lesser offence.

There is One who seeks it. He does not defend his reputation but entrusts it to God (1 Peter 2:23). Called a Samaritan and a demoniac in public, he says his reputation is somebody else’s business, and the judge will see to it in his own time. The man in this verse was executed on a false charge the following spring, was publicly vindicated on the third day after it, and did nothing whatever to arrange either.

In everyday life. Think of the last time you were described unfairly, and count how much of the following week went on it: the conversations, the mental rehearsals, the replies drafted and not sent. The injustice matters, enough that God has appointed himself to deal with it; it has been taken out of your hands and put into better ones.

Should I never defend myself when I am slandered? Not never, but rarely in the way we want to. Paul defended himself when the gospel was at stake (2 Corinthians 11), and it can be right to correct a falsehood calmly, or to seek justice when real harm is being done; abuse and lies that endanger others should be brought into the light. But much of our self-defence is about our reputation rather than the truth, and it is exhausting, never finished, and turns every insult into an emergency. Jesus shows another way: state the truth once, without heat, and then entrust your name to God, who judges justly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.' The Jews said to him, 'Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps Jesus’ word will never meet death as the penalty for sin; his hearers, thinking only of the grave, are now sure he is mad.

He will never see death. “Keeps” (tērēsē): holds fast, obeys, treasures. The believer will die physically, but will never experience death as the wages of sin, separation from God (5:24; 11:25–26).

Not a promise that the heart will not stop. The verse has troubled people at gravesides, for every believer who heard him say it has died. To “see death” is to meet it as what it really is, the penalty of sin. Believers still go through dying; they never meet that. Paul says the same: “O death, where is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). The sting is drawn; the creature is still there, and Christians grieve at funerals like everyone else and are not asked to pretend otherwise. What has changed is what the bite does.

Now we know. At verse 48 they said he had a demon; now they are sure, since only a madman or God could make such a claim. They have named the alternatives correctly, and chosen the wrong one.

Abraham died, as did the prophets. A serious objection, if death is only physical: the greatest men in history are in graves. His answer comes in chapter 11, at the tomb of Lazarus, four days dead, and it is not an argument. He went down into death and broke it from the inside, and now he holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

In everyday life. If you are afraid of dying, take that fear to him by name; he has been through it and come out the other side. And if you have lost a believer, grieve, but not as those who have no hope.

What happens to a believer at the moment of death? The body dies and is buried, but the soul does not sleep or wait in some intermediate place of punishment. It goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory, because Christ’s death has paid in full, and no soul sleep, because to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord. Nor is that the end: at his return the body will be raised, glorious and imperishable, and body and soul will be with the Lord for ever (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). So the believer can face death as a defeated enemy, still to be endured but no longer to be feared.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?" Jesus answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked whether he thinks himself greater than Abraham, Jesus refuses to glorify himself: the Father, the God they claim, is the one who glorifies him.

Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The Greek expects the answer no, as when the Samaritan woman asked about Jacob (4:12). The answer is, of course, yes. They cannot stop mentioning that Abraham is dead (vv. 52–53): the whole exchange has been about descent from a man in a grave, and the one they are arguing with is about to say that he was there before Abraham was born.

Who do you make yourself out to be? The question of the chapter again (v. 25), asked with contempt: they assume he is inflating himself.

If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. He makes no claim of his own, and agrees entirely that self-declared greatness is worthless.

My Father who glorifies me. If the God they profess is real, he is the one honouring Jesus, and their quarrel is with him. The Father glorified him at the Jordan, on the mountain of transfiguration, at the empty tomb, and at his right hand. The patriarchs and prophets are stars in the night; he is the sun.

How is Jesus greater than Abraham? In every way. Abraham was a creature; Jesus is the Creator (1:3). Abraham received the promise; Jesus is the promise kept (Galatians 3:16). Abraham believed God; Jesus is God. Abraham was justified by faith; Jesus is the one in whom we are justified. Abraham died and was buried; Jesus died and rose, and lives for ever. Abraham is the father of the faithful; Jesus is the Lord of the faithful, Abraham included, who rejoiced to see his day (v. 56). To honour Abraham rightly is to bow before the one Abraham longed for.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus truly knows the Father, and Abraham himself looked forward with joy to the day of Christ, and saw it.

You have not known him. Jesus knows him perfectly, and to say otherwise would make him a liar like them: false modesty would be a lie.

Abraham rejoiced. “My day” is the time of the Messiah’s coming. Abraham received the promise that in his offspring all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18), and looked forward to it with joy. Some rabbis taught that God showed Abraham the future ages (from Genesis 15). He rejoiced in the anticipation, and then he saw it: not a vague hope, but something shown to him.

He saw it and was glad. How? By faith, through the promise, and perhaps especially at Mount Moriah, when God provided the ram in Isaac’s place (Genesis 22:8, 13–14). He had almost nothing to go on: no Gospel, no creed, no resurrection to look back on; a promise, a son given back to him from under a raised knife, and a ram in a bush. And it was enough to make him glad.

On the mountain of the LORD. Abraham walks up with his son, the wood on the boy’s back; the boy asks where the lamb is, and at the top a ram is caught in a thicket. The narrator adds: “as it is said to this day, ‘On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided’” (Genesis 22:14): a father, an only son, a substitute supplied at the last moment, and a name that points forward rather than back. And 2 Chronicles 3:1 says the temple was built on Mount Moriah; if, as Jewish tradition has long held, that is the place of Genesis 22, Abraham gave a prophetic name to the very ridge these men were standing on as they argued.

No ram in the thicket for Jesus. Abraham came down the mountain with his son alive, because God provided a substitute. Two thousand years later, near that ridge, God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). There was no ram in the thicket for Jesus. He was the Lamb, and the name Abraham gave the place has been true ever since: the LORD has provided.

What did believers before Christ actually believe? The same Christ, seen at a distance, through promise and shadow, not a religion of law-keeping later replaced by grace. “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). Old Testament believers were saved exactly as we are: by grace, through faith in God’s promise of a Saviour, whose work they saw dimly and we see plainly (Romans 4:3, 23–25). There has only ever been one Saviour. And if Abraham, with a promise and a ram in a thicket, was glad, we who have the cross and the empty tomb have more reason for joy than he had. When your faith feels dutiful and grey, read Genesis 22 beside John 19, and thank God for the day Abraham saw only from afar.

parallels.desc: having seen them and greeted them from afar

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not say that he existed before Abraham but that he is: the eternal God, who never began, speaking his own name. His hearers understood exactly what he meant.

You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham? They twist his words, as people do when they have stopped listening: he said Abraham saw his day; they ask whether he has seen Abraham, who lived some two thousand years before. Fifty was a round number for the end of a man’s working life (Numbers 4:3), and Jesus was in his early thirties (Luke 3:23): you are not even at the end of a working life, and you talk about the patriarchs?

Before Abraham was, I am. The climax of the chapter, and everything turns on the two verbs. “Was” (genesthai) means came into being: Abraham was born, had a beginning. “I am” (egō eimi) is present tense, timeless. Ordinary grammar calls for “I was”, which would mean only that he existed earlier; he breaks it on purpose, claiming eternal, uncreated existence and the divine name of verse 24 (Exodus 3:14). The bare name has already been spoken at verses 24 and 28; here he sets it beside Abraham, and the crowd finally understands. Abraham had a first day, and the Son never did; there was never a time when he did not exist (1:1–2).

His enemies are the best witnesses. Nobody picks up a stone because a man has claimed to be wise, or even a prophet; the penalty for blasphemy was stoning (Leviticus 24:16), and they went straight for it. They are among the best witnesses in the New Testament to what he was claiming, for they had no motive to exaggerate it and every motive to wish he had not said it. A sceptic may reply that John wrote decades later and sharpened the words. But the earliest Gospel, Mark, already has Jesus answer the high priest with “I am”, and the council condemn him for blasphemy on the spot (Mark 14:62–64), so the charge John records is not his invention.

The I AM consented to have a birthday. Before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, he is God (Psalm 90:2). The I AM, without beginning, consented to have a birthday, a hometown and a grave, and came near enough to be stoned, so that creatures who began could live with him for ever.

In everyday life. The one who says “I am” has no yesterday that has slipped away from him and no tomorrow he is anxious about. Bring him the regret from your past and the fear about your future. He was there before both, and he is there now.

If Jesus is eternal, how could he be born, grow and die? Because the eternal Son took a true human nature without ceasing to be God. As God he has no beginning; as man he was conceived in Mary’s womb, grew, learned, hungered, wept and died: one person, two natures, without mixture and without division. The Word who is from eternity became flesh (1:14). When we say that Jesus was born at Bethlehem, we mean that the eternal I AM entered time as a baby. He did not stop being who he always was; he added to himself what we are, so that he could save us.

Where Christians differ: what does “I am” mean here? Some, especially Jehovah’s Witnesses, translate “before Abraham was, I have been,” to make it a claim only to pre-existence, not deity. This commentary’s view: the Greek present tense, set against the past tense of Abraham’s coming to be, marks a contrast between created and eternal being. And the hearers’ reaction settles it: they pick up stones, the penalty for blasphemy (v. 59; 10:33). They understood that he was claiming to be God.
verseByVerse.note: “I am” without anything added echoes the name God gave himself at the burning bush.

parallels.desc: “I AM WHO I AM”
from everlasting to everlasting

verseByVerse.quote: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They try to stone him for blasphemy, but his hour has not come, and the one in whom God dwells walks out of the temple.

They picked up stones. They are about to lynch him. Those who had “believed” (v. 31) now want to kill him: shallow faith, confronted with the full truth of Jesus. Building stones lay around in the courts, and men who had come to worship picked up the building material of the house of God to kill the one it was built for.

Jesus hid himself. Perhaps he simply slipped away in the crowd; John describes no miracle, and in any case his hour had not come. There may be a deeper sign: the glory of God leaving the temple, as in Ezekiel 10, as the one in whom God dwells walks out of the house that has rejected him. The Word who made the stone walks out through a crowd holding pieces of it, and nobody notices that the glory has gone.

What stones could not do. The stones would wait until the hour came, and then nails would do what stones could not, and the guilty would go free because the innocent was condemned. The true temple, his body, was torn down and raised in three days, and now he builds a living temple out of people who once picked up stones against him.

In the flow. With the stones the argument that began in chapter 7 ends; they understood verse 58 exactly. Chapter 9 follows straight on: the one who has left the temple opens a blind man’s eyes, and the man thrown out by the same leaders (9:34) is found by Jesus (9:35). The light the temple drove out goes on shining outside it.

In everyday life. The same Jesus who walked out of their temple is willing to dwell in the humblest heart that receives him. When his word presses on something in your life that you would rather keep, that is the moment the stones come out. Put them down. Let him stay.

Can people who once seemed to believe turn so completely against Christ? Sadly, yes, and the New Testament warns of it (Hebrews 6:4–6; 1 John 2:19). Those truly born of God are kept by him, but interest in Jesus can stop short of the heart, and when his full claims are pressed it can turn into hostility. That is why Jesus tested these hearers so hard. It should not make true believers anxious, for being troubled by the possibility shows a heart that wants Christ. But it should make all of us honest: not resting in a past moment of interest, but abiding in his word, the mark of the real thing (v. 31).
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.<sup>2</sup>Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.<sup>3</sup>The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst<sup>4</sup>they said to him, “Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery.<sup>5</sup>Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?”<sup>6</sup>This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.<sup>7</sup>And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.”<sup>8</sup>And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.<sup>9</sup>But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him.<sup>10</sup>Jesus stood up and said to her, “Woman, where are they? You are of this world; I am not of this world.<sup>24</sup>I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins.”<sup>25</sup>So they said to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Just what I have been telling you from the beginning.<sup>26</sup>I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him.”<sup>27</sup>They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father.<sup>28</sup>So Jesus said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me.<sup>29</sup>And he who sent me is with me.
