Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, ’If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’<sup>53</sup>Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?”<sup>54</sup>Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ’He is our God.’<sup>55</sup>But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word.<sup>56</sup>Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.”<sup>57</sup>So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”<sup>58</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.”<sup>59</sup>So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
8.overview:
Where we are. We are still in the temple at the Feast of Booths, the morning after the council broke up without a verdict (7:45–53). Chapter 7 asked where Jesus comes from; chapter 8 presses on to who he is. First comes the bracketed story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), missing from the earliest manuscripts of John but very probably a true memory of Jesus.

The message. Jesus is the light of the world and the great I AM, the God who named himself to Moses at the burning bush, standing in the temple in a human body. Everything turns on believing that. Those who follow him walk out of darkness, and those the Son sets free are free indeed; those who refuse him die in their sins, however proud their ancestry or careful their religion.

Why it was said. John’s first readers were told that faith in Jesus cut them off from Abraham and Israel’s God (see the introduction). This chapter answers that Abraham’s true children believe as he did, and that to know Jesus is to know God. Because its words have been misused to fuel hatred of Jewish people, they need care: Jesus speaks as a Jew to particular opponents seeking to kill him, and his words search every religious person, not one people.

How the chapter makes its case. The woman’s accusers are sent away by one sentence, and Jesus neither condemns her nor excuses her sin (7:53–8:11). He declares himself the light of the world, with the Father as his second witness (vv. 12–20), and warns that unless they believe “I am” they will die in their sins; the cross will show who he is (vv. 21–30). He tests those who had believed: true disciples abide in his word, the Son frees slaves of sin, and a person’s real father shows in what he does (vv. 31–47). Called a Samaritan with a demon, he promises that his followers will never see death, and at last says, “before Abraham was, I am”, and they pick up stones (vv. 48–59).

Where it leads. The chapter begins with a sinner who deserved stoning and was spared, and ends with the sinless one nearly stoned himself: the gospel in miniature. The stones had to wait for his hour; then he would be “lifted up” (v. 28), condemned in the place of the guilty, so that the one who said “neither do I condemn you” could say it justly. On the cross the I AM, who always did what pleased his Father (v. 29), bore the sin of slaves so that the Son could make them sons.

For us. Religion, ancestry and good intentions free no one; only the Son can, and he does it for any who come. Stop resting on what you have inherited or achieved, bring him the sin you cannot break, and keep living in his word: whoever follows him will not walk in darkness.

keyVerse.quote: Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter climbs to this sentence. The light of the world (v. 12), the one whose identity decides whether people die in their sins (v. 24), the Son who alone can set slaves free (v. 36), is the eternal I AM who spoke to Moses at the bush, and his hearers understood him well enough to pick up stones. Before Jesus is our helper or example, he is our God.

8.reflection:
The woman’s accusers were fierce about her sin and silent about the man’s (vv. 3–6). When are we tempted to use other people’s failures for our own ends, and how can we call sin what it is without picking up a stone?

Jesus says, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (v. 11). Why does the order of those two sentences matter, and how does it change the way you fight a sin you keep falling into?

Jesus promises that the truth will set us free, yet says that everyone who practises sin is a slave (vv. 31–36). What do people around you mean by freedom? Where do you still live like a slave rather than a son or daughter in the Father’s house?

The crowd understood that “before Abraham was, I am” (v. 58) was a claim to be God. How does it change your prayers, your fears and your hope in death to know that the one who loves you is the eternal I AM?

9.title: The Man Born Blind

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–41 — Sight and Blindness: The Light of the World at Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Light of the world gives sight to a man born blind, and the same light exposes the blindness of those who are sure they see. Jesus sees the beggar first, refuses the disciples’ search for someone to blame, and sends him to wash in Siloam (vv. 1–7). The neighbours cannot agree who he is (vv. 8–12). The Pharisees question him, divide over Jesus and summon his frightened parents (vv. 13–23); questioned again, the man argues them into a corner and is thrown out (vv. 24–34), his understanding of Jesus growing at every step. Then Jesus finds him, and he believes and worships, while the leaders who say “We see” keep their guilt (vv. 35–41).
verseByVerse.theology: Physical sight and spiritual sight run side by side through the chapter. The man born blind is a picture of every person by nature, needing God to open his eyes; the Pharisees are blind precisely because they are sure they see (see the note on vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: The healed man’s words about Jesus grow under pressure, from a name to worship (the steps are traced in the note on vv. 10–11), and the questioning meant to break his testimony drives him further into faith (see vv. 26–27). The leaders cast him out (v. 34), and Jesus finds him (v. 35).

verseByVerse.quote: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees a man born blind before the man asks for anything, while his disciples see only a puzzle about whose sin caused it. Grace begins with his seeing, not with our seeking.

As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. Jesus sees him first; the man asks for nothing. The verse just before says that Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple (8:59): if the scenes follow closely, he has just escaped being stoned, and on the way out he stops for a beggar. This is the only healing in the Gospels of someone born with his condition. Medically it was hopeless, and it pictures the spiritual blindness we are all born with (2 Corinthians 4:4). That blindness does not stop us being religious; it means we can look straight at Jesus and see nothing worth worshipping, until God shines in our hearts “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents? Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin. If a man was born blind, either his parents had sinned (a misreading of Exodus 20:5), or he had sinned in the womb, which some rabbis, in writings later than the New Testament, thought possible, citing Jacob and Esau struggling before birth (Genesis 25:22). Job’s friends made the same mistake. The disciples had been taught this, and most people still think this way: when something terrible happens, the mind goes looking for the cause in the sufferer. What did they do? What did I do?

A man turned into a case. They discuss him in front of him as a theological problem, as had presumably happened all his life; nobody in the verse speaks to him. That is the other reason people still ask the question: once we have explained someone’s suffering, we feel that nothing more is asked of us. Jesus refuses their explanation, and puts his hands in the dust of the road to heal the man.

In everyday life. When you see someone suffering, ask first not whose fault it is but what God might do, and what you might do. Someone you know who is disabled, ill or struggling is more often talked about than talked to. Christ saw you before you asked for anything; go and speak to them this week, as a person, not a case.

Is my suffering a punishment for my sins? Not in the way the disciples meant. All suffering exists because we live in a fallen world, and sometimes a particular sin brings painful consequences: drunkenness ruins a liver, lies ruin a friendship. But Scripture refuses to let us read every illness, disability or loss as God’s verdict on someone’s private sin (Luke 13:1–5; Job 42:7). If you are a Christian, Christ has borne your punishment; there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Your Father may discipline you in love (Hebrews 12:6), but that is a child’s training, not a judge’s sentence. So do not torment yourself hunting for the sin behind your trouble. Bring it to God, ask what he wants to do in it, and trust him.
verseByVerse.note: Many assumed that disability was punishment for a particular sin, even a parent’s.

parallels.desc: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns the question from whose fault the blindness was to what God will do through it, and then goes and does that work while the day lasts.

It was not that this man sinned, or his parents. Jesus rejects the simple link between a particular sin and a particular suffering. All suffering exists because of the fall (Romans 8:20–22), and some results directly from a particular sin (5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but not all, and not here.

That the works of God might be displayed in him. Jesus moves from cause to purpose: not why, but what for. That does not make the suffering less real, but it gives it meaning, and it is the key to the chapter: everything that follows displays God’s works in this man. The deepest work of God is “that you believe in him whom he has sent” (6:29), so the display is finished not at the pool but in verse 38, when he falls down before Jesus.

We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. “We”: Jesus includes his disciples. “Must” (dei): it is God’s will, so it has to be done. “While it is day”: while the opportunity lasts. The disciples asked about the past; Jesus answers with what God will do now, and goes and does it.

Night is coming, when no one can work. For Jesus the night is his death; for us, our death or his return. The night came for Jesus at the cross, and through it he brought the morning that will never end. The servant who knows the time is short neither coasts nor panics; he does today’s work.

What does working the works of God look like for me? Not frantic activity, and not finishing what Jesus came to finish: he did the work only he could do, and on the cross he said, “It is finished” (19:30). Our share is to go on doing what he did that afternoon, as people he has already rescued. Believe first (6:29); every other work grows from that. See the person, not the case. Do the good in front of you: he did not plan a campaign; he stopped for one beggar. A visit, a meal, a word about Christ, a wrong put right: do it while it is day, not when life is less busy. And leave the rest with him: night will come with work unfinished, and that is in his hands, not yours.

Did God blind a baby to set up a miracle? Put like that, the question sounds intolerable, and no one should pretend otherwise. But the verse says less than the objection assumes. It does not say God caused the blindness to show off; it says God’s works will be displayed in this man, and the display is that Jesus gives him his sight, goes looking for him when he has been thrown out, and gives him himself. Whatever the years cost, the man ends the chapter seeing, worshipping and known by the Son of God, which is more than his questioners ever got. The sentence may not even give a reason for the blindness (see the box below), and on either reading God does not waste the suffering of those he loves.

If God is good, why is there suffering at all? Epicurus asked it long before Christ, and David Hume sharpened it: if God wants to stop evil and cannot, he is not almighty; if he can and will not, he is not good. Parents in hospital corridors ask it without the philosophy, and it deserves to be met, not managed. Jesus gives neither the moralist’s answer, the disciples’ ledger of what people deserve, nor the sceptic’s, that suffering is simply what happens in a universe that does not care, which takes away the outrage along with God. C. S. Lewis recalled that his own case against God had been that the universe seemed so cruel and unjust, until he asked where he had got his idea of just and unjust: “A man does not call a line crooked unless he has some idea of a straight line.” The protest itself points to a standard beyond the world. God has not told us the whole reason for evil. Instead of a lecture, Jesus stoops to the dust for a man nobody would speak to; and God has given us his Son, who went on to suffer evil himself, and who will not stop until every tear is wiped away (Revelation 21:4).

How can I believe my suffering has a purpose when I cannot see it? You may not see it yet, or all of it in this life. This man waited many years, and the explanation, when it came, was not a theory but a person. Scripture does not promise that every sorrow will make sense now, but that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that our light and momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). Hold on to his character, revealed in Christ, while you wait for what you cannot yet see of his purpose, and look for his works in small things: comfort given, faith deepened, others helped through what you have suffered (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). Stop asking only why, and start asking what for: “Father, display your works in this.”

Uncertain wording. Early Greek manuscripts have little or no punctuation, and these verses can be divided differently: neither this man nor his parents sinned; but that the works of God might be displayed in him, we must work the works of him who sent me. Then Jesus gives no reason for the blindness at all, but turns from its cause to the work to be done. The ESV’s reading is the more natural Greek, and means that God had a purpose in this man’s blindness from the start. Either way, the blindness is not a punishment, and God’s works are displayed in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world." Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man's eyes with the mud
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light of the world is about to give light to a man who has never seen it, and he does it by making eyes out of the dust, as he once made a man.

As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. The claim of 8:12, about to be shown in action. The world will not go dark when he leaves it: his disciples too are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14).

Mud with the saliva. Saliva was widely believed to heal, and Jesus used it elsewhere (Mark 7:33; 8:23). But God formed man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7), and these eyes had never worked; there was nothing to repair. So the hands that made dust into a man make dust into eyes: creation, not medicine. The God who said “Let there be light” made light enter eyes that had never known it. Kneading mud was also work the rabbis’ rules forbade on the Sabbath (see the note on vv. 14–15).

He anointed the man’s eyes. Jesus often healed by a word, even from miles away (4:50). Here he uses fingers and wet earth, perhaps to engage the man’s faith by sending him to wash, perhaps to challenge the Sabbath traditions. The man can only feel a stranger’s fingers putting mud on his face. If God’s work in your life has felt less like a miracle than like being roughly handled, you are in his company: for him too the process was messy, and he had no idea what was happening while it went on.

Does God still heal today? Yes, in answer to prayer and through doctors and medicine, which are also his gifts (James 5:14–16). But Scripture does not promise healing now to every believer who prays in faith: Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20) and lived with his own thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). So pray boldly, use every good means, and trust God with the answer. The final healing of every believer is certain, at the resurrection, when he makes all things new.

Where Christians differ: do gifts of healing continue? Many faithful believers expect them to continue in the church as in the apostles’ day. This commentary’s view: the sign-miracles of Jesus and his apostles confirmed who he was and launched the church, and with many Reformed churches this commentary holds that the apostles’ sign-gifts ceased with them. Both sides agree that God still hears and answers prayer for the sick.
verseByVerse.note: Saliva was widely believed to have healing power. Kneading mud counted as work on the Sabbath under the traditions.

parallels.desc: the LORD God formed the man of dust

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent by the Sent One to a pool called Sent, the man obeys with no promise attached and comes back seeing.

The pool of Siloam. It lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel, cut through solid rock to bring the Gihon spring inside the walls (2 Kings 20:20); the remains of a large stepped pool were uncovered there in 2004. At the feast just past, the golden pitcher had been filled here every morning (7:37). Like Naaman told to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:10), the man must obey.

Which means Sent. John rarely explains place names, but he explains this one (from the Hebrew shalach, to send), because “Sent” is this Gospel’s own word for Jesus, the one the Father sent (v. 4).

Came back seeing. Simple obedience, immediate result. He walks, probably across much of the city, with mud on his face, at the word of a voice he does not recognise, and with no promise attached: Jesus did not say, “and you will see”. He said, “Go, wash”.

The waters of Shiloah, in person. Isaiah speaks of “the waters of Shiloah that flow gently” (the same name as Siloam), a picture of God’s quiet help, which Judah refused (Isaiah 8:6). Now that help has come in person, unhurried and unspectacular, and he is enough: no one who comes to him blind goes away the same. The pool was only named Sent; he is the Sent One himself.

In everyday life. Scripture gives clear instructions without explaining what they will accomplish: to forgive, to give, to confess, to rest. If we will obey only once we have been told how it will work, we are not obeying but bargaining. This man had mud on his eyes and a direction, and that was enough.

Does God heal through my obedience, or is it all grace? It is all grace, and grace works through obedience. The power was entirely Christ’s, but he gave his gift through the man’s trusting obedience, as God works in us both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). The water had no power and the walking earned nothing, but a man who refused to go would have stayed blind. So do what Christ says, not to earn his gift, but because the gift comes along the road of trust.
verseByVerse.note: The pool of Siloam lay at the south end of the city, fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel.

parallels.desc: Hezekiah brought water into the city
the waters of Shiloah

verseByVerse.quote: The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?" Some said, "It is he." Others said, "No, but he is like him." He kept saying, "I am the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The change is so great that his neighbours cannot agree he is the same man, and he keeps insisting that he is.

Is this not the man who used to sit and beg? Blind men had few options but begging, and his neighbours knew him only as the blind beggar. No one uses his name, and John never gives it: to them he was simply his blindness.

He is like him. What stands before them looks like him and does not behave like him: upright, moving freely, meeting their eyes.

I am the man. Here “I am” (egō eimi) has its ordinary sense: “it’s me”. He has to keep saying it, because they will not have it.

The same man, made new. The change is total, yet he is still the same man: Christ did not replace him, but gave him his eyes. The Lord does not discard what he redeems. His own risen body was the same body, bearing the marks of the nails, yet Mary at the tomb did not at first know him (20:14–16, 27); and he “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21).

If I am a new creation, why do I still feel so much like my old self? Because God remakes you without replacing you. What has changed is your standing with God, the life of the Spirit in you and the direction you face (2 Corinthians 5:17); old habits and feelings do not all vanish at once, and the new nature grows over a lifetime, often slowly (Romans 12:2). Like this man, you may find that others notice the change before you do. Measure your new birth not by how new you feel this morning but by Christ, who has made you his, and keep walking in the light.

parallels.desc: they recognized him as the one who sat begging

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then how were your eyes opened?" He answered, "The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So I went and washed and received my sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked how he was healed, the man simply tells what happened, and gives the only thing he knows about his healer: his name.

Then how were your eyes opened? “How” runs through the chapter (vv. 15, 19, 26), and so does the growth of the man’s answer to “who”: “the man called Jesus” (v. 11), “a prophet” (v. 17), one “from God” (v. 33), and at last the Son of Man, Lord, worshipped (vv. 35–38). His sight came in a moment; his understanding grows step by step.

The man called Jesus. He has only the name, reported as you would report a stranger’s, yet without knowing it he said everything. Jesus means “the LORD saves”, a name chosen by heaven before Mary’s child was born (Matthew 1:21), and he had lived up to it on this man’s eyes before the man knew what it meant. He is content to be known at first only by his name, and patiently teaches its meaning until each of his people knows it as the name above every name.

So I went and washed and received my sight. He tells it plainly, and the versions get shorter: here a full sentence with the name and the instruction, to the Pharisees a dozen words (v. 15), under real pressure only the core (v. 25). Invented stories tend to grow in the telling; this one shrinks. And this is a beggar, whose living had depended on telling his story well. Given a real audience for the first time, he tells it plainly.

I do not have a dramatic testimony. Do I have anything to say? Yes. Your testimony is not how bad you were or how sudden your conversion was, but what Jesus has done for you, and that is never small. This man’s three plain sentences set off an investigation that ran the length of a chapter and defeated the best-trained men in Jerusalem. If you cannot remember not believing, your testimony is that God kept you and opened your eyes early. Say in your own words what Christ is to you, what he has forgiven and changed, and why you trust him. That is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is he?" He said, "I do not know." They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man cannot say where Jesus is, and he is taken to the Pharisees to stand on what Jesus has done before he has even met him.

Where is he? I do not know. The crowds at the feast asked the same question (7:11); where Jesus is, and where he comes from, runs through chapters 7 to 9. The man has never seen him, and will not until verse 35. So the defence he is about to make, against trained interrogators and at the cost of his place in the community, is made for a man he could not pick out of a crowd, on the strength of an event and a name.

They brought to the Pharisees the man. Perhaps for an official ruling, since it was a Sabbath. That is not obviously hostile: an unexplained healing was a religious matter, and a careful neighbourhood would take it to the authorities. It becomes an interrogation because the Pharisees have their authority to lose if Jesus is from God. The man goes willingly, assuming that people who ask questions want answers; he will learn otherwise, and learning it is what makes him a disciple.

The Lord no one can trap. At the feast his enemies could not lay a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (7:30; 8:20); this beggar, who could hunt no one, will be found by him. Jesus is never where men can corner him and always where his sheep need him. His absence is not neglect: it leaves the man, for a while, to stand on what Christ has done before he knows who Christ is. We are held not by our grip on Christ, but by his grip on us.

What if I believe, but there is still so much about Jesus I do not know? You are where this man was. Much real faith begins with something that happened before there was much understanding to attach it to: a prayer answered, a word that struck home, a sense of being found. The understanding comes later, often through trouble, as it did for him. Do not despise your beginnings, and do not stay in them: ask to know him better, read his word, and expect to grow. You may not yet know where Jesus is in every situation, but he always knows where you are.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus healed on the Sabbath in a way he knew would cross the teachers’ rules, and the man answers the Pharisees with nothing but the bare fact.

Now it was a Sabbath day. John has held this detail back. As in 5:9, it is a Sabbath healing. The rabbis’ tradition listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, among them kneading, and making mud counted as kneading; some also forbade putting saliva on the eyes, and they debated whether healing was allowed at all when life was not in danger. A man blind from birth could have waited until sundown.

He chose this on purpose. He could have spoken a word and touched no rule. He chose the one method nobody could miss, forcing the question of who has authority over the Sabbath, as in chapter 5: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (5:17). The God who rested on the seventh day after making the world was at work on this seventh day making a new creation, and he works on until all his people enter his rest.

And I see. No name, no instruction, no explanation. He is getting impatient, not hiding anything: he gives the one fact nobody can argue away.

In everyday life. Do not let human rules stand between people and the mercy of God. Ask whether any expectations in your church, or in your own heart, make it harder for hurting people to come to Christ. Keep what God commands, and hold everything else loosely.

Did Jesus really break the Sabbath? He broke the rules the teachers had added to it, which forbade kneading and healing, not God’s command. The law of Moses never forbade doing good on the Sabbath, and Jesus taught that works of mercy were always lawful (Matthew 12:12). He is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28). The Pharisees’ premise, that he did not keep the Sabbath, was false.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath." But others said, "How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?" And there was a division among them. So they said again to the blind man, "What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?" He said, "He is a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The miracle splits the Pharisees, and the man they are questioning reasons his way to a truth bigger than he knows: Jesus is a prophet.

This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath. Some start from their Sabbath rule, and so the miracle must be explained away. Others start from the miracle, which is a fair argument. The difference is which of the two they treat as beyond question.

A division among them. “Division” (schisma, a tear): Jesus divides people wherever he goes (7:43; 10:19), and now even the Pharisees are split. It is a small mercy: some of the men whose job was to guard the people from false prophets were following the evidence, and said so. A man may belong to a body that has made up its mind and still think for himself.

What do you say about him? A council of trained men cannot agree, and asks the man they are examining, perhaps hoping he will help their case. The question is dismissive, and it starts him thinking.

He is a prophet. His second step, reasoned out under questioning: his faith is being built by the very process designed to dismantle it, and he is more right than he knows. Moses had promised a prophet like himself, whom Israel must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15), and the crowds had wondered whether Jesus was the Prophet (7:40). The smallest true thing about Jesus leads on to the greatest: the prophets carried God’s words, but Jesus is himself the Word of God (1:1). A beggar called him a prophet and was right. Heaven calls him Lord, and is right.

What if I start from the wrong fixed point? Everyone starts somewhere. These Pharisees had made their own reading of the Sabbath unquestionable, so they could not see God at work in front of them. Christians can do the same with a tradition, a political view, a favourite teacher or a past experience. The test is whether you let Scripture and what Christ has done correct your fixed point, or explain away whatever does not fit. Hold firm to what God has clearly said; hold everything else humbly, ready to be corrected.

parallels.desc: a prophet who gives a sign

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight and asked them, "Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unable to break the man’s story, the leaders try to deny he was ever blind, and question his parents to turn the fact into a doubt.

The Jews did not believe. Here “the Jews” means the same Pharisees, the leaders (see the introduction). Unable to fault the man’s account, they deny that he was ever blind.

Until they called the parents. The best witnesses, and a tactic: the leaders have a witness who will not budge, and want one who will. Parents have more to lose.

Is this your son, who you say was born blind? Three questions: is he your son, was he born blind, how does he now see? And the wording plants a doubt: not “who was born blind” but “who you say was born blind”. Before any answer is given, the blindness has become something the family merely claims, and now the family is under investigation. No one has to say the man is lying. People still do this, and it does not even take malice.

The sign they could not undo. The same method was used on the greatest sign of all. The chief priests did not deny that the tomb was empty; they paid the guards to say the disciples had stolen the body (Matthew 28:11–15). Make the witnesses the question, and nobody has to face the fact. But the risen Christ, like the seeing beggar, kept standing in front of people, and no investigation has put him back in the tomb. The Light cannot be argued out of the room; the more closely it is examined, the more clearly it shows.

How should I handle evidence that is inconvenient? Honestly. When a fact threatens what we have decided, the temptation is to turn it into somebody’s opinion and question the person; the honest move is to look at the fact. That applies to the evidence for Christ, which deserves to be weighed, not waved away, and to Christians when something unwelcome comes to light: a hard passage of Scripture, a just complaint against us, a wrong done in our church. Truth is never the enemy of faith, and the God of truth is not served by anyone’s refusal to look.

verseByVerse.quote: His parents answered, "We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parents confirm the two facts that make the miracle undeniable, and then, afraid, step back and leave their son to face the court alone.

We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. They answer the first two questions plainly, and the claim that the blindness was invented dies in their answer.

How he now sees we do not know. They avoid the third. They probably did know; their son must have told them. They are afraid (v. 22).

Ask him; he is of age. A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen, able to give legal testimony, and this man was an adult. So they shift the danger onto him, at the moment he most needs someone beside him.

Be fair to them. Contempt for the parents is too harsh. They had raised a blind child in a world with no provision for one, among people who had already decided someone’s sin was to blame; the disciples’ question in verse 2 is what they had heard about themselves all his life. Now they were being asked to risk exclusion from the synagogue. They did not lie, and they did not stand by their son, and John records it without comment.

The one who stood alone. Within months the same pressure fell on Jesus, and those closest to him did what these parents did: all the disciples left him and fled (Matthew 26:56; Mark 14:50), and he stood before the high priest with no friend beside him. He bore that loneliness on purpose, so that none of those he came for would ever finally stand alone. “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in” (Psalm 27:10). As this son stood alone before a hostile court, the Lord was already on his way to him. He receives those whose families stepped back, and restores those who stepped back themselves; he has never once said of any of his people, “Ask him; he is of age.”

In everyday life. Look for the believer near you who is paying a price for faithfulness: the colleague who refused to lie, the relative who has been shut out. Stand next to them this week, in some visible way.

I have gone quiet about Christ when I should have spoken. Is that the end of me? No. Going quiet when the subject came up at work, letting a remark pass, answering a direct question with something technically true and deliberately empty: that is their failure, and Scripture records it honestly but without harshness. These two are not cursed or written off, and Peter did far worse within months, three times, out loud, and was given breakfast on a beach and a commission (21:15–19). The failure is real, but it need not be final. Beneath most of our silences is the fear of man, which needs the approval of the people in the room more than God’s, and it lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not more willpower but a larger sight of the approval you already have in Christ. Confess it, ask for courage, and take the next opportunity he gives you.
verseByVerse.note: A son was regarded as of age at about thirteen.

verseByVerse.quote: (His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, "He is of age; ask him.")
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parents were afraid because the leaders had already decided that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be shut out of the community.

They feared the Jews. That is, the leaders. Being put out of the synagogue (aposynagōgos, 12:42; 16:2) meant exclusion from the community. Some scholars think this reflects a period after AD 70, but local exclusion could already happen in Jesus’ lifetime, as his warning in Luke 6:22 shows.

What it cost. The synagogue was not a church one might change. It was the school, the court, the welfare system and the register of who belonged. Exclusion could mean that no one would trade with you, marry your children or sit with you: not embarrassment but the loss of every relationship the family had.

Had already agreed. The decision came before this man’s case, so the investigation was never really an investigation. And though he never says “Christ”, only “a prophet” and “from God”, the policy seems to be applied to him anyway (v. 34).

Confess Jesus to be Christ. To confess is to declare openly that he is the Messiah, Israel’s anointed King. But the Christ himself would be put out first: rejected by his people’s leaders, he “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). Every disciple shut out for his name since finds Christ already there, outside with him, and the one who was put out for us has made a home for us that no council can shut.

What if confessing Christ would cost me my family or my job? Then you are in the company of this man, and of believers in many countries today for whom it costs exactly that. Jesus does not hide the price: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). But no one who leaves home or family for his sake will fail to receive a hundredfold now, in the family of his church, and eternal life in the age to come (Mark 10:29–30). Count the cost honestly; seek wisdom about how and when to speak, and the support of other believers; but do not deny him. What you lose for Christ, you never lose for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Being put out of the synagogue meant exclusion from the community’s worship and social life.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." He answered, "Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on oath to call Jesus a sinner, the man refuses to claim what he does not know and holds to the one thing he does: he was blind, and now he sees.

Give glory to God. A solemn formula putting a man on oath to tell the truth, especially to confess wrongdoing, as Joshua said to Achan (Joshua 7:19), who confessed and was put to death for robbing the holy God (Joshua 7:20–25). Here it means: admit this was a fraud. These men use the language of God’s holiness to frighten a beggar, and never ask whether they themselves stand before the holy God.

We know that this man is a sinner. A Sabbath-breaker is a sinner: the verdict is announced before the testimony is taken.

Whether he is a sinner I do not know. He will not be drawn into an argument he is not equipped to win, or give an opinion he does not have: an honesty rare under pressure.

One thing I do know. John Newton echoed it in Amazing Grace. It is his story at its shortest, and unbreakable: they can outrank him, out-argue him and out-quote him, but they cannot make him doubt that he was blind yesterday.

Glory given without knowing it. They told him to give glory to God, and he did, more truly than they meant. In this Gospel God’s glory is seen in the works of the Son (2:11; 11:4, 40), and the plainest way to glorify God is to say what his Son has done; the men demanding glory for God refuse it to the one in whom it shines (8:54).

Is my experience enough to prove Christianity is true? It is part of your witness, not the whole case, and this man shows why: his experience is where he stands, not where he stops, for in verse 33 he reasons from Scripture and history to who Jesus is. Experience can be misread, and people of other faiths report experiences too. The Christian faith rests on what God has done in history, above all the death and resurrection of Christ, and on what he has said in Scripture; your experience of his grace confirms that public truth. So tell what has happened to you, and point beyond yourself to the Christ it all depends on.
verseByVerse.note: “Give glory to God” was a solemn call to tell the truth.

parallels.desc: give glory to the LORD and tell me now what you have done

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" He answered them, "I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Questioned yet again, the man sees that they do not want the truth, and his mocking question shows that he has already taken his side as Jesus’ disciple.

I have told you already, and you would not listen. They go over it again, looking for a contradiction, and he grows bolder. The exasperation is genuine, and funny: he has worked out that they hope the story will come out differently the second time. These men have working eyes and ears and are getting nothing through either.

Why do you want to hear it again? There is a mischievous edge to it. He knows the answer before he asks.

Do you also want to become his disciples? A daring, ironic question. The Greek form expects the answer no, and “also” implies that he is, or is becoming, one himself. It is sarcasm, and also, accidentally, evangelism: the chapter’s first invitation, issued by a beggar to the council’s investigators. Up to now he has been reporting; here he takes sides. What has brought him here is not a conversation with Jesus, whom he has never seen, nor teaching, but being pushed: every question drives him a step further, until by the end of the interview he is a disciple of a man he could not recognise.

The disciple sounds like his Master. Jesus had said the same to the same men only days before: “Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word” (8:43). The beggar never heard that sentence, yet he is already treated as his Lord was treated, and answers as his Lord answered (15:20). The Lord who chooses what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27) had put his wit in a beggar’s mouth and his courage in a beggar’s heart. He does not only rescue his people; he makes them like himself, so that the world, questioning them, finds itself hearing him.

How can opposition make faith stronger? It forces us to decide what we really believe, and to lean on God rather than on comfort. Trials test faith as fire tests gold (1 Peter 1:6–7), and testing produces steadfastness (James 1:2–4). This man had faith the size of a name when the questioning began, and a clear confession when it ended. Hardship can shake faith too; but for those who keep turning to him, God uses it to burn away what is false and make the real thing plain. If your faith is under pressure now, do not assume it is failing. It may be growing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they reviled him, saying, "You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out-argued, the leaders turn to abuse and hide behind Moses, and in saying they do not know where Jesus comes from they name their own blindness.

And they reviled him. “Reviled” (eloidorēsan): abused, insulted. They began with an investigation, moved to intimidation, and end by shouting at a beggar.

We are disciples of Moses. The pronouns draw a line: you are his; we are Moses’. But Moses wrote of Jesus (5:46), so the claim defeats itself: anyone who meets the one Moses wrote about and refuses him is no longer following Moses. The name has become a badge of being on the right side, and religion used that way is the hardest blindness to cure, because it looks like sight.

We know that God has spoken to Moses. That much was true (Exodus 33:11). But for them God’s speaking lies in the past and is finished. The man in front of them is evidence that God has acted today, and their thinking has no room for it.

We do not know where he comes from. Earlier they claimed to know where he came from (7:27); now they mean that he has no credentials. In fact they have named their own problem: they do not know that he came from God.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians, or has Jesus replaced Moses? Jesus has not replaced Moses but fulfilled him. The whole Old Testament is God’s word and points to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44): its promises are kept in him, its sacrifices fulfilled in his once-for-all death, its moral law written on our hearts by the Spirit. The Pharisees’ error was not loving Moses too much but reading him without Christ, so that the book meant to lead them to Jesus became a wall against him. Read the Old Testament gladly, as Christian Scripture, asking how each part leads you to the one Moses wrote about.

verseByVerse.quote: The man answered, "Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beggar turns the experts’ own belief against them: God does not answer impostors, so a man through whom God has done this must be from him.

Why, this is an amazing thing! The beggar becomes the teacher, amazed that the experts cannot see the obvious. The Lord who hid these things from the wise and revealed them to little children (Matthew 11:25) gave a beggar the clearest reasoning in the room.

We know that God does not listen to sinners. He turns their “we know” back on them. It was a common belief, drawn from Scripture, that God does not hear the prayers of the wicked who cling to their sin (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; Isaiah 1:15). So, he argues, God would not answer an impostor by doing what Scripture reserves for God himself, opening the eyes of a man born blind; and because they share the belief, they cannot answer him.

God listens to him. So Jesus must be a godly man whom God hears, and the beggar is more right than he knows. There is one man whom the Father always hears (11:42), who always does what pleases him (8:29), the true worshipper the Father seeks; and sinners are heard at all only through him, whose perfect obedience is counted as theirs.

A sentence that needs a guard. Lifted out of this courtyard and read as a rule about prayer, these words have frightened people badly. They are a new believer arguing from the common piety of his day, not a formula handed down from heaven, and even the psalm behind them says something narrower: “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened” (Psalm 66:18). The word is “cherished”. What closes God’s ear is not the presence of sin in a person but his fondness for it: the man who hugs his sin and demands God’s help at the same time.

In everyday life. Is there a sin you are holding on to while asking God for help? The Son has already borne it; let it go, and pray.

I am a sinner. Will God listen to my prayers? Yes. Jesus told of a tax collector who stood far off, would not lift his eyes, beat his breast and prayed for mercy as a sinner, and went home justified (Luke 18:13–14): declared right with God by God himself, not because of his prayer but because of the mercy he asked for. God listened to a sinner at the very moment he called himself one. If you fear that your sin has stopped God’s ears, see which way the fear runs: the person whose sin has closed God’s ear is not troubled about it. Your trouble is not evidence that he has stopped listening; very often it is the first evidence that he has begun to work. Come to him through Christ, honestly, and he will hear you.

parallels.desc: if I had cherished iniquity, the Lord would not have listened

verseByVerse.quote: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever opened the eyes of a man born blind, the beggar argues, because Scripture keeps that work for God; so Jesus must be from God.

Never since the world began. He is right. Elijah and Elisha each raised a dead child, and Naaman’s leprosy went, but no one in Scripture before this opens the eyes of someone blind from birth. The Old Testament keeps that work for God himself (Psalm 146:8; Exodus 4:11), and promises it as a sign of the days of the Messiah (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7). The beggar’s argument is an accurate survey of the record, from a man who had heard a great deal of Scripture in the synagogue he was about to be thrown out of. The promised new age has begun: the God who made the eye had come to give it sight.

If this man were not from God, he could do nothing. His third step. The question they cannot answer, the beggar answers. He does not say Jesus is the Messiah, which he has no way yet of knowing; he claims only the least that the evidence proves, and it is enough to end the argument. It leaves them nothing to attack except him.

How should I think about the evidence for Christ? Like this man: clearly, honestly and from the facts. Christianity does not ask you to switch off your mind. The signs were written so that you may believe (20:30–31), and the risen Christ was seen by many witnesses, most of them still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Weigh the Old Testament promises, the life and claims of Jesus, the empty tomb and the transformation of the disciples. Evidence alone does not save; the Spirit must open the heart. But God uses evidence, and honest reasoning from what Christ has done points to God, even while some questions remain.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind shall be opened

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?" And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thrown out by the leaders for daring to teach them, the man is sought and found by Jesus, who asks him to believe in the Son of Man.

You were born in utter sin. They return to the disciples’ mistaken assumption (v. 2): your blindness proves you were born in sin. In saying so they finally admit he was born blind, and so admit the miracle. The irony is that it is true of all of us, them included (Psalm 51:5). What the disciples raised as a puzzle, these men use as a weapon.

And would you teach us? Pride: a beggar cannot teach scholars. They never manage to say “you are wrong”, only “who do you think you are?” Having lost the argument, they fall back on their rank. A man whose position has become the one thing he cannot afford to lose weighs only who speaks, not what is said, and such a heart cannot be taught by the gospel, which always comes from below: in a manger, from a cross, through a beggar.

And they cast him out. Out of the room, and probably out of the synagogue (v. 22): he has lost his community and standing for confessing Jesus, a man with new eyes and nothing else. Chapters 9 and 10 are joined more tightly than the chapter break suggests: “they cast him out” (exebalon), and a few sentences later the good shepherd has “brought out all his own” (10:4), with the same verb. The Pharisees threw the man out of their fold; the Shepherd was bringing him out of it.

Having found him. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out (10:3–4). He never casts out anyone who comes to him (6:37); those cast out for his sake, he gathers in. The words suggest that Jesus went looking: the man could not have searched for a face he had never seen, and while he stood in the street with nowhere to go, he was already being sought. The one who saw him first, blind and begging, found him again the moment the world had finished with him. That is the whole Gospel in one man’s afternoon: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10), and he has never stopped looking for those everyone else has thrown away.

Do you believe in the Son of Man? “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself, from Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” comes before God and receives a kingdom that will never end. Jesus asks a man just stripped of his standing in Israel whether he will believe in the one to whom every kingdom is finally given.

In everyday life. Who has been pushed out of the circles you move in: the family, the friendship group, the church? Christ went looking for you; go and look for them.

I have been rejected by a church or by Christians. Has Christ rejected me? No. Sometimes believers are put out unjustly, as this man was, and Christ sees it and comes looking for them; bring it to him, for he has not cast you out. But be honest too: church discipline can be a loving and right response to unrepented sin (Matthew 18:15–17), meant to bring a person home, not to destroy them. Whatever has happened, do not let the failures of Christians keep you from Christ, or make you give up on his people. Seek a faithful church where you can be known and cared for.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “Son of God.” The earliest and best manuscripts read “Son of Man,” and a scribe is more likely to have changed it to the more familiar confession than the other way round. The meaning is not changed: in John the Son of Man is the one who comes from heaven (3:13).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: brought forth in iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?" Jesus said to him, "You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ready to believe before he even knows the name, the man hears Jesus say it plainly: the Son of Man is the one standing in front of him.

And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him? “Sir” (kyrie) can also mean Lord. He commits before he knows the answer: not “tell me who he is and I will consider it”, but “I am ready to believe and need only the name”. And he says it to a stranger, for he has never seen the face.

You have seen him. Since the pool this man has seen his neighbours, his parents and the council, but never this face. The eyes he is using to look at Jesus were made by the man he is looking at, out of dirt.

It is he who is speaking to you. As to the Samaritan woman (4:26): twice in this Gospel Jesus states his identity outright to one person, unpressed, and both times to someone with no standing at all. The men who ran the temple, who kept demanding that he speak plainly, never heard it put to them as simply as this.

A beggar was shown the face. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was shown only his back; a beggar who had lost everything was shown the face. The only Son has made the Father known (1:18), and makes him known still, not to those sure they already see, but to those who ask, “Who is he, Lord?” One day “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), and the first face of the age to come will be the face that sought us when we could not seek him.

How does Jesus reveal himself to people today? Through his word, by his Spirit. He no longer stands in the street to be seen; he speaks in Scripture and the preaching of the gospel, and the Spirit opens hearts to see him there (Romans 10:17; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not second best: those who have not seen and yet believe are blessed (20:29). If you want to know him, go where he speaks: read a Gospel, sit under faithful preaching, and ask him to show himself to you. Like this man, you may find he has been speaking to you all along.

parallels.desc: I who speak to you am he

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man’s journey ends on his face before Jesus as Lord, and Jesus names what the day has shown: his coming gives sight to the blind and exposes the blindness of those who claim to see.

Lord, I believe. Now “Lord” (kyrie) in its full sense, the last step of his confession.

And he worshiped him. “Worshiped” (prosekynēsen): bowed down before him. In John this word is used only of worshipping God (4:20–24; 12:20), and Jesus accepts it, because he is God. Just thrown out of the house of worship, on his face in a Jerusalem street, the man had found the true temple standing in front of him in a body. The council kept the building; the beggar had the Lord of it.

For judgment I came into this world. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), but his coming brings a separation. The verse gathers up the Gospel so far: the light came and his own did not receive him (1:9–11); people loved the darkness (3:19). Chapter 9 is that sentence acted out in a single day, and in chapter 12 John will explain the leaders’ blindness from Isaiah 6 (12:37–41).

That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Those who know they are blind and come to him are given sight; those who are sure they already see are left in their blindness (Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 11:25), as this chapter has shown. Nobody was condemned by a new verdict. They were exposed by a light, which is what light does.

Is it right to worship Jesus? Yes, and this verse is one of the plainest reasons. Scripture forbids worshipping anyone but God (Exodus 20:3–5; Matthew 4:10); when Cornelius bowed before Peter, or John before an angel, they were told at once to stand up (Acts 10:25–26; Revelation 22:8–9). Jesus never says that. He receives this man’s worship, and Thomas’ confession, “My Lord and my God” (20:28), because he is God the Son, to be honoured just as the Father is honoured (5:23). So Christians rightly pray to Jesus, sing to him and bow before him, with the Father and the Spirit, one God.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “He said, ‘Lord, I believe,’ and he worshiped him. Jesus said.” Many scholars think the words are original: they are found in the great majority of manuscripts, including very early ones, and the omission may be accidental.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees’ guilt stays because they insist that they see; only those who admit they are blind can be given sight.

Are we also blind? The Greek form expects the answer no: surely not us? They invite a denial, because they have understood him perfectly well.

If you were blind, you would have no guilt. If they knew themselves to be blind and came to him for sight, their sin would be forgiven; or, if they truly had no opportunity to see, they would be less guilty. The mercy is real, but no one in that crowd is in that position.

Your guilt remains. “Remains” (menei): stays, abides. The most dangerous condition is not blindness but the proud claim to see: a man who knows he is blind will ask for help, and a man sure he can see will not, so nothing more can be done for him while he goes on saying it (compare Revelation 3:17). The chapter ends on John’s word for abiding, but here it is guilt that stays, as at 3:36: “the wrath of God remains on him.” Sin either remains or is carried away by the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (1:29). The men who said “we see” kept theirs.

Two kinds of blind men. That is the chapter in one line. One said, “I do not know”, twice (vv. 12, 25), and ended on his face worshipping. The others said “we know” (vv. 24, 29) and “we see” (v. 41), and ended with nothing but the verdict they had passed on him. They would rather be blind than be taught by a beggar.

Born on the wrong side of this verse. Every one of us was born blind and sure we could see. If any of us now see, it is not because we were humbler than the Pharisees, but because the Light of the world came close enough to touch us, and showed us our blindness before he cured it. Even knowing that we are blind is his gift. The light that exposes is the light that heals, and he never shines it on his own people to shame them, only to bring them home.

How do I know whether I am one of those who think they see? Ask whether you are still teachable; the Pharisees could not be taught by anyone below them. When did Scripture last change your mind, or someone with less standing than you question a doctrine you hold? Do you pray for light, or assume you already have it? This test is meant to catch the confident, not to crush the anxious. If you fear you might be blind and want Christ to open your eyes, that very worry shows you are not where these men were. The humble cry, Lord, that I may see, is the cry he always answers.

parallels.desc: a guide to the blind

Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud<sup>7</sup>and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.<sup>8</sup>The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?”<sup>9</sup>Some said, “It is he.” Others said, “No, but he is like him.” He kept saying, “I am the man.”<sup>10</sup>So they said to him, “Then how were your eyes opened?”<sup>11</sup>He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, ’Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed and received my sight.”<sup>12</sup>They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I do not know.”<sup>13</sup>They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.<sup>14</sup>Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.<sup>15</sup>So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”<sup>16</sup>Some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” And there was a division among them.<sup>17</sup>So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”<sup>18</sup>The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight<sup>19</sup>and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”<sup>20</sup>His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind.<sup>21</sup>But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”<sup>22</sup>(His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue.<sup>23</sup>Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”)<sup>24</sup>So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”<sup>25</sup>He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.”<sup>26</sup>They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”<sup>27</sup>He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”<sup>28</sup>And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.<sup>29</sup>We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.”<sup>30</sup>The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes.<sup>31</sup>We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him.<sup>32</sup>Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind.<sup>33</sup>If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”<sup>34</sup>They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out.<sup>35</sup>Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”<sup>36</sup>He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?”<sup>37</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.”<sup>38</sup>He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”<sup>40</sup>Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”<sup>41</sup>Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ’We see,’ your guilt remains.
9.overview:
Where we are. At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus has declared, “I am the light of the world” (8:12), and has slipped out of the temple as his hearers took up stones (8:59). Now, in the sixth of John’s signs, he shows what that light does. The chapter runs straight on into the good shepherd of chapter 10.

The message. Jesus is the light of the world: he gives sight to the blind who know their need, and his light shows up the blindness of those who are sure they see. A beggar receives his eyes in a moment and comes, step by step, to see Jesus as Lord and to worship him, while men with every advantage talk themselves into darkness. And from first to last it is Jesus who does the seeking.

Why it was said. John’s first readers knew what it could cost to confess Jesus as the Christ: some had been put out of the synagogue for it (v. 22; see the introduction). Here they met a man who paid that price before them, and the Lord who came looking for him.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus sees a man born blind, turns his disciples from whose fault it is to what God will do, and sends him to wash in the pool called Sent (vv. 1–7). The neighbours argue over whether he is the same man (vv. 8–12). The Pharisees question him about a Sabbath healing, divide over Jesus, and summon his frightened parents, who leave him to answer alone (vv. 13–23). Questioned again, he holds to the one thing he knows, argues the experts into silence, and is thrown out (vv. 24–34). All the while his words for Jesus grow: a man called Jesus, a prophet, one from God. Then Jesus finds him, and he believes and worships, while the Pharisees who say “We see” keep their guilt (vv. 35–41).

Where it leads. Opening eyes blind from birth is the work Scripture keeps for God himself and promised for the days of the Messiah (Isaiah 35:5), and the Light of the world still does it in hearts that cannot see him (2 Corinthians 4:6). The man is cast out for Christ and found by him; within months Christ himself would be rejected by the same leaders and suffer outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that all who are shut out for his name would have a home with him.

For us. We were all born blind, and sure we could see. Ask for sight humbly, say plainly what Christ has done for you even when it costs, and if you are ever pushed out for his name, remember who comes looking for you.

keyVerse.quote: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.
keyVerse.note: Jesus himself sums up the day in one sentence. The beggar who knew he was blind ends the chapter seeing and worshipping; the men who were sure they saw end it blind and guilty. Jesus did not come to condemn, but his light divides: it heals all who admit their need, and exposes all who will not.

9.reflection:
The disciples looked at the blind man and asked whose fault his blindness was (v. 2); Jesus spoke of what God would do (v. 3). When you meet suffering, in others or in your own life, which question comes to you first? What would change if you began with his?

The man’s words for Jesus grow under pressure: “the man called Jesus”, “a prophet”, one “from God”, and at last “Lord” (vv. 11, 17, 33, 38). How has your own understanding of Jesus grown, and what part have hard times played in it?

His parents told the truth but stepped back out of fear (vv. 20–23), while he would not deny what he knew (v. 25). Where are you tempted to go quiet about Christ, and what would it look like to say plainly what he has done for you?

Jesus went and found the man after he had been thrown out (v. 35), and warned the Pharisees that saying “We see” left their guilt in place (v. 41). How can we stay teachable before Christ, and who around us has been pushed out and needs to be looked for?

10.title: The Good Shepherd

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the true shepherd of God’s flock, and he proves it by dying for the sheep. Against the leaders who have just cast out the man born blind, he describes a shepherd who comes in by the door and calls his own sheep by name, while thieves climb in another way (vv. 1–6). He is the door, the only way into safety and pasture, where the thief comes only to destroy (vv. 7–10). He is the good shepherd who, unlike the hired hand, lays down his life for the sheep, knows them as the Father knows him, and will bring other sheep into one flock (vv. 11–16). He lays his life down of his own accord, and will take it up again (vv. 17–18). His words divide his hearers (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd picture draws on the whole Old Testament: God as the shepherd of his people (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34), the promised shepherd from David’s line (Ezekiel 34:23–24; Jeremiah 23:4). Jesus takes all of it to himself. He is the door, the only way to God; the good shepherd, who gives rather than takes; and the one who lays down his life freely, as no hired hand would. The picture cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice because they are already his, and the Pharisees cannot hear because they are not (see the note on vv. 26–27); the church hears because the Shepherd has given her ears.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who climbs into God’s flock by another way is a thief; the true shepherd comes in openly, by the door that belongs to him. Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees who have just thrown a sheep of God’s flock, the man born blind, out of theirs (9:34), and he is telling them who the true shepherd is.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The solemn double Amen marks a saying with his full authority: where the prophets said, “Thus says the LORD”, Jesus says, “I say to you”.

The shepherds of Israel. Behind the whole chapter lies Ezekiel 34, where God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock (“Should not shepherds feed the sheep?” 34:2), and promises, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (34:15). Jesus is saying, in effect: I am that shepherd.

By another way. Two kinds of sheepfold explain the passage. The one described here was a walled enclosure in or near a village, often a courtyard beside a house, holding several families’ flocks overnight, with a solid door and a man paid to watch it. The other, described by travellers in the region in later centuries and very likely as old as the trade, was used out in the hills: a rough circle of piled stones with a gap and no door, because the shepherd lay across the gap and slept there. Nothing came in or went out except over him. He was the door (see v. 7).

That man is a thief and a robber. The two words are not synonyms. A thief (kleptēs) works by stealth; a robber (lēstēs) is a bandit with violence in hand, the word John uses of Barabbas (18:40). Every generation of the church has met both kinds, and the marks are the same: they did not come in by the door, and they want what they can get out of the sheep.

By the door. The true shepherd need not climb, because the door belongs to him, nor hide, because he has nothing to take. He came as the prophets said he would, born in David’s city, announced by the forerunner, doing in public the works promised of the Messiah: he walked in by the door his Father had built for him over a thousand years of promise.

How do I tell whether a leader has come in by the door? Ask three questions. First, does he come through Christ and his word, or around them? A true shepherd sends you to Christ and is content to be measured by Scripture; a false one needs you to depend on him, his insight or his new revelation. Second, is he accountable? Doors have keepers, and a man who answers to no elders, no church and no one but himself has climbed the wall, however gifted (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 1 Peter 5:1–4). Third, what is he taking? Watch where the money, the admiration and the control flow. A shepherd spends himself on the sheep; a thief spends the sheep on himself.
verseByVerse.note: A sheepfold was a walled enclosure where several flocks might be kept overnight, with a single doorway.

parallels.desc: the false shepherds of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true shepherd knows each of his sheep by name, leads them out, and walks ahead of them, and they follow because they know his voice.

To him the gatekeeper opens. Some say the gatekeeper is the Father, the Spirit or John the Baptist, but not every detail of a parable stands for something. The point is that Jesus is no intruder: heaven opens to him.

By name. Shepherds in that world led their flocks rather than drove them, and often named their sheep for a marking, a habit, an injury. With several flocks mixed in the fold overnight, in the morning a shepherd stands at the door and calls, and out of the mass his own animals detach themselves and come. “His own” (ta idia) is a warm phrase: they belong to him, as God said to Israel, “I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1).

Leads them out. The word (exagei) is used of God leading Israel out of Egypt, and John has just shown it happening: the authorities threw the man born blind out of their fold, and Jesus went and found him (9:35). What looked like being thrown out was being led out to freedom, and towards pasture (v. 9).

He goes before them. A dog behind a flock drives it. Here the sheep move because someone they trust is already moving, a few paces ahead on every step of the road he asks them to walk. There is no stretch of it he has not covered, including death itself, which he went through entirely alone so that nobody following him would ever have to face it alone.

In everyday life. Whatever is waiting for you this week, a hard conversation, a hospital appointment, a decision you dread, he has gone ahead of you into it. You are following someone who is already there. Listen for his voice in his word before you walk into the day.

Does Jesus really know me by name, among so many? Yes, and the number is no strain on him: our attention is divided because we are finite, and his is not. The one who names the stars (Psalm 147:4) knows the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30). He knows your history, your temperament, the sin you are fighting and the sorrow you have told no one, and he calls you as you are. On days when you feel invisible to everyone, including the church, you are not invisible to him.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds in the East led their flocks rather than drove them, and named their sheep; the sheep knew their shepherd’s call.

parallels.desc: who shall go out before them and bring them in

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s sheep will not follow a stranger, because they know their shepherd’s voice; the Pharisees could not understand the picture, because it was about them.

A stranger they will not follow. The healed man would not follow the Pharisees: he had heard the voice that opened his eyes, and theirs did not sound like it. What protects the sheep is not constant watchfulness but knowing his voice well, the voice that called them out of the dark. Ten thousand strangers have spoken since, clever, confident, sometimes in his name, and his flock has gone on recognising him.

They will flee from him. The sheep move away quickly, without giving the stranger a hearing out of politeness. Not every voice claiming to speak for God deserves a debate. Some deserve a closed door (2 John 10).

This figure of speech. The word (paroimia) means a proverb, a veiled saying, a picture with something hidden inside it.

They did not understand. It is the same failure as Nicodemus over the new birth (3:4), the Samaritan woman over living water (4:15), the disciples over his food (4:33) and the crowd over the bread of life (6:34). These trained teachers of Scripture cannot follow a picture of themselves, and in missing it they prove the point: they are not his sheep, and his voice sounds to them like noise.

The way to know a forgery. Bank staff, it is often said, learn to spot forged notes by handling genuine ones. The way to recognise a false teacher is not first to study false teaching, which is endlessly inventive, but to know the real voice so well that the wrong one grates: hours spent in the Gospels rather than on the internet.

Christians do get deceived, so what does this promise mean? That the elect, those God has chosen as his own, will not be finally and fatally led away from Christ, not that no believer is ever confused. Sheep can be frightened, scattered and misled for a time; true believers in Galatia had been bewitched (Galatians 3:1). But the Shepherd guards his own, and they come back to his voice. This is no licence for carelessness: the apostle who recorded this promise tells us to test the spirits (1 John 4:1), and the Shepherd keeps his sheep from deception by their knowing his word. So if you have been taken in by something, do not conclude you were never his. Go back to the voice, and let it correct you.
