verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the one door into God’s flock; those who came as saviours apart from him were thieves, and God’s true sheep did not listen to them.

I am the door of the sheep. This is the third great “I am” saying, after the bread of life (6:35) and the light of the world (8:12). The hill fold without a gate explains the picture: the shepherd’s own body closed the gap (see the note on vv. 1–2). Shepherd and door are one image seen at two hours of the day: he leads them out in the morning and lies across the entrance at dusk, and anything that wants them must get past him first. On a Friday outside Jerusalem the wolf came, the shepherd died in the doorway, and not one sheep was lost. There is only one way into God’s flock, and he is it (14:6).

All who came before me are thieves and robbers. Not Moses and the prophets, who wrote about him and pointed to him (5:46; 8:56), but those who claimed to be saviours apart from him, such as the two men Gamaliel names, Theudas and Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:36–37). They all came for themselves.

In everyday life. Most of us have little doors we are tempted to use instead of him: being good enough, being busy enough in church, having grown up in it, feeling the right things. Come to God today the only way anyone has ever come, through Christ, with nothing in your hands.

Is Jesus really the only way? Yes. He is not a door, one entrance among many, but the door. That is not narrowness but reality: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Salvation comes through conscious faith in him, which is exactly why the church sends missionaries: the door must be shown to those who have not yet heard of it (Romans 10:14–15). But the door is open: the saying that excludes every other way invites everyone to this one. Nor is it arrogant to say so. It would be, if Christians had found the door by their own cleverness or goodness; to point to a door you did not build, and went through only because you were called, is the humblest thing a sinner can do.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever comes in through Christ is safe and fed; the thief only takes, but Christ came to give life in overflowing measure.

If anyone enters by me, he will be saved. Open to anyone at all, through one person.

In and out. To “go in and out” is a Hebrew way of speaking of living in safety, coming and going without fear. Moses asks God for a leader who will go out and come in before the people, “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). The promise is freedom under protection, a door that opens both ways with someone trustworthy standing in it. Salvation is not a cage, and the sheep do not merely survive; they feed.

The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. He takes, he kills, he ruins, and nowhere in the list is the word “give”. False shepherds use the flock for themselves, and behind every false shepherd stands the one who was a murderer from the beginning (8:44).

Abundantly. The word (perisson) means over and above, overflowing. Jesus gives the fullness of eternal life, which is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3): not only rescue from death but life, not only pardon but adoption and an inheritance. He did not come to take a little less from us than the thief; he came to give more than we could hold, and the cost of the giving was his own life.

The suspicion that God is the thief. Many assume the reverse: that God is the one who takes, and faith means a smaller, greyer life. The Victorian poet Swinburne put it in a line addressed to Christ: “Thou hast conquered, O pale Galilean; the world has grown grey from thy breath.” The suspicion is as old as the serpent’s first suggestion, that God was holding something back and that real life lay on the far side of his command (Genesis 3:1–5). Every idol since, a career, a pleasure, being in control, promises life and, given time, takes it: first our evenings, then our friendships, then our peace. Jesus turns the suspicion inside out. The one we feared would take everything from us is the one who gave everything for us, and the life he gives is the life the thief promised and never delivered.

What it does not mean. The prosperity gospel reads this as a promise of health, money and success. The word says nothing about possessions, and the verse sits one sentence away from a shepherd being killed: the abundance is defined by the man offering it, who is about to hand over his life. Paul lists what his own abundant life came to, beaten, shipwrecked, cold, hungry, in prison (2 Corinthians 11:23–27), and then counts everything as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). Abundant life is life with God, rich in him, whatever our circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13).

Then why does my Christian life feel so ordinary? Because abundance here is measured by what you have in Christ, not by how vivid each day feels. A king’s child is no less an heir on a wet Monday than on coronation day. The life Jesus gives is real now: complete forgiveness, a Father who hears, the Spirit within, a people to belong to, a future that cannot be taken. But much of it is still hidden with Christ (Colossians 3:3–4). If your life with God feels thin, the answer is not to look for a new experience but to go back to the pasture: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the company of his people. Sheep that are fed grow strong slowly.
verseByVerse.note: “Go in and out” is a Hebrew expression for living in safety.

parallels.desc: this is the gate of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the shepherd God promised, and what makes him the good shepherd is that he dies for his sheep, where the hired hand runs.

I am the good shepherd. The fourth “I am” saying. Kalos means fine, noble, attractive: the model shepherd, by whom every other is measured. And the claim is enormous. In the Old Testament the shepherd of Israel is God himself: “The LORD is my shepherd” (Psalm 23:1); “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms” (Isaiah 40:11). In Ezekiel 34 God promises both to shepherd his people himself (34:11–16) and to set over them one shepherd, his servant David (34:23). Jesus is both: God himself come to find his sheep, and David’s son set over them.

Lays down his life. Shepherds did risk their lives against wild animals and thieves: David fought a lion and a bear for his father’s flock (1 Samuel 17:34–36). But David won and lived; a dead shepherd is a failure, since the saving depends on his surviving. This one saves the flock by dying: his death is not a risk he runs but the way he saves them.

For the sheep. The little word (hyper) means on behalf of, and where one dies so that others live, in their place. This is substitution. The sheep were under a sentence they could not bear, and he stepped between them and it.

Who does not own the sheep. The hired hand is not wicked. He does the sensible thing: a wolf arrives, the animals are not his, and no wage is worth being killed for. The good shepherd is not a better employee but a different kind of person: he owns the sheep, given him by the Father (v. 29), and losing one would be losing his own. The cross is not imposed on Jesus from outside; it is the act of the owner, who would rather die than lose one of his own.

The wolf snatches them. The wolf stands for anything that attacks God’s people: false teachers, whom Paul calls “fierce wolves” that will not spare the flock (Acts 20:29), persecutors, and the devil himself. The verb “snatches” (harpazei) returns in verse 28: no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand.

All the way into the dark. The God of Psalm 23 did not stay at a safe distance with a rod and a staff. He went down into the valley of the shadow of death himself, all the way into the dark, so that his sheep could walk through it and fear no evil.

What does it mean that he died in my place? That the punishment your sins deserved fell on him instead of you: God’s justice was not set aside at the cross but carried out, on the Shepherd. He was “pierced for our transgressions”, and “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:5–6); he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). This is called penal substitution: penal because it is a penalty, substitution because another bears it. For you it means that God will never punish you for a sin Christ has already paid for. When guilt accuses you, do not answer it with your record. Answer it with his death.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds risked their lives against wild animals and thieves.

parallels.desc: David rescues a lamb from a lion

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hired hand runs because he cares only for himself; Jesus stays with his sheep, and knows each of them personally, as they come to know him.

He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. He does not steal or mislead; he runs, at the one moment when staying is all that matters. His real master is his own comfort, and a man who serves his comfort always runs when the wolf comes.

The shepherd who stayed. The Good Shepherd has never left his flock because staying became too dangerous. He stayed in Gethsemane while the disciples slept, stayed before the high priest while Peter warmed himself at the fire, and stayed on the cross until it was finished (19:30).

I know my own and my own know me. To know (ginōskō) here is the knowledge of love and relationship, as when God says to Israel, “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). And they know him: they trust him, pray to him, listen to him in his word, and find over the years that he is who he said, the way a wife knows her husband and not only facts about him (Philippians 3:10).

The order of the knowing. His knowing comes first and holds the relationship together; it does not rise and fall with how well you know him. Your grasp of him will always be partial in this life. His grasp of you is complete.

In everyday life. The hired hand is a warning for every pastor: “shepherd the flock of God that is among you ... not for shameful gain, but eagerly” (1 Peter 5:2–4). And for every parent, elder and friend whose care evaporates when caring becomes costly. Is there someone in your church whom you have quietly left for someone else to care about? Be there for them this week. None of us stays as faithfully as he did, but his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and on that ground we go back and try again.

What should I do if my pastor behaves like a hired hand? First be fair: tiredness, mistakes or a different style are not the same as not caring. Pray for him, and speak to him directly and kindly (Matthew 18:15); if the problem is real and continues, take it to the other elders, who are there to guard the flock. But if a leader is abusing anyone, spiritually, emotionally, physically or sexually, that is not a matter for patience. It must be reported, to the church’s leaders and, where the law is broken, to the authorities, and the vulnerable must be protected. The Good Shepherd’s care for the sheep never covers for the wolf.

parallels.desc: woe to my worthless shepherd
the Lord knows those who are his

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knows his sheep as intimately as the Father knows him, he dies for them, and he will bring sheep from outside Israel into one flock under himself.

Just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. The largest claim in the discourse: the knowing between shepherd and sheep is compared to the knowing between the Father and the Son. It is no faint likeness, for he uses “just as” again when he prays that his people may be one as the Father and he are one (17:21–23). The closeness between Christ and a Christian is modelled on the closeness between the Father and the Son.

And I lay down my life for the sheep. Said again, now of the sheep he knows, and twice more to come (vv. 17–18): the death is the centre of the picture.

Other sheep. Gentiles who would believe. Verse 16 uses two words that the KJV translated alike. A fold (aulē) is a pen, and this fold is Israel, with its law and temple; a flock (poimnē) is the animals themselves. The other sheep are not brought into this pen; there will be one flock under one shepherd. And before they have heard of him they are already his, given him by the Father. God told Paul in Corinth, “I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:10), before most of them had believed.

I must bring them also. “Must” (dei): it is the Father’s plan, already settled, not a hope.

And they will listen to my voice. Not “might”, but “will”: his voice will reach them through the gospel his servants preach, and they will respond, for “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48).

So there will be one flock, one shepherd. Jews and Gentiles, one people of God, the dividing wall broken down (Ephesians 2:14–16): one not by organisation but by having one Shepherd.

What it does not mean. Mormon teaching claims the other sheep were people in the Americas whom Christ visited after his resurrection. But the context is Israel’s fold and the Gentiles outside it, whom Jesus would gather through the apostles’ preaching (11:52; 17:20) into one flock, not two churches with two scriptures.

In everyday life. If you came into the faith from outside, the wrong background, the wrong family, arriving late and by a side door, Jesus spoke of you in advance; you are not an afterthought or a second tier. Before there was a church in Rome or Corinth or anywhere beyond Judea, the Shepherd stood in the temple and spoke of sheep he already owned on the far side of the world.

If the sheep will certainly come, why should I evangelise? Because he brings them through his voice, heard in the gospel his people speak. “They will listen to my voice” promises the means as well as the result: “how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14). Election, God’s choosing of his people before they chose him, is not a reason to keep quiet but the reason evangelism is not hopeless. Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth because God had many people there (Acts 18:10–11). So speak of Christ with confidence. You need not know whether your neighbour is one of the other sheep; only let him hear the voice.

Then can I tell anyone that Christ died for them? You can tell everyone, with full sincerity, that Christ is offered to them, that his death is enough for any sinner, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (6:37). The apostles did not first work out who the elect were; they called all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30). The moment someone trusts Christ, he may say with Paul that the Son of God “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Definite atonement, the teaching that Christ died to save his sheep in particular, does not make the invitation less real; it makes it certain that it will not be refused by everyone, because the Shepherd has sheep and his death will bring them home.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many godly Christians believe Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all (1 Timothy 2:6; 1 John 2:2). This commentary’s view: here Jesus lays down his life for the sheep, and in v. 26 tells some hearers they are not his sheep; his death was designed to save, and actually saves, those the Father has given him (6:37–39; 17:9), while the offer goes to all and his death is enough for all.
verseByVerse.note: The “other sheep” are Gentiles who would believe.

parallels.desc: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ death is neither an accident nor a defeat: he lays down his life freely, in obedience to his Father, with authority to take it up again.

For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life. The Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world (17:24), so the Son does not earn that love by dying; the Father delights to see his eternal love returned in perfect obedience, as a father’s face lights up when his son freely does the very thing he longed for.

That I may take it up again. He lays down his life in order to take it up again: the cross and the empty tomb are one plan.

Of my own accord. Jesus’ death was not merely something that happened to him. Judas will decide to sell him, the council to condemn him, Pilate to hand him over, and soldiers where to put the nails. Each is a real human decision; none is the deepest reason he died. At the arrest the soldiers fall back at his word (18:6); on the cross he bows his head and gives up his spirit (19:30). They thought they had arrested, judged and finished him, and all the while the Son of God was laying down what he alone had the right to lay down.

I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. Authority (exousia) is the right and the power to act. A man might give his life away; nobody has ever had the right to pick it back up. So the resurrection is not a rescue from disaster but the second half of one continuous act by the same person. He had said the same at the start of his ministry: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, speaking of his body (2:19–21).

This charge I have received from my Father. His death and resurrection are the Father’s command, freely obeyed. The most voluntary act in history was also an act of obedience, and only in Jesus are the two so perfectly joined.

Voluntary is not the same as easy. It was not painless, as if his humanity were a costume and Gethsemane theatre. The man who says “No one takes it from me” will be in agony and ask for the cup to pass. Keep only the first and you have a Jesus who never really suffered; keep only the second and you have a victim who was overwhelmed. He was neither.

In everyday life. If you think of Jesus’ love for you as reluctant, a grim duty he could not escape, remember this verse: he was not trapped; he chose you with open eyes. And when you are called to lay something down for others, you do not do it alone: the Spirit who raised him from the dead now lives in you (Romans 8:11), and by him you can give freely, as he did.

But does not Scripture say the Father raised him? Yes: “God raised him up” (Acts 2:24; Romans 6:4), and the Spirit gives life to mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). There is no contradiction: Father, Son and Spirit act together in all God’s works. The Son took up his life by the authority the Father gave him, as the next clause says, and by the Spirit’s power; one God raised Jesus, each person at work in it.

If no one took his life, are those who killed him not guilty? They are guilty. Peter holds both truths in one sentence: “this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). God’s purpose never makes human sin innocent, and human sin never defeats God’s purpose. That comforts us too: the wrongs done to you are truly wrong, and God will judge them, yet none is outside his hand, and he can work even them for good (Genesis 50:20).

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His words divide his hearers again, and many try to dismiss him as possessed or mad rather than face what he has claimed.

There was again a division. Division is a tear (schisma), the word for cloth pulled apart, and this is the third in four chapters (7:43; 9:16; here).

He has a demon, and is insane. Two charges that do not usually go together: possession, alleged again and again (7:20; 8:48, 52), and madness. People reach for both at once when a claim is too great to face.

Why listen to him? Not an argument but advice to stop listening, still the surest way to protect an opinion: do not answer the claim; persuade people it is not worth hearing.

There is no middle ground. The famous choice between madman, liar and Lord is set out starkly here by people who understood the options. A man who says he will lay down his life and take it up again is not a misunderstood moral teacher. He is possessed, or deranged, or telling the truth. The usual modern reply is that sayings like this are legend, put on his lips later. That is a fair question about whether the Gospels are reliable, and it must be weighed on that ground; but it is not the same as calling him a good teacher who meant something smaller.

What if my faith divides my own family? It is painful, but not a sign that you have failed: Jesus said it would happen (Matthew 10:34–36). Make sure the offence they feel is the offence of Christ and not of your manner: be patient, humble, honest, and kinder than you have to be (1 Peter 3:15–16). Do not argue at every meal; let them see the change. Keep loving them and praying for them, and remember that in this very crowd the same words that drove some to say “why listen” drove others to ask whether a demon can open the eyes of the blind. Families divided over Christ are often families on the way to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others see that neither his words nor his works fit a man with a demon, for only God opens the eyes of the blind.

Not the words of one who is oppressed. A shepherd laying down his life for his sheep does not sound like a man with a demon.

Can a demon open the eyes of the blind? They point back to the man born blind, and their reasoning is sound. Opening blind eyes is God’s work: “the LORD opens the eyes of the blind” (Psalm 146:8). The enemy of souls has three verbs, steal, kill and destroy (v. 10); he has never restored anything, and every genuine healing in the Gospels is evidence that the power behind it is God’s, not the devil’s.

The man who is not in the room. The beggar is not there, and John never mentions him again, yet his healed eyes still bear witness, and for some the argument is settled. What God has done in you may also be speaking to people you will never meet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the winter Feast of Dedication Jesus says that he and the Father are one, and that his sheep are safe for ever in their hands. The leaders surround him in Solomon’s colonnade and demand a plain answer (vv. 22–24). He points to his works and tells them they do not believe because they are not his sheep; his sheep hear him, follow him and will never perish (vv. 25–30). When they take up stones for blasphemy, he answers from Psalm 82 that the Father consecrated him and sent him, and urges them at least to believe the works (vv. 31–38). He escapes and goes back to the Jordan, where John’s witness bears fruit (vv. 39–42).
verseByVerse.theology: “I and the Father are one” is the high point of the shepherd discourse, and his hearers rightly take it as a claim to be God (see the note on vv. 30–31). His defence from Psalm 82 (vv. 34–36) does not shrink the claim; it enlarges it.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends not with hostility in Jerusalem but with a harvest by the river (see the note on vv. 41–42), a reminder that God often gathers his people far from the places that look most important.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the winter feast that celebrated the temple’s rededication, the true temple and the true light walks in its courts.

The Feast of Dedication. The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC by Judas Maccabeus, after Antiochus IV Epiphanes had defiled it with an altar to Zeus and the sacrifice of pigs. It lasted eight days in December, with lamps lit in homes; Josephus calls it Lights. Two months earlier, at the Feast of Booths, Jesus had said among the great lamps of the temple courts, “I am the light of the world” (8:12); now he walks there during the festival of lamps.

A feast about bad shepherds. Hanukkah remembered a rescue from bad shepherds: Antiochus, but also Israel’s own high priests, Jason and Menelaus, who bought their office from the Greek rulers and handed God’s people over to them. That is exactly Ezekiel’s charge (Ezekiel 34:2). The men Jesus has just called thieves and hired hands are keeping a festival that exists partly because their predecessors were just that.

The colonnade of Solomon. A covered portico on the east side of the temple courts, sheltered from the winter wind. The place where Jesus was surrounded and nearly stoned became the place where the early church gathered openly in his name (Acts 3:11; 5:12).

The true temple and the true light. The lamps of Hanukkah were lit for a temple destroyed within forty years of this winter. The one walking through its colonnade was the true temple, God dwelling among men, and the true light, whose light comes not from a jar of oil that might run dry but from the eternal life of the Father, and the darkness has not overcome it (1:5).

If the Maccabees are not in our Bible, how do we know this history? From 1 and 2 Maccabees, Jewish books of the second and first centuries BC, and from the historian Josephus. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include Maccabees; Protestant churches, following the Hebrew canon that Jesus and the apostles used, do not treat them as Scripture (the Westminster Confession 1.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.3). They are valuable history, but they do not carry God’s authority. Nor does Jesus’ presence make the feast a command for Christians: he was a faithful Jew keeping a national festival of thanksgiving, and he used it to show who the true temple and the true light are.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) celebrated the re-dedication of the temple in 164 BC, after Antiochus IV had defiled it. It fell in December. Solomon’s colonnade ran along the east side of the temple courts.

parallels.desc: Solomon’s Portico

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders demand a plain answer and blame Jesus for their doubts, but he has told them already: the problem is not his clarity but their unbelief, and his works show who he is.

Gathered around. Surrounded, hemmed in (ekyklōsan), the verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Psalm 22:16: “For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me.”

How long will you keep us in suspense? There is a complaint inside the question: this is your fault; we would have settled the matter long ago if you had been clearer (see the box below on the wording).

Tell us plainly. They want a political statement they can rally to or report to the Romans. At a feast that remembered Judas Maccabeus, “Christ” meant a liberator with a sword.

I told you. He has said “I am the bread of life”, “I am the light of the world”, “before Abraham was, I am”, “I am the good shepherd”. People who found him vague would not already have reached for stones (8:59).

The works bear witness. Generously, he points them to events: water made wine, a dying boy healed by a word, five thousand fed, a beggar with new eyes walking around Jerusalem. It is the lowest rung on the ladder: believe the evidence if you cannot yet believe the man.

In the flow. The question asked here in public is the one the other Gospels record at his trial before the council (Mark 14:61), and that trial’s charge, blasphemy, comes here in verse 33. In this Gospel Jesus is on trial in the open from chapter 5 onward, so by his arrest the reader has heard the whole case, and knows the verdict was reached against the evidence.

In everyday life. If you are praying for someone who keeps asking for proof, pray not mainly for better arguments but for opened eyes.

Why did Jesus not simply say that he was the Messiah? Because the word in their mouths meant a national liberator who would drive out Rome; a plain yes would have confirmed that error and handed them a political charge, the misunderstanding he had escaped when a crowd tried to make him king by force (6:15). So he told them who he was in fuller terms: the Son who does his Father’s works, the shepherd of Ezekiel 34, the one before Abraham. He said it plainly to a Samaritan woman (4:26) and, at the end, under oath before the high priest (Mark 14:61–62), when the word could no longer be mistaken for a call to rebellion. He is the Christ, but on his own definition.

Uncertain wording. “Keep us in suspense” is literally “how long will you lift up (or take away) our soul?” (heōs pote tēn psychēn hēmōn aireis), an expression found nowhere else in the New Testament. Most translations take it as keeping someone in suspense, and “tell us plainly” supports that. But it can also mean to vex someone, “how long will you annoy us?”, as Greek of later centuries uses it. The ESV’s meaning is the more likely; on either reading they lay the blame for their unbelief on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These men do not believe because they are not Christ’s sheep; his sheep are those who hear his voice, are known by him and follow him.

You are not among my sheep. This sentence is the one most likely to frighten a reader who is already frightened, so look carefully at the order. Jesus does not say they are not his sheep because they do not believe, but that they do not believe because they are not his sheep. Being his sheep comes first; believing follows. Who his sheep are is settled by the Father’s gift (v. 29; 6:37). This is election: God’s free choice, before the world began, of a people to be his own, out of his love and not for anything in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). It does not remove the unbelievers’ guilt (see below), but it explains why some believe and others do not.

Who is being addressed. Read cold, at three in the morning, the verse becomes: what if I am not one? What if the reason faith is hard is that I was never given any? So look at who Jesus is speaking to: men who have watched the signs for a long time, heard the claims to their faces repeatedly, already reached for stones once, and are now trying to extract a sentence to use at a trial. He is not describing a person anxious about whether he belongs, but men entirely untroubled, their minds made up.

The mark of a sheep. It is not a feeling. They hear; they are known; they follow. Nothing suggests they are confident or can tell by looking inward: he knows them as his own (v. 14), and faith shows itself in following.

How do I hear his voice today? Not by waiting for an inner sensation or a sentence forming in the head. The Shepherd’s voice is his word, which the Spirit who gave it opens to his people (16:13–14), and he speaks first: hearing him is not a technique to master but attention paid to someone already talking. Go where he speaks. Read Scripture slowly as his words to you, and sit under its preaching with his people. Listen in order to follow. Ask of each passage what he is calling you to trust and to do, then do the next plain thing. Let him correct you. His voice will sometimes say what you did not want to hear; strangers usually flatter. Answer him. Turn what you have read into prayer, because sheep who know a voice come when it calls.

What if I am afraid I am not one of his sheep? Do not ask whether you feel like a sheep; ask what you have done with the voice. Someone who has heard something in Christ that will not let him go, and keeps turning back to him after every failure, is following, and that is the evidence this passage offers. Then do the plainest thing, which no doctrine of election has ever qualified: come to him. Nobody who came was turned away for not being on a list: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37). The anxiety that whispers that perhaps you are not one is answered as it always has been. Come, and find out.

If they could not believe, how can they be blamed? Because their inability was not a lack of evidence but a refusal: they did not want him. No one is kept from Christ while longing to come; the trouble with the fallen heart is that it does not want to (5:40; 3:19). God is not unjust in leaving people to the choice they love. The wonder is that any are drawn, and that he draws such people as us.

Where Christians differ: does faith make us his sheep, or does being his sheep produce faith? Arminian Christians read the verse the other way round: people are not his sheep because they do not believe, and they could have believed if they would; God’s choice follows his foreknowledge of their faith. Many godly believers read it so, out of real concern for human responsibility and the sincerity of the gospel offer. This commentary’s view: Jesus states the opposite order: you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. Belief is the mark of the sheep, not the way of becoming one: all that the Father gives me will come to me (6:37), and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48). God’s choice is unconditional, resting on his own grace and not on anything foreseen in us (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11–16). And yet these hearers were fully responsible for their unbelief, for they refused to come (5:40). Scripture holds both together, and so must we.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gives his sheep eternal life now, and they will never be lost, because he holds them and his Father holds them, and no one is greater than the Father.

I give them eternal life. Present tense: a gift already handed over, not a prize at the end.

They will never perish. As emphatic as Greek gets (ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna): a double negative strengthened by “for ever”, the construction of “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37). Eternal life that could end would not be eternal.

No one will snatch them. The wolf’s verb of violent seizure (harpazō, v. 12). Jesus does not deny that anything will try, only that anything will succeed.

The Father’s hand. The same promise is made twice, by two persons, about the same sheep, and it rests not on the sheep’s grip but on the Father’s greatness. Two hands hold the sheep, and neither hand is yours.

No wolf strong enough. Within months those hands were opened with nails, and the holding did not stop. There is no wolf strong enough, no night long enough, no wandering far enough to take one sheep out of the hands of God.

The preservation of the saints. The perseverance of the saints, the teaching that true believers continue in faith to the end, could as well be called their preservation, for the holding is in his hand, not theirs (the Westminster Confession 17.1). They persevere because they are preserved by one greater than all. “This is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (6:39).

Against presumption. This is said of sheep who hear and follow (v. 27), not of a decision made once at fifteen and then abandoned; some went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Anyone who reasons that he is safe and so can live as he likes has not heard the Shepherd’s voice here at all.

Against despair. The fear is usually not that something will snatch, but that the sheep will wander off, as sheep do. The Shepherd answers it himself: he leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that is lost until he finds it, and when he has found it, “he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:4–5). The promise that they will never perish covers every way of perishing, including their own wandering.

What about Christians who fall into serious sin? A true believer can fall badly and for a time, as David did with Bathsheba and Peter did by the fire. Sin grieves the Spirit, darkens assurance, harms others and brings the Father’s discipline (Hebrews 12:5–11; Westminster 17.3; 1689 17.3). But a sheep of Christ will not be left there. The Shepherd pursues, convicts and restores, as he restored Peter on the shore (21:15–19). So if you have fallen, do not reason that you are lost; reason that he is coming after you, and turn back now. If you feel no grief at all about a sin you are living in, take that as a serious warning. But if this very question troubles you, the trouble is itself a sign of the Shepherd’s voice at work in you.

What if someone I love has walked away from the faith? Grieve and pray, and do not give up: you cannot see the heart or the end of the story. Some who wander will be brought back, sometimes after many years; others were never truly his (1 John 2:19), and only God knows which. Your part is not to pronounce, but to love, to keep the door open, to speak of Christ when there is an opening, and above all to bring him or her to the Shepherd in prayer. He goes after the lost one, and he is better at finding than we are at waiting.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be lost? Some argue that while no one else can snatch the sheep, a sheep may choose to leave; earnest believers hold this, often out of concern that grace should not be abused. This commentary’s view: “no one” includes the sheep themselves, and Jesus says plainly that his sheep will never perish. The sheep are kept not by their own grip on Christ but by his grip on them (Romans 8:38–39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). This is the perseverance of the saints. Those who fall away for good show that they were never his sheep (1 John 2:19). True sheep may stray and stumble, but the Shepherd brings them back.

Textual note. The Greek of verse 29 is genuinely uncertain. The manuscripts divide between “My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all”, and “What my Father has given me is greater than all”. Translations differ and both readings are defensible. Nothing in the assurance depends on which is right; on either reading the sheep are held by someone nothing can overpower.

parallels.desc: there is none that can deliver out of my hand

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus claims to share the Father’s very being, distinct from him yet one with him, and his hearers understand him well enough to reach for stones.

I and the Father are one. “One” (hen) is neuter, one thing, one in being, not the masculine (heis), which would mean one person. “I” and “the Father” are two, and the verb is plural: the verb keeps them distinct, and the “one” keeps them undivided. Here, for the Father and the Son, is the heart of the doctrine of the Trinity: distinct persons, one God.

Two errors settled at once. The word “one” rules out the view that the Father and the Son are merely two names or modes of one individual, a view the early church met in Sabellius and which is taught today by Oneness Pentecostalism. The Word was with God (1:1), and you cannot be with yourself. It equally rules out the opposite error, pressed by Jehovah’s Witnesses, that they are one only in that their wills agree. Men do not pick up stones over a shared policy, and they tell us what they heard: “you, being a man, make yourself God.”

Stones again. The first attempt (8:59) followed “before Abraham was, I am”; this one follows “I and the Father are one.” What the church later put into the creeds was no invention of the fourth century. It was already there in a sentence spoken in a temple colonnade in winter, by a man about to be stoned for saying it.

In everyday life. When you pray to Jesus, you are not praying to a lesser being who will pass the message on. And when you feel unsure of the Father’s love, look at the Son: the Father is not different from him. They are one.

How can three persons be one God without contradiction? Because one and three are not said in the same sense. God is one in being: there is one divine nature, one will, one power, one glory. He is three in person: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly distinct, relating to one another in love (17:24). A contradiction would be one God who is three Gods, or one person who is three persons, and the Trinity is neither. Every illustration fails somewhere, as we should expect if God is greater than his creation; we believe it not because we can picture it but because the Son himself stood in the temple and said both “I and the Father” and “are one”.

Where Christians differ: is this only unity of will? Some say this means only unity of will and purpose, as believers are to be one (17:22). This commentary’s view: it includes unity of purpose, but cannot stop there. The hearers took it as a claim to be God, and Jesus did not correct them; instead he went on to say the Father is in him and he in the Father (v. 38). Believers share a unity of love; the Son shares the Father’s very being (1:1; 5:18).
verseByVerse.note: “One” is neuter in Greek: one in nature and purpose, not one person.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressed to name their charge, his enemies state exactly what he has claimed: to be God.

For which of them are you going to stone me? A calm question with stones raised above him. “Good” is kala again, the word of the good shepherd: fine, beautiful works. Asked to name the beautiful thing they object to, they state their real charge, accurately: not a good work, but blasphemy, for which stoning was the law’s penalty (Leviticus 24:16).

You, being a man, make yourself God. Had they misheard a lesser claim, Jesus could have corrected them in one sentence and saved his life. Instead he goes on to say the Father is in him and he in the Father (v. 38): he let their understanding stand.

The direction is reversed. Their mistake was to think that a man was making himself God. The truth is the opposite: he was God, making himself man (1:14; Philippians 2:6–7). They are right about the man too. His humanity was standing in front of them, tired and dusty and not yet fifty (8:57). What they could not do was hold the two together: a man, and God.

Did Jesus ever actually claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies are the clearest witnesses. Some say the church invented the idea later; but the earliest Gospel, Mark, already has him forgiving sins and condemned for blasphemy (Mark 2:5–7; 14:61–64), and Paul’s letters, earlier still, call him Lord and pray to him (1 Corinthians 16:22; Philippians 2:6–11). Here men tried to kill him for that claim, and he did not withdraw it. He took the divine name “I am” (8:58), received worship (20:28), and said that to see him is to see the Father (14:9). A man who said these things and was not God would not be a good teacher. The only reason to worship him is that he is who he said.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Scripture that cannot be broken Jesus shows that their charge fails: if God’s word called Israel’s judges “gods”, it is no blasphemy for the one the Father sent to call himself the Son of God.

Is it not written in your Law? “Law” here means the whole Old Testament. The quotation, from Psalm 82:6, calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they exercised God’s authority and justice among his people (compare Exodus 21:6; 22:8–9, where the KJV, among others, takes elohim to mean the judges).

Read the whole psalm. God puts the gods on trial for judging unjustly and failing the weak and the fatherless (82:2–4), then sentences them: “nevertheless, like men you shall die” (82:7). “Gods” is a title of office for men entrusted with God’s authority to judge, and the psalm strips it off them.

To whom the word of God came. The argument runs from lesser to greater: if human judges can be called gods, how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent to call himself the Son of God? His hearers did not take it as a retreat; they try again to arrest him (v. 39). The claim of verse 30 stands.

Scripture cannot be broken. He rests his argument on one word in a short psalm, and says it cannot be set aside. Here is a foundation of the doctrine of the inerrancy and authority of Scripture: because it is God’s own word, Scripture is true in all it affirms and binds all who hear it. Jesus himself held this, and his followers can hold no lower view than their Lord’s.

In him, God has arisen. The eternal Word stood under the written word and rested his defence on one phrase of an old psalm. And he alone does what the judges of Psalm 82 failed to do: he defends the weak and the fatherless, and he will judge the earth in righteousness. “Arise, O God,” the psalm ends, “for you shall inherit all the nations” (82:8). In him, God has arisen.

What it does not mean. “You are gods” is quoted by Mormonism to teach that faithful men and women may themselves become gods, and by Word of Faith teachers to tell congregations they are little gods with creative power in their mouths. But the psalm is a charge against those judges, not a promise; to quote it as a promise of divinity is to mistake the accusation for a reward. Nor is Jesus a god only in the judges’ sense. Having shown that his claim cannot be blasphemy in itself, he goes further than they ever could: “the Father is in me and I am in the Father” (v. 38). No creature is ever promoted to be God.

What are we promised instead? Something better: not deity by nature, but adoption by grace. We become children of God (1:12), sharers in his life and holiness, and one day “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Sons, not gods. The offer of godhood was first made in a garden by someone else (Genesis 3:5), and it has never once been kept.

If Scripture cannot be broken, what about the parts that seem to contradict each other? Take them seriously and humbly. Most dissolve with careful reading: different writers choosing different details, rounding numbers, arranging events by theme rather than strict order, or using words in different senses, as Paul and James do with “justify”. Some remain hard, and it is honest to say so. But a difficulty we cannot yet solve is not an error we have proved. Consult a good study Bible or commentary, ask your pastor, and hold on to the Lord’s own conviction while you wait for light.

Where Christians differ: who are the gods of Psalm 82? Some scholars read them as heavenly beings, the spiritual powers set over the nations, judged by God for their injustice. Others read them as Israel’s human judges. This commentary’s view: the second is more likely. Jesus’ argument is that the word of God came to them (v. 35), and the psalm says they will die like men (Psalm 82:7), which fits human rulers far better. They were called gods because they held God’s authority, and judged because they abused it.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm calls Israel’s judges “gods” because they represented God’s authority. “Your Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole.

parallels.desc: “I said, ‘You are gods’”

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father set Jesus apart and sent him into the world, so his claim to be the Son of God is not blasphemy but the truth.

Consecrated. To consecrate (hagiazō) is to set apart as holy, to dedicate. And they are keeping the Feast of Dedication (Greek ta enkainia, the renewing; Hebrew Hanukkah, dedication), the festival of an altar defiled, rebuilt and set apart again for God. Jesus says: the Father has consecrated me.

The true temple. He has already called himself the true temple (2:19–21). Now, at the feast of the temple’s reconsecration, he tells them that what they commemorate has been fulfilled in a person.

Sent into the world. Sending implies somewhere to be sent from: consecrated before he was sent, he was with the Father before coming. The two words, “consecrated” and “sent”, contain the incarnation, God the Son coming into the world as a man, stated in the middle of a legal defence.

You are blaspheming, because I said, I am the Son of God? Blasphemy is a man claiming for himself a place God has not given him. But if the Father himself set the Son apart and sent him, the Son is only reporting what the Father has done, and the accusation collapses: not because the claim is smaller than they thought, but because the Father himself stands behind it.

Christians are called sanctified too, so is it the same thing? Related, but different: Jesus was consecrated as the holy Son, with no sin to be cleansed from; we are sinners made holy because of him. In his prayer he says, “for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (17:19). He set himself apart for the cross so that we could be set apart for God. Your holiness is borrowed from his, and the Spirit is working it out in you day by day.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus invites them to test him by his works, and to let the works bring them to know that the Father is in him and he is in the Father.

Then do not believe me. He hands them a test that could destroy him: without the works, they may dismiss him. Jesus invites testing; he does not ask for blind faith.

Believe the works. He does not stand on his dignity or require the front door of full faith; he tries to get them in by any opening still ajar. The works are evidence (14:11).

The Father is in me. The goal is not mere agreement but knowledge, of the very thing they are about to try to arrest him for, and no judge of Psalm 82 could have said it. The Father and the Son dwell in each other; later theologians call it perichōrēsis, the mutual indwelling of the persons. It is the deepest statement of their oneness (14:10–11; 17:21).

Counting the works. When Christ no longer seems real and you feel little love for him, this verse allows a smaller step: look not at what you feel but at the record of what he has done. Faith that has lost its warmth can still count the works, and this passage says that is a legitimate place to stand while the rest comes back.

Is it all right to believe because of evidence, rather than simply by faith? Yes. Biblical faith is not believing without reasons but trusting God on the basis of what he has shown. Jesus himself points to his works, John writes so that by reading the signs we may believe (20:31), and the resurrection was proved by many proofs (Acts 1:3). Evidence alone cannot change a heart; only the Spirit can do that, as these hearers show. But the Spirit uses evidence. So do not be ashamed of questions, or despise friends who need reasons. Point them to the works, and pray that the Spirit will open their eyes to the one who did them.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can seize Jesus before his hour, and he withdraws for a time to the place where his ministry began.

He escaped from their hands. Another failed attempt (7:30, 44; 8:20, 59; 10:31), and John’s only explanation is that his hour had not yet come. No one can snatch the sheep out of his hand (v. 28), and no one can seize him out of the Father’s plan. The withdrawal is not a retreat from danger: no mob in Jerusalem could hurry him to the cross a day early, and no fear could keep him from it a day late.

Where John had been baptizing. This is Bethany beyond the Jordan (1:28), where this Gospel started: the Baptist standing in the water, pointing at Jesus and saying, “Behold, the Lamb of God.” The public ministry closes where it opened, where the first two disciples turned and followed him. He will cross the river again to go to the tomb of Lazarus at Bethany (11:7), and from there to his own tomb.

And there he remained. After a winter of stones and interrogations he stays by the river. Before the raising of Lazarus and the last week there was a quiet stretch, and he took it.

Is it cowardice for a Christian to step back from conflict or to rest? Not when done for the right reasons. Jesus withdrew more than once, not from fear but because his hour had not come, and he took his disciples apart to rest (Mark 6:31). Courage is not walking into every fight. Withdrawing is wrong when it means abandoning a duty God has given you, as the hired hand did. It is right when it means waiting for God’s time, guarding your soul, or refusing to let other people’s hostility set your agenda. Rest is not desertion. It is often preparation.
verseByVerse.note: “Across the Jordan” is Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John had baptized.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away from Jerusalem, people who had heard John the Baptist see that everything he said about Jesus was true, and many believe.

John did no sign. No one else in the New Testament is described so, and it is said of the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11): no miracle, not one healing, nothing to draw a crowd. John’s greatness was in his witness.

Everything that John said about this man was true. Probably after his death (the other Gospels report it before the feeding of the five thousand), ordinary people say it where he had worked: when the one he pointed to came back to that river, they knew him because of what a dead man had told them. He had called him the Lamb of God (1:29), the one who would baptise with the Spirit (1:33), the Son of God (1:34), and every word had proved true. It is a beautiful epitaph, and the best thing that can be said of any servant of Christ: what he said about Jesus was true.

Many believed in him there. Jerusalem, with its temple, scholars and festivals, produced stones; the riverbank, prepared by John’s witness, produced believers. It closes a circle. The prologue said John came as a witness, “that all might believe through him” (1:7), and here, at the place where he worked, that purpose is fulfilled. Christ let his greatest prophet die in a prison cell without seeing this fruit, and then walked back to the very riverbank where that prophet had preached and gathered the harvest himself.

Should I expect miracles to confirm my witness? No, and this verse is a relief: the greatest of the prophets did no sign, and his witness bore fruit years later. The miracles of Christ and the apostles had a special purpose: to confirm the new revelation as it was given (Hebrews 2:3–4). This commentary holds, charitably, that the sign gifts of that foundational age have ceased, while God still answers prayer and can heal as he wills. Many brothers and sisters see this differently, and we honour them. But on any view, the ordinary means God uses to bring people to faith is the faithful word of witness, spoken plainly and backed by a life. You do not need a sign. You need to tell the truth about Jesus.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber.<sup>2</sup>But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.<sup>3</sup>To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.<sup>4</sup>When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.<sup>5</sup>A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers.”<sup>6</sup>This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.<sup>7</sup>So Jesus again said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.<sup>8</sup>All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.<sup>9</sup>I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture.<sup>10</sup>The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.<sup>11</sup>I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.<sup>12</sup>He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.<sup>13</sup>He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep.<sup>14</sup>I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,<sup>15</sup>just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.<sup>16</sup>And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.<sup>17</sup>For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again.<sup>18</sup>No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father.”<sup>19</sup>There was again a division among the Jews because of these words.<sup>20</sup>Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?”<sup>21</sup>Others said, “These are not the words of one who is oppressed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”<sup>22</sup>At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter,<sup>23</sup>and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.<sup>24</sup>So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me,<sup>26</sup>but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep.<sup>27</sup>My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.<sup>28</sup>I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.<sup>29</sup>My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand.<sup>30</sup>I and the Father are one.”<sup>31</sup>The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.<sup>32</sup>Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?”<sup>33</sup>The Jews answered him, “It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ’I said, you are gods’?<sup>35</sup>If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—<sup>36</sup>do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ’You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ’I am the Son of God’?<sup>37</sup>If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me;<sup>38</sup>but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”<sup>39</sup>Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands.<sup>40</sup>He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.<sup>41</sup>And many came to him. And they said, “John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true.”<sup>42</sup>And many believed in him there.
10.overview:
Where we are. The Pharisees have just thrown the man born blind out of the synagogue, and Jesus has found him (9:34–35). Speaking to the same men, he now tells them who the true shepherd is; two months later, at the winter Feast of Dedication, the argument resumes, and the public ministry ends where it began, at the Jordan.

The message. Jesus is the shepherd God promised: God himself come to seek his sheep, and David’s son set over them. Unlike leaders who use the flock, he knows his sheep by name, lays down his life for them of his own accord, and holds them where no one can snatch them, because he and the Father are one.

Why it was said. The first hearers had just watched Israel’s shepherds cast out a sheep for confessing Jesus, and John’s readers knew that cost too (see the introduction). They needed to know that being thrown out by men cannot take anyone out of his hand.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a picture from village life: the shepherd comes in by the door and calls his own by name, while thieves climb in another way (vv. 1–6). He is the door, the only way in, through whom the sheep find safety and pasture (vv. 7–10). He is the good shepherd who, unlike the hired hand, lays down his life for the sheep and will gather other sheep into one flock (vv. 11–18). His hearers divide (vv. 19–21). At Dedication the leaders demand a plain answer (vv. 22–25); he tells them they do not believe because they are not his sheep, promises his sheep a life no one can take, and says that he and the Father are one (vv. 26–30). When they take up stones for blasphemy, he answers from Psalm 82 and points to his works (vv. 31–39), then withdraws beyond the Jordan, where many believe (vv. 40–42).

Where it leads. Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 promised that the LORD would shepherd his people himself; here he stands in the temple. No shepherd before him saved the flock by dying, yet that is this shepherd’s whole purpose (v. 11). Within months he laid down his life and took it up again, as he said (vv. 17–18). He is now “the great shepherd of the sheep”, brought again from the dead (Hebrews 13:20), and he will shepherd his people for ever (Revelation 7:17).

For us. You do not belong to Christ because you held on tightly enough; you belong to him because he laid down his life for you, and he holds you in hands no one can open. So listen for his voice in his word, follow him, and let no other voice, and no fear, tell you that you are not safe with him.

keyVerse.quote: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the chapter. Every other shepherd risked his life to save the flock and needed to survive to do it; this one saves his flock by dying for it, freely and in their place (vv. 17–18). Everything else in the chapter, the voice that calls by name, the one flock, the hands no one can open, rests on this death.

10.reflection:
Jesus sets himself against thieves, robbers and the hired hand (vv. 1–13). What marks of a true shepherd does he give, and how do they help you to recognise faithful leaders, and to care for the people God has put in your own life?

“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (v. 11). How does it change the way you see the cross to know that no one took his life from him, but that he laid it down of his own accord (v. 18)?

His sheep hear his voice, are known by him and follow him (v. 27). Where do you listen for his voice, and which other voices most often compete with it?

Jesus says that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand or the Father’s (vv. 28–29). How does this promise answer the fear of falling away, and why does it give no room for carelessness?

11.title: The Resurrection and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The raising of Lazarus shows that Jesus is the resurrection and the life, and that the one who loves us is stronger than death. Because he loves the family, Jesus waits two days, then walks back into danger to wake his friend (vv. 1–16). Martha, holding the true hope of the last day, learns that the resurrection is a person, and is asked whether she believes it (vv. 17–27). Mary falls at his feet, and Jesus weeps, indignant at death (vv. 28–37). At the open tomb he thanks his Father and calls Lazarus by name, and the dead man comes out (vv. 38–44). Every believer’s grave now waits for that voice.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle looks ahead to Jesus’ own resurrection and, through it, to the raising of all who are in him. “I am the resurrection and the life” (v. 25) is a claim not only about what Jesus can do but about who he is: the source of the life of the age to come, already present. On what it means that those who believe in him will never die, see the note on vv. 25–26.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus weeps (v. 35) while knowing he is about to raise Lazarus (see the note on vv. 35–36). God in the flesh does not watch human sorrow from a distance; he enters it and weeps in it before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest of Jesus’ signs begins with an illness in a home he loved, and from the first verses John lets the shadow of Jesus’ own burial fall across it. This is the seventh sign in John, as the signs are usually counted, and the turning point that leads to the cross (v. 53).

Lazarus of Bethany. Lazarus is a short form of Eleazar, God helps, and the chapter will show what that name means when God’s help arrives in person and calls the sick man by name. This is very probably the household Jesus stayed in when he came to Jerusalem (Luke 10:38; Mark 11:11). So the illness is not a case: it is somebody’s brother, in a house Jesus loved.

It was Mary who anointed the Lord. John identifies Mary by an act she has not yet performed in his story; the anointing comes in the next chapter (12:1–8). So the shadow of Jesus’ burial falls across his friend’s illness from the start.

From one Bethany to the other. Jesus is now in Bethany across the Jordan, where the Baptist worked (10:40; 1:28); the message concerns Bethany near Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives (v. 18). The chapter is the journey from the place where his ministry began to a tomb two miles from the city that will kill him.

A house and three friends. The eternal Son chose a house in a village and three friends to love, and let himself be fed, housed and grieved over. When illness came to that house it came to him.

Is this Mary the sinful woman of Luke 7, or Mary Magdalene? No. Luke 7:36–50 describes an earlier and different anointing, in Galilee, by an unnamed woman known as a sinner, in a Pharisee’s house. Mary of Bethany anointed Jesus at Bethany days before his death (12:1–8). Mary Magdalene, from Magdala in Galilee, is a third woman, from whom Jesus had cast out seven demons (Luke 8:2). Later tradition merged the three, but the Gospels keep them distinct, and so should we: each is a separate testimony to his grace.

Did Jesus really need friends? Not as God, who is complete in himself. But he was truly man, and a true man is made for friendship. A home, people he loved by name, a table where he could rest: that is no weakness, but the Son of God come near enough to be your friend (15:15). It also honours ordinary Christian hospitality: a house where Christ is loved and his people are welcome is doing something he himself valued.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem. John mentions Mary’s anointing ahead of time; it comes in chapter 12.

parallels.desc: Martha and Mary

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." But when Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sisters bring their brother’s illness to Jesus, resting everything on his love, and he declares that it will end not in death but in the glory of God and of his Son.

He whom you love is ill. A short message, and a model of prayer. There is no request in it: they state the need and the relationship, and stop, trusting not their wording but his love, and his knowing what to do with it. “Love” here is phileō, the love of friendship; two verses later John uses agapaō, with no clear difference of weight.

This illness does not lead to death. A bereaved reader will stop here, because Lazarus dies. But the Greek, pros thanaton, means toward death. Jesus is not predicting whether the man’s heart will stop, but saying where the illness is aimed: its end is not death but resurrection.

For the glory of God. As with the man born blind (9:3), the purpose is God’s glory, and the Father is honoured when the Son is honoured (5:23). The Son will be glorified by the miracle, and also by the death it brings him to (v. 53; 12:23): the sign that shows his glory sends him to the cross.

If I pray for healing and the person dies, did God fail? No, and this verse must not be made to promise what it does not; quoted over sickbeds, it has later looked like a broken promise. What it says is stranger and better: for those who belong to him, an illness can pass straight through death and still not have death as its destination. God may heal, and we should ask him to, but his answer is never limited to healing or failure. For a believer, death is not God’s defeat but the doorway to his presence and the road to resurrection. Pray boldly, and leave the shape of the answer to his love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus waits two days because he loves the family, not in spite of it: he means to give them far more than a healing.

Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. John says it before he tells of the delay, so that we cannot misread the delay as indifference.

So he stayed two days longer. The little word “so” is the hinge of the chapter, and should be felt as a shock. The delay is the consequence of the love, not a suspension of it. He meant to give them a resurrection, and a deeper knowledge of who he is. Beyond the Jordan he was carrying the whole of Bethany in his heart, and walking toward it on his own schedule.

The arithmetic. Lazarus has been four days in the tomb when Jesus arrives (v. 17). The journey probably took a day, he waited two, and the messenger needed perhaps a day to reach him. Lazarus may well have died soon after the messenger set out. The two days did not cause the death, but they ensured no one could doubt it.

The comfort for “if only”. One form of bereavement spends years on the timing: if the appointment had been a week earlier, if the prayer had started sooner. This passage lets a family say that sentence twice (vv. 21, 32), and quietly shows that the sums never worked: no hurrying would have brought him in time. He allowed a death he could have prevented, in a family he loved, to give what a healing could not. John does not pretend the four days were anything but painful.

Why does God delay answering my prayers? Scripture gives no single reason for every case, but this chapter gives the deepest one: his delays are governed by love, not neglect. Sometimes he means to give more than we asked; sometimes the waiting teaches us to trust him rather than our timetable. Often we will not know why until later, some things not until we see his face. What you can know now is the sentence John put first: Jesus loved them. Read every delay with that sentence in front of it, and keep praying.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns back toward Judea, where men have just tried to stone him, taking his disciples with him and walking with open eyes toward the cross.

Let us go to Judea again. Not “to Lazarus”, the errand, but “Judea”, where men had tried to stone him. And he neither goes alone nor sends them: they go together. The road to Bethany was the road to Calvary, and he took it having counted the cost.

Seeking to stone you. The disciples are not cowards. The authorities had tried twice in a few months (8:59; 10:31, 39), the last time at the Feast of Dedication not long before.

And are you going there again? “Again” comes from both sides. For him it is a return to unfinished business; for them, a second walk into a place that nearly killed him. That is often how God’s call sounds: the one who gives it sees the whole, and those who receive it see only what happened last time. Costly obedience rarely looks heroic. More often it looks like this walk back to Judea: an awkward hospital visit, a costly conversation, a return to where you were once hurt.

Should I take risks for Christ, or be prudent? Both, in their place. Prudence is not sin: Jesus withdrew when his hour had not come (10:40; 11:54), and told his disciples to flee from town to town under persecution (Matthew 10:23). But prudence becomes sin when it excuses disobedience. The question is not “Is this safe?” but “Is this where he is going?” If Christ calls you to a costly duty, to love someone difficult, speak the truth or serve in a hard place, danger is no reason to refuse. If he has not called you, there is no virtue in seeking danger for its own sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ time is fixed by his Father, not by the men holding stones, and whoever walks with him, the light, walks safely until the work is done.

Are there not twelve hours in the day? Daylight was counted as twelve hours from sunrise to sunset in every season, so the hours were longer in summer and shorter in winter. When the light went, work stopped, and a man on a stony Judean track after dark would fall. Jesus’ day is the appointed time of his ministry (9:4), and it cannot be cut short until it is finished. The danger is real, but the clock is not kept by the men holding the stones.

He does not stumble. The one who walks in God’s will walks safely: the disciples’ safety lies not in the route but in whom they follow. Twelve hours is a fixed allowance; enemies cannot shorten it, and caution cannot lengthen it. The only truly dangerous place is somewhere he is not going.

The light is not in him. The picture moves from the sun outside to a light within. In this Gospel that light is Jesus himself (1:4–5; 8:12), and whoever does not have him stumbles (12:35).

Does this mean nothing bad can happen to me if I obey God? No. It is not a promise of long life or freedom from harm: Jesus’ own twelve hours had only weeks to run, and by early tradition many of the men listening would die violently for him. It promises that the ending is not in the hands of whoever throws the stones. Your days are written in God’s book (Psalm 139:16), and nothing can cut them short before he says. That frees you from two fears: that your enemies control your life, and that you must control it yourself by endless caution.
verseByVerse.note: The daylight hours were counted as twelve, from sunrise to sunset.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls death sleep, because for those who belong to him it is temporary and he is going to wake his friend; the disciples hear only good news about an illness.

Our friend Lazarus. Not “my friend”: he includes the disciples in the friendship before he tells them the man is dead.

Fallen asleep. Sleep was a common picture of the death of believers (Matthew 9:24; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), and the related noun koimētērion, a sleeping place, gives us our word cemetery. Sleep is not a gentler word for extinction but a claim about what death now is for those who belong to him: temporary, and ending the ordinary way, when somebody says your name, as is about to happen at the mouth of a cave.

I go to awaken him. The everyday language of rousing someone in the morning: to him a resurrection is going in to wake somebody up.

He will recover. They take it literally, and with relief: sleep is a good sign in illness, so there is no need to walk into Judea. The literal meaning is the one that suits them, as it often suits us.
