What it does not mean. Not that the soul sleeps unconscious between death and resurrection, as some teach. Sleep describes the body’s rest and the certainty of waking; the believer’s spirit goes at once to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

What actually happens when a Christian dies? The body returns to dust, but the person, the soul, is immediately with Christ, made perfect in holiness, in conscious joy, awaiting the redemption of the body (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). There is no purgatory and no unconscious waiting. When Christ returns, the body will be raised, transformed and reunited with the soul, never to die again (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 51–53). So a believer has truly fallen asleep, and is truly with the Lord: the first of the body, the second of the soul.
verseByVerse.note: Sleep was a common picture of death for believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples misunderstand, Jesus takes away their comfortable mistake and tells them plainly that Lazarus has died.

They thought he meant sleep. Another of John’s misunderstandings, recorded decades later with no attempt to make the twelve look better: a small mark of an honest witness, for an inventor of a founding story would have little reason to write his leaders like that.

Lazarus has died. Jesus now speaks “plainly” (parrēsia: openly, without veiling). Rather than let them travel with a comfortable misunderstanding, he takes the comfort away and gives them the fact. The Lord who spoke so gently of sleep was not afraid of the word “death”. He called it by its name and walked toward it, because he had come to deal with it.

How should I speak about death, especially to children? Plainly first, then with hope. Tender words must not become an anaesthetic that leaves people confused; children especially can be frightened by vague phrases such as “gone away”, “lost” or “gone to sleep”, left unexplained. Say that the person has died, that their body has stopped working and will not work again in this life. Then give the hope clearly: if they trusted Jesus, they are with him now, and he will raise their body one day. Jesus kept that order, first the fact, then the promise. The picture of sleep can be explained afterwards, when it will mean something.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is glad he was absent, because what he is about to do will grow his disciples’ faith; and Thomas, expecting to die, chooses to go with him.

Glad that I was not there. Not glad that Lazarus died, but that he was absent: his presence would have brought a healing, and a healing a smaller faith than is now possible. The disciples already believed (2:11), but faith grows, and “so that you may believe” is the aim of the whole Gospel in miniature (20:31). Within days they will see him arrested and killed, and they will need to have seen him empty a grave before they see him laid in one.

Let us go to him. To him, though dead: to Jesus the dead are not beyond reach.

Thomas, called the Twin. Thomas means twin in Aramaic, and Didymus is the Greek equivalent. But something is twinned in the man himself all through this Gospel: he says the brave thing and the doubting thing, and both come from the same place. He will not pretend to a confidence he does not have.

That we may die with him. He is remembered for one sentence of doubt after the resurrection (20:24–25), and has been “doubting Thomas” ever since. But this is the first time he speaks in the Gospel. He has concluded, reasonably, that going to Judea means execution, and he proposes they go. That is not doubt but loyalty without hope, rarer and harder than loyalty with it: he would rather die with Jesus than live without him. And the one Thomas expected to die with did die, not with them but for them, and then came back through a locked door to show his hands to the man who had followed him in despair.

Is it all right to follow Christ while I am full of doubts and fears? Yes. Jesus did not wait for Thomas to become cheerful, or his faith perfect. He works with what is offered and refines it on the way, as he did with Thomas a few weeks later (20:27–28). What matters is not how confident you feel but where you are walking. Bring your doubts, tell him honestly, and keep going in his direction. Many of the best saints have followed in a flat voice for long stretches.
verseByVerse.note: Thomas’s name means “twin” in Aramaic; Didymus is the Greek equivalent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lazarus has been dead and buried four days, beyond any hope of revival, in a village so near Jerusalem that what happens next cannot be hidden.

Four days. Burial was usually on the day of death: the body was washed, wrapped with spices and laid in a rock tomb within hours, as the climate required (see burial customs). Four days in the tomb means four days dead, with decay well under way. A popular Jewish belief, preserved in later rabbinic writings, held that the soul lingered near the body for three days hoping to return, and left on the fourth when the face became unrecognisable. That is probably why John gives the number twice, here and in Martha’s objection (v. 39): Lazarus was beyond any hope of revival.

About two miles off. Literally about fifteen stadia, well under an hour’s walk: near enough for mourners to come from the city, and for the news to reach the temple courts by evening. Everything in this chapter happens in the open, on a road, before a crowd, at the mouth of a cave; the sign was never only for the family. It will be neither deniable nor quiet, and for exactly those reasons it is the one that gets him killed.

In everyday life. Is there something you have written off as four days dead: a relationship, a habit you cannot break, a person you have stopped praying for? Bring it back to him. Nothing is beyond his reach.

Could Lazarus simply have been in a coma? Not after four days in a sealed tomb, bound in linen, in that climate, without water. Everyone present had buried their own dead; Martha expected the smell of decay (v. 39). The authorities, who had every reason to explain the event away, are not recorded as trying; they plotted to kill Lazarus too (12:10–11). John gives the details so that we know what kind of event this was: not a recovery, but a dead man called back to life.
verseByVerse.note: After four days there could be no doubt that he was dead. The ESV notes that the distance is literally fifteen stadia.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grieving sisters are surrounded by mourners from Jerusalem when Jesus comes, and each goes to meet him in her own way.

To console them. Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends and neighbours sitting with the family, weeping and bringing food. These visitors had come from Jerusalem and were still there on the fourth day, which suggests the family was well known. Every word the sisters say to Jesus, and every word he says back, is spoken before an audience.

What the mourners were doing. Consolation was a duty, not a social call: mourners sat with the bereaved, said little, and stayed. Later Jewish custom was not to speak until the grieving person spoke first, a discipline the friends of Job kept for seven days (Job 2:13); it was when they began explaining that everything went wrong. The mourners at Bethany came, stayed four days, and when Mary got up they followed her so that she would not cry alone.

Martha went and met him. Martha, the active one, goes out; Mary, perhaps more crushed, stays seated, as mourners did. One needed to move and one could not, and both receive everything (see vv. 31–32).

Walking in a body toward a grave. Many came from Jerusalem to console, but none could do anything about the cave. He is the God of all comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3) walking in a body toward a grave, who does not sit beside death and sympathise with it, but has come to overturn it.

What should I say to someone who is grieving? Often very little, at first; your presence matters more than your words. Say you are sorry, use the name of the one who has died, and do not hurry to explain the loss or rush to the hope. Avoid clichés that make grief smaller. Offer practical help: meals, errands, company on hard evenings. Keep coming after the funeral, when most people stop; Christ came to grieving Bethany in person, so go in his name to someone everyone else has stopped visiting. When the time is right, especially if the one who died was a believer, the hope of the resurrection is the greatest comfort there is; but give it as a gift, not as a reason to stop crying.
verseByVerse.note: Mourning for a close relative lasted seven days, with friends coming to console the family.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha tells Jesus honestly that he came too late, yet still trusts that God will give him whatever he asks. Her faith is real, but not yet complete.

If you had been here. Grief, perhaps with a note of complaint. Mary will say the same sentence word for word (v. 32), which probably tells you what had been said in that house for four days, in the kitchen, in the night and to every visitor, until it had worn a groove. Jesus does not point out that he could not have arrived in time. He lets both sisters say it, corrects neither, and answers them with himself.

Even now. She does not quite dare to ask for resurrection; at the tomb she objects to the stone being moved (v. 39). What she has is less specific and more lasting: a conviction that his access to God is not affected by its being too late. That is a good place to pray from, open to anyone who has run out of requests. But she still thinks of Jesus as one who asks God, not yet as the one who is himself the life.

Is it wrong to say to God, “if you had been here”? No. It is honest, and God would rather have your honest grief than polite silence. The psalms are full of it: “How long, O LORD?” “Why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 13:1; 22:1). Martha said it to Jesus’ face, and he did not rebuke her. What matters is where you say it: she brought her complaint to him, not away from him, and then added “but even now”. Lament spoken to God is a form of faith. The danger is not in asking why, but in turning your back and refusing to wait for his answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha rightly holds the hope of resurrection on the last day, but her brother is in a cave now, and that is the gap Jesus is about to close.

Your brother will rise again. Deliberately open words: now, or at the end. It was the standard consolation at a Jewish funeral, and Martha takes it so. He lets her, and waits to see what she does with it.

On the last day. Martha is often said to have missed the point, and she has not. The Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age, from texts like Daniel 12:2, “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake”, and Isaiah 26:19. Martha holds the orthodox hope, and Jesus never suggests she is wrong.

The gap the doctrine does not cross. Her belief is true, but its resurrection is at the end of the world, and her brother is in a cave a short walk away. Jesus closes the gap not by moving the last day nearer, but by telling her that what she is waiting for is a person, standing in front of her.

What exactly is the resurrection on the last day? When Christ returns, all the dead will be raised bodily: “those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (5:28–29). Believers will be raised with bodies that are real, recognisable and their own, yet transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, fitted for the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Not the soul escaping the body, but the whole person made new. The body you bury is sown like a seed, and what rises will be more fully you than you have ever been.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees and most Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells Martha that the resurrection she awaits on the last day is present in him now: believers who die will live, and believers who live will never die the true death. Then he asks whether she believes it.

I am the resurrection and the life. The fifth “I am” saying, and the one most often read at funerals. Martha has placed resurrection at the end of history; Jesus places the whole doctrine in himself. What she awaits is not an event he will attend but who he is: the power that will raise the dead at the end is present in him now. He has said it before, that the dead will hear his voice and live, now and on the last day (5:21, 25, 28–29). Martha hears the sermon of chapter 5 spoken to one grieving woman, by name.

Though he die. The two halves do not say the same thing twice. The first is for the dead. It admits plainly that believers still die, but does not end there: believers who die will live, raised by him (5:28–29). This is the resurrection.

Shall never die. The second half is for the living, and it is the life. “Never die” means never die the true death, separation from God (8:51). Eternal life is knowing God (17:3), and a believer has it already; the friendship with God begun on earth carries straight on through the grave. A mourner stands between the two halves: one brother dead, one sister alive, and a promise covering each.

He said “I am” before the stone was moved. Every believer’s grave now lies inside this sentence, and on the last day every one will open at his word.

What it does not mean. The verse is quoted badly in both directions. It does not promise that Christians will not die physically: Lazarus dies again, and so does everyone in the story. Nor does it shrink to a metaphor about living on in memory or influence. The man saying it is about to show what he means by shouting into a cave.

Do you believe this? The question is put to Martha, and to every reader. Not whether she believes in a resurrection, which she had confessed one verse earlier, but whether she believes this, about him, on a day when it has already seemed to fail. He does not raise Lazarus and then ask. He asks first, with the stone in place and the smell expected, and she must answer on nothing but his word.

Is this not just wishful thinking, the kind of thing people say at funerals? Graveside words cost nothing. But Jesus stakes this one on a public event, a named man four days dead before a crowd that included his enemies, and soon afterwards on his own body, in a tomb the authorities had every reason to keep sealed. Wishful thinking does not volunteer for that kind of test. A sceptic may answer that the story was invented, a fair question about the Gospels’ reliability, worth weighing on its own ground; but the claim was made in public, while people who could check it were alive. Paul put it bluntly: if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The Christian hope has always been willing to stand or fall on whether a grave was empty.

What about those who die without believing in him? The promise is to “whoever believes in me”, and Scripture offers it to no one else. Those who die outside Christ will also be raised, but to the resurrection of judgment (5:29), to conscious, eternal punishment, separated from the life that is in him (Matthew 25:46). That solemn truth should make us earnest, not cold. It is why Jesus asked Martha the question, and why we must ask it of others while there is time. And it is why we can leave the dead, whom we cannot judge, with the God who always does right (Genesis 18:25), while we plead with the living.
verseByVerse.note: This is the fifth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha makes the confession John’s whole Gospel was written to produce, and at once goes to bring her sister to Jesus.

Yes, Lord; I believe. This confession is larger than it looks. John wrote “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (20:31), and Martha says it almost word for word. In Matthew it is Peter who says it and is called blessed (Matthew 16:16); here it is Martha, and her confession is as great as his (compare John 6:69). “I believe” is in the perfect tense: I have come to believe, and still believe. She believes who he is before she sees what he will do, the usual order with God: we confess Christ first, and see his full power afterwards.

Who makes the great confessions in John. Not the temple’s rulers, but a Samaritan woman with five husbands behind her, an excommunicated beggar who had been blind, and now a woman at the edge of a village who has just told him he arrived too late.

She called her sister. In private, perhaps so as not to alert mourners hostile to Jesus, Martha gives her sister the chance to go to him without an audience. She knows Mary is sitting in a dark house and will not come for an invitation, but will come for a summons. He calls each one personally, and Martha, who has just met him, does the first thing a believer does: she brings someone else to him.

In everyday life. Who do you know who is sitting in a dark house, too weighed down to come out alone? Go and tell them, gently and in private if need be, that the Teacher is here and is calling for them.

Is it enough to believe the right things about Jesus? Martha’s confession is right in every word, but it is more than facts. To believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, in John’s sense, is to trust yourself to him, as Martha did with her brother in a tomb. The demons believe facts, and shudder (James 2:19); faith says “Yes, Lord”, and leans its whole weight on him. So hold the truth about Christ carefully, because it matters, and make sure it is not only in your head but the ground you stand on when everything else gives way.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the word that Jesus is calling her, Mary rises at once and goes to him, and he waits outside the village until she comes.

She rose quickly. Mary has spent four days in that house receiving visitors, and has not gone out to meet him. John does not say why. He does say that the moment she hears Jesus is asking for her, she is on her feet.

In the place where Martha had met him. He had not moved. He waits outside, perhaps to meet the sisters away from the crowd, or near the tomb, which would lie outside the village. He sends for one of them and stays put until she comes.

Inside the sound of it. Professional mourners, flute players and wailing women, could be heard from some distance. He waits at the edge of the village within earshot of all that grief, and what he will do there next is weep.

In everyday life. When his word calls you, a passage that will not let you go or a plain summons to come back to him in prayer, do not wait until the grief has lifted or the house has emptied. Get up and go to him as you are; he is waiting where he said he would be.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary falls at Jesus’ feet with the same words as her sister, and the mourners who follow her become witnesses of what he does next.

They followed her. Out of ordinary kindness, the mourners assume she is going to the tomb to weep. So the whole crowd from Jerusalem ends up with Jesus, and then at the graveside, witnesses to something none of them came for, whose report will within days get Jesus condemned (vv. 46–53).

She fell at his feet. The difference from her sister is in posture, not words. Martha met him standing and talked theology in the road; Mary fell at his feet, where she always is: listening (Luke 10:39), grieving here, worshipping (12:3). The feet she fell at would soon be anointed by her hands and then pierced by nails.

The same words. Mary says Martha’s sentence and nothing more, from the ground. Martha received a conversation, a question and one of the great sayings of the Gospel. Mary receives not an argument but his tears, which is what she needed.

Grief that cannot stand upright. He did not ask Mary for a confession before he wept with her. The Lord who receives the speechless was himself led like a lamb that is silent before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7), and in Gethsemane he too fell on the ground (Mark 14:35). He knows that grief from the inside.

Is one way of grieving more spiritual than another? No. Martha talked and Mary wept, and Jesus received both with the same love; neither grieved wrongly. Some believers grieve with questions and activity, others in silence and tears, most of us in both ways at different times. Do not measure your faith by how composed you are, or anyone else’s by how they cope. What matters is that both sisters brought their grief to him, and he met each in the way each needed.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the grief that death has caused, Jesus is stirred to anger and deep distress, and asks to be taken to the grave.

Deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. Mary and the mourners weep aloud (klaiō), the public lament a Jewish funeral expected. Jesus’ first verb (embrimaomai) most likely carries indignation (see the box below). “Greatly troubled” is literally “he troubled himself”: a deep inner agitation that does not merely come over him; he takes it on himself.

Angry at what? Not at Mary, who has only fallen at his feet, nor at the mourners, who are doing what neighbours should. Some suggest their unbelief, but the text gives no sign of it, and he rebukes no one. The answer that fits is death itself, the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), the devil who brought it, and the ruin sin has made of God’s world. He stands before a family destroyed by the thing he came to destroy, and at his friend’s grave he faces the power he came to break.

Where have you laid him? He who knows all things is not asking directions; he is doing what a man does at a house of mourning, asking to be taken to the grave. “Come and see” echoes his own words to the first disciples (1:39) and Philip’s to Nathanael (1:46). He goes.

God is not serene about death. The Maker of the world stands in a village road, indignant at what has been done to it. Death is not natural, not friendly, not simply part of the circle of life. It is an intruder, and the Son of God is angry at it. On another day he walked into death itself, through it and out the other side, so that death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55).

Is it right to be angry at death, or even at God, when someone dies? It is right to be angry at death, because Jesus was; you need not pretend otherwise. Anger at God is different, and must be handled honestly: bring it to him rather than nursing it, as the psalmists did. He can bear your raw words and will not despise them. But do not let it settle into a grudge that accuses him of evil, for the one who stood at Lazarus’s grave was not the author of death but its enemy, and he has already gone to war against it on your behalf.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “deeply moved” (embrimaomai, also v. 38) is used elsewhere of a stern warning or an angry rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5), and the ESV’s margin offers “was indignant”. Some translations soften it here to deep emotion. The most likely meaning is a deep, indignant distress, anger and grief together, aimed not at the mourners but at death and all that brought it.
verseByVerse.note: The words behind “deeply moved” carry a sense of anger or indignation, at death itself and the grief it brings.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Minutes from raising his friend, Jesus weeps at what death has done to people he loves: his love is real, his humanity is real, and God is not untouched by our grief.

Jesus wept. The shortest verse in most English Bibles hides a distinction. The mourners wail (klaiō, v. 33); Jesus’ verb, found nowhere else in the New Testament, is dakryō, to shed tears. The picture is probably not a man joining a wail, but a man in a road, surrounded by noise, with tears running down his face.

When it happens. Not at the news, a day’s journey away; not at the tomb; but here, at the sight of Mary on the ground and the crowd behind her. What breaks him is not the fact of the death but what it has done to people he loves.

He weeps anyway. He knows the man will soon walk out of that cave, and that he will do it. He weeps because he truly loves and grieves with those who grieve (Romans 12:15), because death is a real evil, and because he is truly man. That disposes of the common and quietly cruel idea that grief is a failure of faith, that a Christian who really believed in the resurrection would not be undone by a funeral. Here is the resurrection and the life, minutes from proving it, in tears. If knowing the outcome were enough to stop the crying, his would have stopped.

See how he loved him! Some of the mourners read the tears correctly. They could have said it at the cross, where the grave he faced was his own.

He came to stand in the grief. He could have raised Lazarus from across the Jordan with a word, as he healed the official’s son at a distance (4:50). Instead he walked a day’s journey to stand in the middle of the grief and let it reach him. This short verse answers the oldest suspicion about God, that he is untouched by grief.

If Jesus is God, how could he weep? Because he is also truly man. The eternal Son took a full human nature, body and soul, and in it felt real sorrow. God in his own divine being is not overwhelmed by emotion or changed by what happens to him, but that does not make him cold: the tears of Jesus show us the heart of God in a form we can see, a love moved toward us. When you grieve, you pray to a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), because he wept at a grave.

Should we learn to love less, so that we grieve less? Much human wisdom has said so. The Stoic teacher Epictetus advised that when you kiss your child you should remind yourself you are kissing a mortal, so that you will not be disturbed when the child dies. Buddhism traces suffering to craving and attachment, and a culture that hurries the bereaved toward closure says something similar in the language of therapy. Each makes the heart safe by making it smaller. Jesus does the opposite, loving so fully that it costs him tears. Augustine, looking back on a friend whose death had shattered him as a young man, concluded that his mistake had not been loving too much but loving a man who must die as though he never would; the answer was not to love less but to love his friend in God, who cannot be lost. Grief is the price of love, and here God pays it with us. Because he will one day empty every grave, we can afford to love without holding back, and to weep without despair.

How long is it right to grieve? There is no fixed limit. Grief can return in waves for years, and that is not failure. Christians grieve, but not as others who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13): our grief is not shorter, but held inside a larger hope. If grief has become despair, so that you cannot function or pray, tell your pastor or a trusted friend, and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; if medicine is needed, taking it is no failure of faith. If you no longer want to live, tell someone today and get medical help today. That is not weakness of faith. It is the kind of burden God gives his people to bear together.
verseByVerse.note: This is the shortest verse in the English Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: But some of them said, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?" Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some ask why the healer of the blind did not prevent this death; Jesus gives no explanation, but, indignant again, walks to the tomb to act.

Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man…? The question deserves to be taken at full strength. To ask it they concede, without argument, the miracle of chapter 9, done a couple of miles away. Their difficulty is not whether he can but why he did not. John leaves the tone open: a cynical taunt, or bewilderment. If bewilderment, it is where a great many people are, a more painful place than unbelief. Doubting God’s power is one kind of trouble; believing in it completely and standing at a graveside is another.

Deeply moved again. He does not answer. Nobody at the tomb is told why the two days happened; only the disciples had been told (vv. 4, 15). Instead he grows indignant again (the same word as v. 33), and walks to the tomb with tears still on his face, to do something about it. At the end of all things he will answer every “why” of every grave the same way: not with an explanation, but with a voice that empties tombs.

A cave, and a stone. Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance against animals and robbers (see burial customs). Within weeks a stone will turn up again, at a different tomb, rolled away.

Why does God not explain my suffering? Often he does not, and Scripture is honest about it: he did not explain to Job, or to the crowd at Bethany. But he did something better than explain: he came. The answer to “why” is often not a reason but a presence, God coming to where the grief is and acting in a way that transforms the question. You may never know in this life why it happened. You can know who is with you in it, and the end of the story: resurrection, and every tear wiped away. Faith is not having every answer; it is trusting the one who walks to the tomb.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were caves or rock chambers, with a large stone across the entrance.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, "Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days." Jesus said to her, "Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus orders the stone removed; Martha protests that the body has begun to decay, and Jesus recalls his promise that if she believes she will see the glory of God.

Take away the stone. He could move it with a word; he tells them to do it. God often uses human obedience in his works, and what he asks here is not faith to raise the dead but strength to move a stone. Obedience is usually something quite ordinary, done before there is any evidence it will matter.

The sister of the dead man. A quiet, painful touch: the man who has been Lazarus all chapter becomes, at the mouth of the cave, “the dead man”.

By this time there will be an odor. One of the most human sentences in the chapter, and no lapse: anyone who has believed something on Sunday and not managed it on Tuesday will recognise Martha. And she is right: spices did not stop decay, and after four days in that climate it was well under way. She is protecting her brother’s body, the last thing left to protect. Her faith of verse 27 is real, but she cannot imagine what Jesus will do.

Did I not tell you…? A reminder, not a rebuke. He does not dispute what she says about the body; he recalls his promise of glory (v. 4), presumably carried back by the messenger, and his “Do you believe this?” (vv. 25–26). In this Gospel faith comes before sight, and the glory of God has a face: “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (1:14). What Martha is about to see is not a general display of power, but the glory of God shining in the man beside her, who has just told her to open the grave.

In everyday life. What stone is Christ telling you to move: a confession put off, a reconciliation you think hopeless, a habit of prayer abandoned because nothing seemed to happen? Your obedience will be as mixed as Martha’s, but it was never meant to carry you: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his obedience is counted as yours, and his Spirit in you gives strength for the next stone.

Does God need my faith before he can act? Does my weak faith stop him? God is not limited by our faith; he raised Lazarus, who had no faith at all, being dead. Faith is not a power that makes God able, but the empty hand that receives what he gives and the eye that sees his glory when he shows it. Martha’s faith was weak at that moment, and Jesus did not cancel the miracle; he called her back to his word. So do not try to manufacture enough faith to earn an answer. Look at his promise, take the next step of obedience, roll the stone, and leave the power to him.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were not embalmed; after four days decay was well under way.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the open tomb Jesus thanks his Father for having already heard him, and says so aloud, so that the crowd will know the sign comes from the Father who sent him.

He lifted up his eyes. Jews commonly prayed looking upward (17:1; Psalm 123:1). The stone is gone, the smell is expected, the crowd is waiting, and the first thing he does is look to his Father.

Father, I thank you that you have heard me. The tense is past: he gives thanks before the miracle for a prayer already answered. The asking happened earlier, unrecorded, perhaps when he first heard of the illness; the two days beyond the Jordan were not idle.

I knew that you always hear me. No one else in Scripture could say this. Elijah on Carmel prayed, “Answer me, O LORD, answer me” (1 Kings 18:37): a man hoping. This is the Son stating a fact about his Father.

On account of the people. He does not need to speak to be heard; he prays aloud so that the crowd will know where the power comes from. Without the prayer the raising would prove the wrong thing. A man who shouts into a tomb and gets a result looks like a wonder-worker, and the district had seen those. The prayer shows what the sign is for: the miracle comes from the Father, and the Father sent him.

Should I thank God before I see the answer? What if the answer is no? Give thanks, but be clear what for. Jesus knew the Father’s will; we often do not. So we thank God not for an outcome we have decided on, but because he hears us, he is good, and he will do what is best (Philippians 4:6–7; Romans 8:28). That thanks is never misplaced: even when the answer is no or not yet, he has heard, and his answer is love. Thanking God in advance is not a technique to secure results. It is trust speaking before it sees.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed looking upward.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls his dead friend by name, and the dead man comes out: a foretaste of the last day, and a picture of how Christ’s voice gives life to the spiritually dead.

Lazarus, come out. A shout (kraugazō), the word used of a crowd bellowing (19:6): he prayed quietly to his Father, but to the dead man he shouts a command. An old saying, often credited to Augustine, has it that if Jesus had not named Lazarus, all the dead would have come out. And the name is the whole of it: the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (10:3) does exactly that, into a cave.

The man who had died came out. John does not dramatise it. The Word through whom all things were made spoke into a cave, and death let go of what it held, because it has no answer to that voice.

Bound with linen strips. Bodies were wrapped in linen strips, with spices between them and a separate cloth for the face (see burial customs). Lazarus comes out still wrapped; Jesus will rise and leave his grave clothes behind (20:6–7). Lazarus will die again; Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). This is a return to mortal life; Jesus’ resurrection will be the first of the new creation.

Unbind him, and let him go. Again, others help: Christ alone gives life, and his people help the newly living out of their grave clothes.

A picture of salvation. We were dead in sins (Ephesians 2:1–5), no more able to respond than Lazarus. This is regeneration, being born again (3:3–8): God giving new life to a dead heart, so that it begins to love and trust him. And it is the effectual call, a call that does what it says. The gospel invitation goes out to everyone, but when God calls his own by name, as Jesus called Lazarus, the call creates the answer: the dead hear and live (5:25). Lazarus did not decide to live and then hear; he heard because the voice made him alive. And one day that voice will call your body from the grave: “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (5:28–29), and the whole sleeping church will rise.

What does unbinding look like in a church? Nobody in that crowd could call Lazarus out, but every one of them could pick at a knot. New believers often come out of the tomb still wrapped in old habits, fears, addictions, shame and confused ideas. The church’s work is patient: teaching them the word, welcoming them to the Lord’s Table after baptism, walking with them, praying, bearing burdens, and refusing to be shocked by the smell of the grave on them. We cannot give life. We can help someone who has been given it to walk freely.

Why do Matthew, Mark and Luke say nothing about it? It is the objection most often raised against this chapter: if a man four days dead walked out of a tomb outside Jerusalem, and it decided the authorities to kill Jesus (v. 53), why do the other Gospels not mention it? Partly because of how the books are shaped: the first three concentrate on Galilee and bring Jesus to Jerusalem once, at the end, while John fills in the Judean ministry and the repeated visits to the city. None of them tries to be complete; John says so twice (20:30–31; 21:25). Nor were they shy of raisings: Mark and Luke both record Jairus’s daughter, and Luke the widow’s son at Nain.

Protecting Lazarus. A further suggestion is worth weighing. The chief priests planned to kill Lazarus too (12:10–11), and a man so placed, a short walk from the temple, would not be helped by having his name published across the empire. The earlier Gospels leave several people anonymous whom John alone names: only John tells us that the disciple with the sword was Peter and the servant was Malchus (18:10). John writes last, a generation on, when those who might have suffered for being named were beyond harm. That may be the whole explanation or part of it; either way it is better than assuming a story this size was invented late.

What did Lazarus experience in those four days? Scripture does not say, and the silence is deliberate: Lazarus is given no story to tell. What we know of death we know from Christ’s word, not from those who claim to have returned (Luke 16:31). For the believer, what we are told is enough: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). So be wary of books that claim to describe heaven or hell from a near-death experience: they may be sincere, but they are not Scripture, and often contradict it. We have the word of the one who has the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth over the face.

parallels.desc: all who are in the tombs will hear his voice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–57 — The Decision to Kill Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest sign brings the decision to kill the one who gave it. Many believe, but others report to the Pharisees, and the council admits the signs and fears for its place and nation (vv. 45–48). Caiaphas argues that one man should die for the people, and John explains that God spoke through him: Jesus would die in the place of his people and gather God’s scattered children into one (vv. 49–52). From that day they plan his death. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim until his hour, while Passover crowds wonder whether he will come and the authorities order his arrest (vv. 53–57). The life he gave Lazarus will cost him his own.
verseByVerse.theology: Caiaphas’ calculation, sacrifice one man to save the nation, is both cynical politics and unconscious prophecy (see the notes on vv. 49–50 and 51–52). The cross is always more than its perpetrators intend, and exactly what God intends.
verseByVerse.examples: The council’s decision carries out what God had planned beforehand (Acts 4:27–28). The leaders plot what God has purposed, and the victim goes willingly to what they intend as murder and he intends as sacrifice. God works through human wickedness without being stained by it, and nowhere is that plainer than at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same sign brings many to faith and sends others to inform against Jesus: evidence alone does not change a heart.

Many believed in him. The sign leads to faith, as it was meant to (20:31).

Some went to the Pharisees. The same event, the same crowd, and two responses as far apart as can be: a plain answer to the idea that a sufficiently impressive miracle would settle faith for everybody. Those who reported the climax of the signs to the Pharisees did not deny it. They accepted the evidence and acted against it, because believing would have cost what they loved more, as the council is about to say aloud: their place and their nation (v. 48). The heart often has a say in what the mind will accept, in believers and sceptics alike, though not every honest doubt is a hidden refusal. That is why, in the end, the remedy is not more evidence but a new heart.

Neither will they be convinced. Abraham says it in the parable: “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31). Then a man named Lazarus did rise from the dead, and they were not convinced, and soon they were planning to kill him too (12:10).

Feeding the machinery. John does not say why some went. Some may have gone in genuine excitement, thinking the authorities would want to know. What the authorities did with the news was not necessarily what the messengers intended: a small warning that the machinery of a great wrong is often fed by people who thought they were being helpful.

If miracles do not convince people, what will convince my unbelieving friend? Only God himself, by his Spirit opening the eyes of the heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is a reason not for despair but for prayer. The Spirit uses means: the word of the gospel, the testimony of what Christ has done, the love of his people, honest answers to honest questions. So keep telling your friend what Christ has done, as the believing mourners did, live in a way that adorns it, and pray that God will give new life. Arguments do not raise the dead. The voice of Christ does, and it is heard through the gospel you speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, "What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In closed session the council admits that Jesus’ signs are real, and turns against him to protect its place and its nation, the very things it would lose.

The council. The council (synedrion) is the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish court, traditionally of seventy-one members, led by the high priest.

What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. The question is exasperated: something has got out of hand. And they do not deny the miracles; they cannot. In closed session, with no crowd to satisfy, the highest court in Israel records as fact that the miracles are real. Everything they do from here is done with that on the record. The problem was never the evidence.

Everyone will believe in him. The disaster they mean to prevent is the very outcome the Gospel was written to produce (20:31). And the Lord has been granting their fear for two thousand years, in every tongue under heaven.

Our place and our nation. “Our place” means the temple, and perhaps their own positions. Rome allowed Jewish self-rule as long as there was order, and a popular messianic uprising could end it. The terrible irony is that they were right about the outcome and wrong about the cause: they killed Jesus to save the temple and the nation, and in AD 70 the Romans destroyed both.

The true temple. John has already shown what they could not see: the temple Jesus would raise in three days was his body (2:19–21). The council moved to save a building by destroying the true temple, where God now dwells with men, and on the third day God raised it up. He who sits in the heavens laughs at such counsels (Psalm 2:4), and makes the very council called against his Anointed serve his Anointed’s glory.

Can churches fall into the same trap? Yes, and often. Whenever a church or ministry protects its reputation, building, income or leaders at the cost of truth, it speaks the council’s language. The worst form is hiding abuse to protect the institution. That is never acceptable: victims must be heard and protected, wrongdoing reported to the proper authorities, and the truth told, whatever it costs the church’s name. The church belongs to Christ, not to us, and he does not need us to protect his reputation by sin. A church that loses its place for the sake of righteousness has lost nothing.
verseByVerse.note: “Our place” means the temple. The leaders feared a messianic movement would bring Roman retaliation, as happened in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caiaphas, with contempt for his colleagues, proposes that one man die so that the nation may be spared: political murder dressed as responsibility, in words truer than he knows.

Caiaphas, high priest that year. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long term, kept in office by the Romans, which shows how good he was at political survival. His father-in-law Annas, high priest before him, was still powerful (18:13). The office was not annual, yet John says “that year” three times (here, v. 51, and 18:13): not, almost certainly, because it rotated, but because this was that year, the year everything turned on.

You know nothing at all. Caiaphas opens with contempt for his own council, rude in a way the Jewish historian Josephus thought typical of Sadducees. Then comes the calculation: kill Jesus before the Romans kill us all. Nobody at the table asks whether the man is guilty of anything. It is the oldest political arithmetic there is, one life against many, always framed as responsibility, and always paid by somebody else.

For the people. One man should die on behalf of, in place of (hyper), the people: the word Jesus used of the shepherd laying down his life for the sheep (10:11), and one Paul often uses of the atonement. Arguing for a judicial murder, the high priest of Israel reaches instinctively for the language of sacrifice. He is a priest; it is the language he has.

The same sum in smaller rooms. It is still done: the colleague quietly blamed so the team keeps its contract, the awkward member eased out so the church keeps its peace. When you hear yourself reasoning that it is better for one person to bear the cost so that everyone else is spared, stop and ask whether anyone has asked what he deserves, and remember that the only substitute God accepts is the one who offered himself.

Why do we take the victim’s side? It feels obvious to us that the innocent victim of a crowd deserves sympathy; for most of history it was not. The French thinker René Girard, who came to Christian faith through his study of literature, argued that communities have again and again held together by uniting against a victim whose removal brings the crowd its peace, and that the old myths tell those stories from the crowd’s side: the victim was guilty, and the gods approved. Girard heard that logic spoken aloud in Caiaphas’s sentence. The Gospels tell the story from the side of the victim, and he is innocent; our instinct for the underdog comes from here, though we still form crowds and look for someone to blame. And the Gospel goes beyond the insight: the innocent victim truly did die for the people, of his own accord, and so ended the need for any other. The crowd’s peace is always bought with someone else’s blood. God’s peace was bought with his own.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; “that year” means that fateful year.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without knowing it, Caiaphas spoke God’s truth: Jesus would die in the place of his people, and by his death gather God’s scattered children from every nation into one.

He prophesied. John claims that God spoke through a man who was arranging a murder, and not despite his office but through it, as he once spoke through Balaam (Numbers 23–24). The high priest was to speak for God to the people and for the people to God, and on the one occasion in the Gospels when Caiaphas does so, he speaks accurately, without the faintest idea what he is saying. That does not make him a good man or excuse anything. God’s purposes do not depend on the character of those he uses: he can speak even through wicked men, and overrule their evil for good (Genesis 50:20; Acts 4:27–28).

That Jesus would die for the nation. Caiaphas meant a political substitute; God meant a saving one. On the cross Christ took the punishment sin deserves, in the place of his people, so that they will never bear it (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

To gather into one. John finishes the sentence Caiaphas started: not the nation only, not rescue from Rome, but a gathering that runs to the ends of the earth. “The children of God who are scattered abroad” are most naturally the elect among the Gentiles, the other sheep of 10:16. In the next chapter the first of them arrive, Greeks asking to see Jesus (12:20–21), and he answers that, lifted up, he will draw all people to himself (12:32). His death does not merely make a gathering possible; it brings it about. The scattering is what sin did at Babel and exile did to Israel, and the cross undoes it. The high priest of the old covenant pronounced the terms of the new one, out loud, in council, and voted for it.

Does God still speak through people like this today? God is sovereign over every word spoken, but this was a unique moment, tied to the office of high priest at the climax of redemption. It is no reason to look for new revelations in the words of people around us: God’s revelation is complete in his Son and his written word (Hebrews 1:1–2; the Westminster Confession 1.1, 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.1, 1.6). What the verse teaches is not to seek new messages, but to trust that no plot, no wicked decision and no cynical politician is outside his control.

parallels.desc: I will gather yet others

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that day the council resolves to kill Jesus, and he withdraws to a quiet town near the wilderness, not from fear, but because he, not they, will set the hour.

From that day on. John dates it. There had been hostility for a long time, and stones twice, but here the decision becomes a formal resolution of the council, and everything after is the working out of it: the anointing for burial, the entry into Jerusalem, and the Greeks whose request makes him say the hour has come (12:23). What turned them was not a blasphemy but a resurrection, an act of pure kindness to a family in Bethany.

No longer openly. His hour is close, but not yet, and his public ministry is drawing to a close. This is not fear. He has walked into Judea twice knowing what was waiting, and soon he will walk in again and let them take him. What he will not do is let them set the date. A Passover is coming, and he intends to die at it, and not before.

A town called Ephraim. Probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness that drops toward the Jordan valley (see the box below). John notes the wilderness deliberately: it is where the Baptist worked, and where Israel was shaped into a people before crossing into the promised land.

He stayed with the disciples. Not preaching, not travelling, nothing John thinks worth recording: before the last week, a stretch of quiet in a small town on the edge of the desert, with twelve men who did not know what was coming, and a Master who knew all of it.

Uncertain wording. This Ephraim is named nowhere else in the New Testament, and its site is not known for certain. It is often identified with the Old Testament Ophrah (Joshua 18:23), at the modern village of et-Taiyibeh, a dozen miles or so north-east of Jerusalem, overlooking the wilderness. That fits John’s description well, but it is likely rather than proven, and nothing in the meaning depends on it.
verseByVerse.note: The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Passover pilgrims purify themselves and wonder whether Jesus will dare to come, never imagining that he will come as the Lamb who alone can make them clean.

Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand. The third Passover in John (2:13; 6:4), the one at which Jesus will die as the true Passover Lamb (1:29; 19:36).

To purify themselves. A real and demanding business. Pilgrims came up a week or more early, because anyone ceremonially unclean needed time to be cleansed before he could eat the Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18). Contact with a corpse was a common cause, and its cleansing took seven days (Numbers 19:11–12). Those laws were not fussiness: they taught Israel that God is holy, that death and sin are the opposite of his life, and that no one may come near him carelessly (Leviticus 10:3). Just after a man four days dead has walked out of a tomb, John shows a city preoccupied with the defilement of corpses. They purify themselves for a feast at which they will kill the Lamb who alone can make them clean.

What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all? The Greek expects that he will not: surely he will not dare? It is the talk of a crowd with time to fill, speculating about a celebrity with a warrant out: not whether he is the Christ, only whether he will turn up. He will come within the week, on a donkey, precisely to be arrested, the one possibility hardly anyone in that temple seems to have considered. Days later they will be cutting branches and shouting “Hosanna”, and five days after that a crowd in the same city will shout for his death. The distance between those two noises is very short.

How am I made clean to come to God? Not by rituals, effort or a week of religious preparation. The pilgrims’ washings dealt only with outward defilement, and only for a time. The uncleanness that keeps us from God is sin, and only one thing removes it: “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). You come to God clean not because you have prepared yourself well, but because Christ the Lamb was sacrificed for you. So come now, as you are, trusting him. Then, as one already washed, you will want to put away whatever defiles, out of love and not to earn your place.
verseByVerse.note: Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter that began with two sisters’ private message ends with a public order for Jesus’ arrest, yet the hunted man is still the one who will lay down his life.

Given orders. Jesus is now a wanted man, and the authorities enlist the city. In the end they did not need the public; they needed one man who already knew where he would be, and he was inside the twelve. John records the warrant seven chapters before it is carried out, setting the scene for Judas (12:4; 18:2–3).

So that they might arrest him. The net is closing, but the one they plan to arrest has authority to lay down his life (10:18). Four attempts in this Gospel have already failed (7:30, 44; 8:20; 10:39). The next will succeed only because he walks out of a garden and asks the soldiers whom they are looking for (18:4–8).

The cost of Bethany. The one who called Lazarus by name and gave him back to his sisters is a wanted man because he did it: raising his friend cost him his life. They issued a warrant for the arrest of the resurrection and the life, as though life itself could be taken into custody. When the one man who knew the place led them to it, the hunted one stepped forward into the torchlight, and asked only that his friends be let go (18:8). He was bound so that his own could go free, as Lazarus was unbound and let go.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.<sup>2</sup>It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.<sup>3</sup>So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.”<sup>4</sup>But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”<sup>5</sup>Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.<sup>6</sup>So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.<sup>7</sup>Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”<sup>8</sup>The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”<sup>9</sup>Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.<sup>10</sup>But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”<sup>11</sup>After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”<sup>12</sup>The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”<sup>13</sup>Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.<sup>14</sup>Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,<sup>15</sup>and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”<sup>16</sup>So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”<sup>17</sup>Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.<sup>18</sup>Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off,<sup>19</sup>and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.<sup>20</sup>So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.<sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.<sup>22</sup>But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”<sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”<sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live,<sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”<sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”<sup>28</sup>When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”<sup>29</sup>And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him.<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.<sup>31</sup>When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.<sup>32</sup>Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”<sup>33</sup>When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.<sup>34</sup>And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus wept.<sup>36</sup>So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”<sup>37</sup>But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”<sup>38</sup>Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
Where we are. Jesus has withdrawn across the Jordan to the place where John first baptised, after the leaders in Jerusalem tried once more to stone him (10:31, 39–40). Now word comes from Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, and the seventh and greatest of John’s signs begins. It is the hinge of the Gospel, the sign that sends Jesus to the cross.

The message. Jesus is the resurrection and the life. Death, the enemy that grieves even him, has no answer to his voice, and whoever believes in him, though he die, will live. And the one who gives life to his friend will give his own life to do it, dying in the place of his people to gather God’s scattered children into one.

Why it was said. John wrote so that his readers might believe and have life (20:31; see the introduction). They buried their dead in a world that saw death as the end, and some faced authorities like those who plot here. Here they see whose voice will speak over every Christian grave, and that even the schemes of the powerful serve his purpose.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus hears of the illness, waits two days because he loves the family, and leads his frightened disciples back into Judea (vv. 1–16). He meets Martha, who holds the true hope of the last day, and tells her that the resurrection is standing in front of her (vv. 17–27). He meets Mary at his feet and weeps, indignant at death (vv. 28–37). At the tomb he thanks his Father and calls a man four days dead out of the cave (vv. 38–44). Many believe, but the council meets, Caiaphas argues that one man must die for the people, and from that day they plan to kill him (vv. 45–53). Jesus withdraws to Ephraim while the Passover crowds wonder whether he will come (vv. 54–57).

Where it leads. Everything points beyond Lazarus, who came out still bound and would die again, to Jesus’ own tomb, which he would leave with his grave clothes lying behind him, never to die again. Caiaphas spoke better than he knew: Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only. And the voice that called Lazarus by name will call every believer from the grave on the last day (5:28–29).

For us. Christian grief is real, for Jesus wept, but it is not hopeless, because the one who wept is the resurrection. Bring him your “if only” and whatever you have written off as four days dead, answer his question, “Do you believe this?”, and help those he has raised to be unbound and set free.

keyVerse.quote: I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.
keyVerse.note: Martha had placed the resurrection at the end of history; Jesus places it in himself. The whole chapter turns on this saying: the sign at the tomb shows it is true, and the death and rising that the sign sets in motion make it true for everyone who believes. It is the promise read at Christian gravesides, and it ends in a question each reader must answer: “Do you believe this?”

11.reflection:
John tells us that Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and so stayed two days longer (vv. 5–6). How would reading a delay in your own life with “Jesus loved them” in front of it change the way you wait and pray?

Martha believed in the resurrection on the last day, and Jesus answered, “I am the resurrection and the life” (vv. 24–25). What difference does it make that our hope is a person and not only a doctrine? How would you answer his question, “Do you believe this?”

Jesus wept at the grave, though he knew he was about to raise Lazarus (v. 35). What does that teach us about grief and faith, and how can we grieve with others in a way that is both honest and hopeful?

Some who saw the sign believed, and others reported it to the authorities, who decided to kill him (vv. 45–53). Why does evidence alone not settle faith? And how can we, like the bystanders at the tomb, help those whom Christ has raised to be unbound and set free (v. 44)?

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus comes to Jerusalem as the King who is going to die, and the people around him show what they make of him. At a dinner in Bethany, with Lazarus at the table, Mary pours costly nard on his feet, Judas complains of the waste, and Jesus says she has anointed him for burial (vv. 1–8). Crowds come to see the man raised from the dead, and the chief priests plan to kill him too (vv. 9–11). Next day pilgrims go out with palm branches to hail the King of Israel; he rides a young donkey, the king of peace Zechariah foretold, though his disciples understood only after his glory (vv. 12–16). Lazarus is why the crowd came, and the Pharisees despair that the world has gone after him (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Mary’s extravagance is the fitting response to Jesus: Matthew records him calling it “a beautiful thing” (Matthew 26:10). Judas uses the language of charity to cover his own greed (see vv. 5–6). The contrast between Mary’s love and Judas’ arithmetic is the contrast between true discipleship and a discipleship that has never left the world’s way of counting.
verseByVerse.examples: The crowd hails Jesus as king, right about the title and wrong about its meaning (see vv. 12–14). Jesus comes on a donkey, the humble king of peace (v. 15), and the disciples understand it only after he is glorified (see the note on v. 16).

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days before Passover, Jesus walks back into danger to share a thankful supper with the family whose brother he raised from the dead.

Six days before the Passover. Probably the Saturday evening before Passover week, once the Sabbath had ended. John has started a clock that runs to the end of the book: nearly half this Gospel covers one week.

Jesus therefore came to Bethany. “Therefore” reaches back to the order that anyone who knew where he was should report it (11:57). He comes within an hour’s walk of men with a warrant, knowing they are looking for him.

A dinner for him. Mark and Matthew place what is very likely the same dinner in the house of Simon the leper (Mark 14:3): a dinner of gratitude, in the village of resurrection, at the last resting place before Jerusalem.

Martha served. Martha is still serving, as in the one other scene we have of that house (Luke 10:40), now without complaint. That is not a failure to learn but a woman doing what she is good at for the man who gave her brother back. Service offered in love is worship too.

Lazarus at table. Lazarus, four days dead, is reclining at dinner as guests did (see meals and reclining at table). Resurrection produces not a spectacle or a ghost but a man having supper with his sisters.

Supper, six days from a cross. With a cross six days away, the Lord of life sat unhurried at supper with a man he had raised. It is a small picture of what is coming: all whom he raises will one day recline with him in his Father’s house, and he himself will serve them (Luke 12:37).

Did Jesus really spend his last week at dinners? Among other things, and it was no waste. He taught, wept over the city and prayed; he also ate with friends, and his last free evening was spent at a meal (13:1–2). Not only overtly religious activity counts. Eating together in gratitude, with Christ honoured at the table, is part of the life of his people, and a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary pours her most precious possession on Jesus’ feet, in the lowliest way and at cost to her dignity, while at the same table Judas calculates.

Pure nard. An aromatic oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas, imported from India and very costly, perhaps a family treasure put by for her own burial or her dowry. As Judas will calculate in a moment, it was worth about a year’s wages.

His feet, and her hair. Anointing the head honoured a king; the feet were a servant’s place. And a respectable woman, it is often said, did not let down her hair in public. She gives the best she has, in the lowest place, without a word.

Feet wiped twice. John uses the same verb for what Jesus does a few nights later, when he wiped his disciples’ feet with the towel tied round him (13:5). A disciple kneels at his feet in love; then the Lord kneels at theirs, Judas’s among them, and washes what she only anointed. His is the deeper humbling, the Lord of glory in the servant’s place, and it points to the cross, where he would lay down his life to make them clean (13:8–10).

The fragrance of the perfume. Her devotion fills the house, and the story fills the world. Matthew and Mark record Jesus’ promise that wherever the gospel is preached, what she has done will be told in memory of her (Mark 14:9). John does not record the promise; he keeps it.

But Judas Iscariot. John tells us who Judas is before we hear what he says: the fragrance of devotion and the coldest calculation at one table.

What would extravagant love for Christ look like for me? Rarely a jar of nard, but always something that costs: time when you have little, money beyond what is sensible, a reputation risked by being openly his, a long, quiet service no one sees. The mark of Mary’s act is not its size but its direction: it was all for him, and it was not calculated. Ask what you are keeping back because it is too precious, and whether he is worth more. He is the only one who has ever deserved everything, and the only one who gave everything first.

Is this the same anointing as in Matthew and Mark? Very probably, and the differences can be reasonably harmonised. There the unnamed woman anoints his head (Mark 14:3); John has the feet. A pound of nard poured out over a reclining man would reach both: she probably did both, and each writer keeps what struck him; John remembers the hair. The host is Simon the leper, with Martha serving and Lazarus a guest. Mark and Matthew have several objectors; John names the one who started it, as he alone names Peter with the sword and Malchus (18:10). John’s six days date the arrival at Bethany; Mark’s two days (Mark 14:1) date the plotting, and he tells the anointing there because Judas’s betrayal follows from it. This is not the sinful woman of Luke 7, an earlier and different anointing in Galilee. Not every detail can be settled, but nothing here forces us to doubt either account.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. A respectable woman did not normally let down her hair in public.

parallels.desc: a different woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas dresses greed up as concern for the poor, and John strips off the disguise: he was a thief.

Three hundred denarii. A denarius was a day’s wage, so three hundred, once Sabbaths and feasts are taken out, is about a year’s pay for a labourer. The objection sounds pious, and the arithmetic is right: had his motive been what he claimed, it would have been a fair point. Mark and Matthew say others shared the indignation (Mark 14:4; Matthew 26:8); John names Judas as the one who voiced it.

Because he was a thief. The moneybag was the common purse, from which the poor were helped (13:29). Judas was the treasurer, and “used to help himself” is continuous: not once, but habitually, over a long time. Love of money opened the door to his betrayal (Matthew 26:14–15; 1 Timothy 6:10).

The disguise of a good cause. Judas argues not for theft but for the poor. A concern for the poor can be perfectly genuine, and it can be the most effective disguise, and from outside the two cannot be told apart. The only person in the room who could tell was the one being anointed.
