Worth more than a year’s wages. The Lord who knew what was in the bag let Judas carry it for three years and never shamed him before the others. The one Judas valued below a year’s wages was worth more than all the world’s treasure, and he gave himself freely for people who had robbed God.

Why did Jesus choose Judas, and let him keep the money? Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (6:64, 70–71). He chose Judas so that Scripture would be fulfilled (13:18), and gave him every privilege of an apostle for three years: his teaching, his miracles, his friendship, his trust. Judas was not kept out; he was kept close and loved, and he chose silver. Nearness to Jesus, even a ministry in his name, saves no one who keeps his heart for something else. And Jesus’ patience with him is a picture of God’s long patience with every sinner.

How do I guard against the love of money? Give regularly and generously, so that money learns who is master (2 Corinthians 9:6–8). Never handle other people’s money alone. Watch for the moment you begin to justify small dishonesties. Be content with what you have, because he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). And treasure Christ: the cure for loving money is not merely having less of it but loving him more.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus defends Mary: she has anointed him for his burial, and while he is still with them, devotion to him comes first. He does not dismiss the poor; he quotes the command to open your hand to them.

Leave her alone. Mary has said nothing, and he speaks for her.

For the day of my burial. Bodies were anointed with spices for burial (see burial customs), and Jesus takes her act as preparing his body for death (on the wording, see the box below). Nicodemus will bring spices to a body already dead (19:39–40); Mary comes six days early, while he can still smell it. She who sat at his feet may have understood what the disciples missed. Her nard prepared his body for the grave; his body, given for us, prepared the way out of ours.

The poor you always have with you. Often quoted as a shrug, as if nothing can be done about poverty. But Jesus is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11, and the rest of the verse is usually left off: “For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, ‘You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.’” That there will always be poor people is the reason for the command, not an excuse. His people must help them, and there will always be time to (Galatians 2:10).

You do not always have me. In a few days he would be gone. Devotion to Christ himself comes first, and care for the poor flows from it. And Judas, who raised the objection, had had every day of three years to open his hand to the poor, and used the moneybag to fill his own.

So should churches spend money on beauty and worship rather than the poor? This verse neither makes the poor unimportant nor licenses luxury; Mary’s act was a unique gift to Christ in person before his burial. Christ is worthy of our best, and worship is not wasted when it costs. Care for the poor is commanded, and the early church organised it from the start (Acts 6:1–6). The two are not rivals: those who love Christ most will be most generous to the poor, because he is found among them (Matthew 25:40). Be suspicious of any argument, for spending or for saving, that happens to serve the arguer’s own comfort.

Uncertain wording. “So that she may keep it for the day of my burial” is genuinely difficult, because the ointment has just been poured out and there seems nothing left to keep. Some take it to mean that she should keep what remains for the burial itself; some translations make it a statement, that she has kept it for this day. Most likely she had been keeping this jar, and has spent it on the right day. Either way, her act looks ahead to his burial.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lazarus has become a walking sign that draws people to Jesus, and the chief priests, rather than believe the evidence, plan to destroy it.

Also to see Lazarus. Not a word of Lazarus is recorded anywhere in this Gospel. He does not need to preach: his silent, breathing life is a standing testimony to the one who called him out.

To put Lazarus to death as well. One of the darkest sentences in the New Testament, and nearly comic in its futility: they propose to kill a man who has already been dead once, and got up. The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8), and a resurrected man was an embarrassment. But the man was alive because the Lord of life had spoken, and no council could reverse that word.

When religion becomes control. When religion becomes a way of keeping control, even a resurrection stops being good news and becomes a threat to be managed. Anyone who wants God on his own terms will find a living Christ inconvenient.

I have no dramatic story, so do I have a testimony? Yes. Lazarus’s whole testimony was that he was alive at dinner, and it drew crowds to Christ. Yours is the same in kind: you were dead in sin and are now alive to God (Ephesians 2:4–5), whether your conversion was sudden or too gradual to date. The evidence is your life now: a love for Christ you did not have by nature, a fight against sin, a hope that death cannot shake. You need not have been a criminal or an addict. Say, truthfully and simply, what he has done for you, and let your changed life back it up.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The festival crowds hail Jesus as a national liberator, and he accepts their welcome as King while, by riding a donkey, he declines the kingdom they have in mind.

The next day. On the usual reckoning, Palm Sunday.

Branches of palm trees. Only John mentions palms, and they were a political symbol. Since the Maccabees they had stood for national victory: when Simon retook the citadel in Jerusalem, the people entered with praise and palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7). Waving them at a man entering the capital was like waving a national flag at a returning general, and going out to meet him (hypantēsis) was how cities greeted a visiting king or conqueror.

Hosanna. Hebrew for “save us, we pray” (Psalm 118:25). By this time it had become a shout of praise, rather as “God save the King” is a shout of loyalty more than a prayer, but its meaning is a cry for salvation. The blessing is from Psalm 118:26, one of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover and the Feast of Booths, a pilgrim psalm of welcome.

Even the King of Israel! The title is not in the psalm, and it is the whole misunderstanding in a phrase: a pilgrim welcome turned into the coronation of a liberator. Jesus is king, but not the kind they expect (6:15; 18:36). John heard the title from Nathanael under the fig tree (1:49), and will see it again, fixed above the cross in three languages as “the King of the Jews” (19:19–20).

A young donkey. The other Gospels tell how he found it (Mark 11:1–7). The donkey is his answer to the palms. A king on a warhorse comes to take a city; a king on a donkey has come in peace. He lets them crown him, and quietly declines the kingdom they have in mind.

John saw the palms again. Within the week the city had dropped its palms. But in his vision of heaven John saw a multitude no one could number, from every nation, standing before the throne with palm branches in their hands, crying that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10). Every palm the crowd let fall will be lifted again, by people he has truly saved.

Was this the same crowd that shouted “Crucify him” a few days later? Probably not entirely. The crowd on the road was largely pilgrims and witnesses from Bethany; the crowd before Pilate gathered early in the city, stirred up by the chief priests (Mark 15:11). But some may well have been in both, and popular enthusiasm is fickle: people who wanted a king on their own terms turned against him when he would not be that king. Beware a faith that follows Jesus only while he seems to be giving us what we want.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus fulfils Zechariah’s promise of a humble king who comes in peace, though his disciples understood it only after he was glorified.

Fear not, daughter of Zion. From Zechariah 9:9, with its opening “rejoice greatly” exchanged for “fear not”, the standard word to a frightened Israel (Isaiah 40:9; Zephaniah 3:16). “Daughter of Zion” is Jerusalem. The crowd needs no telling to rejoice; they are doing it loudly, and about the wrong thing. What they will need in five days, at the cross, is the other word: “fear not”.

A king of peace. Zechariah goes on to say that this king will cut off the war horse and speak peace to the nations, with a rule from sea to sea (Zechariah 9:10). The King of the universe came into his capital on a borrowed donkey, not to terrify but to save, not with chariots but with peace.

They did not understand at first. Two of them had fetched the animal, and all of them walked in the middle of the noise, yet none of it meant anything to them at the time.

When Jesus was glorified. “Glorified” is a large word in John: it takes in his death, resurrection and return to the Father as one great event, the moment when who he is was fully shown (7:39; 17:5). Afterwards, with the Spirit’s help (14:26), they remembered the same events and at last saw what the Scriptures meant (2:22). Their confusion at the time did not stop the prophecy being fulfilled.

How do we know the apostles did not simply read prophecy into the events afterwards? They tell us honestly that they understood only later, which does not flatter them. Many fulfilments were outside anyone’s control: the place of birth, the manner of death, the piercing, the grave; and Jesus himself acted deliberately to fulfil Scripture, as here. Above all, the resurrection opened the Old Testament to them, and it rests on many witnesses, more than five hundred at one time, most still alive to be questioned when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The apostles did not create the pattern. They discovered it, once the risen Lord explained it.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The entry into Jerusalem was set off by Lazarus: the crowd went out to hail a king who had emptied a grave.

Continued to bear witness. The tense is continuous: they had not stopped talking about it.

They heard he had done this sign. The palm branches, the shouting, the psalm, the improvised coronation were all set off by a resurrection in a village two miles away. The King they hailed had not won a battle. He had emptied a grave, and the only kingdom worth hailing is one whose king has authority over death.

Two crowds. One, from Bethany, tells what it saw (v. 17); the other comes out from Jerusalem because it heard (v. 18). The second saw nothing. That is how almost every Christian who has ever lived came to faith: not by seeing, but by believing people who did, as Jesus will say to Thomas: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (20:29).

Is believing on the testimony of others really enough? Yes, when the testimony is true and comes from God. Most of what we know of history we know from witnesses, and the apostles told what they had seen and heard (1 John 1:1–3), wrote it down, and suffered for it. Their testimony is preserved in Scripture, and the Holy Spirit himself bears witness through it to our hearts (the Westminster Confession 1.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.5). Faith is not believing without evidence. It is trusting God’s own testimony about his Son, delivered through those he chose.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees admit defeat, and in their frustration announce, without knowing it, what Jesus has come to do: the world will go after him.

You are gaining nothing. Said to one another, which suggests recrimination: the policy is not working, and they are turning on each other.

The world has gone after him. An exaggeration, but a prophetic one, for John’s next sentence is: “Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.” Like Caiaphas, they speak more truly than they know (11:50–51). His enemies said in despair what heaven says in joy.

A second irony. The Pharisees think the crowd’s enthusiasm is their defeat. In five days the same city will be shouting for a crucifixion, and they will have won everything they wanted. And the world will go after him anyway, by exactly the route they arranged: lifted up on a cross, he will draw all people to himself (12:32).

Is the world really going after him today? More than ever. The church that began with a handful of believers in Jerusalem is now in almost every nation, often growing fastest among the poor and the persecuted, though many peoples still have no church at all. But it fulfils what the Pharisees feared and Jesus promised: people from every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 5:9). You are part of that crowd. This week, pray for one nation where the church is small or suffering.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hour of Jesus’ death has come, and it is his glory, the means by which he will draw the world to himself. Greeks ask to see him, and he answers that the grain of wheat must die to bear fruit, and that his servants must follow him (vv. 20–26). Troubled, he prays that the Father glorify his name; a voice answers from heaven, and he says the cross will judge the world, cast out its ruler and draw all people (vv. 27–33). He urges the puzzled crowd to believe while the light is with them, then hides himself (vv. 34–36). John explains their unbelief from Isaiah and exposes secret believers (vv. 37–43), and Jesus’ last public words declare that he speaks the Father’s life-giving word (vv. 44–50).
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is at the centre of John’s Gospel (see the note on v. 23): the Son of Man is lifted up in humiliation and glorified in the same act. The cross is not the Father’s defeat but his decisive victory, not the Son’s shame but his glory, and it cannot be separated from the resurrection: both belong to the one hour.
verseByVerse.examples: The grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die before it bears much fruit: life through death. On hating one’s life, see the note on v. 25; the call to follow him is a call to follow him even into death (v. 26).

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentiles who could go no further than the temple’s outer court ask to see Jesus, and their request is the sign that his hour has come.

Some Greeks. Gentiles by birth, not Greek-speaking Jews. They had come to worship at the feast, which probably places them among the God-fearers: Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel without becoming full converts, like Cornelius (Acts 10:2; 17:4). And there was a wall for them. The temple’s outer court was as far as a Gentile could go, and stone notices in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner who passed the barrier had only himself to blame for the death that followed. That is where they stand as they ask.

Philip of Bethsaida. Philip has a Greek name, and Bethsaida was a mixed border town near Gentile areas, where Greek was spoken daily.

We wish to see Jesus. To meet him, to come to know him. The words are carved on the inside of many pulpits, where only the preacher can see them.

The Son they wished to see. Carved letters told them where to stop, and they asked for the one person who could take them further. He was himself the true temple, and through his death the dividing wall of hostility came down (Ephesians 2:14), so that Gentiles who once stood outside the inscriptions are brought near by his blood.

What does it mean to see Jesus today? Not a vision, but to know him truly by faith. We see him in the Gospels, written so that we may believe (20:31); in preaching that sets Christ before us as crucified (Galatians 3:1); in the Lord’s Supper; and something of him in his people, when they love one another as he loved them (13:35). One day we shall see him face to face (1 John 3:2). Until then, every Sunday ought to answer this request.
verseByVerse.note: These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, like the centurion Cornelius. Philip had a Greek name.

parallels.desc: other sheep

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Gentiles come asking for him, Jesus announces that the hour of his death and glory has arrived. The whole Gospel turns on this sentence.

Philip and Andrew. Philip is oddly hesitant: he does not take them straight to Jesus but goes to Andrew, probably because the enquirers are Gentiles and Jesus had said he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel (Matthew 15:24). He is the man who did the arithmetic on the loaves and concluded it could not be done (6:7). Andrew is the man who brought the boy with the lunch anyway (6:8–9), and who brought his brother Peter in the first place (1:41).

The hour has come. Jesus’ hour is the time of his death and glorification. Three times John has told us it had not yet come: at Cana (2:4), at the feast when no one laid a hand on him (7:30), in the treasury (8:20). Now the clock strikes, and what makes it strike is not the arrest, the plot or the entry into Jerusalem, but a handful of foreigners asking to see him, because the Gentiles can truly see him only through his death, when he is lifted up and draws all people (v. 32).

The Son of Man. The title comes from Daniel 7, where “one like a son of man” is given dominion over all peoples, nations and languages (Daniel 7:13–14). Greeks ask for him, and he answers with the title that has the nations written into it; and his dominion over every people was bought with his blood.

To be glorified. “Glorified” takes in the cross, resurrection and return to the Father as one (see the note on v. 16). The cross is not a defeat followed by glory; the cross is itself the glory.

How can a crucifixion be glorious? Glory in Scripture is the shining out of who God is, and nowhere does it shine more brightly than at the cross: his holiness, which will not overlook sin; his justice, which punishes it fully; his love, which bears that punishment himself for his enemies; his power, which turns the worst crime in history into the salvation of the world. A crucifixion was meant to be the most shameful death imaginable; God made it the place where he is most honoured. That is why Paul could say, “far be it from me to boast except in the cross” (Galatians 6:14).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus must die, as a seed is buried, to bring a harvest from every nation; and whoever clings to his own life loses it, while whoever lets it go for Christ keeps it for ever.

Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth. He answers a request from Gentiles with a fact about farming: they want to see him, and he tells them what it will cost to be seen. In the gentlest image available, days before it happens, he is telling them he is going to die. A seed kept in a jar stays exactly what it is. It “remains alone”, an odd word for a seed and the right word for him.

It bears much fruit. Planted, the seed is truly lost, and a plant grows with many seeds. The grain of wheat fell into the ground outside Jerusalem and lay there until the third day, and from it has come a harvest that fills the earth, including the Greeks who have just asked for him: the wall that kept them out comes down because the seed goes into the ground.

Whoever loves his life loses it. “Life” here (psychē) means the self, one’s earthly life. Clinging to it, living for yourself, is the way to lose everything.

Whoever hates his life. “Hates” is a Hebrew way of saying loves less, prefers something else, as when Jesus says a disciple must hate his father and mother (Luke 14:26), or God says, “I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated” (Malachi 1:2–3), where the sense is choosing and setting aside rather than malice. It is not self-loathing but ranking Christ above self. Whoever holds his life as the thing to be preserved at all costs finds he cannot keep it; whoever holds it loosely, because something matters more, gets it back.

The loneliness of the kept life. Our culture sincerely tells us the opposite: protect yourself, keep your options open, let nothing cost you too much. But notice the word Jesus chooses for the seed kept safe: it “remains alone”. Martin Luther described the human heart as curved in on itself, and a heart bent inward is safe as a seed in a jar is safe: untouched, unfruitful and alone. It is perhaps no accident that an age so devoted to self-protection is also so lonely.

He goes into the ground first. Jesus does not answer by telling us to try harder at self-sacrifice, which would only make the self a new project; nor is letting go a way of earning eternal life. The grain of wheat that wins the harvest is Christ, not us. Our letting go follows his, and is possible only because he has already given his life for ours. A person who knows he has been loved by someone who would not keep his own life can at last afford to spend his.

What does falling into the ground look like in ordinary life? Usually not martyrdom, but many small deaths: the evening you wanted, given to someone who needs you; a grudge you had every right to hold, let go; obedience that costs a promotion or a friendship; years poured into children, a church or a neighbour without seeing the fruit. Each feels like loss, and each is a seed. Ask a plain question: what would you be unable to obey God about, if he asked? Not what you would find hard; what is genuinely not on the table. That is the part of your life you are still loving in the sense this verse means. Bring it to the one who gave up his life for you before you gave up anything for him. You do not let go by willpower: the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you (Romans 8:11), and he gives the strength to plant it and wait for the fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To serve Jesus is to follow him on the road of the grain of wheat, and the Father will honour those who do; Jesus himself, deeply troubled, does not turn back from the hour he came for.

He must follow me. His servants will be with him in glory (14:3; 17:24), but first they follow him on the road there, and the place he is going in a few days is a cross.

The Father will honor him. Not human glory but the Father’s approval, the very honour the authorities in verse 43 gave up for the approval of men. Wanting it is not a holier vanity: Jesus, who obeyed to a cross and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:8–9), offers a share in his own honour: to hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21), and to be acknowledged before his Father (Matthew 10:32). It is not wages earned; it comes to sinners who belong to Christ, as children are honoured in their father’s house because they are his. So you are free to serve where nobody notices: stack the chairs, visit the person no one visits, give without your name on it. The Father sees in secret (Matthew 6:4), and his is the only honour that lasts.

Now is my soul troubled. This is John’s Gethsemane, and it is easy to miss that he has one. John has no agony in the garden; in chapter 18 Jesus walks out to meet the soldiers. The struggle is here, in public, days early. “Troubled” (tetaraktai) means agitated, shaken, like water stirred up. Jesus is truly human and feels the horror of what lies ahead: not just physical death, but bearing the wrath of God against sin (Mark 14:34).

And what shall I say? The sentence is the whole of Gethsemane compressed: a genuine recoil, and a genuine refusal to act on it (on the wording, see the box below).

For this purpose I have come to this hour. He says out loud, before Greeks, disciples and crowd, that his soul is in turmoil. Entirely certain of the Father’s will, entirely committed to it, and churned up about it, he does not let the trouble weaken his obedience by a syllable. Ours wavers at far less, which is why it matters that his did not: by his obedience, offered in our place, the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

Is it a sin to feel troubled about what God is asking of me? No. Jesus was troubled, and he never sinned (Hebrews 4:15). Dread, grief and fear in the face of suffering are part of being human in a fallen world; what matters is what you do with them. Jesus brought his trouble to the Father, named it honestly, and chose the Father’s glory over his own escape. You may do the same: tell God exactly how you feel, ask for help, and then say, “for this purpose I am here.” Obedience does not require that you stop feeling. It requires that you keep going.

Uncertain wording. The Greek was written with little or no punctuation, so “Father, save me from this hour” can be read as a question he considers and rejects, as the ESV prints it, or as a real prayer, like “let this cup pass” in the garden, answered by himself in the next breath. The Greek allows either, and the meaning is the same both ways: the recoil is real, and so is the refusal to act on it.

parallels.desc: Gethsemane

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays not to escape but that the Father’s name be glorified, and the Father answers aloud from heaven, though many heard only noise.

Father, glorify your name. Not “save me”, but “glorify your name”, like “your will be done” in Gethsemane. God’s name is God himself as he has made himself known: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, and by no means clearing the guilty (Exodus 34:5–7). To ask the Father to glorify his name is to ask that who he truly is be seen and honoured, and Jesus knows where it will be seen most clearly: at the cross.

A voice came from heaven. The third time in the Gospels, after the baptism (Mark 1:11) and the transfiguration (Mark 9:7).

I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again. He has glorified it in Jesus’ life and signs; he will glorify it again in his death and resurrection. All that has happened and all that is about to happen is one work. The Father answered the Son in the hour of his trouble, and the answer was glory.

It had thundered. Others said an angel had spoken. Some heard only noise; others knew it was speech, but not whose (compare Paul’s companions on the Damascus road, Acts 9:7; 22:9). In the Old Testament God’s voice is likened to thunder (Psalm 29:3; Exodus 19:19). They could not receive it as words spoken to them, so it became mere weather, which asks nothing of anyone. People still do this with God: they do not deny that something happened; they call it coincidence or psychology, and so need not answer it.

Should I expect God to speak to me with an audible voice? That is not how he has promised to guide us. Many sincere Christians see this differently, and God is free to work as he pleases, but the guidance he has promised is his word; the voice from heaven was a rare act at the climax of redemption. God has now spoken fully in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and his word is written in Scripture, complete and sufficient for all we need for salvation and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17; the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). The Spirit speaks through that word, opening it to our hearts. So when you want to hear God, open the Bible; and when he speaks there, do not file it as thunder.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cross is the hour when the world is judged and Satan thrown out: what looks like the world’s verdict on Jesus is God’s verdict on the world.

For your sake, not mine. Jesus did not need the voice; as he said at the tomb, “I knew that you always hear me” (11:42). It was for the crowd, to confirm him.

Now is the judgment of this world. Not at the end of history: now. The trial in which the world condemns Jesus is the trial in which the world is condemned. And the cross shows what a holy God thinks of sin: laid on his own Son, it was not spared (Romans 8:32). No one should imagine sin a small thing to God.

The ruler of this world cast out. “The ruler of this world” is Satan (14:30; 16:11; 2 Corinthians 4:4). The verb is ekballō, the ordinary word for throwing something out and the word used all through the Gospels for casting out demons: the exorcist’s word, applied to the chief of them. By the cross Christ removed the ground of Satan’s accusation, our sin (Colossians 2:14–15; Hebrews 2:14–15; Revelation 12:9–11). Satan still works, but he is a defeated enemy.

The enemy’s own plan. The enemy arranged that execution. He entered Judas (13:27) and got exactly what he wanted, and it became the means of his eviction, in the very hour of his apparent triumph: the oldest pattern in Scripture, the thing meant for harm becoming the thing that saves, at full scale. The Lamb overcame him, and so do all who belong to the Lamb, by his blood and by the word of their testimony (Revelation 12:11).

If Satan has been cast out, why is there still so much evil, and why am I still tempted? He is defeated but not yet destroyed, like an enemy fighting on in pockets after the decisive battle is lost: still a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), still tempting and accusing, with the world under his influence (1 John 5:19). But he cannot stop the gospel, cannot snatch a single sheep from Christ’s hand (10:28), and cannot condemn anyone for whom Christ died (Romans 8:33–34). So resist him, firm in your faith, knowing the outcome is settled. The day is near when he will be crushed under the feet of the church (Romans 16:20).

Where Christians differ: the binding of Satan. Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth, often teach that Satan will be bound only in that future reign. Many godly believers hold this, out of a desire to take prophecy at face value, and some also expect a rapture of the church before it. This commentary’s view: Jesus says Satan is cast out “now”, at the cross. Revelation 20’s binding of Satan describes this present age, in which he can no longer deceive the nations or stop the gospel going to them (Matthew 12:29). This is the amillennial view: the thousand years are the gospel age between Christ’s first and second comings. Christians on every side agree that Christ will return in glory and that Satan’s defeat is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lifted up on the cross, and by it to his throne, Jesus will draw people of every kind and nation to himself.

Lifted up from the earth. The third and last of the “lifted up” sayings in John (3:14; 8:28). It means both the cross and his exaltation (Isaiah 52:13), and it is also, brutally and literally, what happened to him: a man raised off the ground on a beam. The two meanings are one movement.

Will draw all people to myself. “Draw” (helkō) is the verb of 6:44, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”: a pulling that succeeds. The Greeks have just asked to see him, and this is the answer: through the cross he will draw people from every nation. What draws is not his teaching or miracles but a man being executed: at his most powerless he will pull the world in.

By what kind of death. John stops to explain, the only time he does so with these sayings, which settles that he means the cross without cancelling the other meaning. He was lifted up to die, and lifted up to reign, and from that throne he is drawing to himself a people no one can number.

Does this mean everyone will finally be saved? No. Some have read “all” as a promise of universal salvation, but this same Gospel records that many turned back (6:66), that some will die in their sins (8:24), and that the word Jesus spoke will judge on the last day (12:48). John does not contradict himself a few verses apart. The barrier between Jew and Gentile is down, and the cross now draws from every nation, the same promise as the other sheep who will become one flock under one shepherd (10:16). Everyone who comes to him is drawn, and everyone who is drawn will come.

Where Christians differ: does Christ draw every person? Some take “all people” to mean every individual, drawn with a resistible grace, that is, a grace that can be finally refused. Many earnest Christians read it so, out of love for the wideness of the gospel. This commentary’s view: in 6:44 the one who is drawn is raised up on the last day. If every person were drawn in that sense, every person would be saved, which Scripture denies. Here “all people” means all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews, as the context of the Greeks shows (compare 11:52). The cross draws, effectively, people from every nation.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd cannot fit a dying Messiah into what they know of Scripture, and Jesus, instead of debating, warns them to walk in the light while it is still with them.

We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. A serious objection, from the Old Testament as a whole (see the box below). They could not imagine the Messiah reaching his everlasting throne through death.

How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? They understand “lifted up” as death, and a dying Messiah made no sense to them. Paul would meet the same objection all his life: “Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Who is this Son of Man? The honest question. They have noticed that he has quietly changed the title: they said “the Christ”, he said “the Son of Man”, and they want to know whether these are the same person.

The light is among you for a little while longer. Jesus does not argue; he warns. The season for standing about asking questions is nearly over: questions can be put off, but the daylight will not wait.

Lest darkness overtake you. “Overtake” (katalabē) is the word of 1:5, where the darkness has not overcome the light. Now the darkness will overtake those who refuse the light.

Is it wrong to have unanswered questions before I believe? No. Honest questions are not sin, and many believers carry some for years. But do not make every question a condition of coming to Christ. The crowd’s question had a real answer, the Messiah would reign for ever by dying and rising, but they would see it only if they walked in the light they had. You trust what you can see of Christ now, and understanding grows as you follow. Waiting to have everything solved first is itself a choice.

Uncertain wording. No Old Testament verse says in so many words that the Christ remains for ever, so we cannot be sure which text the crowd had in mind. Several promises fit: David’s throne established for ever (Psalm 89:36–37), Isaiah’s child reigning from this time forth and for evermore (Isaiah 9:7), Ezekiel’s David prince for ever (Ezekiel 37:25), and Daniel’s son of man with a dominion that would not pass away (Daniel 7:14). Psalm 89 is often thought the likeliest: “His offspring shall endure forever” (Psalm 89:36). Most likely they mean that the Scriptures as a whole promise the Messiah an everlasting reign.

parallels.desc: his offspring shall endure forever

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus makes his last appeal to believe in the light, then hides himself; and John gives the verdict on his public ministry: after all the signs, they still did not believe.

That you may become sons of light. A Hebrew way of saying people who belong to the light and share its character (Luke 16:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). Light here is the truth of God shining in Jesus, and those who belong to it stop hiding from it (3:21): they start to love honesty, to hate the sin they once covered, and to want what God wants (Ephesians 5:8–9).

He departed and hid himself from them. The light withdraws. It is the last thing Jesus does before a crowd in this Gospel; from here on he teaches only his disciples. John used the same phrase at the end of chapter 8 (8:59), and both times it follows a moment when the light was offered and refused.

They still did not believe. Verse 37 begins John’s closing comment on the first half of his Gospel, and it takes up its great mystery: why did God’s own people reject their Messiah? The signs were many and clear, from water into wine to a man four days dead walking out of a cave. The prologue said it: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (1:11). John writes the verdict flatly, a warning against assuming that unbelief is always a failure of evidence or presentation. The second half of the book turns to those who did receive him: a few men in a room with their Lord.

Can a person put off believing for too long? Yes, and this verse is a solemn warning. The light was among them, and then it withdrew. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), because no one is promised tomorrow, and a heart that keeps refusing grows harder. But if you are concerned about your soul and want to come to Christ, that very desire shows the light has not left you. No one who comes to him is turned away (6:37). The danger is not for those who are anxious to come, but for those who are content to wait.

parallels.desc: walk as children of light

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s unbelief did not take God by surprise: Isaiah foretold it, and in judgment God confirmed those who refused the light in their refusal.

That the word might be fulfilled. John reaches for Isaiah twice to explain what he has just reported, and it matters which parts of Isaiah he takes.

Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? From Isaiah 53:1, the opening line of the great Suffering Servant passage: the man despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, led like a lamb to the slaughter. The prophet given the fullest description of the cross in the Old Testament opens it by asking who will believe the report, and the question has its answer built in: almost nobody. Seven centuries later the answer is a rejected Messiah walking away from a crowd. The unbelief is neither a surprise nor a defeat; it was written into the very passage that describes the whole work. “The arm of the Lord” is God’s power in salvation, revealed in Christ’s signs and in his cross.

Therefore they could not believe. Not merely “did not”, but “could not”: the hardest phrase in the chapter, not to be softened but to be read in order. Verse 37 says they did not believe though they had seen everything; verse 39, that at a certain point they could not. The inability follows the refusal, as it consistently does in Scripture. Pharaoh hardened his own heart through several plagues before the narrative says that God hardened it, though God had told Moses beforehand that he would (Exodus 4:21; 9:12). Romans 1 says three times that “God gave them up”, to what they had already chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). The judgment is that a man is finally given what he has insisted on; Isaiah says it in the lines John quotes next (Isaiah 6:10).

Does this mean God stops people who want to believe? No. Scripture never shows anyone truly seeking God and being turned away. Behind all human unbelief lies the fallen heart, which does not want God (3:19–20), and God in his justice may confirm a person in the refusal he has chosen. But he never turns away a sinner who seeks him. If you want Christ, that desire is itself evidence of God’s grace at work in you, not of his rejection. Come to him. The doctrine of hardening is a warning to the careless, not a threat to the seeking.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hardening Isaiah foretold is God’s judgment on unbelief, and the Lord whose glory Isaiah saw on the throne was Jesus.

He has blinded their eyes. From Isaiah 6:10, quoted freely. The passage is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts to explain Israel’s unbelief (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; Acts 28:26–27).

Lest they turn. Hardening is God’s judgment on persistent unbelief (2 Thessalonians 2:11).

He saw his glory. Isaiah 6 is the vision of the Lord on his throne, with the seraphim crying, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:1–5), and John says that glory was Christ’s. Some take him to mean only that Isaiah foresaw Christ’s glory, but John has just quoted Isaiah 6, and the glory seen there was the Lord’s on his throne. This is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is the Lord of the Old Testament, Yahweh himself, and John makes it almost in passing.

High and lifted up. Isaiah saw him “high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1); the same pair of words describes the Servant in Isaiah 52:13, at the start of the passage John has just quoted; and “lifted up” is Jesus’ own phrase for his death. The throne and the cross are described in the same language. The glory the seraphim could not look at is the glory of a man on a Roman cross outside a city wall, and this Gospel has said so since the prologue: “we have seen his glory” (1:14).

Paid for by the King himself. Isaiah cried “Woe is me” before that throne, and a seraph touched his lips with a burning coal from the altar, and his guilt was taken away (Isaiah 6:6–7). That cleansing was paid for, in the end, by the King himself, who became the sacrifice every altar pointed to, so that unclean lips like Isaiah’s and ours might be made fit to sing his praise.

What it does not mean. Not that God is the author of sin, or that they were innocent victims: they had seen and rejected the light first (see the note on v. 39). Nor that all Israel is hardened for ever: Paul says a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11:25), and many Jews have believed and will believe.

How far does God’s hand reach in hardening? Some read hardening only as God giving people over to the unbelief they have chosen; others, with Romans 9:17–24, see his sovereign purpose behind it. Scripture holds both: God hardens, and those hardened are responsible, “for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God” (v. 43). On those who seek him, see the note on vv. 38–39.

Has God then rejected the Jewish people? No. Paul answers directly: “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). There has always been a remnant chosen by grace, Paul among them. Christians differ on how Romans 11:25–26 will be fulfilled: some expect a large turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, others read “all Israel” as the full number of the elect from Jews and Gentiles together. But all agree that God’s promises do not fail, that Jewish people are saved in the same way as everyone else, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians owe them love, humility and the gospel, never contempt.

Could I be hardened? If you are worried that you might be, that worry is a sign you are not: hardened hearts are not anxious about God but indifferent. The warning is for anyone who has heard the gospel many times and keeps saying “not yet”, and the answer is what it always has been: turn to Christ today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13–15). He has never refused anyone who came.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple; John says that glory was Christ’s.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull
I saw the Lord, high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the leaders believed but kept it hidden, because they valued the approval of men above the approval of God.

Many even of the authorities believed in him. John uses his full phrase, “believed in him”; by his own vocabulary these are not mere admirers. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were probably among these secret believers (19:38–39).

For fear of the Pharisees. Belief without confession. The threat was being put out of the synagogue, which the parents of the blind man also feared (9:22). It meant being cut off from the community’s worship and much of its family, social and business life (compare 16:2).

The glory that comes from man. “Glory” (doxa) here means honour, approval, reputation. Isaiah saw the glory of Christ enthroned; these men preferred the approval of the room. Jesus had made the same charge: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (5:44). So the issue is not chiefly cowardice but whose approval a man is living for.

Naming the cost. More useful than resolving to be braver is to name precisely what would be lost, the promotion, the friendship, the family meal, the standing in a particular room, and ask what it is worth, and whose opinion is being bought with it. In Christ the Father has already welcomed you as his child, so you can afford to lose the room’s. Pick one place where you have kept quiet about Christ, and ask him for an opportunity to speak there.

Is this saving faith? Jesus said that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (Mark 8:38), and Scripture joins confession with the mouth to belief in the heart (Romans 10:9–10). Their faith is at best weak and immature, at worst not real.

Am I saved if I have kept my faith secret? This needs care, because these verses can be preached so as to produce despair in exactly the wrong people. Look at whom John places in this category. Nicodemus came at night, yet he brought about seventy-five pounds of spices to the cross (19:39). Joseph was a disciple secretly, for fear of the Jews, yet he asked Pilate for the body when the twelve had scattered (19:38). Both came through: a hidden faith is a dangerous condition, not a settled verdict. If you are hiding your faith, do not conclude you are lost. Conclude that you must come out, and ask Christ for the courage he gave those two men. Start with one person this week.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To believe in Jesus is to believe in the Father who sent him, and to see Jesus is to see the Father: there is no other God behind him.

Jesus cried out. A shout, the verb used on the last day of the feast (7:37), much like the cry at the tomb (11:43). He hid himself in verse 36, and no new scene is described, so these verses (vv. 44–50) are probably a summary of his public teaching, placed here as his last word to the world.

Not in me but in him who sent me. Faith in Jesus does not stop with him but reaches the Father: it is not a dead end but a window.

Whoever sees me. Jesus is the perfect revelation of the Father (1:18; 14:9). There is no hidden God behind Jesus who is different from him. The one who wept at Lazarus’s grave, washed his disciples’ feet and died for his enemies is not a softer image of a harder God. So when you wonder what God is like, how he feels about you, whether he can be trusted, do not guess: look at Jesus in the Gospels. That is the Father’s face.

Do other religions worship the same God, just without Jesus? Not according to Jesus. If to see him is to see the Father, then to reject him is to reject the Father; whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (5:23). People of other faiths may truly know that God exists and that they are accountable to him (Romans 1:19–20), and they deserve respect and love. But the God who is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is known and worshipped truly only through his Son (14:6). That is why we share the gospel with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came as light to bring people out of darkness; the purpose of his coming was to save the world, not to condemn it.

I have come into the world as light. The prologue said it of him (1:9); in his last public words he says it once more, and adds what it is for.

May not remain in darkness. “Remain” assumes that everyone starts there. Darkness is not a mood but life without the knowledge of God: not seeing him truly, loving what he hates, and standing under his judgment without knowing it (3:19; Ephesians 4:18). Faith brings us out.

I did not come to judge the world. This is 3:17 again: whatever else is said about judgment, the purpose of his coming never changes.

So does Jesus judge or not? Both, in different senses. He came the first time to save, not condemn, and anyone who comes to him finds mercy. Yet light exposes darkness, so his coming divides (3:19–21; 9:39), and on the last day he will judge all (5:22, 27). How the two fit follows at once (v. 48): he need not pronounce a new sentence on those who reject him, for the word they refused will itself be the standard. The purpose of his coming is salvation; judgment is the consequence of refusing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever sets Jesus aside will be judged on the last day by the very words he spoke, because those words are the Father’s.

The one who rejects me. The word means setting aside, disregarding, rather than arguing against. Nobody in John 12 has refuted Jesus: the council admitted the signs, the crowd hailed him as king, and some authorities believed. Most rejection of Christ happens this way: not a conclusion reached, but a subject dropped.

The word that I have spoken will judge him. His words themselves will be the evidence: spoken publicly, written down, and available ever since in a great many languages. To hear the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility (Matthew 11:20–24; Hebrews 2:1–3). It is never neutral once heard: it arrives as an offer, and it stays as a standard.

Not on my own authority. His words are the Father’s, which is why rejecting them is so serious. To refuse them is not to disagree with a Galilean rabbi. It is to have been handed, by the Father through the Son, a commandment whose content is eternal life, and to have put it down.

What about those who never heard Christ’s words? They will not be judged for rejecting a message they never received. God judges each person justly, by the light he was actually given, and every person has some light: the witness of creation and of conscience, enough to leave them without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). But that light cannot save, because salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–14). Infants who die in infancy and are elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). Grieving parents may entrust their little one to the Lord who took children in his arms (Mark 10:16), and to the Judge of all the earth, who always does right (Genesis 18:25). And this is why the church sends missionaries: so that those who have never heard may hear the words that give life.

parallels.desc: I will put my words in his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father’s commandment that Jesus speaks is itself eternal life, and he has spoken only what the Father told him.

His commandment is eternal life. Not that his commandment leads to eternal life, as we might expect: it is life. The words are the thing itself, as he said in Capernaum when the crowd was leaving: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (6:63). And the life they give is not mere endless existence but knowing the Father and the Son he sent (17:3), a life that begins the moment a person believes. So the public ministry ends where the prologue began: “In him was life, and the life was the light of men” (1:4).

As the Father has told me. Jesus’ last public words in John are complete obedience to the Father; from chapter 13 he is alone with the Twelve.

Three years of speaking. For three years he talked to anybody: crowds who wanted bread, a woman at a well at noon, a teacher by night, men who twice picked up stones, a beggar the synagogue threw out. His last word to them all, at the top of his voice, is that the message was never his own, and that its content is life. Then he went from that street to give that life at the cost of his own. “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (6:68).

How do I read Jesus’ words so that they give me life? Read them as the Father’s words to you, not as information about the past: slowly, asking what each passage shows you of Christ and asks of you; with prayer, asking the Spirit who inspired them to open them (14:26); and with others, in your church, where the word is preached. And obey what you understand: the words of Christ give life to those who keep them, not to those who only admire them (8:51). Life does not come from reading as a technique, but from the living Christ who speaks through what is read.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.<sup>2</sup>So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.<sup>3</sup>Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.<sup>4</sup>But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,<sup>5</sup>“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”<sup>6</sup>He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.<sup>8</sup>For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”<sup>9</sup>When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.<sup>10</sup>So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well,<sup>11</sup>because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.<sup>12</sup>The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!”<sup>14</sup>And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,<sup>15</sup>“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!”<sup>16</sup>His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.<sup>17</sup>The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness.<sup>18</sup>The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.<sup>19</sup>So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”<sup>20</sup>Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.<sup>21</sup>So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”<sup>22</sup>Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.<sup>23</sup>And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.<sup>25</sup>Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.<sup>26</sup>If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.<sup>27</sup>“Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ’Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.<sup>28</sup>Father, glorify your name.“ Then a voice came from heaven: ”I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”<sup>29</sup>The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”<sup>30</sup>Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine.<sup>31</sup>Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.<sup>32</sup>And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”<sup>33</sup>He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>34</sup>So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”<sup>35</sup>So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.<sup>36</sup>While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them.<sup>37</sup>Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,<sup>38</sup>so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”<sup>39</sup>Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,<sup>40</sup>“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.”<sup>41</sup>Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.<sup>42</sup>Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue;<sup>43</sup>for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.<sup>44</sup>And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me.<sup>45</sup>And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.<sup>46</sup>I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.<sup>47</sup>If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.<sup>48</sup>The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.<sup>49</sup>For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment—what to say and what to speak.<sup>50</sup>And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.”
12.overview:
Where we are. Lazarus has walked out of his tomb, and the council has resolved that Jesus must die (11:47–53). Chapter 12 opens the last week and closes the first half of the Gospel, the book of signs: after it Jesus speaks only to his disciples, and then goes to the cross.

The message. The hour has come. The King has arrived in Jerusalem, and he will be glorified not by seizing a throne but by dying, like a grain of wheat that falls into the earth and bears much fruit. Lifted up on the cross, he will cast out the ruler of this world and draw people of every nation to himself.

Why it was said. John’s readers, Jews and Gentiles, some of whom had been put out of the synagogue for confessing Jesus (see the introduction), needed to know why God’s own people had largely refused their Messiah, that this was foreseen and did not defeat God’s purpose, and that God’s approval is worth more than the room’s.

How the chapter makes its case. At Bethany Mary pours out a year’s wages on Jesus’ feet, and he receives it as anointing for his burial, while the chief priests plot against Lazarus (vv. 1–11). The crowds, stirred by Lazarus, hail him as King of Israel, and he answers their palms with a donkey, Zechariah’s king of peace (vv. 12–19). When Greeks ask to see him, he announces that his hour has come: the seed must die, and his servants must follow (vv. 20–26). Troubled, he prays that the Father glorify his name, heaven answers, and he says his death will judge the world, cast out its ruler and draw all people (vv. 27–36). John explains Israel’s unbelief from Isaiah and exposes believers who would not confess (vv. 37–43), and Jesus’ last public cry declares that the Father’s word he speaks is eternal life (vv. 44–50).

Where it leads. The anointing, the entry and the seed all lean toward the death six days away, and John shows that death as glory: the Lord Isaiah saw “high and lifted up” is the one about to be lifted up on a cross (vv. 32, 41). His death is not defeat but harvest: Greeks who could go no further than the temple court are drawn to him, and the world is still going after him.

For us. Christ held nothing back, and he deserves Mary’s nard, not Judas’s calculation. To follow him is to let go of the life we cling to, trusting that the seed that dies bears fruit and that the Father honours those who serve his Son. While the light is with us, believe him openly, and do not trade his approval for anyone else’s.

keyVerse.quote: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
keyVerse.note: Here is the chapter in one picture. Greeks have just asked to see Jesus, and he answers that his death is the way the harvest comes: kept back, he would remain alone; buried, he will bear fruit from every nation. The same pattern then shapes everyone who follows him, who keep their lives by letting them go (v. 25).

12.reflection:
Mary poured out a year’s wages on Jesus, and Judas called it waste (vv. 3–6). What would extravagant love for Christ look like in your life, and where do you find yourself calculating instead?

The crowd hailed Jesus as King of Israel but wanted a king on their own terms, and he answered with a donkey (vv. 12–15). In what ways are we tempted to follow Jesus only while he seems to give us what we want?

“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (v. 24). What small deaths is following Christ asking of you now, and how does his going into the ground first make them possible?

Some of the authorities believed but would not confess him, because they loved the glory that comes from man (vv. 42–43). Whose approval would you find hardest to lose, and where might God be asking you to speak?

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus loves his own to the end, and shows it by doing a slave’s work, washing feet that stand for hearts. Knowing that all things are in his hands, he lays aside his garments and kneels with a towel (vv. 1–5). Peter’s protests draw out the meaning: unless Christ washes us we have no share with him, yet the one who has bathed needs only his feet washed, and Judas, though washed, is not clean (vv. 6–11). Then Jesus makes the act a pattern: if the Lord serves, his servants must serve, and blessing lies in doing it (vv. 12–17). One at his table will turn on him, as the psalm foretold, and when it happens they are to believe that he is who he claims to be (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The footwashing is both a moral example (“do just as I have done to you”) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (“If I do not wash you, you have no share with me”). The one already bathed needs only his feet washed (see the note on vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus washes feet because he knows exactly who he is, and that security is what frees his people to serve (see the note on vv. 3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing that his death is upon him, Jesus loves his own to the very end and to the uttermost, with the betrayer already at the table. The second half of the Gospel begins here, and at the centre of its last evening John sets what the others leave out: the Lord of glory on the floor with a towel.

The setting. It is Thursday evening in an upper room in Jerusalem, at Passover, and before the sun sets again the true Passover Lamb will be dead and buried. Everything to the end of chapter 17 is said in a few hours, to men who will all run away before morning.

His hour had come. All through the Gospel the hour has not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now it has, and John’s word for his death is gentle: a departure (metabē, a crossing over) out of this world to the Father, at the feast that remembered the night the LORD passed over Israel’s houses. For Jesus the cross is not the end of a road but a doorway home.

His own. John used this word (idios) twice in one of the saddest verses of the prologue: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (1:11). Now, on the last night, he has his own again, eleven men in a room and one who is leaving, and this time the sentence ends differently. His own are those the Father gave him (10:3–4; 17:6), the sheep he calls by name.

He loved them to the end. “To the end” (eis telos) means both to the end of his life and to the uttermost. John does not choose between how long and how much, because both are true: he loved them to his last minute, and as far as love can go. Chapters 13–17 express this love, and so does the cross that follows.

Into the heart of Judas. The money is already agreed (Mark 14:10–11). The devil planted the idea, and Judas welcomed it. John tells us before the basin comes out, so that we watch the whole washing knowing it: love and treachery at one table, and Jesus, knowing it all, washes Judas’s feet anyway.

In everyday life. Most of us have a quiet stopping point in our love: the colleague who let us down once, the relative privately written off. Love one of them past that point, with an act that costs something. You can love one step further than you did, because you have been loved all the way.

Does “to the end” mean Jesus’ love for me could still run out? No; it means the opposite. It is the measure of a love tested at its worst point and found to hold: when one of the Twelve was selling him, when Peter was about to deny him, when all were about to run. If it did not fail them that night, it will not fail you on yours. No one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (10:28), and nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38–39). The question is not whether his love will last but whether you are one of his own, and his own hear his voice and follow him. If you want to follow him, however falteringly, that wanting is itself his voice at work in you.

Is there a contradiction about the date? John places this before the Feast, says the authorities avoided the governor’s headquarters so that they might eat the Passover (18:28), and calls the day of the crucifixion the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14); the other Gospels present the Last Supper plainly as the Passover meal. The tension is real but smaller than it looks. Preparation is the ordinary Greek word for Friday, as it still is, so the phrase most naturally means the Friday of Passover week. And Passover was used loosely for the whole seven-day festival (see the Feast of Unleavened Bread), so to eat the Passover at 18:28 can mean the festival meals that followed. Read that way, all four agree: the supper was the Passover meal, and Jesus was crucified on the Friday of the feast. Another long-standing solution is that different groups reckoned the feast a day apart. Neither can be proved, but both show that the accounts can honestly be read together. What should not be said is that John invented a date to make a point: Jesus really did die at Passover, and John’s theme, behold the Lamb of God, was handed to him by the calendar, not the other way round.

Where are the bread and the cup? The other three Gospels record the institution of the Lord’s Supper at this table, and Paul had already written it down for the Corinthians. John gives us a basin and a towel instead. Writing last, with the other accounts long in circulation and the church keeping the Supper for some sixty years, he supplies what is missing rather than repeating what everyone has. He had already given the meaning of that meal in chapter 6, the bread from heaven, the flesh given for the life of the world; here he shows what it requires.

Uncertain wording. The King James Version reads “supper being ended”, but “during supper” fits what follows: Jesus rises from the meal (v. 4), and it is still going on at verse 26. And verse 2 is compressed, literally “the devil having already put into the heart that Judas should betray him”. Nearly all translations take it, as the ESV does, as Judas’s heart; a few interpreters read it as the devil’s own, meaning he had already resolved on the betrayal. Either way the plan was Satan’s, Judas made it his own (v. 27), and Jesus knew.
verseByVerse.note: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17). “Simon’s son” is a different Simon from Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stoops to a slave’s work not because he has forgotten who he is, but because he knows exactly who he is. John gives him the largest possible credentials, all things in his hands (3:35), come from God, going to God, and the next thing those hands do is pick up a towel.

Rose from supper. In the middle of the meal, not at the door, where a servant would have done it. Apparently nobody had. Luke tells us that at this same supper the Twelve argued about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24); Jesus may well have got up in the middle of it.

He laid aside his outer garments. Laid aside (tithēmi) is the word he used repeatedly in chapter 10 of his life: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11, 15, 17, 18). In verse 12 he takes his garments again, with the verb he used for taking his life up again (10:17–18). The washing is an acted picture of his death and resurrection, hours before they happen, and behind it lies the whole movement of the incarnation: he who was in the form of God emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the point of death (Philippians 2:6–8).

This is what his glory is like. With a towel he dresses as a slave, the lowest person in the household, whose task it was to wash the guests’ feet (see sandals and washing feet). The hands that hold all things together tied it round his waist. He had come from God and was going to God, and between the two he went down to the floor, not because he lost sight of his glory, but because this is what his glory is like. The God of glory knelt, and he knelt for us.

Where does the freedom to serve come from? Not from thinking little of yourself. John has just told us in the most extravagant terms who this man is, and gives that as the reason he can kneel. Nobody still trying to establish his position can afford to take the towel. So the Christian’s freedom to serve grows out of knowing who he is in Christ: a child of God, forgiven, loved, his future secure. A man accepted by the Father no longer needs the best seat to prove anything.

Isn’t humility just weakness dressed up as virtue? Friedrich Nietzsche thought so, and he was not a fool. He called Christianity a slave morality: the weak, resenting the strong, had renamed their weakness goodness. He was right that the ancient world did not admire humility: the Greek word for lowly described the servile and abject, and Aristotle’s ideal man claimed the honour he knew he deserved. That we count humility a virtue at all is largely the legacy of this scene and the cross it points to. But Nietzsche had the origin backwards. The man with the towel is not one of the resentful weak; all things have been given into his hands. Humility here does not rise from below as envy; it comes down from above as love, the shape strength takes when it has nothing to prove and someone to save.
verseByVerse.note: Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; roads were dusty and people wore sandals.

parallels.desc: I am among you as the one who serves

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord of glory kneels to do the lowest job in the house, even for Judas, and Peter is shocked, because grace turns everything the wrong way up.

A basin. Footwashing was no quaint courtesy: feet arriving at a house were filthy, and washing them was the bottom job on the household list. Later rabbinic writings say that a Jewish slave could not be required to do it, and record a rabbi teaching that a disciple should do anything for his teacher except loosen his sandal. A basin had stood in that room all evening, untouched. Then the Lord of glory kneels at each pair of feet in turn.

He came to Simon Peter. Peter’s objection seems to come partway round the table. At some point Jesus knelt in front of Judas, Judas put his feet in the water, and neither said anything John thought worth recording.
