Lord, do you wash my feet? In Greek “you” and “my” stand side by side: Lord, you, my feet? Peter is not being falsely modest, and his instinct is right as far as it goes: lords do not wash feet. What he cannot yet accept is a Lord who does, and within a day he will have to accept a Lord who is executed, the same problem at full scale. The incarnation (God the Son becoming man) and the atonement (his death for our sins) are this same reversal: the Holy One serving the unholy, the Judge kneeling before the guilty to make them clean.

In everyday life. Think of the person whose feet you would least like to wash: the one who has used you, or criticised you, or simply wearies you. Do that person one hidden kindness this week, as he did for Judas without a word.

Why did Jesus wash Judas’s feet if he knew? Because his love is not a reward for loyalty. He knew Judas had already sold him, and the knowledge did not change the service by one degree. It was a real kindness and, like the morsel in verse 26, a real appeal, though it was refused. It also shows that the command to wash one another’s feet reaches even those who will wrong us (Luke 6:27–28). It does not mean Judas was cleansed; verse 10 says plainly he was not. Outward kindness from Christ is not the same as inward cleansing by Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless Christ washes us we have no part in him, so refusing his washing, however humble it looks, is refusing salvation. What Peter cannot understand now, he will understand after the cross.

Afterward you will understand. The explanation comes a few verses later, but the fuller understanding is promised for after the cross and resurrection, when the Spirit would bring these things to mind (12:16; 14:26) and Peter would see that this washing pointed to Jesus’ death for him. Much of the Christian life is lived from here: something is being done that makes no sense while it happens, and we are given not an explanation but Jesus’ word that it will make sense later. John, writing some sixty years afterwards, had seen the afterward arrive.

You shall never. He is not hesitating; he is forbidding. It is pride dressed up as humility, and refusing grace is not humility.

No share with me. The word means an allotted share (meros). The washing now clearly means more than feet: unless Christ cleanses us from sin, we have no part in him or his kingdom. Peter thinks he is defending his master’s dignity, when in fact he is refusing his own salvation, and to him the two feel exactly the same. But Christ will not be refused, because his love will not leave us dirty.

The refusal that looks like reverence. Some refusals of grace look like humility: “I could not ask that”, “others need it more”, “I will manage”. Ask what each protects. Reverence protects God’s honour; this refusal protects our picture of ourselves as people who do not need to be carried, and it can keep a man out of the kingdom while he is admired for it. “I am not worthy” can be a deeper refusal than “I do not need it”.

What if I feel too dirty or too unworthy to come to Christ? Then you are exactly the person he washes. The basin is for dirty feet. Feeling unworthy is not the obstacle; refusing to let him do what only he can do is. You do not clean yourself up first: you come as you are and let him wash you, and that is what faith is. His word to Peter is his word to you: unless he washes you, you have no part with him, and if he washes you, you are completely clean (v. 10).

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one Christ has washed is completely clean and never needs saving again, but he does need the dust of each day washed away. One bath, many footwashings.

Not my feet only. Peter swings to the opposite extreme, entirely in character. He is wrong twice in ninety seconds, in opposite directions, and both times because he is trying to set the terms: first he will have none of it, then more than is offered. What he never does is simply put his feet in the water.

Bathed and completely clean. The one who has bathed (louō, to wash the whole body) does not need to wash (niptō, to wash a part). Guests bathed at home before a banquet and walked through the streets, so that on arrival only their feet needed attention. Nobody had a second bath at the door.

Justification once, cleansing daily. Here is the doctrine of assurance and confession in a household image. The one cleansed by Christ once for all, in justification and in regeneration, the new birth (Titus 3:5), does not need to be saved again. Justification is God’s verdict that a sinner is right with him because Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5); it is not lost when a believer stumbles and won back, because it never rested on how well he walks. Yet the walking does soil, daily and genuinely, and the feet do need washing (1 John 1:7–9). Justification happens once; confession and forgiveness go on.

But not every one of you. The disciples are clean by the word he has spoken to them (15:3), but not all. Twelve pairs of feet were washed; eleven men are clean.

When I sin as a Christian, do I need to be saved all over again? No. If you have truly trusted Christ, you have had the bath, and you are completely clean in God’s sight; your standing as his child does not lapse every time you fall. What you need is the footwashing: bring that sin to him in honest confession, trust that he forgives it (1 John 1:9), and get up and walk on. A believer who keeps asking to be saved again is like Peter asking for his head to be washed; a believer who never confesses is walking about with dirty feet. Both the once-for-all and the daily belong to the Christian life.

Textual note. One important early manuscript and some early Christian writers lack the words except for his feet, and a footnote may appear in a modern Bible. The shorter reading gives essentially the same sense, that the bathed man does not need washing, and the distinction between the bath and the feet is carried by the two verbs regardless.
verseByVerse.note: Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival.

parallels.desc: you are already clean

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus knew all along who would betray him, and having finished the washing he sits down again as Teacher to explain what he has done.

For he knew. We are told twice, at verse 2 and here, that nothing about Judas was hidden. This is not a story about a man who was fooled.

Resumed his place. He took (elaben) his garments, the verb of taking up his life again (10:17–18), completing the picture verse 4 began: he went down, and he came back. He knew who would betray him and knelt anyway; he knew the whole cost of the cross and laid down his life anyway, and took it up again. Nothing about us takes him by surprise, and nothing in us made him withdraw.

Do you understand what I have done to you? The sign first and the explanation after is his method throughout this Gospel: water into wine before anyone knew what to make of it, the five thousand fed before the discourse about bread, the blind man healed before he spoke of who is truly blind (9:39–41). Here he washes twelve pairs of feet in silence and then asks what they made of it, not to expose them (v. 7) but to begin the explanation: the washing has a second meaning, as an example for them to follow.

The warning of the means of grace. Judas received the footwashing with the eleven, but without the cleansing it signified. Taking part outwardly in the means of grace (baptism, the Lord’s Supper, the preaching of the word) does not by itself produce inward cleansing. They are genuine means by which God blesses his people, but they bless through faith, not apart from it: they feed the faith of those who trust his Son, and to the one who does not trust him they bring only greater accountability (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

Can a person go to church, be baptised and take communion, and still not be saved? Sadly, yes, and Judas is the warning. He was chosen as an apostle, lived with Jesus for about three years, preached, saw miracles, and had his feet washed by the Son of God, and he was not clean. This is said not to make sincere believers anxious but to stop anyone resting on outward things. The question is not whether you have been near Jesus but whether you have trusted him. If you have come to him as a sinner and rest on him alone, the outward signs are real blessings to you. If you have not, no amount of religious contact will substitute. Come to him today.

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Jesus, who really is Lord and Teacher, washed their feet, his followers owe one another the same lowly service.

Teacher and Lord. Jesus does not disclaim the titles. His service does not lessen his authority; it shows what kind of Lord he is.

You also ought. If the Lord serves, how much more the servants. Ought (opheilete) is the language of a debt owed (on the pattern, see v. 15).

The harder obedience. A church that does not wash feet is under exactly the same obligation, and has a harder time discharging it, because the substance is not a ritual with a towel but the willingness to do for one another the job nobody wants. A footwashing service can be got through in twenty minutes once a year; what he describes has no fixed occasion and no end.

What does washing one another’s feet look like today? Doing the needed thing nobody notices or wants: cleaning up after the church meal, visiting the elderly member who repeats herself, changing the nappy, sitting with the dying, driving the person without a car, doing the paperwork for the widow, listening to the same trouble for the fifth time. It includes the humbler work of forgiving, of bearing with someone’s faults, and of gently helping a brother with his sin (Galatians 6:1–2). The mark of footwashing is that it is beneath your dignity and meets a real need.

Where Christians differ: is footwashing an ordinance? Some churches practise it as a regular ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and they are not being silly: the sentence says you also ought to wash one another’s feet. This commentary’s view: Jesus calls it an example (v. 15), not a sacrament. There is no record that the apostles practised or commanded it as a church rite; in 1 Timothy 5:10 it appears as an act of humble hospitality. The command is to do humble, menial, loving service that meets real needs, whatever form that takes today. A literal footwashing can be a moving act, but the point is the lowly love behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Jesus has done is a pattern to copy, and no servant of his may think himself too great for what his Master has done.

For I have given you an example. A pattern laid down to be copied (hypodeigma; compare 1 Peter 2:21).

Just as I have done. The measure is the original act, done by someone with all things in his hands, for people arguing about rank, one of whom was selling him. The pattern has specifications: it is voluntary, it goes downward, it is done for people who will not repay it, and at least one recipient does not deserve it.

A servant is not greater than his master. If the master is not too proud to wash feet, the servant cannot be. The proverb returns in chapter 15 with a harder edge: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (15:20). It cuts twice: it limits how high a disciple may hold himself, and warns him not to expect gentler treatment than his master received.

Nor is a messenger greater. The word for messenger is apostle (apostolos), its only appearance in John’s Gospel, in a sentence about not being above the job. It cuts against the servant who begins to think the work is his. Everything an apostle has, the message, the authority, the commission, came from someone else.

In everyday life. If you serve in church in any visible way, watch for the sign that you have begun to think of the work as yours: the sting when someone else gets the credit, or when your role is changed without your being consulted.

Am I meant to copy everything Jesus did? Not everything. Some of what he did belongs to him alone: he alone died for sins, rose from the dead, and is Lord. We follow him as servants, not substitutes. But in his humility, his love and his patience toward the undeserving he is meant to be copied, and the footwashing is given as exactly that kind of example. Peter says Christ left us an example so that we might follow in his steps, and in the same breath that he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:21–24). He is first our Saviour, and then our pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessing lies in doing what Jesus has shown, not merely knowing it; and the betrayal at his table is no surprise to him but Scripture fulfilled.

Blessed are you if you do them. Knowing is assumed; the blessing hangs on the doing (James 1:22–25), and between the two there is a gap. Yet it is spoken to men already washed and clean (v. 10): the blessing is the joy of children doing their Father’s will, not the price of becoming his, and the Helper he is about to promise (14:16–17) is the power that carries them across the gap.

What “blessed” means here. Not lucky, but favoured by God and truly well off: the word that opens the Beatitudes (makarios; Matthew 5:3). What is new is where Jesus puts it. We assume the blessed person is the one being served, as the disciples arguing over rank that evening did (Luke 22:24). Jesus puts the blessing on the floor by the basin, because that is where he is, on his way lower still, to a cross, so that we need never climb to be accepted. Timothy Keller often pointed out, following C. S. Lewis, that gospel humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. When a job feels beneath you this week, take it as the place where this blessing is offered.

Whom I have chosen. Jesus chose the Twelve, Judas included (6:70), but here he probably means chosen for salvation: he knows his own, and Judas is not among them. When he chose Judas as an apostle he was not deceived about him; he chose with open eyes, within God’s sovereign purpose, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

He who ate my bread. The words come from Psalm 41:9, where David laments a close friend’s betrayal. To eat someone’s bread was to bind yourself to him in friendship, and Judas would betray the friend who had just fed him and washed his feet.

What he leaves out. The psalm says “my close friend in whom I trusted”, and Jesus drops those words. He could not say it: he had known from the beginning who would betray him (6:64). He was betrayed by someone he had not trusted, yet had kept beside him for about three years, and whose feet he had just washed.

Was Judas, then, chosen to be lost and so less guilty? Jesus chose him to be an apostle (6:70), not to be saved. Judas acted willingly, for money, and was fully responsible; Scripture foretold his act but did not force it (Acts 1:16). Jesus said it would have been better for that man not to have been born (Matthew 26:24). God’s sovereignty and Judas’s guilt stand side by side, as they do at the cross itself (Acts 2:23).

Could I turn out to be a Judas? If you ask that with fear and a longing to be true to Christ, it is very unlikely. Judas was not a tender believer who fell but a thief all along (12:6), who showed remorse that ended in despair, never grief before Christ. The warning is for those comfortable near Jesus without loving him. If you hate your sin, run to Christ with it, and want him more than what he gives, those are the marks of the Spirit’s work, and he who began that work will finish it (Philippians 1:6).

Uncertain wording. Lifted his heel against me is a Hebrew picture of treachery whose exact image is unknown: perhaps an animal lifting its hoof to kick, perhaps tripping someone up, perhaps showing the sole of the foot, still a deep insult in much of the Middle East. The meaning is clear: a friend who has shared your table turning on you with contempt.
verseByVerse.note: Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus foretells the betrayal so that, when it comes, it will strengthen their faith in him as the God who knows the end from the beginning, and he still sends them out as his representatives.

Before it takes place. The reason is pastoral rather than merely predictive. If one of the hand-picked Twelve had sold him without warning, the obvious conclusion would be that Jesus had been taken in. Told in advance, they will see the thing that looks most like a failure of his judgment as evidence of the opposite.

That I am he. Again “I am” (egō eimi), the words of 8:24 and 8:28. The God of Isaiah declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10; 48:5), and Isaiah 43:10 is closely echoed: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.” Jesus claims to be not a prophet who happens to know what is coming but the God who planned it. Prophecy in John’s Gospel is given not to satisfy curiosity about the future but to strengthen faith when it arrives.

Whoever receives the one I send. He has been speaking of a man who was sent and went wrong; now he tells the other eleven what it will mean when they are sent. The chain runs unbroken from the Father through the Son to them (Matthew 10:40), and even after Judas’s betrayal their mission stands. He does not wait until they have proved reliable.

How do I receive the ones Jesus sends today? The apostles were sent once, and their message stands written in the New Testament; to receive their word is to receive Christ, and to reject it is to reject him. So first, receive the apostolic Scriptures as the very word of the Lord. Then, in a secondary way, welcome those who faithfully bring that word to you, a pastor, a missionary, a friend who shares the gospel, for the sake of the one whose message they carry, not for their eloquence (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe that I am he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The love that washed the disciples’ feet now meets treachery and does not change. Troubled in spirit, Jesus announces that one of them will betray him; he identifies Judas with a morsel of honour, and Judas goes out into the night (vv. 21–30). With the betrayer gone, Jesus declares that the Son of Man is now glorified, because his death will display the glory of God (vv. 31–32). He gives his little children the new commandment, to love one another as he has loved them, the badge by which the world will know them (vv. 33–35). And when Peter vows to die for him, Jesus foretells that he will deny him three times before the rooster crows (vv. 36–38).
verseByVerse.theology: The new commandment is new in its measure: as I have loved you (see the note on vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter’s denial answers Peter’s most confident declaration. Jesus does not shame him but tells him the truth he needs (on Peter’s confidence, his failure and his restoration, see the note on vv. 37–38).

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus feels the full grief of a friend’s treachery and names it openly, and the disciples, unable to point at Judas, can only wonder about themselves.

Jesus was troubled in his spirit. The third time John uses this verb of him, marking the stages of his approach to the cross: at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33); in the temple courts, when the Greeks came, “Now is my soul troubled” (12:27); and now at the table. The Son of God was not serene in the sense of untouched. He felt the full weight of a friend’s treachery and went on loving.

And testified. A solemn declaration, the language of a witness on oath, not a guess or a mood.

Uncertain of whom he spoke. Judas had been helping himself from the moneybag (12:6), had gone to the chief priests, taken money, and come back to supper, and not one of the men who had lived on the road with him suspected anything. A man can be indistinguishable from a disciple for years, not by clever acting but by doing the same things and going to the same places, and be nothing of the kind.

Is it I? Matthew and Mark record that each of them asked, “Is it I?” (Mark 14:19). Told there was a traitor at the table, they looked inward rather than round the room. It is the healthier instinct, an honest suspicion of oneself, and one Judas never had.

Is it wrong for Jesus to be troubled, if he is God? No. He is truly God and truly man, and as man he had a real human soul that could be grieved, shaken and pained, without any sin (Hebrews 4:15). His trouble was not doubt or panic but the holy grief of a pure heart facing treachery and death. When you are troubled by betrayal or loss, you are not praying to a Saviour who cannot understand. He has sat at a table with a friend who had sold him.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciple who will write this Gospel is lying close to Jesus’ heart, and he names himself not by his love for Jesus but by Jesus’ love for him.

One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved. His first appearance under a title that recurs but is never attached to a name: at the cross (19:26), at the empty tomb (20:2), on the beach (21:7, 20), and named at the end as the one who wrote these things (21:24). He is most probably John, son of Zebedee, as early tradition says (see the introduction), and he never uses his own name.

At Jesus’ side. Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, so the man to the host’s right had his head near the host’s chest and could lean back to speak privately (see meals and reclining at table). The Greek is literally “in the bosom of Jesus”, the words the prologue used of the Son at the Father’s side (1:18). As the Son rests against the Father’s heart, a disciple rests against the Son, and he is the one who will write it all down: he tells us who Jesus is because he was lying against him when he found out. The eternal love between the Father and the Son has opened to take in sinners.

Peter motioned to him. Peter, apparently further away, signals to the man who can ask quietly. Peter, who will soon fail most visibly, organises the inquiry; John, who will stand at the cross, is already in the place of intimate witness.

Did Jesus have favourites? Not in any sense that slights the others. He loved all his own to the end (v. 1) and died for each. John’s title is not a claim to be loved more but wonder that he was loved at all, and every believer may say the same: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Jesus did have friendships of different closeness, as any true man does: the Twelve, then Peter, James and John, then John. Closeness in friendship is not partiality in salvation.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right lay with his head near the host’s chest. The disciple “whom Jesus loved” is traditionally identified as John, the Gospel’s author.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus identifies his betrayer with a gesture of honour, offering Judas a last token of love even as he exposes him.

This morsel of bread. Bread seems to have been dipped into a common dish, perhaps of bitter herbs or sauce, and handed to a particular guest: a host singling somebody out for favour, like serving him first. The morsel itself is not a mark of guilt.

The seating plan. The place of highest honour was beside the host, within easy reach. The beloved disciple is on Jesus’ right, since he leans back against his chest, and Jesus hands the morsel to Judas with no sign of getting up or passing it along, which puts Judas within arm’s reach on the other side, perhaps in the place of honour. Deliberate or not, the two men closest to Jesus that night may well have been the disciple he loved and the man who had already sold him. With the betrayer at arm’s length, he offered honour.

He gave it to Judas. A final offer of love. Only the beloved disciple knew what the gesture meant; the others saw a kindness, which is why they do not understand when Judas leaves. Jesus knew everything, the arrangement, the money, the hour, and with that knowledge he offers the man the best piece of bread. It is the last thing he ever gives him (on what the refused kindness did to Judas, see v. 27).

Was Judas present for the Lord’s Supper? Luke places the warning about the betrayer after the cup (Luke 22:21), while Matthew and Mark place it before, and John has Judas leave right after the morsel. Luke sometimes arranges events by topic rather than strict order, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the bread and cup were shared. Christians have read the order differently since early times, and nothing in the faith hangs on it.
verseByVerse.note: Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Judas takes the last kindness and refuses its appeal, Satan enters him; yet even now it is Jesus, not Judas or Satan, who sets the hour.

Satan entered into him. The only time John uses the name Satan, and the timing is exact: after the morsel. The last kindness offered was the point at which the door closed. Verse 2 said the devil had already put the idea into his heart; now he enters; Luke speaks of Satan entering him earlier still, when he struck the bargain (Luke 22:3). Grace refused does not leave a man where it found him; refused love hardens. Judas is not a puppet: he chose, and his choice gave Satan entry.

Do quickly. Jesus sets the timing of his own betrayal. Judas thinks he is running an operation and has fooled eleven men, but the man he is selling tells him to get on with it, he goes when he is told, and the arrest happens on the night Jesus intends to die. Satan entered Judas, and still it was Jesus who said when.

Not approval, but a dismissal. These are Jesus’ last words to Judas: a man who has decided is allowed to go. God compels nobody’s betrayal, but there comes a moment when he stops restraining it.

No one at the table knew. The most decisive moment of the evening passes before eleven witnesses and registers as nothing. The cross is not understood until the Spirit interprets it in the light of the resurrection.

In everyday life. If there is a sin you keep hearing warnings about and keep putting off, every refusal of grace makes the next one easier. Confess it today, tell a trusted friend, and remove what feeds it. And if this warning frightens you, take heart: a hardening heart seldom worries about it, and your concern is a sign that grace is still at work.

Can a Christian be possessed by Satan like Judas? No. A true believer belongs to Christ and is indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Satan can tempt, accuse and harass a Christian, and a Christian can give him a foothold by sin (Ephesians 4:27), but he cannot own one whom Christ has bought. Judas was never a believer (6:64, 70); he kept company with Jesus while his heart belonged elsewhere. Resist the devil by submitting to God and keeping near to Christ (James 4:7–8), not by living in fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas walks out from the Light of the world into the night, and no one at the table suspects a thing.

Buy what we need for the feast. The disciples’ two guesses show how normal Judas seemed. Buying for the festival was an ordinary errand for the man with the moneybag, and giving to the poor at Passover was a custom, the very cause Judas had championed so publicly over Mary’s ointment (12:5). Betrayal usually leaves a room like that: not with a slammed door but with a plausible explanation everyone accepts.

And it was night. A statement of fact: the meal was eaten after sundown. But John does not write about darkness by accident. He opened the book with it: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (1:5). Jesus had said that anyone who walks in the night stumbles, because the light is not in him (11:10; compare 12:35). Judas got up from a table where the Light of the world was sitting and went out, and the night outside the door was already inside the man.

The night is not the last word. The darkness could not overcome the Light, though a man walked out into it to bring him down. For all his own the night is not the last word: the Lamb is the lamp of the city where there is no night (Revelation 21:23–25).

Is it ever too late to come back? For anyone who wants to come back, no. Judas did not go out because the door was locked against him; he chose the dark, and he never came back to Christ even when remorse came (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter fell that same night, wept, and was restored (on the difference, see the note on vv. 37–38). If you feel the pull to return to Christ, that pull is grace, and he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom.

parallels.desc: send portions to anyone who has nothing ready
the power of darkness

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Judas gone and the cross now certain, Jesus declares that his glory has begun: in his death the Son and the Father are both glorified.

When he had gone out. With the betrayer gone, the events are set in motion, and the great discourse of chapters 14 to 17, the vine, the Spirit, the peace, the prayer, begins the moment the door shuts behind Judas.

Now is the Son of Man glorified. The betrayer is on his way to the chief priests, and the situation is now irreversible. Not on the third day but now, with the trial and the nails still ahead, Jesus greets the darkest night of his life by announcing that his glory has started.

Glorified, five times. The verb appears five times in two verses, and the glory flows both ways: the Son is glorified, God is glorified in him, and God will glorify the Son, at once. At the cross the Son’s love and obedience shine most brightly, and the Father is shown to be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

The dying itself is the glory. God did not merely bring good out of the cross afterwards: the dying itself is the glory. Everywhere else glory and humiliation are opposites; here they are one event. The light of the knowledge of the glory of God shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and most brightly from the face that was spat on, crowned with thorns, and lifted up for sinners.

How can a death be glorious? Glory in the Bible is the weight and beauty of God shining out, and at the cross, in a man bearing a punishment he did not deserve, more of God is seen than anywhere else: his holiness, which will not overlook sin; his justice, which punishes it fully; his love, which bears that punishment himself in his Son; his wisdom, which saves sinners without compromising his righteousness; and his power, which turns the devil’s victory into his defeat. The cross is ugly as a human deed and glorious as a divine one. That is why Christians sing about it, and why Paul would boast in nothing else (Galatians 6:14).

Uncertain wording. In himself (v. 32) may mean in God himself, that is, in his own presence, or in the Son himself. The first fits Jesus’ prayer, “glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (17:5), and is the likelier sense. Either way the Father will answer the Son’s self-giving with glory, and soon.

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he leaves them, Jesus gives his disciples a new commandment: to love one another with the love he has shown them, a love they must first receive before they can pass it on.

Little children. A tender word (teknia), the word of a father about to leave his children. John will use it seven times in his first letter, decades later, evidently having kept it.

Where I am going you cannot come. He said it before to the men who wanted him dead (7:34; 8:21). Now it is turned to his friends, with the difference that for them it is temporary: not yet (v. 36).

A new commandment. Loving one another is not itself new: Leviticus 19:18 had said you shall love your neighbour as yourself, and Jesus had called it the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:39). What is new is the standard, as I have loved you, the love that washes feet and lays down its life; the community, a family of disciples bound to one another in Christ; and the covenant, for this is the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). The old law stood outside a man, on tablets of stone; in the new covenant God puts his own Spirit within his people and changes what they want, so that they begin to love what he commands (Ezekiel 36:26–27). The Latin for commandment, mandatum, is the likely source of the name Maundy Thursday.

As I have loved you. Leviticus gave a measure everybody carries with them, as yourself; Jesus gives one outside the self altogether, shown that evening with a basin and the next afternoon on a cross.

Impossible on purpose. “As yourself” can be attempted. “As I have loved you” cannot be attempted at all in the ordinary sense; it can only be received first and then passed on. That is why the Spirit is promised in chapter 14, the Spirit who raised Jesus now living in his people (Romans 8:11), and why the vine follows in chapter 15. His love is both the pattern and the power for ours: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). And where our loving falls short, as it does every day, his own perfect love, kept to the end, is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so failure sends us back to him, not out of his love. The rest of the discourse is the provision for this commandment.

In everyday life. Pick one believer you find hard to love and ask what the love that washes feet would look like toward him this week. Pray for him first, asking the Lord who loved you for more of his love, and then do one thing.

Does one another mean only Christians? In this verse, yes: Jesus is speaking of his disciples’ love for each other, the family love of the church. Elsewhere he commands love for neighbours and even enemies (Luke 6:27–36; 10:25–37), so this is no permission to love Christians only. But there is a particular, covenant love owed within the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), and it is this love the world is meant to see (v. 35). Often the hardest test is not the stranger but the fellow member you find difficult.
verseByVerse.note: Love of neighbour was old; the new standard is “as I have loved you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for one another is the badge by which the world will recognise Jesus’ disciples; and Peter, who cannot follow him now, is promised that he will follow later.

By this all people will know. The badge is not what we might expect: not doctrine, though he cared enormously about truth; not miracles, numbers, buildings, learning or zeal. The mark of a Christian community before the watching world is its love. He hands the world a test and invites it to use it.

Vindication and humiliation. The second-century writer Tertullian reported pagans saying of Christians, “See how they love one another”, and the early church’s care for its poor and its plague victims was noticed across the empire and is often thought to be one reason it grew. The same church has produced schisms, wars and cold congregations, and whenever the love is missing the sentence hands unbelievers a fair objection. He said it anyway. The world can argue with theology; it finds it far harder to argue with a community that loves the unlovable, forgives the unforgivable and serves the unworthy.

Lord, where are you going? Peter skips over the new commandment to ask about the departure; he is still back at verse 33.

You will follow afterward. Not a refusal but a postponement and a promise. What Peter cannot do tonight he will do later: in death, as a martyr (21:18–19), and into glory. The cross that separates them now is the path Peter himself will one day walk.

Does this mean doctrine matters less than love? No. The same Lord prays in chapter 17 that his people be sanctified in the truth, and John’s letters insist that love and truth belong together (2 John 1–6). Love without truth is not Christ’s love, for he loved us by telling us the truth and dying for it; truth without love fails the very test he gives the world. Hold both: be as careful with one another’s souls as with one another’s doctrine.

parallels.desc: the death by which Peter would glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter sincerely vows to die for Jesus, but Jesus, who will lay down his life for Peter, tells him that before morning he will deny him three times, and loves him still.

I will lay down my life for you. Peter uses the very words Jesus has used of himself: lay down (tithēmi), the verb of the good shepherd (10:11, 15) and of laying aside his garments at the start of the evening. And he means it. Peter is often treated as a braggart here, and he is not: within hours he will draw a sword against an armed band in the dark (18:10). He was willing to die; what he could not do was survive a servant girl’s question by a fire. Courage often fails not at the point it braced for: Peter had prepared for a fight and was undone by a conversation.

A quiet idol. Hidden in his promise is trust in his own devotion. The religious heart is always tempted to rest on the strength of its love for Christ, when the only safe resting place is the strength of Christ’s love for it.

Will you lay down your life for me? Gently, Jesus echoes his words back as a question. Peter says he will lay down his life for Jesus; in fact Jesus will lay down his life for Peter (10:11), and then come back to find him.

The rooster will not crow. The denials follow in 18:15–27, and the exactness of the warning is a mercy. A general warning would have been forgotten or argued with; this one is so precise that when it happens there can be no doubt it was foreseen. Luke records the moment it lands: the rooster crows, the Lord turns and looks at Peter, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

Two failures, two endings. Judas also failed that night, and the warnings did not bring him back; he went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). The difference is not the size of the sin. Peter had been prayed for (Luke 22:32) and told in advance, so he knew at the worst moment of his life that he had not surprised the Lord who had washed his feet. Jesus restores him with three questions by the lake (21:15–17).

He had washed all twenty-four feet. He knew what every one of them was about to do, Judas in the night, Peter by the fire, the rest scattering, and he had already washed all twenty-four feet. Our hold on Christ fails within hours; his hold on us does not fail at all.

What if I have failed Christ badly, after promising him much? Then Peter is your brother. He made the boldest promise in the room and broke it three times within hours, with curses. Jesus knew it would happen, loved him through it, prayed that his faith would not fail, and went looking for him after the resurrection. Your failure does not surprise Christ, and it does not cancel his love. Do what Peter did: weep over it honestly, do not run from him as Judas did, and let him restore you. Then strengthen your brothers out of what you have learned (Luke 22:32).
