He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.<sup>5</sup>Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.<sup>6</sup>He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”<sup>7</sup>Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”<sup>8</sup>Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”<sup>9</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”<sup>11</sup>For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”<sup>12</sup>When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?<sup>13</sup>You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am.<sup>14</sup>If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.<sup>15</sup>For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you.<sup>16</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.<sup>17</sup>If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.<sup>18</sup>I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ’He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’<sup>19</sup>I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”<sup>21</sup>After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”<sup>22</sup>The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.<sup>23</sup>One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side,<sup>24</sup>so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.<sup>25</sup>So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.<sup>27</sup>Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”<sup>28</sup>Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.<sup>29</sup>Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.<sup>30</sup>So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.<sup>31</sup>When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him.<sup>32</sup>If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.<sup>33</sup>Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ’Where I am going you cannot come.’<sup>34</sup>A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.<sup>35</sup>By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”<sup>36</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”<sup>37</sup>Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”<sup>38</sup>Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.
13.overview:
Where we are. The public ministry closed in chapter 12 with Israel’s unbelief and Jesus’ last call to the crowds; chapter 13 opens the book of glory (see the introduction). For five chapters (13–17) Jesus is alone with his disciples on the night before he dies.

The message. Jesus loves his own to the uttermost, and the love that kneels to wash them is the love that will die to make them clean. No one has a share in him unless he washes them, and those he has washed are to love one another in the same way. His love is not defeated by our failure: he washes the feet of the man who has sold him and of the man who will deny him, and he goes to the cross calling it glory.

Why it was said. John’s readers knew the Lord’s Supper well but needed to see the love behind it, and they lived in churches under pressure, where betrayal, failure and rivalry were real (see the introduction). Jesus, they learn, foresaw every failure, chose his cross with open eyes, and left his people one badge before the world: their love for one another.

How the chapter makes its case. Knowing who he is and where he is going, Jesus takes a slave’s towel and washes their feet (vv. 1–5). Peter’s two protests draw out the meaning: without Christ’s washing there is no share in him, and the one who has bathed needs only his feet washed (vv. 6–11). Then Jesus gives the washing as an example for servants to follow, though one of them will lift his heel against him (vv. 12–20). Troubled, he exposes the betrayer with a morsel of honour, and Judas goes out into the night (vv. 21–30). With the door shut, Jesus announces that his glory has begun, gives the new commandment, “just as I have loved you”, and foretells Peter’s denial (vv. 31–38).

Where it leads. The footwashing is the cross in miniature. Jesus lays aside his garments and takes them up again with the verbs he used of laying down his life and taking it up again (10:17–18), and the cleansing he gives at the basin is the cleansing his death will win. The towel leads to the nails, and John calls it glory: a love that goes all the way down for the unworthy.

For us. You cannot wash yourself: let him wash you, and when you stumble, bring him your feet, not a request to be saved again. Then take up the towel for others, the ones who have wronged you included, because he has loved you to the end.

keyVerse.quote: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.
keyVerse.note: Here the evening’s acted parable becomes a command. The old law said to love your neighbour as yourself; Jesus sets a measure outside ourselves, his own love, shown at the basin and soon at the cross. It cannot be met by effort alone: it must first be received, which is why the rest of the discourse promises the Spirit and the vine.

13.reflection:
Jesus washes feet “knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (v. 3). How does being secure in who you are in Christ free you to serve? When you avoid a lowly task, what are you protecting?

Peter first refuses to be washed and then asks for more than is offered (vv. 6–10). Which of his two mistakes are you more prone to, and what does “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me” teach about grace?

Jesus washed Judas’s feet and offered him the morsel of honour, knowing everything (vv. 21–30). What does this show about Christ’s love, and who in your life might need a hidden kindness from you?

Jesus sets the measure “just as I have loved you” and makes love the badge the world will see (vv. 34–35). Where would an outsider see that love in your church, and where might they find it missing?

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus answers his disciples’ troubled hearts by pointing them to himself. They are to trust him as they trust God, for he is going to prepare a place in his Father’s house and will come back for them (vv. 1–4). When Thomas says they do not know the way, Jesus says he is the way, the truth and the life, the only way to the Father (vv. 5–7). When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (vv. 8–11). And because he is going to the Father, believers will do greater works, and he will do what they ask in his name (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” is both a comfort and an exclusive claim (see the note on vv. 5–6). It follows from the incarnation: if God has come in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home.
verseByVerse.examples: “Whatever you ask in my name” (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus’ name is not a formula attached to the end of requests (see the note on vv. 13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers his friends’ fear by calling them to trust him as they trust God, and by telling them where he is going: to prepare a home for them with his Father. Read at countless funerals, these words were first spoken to the friends he was about to die for.

Let not your hearts be troubled. There is no break after 13:38. Judas has gone out into the night and Peter has just been told he will deny his Lord, and the comfort comes straight after the warning, to the man who will fail and to the others who will scatter. Troubled (tarassesthō) means stirred up, agitated, and John has used it of Jesus himself three times: at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), in the temple (12:27), and at this table an hour ago (13:21). He has just brought his own troubled soul to his Father in trust (12:27–28), and will do it again in a garden before dawn. He was troubled so that they need not be.

Hearts, and one heart. In Greek “your” is plural but “heart” is singular: ordinary idiom, yet it fits one shared fear in eleven men. The command does not forbid the feeling, but letting it settle in and take charge.

Believe also in me. The remedy is not an explanation but trust (on the form of the verbs, see the box below): whatever trust they place in God, they are to place in the man sitting opposite them. No faithful Jew could have said that sentence, unless it was true.

Many rooms. The rooms are dwelling places (monai), a noun from menō, the abiding word of chapter 15; the old translation “mansions” (Latin mansiones) once meant simply places to stay. The promise is not grand apartments but room to stay, permanently, in a great family house, and the emphasis falls on many: there is room for all the Father has given the Son. “My Father’s house” is also what Jesus called the temple when he cleared it (2:16); what that building only pictured, he now promises: a home with the Father himself.

How can I stop my heart being troubled? Not by pretending the trouble is not there. The darkest night of their lives is a few hours away, and Jesus does not deny it. He gives them something to do with the trouble: trust God, and trust him. Take the specific thing that troubles you and place it, in prayer, in the hands of the God who has shown his heart in Jesus; remind yourself of what he has promised, a room, his return, his presence, his peace, and say them back to him. The feelings may not go at once, but a troubled heart that keeps turning to Christ is already obeying this verse.

Uncertain wording. Two points of grammar are genuinely uncertain. In v. 1 each “believe” can be read as a statement (“you believe”) or as a command; most likely both are commands: keep trusting God, and keep trusting me. In v. 2 the ESV reads a question; its margin gives a statement instead, “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you”, close to the familiar KJV. Either way, Jesus would not have let them believe in a home that was not there, and he is going ahead to make it ready.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.” Family houses were often extended with rooms as the family grew.

parallels.desc: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will come back for his people himself and take them to be with him; and they already know the way, because they know him.

Prepare a place. By his death, resurrection and ascension he opens the way into the Father’s presence, entering as our forerunner behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20; 9:24). The high priest went in once a year with blood (Hebrews 9:7); Jesus has entered God’s very presence by his own blood (Hebrews 9:12), and because he is there, the way is open for us. The place is prepared by the cross.

I will come again. This has been read of the resurrection, three days off; of Pentecost; of his coming to each believer at death; and, most often and rightly, of his visible return at the end of the age (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). The purpose settles it: “that where I am you may be also.” Neither the resurrection appearances nor Pentecost did that; this is a fetching, and a permanent one.

Take you to myself. The verb (paralambanō) is domestic rather than judicial: to take someone along with you, to receive them to yourself, the word for collecting a person rather than summoning him. In effect he says: I am going to get a room ready, and then I am coming back for you personally.

Where I am. The purpose is not that you may be comfortable at last, but that you may be with him. Scripture says much elsewhere about a body, a city and a new earth, but the reason given here is that he wants them where he is (17:24; Philippians 1:23). The heart of heaven is not the place but the person.

You know the way. Jesus says they know it; Thomas is about to say flatly that they do not. Both are true: they had been walking the way for years without hearing it named. They know him, and he is the way (v. 6).

What happens to a Christian who dies before Jesus comes back? He goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no sleep of the soul and no purgatory: the believer’s soul, made perfect in holiness, is received into heaven at death, while the body rests in the grave until the resurrection (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). When Christ returns, the dead in Christ will be raised with glorified bodies, and all his people together will be with him for ever. So this promise holds for those who have already died: he will come for them too.

Where Christians differ: the coming again and the rapture. Dispensationalists (Christians who read God’s dealings with Israel and with the church as distinct stages) see here a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation, distinct from Christ’s visible return. They long for his coming as much as anyone; the question is how many comings Scripture describes, and the passage most used for a secret rapture speaks of a shout, an archangel’s voice and the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). This commentary’s view: Scripture speaks of one return of Christ, visible, glorious and final, at which the dead are raised, believers are caught up to meet him, and the world is judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). There is no secret rapture. The Lord comes once, and takes his people to be with him for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not merely show the way to the Father; he is the way, because he is the truth about God and the life of God, and no one comes to the Father except through him.

Thomas’s question. Give Thomas (11:16; 20:25) his due: he is the one man in the room willing to say he is lost, and his question draws out one of the most quoted sentences in the Gospel.

I am the way, and the truth, and the life. This is the sixth of Jesus’ great “I am” sayings in John, and perhaps the most comprehensive. He says “the” three times: not a way, not one truth among others. And he does not say “I show the way” but “I am the way”: he does not point to a road; he is the road. The truth is God as he is, revealed (1:14, 17); the life is the life of God shared with us, now and for ever (1:4; 11:25). A road that does not correspond to reality leads nowhere, and a road that cannot carry you alive is no use either.

No one comes to the Father except through me. Now the hard half, the sentence that makes Christianity intolerable to many decent people: there are not many ways to God, but one (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). Three things need saying. First, the offence cannot be removed. Every attempt to soften this into “Jesus is the way for Christians” breaks on the words “no one”. If it is not true it is monstrous; if it is true it is the best news there has ever been.

Not a boast. Second, it is no boast about the people who hold it, and Christians who use this verse to feel superior abuse it. It says there is one bridge; it says nothing about the merit of those crossing it, and this Gospel has taken pains to show they have none. Nor are Christians alone in making an exclusive claim: whoever says that all religions lead to God is saying that every religion which denies it is wrong. The only question is whose exclusive claim is true, and this one was made by a man who backed it by rising from the dead.

An answer to a frightened man. Third, notice what the sentence is doing where it stands. It is not a boundary marker put up against outsiders but an answer to a frightened disciple asking how to get home: the way is not a map, a technique or a standard, but the man who is talking to him. He did not hand us a map and leave; he took our hand and became the road himself, laid down through his own body to the Father’s house.

In everyday life. Think of someone trying to reach God by another road: good works, another religion, spirituality without Christ, or simply hoping it will be all right. Bring them to the Father in prayer today, and if the opportunity comes, tell them gently and plainly that Jesus said he is the way, and that the way is open to them.

What about those who never heard? No one is saved except through Christ. Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a message they never received, but for their sins against the light of creation and conscience they did have (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12–16). Some Christians hope that God may save people who respond to that light without knowing Christ (see the box below). Infants dying in infancy, and those unable to understand, are a different case: the elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases, and there we may rest in the mercy of the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Parents who have lost a little one may hold on to that: David, grieving his infant son, expected to go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and many Reformed pastors have taught that God’s mercy to such little ones is large. The right response to this question is not speculation but sending.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways to God? Many today hold that all religions lead to God (pluralism), or that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him, by following the light they have (inclusivism). This commentary’s view: “No one comes to the Father except through me” leaves no exceptions, and Acts 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church must send missionaries. It is not arrogance to say this; Jesus himself said it. And the way is open to anyone, from any background, who comes through him.
verseByVerse.note: This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: no other name
the Way

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To know Jesus is to know the Father, and from now on the disciples do; Philip’s request to be shown the Father has been granted all along without his noticing.

From now on you do know him. To know Jesus is to know the Father (8:19), and from the coming hour of the cross and resurrection something changes: not what there is to see, which has stood in front of them since Cana, but their ability to see it. For anyone who has read the Gospels a long time and found them flat, the problem is usually not the light but our eyes, and opening them is the Spirit’s work (v. 17).

Show us the Father. The request is one of the oldest in the Bible. Moses asked, “Please show me your glory” (Exodus 33:18), and was told he could not see God’s face and live; hidden in a cleft of the rock while the glory passed, he saw only God’s back. Philip asks the same thing, and he is right that it would be enough. The answer is not a refusal: the request has been granted all along.

What Philip assumes. He assumes that the Father is somewhere else, and that Jesus might arrange an introduction: the natural religious instinct, that the visible teacher gives access to the invisible God behind him. This whole Gospel has been taking that idea apart, and here it is again, sincerely meant, from a man who has been present for all of it. The conversation moves by such interruptions, Peter (13:36), Thomas (v. 5), Philip (v. 8) and Judas (v. 22), each answer going deeper: the only Son making the Father known (1:18).

Close enough to be misunderstood. Moses was hidden in the rock while the glory passed by. Philip was sitting at the table with it, and the glory had just washed his feet. The God whom no one could look on and live has come close enough to be looked at, touched and misunderstood, and to have him is to have enough. What was refused to the greatest of the prophets has been given to the least of the believers.

Will I ever see God? Yes. The pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4), when we see Christ as he is and are made like him (1 John 3:2). Now we see by faith, through the Son whom the Scriptures show us. But the God you will one day see face to face is not a stranger behind Jesus; he is the Father whose heart you have already seen in the Son. It will not be meeting someone new, but seeing fully the One you have known.

parallels.desc: please show me your glory

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father, because the Father is in him and he is in the Father: there is no God behind Jesus who is unlike him.

Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? A gentle rebuke, with sadness in it rather than anger: three years together, and Philip still asks. It is one of the very few places where we hear what it cost him to be misunderstood by his friends.

Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. It does not say Jesus is the Father: the Word was with God and was God (1:1), a distinct person from the Father. Nor does it say merely that Jesus resembles the Father or teaches accurately about him. It says that looking at the one is seeing the other. Jesus is the image of the invisible God, the exact imprint of his nature (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3).

I am in the Father and the Father is in me. Each is in the other (10:38); the church later called this the perichoresis of the persons. The Father and the Son are two persons, not one person wearing two masks, yet not two Gods side by side: each is wholly in the other, sharing the one divine life (10:30). Jesus offers this not as speculation but as the reason his words and works are what they are: he speaks not on his own authority, and all he says and does is God’s own.

No God behind Jesus. A suspicion, very old and still current, says that behind the kindness of Jesus stands a different sort of God: sterner, more remote, harder to please. It survives in people orthodox on paper, who trust Christ and are afraid of God, and it governs how they pray. This verse forbids it. The face that wept at a grave, knelt with a towel and did not break a bruised reed is the face of God.

But is the God of the Old Testament not harsher than Jesus? No; he is the same God, as Jesus himself said. The God who thundered at Sinai proclaimed his name as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6), and Jesus is the full showing of that name. Nor is the Jesus of the Gospels soft: he drove traders from the temple, pronounced woes on hypocrites and, it is often said, spoke more about hell than anyone else in Scripture. Holiness and love meet in both Testaments, perfectly in Christ, and supremely at the cross. Read the Old Testament through him, and the one God comes into focus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus is going to the Father, those who believe in him will do greater works than his: not greater miracles, but the gospel carried to the nations and souls raised to life by the Spirit he sends.

Believe me. His own word is the first and best ground of faith; failing that, let them believe because of the works. He meets weak faith where it is and gives it something to hold.

Greater works than these. “Whoever believes” means every believer, not the apostles only or the specially gifted. The promise is claimed too much and believed too little. It cannot mean more impressive miracles: nobody in Acts or since has fed five thousand from a boy’s lunch or called a man four days dead out of a cave. Jesus gives the reason himself, “because I am going to the Father”: the promise is not about the disciples’ capacities but about what becomes possible once he has ascended and the Spirit has come (16:7).

Greater in scope and in effect. In his earthly ministry Jesus was one man in one province; within thirty years the message was in Rome, carried by people in a hundred places at once. On the day of Pentecost one sermon brought about three thousand people to faith (Acts 2:41). And Peter could preach a finished atonement (Christ’s death fully paying for sin) and a risen Lord, where Jesus in his earthly life preached an atonement still to come. The disciples’ sermons were greater in the only sense that finally matters: they could tell people the thing had been done.

The work is still his. Every conversion since Pentecost is the work of the ascended Christ by his Spirit through his people, greater than the raising of a body, because it raises a soul to everlasting life.

Both guards. Against claiming too much: preachers who have promised deeds more remarkable than Jesus’ have left disappointed and ashamed people behind them. Against claiming too little: it is a real promise, not a figure of speech. The ordinary Christian who says something true about Christ to someone who then believes it has taken part in a work that Jesus, during his earthly life, did not do in that way.

Can I do greater works if I am not a preacher? Yes, because the greater works are not about a platform but about the gospel reaching people. The mother teaching her children the faith, the friend who invites a colleague to church, the believer who gives so that a missionary can go, the church member who prays for the lost by name: all share in bringing people from death to life. The power is not in you but in the Spirit Christ sends, and in the word. You are asked not to be impressive but to be a faithful witness.

Where Christians differ: greater works and miracles. Some take this as a promise that every believer can do greater miracles than Jesus. Others, including many Pentecostal and charismatic brothers and sisters, do not claim that, but do believe the miraculous gifts continue today, and they should be heard with charity. This commentary’s view: no believer has ever done greater miracles than Jesus; the greater works are the saving works of the Spirit through the gospel. The miraculous sign gifts accompanied the apostles to confirm their message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12) and ceased with the apostolic age (the generation of the apostles), because the message they confirmed now stands complete in the New Testament. That does not limit God, who still heals in answer to prayer when he pleases. And the greatest work, new birth, goes on wherever the gospel is preached.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will do whatever his people ask in his name, as his representatives and for the Father’s glory: not a blank cheque, but an invitation to ask what he would ask.

Whatever you ask. This is one of the most quietly resented promises in the New Testament, because people have prayed for something enormous and not received it. Read as a blank cheque, it is falsified by the life of every Christian, including the men it was spoken to. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be taken away and was refused (2 Corinthians 12:8–9); Jesus himself asked that, if it were possible, the cup might pass, and drank it. So it cannot mean “anything at all”: the limit is stated in the middle of the sentence.

In my name. In the ancient world a name stood for a person’s character and authority, and to act in someone’s name was to act as his representative, within his commission, as an ambassador can commit his government to anything it would want and nothing it would not. So praying in Jesus’ name means praying as his representatives, according to his will and for his glory (1 John 5:14). It is not a magic formula, but coming to the Father on the strength of who Jesus is and what he has done, and asking what he would ask. We come on his credit, not our own, and he has never been refused.

That the Father may be glorified in the Son. The purpose of prayer is also its limit. Whatever glorifies the Father in the Son may be asked; beyond that, nothing is promised.

If you ask me anything. Jesus invites prayer to himself as well as to the Father (see the textual note below), at a table of Jews who prayed only to God. Prayer to Christ is right, because he is God (Acts 7:59).

What it does not mean. Underneath the blank-cheque reading lies an old idol: a god who signs whatever we write. Prayer in Jesus’ name hands our plans back to a Father wiser than we are, and that is a relief, not a loss.

In everyday life. Take one thing you are praying for and ask whether Jesus would ask for it and how it would glorify the Father. The prayer may change shape, or you may find you can pray it with new boldness. Then pray it in Jesus’ name, and leave the answer with him.

What about the good prayer that was refused? The honest difficulty is not the greedy prayer but the plainly good one, for a child’s healing, a marriage saved, a friend brought to faith, that was refused. Two things are true. Scripture never explains each case, and any commentary that produces a formula is selling something. But the New Testament everywhere assumes that the refusals are not indifference. In this same Gospel Jesus deliberately waited two days while his friend Lazarus died (11:6), and the family got more than they asked for and nothing like what they wanted at the time. A refused prayer is heard by a Father who is working a greater good than we can see (Romans 8:28), and who will one day show us why.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit “me” in v. 14 (so the KJV). If it stands, as the ESV prints it, Jesus himself invites prayer addressed to him.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is going away, but he will not leave his people alone. Those who love him will keep his commandments, and the Father will give them another Helper, the Spirit of truth, through whom Jesus himself comes to them (vv. 15–20). When Judas asks why he will show himself to them and not to the world, Jesus answers that the Father and the Son will make their home with all who love him (vv. 21–24). The Spirit will teach and remind them (vv. 25–26). Jesus leaves them his peace and rises to meet the ruler of this world, who has no claim on him, out of love for the Father (vv. 27–31).
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (*paraklētos*, one called alongside) is described four ways in the farewell discourse: the Spirit of truth (14:17), who teaches and reminds (14:26), who bears witness about Jesus (15:26), and who convicts the world (16:8). Each is part of one mission: to apply what Jesus accomplished. He brings no new revelation beyond Jesus, but makes what Jesus said and did present to each generation.
verseByVerse.examples: “Not as the world gives” (v. 27). The disciples will need Jesus’ peace before the night is over (on how it differs from the world’s, see the note on vv. 27–28).

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for Jesus shows itself in keeping his commandments, and he will not leave those who love him alone: the Father will give them another Helper, one like Jesus himself, to be with them for ever.

If you love me, you will keep my commandments. This sets love and obedience in an order worth getting right, because reversed it produces only anxiety (see the note on v. 21). “You will keep” is a plain future: a statement of what love does, not a test love must pass (vv. 21, 23; 1 John 5:3). Keep means guard, treasure, obey; and the Spirit who is given writes the law on the heart, creating the desire to obey that the law alone could not create.

Another Helper. Paraklētos means, literally, one called alongside (see the box below): in ordinary Greek, the friend of standing you brought to court, who stood at your side and spoke for you. Another (allon) here means, as the context shows, another of the same kind. Jesus has been their Helper, and John calls him a paraklētos (1 John 2:1). In effect he says: you are losing me, and you are getting one exactly like me. This also shows that the Spirit is a person, not a force: Jesus would not compare himself to a power.

To be with you forever. They have had Jesus in the flesh for a few short years and are losing him tonight; the Helper who is coming will never leave. The Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes: the whole Trinity bending toward eleven frightened men, and toward every believer since.

What if I do not feel that I love Jesus enough to obey him? Then start where love starts: not with your love for him, but with his for you. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19), and love for Christ grows as you look at what he has done: read the Gospels, sit at the cross, remember your forgiveness. Then obey in the small thing in front of you, even without strong feeling. Obedience is often how love is learned, as a child learns love for a parent partly by trusting and doing what he says. And the Helper is given precisely because you cannot do this alone: ask him for love, and he gives it (Romans 5:5).

Uncertain wording. No single English word covers paraklētos: translations give Helper, Comforter, Advocate, Counsellor or simply Paraclete, and the ESV margin offers Advocate or Counselor. The idea of standing alongside is certain, and used of Jesus in 1 John 2:1 the word plainly means an advocate. Less certain is how much of the courtroom John intends here, where the Spirit also teaches and reminds (v. 26). “Comforter” has weakened badly: it once carried the sense of strengthening (Latin fortis, strong). The likely meaning is one who stands beside us to help, strengthen and speak for us, as Jesus did.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Helper is the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive but who will live in the disciples; through him Jesus himself will come to them, so they will not be left as orphans.

The Spirit of truth. He brings and teaches the truth, and the truth is Christ (15:26; 16:13). The unbelieving world, which neither sees nor knows him, cannot receive him (1 Corinthians 2:14), because spiritual sight requires the new birth he creates.

With you and in you. Two small words mark the change from one age to the next: with you now, in the person of Jesus; in you after Pentecost. The Spirit had always been at work: he came upon judges, prophets and kings for particular tasks, and rested on Jesus without measure. But in the old covenant he came and went. What is promised here is permanent residence in ordinary believers, which is what Ezekiel and Joel said would mark the last days (Ezekiel 36:27; Joel 2:28–29).

Not as orphans. Orphans (orphanous) means bereaved children, and disciples whose teacher had died were sometimes called orphans. So he names exactly what they are about to be, and denies it. By tomorrow evening they will look like a school whose master has been executed; he tells them in advance that the appearance will be false.

I will come to you. Not I will send help, but I will come: in the resurrection appearances (v. 19), and by the Spirit, who brings Christ’s own presence (v. 23). The coming of the Spirit is Christ himself coming to his people by another route.

For the one who has lost the person who explained things. There is a particular loneliness in losing the one who made the world make sense: a parent, a mentor, a pastor. This verse was spoken to men about to suffer exactly that loss, by the man they were about to lose, and what he promised was not a replacement but his own return.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Not chiefly by unusual feelings, but by what he does: he makes you confess Jesus as Lord, call God Father, love Christ and his people, and hate your sin; and anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ own life is the guarantee of his people’s life: because he lives, they will live, and when the Spirit comes they will know that they are in him and he is in them.

The world will see me no more. After his death the world will not see him again until he returns; the disciples will see him in the resurrection appearances, and by faith.

Because I live, you also will live. The result follows from the fact, not from anything in the disciples. “I live” is present tense: he is the living one, even facing death, and his resurrection life is the source and guarantee of theirs, now in the new birth and at the last in the resurrection of their bodies.

In that day. The day of resurrection and Pentecost. Three circles of union run outward from the life of God: the Son in the Father, the believer in the Son, the Son in the believer, so that we are drawn into the fellowship of the Trinity (17:21–23). They will know it not by argument, but when the Spirit comes and the whole evening becomes clear.

The key is in his hand. He said “I live” on the night before he died, and it was true even then. Glory to the living one, who died and is alive for evermore and holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18), so that the grave of every believer is a locked room whose key is in the Saviour’s hand.

Where assurance rests. That is where a Christian’s assurance finally rests: not on whether my faith is strong enough to survive, or whether my grip will hold, but on whether he is alive. If he is, the rest follows by the logic of this verse, and my grip is not what holds me.

What does it mean to be in Christ? It means that by faith, through the Spirit, you are joined to him so closely that what is true of him becomes true of you: his death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness as your righteousness, his life as your life, his Father as your Father (Romans 6:4–11; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is not a feeling, though it brings feelings; it is a fact God has made, and every blessing of salvation comes to you in him (Ephesians 1:3). Because it is his work, it does not come undone. The branch does not hold the vine; the vine holds the branch.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves Jesus keeps his commandments and is loved by the Father and the Son, who make themselves known to him; Judas asks why to them and not to the world.

Has my commandments and keeps them. To have his commandments is to know them; to keep them is to do them. Love for Christ is not just a feeling but loyalty that shows in how a person lives.

Will be loved by my Father. Read carelessly it sounds like a bargain: obey, and the Father will love you in return. It cannot mean that, because this Gospel has already said that God loved the world first (3:16), and John’s letter makes it explicit: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). This is not the beginning of the Father’s love but what it goes on to do. Whoever has come to love Christ finds himself inside a love that was there before he arrived, and that now comes toward him in a particular and personal way.

Manifest myself. Manifest (emphanisō) means make visible, show plainly. It promises something experienced rather than merely believed, which is why Judas asks his question.

Judas (not Iscariot). This is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark’s lists (Luke 6:16; Matthew 10:3). By the time John writes, the name is a byword for treachery, and his parenthesis is a small mercy toward a man who did nothing wrong and had his name ruined by somebody else.

Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world? He is not being slow. Israel hoped for a Messiah whom the nations could not miss; if the Messiah is going to make himself plainly visible, surely that is a public event. Why only to them?

Why does Jesus seem more real to some Christians than to me? Part of the answer is in this verse: he shows himself to those who love him and keep his word. Closeness to Christ grows along the path of obedience and his word, not by waiting for a special experience, and where there is unconfessed sin, neglect of Scripture or a divided heart, the sense of his presence often fades. But not every dry season is caused by sin; godly believers have walked through long stretches of darkness while trusting him (Isaiah 50:10). Keep reading, praying and obeying, and keep company with his people. He has promised to make himself known, and he keeps his promises.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father and the Son will come and make their home with everyone who loves Jesus and keeps his word: Jesus shows himself to his people not by a public display but by moving in.

If anyone loves me. Jesus answers Judas indirectly, repeating the condition for the third time in the chapter. Whatever else this indwelling (God living in a person) is, it is not given to those who merely admire Jesus.

Make our home with him. One word turns the whole chapter round, and it is invisible in English: home is monē, the singular of the rooms of v. 2. Jesus goes to prepare a dwelling for us in the Father’s house, and meanwhile the Father and the Son come to make their dwelling in us. That is the answer to Judas. The disclosure is not a display the nations could photograph; it is the Father and the Son taking up residence in a person, which only that person and God can know.

We. Father and Son together, by the Spirit, who is given to be with them for ever and in them (vv. 16–17): so all three persons take up residence in ordinary people, and every believer is a temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). God dwelt in a tent, then in a temple, which the glory left (Ezekiel 10); then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (1:14); now the dwelling moves again, into people. The God whom heaven cannot contain has chosen to make his home in sinners who love his Son. One day we will go to live with him; already he has come to live with us. That is both the deepest comfort and the most searching call to holiness (2 Corinthians 6:16–7:1).

Not mine but the Father’s. Now the other side: to reject Christ’s word is to reject the Father’s. The stakes of hearing the gospel are as high as its source.

In everyday life. Ask what in your life you would be ashamed for the Father and the Son to see: the screen, the grudge, the habit. Clear one room today, not to earn his presence but because he is already there.

If God lives in me, why do I still sin so much? Because the house is being renovated while he lives in it. God does not wait for a believer to be perfect before he moves in; he moves in to make him holy, and his presence is the reason you now hate your sin and fight it. Your body is his temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), so sin now grieves him (Ephesians 4:30), and that should make you serious. But it is no reason to doubt that he dwells in you. He has not moved in to move out again: the work he began in you he will finish (Philippians 1:6).

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit, sent in Jesus’ name, will teach the apostles all things and remind them of all Jesus said, and this promise is the ground of the New Testament.

While I am still with you. They have heard much they do not yet understand. But the Father will send the Helper in the Son’s name: as the Son’s representative, to continue his work.

Teach and remind. The second verb is the more remarkable: a promise about memory, made to men who had misunderstood much of what they were told. As far as we know, nothing had been written down; the teaching of Jesus existed in the memories of eleven frightened men who would have to hand it on.

The promise that grounds the New Testament. The promise is especially to the apostles. The Gospels rest on the memory of men whom the Spirit helped to remember, by his work of inspiration (2 Peter 1:21), and the letters come from men whom he taught. John, writing decades later, reproduces long discourses, exact phrases, the fragrance of the ointment, the number of the water jars. Detail alone does not prove an eyewitness, and some scholars take the discourses as the church’s later reflection; but John’s own claim is that the Spirit reminded rather than invented, and the church received his Gospel as the testimony of one who was there (21:24).

The boundary. The Spirit does not bring new material: both verbs are tethered to “all that I have said to you.” Every claim to fresh revelation that adds to or contradicts these books has this verse against it. His work is to bring home what Christ said to someone who has read it many times and never been moved by it.

Does the Spirit still guide me personally? Yes, but through his word, not beside it. He gives wisdom as you study Scripture, pray and take counsel (James 1:5); he brings to mind what you have read when you need it; he convicts, comforts and directs your heart along the lines Scripture has drawn. Do not treat impressions, dreams or inner nudges as new words from God that bind you or others. Test every impression by Scripture, and where Scripture leaves a choice open, choose wisely and in faith, trusting God’s providence. A feeling may be from the Spirit, but only the Bible is certainly from him.

Where Christians differ: the Spirit’s teaching today. Some claim the Spirit gives new revelation today, beyond Scripture. Most who speak of such words do not mean to add to the Bible, and many test what they hear by it; the real question is whether such words carry God’s authority. This commentary’s view: the promise is first to the apostles, and was fulfilled in the New Testament, which is complete and sufficient (Jude 3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). The Spirit still teaches every believer, not by new revelation, but by illuminating the Scripture he inspired. The canon is closed; the Spirit opens our eyes to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus leaves his friends his own peace, which no circumstance can reach, and tells them to be glad that he is going to the Father; “the Father is greater” speaks of the Son’s humble mission, not of a lesser nature.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Peace (shalom) was how a Jew said goodbye at a door, and still is; and leave is what a man does in a will. He is dying tomorrow and disposing of his estate, and this is what is in it: wholeness, a right relationship with God, the calm that comes from reconciliation (Romans 5:1; Philippians 4:7), bought at the cross by the one who bequeaths it. No thief can steal it and no storm can reach it.

Not as the world gives. The world’s peace is the absence of trouble, sought in control: money, health, the children settled, our reputation safe. It lasts only as long as the circumstances do, which is why it leaves us anxious even while we have it. What he leaves is not a quiet life; within hours these men will scatter into the dark. It is that the thing which makes a person whole, being right with God, has been settled where circumstances cannot reach it. Christ’s peace holds in the middle of trouble (16:33).

Neither let them be afraid. The chapter returns to its start. After a whole chapter the fear is still in the room, so he says it again, and adds the word for what they are actually feeling.

If you loved me, you would have rejoiced. His going is gain for him: he returns to the Father and to the glory he had with him (17:5). And there is tenderness in it: where he is going is better, and if they loved him they would be glad for him.

For the Father is greater than I. How can this be, if the Son is equal with God (5:18; 10:30)? In his incarnation and earthly mission the Son took the role of a servant, sent by the Father and obeying him even to death (5:19, 30; Philippians 2:6–8). That submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook, not to any inferiority of nature.

Four answers to the Arian reading. This was an anchor text of Arius, and it is the verse a Jehovah’s Witness is most likely to open at your door. First, look at what the sentence is for: a reason he gives his friends to be glad, and nobody offers a confession of inferiority as consolation. Second, the word is “greater”, not “better”: the language of position, as a king is greater than his son without being more human. Third, and decisively, the same book tells us that “the Word was God” (1:1), that Jesus said “I and the Father are one” (10:30) and “before Abraham was, I am” (8:58), and it closes with Thomas saying to him, “My Lord and my God!”, which Jesus does not correct (20:28). Fourth, he is hours from the cross, having taken the form of a servant though he was in the form of God (Philippians 2:6–7). A man on his way to be crucified who says the Father is greater is telling you where he has placed himself, not what he is: greater in office, equal in nature.

How do I keep Christ’s peace when life is falling apart? By remembering where it is kept. His peace does not live in your circumstances, so circumstances cannot take it; it lives in your standing with God, which he has settled by his blood. When fear rises, bring it to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7). And do not mistake feeling shaken for having lost his peace: Jesus himself was troubled in spirit while perfectly at peace with the Father. The storm may be loud; the anchor still holds.

Where Christians differ. Arians in the fourth century (followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was the first and highest created being), and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, cite this verse to show that the Son is a lesser being. Some evangelicals who fully confess the Son’s deity also find here an eternal order of authority and submission within the Godhead. This commentary’s view: the verse speaks of his incarnate state, as the one sent; “greater” refers to role and position, not essence, and the Son’s submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook as Mediator, not to any subordination of his being. A son can be equal to his father in nature and still honour his father as the head of the house. Athanasius and the Nicene Creed held both truths together.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells them beforehand so that what is coming will strengthen their faith instead of destroying it: the ruler of this world is coming, but he has nothing in Jesus to lay hold of.

Before it takes place. He did the same with the betrayal (13:19): he foretells the event so that, when it comes, it confirms their faith instead of destroying it. Remembering these words, the disciples will come through the passion with stronger faith.

The ruler of this world is coming. Satan comes through Judas, and through the soldiers and temple police with their lanterns (13:27; 18:3).

He has no claim on me. Literally, in me he has nothing. The enemy will search this man and find nothing belonging to him: no handhold, no debt, no compromise. That is the claim of sinlessness in its most practical form, and everything in the next three days depends on it.

The sting with nothing to inject. Everyone else who has ever died had something in them that death could rightly claim. Hebrews calls the devil the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), and Paul says how death gets its hold on us: “The sting of death is sin” (1 Corinthians 15:56). On Jesus he has no claim. So Jesus dies not because Satan has power over him, but freely, for love of the Father. Those who arrest him in the garden have no rights over him whatever, and he goes anyway: the spotless Lamb walking into the enemy’s hour with nothing in him for the enemy to seize, laying down his life of his own accord.

Does the devil have a claim on me? If you are in Christ, no. His accusations are real, and some of them are true, but they have no legal force, because Christ has paid the debt in full and cancelled the record that stood against you, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). When the accuser reminds you of your sins, agree that they were real, and point him to the cross where they were punished. He has nothing in Christ, and you are in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to the cross freely, doing as his Father commanded, so that the world may see how the Son loves the Father.

As the Father has commanded me. The Son obeys willingly, and so shows the world what love for the Father looks like.

That I love the Father. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus says in so many words that he loves the Father, and it is a startling reason to give for a crucifixion. The cross is a ransom, a substitution (he in our place) and a victory; here he names it also as a demonstration of his love for his Father, made where the world can see it. The love between the Father and the Son, from all eternity, was displayed before the world on a Roman gallows.

Rise, let us go from here. There is a real puzzle here, better faced than ignored: three more chapters follow before anybody leaves, and only at 18:1 does Jesus go out with his disciples across the brook Kidron. Some think they left here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way to the garden, perhaps passing vines (15:1); others that they rose but lingered, as people do who are about to part. Many scholars think an earlier form of the discourse ended here; that would not make the words less his, and John let the sentence stand.

Not the words of a victim. He is the one who ends the meal and sets off toward the garden where he knows Judas will bring the soldiers, because he told him to go and do it quickly. Nobody fetches him from the room; he goes out to meet them, in love, not under compulsion.

Why did Jesus have to obey the Father, if he is equal with him? Because in the plan of salvation the Son freely took the place of the servant, as the second Adam who would obey where the first disobeyed (Romans 5:19); on why that is not inferiority, see the note on v. 28. And it was for us: his perfect obedience in life and death is counted to everyone who trusts him. When you obey God, you are not earning his favour; you are walking in the steps of the Son whose obedience has already won it for you.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.

If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?<sup>3</sup>And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.<sup>4</sup>And you know the way to where I am going.”<sup>5</sup>Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”<sup>6</sup>Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.<sup>7</sup>If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him.”<sup>8</sup>Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”<sup>9</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ’Show us the Father’?<sup>10</sup>Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.<sup>11</sup>Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves.<sup>12</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.<sup>13</sup>Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.<sup>14</sup>If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.<sup>15</sup>“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.<sup>16</sup>And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,<sup>17</sup>even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.<sup>18</sup>“I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.<sup>19</sup>Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live.<sup>20</sup>In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.<sup>21</sup>Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”<sup>22</sup>Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.<sup>24</sup>Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.<sup>25</sup>“These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you.<sup>26</sup>But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.<sup>27</sup>Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.<sup>28</sup>You heard me say to you, ’I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.<sup>29</sup>And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe.<sup>30</sup>I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,<sup>31</sup>but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.
14.overview:
Where we are. It is the last night before the cross. Judas has gone out into the night and Peter has just been told he will deny his Lord (13:30, 38); with no break, Jesus turns to comfort the men about to fail him, in teaching that runs on to his prayer in chapter 17.

The message. Jesus is leaving, but his going is not their loss: he goes to the Father to bring them there. He is himself the way to the Father, and in him the Father is seen. Meanwhile he will not leave them as orphans: the Spirit will come, and the Father and the Son will make their home with all who love him. So their hearts need not be troubled; he gives them his own peace.

Why it was said. The eleven were about to lose their teacher. John’s first readers had never seen Jesus and lived under pressure from synagogue and empire (see the introduction). Both needed to know that an absent Lord is not a distant one.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus answers troubled hearts with trust in himself and a promise: a room in his Father’s house, and his return to fetch them (vv. 1–4). Thomas’s question draws out that he is the only way to the Father (vv. 5–7); Philip’s, that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (vv. 8–11). His going will mean greater works and answered prayer (vv. 12–14). He promises another Helper, through whom he himself comes to them (vv. 15–20), and Judas’s question draws out how: the Father and the Son will make their home with those who love him (vv. 21–24). The Spirit will teach and remind them (vv. 25–26). He leaves them his peace (vv. 27–29) and rises to meet the ruler of this world, out of love for the Father (vv. 30–31).

Where it leads. Everything here rests on the cross. The place is prepared by his death and ascension, the peace bought by his blood, and the Spirit given because he has gone to the Father. And the one who goes to die is the one in whom the Father is seen, so the love that walks out to meet the betrayer (v. 31) is the heart of God himself. The chapter’s two dwellings (vv. 2, 23) meet when he comes again: now God makes his home with us; then we will be at home with him.

For us. We still live between his going and his coming. This chapter offers no technique for calm but a person to trust: he has gone ahead to prepare a place, his Spirit lives in you, and his peace does not depend on your circumstances. Bring what troubles you to the Father in his name, and keep his word because you love him.

keyVerse.quote: I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
keyVerse.note: Thomas asks how to get home, and Jesus answers not with directions but with himself: the way to the Father is a person, who is the truth about God and the life of God in one. Everything else the chapter promises, the room in the Father’s house, the Spirit, the peace, belongs to those who come through him, and the way is open to anyone who does.

14.reflection:
Jesus meets his disciples’ troubled hearts not by removing the trouble but by giving them himself to trust and his promises to hold (vv. 1–3). What troubles you most at present, and which promise in this chapter speaks most directly to it?

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (v. 6). Why is this both the hardest and the kindest thing Jesus could say? How can we say it to friends of other faiths, or of none, without arrogance?

“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (v. 9). Do you ever picture God as sterner or more distant than Jesus? How would your prayers change if you believed there is no God behind Jesus who is unlike him?

Jesus promises that the Father and the Son will make their home with those who love him (v. 23), and he leaves them his peace (v. 27). How is his peace different from the peace the world gives, and what difference does it make on an ordinary Monday that God lives with you?

15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything Christ’s people are meant to be flows from staying joined to him. Jesus is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser, who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones (vv. 1–2). The disciples are already clean, and they must remain in him, because a branch bears nothing by itself (vv. 3–6). Abiding means his words living in them, prayer shaped by them, and life inside his love, kept by obedience (vv. 7–10). Its aim is his joy in them and their love for one another, measured by the love that dies for its friends (vv. 11–14). He calls them friends, reminds them that he chose them, and sends them to bear fruit that lasts (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be (see the note on v. 1), and a branch bears only what the life of the vine produces in it (v. 4).
verseByVerse.examples: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (v. 16). Their following is traced back to his choosing, which does not make them passive: they are appointed to go and bear fruit (see the note on vv. 15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the true vine, the faithful Israel, and his Father tends the branches: he removes the fruitless ones that were attached only outwardly, and he prunes the living ones so that they bear more.

I am the true vine. The seventh and last of the great “I am” sayings in John. The vine was Israel, planted by God and fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; Hosea 10:1); in Isaiah’s song the vineyard yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2). A Jew who heard “vine” heard a story that had gone wrong: a people planted with every advantage who produced nothing worth picking.

True, not a copy. “True” (alēthinē) means real: the genuine article of which the others were copies, as with the true light (1:9) and the true bread (6:32). Everything that vine was meant to be and never was, Jesus is: the real Israel, the faithful Son, who bears the fruit Israel did not. So a place among God’s people comes not by birth, nation or ceremony but by union with Jesus through faith, and a Gentile who trusts him is as much a branch as any son of Abraham (Galatians 3:29).

My Father is the vinedresser. The farmer (geōrgos) tends the vine himself. Nothing happens to the branches by accident; every cut is made by his hand.

He takes away. Judas is the clearest example: outwardly attached to Christ, but never united to him by faith. Some take “takes away” (airei) to mean “lifts up”, as trailing branches are lifted off the ground, but verse 6 describes the same branch thrown out, withering and burned, which is not what happens to a branch that has been tied up. Whether a true believer can be cut off is treated at vv. 5–6.

He prunes. This second knife falls on the healthy branch: cultivation, not punishment. Pruning hurts, but it makes a vine more fruitful, and the Father uses trials, discipline and his word to cut away what hinders fruit (Hebrews 12:5–11). He sometimes cuts away what is good to produce what is better, and what is comfortable to make room for what is fruitful. No cut is careless, no season is wasted, and no living branch is ever thrown away.

The setting. Jesus has just said, “Rise, let us go from here” (14:31), so these words may be spoken as they leave the room or on the walk toward the Kidron valley. They may even have seen a vine: Josephus describes one of gold above the entrance to the temple sanctuary, with clusters as tall as a man, and the Mishnah adds that worshippers gave golden leaves and grapes to hang on it. It cannot be proved that they passed it, and it need not be; but a man saying “I am the true vine” beneath a golden one would not have needed to explain himself.

How do I know whether I am being pruned or punished? If you belong to Christ, the Father’s knife is never punishment that pays for your sins, because Christ has borne that in full (Romans 8:1). It is a Father’s discipline, for your good, that you may share his holiness (Hebrews 12:10). Sometimes he removes a sin; sometimes a comfort, a plan, a reputation, or a good thing grown too large in your heart. You may not know the reason for each cut, but you know the purpose: more fruit, more likeness to Christ, more joy in him. Trust the hand that holds the knife.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples are already clean through the word Christ has spoken, so the command is to stay where they are: remain in him, as he remains in them, because no branch bears fruit on its own.

Already you are clean. The eleven have been cleansed by receiving his word in faith (13:10); Judas has gone. There is wordplay here no English version can carry: he prunes, kathairei; you are clean, katharoi. The words share a root, so the Father’s pruning is first a cleansing, and the knife is chiefly his word, coming home to a person and cutting something away (Hebrews 4:12).

Abide in me, and I in you. The keyword of the chapter: abide (menō), remain, stay. “Abide in me” is the command; “and I in you” is the promise that Christ lives in the one who stays. It is not a mystical exercise but the ordinary word for staying: the disciples stayed with him (1:39); he stayed two days in Samaria (4:40). The branches are already in the vine, so the command is not “get in” but “do not go anywhere”.

How do we abide? The chapter supplies the content: by his words abiding in us (v. 7), Scripture living in us, not visited now and then; by resting in his love (v. 9), not trying to earn it; by keeping his commandments (v. 10); and by prayer, which runs through all three. Ordinary things done continuously, needing no special temperament or technique. The branch does not achieve its place; it simply does not detach. All the life, all the fruit and all the glory are his, and he shares them with branches that could produce nothing alone. This is the dependence pride always resists and grace always establishes.

What does abiding look like on a busy day with no time for long devotions? Staying turned toward Christ in the ordinary hours. Begin with even a few verses read with attention, and carry one with you. Speak to him briefly and often: before the meeting, in the queue, when tempted, when glad. Obey him in the small next thing. When guilt or worry rises, remember that you are loved and forgiven in him. Abiding is measured not by the length of your quiet time but by whether you are depending on him or on yourself. Longer times in Scripture and prayer feed it, and you should make room for them, but a branch abides all day.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joined to Christ, his people bear much fruit; apart from him they can do nothing, and the one who has no living union with him is at last thrown out and burned.

You are the branches. He says it again, plainly, and promises much fruit. What is the fruit? Christlike character, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience (v. 10); love (v. 12); joy (v. 11); answered prayer (v. 7); and people brought to Christ (4:36; Romans 1:13).

Apart from me you can do nothing. The most absolute statement of dependence in the Gospel. “Nothing” means nothing of spiritual value: the separated branch does not produce less fruit; it produces none. That is humbling, and encouraging, because with him, by the Spirit through whom his life flows into us, everything he calls us to is possible (Philippians 4:13).

Thrown away like a branch. Vine wood is useless for building, and pruned branches were burned because they were good for nothing else (Ezekiel 15:2–5). The fire is a picture of final judgment (Matthew 13:40–42), falling on the branch that seemed to be in the vine but had no living connection.

Can a branch in Christ be cut off and burned? The words are severe and the difficulty is real: verse 2 says “every branch in me”, yet the same Lord said that no one is able to snatch his sheep out of his Father’s hand (10:29). The picture itself answers. The vine of Israel was always mixed: full of people who belonged to the covenant community outwardly, carried its sign and kept its feasts, and were not the true people of God at all. One of the Twelve has just gone out into the night to sell him (13:30). Judas was a branch in every visible sense, called and trusted with the common purse, and he bore nothing, because he had no life from the vine. John describes such people: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). So the fruitless branch is not a sheep prised out of the Shepherd’s hand; it is a branch tied on to the vine that never drew a drop of sap. Real union with Christ produces fruit, always, however slowly and however little: not a level of achievement but evidence of life.

Independence is not the goal. Few sentences grate more on a modern ear than “apart from me you can do nothing”. We measure growing up by how little we need anyone. The philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre argued that the self-sufficient adult is a fiction: we begin helpless, spend long stretches ill, ageing or grieving, and flourish only through what he called the virtues of acknowledged dependence. The question is never whether we will depend on something, but on what. A career, a relationship and an approving audience are vines too, and they demand fruit without ever giving sap. Jesus offers the reverse: the branch bears fruit not to earn its place but because the life of the vine is already flowing into it. Dependence on him is the one dependence that sets a person free from all the others.

If this frightens you. The very desire to abide is sap moving. Christ did not say this to leave his friends measuring themselves for the fire. The command is not “examine yourself” but “abide in me”, and abiding is not a feat but staying put. Stay where you are, in him, and the fruit is his business.

How much fruit must I see to be sure I am a true branch? There is no quota. Fruit, more fruit, much fruit (vv. 2, 5) means growth, not a fixed measure. Look for the kind of thing the chapter names, not impressive results: a real love for Christ and his word, a hatred of your sin and a will to fight it, love for his people, some desire that others know him. They may be small and mixed with much weakness, but they are signs of sap. And base your assurance not chiefly on your fruit but on Christ’s promise to keep his sheep and the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16); let the fruit confirm what the promise declares.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off?
