Arminian Christians (who hold that saving grace can be resisted and a true believer can finally fall away) read these verses as warning that genuine Christians can lose their salvation if they stop abiding (compare Hebrews 6:4–6), and they are right that the warning is real. This commentary’s view: the branches burned are those who never truly abide, like Judas, and the warning is one of God’s means of keeping his people abiding, so the warning and the Shepherd’s promise (10:28–29) stand together.
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ’s words live in his people, their prayers are shaped by him and answered, and the fruit they bear makes the Father’s glory visible and shows them to be Christ’s disciples.

My words abide in you. You cannot abide in Christ while ignoring his word; Scripture filling mind and heart is how he dwells richly in us (Colossians 3:16).

Ask whatever you wish. The second of three prayer promises in chapters 14 and 15, and the conditions accumulate: in my name (14:13–14); here, abiding and his words abiding; at verse 16, being chosen and sent. This condition is the most searching: not words added to a request, but whether the one praying is living in Christ, with his words in him.

The prayers change before the answers do. A person saturated in what Christ said begins, over time, to want different things. The wishes are genuinely his own, but Christ’s words have taught them, which is why he can say “ask whatever you wish”.

By this my Father is glorified. The vine’s purpose is the vinedresser’s glory. To glorify God is not to add anything to him but to make his worth visible, as a heavy crop shows the skill of the gardener. When a harsh man grows gentle or a fearful woman brave, people see what kind of God has been at work (Matthew 5:16).

Prove to be my disciples. More literally, “and become my disciples”: discipleship is grown into, not only a status secured at the start. Fruit does not earn the title; it makes it visible.

How can I let Christ’s words abide in me, if I struggle to read the Bible? Start small and steady rather than large and occasional. Read a few verses of a Gospel at the same time each day, twice and slowly, asking what they show you of Christ and what they ask of you. Carry one sentence with you through the day. Listen carefully to Sunday’s preaching and talk about it afterwards. Learn a verse by heart each week. If reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud. The aim is not to finish a plan but to let his words take up residence.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ loves his people with the very love the Father has for him; they are to live inside that love, and obedience is how they stay in its warmth, not how they earn it.

As the Father has loved me. The comparison is easy to read past. The measure of Christ’s love for us is not “a great deal” but the love the Father has had for the Son from before the foundation of the world (17:24). It will not run dry, because it springs from God himself. Nothing we did began it, and nothing can exhaust it.

Abide in my love. This can be heard as a threat: stay in it or you will fall out of it. Read it against the picture. A branch does not generate the sap; it lives in a supply already flowing. Abiding in his love is not keeping his affection at a certain level, which was never asked, but remaining inside something that is there whether one feels it or not.

If you keep my commandments, just as I have kept. Obedience is how we stay in his love, not to earn it but to enjoy it. Nobody supposes the Son earns the Father’s love by good behaviour: his obedience is how a love never in doubt shows itself, and the disciples’ obedience is described the same way. Obedience is love’s response, not love’s price. And his keeping was perfect where ours never is (1 John 1:8). That obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a branch that keeps his commands only haltingly still abides in a love that rests on his record, not its own.

Does God love me less when I disobey? No. His love for his children rests on Christ, not on their performance, and it does not rise and fall with your week (Romans 8:38–39). But sin can cloud your enjoyment of it, as a child who has disobeyed avoids his father’s eyes while his father loves him as much as ever. The way back is not to make up for it first, but to come home: confess, receive his forgiveness, and walk with him again. You do not obey to get into his love; you obey because you are in it, and obedience keeps you in its warmth.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks so that his own joy, the Son’s gladness in the Father’s love, may fill his people to the brim, and so that they love one another as he has loved them.

That my joy may be in you. Not joy in general but his own, the Son’s joy in the Father’s love and in doing his will, handed over by a man who will be dead by tomorrow afternoon. It is not a mood produced by favourable circumstances. Hebrews shows it from the far side: for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

Full. Filled up, brought to the brim (1 John 1:4). Obedience and joy go together, and he has gone through death to make sure that one day our joy will be full for ever.

This is my commandment. The new commandment of 13:34, repeated, and now resting on the picture of the vine: branches of the same vine belong to one another.

For the believer who does not feel joyful. To some readers this verse feels like an accusation. Christians told they ought to be joyful, who are not, conclude that something is wrong with them, which is often untrue and always unhelpful, particularly when their flatness comes from temperament, exhaustion or illness rather than from the soul. Look where the joy is located: it is his, and it arrives by abiding. It is not summoned up, and it has nothing to do with being naturally cheerful. Some of the most joyful Christians in history, Charles Spurgeon among them, fought long battles with depression. And Jesus says this not at a wedding but on the night Judas has gone out to fetch soldiers.

How can I have joy and sorrow at the same time? Because Christian joy is deeper than mood. Paul was sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). This joy is the settled gladness of knowing that you are loved by God, forgiven in Christ and kept for glory, and it can lie beneath real grief like deep water under a stormy surface. You need not pretend to be happy at a graveside or in a hospital ward. You can weep, and still know that the One who loves you is risen and the end of the story is good. That is his joy in you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest love anyone can show is to die for his friends, and Jesus is about to show it for friends who are failing him; his friends show that they are his by doing what he commands.

Greater love has no one than this. The sentence is carved on many war memorials, and it belongs there: a man who dies to bring his friends out is doing what Christ calls the greatest love there is, and no Christian should be grudging about it.

Greater than the greatest. But the verse says what the memorials cannot. He defines the ceiling of human love and goes beyond it the following afternoon. One will scarcely die for a righteous person, Paul says, but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:7–8), indeed “while we were enemies” (5:10). His friends that night were not behaving like friends: one had sold him, one would deny him three times before dawn, and the rest would run. He calls them friends anyway, and the word is warm: philoi, the word the sisters used of Lazarus (11:3). The love that went beyond the highest human love has found us, and it will never let us go.

If you do what I command. This is not friendship on probation; the next verse says he has already called them friends (v. 15). The “if” describes what the friendship looks like, not what it costs: obedience does not make us his friends; it shows that we are. And the command comes from one about to obey a harder one: he asks nothing he is unwilling to do first.

Can I really call Jesus my friend? Yes, and with wonder, because he calls you that first. It does not make him less than Lord; you are friends of the King, not his equals, so the friendship is full of reverence as well as warmth. But it is real: he has laid down his life for you, told you the Father’s plans, hears you, and is for you. You may speak to him openly, bring him your troubles without performance, and trust his loyalty when you feel least loyal yourself. “What a friend we have in Jesus” is sentimental only if it forgets the cross; remembered there, it is the plain truth.

In everyday life. Think of someone in your church who needs a friend who will lay something down for them, time, comfort, convenience or money, and lay one thing down for that person this week, quietly, for Christ’s sake.

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus raises his disciples from servants to friends by opening the Father’s purposes to them, and reminds them that he chose them, not they him, and sent them to bear lasting fruit and to pray in his name.

No longer servants. Moses my servant, David my servant: it was the highest title a Jew could aspire to, and Jesus takes it off them for a precise reason: a slave is told what to do and not why.

I have called you friends. In the whole Old Testament only Abraham is called the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23), and of Moses alone it is said that the LORD spoke to him face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11). Two men in two thousand years, and God shared his plans with them (Genesis 18:17). Now Jesus calls all his disciples friends. The promotion lies in what he tells them: not easier commands, but the reasons, as he has been doing all evening. They are still his servants (v. 20; Romans 1:1), but more than servants: trusted friends.

All, and yet more to come. He has made known all that he heard from his Father, yet he still has many things to say which they cannot bear now (16:12). He has told them all they need as his friends; the rest the Spirit will bring out after his glory, through the apostles (16:13).

You did not choose me. In that culture, as far as we can tell, disciples usually chose their rabbi, and at least two of these men had first followed John the Baptist (1:35–40). Jesus reverses it: a blow to pride and a relief to the anxious, for the one who chose them knew exactly whom he was choosing. We did not find him; he found us. The Bible’s word for this is election: God choosing people for himself before they had done anything good or bad, out of his own love and not for their worth (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11).

Is “I chose you” about salvation, or about the apostles’ office? In the first place it is the choosing of the Eleven for their mission, “that you should go and bear fruit”; Judas, too, was chosen as an apostle (6:70). But it rests on the truth that runs through John, that those who come to Christ come because the Father gave them and drew them (6:37, 44). So it is rightly applied to every believer: our faith began with his choice, the deeper election to salvation (13:18; 17:6).

Appointed to bear fruit, and to ask. Being chosen leads straight to being sent, and the fruit is to abide, the chapter’s keyword again. Prayer belongs with that mission: those he has chosen and sent pray in his name, and the Father answers them.

Does election make my choice meaningless? No. You really did repent and believe; no one did it for you. Election explains why you did. Left to ourselves we would never have chosen him (6:44), so behind your choosing lies his, which made it possible and certain. That makes you not a puppet but a rescued sinner, and it brings two gifts: humility, because you cannot boast of having chosen well, and security, because what began with his choice does not depend on the strength of yours.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything Jesus has said about the vine was aimed at this: that his people love one another.

These things I command you. The vine, the pruning, the abiding, the joy, the friendship and the choosing were all aimed at love among his people. The world will hate them (v. 18); they must love one another. We might have put the emphasis on our own walk with God; he says the point of the whole thing is that they love each other. Good doctrine always runs out into love: election produces humility, grace produces gratitude, and both produce the servant-hearted love of the community of the chosen.

Love that flows from the vine. Fruit is not extracted from a branch by exhortation; it comes from the life flowing into it. Their love for one another is to be Christ’s own love passing through them. He loved them first, he is about to lay down his life for them, and the sap of that love will turn eleven quarrelling men into a family.

To these men, that night. At this supper they had argued about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), and within hours they would all abandon him and spend the weekend locked in a room together, with Peter’s failure in the middle of it. He gives the command anyway, for the third time that evening (13:34; 15:12).

What if the Christian I find hardest to love has really wronged me? Then love will look like forgiveness, which is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It means not holding it against him or seeking to pay him back, because Christ has not held your sins against you (Ephesians 4:32). It may mean a hard conversation (Matthew 18:15), and where there is abuse or danger it means protection and, where needed, the involvement of church leaders and the authorities; love never requires you to stay in harm’s way. But it does mean praying for him, refusing bitterness, and being ready for reconciliation when there is repentance. Ask Christ for his love, because yours will run out.

In everyday life. If anything is unresolved from your last disagreement with a fellow believer, take a step toward peace this week: a message, a call, an apology for your part, a prayer for his good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world will hate Christ’s people because it hated him first, but the Spirit and the apostles will bear witness to him all the same. The disciples should not be surprised: the world loves its own, and he has chosen them out of it (vv. 18–19). Servants share their master’s reception, persecution from some and faith from others, all on account of his name (vv. 20–21). The hatred is without excuse, for he spoke and worked as no one else did, and without cause, as the psalms foretold (vv. 22–25). Yet his case is not lost: the Spirit of truth, sent from the Father, will testify about him, and so will the men who have been with him from the beginning (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology: The world’s hostility to the church is not an accident to be explained away but follows from the conflict between the kingdom of God and a world in rebellion against him. Jesus promises not a strategy to remove it but the Spirit, who bears witness about Jesus alongside the disciples who were with him from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). This is both warning and honour: to suffer for Christ is to share in his sufferings (on manufactured hostility, and on hostility as a sign of belonging to Christ, see the note on vv. 18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world that hated Jesus will hate those he has chosen out of it, and its hatred is not a sign that something has gone wrong with them but proof that they now belong to him.

If the world hates you. The change from love (vv. 9–17) to hatred (vv. 18–25) is abrupt and deliberate: the community commanded to love one another will need to, because nobody outside it will. The world in John is humanity in rebellion against God: not the planet or people as such, for God so loved the world (3:16), but human life arranged without God, its approval, values and loyalties, wherever found, religion included. And the word is not dislike but hatred.

It has hated me before. The hatred is first aimed at Christ, and the disciples share what he suffered because they bear his name (1 Peter 4:12–14).

The world would love its own. The logic is oddly comforting. The hostility is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the disciples, but that they no longer belong to the system doing the hating. Belonging elsewhere is the whole cause.

I chose you out of the world. They now belong to another kingdom (17:14–16), with different loyalties and a different love, and the world resents it. Their chosenness is the source of both their dignity and their danger. The world’s hatred cannot reach the love that chose us; it can only confirm whose we are.

The first readers. John’s first readers probably knew this at first hand: put out of the synagogue (16:2) and suspected by their neighbours for refusing the gods of their cities, they could read these words as their Lord’s forecast of what they were living through (see the introduction).

Two guards. This passage is misused in two opposite ways. First, against manufacturing persecution: much of what Christians suffer in comfortable countries is the result of being rude, ill-informed or needlessly provocative. Peter drew the line: “let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler” (1 Peter 4:15). Being disliked for being disagreeable is not sharing in Christ’s sufferings. Second, against the opposite error: many Christians are imprisoned, dispossessed and killed today, and a church that reads verse 18 as a metaphor for social awkwardness has forgotten much of its own family. The comfortable believer should neither invent a persecution nor decide the verse no longer applies, but pray for the persecuted church.

Should I try to be liked by unbelievers, or expect to be hated? Neither as a goal. Aim to be faithful to Christ and kind to people, and leave the reaction to God. Live such good lives among unbelievers that they may see your good deeds (1 Peter 2:12), walk in wisdom toward outsiders with gracious speech (Colossians 4:5–6), and live peaceably with all as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18). Many unbelievers will respect, even love, a gentle and honest Christian. But when faithfulness to Christ costs you their approval, do not trade him for it. Being hated is not a mark of holiness in itself; being hated for his name is.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Servants share their Master’s reception, persecution from some and faith from others, because what is done to them is done on account of his name by people who do not know God.

A servant is not greater than his master. He said it earlier that evening, at the basin (13:16), as an argument for washing feet. Here it cuts the other way: if the master is hunted, no servant should expect to be exempt. The same proverb produces humility in one direction and realism in the other.

If they persecuted me. The church shares her Lord’s experience (Acts 9:4; 2 Timothy 3:12), because the world sees in her something of him.

They will also keep yours. The parallel runs both ways. Not everyone will be hostile: the disciples will be received as he was, and his reception was mixed. A Samaritan village believed; some of the authorities believed and would not say so; his welcome included Nicodemus and a beggar who worshipped him (9:38).

On account of my name. The blows that land on the church are meant for Christ. Their root is ignorance of the true God (16:3), and the ignorance is not innocent: they have had the opportunity to know and refused.

How should I respond when I am treated badly for being a Christian? Remember that you share your Master’s lot, and that it is an honour (Acts 5:41; Matthew 5:11–12). Do not repay evil for evil or insult for insult, but bless (1 Peter 3:9). Pray for those who mistreat you, as Jesus did on the cross. Speak the truth gently and stand firm without bitterness. Use lawful protections where you have them, as Paul did (Acts 22:25). And keep on with the work: some who now oppose you may later keep the word, as Saul of Tarsus did.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s coming stripped away every excuse: having heard him, those who reject him are guilty of refusing God’s own Son, and to hate the Son is to hate the Father.

They would not have been guilty. He cannot mean they would have been innocent: the whole world is guilty before God (Romans 1–3), and people loved the darkness rather than the light (3:19). He means the particular sin of this chapter, rejecting God’s Son with the evidence in front of them. That sin was not possible before he came; no one can refuse a person he has never met.

No excuse. Excuse (prophasis) means pretext, a cloak: the plausible cover story. His coming did not create the guilt; it removed the covering that had made it deniable.

Whoever hates me hates my Father also. There is no loving the Father while hating the Son (5:23; 1 John 2:23). It is 14:9 turned round: if seeing him is seeing the Father, hating him is hating the Father. This closes off a common, sincerely held position, that one may honour God and set Jesus aside as a good man the church has exaggerated. There is no God behind Christ who can be honoured while Christ is refused.

More light, more responsibility. The principle runs right through the Bible: privilege increases responsibility (9:41; Luke 12:47–48). The well-informed are in more danger, not less. A person who has grown up hearing the gospel and can predict the sermon is the kind of person this verse describes.

What about religious people who worship God but reject Jesus? This verse speaks to them with great seriousness and great love. Many sincerely believe they honour God while rejecting Jesus as the Son, but the Father and the Son cannot be separated. That is why Christians must lovingly and humbly tell their Jewish, Muslim and other religious neighbours about Christ, not to win an argument but because there is no other way to the God they seek. Honour their sincerity and their questions, never despise them, and still say plainly who Jesus is.

In everyday life. If you have grown up in church, ask honestly whether you have ever come to Christ yourself, or only been near him. If not, come today; he casts out no one who comes (6:37). If you have, thank God for the light you were given, and ask what he wants you to do with it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They saw works no one else had ever done and still hated him, fulfilling their own Scriptures: he was hated without a cause, so that sinners might be loved without a cause.

Seen and hated. His works were unique (9:32), as the council itself admitted behind closed doors (11:47). They saw, and still they hated: the clearest evidence of how deep sin goes. When perfect goodness came among them, the world’s enmity against God became fully visible.

Written in their Law. “Their Law” means the Scriptures as a whole, Psalms included. The phrase (8:17; 10:34) does not distance him from Scripture: he quotes it as authoritative, so that his accusers’ own Scriptures testify against them. The words come from Psalm 35:19 and 69:4, laments of David, hated by enemies without reason. Psalm 69 also supplies the zeal for the house (2:17) and the sour wine at the cross (19:28–29). Even their hatred fulfilled Scripture.

Without a cause, and as a gift. “Without a cause” means gratuitously, for nothing (dōrean). The same word appears in Romans 3:24: we are justified by his grace as a gift, dōrean. The world’s hatred of Christ was unearned, the sinner’s acquittal is unearned, they meet at the same cross, and the free gift wins. He received a hatred he had done nothing to deserve; those who hated him receive a righteousness they have done nothing to deserve.

Why would anyone hate Jesus? Because his light exposes what we love in the dark (3:19–20). He was kind, but also holy, and his holiness told people the truth about themselves. He claimed authority over their lives, their religion and their future, and he would not be used. People who wanted a different kind of God found in him the real one, and resisted. The same happens in every heart before the Spirit changes it: we may admire Jesus at a distance, but when he comes close and claims us, the natural heart pushes him away. That is why new birth is necessary (3:3).

In everyday life. When you are treated unfairly today, remember that the Lord was hated without cause and was silent like a lamb. Then remember that you were loved without cause, and let that shape how you answer.
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the world’s hatred Jesus sets two witnesses, the Spirit of truth, whom he will send from the Father, and the apostles who were with him from the beginning, and together they will make him known. Christ’s case before the world looks lost, so he names his witnesses, and they will have the last word.

When the Helper comes. Here paraklētos has its courtroom sense most clearly: the Helper is the Advocate who stands alongside the persecuted church and speaks for Christ. And here the Son sends him, where earlier the Father was said to send him (14:16, 26). Both send.

Who proceeds from the Father. Proceeds (ekporeuetai) means goes out from. Most take it of the Spirit’s mission into the world; theologians have also seen in it his eternal relationship to the Father (see the box below).

He will bear witness about me. The Spirit’s great work is to point to Christ (16:14). He does not draw attention to himself; he is the floodlight that shines on the Son. The Spirit of truth has one subject, and every heart that has seen the glory of Jesus has seen it by his light. The world has never silenced the witness of eleven frightened men, because behind their weak words stood the Spirit who will not let Christ be forgotten. Glory to the Father who sends, the Son who is shown, and the Spirit who shows him.

You also will bear witness. Two witnesses, as the law required, a requirement that runs through this Gospel (8:17). The qualification for the human half is purely factual: not eloquence or bravery, neither of which they were about to show, but that they were there. Their eyewitness testimony (Acts 1:21–22), preserved in Scripture, is the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20).

The pressure taken off. The Spirit’s witness is the one that convinces; the disciples’ task is to say what they saw. Nobody is asked to produce faith in anybody. And “you have been with me from the beginning” was said to eleven men who would, before the night was over, all be somewhere else. He sent them anyway.

I was not an eyewitness, so how can I bear witness? By passing on faithfully what the eyewitnesses saw, and by telling what Christ has done for you. Their testimony is written down (20:31; 1 John 1:1–3), so you need invent nothing; you point people to it. And you can say, as the healed blind man did, “though I was blind, now I see” (9:25). The Spirit still bears witness through such ordinary testimony. You are responsible for being honest and clear about Jesus; leave the convincing to the Spirit who loves to glorify him.

Where Christians differ: does the Spirit proceed from the Son? The Nicene Creed, as agreed in the fourth century, said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, in this verse’s words. The Western church later added “and the Son” (filioque); the Eastern Orthodox church rejected the addition, a major cause of the split of 1054. Each side defends something the verse says. The East protects the Father as the single source within the Godhead; the West protects the Son’s full part, for the same verse says “whom I will send to you from the Father”, and on Easter evening the risen Son breathes on the disciples and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (20:22). This commentary’s view: the Western confession, held by the Reformed churches (the Westminster Confession 2.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 2.3), is right in substance: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9), and the Son sends him, as here. Yet the matter is subtle, and should be held humbly, with respect for Eastern brothers and sisters who confess the same Trinity.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

15.text: <sup>1</sup>“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.<sup>2</sup>Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.<sup>3</sup>Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.<sup>4</sup>Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.<sup>6</sup>If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.<sup>7</sup>If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.<sup>8</sup>By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.<sup>9</sup>As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.
15.overview:
Where we are. On the last night Jesus has washed his disciples’ feet, Judas has gone out, and Jesus has promised the Helper and said, “Rise, let us go from here” (14:31). Chapters 15 and 16 come from those final hours, perhaps on the walk toward the Kidron valley.

The message. Everything that matters in the Christian life flows from being joined to Jesus. He is the true vine, the faithful Israel, and those who stay in him, with his words and his love in them, bear fruit that lasts; apart from him they can do nothing. The same union that makes them his friends makes the world their enemy, but he will not leave his case undefended: the Spirit and the apostles will bear witness to him.

Why it was said. Jesus was about to leave eleven frightened men who would soon be hated, put out of the synagogue and hunted for his name. John’s readers, late in the century, knew that hostility at first hand (see the introduction). They needed to know where their life came from, why the world hated them, and that they were not alone.

How the chapter makes its case. Jesus is the vine and his Father the vinedresser, who removes dead branches and prunes living ones (vv. 1–2). The disciples are already clean, and must stay where they are, because fruit comes only from the vine (vv. 3–6). Abiding means his words in them, prayer shaped by those words, and life inside his love shown in obedience (vv. 7–10). Its aim is his joy in them and their love for one another, measured by the love that lays down its life for friends he has chosen (vv. 11–17). Then the turn: the world will hate them as it hated him, without excuse and without cause (vv. 18–25). But the Spirit of truth will bear witness to Christ, and so will they (vv. 26–27).

Where it leads. The vine was Israel’s old picture of herself, a people God planted who bore wild grapes. Jesus is everything that vine was meant to be, and he gives what no vine ever gave: his own life, flowing into branches that could produce nothing alone. The friend who speaks of laying down his life will do it the next afternoon, for friends who are running away.

For us. The Christian life needs no special technique or temperament, only staying joined to Christ in his word, in prayer, in his love and in obedience. The Father’s knife is never careless, and the world’s hatred cannot reach the love that chose you. Love the other branches, and speak of what Christ has done.

keyVerse.quote: I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers the chapter into one sentence: union with Christ, its promise of much fruit, and the plain fact that without him nothing of spiritual value grows. It humbles the self-sufficient and comforts the weak, because the fruit is not squeezed out of the branch but flows from the life of the vine. Everything else in the chapter, prayer, love, joy, friendship and witness, is this abiding worked out.

15.reflection:
Jesus says “apart from me you can do nothing” (v. 5). Where are you most tempted to live as if you can manage on your own, and what would abiding in him look like in that part of your life this week?

The Father prunes the branches that bear fruit (v. 2). Can you think of a painful season God used to make you more fruitful? How does knowing the vinedresser’s purpose change how you face loss or discipline now?

Jesus calls his disciples friends and shows what that means: he lays down his life, tells them the Father’s purposes, and chose them first (vv. 13–16). Which of these do you find hardest to believe about yourself, and why?

Jesus warns that the world will hate his people as it hated him (vv. 18–21). How can we tell the difference between suffering for his name and being disliked for being difficult, and how should we pray for Christians who face real persecution today?

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ going, which grieves his disciples, is for their good, because it brings the Spirit. He warns them of persecution, even killing done in God’s name, so that it will not trip them, and traces it to ignorance of the Father (vv. 1–4). Their sorrow has silenced their questions, but he tells them the truth: unless he goes, the Helper will not come (vv. 5–7). The Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment (vv. 8–11). And he will guide the apostles into all the truth, speaking what he hears, glorifying Christ by taking what is his, which is all that the Father has (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit convicts the world on three counts: sin, righteousness and judgment (see the notes on vv. 9–11). The Spirit does not force anyone; he opens eyes to what is true. The gospel is not an optional improvement but rescue from real condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all the truth (v. 13): first the apostles, and through their word the church (see the note on vv. 13–14). So the church, reading the Spirit’s word with prayer and humility, can come to the truth Jesus promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns his disciples plainly that they will be expelled and even killed by people who think they are serving God, so that when it happens they will not stumble.

To keep you from falling away. Falling away (skandalisthēte) is being tripped on an obstacle you did not see, not formally renouncing the faith. The obstacle is persecution arriving without warning, and Jesus removes it by placing it in the road ahead where they can see it. Suffering predicted by the one you follow is different from suffering that seems to prove he was not in control.

They will put you out of the synagogues. As had already happened to the man born blind (9:22, 34). For a Jew of that day it meant being cut off from community, worship, family and livelihood (on the synagogue, see the introduction).

Offering service to God. The English softens a chilling word. Service (latreia) is worship, the term for what went on in the temple (Romans 12:1). The killing will be performed as an act of worship, by men who go home believing they have pleased God. Religious zeal without the knowledge of God can become murderous; Stephen was the first recorded to die this way (Acts 7:58–60).

The setting. These words follow straight on from 15:27, late on Thursday night; within hours these men will be asked whether they know him.

The persecutor who became an apostle. Paul had been such a man, sincerely convinced he ought to oppose the name of Jesus (Acts 26:9–11). That is the hope inside the warning: the first man to fulfil it on a large scale wrote much of the New Testament. Nothing in verse 2 puts a person beyond the reach of grace.

Why does God let his people be persecuted at all? Scripture does not explain fully, but it gives enough to trust him. Suffering for Christ joins us to him on his path (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13). It purifies faith like fire refining gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It bears witness to the world, as the blood of martyrs has so often been seed for the church. And it is temporary, while the glory to come is eternal and far outweighs it (Romans 8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17). None of this makes persecution good in itself. But God never wastes the sufferings of his people, and he holds the persecutors, too, in his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persecution springs from not knowing the Father or the Son, and Jesus foretells it now, as he leaves, so that they will remember.

They have not known the Father. The most important sentence in the passage: religious violence comes not from too much God but from not knowing him. That cuts against the common modern view that strong conviction is itself the danger. The men who will kill his followers as worship do not know God too well; they do not know him at all.

A usable test. A conviction that makes a person willing to destroy someone in God’s name shows that he does not know God, who sent his Son to be destroyed rather than to destroy. The test reaches the respectable too: contempt offered as zeal, the cold shoulder and the cutting remark made in God’s name grow from the same root: religion used to prove oneself right, instead of knowledge of the God who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

When their hour comes. The persecutors’ hour. Then the memory of these words will confirm faith: this is what he said would happen.

Not from the beginning. While he was with them, the hostility was aimed at him. There were earlier warnings (Matthew 10:17–22), but tonight he is leaving, and the blows will land on them. God sometimes holds things back, and that is not deception but timing.

Does this mean every religious person who opposes Christians does not know God? It means that no one who truly knows the Father will persecute those who belong to his Son. People disagree with Christians for many reasons, and many in other religions are sincere and morally serious. But the deepest reason for hostility to Jesus and his people is not knowing the Father as he has revealed himself in the Son. That calls for compassion, not contempt: they need what we have been given, the knowledge of God in the face of Jesus Christ. And Christians must apply the test to themselves first: the church has sometimes persecuted in God’s name, and every time it did, it was failing to know him.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is returning to the Father, but his disciples are so full of sorrow at losing him that they no longer ask where he is going or why it might be good.

None of you asks me, “Where are you going?” A careful reader trips here, because Peter had asked exactly that (13:36), and Thomas something close (14:5). But nobody is asking now, and Peter, when he asked, turned at once to his own loyalty. Their questions were about losing him, not about where he was going and why that would be good. The rest of the sentence says why: they are thinking only of their loss.

Sorrow has filled your heart. A true observation about grief: sorrow closes questions down. Jesus does not tell them to stop being sad, or hurry past it. He names it, and takes responsibility for having caused it. Then he gives them the one thing that will turn it round: not an argument but a fact about the Spirit.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve deeply? No. Jesus did not rebuke these men for their sorrow, and he himself wept at a grave (11:35). Paul did not tell the Thessalonians to stop grieving, only not to grieve like those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love feeling the weight of loss, and the Psalms give us words for it. Faith does not remove sorrow but puts a window in it: God is doing something we cannot yet see, and the story does not end here. So grieve honestly, bring your grief to the Lord, and let others carry it with you. In time, ask him to show you what he is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better for the disciples that Jesus goes, because his going opens the way for the Spirit, who will come to them and will put the world on trial.

It is to your advantage that I go away. The most surprising sentence of the farewell discourse. The verb, sympherei, is the one Caiaphas used: “it is better for you that one man should die for the people” (11:50), cold political arithmetic in a council chamber. Caiaphas meant: better for us that he dies. Jesus means: better for you that I go. What Caiaphas meant as murder God meant as salvation, and what the disciples felt as loss God meant as gain.

The Helper will not come. Why not while Jesus was here? The Spirit is sent by the glorified Son, and was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified (7:39). Cross, resurrection and ascension come first, then Pentecost (Acts 2:33): the Spirit applies the finished work, and there was nothing to apply until the work was done.

A distribution of his presence. There is also an implied reason, which touches their grief: a body is in one place, but the Spirit is with every believer everywhere, always, and within them. What is coming does not replace Christ’s presence; it spreads it to all his people. The arrangement they are grieving to lose was the lesser one. He goes away in order to come nearer.

He will convict the world. Convict (elenxei) is a courtroom word: to cross-examine, bring to light, prove a case. The world thinks it has judged Jesus; the Spirit turns the case around and proves the world wrong on three counts (vv. 9–11).

Did Old Testament believers not have the Spirit? They did. David prayed, “take not your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11), and they too were born of God, as Jesus implies when he rebukes Nicodemus, Israel’s teacher, for not understanding the new birth (3:10). What came at Pentecost was the Spirit poured out on all God’s people, dwelling in them permanently on the ground of Christ’s finished work: the gift of the new covenant, which could not come until he had gone.

Would it not be better to have Jesus here in person? It feels that way, and Jesus says plainly that it is not. The men who walked with him in Galilee often misunderstood him; after Pentecost they understood and preached boldly. You are not a second-class Christian for living after the ascension. You live in the age Jesus called better.

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit proves the world wrong about sin, because its root sin is refusing to believe in Jesus, and about righteousness, because Jesus’ return to the Father shows that the one it condemned was in the right.

Not making people feel bad. Convicting is not making somebody feel bad, and confusing the two does real harm. The Spirit shows a person what is true; the accuser presses him about what he is (see the question below).

Concerning sin. Not sins catalogued but the root: the world’s great sin is not first its immorality but unbelief (3:18–19), and every other sin is fruit of this tree. So conviction began at Pentecost: hearers “cut to the heart” over the one they had crucified (Acts 2:36–37).

Concerning righteousness. Jesus was executed as a blasphemer and a criminal. His return to the Father in resurrection and ascension is the appeal court, overturning the sentence and proving him righteous (Acts 2:24, 32–36; 1 Timothy 3:16). So the Spirit convinces people that Jesus was in the right and their own righteousness worthless. And Christ’s righteousness, accepted in heaven, is what God gives to all who believe (Romans 3:21–22). God does not weigh our better days against our worse; he counts Christ’s perfect record as ours the moment we trust him, so that we stand accepted as he is (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is justification: God declaring the guilty righteous because of Christ. The Judge who was judged is the righteousness of all who believe in him.

And you will see me no longer. The verdict in his favour was given out of sight; nobody watched the Father receive him. The Spirit convinces the world of a verdict it never saw.

Why does the word sin sound so old-fashioned? Because we have learned other words. The sociologist Philip Rieff argued in The Triumph of the Therapeutic that the modern West has exchanged the religious self, who wanted to be saved, for the psychological self, who wants to feel well: wrongdoing becomes a mistake, a wound or a dysfunction, never quite guilt. Yet our culture has not stopped judging; online it judges more fiercely than any Puritan town, and rarely forgives. It has lost not the verdict but the absolution. The Spirit’s conviction is kinder than either the moralist or the modern: he goes beneath the offences to the root, the refusal to trust Jesus, and exposes it to point to the one place where guilt is neither managed nor denied but removed, the righteousness of the one who went to the Father.

How can I tell the Spirit’s conviction from false guilt? The Spirit’s conviction is specific: it names a thing that can be dealt with, and there is a door out marked with the name of Christ. The other kind is vague, cumulative, always about the whole self rather than an act, and never suggests anything to do. If what you hear has no exit, it is not this verse. The Spirit leads you to confess and trust Christ’s blood (1 John 1:9), and lifts the burden; the accuser tells you that you are beyond help. Answer him with the cross.

Uncertain wording. The three “concerning… because” clauses (vv. 8–11) are compressed, and exactly how they work is uncertain. The verb can mean to expose as guilty, or to convince. Some read them as exposing the world’s own sin, false righteousness and mistaken judgment; others as convincing it of the truth about sin, Christ’s righteousness and Satan’s judgment. The likely meaning combines them: the Spirit proves the world wrong on all three counts, because its sin is unbelief, the true righteousness is Christ’s, vindicated by his return to the Father, and the true judgment fell not on Jesus but on the ruler of this world.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the cross the ruler of this world stands judged, not Jesus; and Jesus, who has more to teach, gently stops at what his friends can carry that night.

Concerning judgment. The tense matters: “the ruler of this world is judged”. Jesus says it before the cross, about the cross, as a thing already done. The world judged Jesus, but Satan was judged there (12:31), cast out at the very cross where he thought he had won. The Spirit convinces people that the world’s verdicts are wrong and God’s judgment certain (Acts 17:31). When the enemy seems to be winning, remember that the question of who rules was settled on a Friday afternoon, and nothing has reopened it.

You cannot bear them now. One of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. Bear means carry a weight: he has more to say, and he stops, because he can see the limit of what they can carry tonight. This is why the New Testament contains more than the Gospels: the apostles’ letters unfold what Jesus began to teach.

Measured to our strength. If you suspect that God expects more of you than you can manage, here he does the opposite: he measures his words against what they can carry, and stops short. The Spirit will bring the rest. Nothing is held back for ever, only until it will help rather than crush. Mighty to defeat the devil, tender toward the weak: that is our Lord.

If Satan is already judged, why is there still so much evil? Because his sentence has been passed but not yet fully carried out. At the cross Christ disarmed him and broke his claim on God’s people (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14–15), and the gospel now goes out to the nations, freeing his captives. He still prowls like a lion (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, and his time is short. At Christ’s return the sentence will be executed in full (Revelation 20:10). We live between the verdict and the execution. That is why we fight, and why we fight without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of truth will lead the apostles into all the truth about Christ, speaking only what he hears, and in everything he will make much of Jesus.

Into all the truth. A promise first to the apostles, fulfilled in the writing of the New Testament; believers today share in it through their word, as the Spirit opens our eyes to it (1 Corinthians 2:12–13), not as new revelation beyond Scripture. Guide (hodēgēsei) comes from the word for a road: what a guide does for a traveller in unknown country. All the truth means not chemistry or astronomy but the truth about God, salvation and the meaning of Jesus.

Not on his own authority. Jesus states the limit himself. The Spirit does not bring a different message from the Son, any more than the Son brought a different message from the Father. He is not a second source. He reports.

The things that are to come. Not a promise of predictions to individual believers about their futures, but most naturally what the apostles would be given to understand and write: the meaning of the cross, what this present age would be like, and how it will end.

He will glorify me. The Spirit shines the spotlight on Jesus, not on himself, and this is one of the surest tests of any spiritual claim: not whether it is impressive or emotional, but something much harder to fake, whether it makes much of Christ. Much that goes under the Spirit’s name fails, because attention settles on the striking experience or the man producing it. The Spirit habitually stands slightly out of the light and points. His delight is to take what is Christ’s and show it to us, until our hearts burn with the glory of the Son.

No new country. This verse needs a boundary, because every movement that wanted to add something to Scripture has claimed it. A guide does not invent the terrain; he takes people over ground already there. So the church tests every claim to a fresh word from the Spirit by the word the Spirit has already given, and finds in it everything needed to make us wise for salvation and equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). (On words from the Spirit today, see 14:26.)

If the Spirit guides into truth, why do Christians disagree? Because the Spirit’s guidance into all the truth was given infallibly to the apostles, and is in Scripture without error, but our reading of it is not infallible: we are sinners, limited, shaped by our backgrounds and sometimes stubborn. Where Scripture is clear, on Christ, the gospel and the way of salvation, true believers broadly agree, and that is the Spirit’s work. Where we differ, go back humbly to the text, pray, listen to the church’s wiser teachers, and love those with whom you disagree. The Bible is the judge, not our impressions.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the Father has belongs to the Son, so the Spirit who takes from Christ gives the church the whole wealth of God; and in a little while the disciples will lose sight of Jesus, then see him again.

All that the Father has is mine. One of the largest claims in the Gospel, dropped in casually. He does not say “all that the Father has given me”, as a servant entrusted with an estate would speak, but “All that the Father has”. No creature could say it. Father, Son and Spirit share all things (17:10).

He will take what is mine. The Spirit takes from the Son, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son, so what the Spirit brings the church is drawn from the whole wealth of God. In Christ we have all, because in him we have God.

A little while, and again a little while. The first is his death, in a few hours; the second his resurrection, on the third day. Some also see behind it the whole age of the church, up to his second coming, and the New Testament speaks of that long wait in the same way: “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay” (Hebrews 10:37), written nearly two thousand years ago.

What does it mean for me that all the Father has belongs to Christ? That in Christ you lack nothing you truly need. Every spiritual blessing is yours in him (Ephesians 1:3): his righteousness, sonship, inheritance and access to the Father; all things are yours, and you are Christ’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). When you feel spiritually poor, the remedy is not a technique or an experience but Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3). The Spirit’s work is to show you what is already yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The grief of the cross will be turned into a joy no one can take, and the outcome is already settled. The disciples are puzzled by the “little while” and admit they do not understand (vv. 16–18). Jesus answers not with a timetable but with what it will feel like: they will weep while the world rejoices, but their sorrow will turn into joy, as a mother’s labour gives way to the joy of a child (vv. 19–22). In that day they will ask the Father in Jesus’ name, and the Father himself loves them (vv. 23–28). Their sudden confidence will scatter before dawn, yet he is not alone, and he leaves them peace in him and a victory already won (vv. 29–33).
verseByVerse.theology:
The second half of the chapter turns on time. Jesus speaks of what is coming as already settled: the ruler of this world is judged (v. 11), and I have overcome the world (see the note on v. 33). The church lives knowing that the outcome is settled, though it cannot yet be seen.

So the childbirth image governs the section (see vv. 21–22). And prayer in Jesus’ name belongs here, not as a technique for getting results, but as the asking of people whose future is secure (see the note on vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) stands against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. And it sits beside in me you may have peace without contradiction (see “Two locations” at v. 33).

No one will take your joy from you (v. 22) is not a promise of cheerfulness (on where the joy is grounded, see the note on vv. 21–22).

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples cannot work out what Jesus means by “a little while”, and they say so honestly to one another, too unsettled to ask him.

What is this that he says to us? Something almost comic and entirely human: they repeat the riddle word for word, as though saying it again might help, adding what he said about going to the Father in case it is a clue. Then they give up: “We do not know what he is talking about.” They could not imagine death and resurrection.

They do not ask him. He is sitting there, and Jesus knew they wanted to ask, which means nobody did. Probably for the reason anybody sits on a question when the mood has turned: a long evening, the news that one of them is a traitor and that Peter will deny him, and asking would mean admitting before the others that they had not followed.

They had understood very little. After years of the best teaching ever given, on the final evening they cannot make out what he means: not the footwashing, not the vine, not the going away. Whatever is required to follow him, understanding everything at the time is evidently not it. He did not wait for them to understand before he loved them, died for them, and sent them.

The riddle answered by his own body. The puzzle was not one of words. “A little while, and you will see me no longer” was Friday’s tomb; “again a little while, and you will see me” was Sunday’s garden. What changed these men was not a clearer sentence but Easter, and then the Spirit. Christ is himself the meaning of what he says, and those who cannot follow the words are carried through by the deed.

John’s own voice inside it. John was at the table that night (13:23), perhaps among the men muttering, and decades later he could have made the disciples look wiser. Instead he preserves the flat admission as it was said.

Is it wrong to have doubts and questions about the faith? Questions are not unbelief. These men loved Jesus and were confused, and he did not reject them. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to meet him (20:27). The Psalms are full of honest questions put to God. What matters is where you take them: to Christ in prayer, to his word and to mature believers, rather than nursing them in private or letting them harden into a reason to walk away. Some questions will be answered as you grow; some will wait for glory. Faith is not the absence of questions but trust in the Lord while you ask them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his disciples not when but how it will feel: they will weep while the world celebrates, but their sorrow itself will be turned into joy.

Jesus knew. He answers the question they did not put, but not as they wanted. They wanted the timetable decoded; he tells them what it will feel like, which is what they will need.

You will weep and lament. Weep is the ordinary word for shedding tears; lament is formal mourning, the wailing at a funeral. At the cross the disciples will mourn while his enemies celebrate: not only grief, but grief while other people were pleased.

Your sorrow will turn into joy. Not followed by joy, not replaced by joy, but turned into joy. The thing they wept over on the Friday is the thing the church has sung about ever since (Galatians 6:14). Nothing was deleted; the same event changed its meaning. The bad thing is not compensated later by a good thing; it turns out to have been the good thing, which they could not yet see. On the Saturday they needed not a timetable but to have been told, by someone who knew, that what they felt was not the end of the story.

Turned, not erased. The Man who made this promise walked into the sorrow first, and on the third day his own anguish was turned, not erased: the risen Lord still bore his wounds, showed his friends his hands and his side, and then they were glad (20:20). The scars that were the world’s triumph became the sight that filled them with joy. He does not ask us to forget the Friday. He shows us his hands.

Does this mean every sorrow of mine will become joy? For the believer, yes, in God’s time, though not always in the way or when we would choose. God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (8:18). Some sorrows are turned within this life: a loss that later bears fruit, a trial that deepens faith. Others will be turned only when Christ returns and wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). But nothing a Christian suffers is wasted or final. The cross is the proof: if God could turn that into joy, he can turn yours.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a mother’s anguish gives way to joy at her child’s birth, so the disciples’ grief at the cross will give way to the joy of the risen Jesus, which no one can take from them.

Her hour has come. “Hour” is Jesus’ own word, running through this Gospel since Cana (2:4) and almost always meaning the cross. He now lends it to a woman in labour, an Old Testament picture for the pains that come before God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14).

The pain is the way the joy arrives. In childbirth the pain is not a side issue beside the joy; it is the way the joy arrives, and nobody gets the child by another route. The cross is the birth pang of the new creation.

She no longer remembers the anguish. No mother forgets that labour hurt, but the pain stops being what the day is about, displaced by someone who was not in the room before.

I will see you again. He will come to them in the resurrection (20:20), and the direction matters: not “you will see me”, as in verse 16, but “I will see you”. The joy is grounded in his looking at them, not in their managing to catch sight of him.

No one will take your joy. Not “nothing” but “no one”, and in a chapter that has just said the ruler of this world stands judged, that includes the devil. Joy grounded in the risen Christ cannot be taken by persecution, loss or death; the apostles rejoiced after being flogged (Acts 5:41).

But I have lost my joy; was it taken? The joy itself cannot be taken, but your sense of it can be clouded by sin, sorrow, exhaustion, illness or spiritual attack. David prayed, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12), which shows that a true believer can lose the feeling and still have the salvation. Go back to the source: confess any known sin, rest your body if it is worn out, get help if you are ill, look again at the risen Christ in the Gospels, and keep company with his people. The joy has not been stolen; it is waiting where it always was, in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the resurrection the disciples’ puzzled questions will end and a new asking begin: prayer to the Father in Jesus’ name, answered so that their joy may be full.

You will ask nothing of me. That day is after the resurrection, and English uses one word for two things. Ask here is erōtaō, which here means to ask a question, as in v. 19 (it can also mean to request, as in 14:16). They will no longer be confused, because the Spirit will teach them.

Whatever you ask of the Father. This ask means to petition (aiteō). So the sentence does not say that prayer to Jesus will cease, but that their puzzled questions will stop and a new kind of asking begin. After Easter they ask about the timing once, and then go and preach (Acts 1:6–8).

Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Prayer in Jesus’ name is new, made possible by his death and exaltation as our mediator (Hebrews 4:14–16). The disciples had prayed, but not yet on the ground of the Son’s finished work.

At full stretch. The promise must be handled honestly, because every Christian who has prayed long has asked and not received: a parent for a dying child, a wife for twenty years for a husband who never turns. Read carelessly, it leaves them with false hope or the secret conclusion that their faith is at fault.

Not a formula. First, “in my name” means asking as his representative, for what he himself would ask (see 14:13–14): “this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14). The promise is not that God will do our will if we use the right name, but that he will not refuse what he himself wills.

The prayer he did not press. Second, Jesus faced such a prayer himself: “Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour’?” Then he answered his own question: “But for this purpose I have come to this hour” (12:27). He raised the request and declined to press it, because he wanted something more. That is praying in his name, seen in Jesus himself. The Father did not save him from that hour, and the whole world was saved through it.

The stated end is joy. Third, the goal Jesus names is joy, the full joy he has promised all evening, not simply getting what we asked for. Some prayers God grants outright; some he answers with something better than we had the wit to ask; and some he answers with himself, which is why saints who received almost nothing they asked for have so often been the gladdest people in the room. The prayer unanswered in the form we wanted has been taken up by a Father committed to the fullness of our joy, not merely the shortening of our discomfort.

How do I pray in Jesus’ name in practice? Come to the Father as his child because of Christ, not your own record. Bring what is on your heart honestly, without tidying it first, and let what Jesus loves and Scripture promises shape your request. Pray for his kingdom and glory first, as he taught in the Lord’s Prayer, and then for your daily needs without embarrassment. End with “in Jesus’ name”, not as a password but as a confession: I come only through him. Then trust the Father with the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon Jesus will speak plainly about the Father, and his disciples will pray in his name, not through a reluctant go-between but as people the Father welcomes.

In figures of speech. Figures of speech (paroimiai) are veiled sayings, pictures: the same word John used of the shepherd discourse nobody followed (10:6). The vine, the woman in labour, the shepherd, the bread: figures that point beyond themselves. After the resurrection, through the Spirit, their meaning will be plain, and the questions of the last night will stop.

I do not say that I will ask. This does not mean that Jesus will stop praying for them. He always lives to make intercession (Hebrews 7:25), he is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:34), and he is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). What he rules out is the idea of a kind go-between wringing answers out of an unwilling judge. The Son as mediator does not keep us at a distance from the Father; he brings us in. His name opens the door and does not stand between the one praying and the Father, and he says at once why the other picture is wrong: the Father himself loves them (v. 27).

If the Father loves me, why do I need Jesus as mediator at all? Because the Father’s love for sinners is holy love, which will not pretend our sin is nothing. In Christ, love found a way to be just and the justifier (Romans 3:26): the Father gave the Son, and the Son bore our sins, so that we could come near. Christ’s mediation is not the cause of the Father’s love but its gift. The Son did not die to make the Father love us; the Father sent the Son because he already loved us (3:16). So we need Jesus, and we need not fear the Father. Through the one we come confidently to the other.

In everyday life. If you tend to pray to Jesus but avoid addressing the Father, as though he were sterner, begin your prayer today with “Father”, and speak to him as a loved child.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father himself loves those who love and trust his Son, and the Son, who came from the Father into the world, is now returning to him.

The Father himself loves you. “Himself” is emphatic: the Father loves them not because Jesus asks him to, but directly, with no one having to persuade him. Loves is phileō, warm affection. The picture of a severe Father and a merciful Son standing between us and him has no basis in this Gospel (14:9), and it turns prayer into a legal manoeuvre. There is nobody to be got round (on the Father’s love and the Son’s mediation, see the question at v. 26).

Because you have loved me and have believed. Their love and faith are the evidence that they belong to the Father’s family, and are themselves the fruit of his love.

I came from the Father. Jesus’ whole mission in four movements: his life with the Father before he came, his becoming man, his death, and his return to the Father. A creed before there were creeds, said at a supper table, and the disciples’ response is the first sign all evening that something has got through. The Son came from the Father’s side, walked our roads, went to our cross and returned, all to bring us into the love that was there before the world began.

Does the Father’s love, then, depend on ours? No. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Jesus is speaking of the Father’s fatherly delight in and fellowship with those who love his Son (compare 14:21, 23), not of the love that chose them before they loved. The Father rejoices in their love for Jesus.

How can I believe the Father loves me when I feel so far from him? Look first not at your feelings but at what he has done: he sent his Son for you, and that is how you know his love (1 John 4:9–10). He has given you his Spirit, who cries “Abba! Father!” in your heart (Galatians 4:6), even when your own voice is weak. He has adopted you, and a father does not disown his child on a bad day. Feelings of distance are real, and the Psalms are full of them, but the measure of his love is the cross. Speak to him as Father even when it feels hollow, and let his word, not your mood, tell you who you are.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples suddenly declare that they understand and believe; their faith is real, but it rests on slender evidence and has not yet been tested.

Now you are speaking plainly. Touching and slightly absurd, after a sentence arguably no plainer than anything else that evening. They have not solved the riddle; something has simply landed, and their relief is audible.

You know all things. What has convinced them is not the vine or the Spirit but that he answered the question they had not asked aloud (v. 19). It is a real thing to have noticed, but a very small foundation for the test that is coming.

This is why we believe. A real confession, but their confidence runs ahead of their understanding, and has not yet been through the fire of his arrest and death. Faith often fastens on the evidence in front of it, an answered prayer, a coincidence too neat to dismiss: not false, but slighter than it feels, and no one knows in advance how much weight faith will have to carry. Jesus does not disparage their confession. He asks one question about it, and then tells them what will happen before dawn.

Is my faith real if it is weak and untested? Yes. These men truly believed, and Jesus prayed for them as those the Father had given him (17:6–8). Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves, because it is the Saviour who saves, not the strength of the faith. But faith grows by being tested, and God will test it, not to break it but to deepen it (1 Peter 1:6–7; James 1:2–4). So do not despise your faith for being small, and do not trust it for being fervent. Trust Christ, and let him strengthen it through the trials he sends.
