verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before dawn every one of these believers will run and leave Jesus alone, yet the Father is with him, and he goes on to bear the stroke for the scattering sheep.

Do you now believe? There is no mockery in it. He does not deny that they believe; he warns them how weak their faith is, and tells them what these believers are about to do (on whether this is a question, see the box below).

You will be scattered. The language is Zechariah’s: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7; Matthew 26:31). The detail is what hurts: “each to his own home”. They will simply go back where they came from, one by one, the way people do when something ends.

And will leave me alone. All of them would run. The precise prediction is its own mercy: he is not surprised by their failure, but has accounted for it in advance.

Yet I am not alone. The Father never leaves him (8:29). This stands a few hours from a cry that seems to contradict it, that God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34). Both are true, and the church has held them together rather than choosing. The abandonment at Golgotha is real: it is what bearing our sin meant, the cup he asked to be spared, the one thing the Son had never known, suffered in our place. Yet even there the Father’s love for the Son never ceased and the unity of the Trinity was never broken: Jesus could still say “My God” and, at the end, “Father, into your hands” (Luke 23:46). What happens on the Friday is the one exception, brief, and borne in their place: it fell on him precisely so that it would never fall on them.

The Shepherd who was left alone. The Shepherd did not stop loving the sheep he knew would scatter. He went on alone to bear the stroke Zechariah foretold and drink a cup no friend could share. Then he came back, found them behind locked doors, stood among them and said, “Peace be with you” (20:19). The flock that ran has been gathering ever since, around the Shepherd who was left alone so that none of his own ever will be.

What if I feel completely alone? Then you are where Jesus has been, and where he meets you. He knows what it is to have every friend go home, and, as nobody else ever will, to bear the Father’s turning away. So the promise “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) is not a slogan; it cost something to be able to say it. If you are in Christ, the Father is with you as he was with his Son, and will never forsake you, because the forsaking was borne for you. Tell him how alone you feel. Then reach out to his people; loneliness often lies to us about who would gladly come.

Uncertain wording. Greek was first written without punctuation, so “Do you now believe?” (v. 31) can be read as a question or as a statement, “Now you believe!” Either way the sense is close: their faith is real, and Jesus at once warns how soon it will be tested. Most English versions, like the ESV, print a question.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus ends his farewell with the truth about the life ahead: in the world, trouble is certain; in him, peace is available; and the victory is already won.

That in me you may have peace. Peace is the purpose of the whole farewell discourse, and it is found not in circumstances but “in me”, the words of the vine chapter (15:4). It does not depend on the world outside, because it is not stored there.

In the world you will have tribulation. Tribulation (thlipsis) is pressure, distress, affliction: the word used of the woman’s anguish in verse 21. And he says not “might” but “will” (Acts 14:22).

Two locations. “In me”, peace; “in the world”, tribulation. Both are true at once of the same people, which is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon.

I have overcome the world. Take heart (tharseite) means be courageous. And the tense is the thing: I have overcome (nenikēka) is a completed victory with lasting effect, said before the arrest, the trial and the nails. By the cross and resurrection he has defeated sin, death and Satan. John uses its noun in his letter: the victory that has overcome the world is our faith (1 John 5:4), and his people share his victory (Revelation 3:21).

The order of the verse. The trouble is guaranteed, the peace available, and the outcome settled before the fight started. He does not promise to remove the tribulation; he tells them where the peace is kept and who has already won. Anxiety demands a life it can control and keep free of trouble, and Jesus never offers that. He offers himself, and a victory that does not depend on our keeping anything under control.

Before the prayer. The next words out of his mouth are a prayer. By any measure that evening he had overcome nothing yet: the crowds gone, the traitor arranging the arrest, the eleven about to scatter, and himself dead within a day. And he says it as a thing finished, because he had never once been in doubt about how it ends.

If Jesus has overcome the world, why do I keep losing? Because the victory is his before it is yours, and you live between the decisive battle and the final peace. The world still presses, sin still wounds, and you will fall; but the outcome rests on what he has already done. Your faith joins you to the Victor (1 John 5:4–5), and he will finish the work he began. So fight from victory, not for it. When you fall, get up in his strength, not yours. The last chapter is already written, and in it the Lamb has conquered.

In everyday life. When trouble comes today, say both halves of the verse: in the world I have tribulation; in him I have peace. Then do the next right thing with the courage his Spirit gives.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world

Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.<sup>33</sup>I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
16.overview:
Where we are. This is the last part of Jesus’ farewell teaching on the night before he dies. He has just warned that the world will hate his disciples and promised that the Spirit will bear witness with them (15:18–27); after this chapter he prays (chapter 17) and goes out to be arrested.

The message. Jesus’ going away, which breaks his disciples’ hearts, is the best thing that could happen to them. Through his death, resurrection and return to the Father he will send the Spirit, who will prove the world wrong about him and lead his people into the truth; their grief will be turned into a joy no one can take; and they will come to the Father themselves, who loves them. The trouble is certain, but the victory is already won.

Why it was said. The disciples were about to see their Master arrested and killed, and would soon be put out of the synagogue and even killed by men who thought they served God. John’s readers knew that pressure well (see the introduction). Jesus speaks so that, when it comes, they will remember he foretold it and will not stumble.

How the chapter makes its case. He forewarns them of persecution, which springs from not knowing God (vv. 1–4). Their sorrow is real, but his going is to their advantage, because then he will send the Helper (vv. 5–7). The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment (vv. 8–11), and will guide the apostles into all the truth by taking what is Christ’s and declaring it (vv. 12–15). The puzzling “little while” is answered by the picture of childbirth: sorrow now, then a joy no one can take (vv. 16–22). In that day they will pray to the Father in Jesus’ name, for the Father himself loves them (vv. 23–28). Their quick confidence will scatter before dawn, yet he is not alone (vv. 29–32), and he ends with peace in him and a victory already won (v. 33).

Where it leads. Every promise in the chapter hangs on Christ’s going: the cross, the empty tomb and the ascension. The man who will be dead within a day speaks of the ruler of this world as judged and of the world as overcome, because he has never doubted how it ends, and the Spirit he sends exists to glorify him.

For us. Tribulation is not a sign that Christ has failed you; he said it would come. Your sorrow is not the end of the story, the Father himself loves you, and you may come to him in Jesus’ name. Take heart: the decisive battle is already won.

keyVerse.quote: I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.
keyVerse.note: These are Jesus’ last words to his disciples before his prayer, and they gather the whole farewell teaching into one sentence. They are honest about trouble, which is certain, and they locate peace not in circumstances but in him. The victory is spoken of as already won, the night before the cross, by one who never doubted the outcome.

16.reflection:
Jesus says it is to his disciples’ advantage that he goes away, because then the Spirit will come (v. 7). Do you ever feel you would be better off if Jesus were here in person? What does this verse say to that feeling?

The Spirit convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment (vv. 8–11). How is the Spirit’s conviction different from vague guilt or the accuser’s voice, and how have you experienced the difference?

Jesus compares his disciples’ sorrow to a woman in labour, whose anguish gives way to joy (vv. 20–22). Which sorrow in your life, or in the life of someone you love, do you need to bring to this promise?

“In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (v. 33). How would living from Christ’s victory, rather than for it, change the way you face this week’s pressures?

17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every petition in this prayer rests on the Father’s gift of a people to the Son. Jesus asks to be glorified in the hour of the cross so that he may give eternal life, which is knowing the Father and the Son he sent (vv. 1–5). He asks that the eleven be kept in the Father’s name and from the evil one, made holy by the word, and sent into a hostile world as he was sent (vv. 6–19). Then he prays for every later believer: that they may be one, so that the world may believe, and that they may be with him to see his glory (vv. 20–24). It ends with the Father’s love, and the Son himself, dwelling in his people (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer recalls the high priest entering the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. Jesus is both priest and sacrifice (see the note on v. 19). What he asks for them, protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), holiness (v. 17) and unity (vv. 21–23), is what the church still lives on.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on, and drawn from, the unity of the Father and the Son (see the notes on vv. 21–22). It is also how the world is meant to see the truth (vv. 21, 23), so a church at war with itself undercuts its own witness. In Jesus’ prayer, unity and mission belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the hour of the cross upon him, Jesus asks the Father to glorify the Son through it, so that the Son may glorify the Father by giving eternal life to all whom the Father has given him. In his longest recorded prayer, spoken aloud within the hour of his arrest, we overhear the Son speaking to the Father.

He lifted up his eyes to heaven. Eyes open, head up: a common Jewish posture in prayer (bowed head and closed eyes are a later habit, good but not commanded). He did the same at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). On the last evening of his life he looks his Father in the face.

Father. Six times he says it, the family word he taught his disciples, and only twice adds a describing word where the request calls for it: “Holy Father” (v. 11) and “righteous Father” (v. 25), forms of address found nowhere else in the Bible.

The hour has come. Three times the hour was not yet: at Cana (2:4), and twice when men tried to seize him and could not (7:30; 8:20); for three years no hand could touch him before his Father’s time. From the arrival of the Greeks it has come (12:23, 27; 13:1), and the first thing he does in it is pray.

Glorify your Son. Not a selfish prayer: the Son asks to be glorified in his death, resurrection and exaltation so that he can glorify the Father, for their glory is one. In this Gospel the lifting up on the cross begins the lifting up to glory (3:14; 12:32–33). God’s glory is the shining out of who he is, and nowhere does it shine more fully than when he gives his Son for sinners.

Authority over all flesh. Every human being answers to the Son (Matthew 28:18). The man about to be led bound from court to court is the one to whom everyone in those courts already answers, and he uses that authority to give life.

All whom you have given him. The Father’s giving of a people to the Son runs through this prayer (vv. 2, 6, 9, 24): authority over everyone, a saving gift for a particular people. Before anything was made (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4), the Father gave them and the Son undertook to save them, so every believer’s salvation was planned in love before he existed. And none of those given will fail to receive what the Son was given authority to give (6:37–39).

A high priest’s prayer. Like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, he prays for himself, for his priests (the apostles) and for the people; and like the high priest who carried the names of the tribes on his heart into the holy place (Exodus 28:29), he carries his people before the Father before offering himself as their sacrifice.

The Son who looks up and the sinner who cannot. Set beside him the one man in the Gospels who could not lift his eyes: the tax collector in the parable, who “would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast” (Luke 18:13). Both were heard: a Son who looks up because he has every right to, and a sinner who cannot because he has none, and the Father receives them both, the second because of the first.

In everyday life. Pray with your eyes on the Father, not on yourself. Before you bring him a list, say his name the way a child does, and remember who taught you to say it. When the hour you have been dreading arrives, speak to your Father first, and ask that he be glorified in it.

If some are given, can I know whether I am one of them? Not by looking into the secret counsel of God, but by coming to Christ. The Jesus who spoke of those the Father gives him said in the same breath, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37). The giving is the hidden root; the coming is the visible fruit. Nobody has ever come to Christ and been turned away because his name was missing from a list. If you are coming to him, trusting him, wanting him, that is the Father’s gift showing itself. Election is not a wall to keep anyone out. It is the reason anyone comes in at all.

Where Christians differ: what does “given” mean? Some read those the Father has given the Son as those he foresaw would believe. This commentary’s view: Jesus will say, “I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me” (v. 9), which shows that the giving is the Father’s choice, not merely his foresight; faith is the fruit of that choice, not its ground.
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent, and the Son can tell the Father that he has glorified him on earth by finishing, without a flaw, the work he was given to do.

That they know you. Scripture’s nearest thing to a definition of eternal life is not living for ever, nor going to heaven, though both are true: it is knowing. The verb (ginōskō) means the knowledge of a person rather than of a subject (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6); it is the word of the new covenant promise, “they shall all know me”. Two things follow.

Eternal life has already begun. Because it is a relationship, it begins when we come to know God, and dying does not interrupt it, as he told Martha at the tomb: “everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die” (11:25–26). It grows for ever, but it does not wait.

What makes eternal life eternal. Second: to exist for ever without God would not, by this definition, be life at all. What makes eternal life eternal is not its length but who is in it. Heaven without God would be a long exile; a cell with God in it is already the beginning of heaven.

The only true God. Some use this against the deity of Christ, as though it excluded Jesus. But the sentence makes knowing Jesus Christ part of eternal life, joined by “and” to knowing the only true God, and no monotheist would put a creature there. Calling the Father the only true God denies the idols, not the Son, who is included within the one true God (1:1); John wrote of him in his letter: “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20), using the same two words. The verse distinguishes the Father from the Son; it does not divide them.

Jesus Christ. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus uses the full name Jesus Christ of himself. John may have phrased his Lord’s words for later readers, as he sometimes does; nothing turns on it.

Having accomplished the work. The verb means completed, finished, from the same family as the cry “It is finished” (19:30). He speaks from the threshold of the cross as though it were behind him, because his obedience was settled, and every hour of thirty-odd years had been offered to the Father without a single failure. No other human being has ever been able to say, “I glorified you on earth”, without needing to add a confession.

A life that will outlast the stars. The God who made the galaxies has not left us to guess at him. He sent his Son, the only man who could say he had glorified the Father with nothing left undone, and that finished obedience is credited to people whose obedience is full of holes. To know God in the face of Jesus Christ is to have begun a life that will outlast the stars, because the One we know has no end.

Wouldn’t living for ever be unbearably dull? The philosopher Bernard Williams argued so, from Karel Čapek’s play about a woman who has lived more than three hundred years and grown cold, with nothing left to interest her. If eternal life meant simply more time, he would be right: every pleasure wears thin with repetition. But this verse defines eternal life by a person. Things can be exhausted; persons cannot, least of all a person who is infinite. Even the people we love best still surprise us after fifty years. To know God is to be drawn for ever further into a life that has no bottom, and the boredom Williams feared is simply what endless existence without him would be.

How do I actually get to know God better? As you know anyone: by listening, speaking and spending time together. Read Scripture to meet him, asking what it shows you of God and of Christ. Speak to him in prayer, honestly, as a child does. Meet him with his people at his table and under his preached word. And obey what you learn, because Jesus said the one who keeps his commands is the one to whom he shows himself (14:21). Knowledge of God grows slowly, like a friendship, and it grows most in the hard seasons when he is all you have.

Is it not narrow to say eternal life comes only by knowing Jesus Christ? Narrow as any true answer is narrow. If eternal life is knowing God, the question is not which religion is most sincere but whether God can be known at all, and Jesus says he is known in the one he sent (14:6). Every other road asks us to climb to God by devotion or goodness, leaving all but the disciplined and respectable without hope. This road is open to the worst sinner, and closed only to the person who insists on coming as anything other than a receiver. A door that only God could open, held open to anyone who will come, is not arrogance. It is mercy.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks to return to the glory he shared with the Father before the world existed, and tells the Father that he has made his name known to the people the Father gave him, who have received his word.

The glory that I had with you. No prophet ever prayed like it. Moses asked to see God’s glory; this man asks to have his own glory back. Inside the request is the opening of this Gospel (1:1–18) in a clause: he had glory with the Father before there was a world. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem; he came from somewhere, and is about to go back. Since God will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8), the Son is not another: he is God.

The glory set down. Becoming man, he veiled that glory: he “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7). Now he asks for it back, and asks to return to it in his human nature as well. He goes back with pierced hands and a raised body. Our flesh has entered that glory in him.

Your name. The name is God’s character, all that he is (1:18). The whole ministry of Jesus, teaching, signs, foot-washing and finally the cross, is the disclosure of the Father’s name.

Yours they were, and you gave them to me. They belonged to the Father before they belonged to the Son. Chosen before they came (6:37; Ephesians 1:4), they are first the Father’s and then, by gift, the Son’s. Election, God’s choosing of his people, is the Father’s prior claim on those the Son will redeem.

They have kept your word. Startlingly generous. These eleven have understood little all evening, argued that night about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24), and will soon run into the dark; Peter will deny him three times. And his report to his Father is not “they are trying”, but “they have kept your word”. He is neither blind nor flattering: he describes them as what they have become by receiving his word, a different measure from the one we apply to ourselves.

Did Jesus stop being God when he laid his glory aside? No. He laid aside not his deity but its open display, remaining what he was while becoming what he was not, a man. The emptying of Philippians 2 is explained by the next words, “taking the form of a servant”: he emptied himself by adding, not by subtracting. So even in the manger and on the cross he was the eternal Son, upholding all things (Hebrews 1:3). The glory was hidden like the sun behind cloud, breaking through at Cana, on the mountain, at the tomb of Lazarus. Here he asks for the cloud to be taken away.

Does this mean my sin does not matter to him? No. He grieves over it and he will deal with it; after the resurrection, beside the Sea of Galilee, he will restore Peter by name, and it will hurt (21:15–17). But he does not define his people by their failures. He defines them by what grace has made them: people who have received his word and are his. That should make you more serious about sin, not less, because you are being treated as something better than your worst nights. And it should silence the voice that tells you that your stumbles prove you were never his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples have received the words the Father gave the Son, and so have come to know that Jesus came from God and to believe that the Father sent him. They have finally grasped it on the last night, not long before their nerve fails them.

Everything is from you. The teaching, the signs, the authority, the men themselves: nothing in the ministry of Jesus came from him acting on his own, apart from the Father (5:19).

Given, received, known, believed. The chain runs from Father to Son, to disciples, and through them to us. Faith begins by receiving, not by inventing or improving God’s word. Knowing comes first here. They came to know that I came from you: his origin. They believed that you sent me: his commission. Both rest on words handed over, not worked out. In his report to the Father all four verbs are completed actions, credited in full (on how he measures his people, see v. 6).

Two errors corrected at once. Faith is not a leap in the dark with nothing to believe, since there are words to receive. Nor is it a conclusion we reasoned our way to, since the words came from outside us. Christian faith is neither blind nor self-made. It is the open-eyed reception of what God has said.

My faith feels nothing like as solid as that. Does it count? Yes. The disciples’ faith was real, and within an hour shaking badly; Jesus called it faith anyway, because faith is measured by its object, not by its strength. A trembling hand that grasps a strong rope is as safe as a steady one. If you have received his words as true, if you believe that Jesus came from God and that the Father sent him to save sinners, you have the faith this verse describes, however weak it feels. Feed it with the same words that created it, and ask him, as a father once did, to help your unbelief (Mark 9:24).

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ high-priestly intercession here is for those the Father has given him: he pleads for them because they belong to the Father, and in them the Son is already glorified.

I am not praying for the world. The coldest-sounding sentence in the warmest chapter in the Bible, and three things help. First, it concerns how far this one request reaches, not the heart of the one praying. He asks that these men be kept and that what he is about to do be applied to them, and the world that is rejecting him cannot be the subject of that request.

The world in the same prayer. Second, the same prayer turns to the world twice: “so that the world may believe that you have sent me” (v. 21); “so that the world may know” (v. 23). He prays for his church in order to reach the world.

Father, forgive them. Third, within hours he would be praying aloud from a cross for the men driving the nails: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). (These words are missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but many scholars judge them original and most Bibles print them.) So the verse describes one kind of praying, for the particular people the Father gave him: the High Priest with the names on his breastplate, where the naming is the comfort rather than the offence.

For they are yours. He pleads for them on the ground that they belong to the Father. It is the argument of a son to a father: these are yours; take care of what is yours.

All mine are yours, and yours are mine. Anyone could say the first half; no one else the second. “Yours are mine” is a claim to hold the Father’s property as one’s own (16:15). Luther is said to have observed that no creature could utter it. It is perfect equality, spoken quietly, and all that he has he spends on the people he was given.

I am glorified in them. They exhibit what grace produces. The eleven are not much to look at tonight, yet he is glorified in them, as a craftsman is honoured by the work still on his bench.

Is Jesus praying for me now? Yes, if you are his. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and Paul names it as one reason no one can condemn us: Christ Jesus is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand of God, and indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:34). It is not nervous pleading with a reluctant Father but the risen Son presenting his finished sacrifice and asking for what it purchased, and it is never refused. On the days you cannot pray, he is not silent.

Then should I pray only for Christians? No. His high-priestly intercession is unique to him. We are told to pray for all people, kings and those in authority included (1 Timothy 2:1–4), to pray for our enemies (Matthew 5:44), and to plead for the lost as Paul did for Israel (Romans 10:1). We do not know whom the Father has given to the Son, so we pray for everyone and preach to everyone, trusting that he will call his own through those prayers and that preaching.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Reformed readers see here strong support for definite atonement: that Christ died intending actually to save those the Father had given him, not merely to make salvation possible for everyone. Many faithful Christians read the matter differently, holding that Christ died for every person alike and pointing to verses such as 1 John 2:2; they are brothers in the same gospel, and the question is how to hold those verses together with this prayer. This commentary’s view: the High Priest’s pleading has a definite people in view, and his sacrifice and his intercession have the same scope (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). He prays for those for whom he dies, and he dies for those for whom he prays, and they do not miss (10:11, 15). His death is sufficient for all, so the gospel is offered to anyone without reservation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaving his friends in a hostile world, Jesus asks the holy Father to keep them by his name and make them one, as he himself guarded them while he was with them and lost none of them except Judas, the son of destruction whom Scripture foretold.

No longer in the world. He speaks as if already gone, and asks everything with one picture before him: his friends left behind in enemy country.

Holy Father. He adds holy because he asks that these men be kept in an unholy world. The God whose presence on Sinai could not be approached without washing and warning (Exodus 19:10–13) is Father to men like the eleven: that is grace.

Keep them in your name. Keep means guard and preserve; “in your name”, by the power of who you are and in loyalty to your revealed character. The Father has given the Son his name, the divine name (Philippians 2:9–11), and the Son keeps his people by the same name in which he reveals the Father. Here is their perseverance: those God has given to Christ will be kept in faith to the end. They may stumble badly, as Peter did that very night, but they will not finally fall away, because the one who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

That they may be one. The goal of their being kept is a unity like that of the Father and the Son (this is treated fully at vv. 21–22).

The son of destruction. Not one was lost except the son of lostness: the Greek plays on one root (apōleto, apōleias). “Son of destruction” is a Hebrew way of saying one who belongs and is destined to destruction; the phrase recurs once in the New Testament, for the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). It is Judas. He was never one of those truly given; he was lost because he never truly belonged (6:64, 70).

That the Scripture might be fulfilled. The Scripture Jesus means is probably the psalm he quoted of Judas earlier that same evening: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). Jesus did not fail to keep him (on Judas’s guilt and God’s purpose together, see the question below).

A Father who keeps. Our perseverance is not the story of how tightly we held on. It is the story of a Father who keeps, and a Son who guards, and a name that has never once failed those who are kept in it.

Was Judas free? Two things must be held, and the New Testament holds both without strain. Judas is never described as a victim. He is a thief who helped himself to the money bag (12:6), Satan enters him at the morsel (13:27), and Peter says he turned aside “to go to his own place” (Acts 1:25): his own, chosen, fitting. And equally, Scripture had said it would happen, and Peter at Pentecost says the whole event went forward “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, in the same breath as “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). What Scripture never does is derive one from the other. It does not say Judas betrayed him because it was written; it says it was written, and he did it, and both are true. Anyone who claims to have resolved it has usually quietly dropped one half.

Could I be the one exception, like Judas? The verse is not given to classify anybody or frighten the trembling, but to explain why the keeping did not fail: “I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost”. The exception is the man who was never inside the guarding in the first place. Judas loved money, kept his heart closed, and never came to Jesus in sorrow; even his remorse took him away from Christ rather than to him (Matthew 27:3–5). If you fear that you might be a hypocrite and run to Christ with that fear, you are doing the one thing Judas never did. The sheep who worry that they are goats are seldom goats. Bring your fear to the Shepherd, and let his keeping be your confidence.

Textual note. Where the ESV reads “your name, which you have given me”, the KJV, following later manuscripts, reads “those whom thou hast given me”; the earliest manuscripts speak of the name given to the Son.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction: Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays aloud so that his friends may have his own joy in full, even as the word he has given them makes them, like him, strangers whom the world hates.

These things I speak in the world. It is a genuine prayer, and he prays it aloud for their sake (15:11). Being told you are valued is one thing; overhearing it said to someone else is the one that lands. All this prayer says of their being given, kept, loved and sent, they heard him say to his Father, to remember for the rest of their lives. John did remember, and wrote it down, so that we could overhear it too.

My joy fulfilled. Joy keeps returning in the last hour (15:11; 16:20–24). On the worst night of his life, it is his own joy he gives: not a mood they must manufacture, but the joy of the Son in the Father’s love and in doing the Father’s will. That joy did not leave him in the garden; it was the joy set before him for which he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). The world can take a great deal from the people of God, but it cannot reach the joy that lives in the heart of the Son, and that is the joy he has given.

The world has hated them. The sober half: the word that sets them apart draws the world’s hatred, and he does not pray it away.

Not of the world. Their origin is now from above, like his (3:3). The new birth has made them citizens of another country. They are hated not because they are odd but because they belong to the one the world rejected.

In everyday life. Take the joy he gives into the place where you are least welcome as a Christian: the office where your faith is mocked, the family gathering where it is ignored. Joy is not denial of the hostility; it is a deeper possession that the hostility cannot reach.

Why does the world hate Christians, and what if I am not hated? The world’s hatred is first a hatred of Christ, and it falls on his people because they carry his word (15:18–20). Often it is not persecution but scorn or being left out. Many Christians live quietly with kind neighbours, a mercy, not a failure. But if your faith never costs you anything, it is worth asking whether anyone can see it. Do not court hostility by being unpleasant; Peter says we should suffer as Christians, not as wrongdoers or meddlers (1 Peter 4:15–16). Simply be faithful, and let the response be his business.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not ask that his people be taken out of the world, but that the Father keep them from the evil one while they live in it as people who do not belong to it. He refuses both of the available shortcuts, withdrawal and blending in.

Not out of the world. His people must stay in the world for their mission (v. 18). The first shortcut is withdrawal: the Christian bubble, a life arranged so as never to deal with anyone who does not already agree. The wish usually comes from a desire to stay clean. But Jesus declines to ask for it, though the men he loved were about to be hunted.

From the evil one. The danger is not the world itself but the one who works in it, Satan (1 John 5:18–19), and the Father’s keeping is the answer to his strategy.

Protection, not exemption. Not that nothing will happen to them: as early tradition tells it, most of them died for him. But the one who wants them will not get them. Satan may sift them like wheat (Luke 22:31); he will not keep them. A Christian can lose his job, his health, his life for Christ, and lose nothing that the evil one was after.

In, not of. The second shortcut, blending in until no difference is left, verse 16 blocks: staying in the world is not belonging to it. He prays for the uncomfortable middle, not pulling away from the neighbours but loyal to a different Lord: citizens of heaven, sent as ambassadors.

Kept in it, not taken out. He asked not that his friends be taken out of danger but kept in it, and through two thousand years of hostility his church has never been taken out of the world nor swallowed by it. The evil one has never yet taken one whom the Father was asked to keep. Our safety is not distance from danger. It is the hand of God.

So is it wrong to protect my children or avoid certain places? No. Wisdom is not withdrawal. Parents rightly guard young children from what would harm them, and every Christian should flee situations that feed his own particular temptations (2 Timothy 2:22). The question is direction and purpose: are you sheltering in order to grow strong enough to go out, or hiding so that you never have to? Careful choices about schooling, entertainment or work are not the error Jesus refuses. The error is a life that has no unbelieving friends, no presence among the lost, and no intention of having any. He sends his people in, and he keeps them while they are there.

Where Christians differ: separation from the world. Some Christians have sought holiness by withdrawing from society; others have so blended in that no difference remains. This commentary’s view: Jesus prays for neither. His people are to live in the world, engaged in its life, but distinct in character and loyalty, kept by God from evil. Not monasteries, nor conformity, but holy presence.

Uncertain wording. The Greek phrase can be rendered “from the evil one” or “from evil”, as in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13), and the form alone cannot decide. John’s own usage leans towards the person, since his letter speaks of the evil one by the same word (1 John 5:18–19), and most modern translations follow it. Either way, behind the evil stands the evil one.

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks the Father to set his people apart for himself by the truth of his word, because he is sending them into the world as the Father sent him.

Sanctify them. “Sanctify” is not first a word about behaviour. Hagiazō means to set apart for a purpose, as was done to vessels, a day, a priest; the change of life follows, since a thing devoted to God must be fit for him. So to sanctify is both a status (set apart, 1 Corinthians 6:11) and a process (made holy, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). The petition is not first “make them better” but “make them yours, for this work”, which is exactly why the next verse is about being sent.

Your word is truth. Not merely accurate, but truth itself, the standard for everything else: when feelings, culture or reasoning disagree with it, it is not his word that gives way (Isaiah 40:8). And it is the means he names for making them holy: not an experience, a technique or a decision, but the word (Psalm 119:9, 11; Ephesians 5:26; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). When growth stalls we look for a new method; this verse points somewhere quieter, where the pruning came from in chapter 15: “you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (15:3). The Spirit sanctifies, and the sword he uses is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17).

As you sent me. The Son’s mission is the pattern for the church’s (20:21). This is John’s Great Commission, said to their faces on Easter evening. The church goes all the way in, among people at their level and at their disposal. It does not atone; that is his alone. But it goes as he went: humbly, truthfully and at cost.

What if reading the Bible feels dry? The word works anyway. Nobody remembers last month’s meals, but they are why you are alive. Keep reading, and read more of it at a time so that you see its shape. Read it with others, ask questions of it, hear it preached, and pray before you open it: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Read it to meet Christ, not only to tick a box. And remember that sanctification is the Father’s work in answer to the Son’s prayer. You are not making yourself holy by effort; you are putting yourself where he has promised to work.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sets himself apart as both priest and sacrifice for his people’s sake, so that they too may be made holy, and then widens his prayer to everyone who will believe through the apostles’ word.

I consecrate myself. Consecrate is the same word as sanctify in verse 17, and Jesus was already holy. He means that he sets himself apart for the sacrifice, as a priest was consecrated and as an offering was consecrated (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). He dedicates himself to death for their sake (hyper, on their behalf and in their place). In the old ritual the priest offered the animal; here one person is both priest and offering.

That they also may be sanctified. Their being set apart depends on his offering of himself. We are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all, and by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:10, 14).

Those who will believe. Now the prayer opens out to the whole church in every century. If you believe, Jesus prayed for you that night.

Through their word. This is how faith spreads: the eleven spoke, people believed and spoke, and it has not stopped. The word is still theirs: the apostolic word we have in the New Testament, which is why the church has always measured its preaching by Scripture. So all that follows is asked not for apostles alone but for the ordinary Christian who has never seen a miracle and finds prayer difficult.

Nobody has ever been prayed for like that. With the arrest drawing near, the Son of God spent his last quiet moments on strangers who had not been born. Then the One who prayed for them, priest and lamb in one, walked out into the night to be the offering that would make them holy. Every believer since has been brought near to God on that prayer and that blood, and the High Priest who prayed it has never stopped praying.

How can my holiness depend on his? Because holiness is first belonging to God, and then becoming like him (see v. 17). By his death Christ has set you apart for God once for all (1 Corinthians 6:11), and a bad week cannot undo it. Out of that settled status comes the daily growth in holiness, as the Spirit uses the word to make you in practice what Christ’s sacrifice has already made you in standing. So you fight sin not to become God’s but because you are his, and your victory was bought before the battle started.

How can he have prayed for me if I did not exist yet? Because he is the eternal Son, and he knew the people the Father had given him before the foundation of the world (v. 24; Ephesians 1:4). He named you in the only way a person can be named who does not yet exist, “those who will believe in me”, and the Father, who knows every one of them, heard the request as a request for each. And he did not merely foresee you. He prayed for you, and then he went out and made it possible.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays that all believers may be one with a unity drawn from and patterned on the life of the Father and the Son, a unity the world can see, so that the world may believe that the Father sent him.

That they may all be one. This is the verse on which the whole question of a divided church turns (see “Where Christians differ” below). The “all” is every believer of every century for whom he has just begun to pray (v. 20).

As you, Father, are in me, and I in you. The unity he asks for is modelled on the life of the Trinity, where the persons are genuinely distinct and the unity is one of love, life and will rather than of administration.

That they also may be in us. Christian unity is not first something we build but something we are brought into, union with the Father and the Son, which is why breaking it is serious.

So that the world may believe. Unity is a witness, so it must show: a love between Christians that outsiders can actually observe and cannot account for (13:35). Every time two estranged believers are reconciled, the world catches a glimpse of what God is like.

The glory that you have given me. “I have given” is said before the cross, of eleven men about to run, so it is no reward. The prayer says what it is for in the same breath: “that they may be one even as we are one”. It is not radiance or status but a share in the life the Father and the Son have between them.

Unity and truth in one prayer. Four verses earlier Jesus asked, “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” (v. 17). Unity and truth are petitions of one prayer and cannot be traded against each other. A unity bought by saying less than the gospel says is a counterfeit, as the Reformers, who did not leave lightly, understood. Nor does truth excuse needless division among true believers, who should stop treating each other as enemies. And it searches the heart: much division among believers is not a stand for truth at all, but the old idol of being right, and being seen to be right, dressed up as zeal.

When should I leave a church, and when should I stay? Stay through disagreements over secondary matters, disappointing preaching and personalities that grate; those are the places where the unity Jesus prayed for is proved. Leave, peaceably and without slander, when a church abandons the gospel itself, denies the authority of Scripture, or will not deal with serious sin or abuse, and only after you have raised your concern honestly with its leaders. Even then, do not burn the bridge to brothers and sisters you will spend eternity with. And never leave a church simply to escape a person you have refused to forgive.

Can I be united with Christians whose baptism or church order differs from mine? Yes, more practically than many think. A Baptist and a Presbyterian who both trust Christ alone are already one in the Father and the Son. They may not be able to form one congregation, because each must act on his convictions about baptism with a clean conscience. But they can pray together, honour each other’s ministers, share platforms for the gospel, help each other’s churches in need, and speak of each other with warmth. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, and holds it alongside a glad affection for paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) who love the same Lord.

Where Christians differ: what unity does Jesus pray for? Three answers have been given. Rome reads it as asking for one visible institution under one visible head, with separated churches the wound it was meant to prevent. The ecumenical movement read it as a mandate to merge structures. Many Protestants have read it as invisible unity only, assuming that since true believers are already one in Christ, visible divisions cost nothing. This commentary’s view: the prayer itself rules out each of the three. Against the single-institution and merger readings stands the pattern Jesus gives: nothing in the life of the Trinity requires a single earthly organisation, and the apostolic churches of the New Testament were plainly many congregations, not one structure. Against the invisible-only reading stands the purpose, “so that the world may believe”. The true answer is harder: not merger, and not comfort with division, but believers who honour one another across the lines, refuse to caricature, and are visibly glad of grace wherever it appears.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Christ living in them, believers are to be made perfectly one, so that the world may know that the Father loves them as he loves the Son; and the Son wills that they be with him to see the glory the Father gave him in love before the world began.

Perfectly one. “Perfectly” means brought to completion; it belongs to the same word family as “accomplished” (v. 4) and “It is finished” (19:30). What his finished work secured, his people grow into.

Loved them even as you loved me. Two clauses here are among the hardest things in the Bible to believe about oneself. The first, “even as you loved me” (as at 15:9), is said to the Father in prayer, so it is no exaggeration meant to cheer anyone up. The Father loves believers as he loves the Son: not that we are equal to the Son, but that we are loved with the same love, because we are in him. Most Christians, if pressed, would describe God’s love for them as something cooler, a settled goodwill, perhaps a determination to put up with them. This verse forbids it. The measure is the love between the Father and the Son from before the world was made, and the sentence has no qualifier anywhere.

I desire. The second hard thing to believe is in verse 24, and the verb changes. Until now he has been asking. Here it is thelō, “I will”: not a request but the confident will of the Son, in perfect agreement with the Father. He spends it not on escaping the cross but on securing our company: that the people he is leaving should end up where he is (14:3).

To see my glory. Heaven is seeing Christ’s glory. A second time he looks back before the world (v. 5), now to say why the Father gave him glory. God did not need to create to have someone to love; he is love, from all eternity (1 John 4:8). Before light and time there was a Father loving a Son, and this prayer asks that a crowd of latecomers be brought in to watch. We will see the glory of the Son with our own eyes, and we will not grow tired of looking.

In everyday life. Say it to yourself before you get out of bed: the Father loves me as he loves his Son. A person who knows he is loved like that does not need to win every argument or be noticed in every room.

How can God love me like that when I am so sinful? Because he does not love you on the strength of what you are in yourself. He loves you in his Son. You have been united to Christ by faith, clothed in his righteousness, adopted into his sonship (Galatians 4:4–7). When the Father looks at you he sees you in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6), and the love that rests on the Son rests on you there. Your sin is real, and it grieves him; but it was laid on Christ and punished in him, so it cannot shut you out of the love that Christ enjoys. You will not feel this every day. It is true every day.

What will heaven actually be? Before rest or reunion, it is being with Christ and seeing him. The reunions are real, the end of pain is real (Revelation 21:4), the renewed creation is real; but the centre is the face of the Lamb (Revelation 22:4). Paul said that to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23), and John said that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). If heaven seems vague or dull to you, it is usually because Christ seems vague to you now. Get to know him here, and you will long to see him there.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer ends with the righteous Father, the Son who knows him and goes on making his name known, and the goal of it all: the Father’s love for the Son, and the Son himself, living in his people.

O righteous Father. “Righteous”, the second word he adds to “Father” (see v. 11), is the word for a judge who gets the verdict right, used when every human court he will stand in before morning is about to get it wrong. The courts of men will condemn him; the righteous Father will raise him.

I know you. Three groups: the world that does not know God, the Son who knows him perfectly, and the disciples who know that the Son came from him. The only way out of the first group into the third is through the second. Nobody comes to know the Father except through the Son who knows him (Matthew 11:27).

I will continue to make it known. Two tenses, and the future is the striking one. He said at verse 4 that he had accomplished the work he was given, and here he says the making known continues. The accomplishing is the cross; the disclosing does not stop there. It goes on through the Spirit, the word and the church’s preaching.

That the love may be in them. Not that they may know about the love, but that the Father’s actual love for the Son should live inside them. The eternal love that flowed between the Father and the Son before there was a world has been poured into the hearts of sinners.

And I in them. The prayer ends not with a petition but a destination, and it is not a place: after four chapters of farewell, the last words are “in them”. The farewell leads not to a system or an institution, nor even to heaven as a place, but to the Son of God making his home in ordinary people.

In the flow. The next sentence has him crossing the Kidron (18:1). Everything he has just asked, keeping, holiness, unity, the Father’s love in his people, he goes out to secure by being arrested, condemned and lifted up.

What does it mean in practice that Christ is in me? It means you are never alone and never left to your own resources. By his Spirit the risen Christ lives in every believer (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27). So you can love people you could not love by nature, endure what would crush you, and keep praying when prayer feels empty. You will not usually feel it as a sensation. You will see it, over years, in a growing likeness to him and a love for him that was not there before. It is also why you can face death calmly: what is in you cannot die.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you,<sup>2</sup>since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him.<sup>3</sup>And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.<sup>4</sup>I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do.<sup>5</sup>And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.<sup>6</sup>“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.<sup>10</sup>All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.<sup>11</sup>And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
17.overview:
Where we are. The farewell discourse (chapters 13–16) is over. Jesus has told his disciples that they will be scattered and that he has overcome the world (16:32–33). Now, before he crosses the Kidron to the garden of his arrest (18:1), he prays aloud in their hearing.

The message. On the night before he dies, the Son speaks to the Father about his people, and we are allowed to listen. He asks to be glorified through the cross so that he may give eternal life, which is knowing the only true God and the Son he sent. He asks that those the Father gave him be kept, made holy by the word, made one, and brought at last to see his glory. Everything he will do on the cross, and still does at the Father’s right hand, is in this prayer.

Why it was said. Within the hour the disciples would run; in years to come they would be hated, expelled and killed. John’s readers knew that hatred, expulsion from the synagogue and false ideas about Jesus (see the introduction). They needed to know that they had been prayed for by name, and that the one who prayed was still praying.

How the chapter makes its case. The prayer moves outward in three circles. Jesus prays for himself: that the Son be glorified in the cross, so that he may give eternal life, and return to the glory he had before the world (vv. 1–5). He prays for the eleven, to whom he has made the Father known, asking that they be kept from the evil one, made holy in the truth, and sent into the world as he was sent (vv. 6–19). Then he prays for all who will believe through their word: that they be one, so that the world may believe, that they be with him to see his glory, and that the Father’s love and the Son himself may live in them (vv. 20–26).

Where it leads. Since the sixteenth century this has rightly been called the high-priestly prayer. Jesus consecrates himself as the sacrifice (v. 19), carries his people’s names before the Father as Israel’s high priest carried the tribes on his heart, and walks out to die for those he has prayed for. The prayer is not finished at the cross: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. If you belong to Christ, he prayed for you that night, and he is praying for you now. Your keeping rests not on your grip but on his intercession, so you can face a hostile world without leaving it, love believers you differ from, and live toward the day when you will see his glory.

keyVerse.quote: And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of his prayer Jesus defines what he came to give. Eternal life is not first a length of days or a place but a relationship: knowing the Father in the Son he sent. It is what the whole Gospel was written to bring us to (20:31), and it begins the moment we come to know him.

17.reflection:
Jesus defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (v. 3). How does this change the way you think about heaven, and about what eternal life looks like on an ordinary weekday?

Jesus asks the Father not to take his people out of the world but to keep them from the evil one (v. 15). Are you more tempted to withdraw from the world or to blend into it? What would it look like to be “in” but not “of” the world where you live and work?

Jesus prays that believers may be one “so that the world may believe” (v. 21). What divides Christians in your area or your own church, and what is one step you could take toward a unity that outsiders could see without giving up the truth?

The disciples overheard Jesus telling his Father that they were his, kept, loved as he is loved, and wanted where he is (vv. 6, 23–24). Which of these is hardest for you to believe about yourself, and how might it change the way you face this week?

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to his arrest as the one in control, and stands firm while his boldest disciple falls. In the garden he steps forward, his “I am he” sends the arresting party to the ground, and he wins his disciples’ freedom and refuses Peter’s sword, because he means to drink the cup his Father has given him (vv. 1–11). Bound, he is taken to Annas (vv. 12–14). John then alternates the scenes: Peter denies him at the door (vv. 15–18); inside, Jesus answers openly, is struck and is sent on to Caiaphas (vv. 19–24); at the fire Peter denies him twice more, and the rooster crows (vv. 25–27). The faithfulness that saves is his, not ours.
verseByVerse.theology: “I am he”, in Greek *egō eimi*, is the divine name, and at it armed men fall to the ground (see the note on vv. 5–6). He gives himself up not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to: the Shepherd lays down his own life for the sheep (10:11, 18). The arrest is at once his most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter’s denials come at a charcoal fire among the servants and officers, three times as Jesus had said, and then the rooster crows. On what fails here, and the restoration to come, see the notes on vv. 15–16 and v. 27.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes, as he often did, to the garden across the Kidron, the very place Judas knows: he is going to meet his betrayer, not to escape him.

Across the brook Kidron. The Kidron Valley lies east of the city, below the Mount of Olives. John calls it a cheimarros, a winter torrent: a stream bed that runs only after rain. A tradition, impossible to verify, says the blood of the temple sacrifices drained into it, at Passover the blood of thousands of lambs. Whether or not that is so, the Lamb of God now crosses it on his way to his own death.

A garden. Matthew and Mark name it Gethsemane, “oil press” (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the Mount of Olives. Only John calls it a garden (kēpos), and he will use the word again: “in the place where he was crucified there was a garden” (19:41). He does not spell out an echo of Eden, but many readers have heard one: Adam fell in a garden; the second Adam is arrested in one, and will be buried and rise in another. The story that went wrong in a garden is being put right in one.

Judas also knew the place. It was not discovered but known, because it was theirs. Judas could find him in the dark only because he had been welcome there; betrayal by a friend always uses what it learned when it was trusted. And Jesus did not change his habits that night. He went where Judas would find him. Nothing forced him; love led him.

The king who crossed the Kidron weeping. A thousand years earlier another king left Jerusalem betrayed: “And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron” (2 Samuel 15:23). David was fleeing Absalom, going up the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered and feet bare. His betrayer was Ahithophel, his own counsellor, whose advice had been “as if one consulted the word of God” (2 Samuel 16:23), and who hanged himself when it was not followed (2 Samuel 17:23). The Son of David now walks the same ground with the opposite purpose. David crossed it to save his life. This King crosses it to lay his down.

In everyday life. If a place where you have known Christ’s company has become the place of a wound, a betrayal in the fellowship, a hurt in the church, your Lord knew that too. He did not stop going to the garden because Judas knew it. Do not abandon the places of fellowship because one person abused them. (Where someone has been harmed or is not safe, getting safe comes first; that is not abandoning fellowship.)

Was it right for Jesus to walk into danger like that? Yes, because his hour had come. For three years he had withdrawn when men tried to seize him early (7:30; 10:39), because his time was not yet; now to avoid the garden would have been to refuse the cup. This does not teach us to court danger or despise our lives: ordinary prudence is right for us, as it was for him in the years before. It shows us a Saviour who laid down his life when it was required, and not one moment before or after.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas comes with soldiers, police and weapons, but Jesus, knowing all that awaits him, steps out to meet them and asks whom they want.

A band of soldiers. Two things about the arresting party are absurd. The first is its size. The band was a cohort (speira), a tenth of a Roman legion, nominally six hundred men, though probably only a detachment came; either way, Rome was involved from the start. With them came the temple police (“officers”). All this, at night, for a man who had taught openly in the temple every day and could have been taken there at noon (v. 20).

With lanterns and torches. The second is the equipment. Passover falls at full moon. On the brightest night of the month they come out carrying fire to look for the light of the world (8:12), and they will not find him until he steps out and tells them where he is.

Knowing all that would happen. He was not found or seized: he “came forward”, and that verb governs John’s whole account of his suffering. He knew all of it, the ropes, the slap, the flogging, the nails; he had foretold it in detail (Mark 10:33–34). Some courage depends on not knowing how bad it will be. This is the rarer kind: he walked out of the trees toward the torches with the whole of the next day in view.

Whom do you seek? His first words in the account of his suffering echo his first words in this Gospel, “What are you seeking?” (1:38), and he will ask Mary much the same at the tomb (20:15). The book, the arrest and the resurrection morning all open with him asking what people are looking for. Here the hunters are asked to name their quarry, as though he were in charge of the proceedings, which he is.

The hunted one is the great Seeker. Men came with torches to find him, and he let himself be found, because he had come to look for people who were not looking for him (Luke 19:10). The Lamb went to the altar on his own feet, and his searching love found us in our darkness long before we lifted a lantern toward him.

Did Jesus really know everything that would happen? Yes. As the eternal Son he knows all things, and in his human mind he had been given to know his path. Nothing took him by surprise, and that is what makes his going forward so astonishing. It is also a comfort: the Christ who goes before you into your sufferings is not improvising. He knows the road you are on, and he walked a harder one with his eyes open.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion: Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Jesus’ “I am he”, words that echo the divine name, the armed men fall to the ground: they will take him only because he allows it.

Jesus of Nazareth. The name of a man from a despised village (1:46), and the name that will be nailed above his head in three languages (19:19).

I am he. In Greek it is barer: two words, egō eimi, with no “he” (the ESV notes that it is literally “I am”). On one level it simply means “I am the one you want”. But John’s readers have heard Jesus use these words as the divine name (8:24, 28, 58), the words that made his hearers pick up stones at 8:58, echoing what God said to Moses out of the bush (Exodus 3:14).

Judas was standing with them. John will not let it pass. In the middle of the sentence about the divine name, he records where the man was standing: among the soldiers.

They fell to the ground. They could not take him unless he let them (10:18), and Judas, standing among them, presumably went down too. The great I AM who spoke to Moses from the fire stood among the olive trees in a carpenter’s body, and the soldiers of the strongest empire on earth could not stay on their feet before his name. It is not a rescue or a threat; they get up and do their job. It is a demonstration placed where the reader most needs it. From here on everything is done to him by others: he is bound, struck, tried, flogged, sentenced, nailed. At the front of that sequence John sets one moment in which armed men go over backwards at two words, so that nobody can say he was overpowered.

In everyday life. When Christ seems weak in your world, mocked at work, ignored in the news, outvoted in the culture, remember the garden. He has never been overpowered, only patient. Let that steady you, and humble you whenever you think his cause depends on your cleverness.

Why did they fall? John does not explain the mechanism, and we should not invent one. Shock or confusion would hardly explain why men who had come for this very purpose went down together. The plain sense is that for a moment the majesty of who he is broke through, as on the mountain of transfiguration, and creatures fell before their Creator. Every knee will one day bow at that name (Philippians 2:10). In the garden, a company of armed men bowed early.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8: the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus names himself a second time and uses the moment to win his disciples’ freedom: take me, and let them go.

So he asked them again. He is directing his own arrest, identifying himself a second time to men who have just been knocked down by the first.

Let these men go. It is a condition, put to a cohort that has just been knocked off its feet, and the only thing he asks is that his friends be allowed to walk away. Not a hearing, not fair treatment, not time: he uses the one piece of leverage he has to get them out of the garden, the Good Shepherd standing between the wolf and the sheep (10:11–12).

And it worked. Every one of the eleven survived that night, which is not what usually happened to the followers of an executed insurrectionist. Hours earlier he had prayed aloud that the Father would keep them (17:11). Now he keeps them himself, and keeping them cost him the very arrest and death he was keeping them from.

Is this really a picture of the cross? Yes, and John means it to be. The arrest is not the atonement; that happens on the cross, where Jesus bears God’s wrath against sin. But the garden shows its shape in advance: the Shepherd stepping between his sheep and the danger, taking what was coming for them so that they go free. At the cross the law’s sentence against his people falls on him, and they are released. Whenever you feel the accusation of your sins, hear him say to it: “if you seek me, let these men go.”

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples’ escape fulfils Jesus’ promise to lose none of them, while Peter, brave and mistaken, draws a sword to stop what Jesus has come to do.

To fulfil the word. Jesus’ words are fulfilled like Scripture, because they are Scripture. The word is from 17:12 (and 6:39). It promised that none would be lost eternally, and John applies it to their safety on one night. That is not a misuse of it but a window into it: the man who will not let them be arrested in a garden will not let them be lost at the end, and watching him keep the first promise makes the second credible.

Simon Peter, having a sword. Only John names Peter as the swordsman. He acts as he promised (13:37), bravely and foolishly, against a cohort. Be fair to him: hopelessly outnumbered, he drew anyway. Yet the same man will be denying everything before morning, which tells us something uncomfortable: being brave in one kind of danger does not make us brave in another.

The servant’s name was Malchus. An eyewitness detail. If, as many think, John is the other disciple known to the high priest (v. 15), he knew the household; the other Gospels say only that someone struck the high priest’s servant. John gives the wounded man a name, and mentions him again when a relative of his recognises Peter (v. 26). To Peter he was a target. To Jesus, as Luke the doctor tells us, he was a man to be healed (Luke 22:51): the last healing before the cross was done for an enemy, mending what a disciple had broken.

What Peter got wrong. Not his courage but his reading of the situation. He had heard about the cup and the hour and the Good Shepherd laying down his life, and he came to the garden believing his job was to stop it. Ask what you are defending God from. If it means preventing something he has said he intends to do, a loss, a humbling, a door closing, then the sword is out, and the likeliest result is somebody else’s ear.

How can I tell whether my zeal is Peter’s sword? Ask three questions. Is it in line with what Christ has actually said, or with what I assume he must want?
