Am I using the weapons he gave, truth spoken in love, prayer, patient witness, or the world’s weapons of force, manipulation and contempt? And who is getting hurt? Zeal that wounds the people Christ came to save, or that would have kept him from the cross, is zeal without knowledge (Romans 10:2). Real zeal for Christ looks like his own: willing to suffer, quick to heal, never needing to win by cutting someone down.
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stops Peter because he means to drink the cup his Father has given him, and he lets himself be bound.

Put your sword into its sheath. His kingdom does not advance by the sword (v. 36; Matthew 26:52), and he has to rescue his disciples not only from the soldiers but from themselves.

Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? The cup pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had appointed for him. In the Old Testament it is often the cup of God’s wrath (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15): not a sudden flare of irritation but the holy resistance of a pure God to evil, his just response to sin (Romans 1:18). It would be a lesser God who looked at the world’s cruelty and felt nothing. Jesus will drink the cup of God’s anger against sin, so that his people never have to. And it is the cup the Father has given: not Judas’s, not Caiaphas’s, not Pilate’s. Behind every human hand that night stands the Father’s purpose, and the Son receives it from him.

Where is Gethsemane? The other three Gospels place here the most famous prayer ever prayed in a garden: Jesus on his face in anguish (Luke’s detail of sweat like drops of blood is missing from some early manuscripts), asking that the cup might pass (Mark 14:36), and the disciples asleep a stone’s throw away. John gives none of it, but he assumes it. Jesus speaks of the cup as something already settled between him and his Father, and you cannot resolve a struggle you never had. John has told the agony in his own place, in chapter 12, in daylight, before a crowd: now is my soul troubled, and shall I ask to be saved from this hour? No, for this purpose I have come to this hour (12:27). It is much the same prayer, moved out of the dark into the open.

Both pictures are needed. The others show a man overtaken by horror and holding on; John shows a man walking into it with his eyes open. Take John without the others and you may forget what it cost him. Take the others without John and you may forget that nobody took his life from him.

And bound him. The captain is a commander of a thousand (chiliarchos), a senior Roman officer. They bind the one who had just floored them, and he lets them. Israel remembered a son bound by his father and laid on wood on a mountain (Genesis 22:9), who, Jewish tradition said, was old enough to have resisted and did not; tradition called it the Akedah, the Binding, and some linked it with Passover. Isaac was released and a ram was found. This time the ropes stay on.

The cup was ours. We filled it with every sin we ever committed, the Father put it into the hands of his Son, and the Son did not set it down. The next afternoon he drank it to the bottom, so that not one drop of wrath is left for those who are his. What remains for us is another cup altogether, the cup of blessing at his table (1 Corinthians 10:16), filled not with anger but with the new covenant in his blood.

Did Jesus resist the Father’s will in the garden? No. His human soul shrank from the cup with all the horror of a holy man facing God’s wrath against sin, and he said so honestly. But each time he added, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). To feel the full weight of something terrible and still embrace God’s will is not resistance but the deepest obedience there is. So when you pray in agony, asking God to take something away while longing to do his will, you are not sinning. You are praying the way your Lord prayed.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is taken first to Annas, the power behind the high priesthood, in a process whose verdict Caiaphas had pronounced long before: one man must die for the people.

First they led him to Annas. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until the Romans removed him, but five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, so for half a century the high priesthood was a family business run out of one house. Many Jews still regarded him as the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life (Luke 3:2). Only John records this hearing: a private call, before anything official begins.

Father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. The family dominated the temple, and it is often thought that they profited from its trade, the very trade Jesus had disrupted (2:13–16). So Jesus is taken first to the house of the man whose family had most to lose. “That year” does not mean the office changed hands yearly: Caiaphas held it for some eighteen years, and John means that year of all years (see the note on 11:49–50).

Expedient that one man should die. The verdict was decided before the trial (11:49–52), when Caiaphas spoke a prophecy he did not know he was uttering. Now the prophet presides, accomplishing it without understanding it. One man did die for the people, and for children of God scattered through every nation and century, and we are among them.

A night of irregularities. Jewish law as later written down forbade capital trials at night or on the eve of a festival, required a day to pass before a death sentence, and required the court to sit in its own chamber. Every one of these appears to be broken in the next few hours. How much of it applied in the AD 30s is disputed, but the guardians of the law are at work at midnight in a private house.

Why did God let such corrupt men hold the high priesthood? Because he was bringing the old priesthood to its end and replacing it with a better one. The men who should have recognised the Lamb of God handed him over, and so fulfilled the purpose of the priesthood without knowing it: a sacrifice was offered for the people. The true High Priest stood bound before the false ones, and by the next afternoon the temple curtain would be torn in two (Matthew 27:51).
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter follows Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard, let in by a friend’s kindness, and the courtyard becomes the place of his fall.

Simon Peter followed. Bravely, after the others had fled (Mark 14:50). He fails in a place most of them never went.

And so did another disciple. He is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John himself (20:2), which fits the way this Gospel refers to its author in the third person and never by name. The difficulty is that he was known to the high priest, and a Galilean fisherman’s acquaintance with the household of Annas is not obvious; perhaps it came through business or family, and some think he is someone else entirely. The Gospel does not say.

Into the courtyard. A large house built round a central courtyard, which Annas and Caiaphas may have shared. The other disciple used his access to bring Peter in. The kindness was real; left in the street, Peter might have gone home. That is no reason to be wary of kindness, but it is a reason to be honest about how failure arrives: seldom through malice, often through a door somebody opened for us in love. And the door is kept by a servant girl, whose idle question will draw out the most famous denial in history.

Two men through one gate. John sets Master and disciple in the same courtyard on purpose. Jesus goes in bound, knowing exactly what is about to happen at the fire; Peter goes in free, confident and unaware. One will be questioned and tell the truth; the other will be questioned and lie. The Lord did not go in to keep Peter from falling that night. He went in to be condemned in Peter’s place, and he had already prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

Should I avoid places where I might be tempted? Often, yes, and with no shame in it: flee youthful passions (2 Timothy 2:22), and make no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). But Peter’s problem was not that he went into the courtyard; following his Lord into danger was right. It was that he went in sure of his own strength, having brushed aside the warning (13:37–38). Go where Christ calls you, even into hard places, but go praying, aware of your weakness, leaning on him and not on your record of loyalty.
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked an idle question by a servant girl, Peter denies being Jesus’ disciple, then warms himself at the fire of the men who arrested his Lord.

You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you? She frames the question to invite a no. She is not accusing him; she is a girl at a door making conversation, probably without much interest either way. “Also” means like the other disciple, whom she knows to be one of them and who has come to no harm.

I am not. No threat has been made. And Peter, who hours ago swung a sword at an armed man’s head in the dark, says ouk eimi, “I am not”. The contrast with Jesus’ “I am he” in the garden is deliberate (vv. 5, 6, 8). The Lord named himself and a cohort went over backwards; the disciple denies who he is to a girl minding a gate.

A charcoal fire, because it was cold. Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. The word (anthrakia) appears only here and in 21:9, where the risen Jesus cooks breakfast and restores Peter beside another charcoal fire; he may have lit the second to heal what the first had witnessed. For now Peter stands among the officers who arrested his master, at their fire, getting warm.

How denial usually happens. Rarely dramatically. Far more often it is what Peter does here: taking the answer somebody has already assumed, because correcting them would be awkward and nothing seems at stake. It costs nothing at the time, which is why it is easy. Underneath is the fear of man, the wish to be accepted by the people round the fire, and Scripture calls that fear a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The cure is not a stronger will but a greater fear: the fear of the Lord, whose opinion matters more than any circle we want to belong to.

Is keeping quiet about my faith the same as denying Christ? Not always: there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and tact is not cowardice. But silence becomes denial when someone asks you directly, or assumes something false about you, and you let it stand to protect yourself. The test is the motive: am I silent because this is not the moment, or because I am ashamed of him? If it is shame, Jesus’ words apply: whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed (Mark 8:38). Ask him for courage before the question comes. And if you have already failed in exactly this way, the man who stood at this fire was restored by the same Lord and sent out to preach.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Questioned about his disciples and his teaching, Jesus shields the one and stands openly by the other: he has taught nothing in secret.

About his disciples and his teaching. A security official’s question, fishing for evidence of sedition or false teaching.

He would not name them. Jesus answers only about his teaching, not one word about the disciples. He has just got them out of the garden; he is not going to name them in a courtyard. Meanwhile, a few yards away, one of them is refusing to name him. The Shepherd who has nothing to hide hides his sheep.

Openly to the world. “Openly” (parrhēsia) is John’s word for speaking boldly, in public, without concealment, so what he taught can be checked. Nor does “nothing in secret” deny that he taught the Twelve privately (chapters 13–17): his private teaching explained the same message he preached openly (Mark 4:34). There was no secret doctrine for insiders.

Why John leaves out the trial before the council. Matthew and Mark record a full session of the council, with witnesses and the verdict of blasphemy; John covers it in a single sentence (v. 24). The likeliest reason explains most of his omissions: the other accounts were long in circulation, and he supplies what they lacked, here the hearing before Annas.

The God who did not speak in secret. Jesus is using the language of the God of Israel, who said through Isaiah, “I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness” (Isaiah 45:19), setting himself against the idols and oracles with their hidden whispers. The prisoner says the same of his own ministry, because he is the Word made flesh (1:14). Annas wants secrets. He is standing before the one in whom God has hidden nothing he means his people to know.

Is there any hidden teaching for advanced Christians? No. From the Gnostics of the second century to modern movements promising a deeper revelation, teachers claiming knowledge beyond the Bible are answered by this verse. What Jesus taught he taught openly, and what the apostles received they wrote down for the whole church (1 John 1:3). The deepest things of God are in the same Scriptures a child can read. Growth in Christ is not access to hidden knowledge but going further into what has been openly given.

Uncertain wording. Which high priest is questioning him? John calls both Annas and Caiaphas high priest (vv. 13, 19, 24). Annas had held the office and still bore the title, and many read vv. 19–23 as his questioning; others take the high priest of v. 19 to be Caiaphas, named in v. 13. The first is more likely, because v. 24 sends Jesus on to Caiaphas only once the questioning is over.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks for what any fair hearing requires, witnesses, and for saying so he is struck in the face.

Why do you ask me? “Ask those who have heard me.” Under Jewish law a case had to be established by witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and later Jewish tradition would not let the accused be made to testify against himself. Jesus calls for a proper trial. The hearing is already breaking the rules, and he says so.

Struck with his hand. Most likely an open-handed blow across the face (see the note on the wording below), illegal and humiliating. It is not mainly meant to hurt; it is the standard gesture for putting an inferior back in his place.

Is that how you answer the high priest? The officer is showing off to his master. So the first violence done to Jesus is not a court’s sentence, and not even angry: it is a junior official enforcing good manners because he disliked the prisoner’s tone. The one through whom all things were made stands bound in a courtyard, corrected on his manners by a member of the temple staff.

I gave my back. Isaiah had described it: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). The verbs are active. The Servant is not overwhelmed; he presents himself. The face slapped in Annas’s courtyard is the face we will see in glory, and the shame he carried there is the reason we will be able to look on it without shame.

Why did God allow his Son to be humiliated like this? Because our sin is not only guilt but shame, and he came to bear both. We dishonoured God; the Son received dishonour. We exalted ourselves; he was struck and put in his place. He endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and the shame began here, with a blow from the temple’s own servant: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (1:11). If you carry shame, for what you have done or for what was done to you, your Lord has stood in this courtyard. He knows what it is to be treated as worthless by those who should have honoured him, and he bore it so that you could be clothed with honour as a child of God.

Uncertain wording. The Greek says only that the officer gave Jesus a rhapisma, which can mean a blow with a rod as well as a slap. The ESV’s “with his hand” takes it as a slap, as most translations do, and a rebuke for disrespect fits that best, but certainty is not possible.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus neither hits back nor pretends the blow was just: he names the injustice calmly, leaves his cause with God, and is sent on, still bound, to Caiaphas.

If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? The reply shows what to do with an injustice. Most of us know only two responses, to swallow it in silence or to hit back, and he does neither. There are two possibilities, and the blow is wrong under both: if what he said was wrong, produce the evidence, which is what a court is for; if it was right, the blow has no justification at all. And he does not appeal to who he is, though he could have. His argument would protect any prisoner in any courtyard.

Sent bound to Caiaphas. The formal trial before the council is told by the other Gospels (Mark 14:53–65). Nothing has been established and no charge produced; he is simply moved on, still bound, in a process decided long before (11:53).

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Peter wrote about it afterwards: “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). The last clause explains how he could do it. You can say plainly that a thing is unjust and still not fight it, if you truly believe a court will sit later. Every injustice ever done to his people will be put right in a court that cannot be rigged, presided over by the one who was struck in Annas’s house.

Turning the other cheek. Jesus does not literally turn the other cheek here (Matthew 5:39), but neither does he retaliate. Turning the other cheek means refusing revenge, and it evidently permits a person to say plainly that what has been done to him was unjust.

When should I speak up against wrong done to me, and when should I stay silent? Speak when truth or justice needs it, calmly, without insult or threat, as Jesus did here and as Paul did when he appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 22:25). Use the proper channels: a complaint, a court, the elders of the church. If you are being abused, tell someone and get safe, because Scripture never asks you to stay under harm. Stay silent when speaking would only be revenge, self-display or a fight for your pride. Either way the heart beneath is the same: you entrust yourself to God, who judges justly, and refuse to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus inside will not name his disciples, Peter at the fire is asked again, by a group and then by a man who saw him in the garden, and denies again.

Warming himself. John has interleaved the scenes on purpose: Peter denies (vv. 15–18), Jesus is questioned and struck (vv. 19–24), Peter denies twice more (vv. 25–27). Both men are being asked who they are. One says no; the other will not name a single one of his disciples. Our salvation has never depended on the faithfulness of the one by the fire. It depends on the faithfulness of the one inside, who kept his silence about Peter and went on to die for him.

The second denial. The pressure rises: not a servant girl at a gate but several men at once (“they said to him”), and the question is again worded to invite a no.

A relative of Malchus. Now the danger is real. “Did I not see you in the garden with him?” expects the answer yes. This man was there: he has a family grievance and an eyewitness identification, and Peter is standing in the household of the injured party, warming his hands. Peter’s one act of courage that night has become the evidence against him. Bravery of the wrong kind stores up no credit for later.

Before we feel superior to Peter. The first denial cost him nothing; by the third he had something to fear, for it might have cost his life. Nothing suggests any of us would have done better, and the others are not in the courtyard at all.

In everyday life. Peter’s first lie made the second necessary, and the second made the third almost automatic. If you have told a small untruth this week to avoid embarrassment, go back and correct it before it grows. You can do it without dread: the Lord who told the truth inside while Peter lied outside kept the law perfectly in your place, and his record, not yours, is your standing before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter denies Jesus a third time and at once the rooster crows, exactly as Jesus said; John tells it in a handful of words and keeps Peter’s restoration for later.

Peter again denied it. Matthew and Mark say he swore and called down curses (Mark 14:71). John says nothing more: no weeping, no look, no comment. The worst night of Peter’s life is reported in a few words, and the narrative moves on to Pilate.

A rooster crowed. Exactly as Jesus said (13:38). Luke supplies what happened next: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter”, and Peter remembered, and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). The crow did not condemn him. It reminded him that the worst moment of his life had been foreseen by the man he had just disowned.

The four accounts. The Gospels name different questioners, a servant girl, another girl, the bystanders, and in John alone a relative of Malchus, and place Peter differently in the courtyard. They agree on three denials and the rooster; questions were flying round a crowded fire. Mark adds that the rooster crowed twice (Mark 14:72).

The mercy hidden in the prediction. That is why Jesus made it. A failure your Lord described to your face beforehand is one he has already taken into account; it is not the end of the story. In Peter’s case he announced it, washed the man’s feet anyway, prayed for him by name, arranged his escape from the garden, and on the third day sent word to him by name through the messenger at the tomb: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). John will tell of his restoration (21:15–19): three questions of love to match the three denials, and a man given his work back. There is no failure of ours that his faithfulness has not already outrun.

Judas and Peter. Both failed Jesus that night. Judas went out into the night (13:30); Peter would be brought back. What separated them was not that one sin was large and the other small. It was Christ. Jesus had prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32), and Peter was among those the Father had given the Son, of whom not one had been lost except the son of destruction (17:12).

Can a Christian who has denied Christ be forgiven? Yes. Peter is the proof, and he became the preacher of Pentecost. Jesus’ warning that he will deny before the Father whoever denies him (Matthew 10:33) speaks of a settled, final rejection of Christ, the life that disowns him and never returns, not of a believer who falls in weakness and comes back weeping. The warnings of Hebrews 6 describe those who fall away for good, not those grieved by their fall; if you are troubled that you have denied him, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Confess it as plainly as Peter wept over it, and believe that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7–9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pilate judges Jesus, but it is Pilate who is being tested, by the truth standing in front of him. The leaders will not enter a Gentile house for fear of defilement, yet they hand over the Passover Lamb and press for a Roman death (vv. 28–32). Inside, away from the accusers, Jesus tells Pilate that his kingdom does not come from this world and does not fight, and that he came to bear witness to the truth, which his people hear (vv. 33–37). Pilate asks what truth is and does not wait for the answer. He declares Jesus not guilty, then bargains instead of releasing him, and the crowd chooses Barabbas (vv. 38–40).
verseByVerse.theology: “Are you the King of the Jews?” is the question of this trial, and the title Pilate later fixes over the cross (19:19) will turn out to be the truest sentence anyone writes that day. Jesus’ kingdom is not from this world (see the note on vv. 36–37), and Pilate asks what truth is while standing in front of the answer (v. 38).
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free and the innocent is condemned (see the note on v. 40).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At dawn the leaders hand Jesus over to Pilate but will not enter his house, keeping themselves clean for the Passover while they deliver up the Passover Lamb.

To the governor’s headquarters. The praetorium: either Herod’s old palace near the city’s western wall or the Antonia Fortress at the corner of the temple. Pilate, governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, normally lived in Caesarea but came to Jerusalem at the feasts to keep order. Roman officials began work at dawn, and the leaders want the matter finished before the festival crowds wake; the night has produced a prisoner and no case.

So that they would not be defiled. Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean, barred from the festival meals of that day. So they stand in the street and make Pilate come out. The irony is crushing: men who will not step over a threshold because of a ceremonial rule are arranging a judicial killing on the other side of it (Matthew 23:24). This is not hypocrisy in the crude sense of knowing better and pretending. They were sincere about the purity rule, which is what makes it frightening: a real conscience about small things can stay in perfect working order while the large thing goes past unnoticed.

Eat the Passover. This raises a famous question. The other Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16); here the Passover seems still to come. The answer given at the end of this note is the likeliest harmonisation, not a certainty.

What accusation do you bring against this man? Pilate opens a formal Roman trial, and by going out to them he sets its direction: a governor was not obliged to do business in the street to suit a subject people’s scruples, and by the end of the morning he will have conceded everything. When authority loses the will to be just, it becomes the instrument of injustice, however correct its procedures appear.

Clean for the feast, outside the Lamb’s door. Jesus is handed over on the day of Preparation (19:14), and not a bone of his is broken (19:36), the rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46). The men guarding their purity for the Passover meal are delivering up the Passover Lamb himself: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). They would not cross a Gentile threshold to stay clean; he crossed from heaven to earth, and into death, to make the unclean clean.

Slain by Jew and Gentile together. Handed across the threshold the priests would not cross, the Lamb of Israel was slain by Jew and Gentile together, for Jew and Gentile together. The wall they guarded so carefully that morning he broke down in his flesh (Ephesians 2:14), and now the unclean of every nation are made clean and welcomed to his feast.

How do I know if I am straining gnats and swallowing camels? Look at where your conscience is loudest. If small matters of practice trouble you, the right wording, the right music, while bitterness, greed, a harsh tongue or an unreconciled brother do not, the scale is wrong. Jesus did not say the small things do not matter: “These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” (Matthew 23:23). Ask God to recalibrate you by his word, especially by the weightier matters of justice, mercy and faithfulness, and ask a trusted friend where your blind spot lies.

Where Christians differ: the date of the Passover. Some say John has moved the date for theological reasons, so that Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered; others that different groups followed different calendars. This commentary’s view: “eat the Passover” can refer to the whole seven-day feast of Unleavened Bread, which was also called Passover (Luke 22:1), including the festal offering eaten on the next day (2 Chronicles 30:22). The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and the leaders here wished to stay clean for the feast’s continuing meals. The Gospels do not contradict one another.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders name no crime, only insist that Jesus is an evildoer, and they show what they want: a death sentence that only Rome can pass.

If this man were not doing evil. Their first answer is not an answer, and Pilate notices. They are asking a Roman court to confirm a verdict they have already reached without telling it the grounds.

Judge him by your own law. Procedurally correct, and an attempt to be rid of the case: Rome generally left internal religious matters to local courts.

Not lawful for us. Now their goal shows: in Judea Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself. Stephen was stoned (Acts 7), but by a mob, not by a formal judicial execution, which in a Roman province was reserved to the governor. Killing Jesus legally requires Pilate.

A prisoner with no charge. They cannot name a crime because there is none. Jesus had asked them openly, “Which one of you convicts me of sin?” (8:46), and no one had answered. The emptiness of their case is the first testimony of the morning to what Pilate will say three times: “I find no guilt in him.” The Passover lamb had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5), and the men handing him over are proving, without meaning to, that he is.

Why does John keep saying the Jews handed Jesus over? He uses the phrase for the Jerusalem leaders and those who followed them, not for the whole people; Jesus, his disciples and the first believers were all Jews (see the introduction). Pilate himself says, “Your own nation and the chief priests” (v. 35). The guilt for the cross belongs to those who planned it, to Pilate who allowed it, and, in the deepest sense, to all of us whose sins put him there. Peter says the Jerusalem crowd and their rulers acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and the gospel was preached to them first. The charge of collective Jewish guilt, used to justify persecution, has no ground in John or anywhere in Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because only Rome could execute, Jesus would die not by stoning but lifted up on a cross, as he had said; and Pilate takes up the one charge Rome cares about: is he a king?

By what kind of death. Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” meant crucifixion, the Roman penalty (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–33). Had the council been able to act alone, he would have been stoned. So a legal technicality about who could execute became the means by which he died on a cross, as he had said he would. To be hanged on a tree was to be under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23), and he had to die under that sentence: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The men insisting on the correct paperwork were arranging it.

Are you the King of the Jews? The charge is now political: they accused him of forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be Christ a king (Luke 23:2). In Greek Pilate’s “you” is emphatic, placed first: su, you? This beaten, bound man, a king? It is contemptuous, and understandably so: an unarmed man, tied up, handed over by his own nation’s leaders, with no supporters anywhere in the building. Pilate has managed real insurgencies, and knows what a claimant to a throne looks like. This does not.

The only charge that could interest Rome. Treason, a rival king, is the only charge a Roman court would care about, and everything the priests want depends on making it stick. Blasphemy, which Pilate would have thrown out, surfaces only later (19:7). They were right that he was a king, and wrong about what kind, and Pilate will be right for the wrong reasons and write it on a board (19:19).

In the room they would not enter. The one conversation in which Jesus explains himself happens in a room the accusers refused to enter. Pilate meanwhile goes out (v. 29), comes in (v. 33), goes out again (v. 38), and never settles anywhere, not even with his own verdict.

What does it mean that Christ became a curse? That he stood where the law’s judgment falls. The law pronounces a curse on everyone who does not keep it (Galatians 3:10), and that is all of us. On the cross the Father treated his Son as the bearer of that curse, not because Jesus had sinned, but because our sin was laid on him (2 Corinthians 5:21). The tree was the outward sign of the inward reality: the Holy One under God’s judgment in our place. So for the believer the curse is not merely lessened. It has been exhausted on Christ, and the blessing of Abraham comes to us instead (Galatians 3:14).
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns the question back on Pilate, inviting him to ask for himself, and Pilate refuses to be involved, though he can see he is being used.

Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me? The prisoner starts questioning the judge. If Pilate means a political rebel king, the answer is no; if he means the Messiah, the answer is yes. That is not evasion. It separates two entirely different conversations, and it invites Pilate to ask for himself: the invitation Jesus gave Nicodemus, the woman at the well and the man born blind, now extended to the Roman prefect of Judea. He was the one on trial, and he spent his breath trying to reach his judge.

Am I a Jew? Contempt: why would a Roman care about Jewish religious ideas? It is also self-revealing. He declines to be personally involved; whatever this is about, it is not his world and he does not intend to enter it. So he shuts the door on the only conversation in the room that could have done him any good.

Your own nation. Having refused to be interested, Pilate still wants to know. That is his tragedy: neither monster nor fool, he asks good questions and declines to stay for the answers. He knows he is being used, and says so, and goes through with it anyway, which is the difference between seeing a thing clearly and being willing to pay for acting on it. What he would not pay was his standing with Caesar, and when the crowd cries that releasing this man would make him no friend of Caesar, that settles it (19:12). Many who see clearly enough who Jesus is are held back by the same thing: not a lack of evidence, but the fear of what following him would cost.

Can I keep Jesus at arm’s length, like Pilate? Many try: interested in him as a historical figure, a moral teacher, a subject for discussion, but unwilling to let the question become personal. Jesus will not leave it there. He asked Pilate, in effect, are you asking this for yourself? and he asks every reader the same. Neutrality about Christ is not available, because he is the King to whom every person will answer (Acts 17:31). Pilate tried to be a spectator at his own trial of Jesus, and ended as the man named in every recitation of the Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is a King, but his kingdom does not come from this world or fight with its weapons; he came to bear witness to the truth, and his people are those who listen to his voice.

My kingdom is not of this world. “Of” means out of, from (ek); the ESV renders the same word “from” at the end of the verse: “my kingdom is not from the world”. It is a statement about origin, not location. His kingdom does not come from this world or work the way its kingdoms do: its source is heaven, and its power is truth, not swords. Its territory is very much this world, which is why he is standing in a Roman courtroom.

Why the preposition matters. Read as location, the sentence becomes an excuse for a Christianity that hands the real world to other powers and retreats into private religion, an arrangement every tyranny has been happy to grant the church. Read as origin, it is far more disturbing to Pilate: a kingdom is at work in his province whose authority did not come from Rome, does not depend on Rome, and will outlast Rome. Rome has fallen. His kingdom has spread to every nation by nothing but the word of the cross and the power of the Spirit, and it will stand when every throne on earth is dust.

My servants would have been fighting. Jesus gives evidence Pilate can check: exactly one sword had been drawn in the garden, and its owner had been told to put it away. The absence of a fight proves the kingdom’s origin. Every time the church has reached for the sword to advance the faith, and it has, it has contradicted the sentence its Lord spoke at his own trial.

So you are a king? Pilate seizes on the word, and Jesus’ answer amounts to a yes, though not in Pilate’s sense (see the note on the wording at the end).

Born, and came. He was born, as every man is, and he came into the world from elsewhere: the eternal Son become man, in one phrase. It is the only time in this Gospel he speaks of his birth.

To bear witness to the truth. He conquers by testimony, describing himself to the governor as a witness: the humblest of job descriptions, and the one that gets him killed. His subjects are those who listen to his voice, as the sheep hear the shepherd (10:27), and the sentence is an invitation even to Pilate.

In the flow. Nathanael hailed him as King of Israel (1:49); the crowd tried to make him king by force (6:15); he rode in as Zechariah’s king (12:13–15). Now he tells a Roman what kind of king he is, and Pilate will write the title over the cross (19:19–20): this King is never more truly enthroned than when he is lifted up.

In everyday life. In your workplace, your vote, your conversations about public life, refuse the weapons of slander, manipulation and contempt even when your cause is right. The King you serve won without them.

Does this mean Christians may never fight? Some Christians, pacifists, read it so, and their earnest witness against violence deserves respect. But Jesus is speaking of his kingdom: it will never be advanced by force. That does not abolish the state’s God-given sword (Romans 13:4), nor forbid a Christian to serve as a soldier or police officer (Luke 3:14), nor to defend life. A Christian citizen may share in the just defence of others.

What does it mean to be of the truth? To belong to the truth, not merely to hold opinions about it: to have been born of God, so that his voice sounds like the voice of home. It is not that some people are naturally better at truth, but that those whom God has drawn hear the Shepherd when he speaks (6:44–45; 10:26–27). It shows in a willingness to be corrected by Christ, to come to the light even when it exposes you (3:21), and to keep listening when his word is unwelcome. If his voice is the one you want to hear above all others, you are of the truth.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and the state. Some have sought to establish Christ’s kingdom by political power or force; others have concluded that faith has nothing to say to public life. This commentary’s view: Christ’s kingdom advances by the word and Spirit, not by the sword. The church must not use the state’s weapons to spread the gospel. Yet Christ is king over all, and his truth addresses rulers too, as here.

Uncertain wording. “You say that I am a king” can be read as a guarded yes (the word is yours, but it is true), as a plain yes, or, since the Greek for “that” can also mean “because”, as you say it, because I am a king; a few take it as non-committal (compare “You have said so”, Mark 15:2). What follows settles it: he goes straight on to say why he was born and came into the world, which no one denying the title would do. The likely meaning is a real yes, held apart from Pilate’s idea of kingship.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate asks what truth is but does not wait for the answer; he declares Jesus not guilty and then, instead of releasing him, tries to bargain him away.

What is truth? It can be heard two ways. As a sneer: the cynicism of a career official who has watched every faction in a difficult province dress up its interests as principle, and has decided that truth is a word people use when they want something. That is the usual reading, and it fits the man. Or as genuine: he has just been told by a bound prisoner that there is such a thing as truth and that people can be of it, and for one moment he may be actually asking. Either way, the Truth is standing in front of him (14:6).

He did not stay. What settles it is not the tone but the timing. Francis Bacon wrote: “What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.” He asked the largest question a person can ask, in the presence of the only one who could answer it, and left the room. Many still ask it without wanting the answer.

I find no guilt in him. The first of three times (19:4, 6). Three times the Roman court, in the person of its highest local representative, returns a verdict of not guilty, and three times it proceeds anyway. He was declared innocent three times by the court that crucified him, so that we who are guilty might be declared righteous by the court of heaven.

A custom. Having acquitted him, Pilate does not release him but offers a deal, so from this moment Jesus is no longer being tried but negotiated over. No source outside the Gospels mentions this custom, though governors are known to have released prisoners to please a crowd. By offering them “the King of the Jews” he is trying to wriggle out, and mocking the leaders with the title.

The suspicion that truth is only power. Pilate’s cynicism has since become an intellectual school. Nietzsche, and after him Michel Foucault, taught many to ask of every claim to truth whose interests it serves, and the suspicion is not paranoid: churchmen among others have used “the truth” as a club. But look at who holds what in this room. The man with the power has given up on truth, and the man who claims to be the Truth has no power at all: bound, struck, about to be traded for a bandit. A truth used as a weapon would look like Pilate. This truth looks like a prisoner who will not let his servants fight, and who uses his authority to lay down his life for the people condemning him. That is the one truth claim that cannot be a grab for power, and it judges every Christian who has turned it into one.

How do I answer a friend who says there is no such thing as truth? Gently, and with a question: is that statement true? If it is, there is at least one truth; if not, there is no reason to believe it. Then move from argument to a person. Christianity claims not merely to have found some true ideas but that the Truth became a man, lived, died and rose, and that his resurrection is a public fact that can be examined (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Invite your friend to read one of the Gospels with you. Pilate’s problem was not a lack of evidence but that he would not stay for it. Ask your friend to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offered the King of the Jews, the crowd demands Barabbas, a violent rebel, and the guilty man goes free while the innocent one goes to the cross: substitution acted out before anyone explained it.

Not this man, but Barabbas! Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7): an armed nationalist with blood on his hands, of exactly the kind Rome crucified in batches, and of exactly the kind Jesus had been accused of being.

Barabbas was a robber. The word (lēstēs) means a bandit, often a violent rebel; Josephus uses it of the insurgents of the period, and it is the word for the thieves and robbers who climb into the sheepfold by another way (10:1, 8). They chose the robber over the Good Shepherd, the violent, political liberation that Rome could crush, and refused the liberation no power can overcome.

Son of the father. His name means “son of the father” (bar abba). Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17), which, if it stood, would mean Pilate asked the crowd to choose between Jesus son of the father and Jesus who is called Christ. The evidence is divided. But the scene makes the point the name suggests: a guilty son of a father goes free, and the innocent Son of the Father dies.

The exchange acted out. Here substitution, one person taking another’s place, is acted out in front of witnesses before anybody had a word for it. The man guilty of insurrection and murder walks free; the one the judge has declared innocent is taken to the cross that had been prepared for Barabbas. Barabbas is the first person whose life was saved by Jesus’ death in a literal sense, and then he walks out of history. He did not choose it, did not deserve it, and as far as we know never thanked anybody. That is the exchange: not a bargain or a reward, but a guilty man’s sentence served by an innocent one, arranged by people trying to do something else entirely.

The prison stands open. Barabbas walked out into the morning light, and the Lord of glory walked toward the cross Rome kept for men like him. Every rebel who trusts in Christ goes out through that same door. The prison stands open because the cross was occupied, and the one who hung there was the King of the Jews, our substitute.

In everyday life. You are Barabbas. When someone wrongs you, remember how much you were released from, and let that make you quick to forgive.

Was Barabbas saved? Scripture does not tell us, and we should not guess. He was spared a Roman cross, which is not the same as being forgiven by God. To be saved from God’s judgment a person must trust in the one who took his place (3:16, 36). Barabbas is a picture of substitution, not proof that everyone it pictures receives it. So the picture ends with a question for us: you have heard that Christ died in the place of sinners; have you received him as dying in yours?

Is it just for an innocent man to be punished in place of the guilty? It would be unjust if the substitute were unwilling or dragged in against his will, or if the judge simply waved the guilt away. None of those is true at the cross. The Son came willingly (10:18); the Judge whose law was broken is the same God who provides the substitute (Romans 3:25–26); and the Son is united to his people as their head, so that what he does, he does as one of us and for us. Barabbas’s release was an injustice by Pilate. Ours is the justice of God satisfied by the love of God, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. To justify means to declare a person righteous in God’s court: not to make him better by degrees, but to pronounce the verdict in his favour, because his penalty has been borne and Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.

So, if you seek me, let these men go.”<sup>9</sup>This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.”<sup>10</sup>Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)<sup>11</sup>So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?”<sup>12</sup>So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.<sup>13</sup>First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.<sup>14</sup>It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.<sup>15</sup>Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.<sup>17</sup>The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”<sup>18</sup>Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves.
