I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.<sup>21</sup>Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said.”<sup>22</sup>When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?”<sup>24</sup>Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.<sup>25</sup>Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”<sup>26</sup>One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”<sup>27</sup>Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.<sup>28</sup>Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.<sup>29</sup>So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”<sup>30</sup>They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.”<sup>31</sup>Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”<sup>32</sup>This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>33</sup>So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?”<sup>35</sup>Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”<sup>36</sup>Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”<sup>37</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world— to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
Where we are. The teaching in the upper room and the great prayer are over (chapters 13–17), and Jesus walks out of the city into the hour he has spoken of since Cana (2:4; 12:23). This chapter takes us from a garden across the Kidron, through a night hearing in the high priest’s house, to the trial before Pilate at dawn.

The message. Jesus is not a victim caught by stronger men but the King going freely to his death for his people. He gives himself up, shields his friends, receives the cup from his Father’s hand, and stands firm while his boldest disciple collapses. Before the Roman governor he declares a kingdom that does not come from this world and does not fight with its weapons, and he names its power: the truth, heard by everyone who belongs to it.

Why it was said. John’s readers lived under Rome’s power and knew what it was to be put out of the synagogue (see the introduction). A crucified Messiah looked like a defeated one. John shows them that nobody took Jesus’ life from him (10:18), that his kingdom outlasts the courts that condemn his people, and that even a disciple who denies him is not beyond his reach.

How the chapter makes its case. In the garden (vv. 1–11) Jesus steps forward, his “I am he” throws the arresting party to the ground, and he wins his disciples’ release and sends Peter’s sword back into its sheath. John then sets two scenes side by side (vv. 12–27): inside, Jesus answers Annas openly, is struck and is sent bound to Caiaphas; outside at the fire, Peter three times says “I am not”. At dawn (vv. 28–40) the leaders, careful not to be defiled, hand Jesus to Pilate. Inside, Jesus speaks of his kingdom and the truth; outside, Pilate declares him innocent, and the crowd asks for Barabbas.

Where it leads. The chapter points straight to the cross. The Good Shepherd says, “if you seek me, let these men go”, and drinks the cup so that it is not left for his people. The Passover Lamb is handed over by men keeping themselves clean for the feast. The innocent one is condemned and the guilty Barabbas walks free: substitution is acted out before it is explained.

For us. You are not saved by your faithfulness at the fire but by his faithfulness inside, so a fallen believer can come back as Peter did. And Christ’s kingdom asks you not to fight for him with the world’s weapons but to listen to his voice and bear witness to the truth, whatever it costs.

keyVerse.quote: Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?
keyVerse.note: In one sentence Jesus refuses both rescue and resistance, and shows how he goes to the cross: freely, as a Son receiving his Father’s will, to drink the cup of judgment that would otherwise be ours. The whole chapter, from the soldiers on the ground to Barabbas walking free, shows the same willing Saviour and the same kingdom that does not advance by the sword (v. 36).

18.reflection:
Jesus steps forward to meet the soldiers, wins his disciples’ release and refuses Peter’s sword (vv. 4–11). What difference does it make to you that nobody took his life from him, but that he gave it? How might his words “if you seek me, let these men go” speak to guilt you still carry?

Peter’s first denial was an answer to a servant girl’s idle question, with nothing apparently at stake (v. 17). Where are you most tempted to let people assume you are not his, and what helps you stand when the question comes?

When he was struck, Jesus named the injustice calmly without hitting back (v. 23). When have you swallowed a wrong or struck back, and what would it look like to speak plainly and still entrust yourself to the God who judges justly?

Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world and that everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice (vv. 36–37). How should that shape the way Christians speak and act in public life? And where are you, like Pilate, asking questions without staying for the answer?

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The innocent King is condemned because the men around him love their position more than the truth, yet even his enemies end up proclaiming who he is. Pilate has Jesus flogged to satisfy the crowd and presents him in a mock crown and robe, declaring him innocent again (vv. 1–6). The charge that he made himself the Son of God frightens Pilate, but Jesus tells him his authority is lent from above (vv. 7–11). The threat about Caesar ends the trial: the chief priests disown every king but Caesar, and Pilate hands Jesus over (vv. 12–16). He carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, under a title in three languages that Pilate refuses to change (vv. 17–22).
verseByVerse.theology: “Behold the man!” (v. 5) and “Behold your King!” (v. 14) are Pilate’s two presentations of Jesus, each truer than Pilate knows (see the notes on vv. 5–6 and vv. 13–14). Pilate intends mockery; God intends revelation. The crown of thorns and the purple robe are meant as a parody of kingship (vv. 2–3).
verseByVerse.examples: Crucified between two others (v. 18): the innocent numbered among the guilty. On the title in three languages, and Pilate’s refusal to change it, see the notes on vv. 19–22.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate has an innocent man savagely flogged to buy him off the cross, and the soldiers mock him with a crown and a robe that, without their knowing it, tell the truth about him. John tells the cross as the King’s enthronement, and it begins here, with a crown of thorns.

Flogged him. Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it tore the flesh to ribbons and sometimes killed the prisoner before crucifixion. This one comes mid-trial, before any sentence. Pilate has found no guilt and is looking for a cheaper way out than justice, as Luke records in his own words: “I will therefore punish and release him” (Luke 23:16, 22). That is in some ways worse than a plain miscarriage of justice: a man he has publicly declared innocent is savagely beaten, not as a sentence but as a bargaining chip.

A crown of thorns. Not the usual word for a king’s crown (diadēma) but stephanos, above all the victor’s wreath, given to the winner of the games or a general returning in triumph. They meant it as a joke. Within days the man wearing it will be seen to have won, and stephanos is the New Testament’s word for the crown he gives away: the crown of life, of righteousness, of glory that does not fade (James 1:12; 2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4).

The thorns of the curse. Thorns were part of the curse on the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:18), and a handful of that curse is pressed onto his head by laughing men. The King bears the sign of God’s just sentence on a world gone wrong, so that those who trust him receive blessing instead: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

A purple robe. Purple, made from costly dye, was the colour of royalty; this was perhaps an old soldier’s cloak. Without knowing it, the soldiers are robing and crowning the King for his throne.

The King’s first crown was made of thorns. He wore it without complaint for people who had brought thorns into the world. The head they mocked is crowned now with many diadems (Revelation 19:12), and he wears them still bearing the marks of the first. There is no crown in heaven that was not won under that one.

Why did Jesus have to suffer so much? Would his death alone not have been enough? Scripture does not treat his sufferings as a mere preliminary. His whole humiliation, the flogging and mockery as well as the death, was part of his obedience and his bearing of our sin: Isaiah links the wounds themselves to our healing (Isaiah 53:5), and Peter says he bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The suffering also shows what sin is: something that, when it fell on the holy Son, looked like this. And there is no pain you can suffer that he has not entered; he is a High Priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

In everyday life. When you suffer in your body, tell the Lord who was flogged. You do not have to explain pain to him.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in mockery the soldiers hail the truth, and Pilate’s second verdict of innocence exposes the injustice of everything being done to Jesus.

Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” by soldiers, probably auxiliary troops in Roman service, who mock him with the truth. Robe, crown, acclamation and homage: every part of a coronation is there, turned into a joke. Heaven will one day ring with the same acclamation, sung in earnest by people from every nation.

I find no guilt in him. The second declaration of innocence (18:38). The horror is quiet and official: the verdict is innocent, and the prisoner has just been flogged (see the note on vv. 1–2). Pilate wants his fairness noticed in the same breath in which he brings out a man beaten half to death for no offence.

Why does God let people mock Christ, then and now? Because he is patient, and he is not threatened. The soldiers’ mockery was the means by which the King was led to his throne, and today’s jokes and casual blasphemy threaten his reign no more than theirs did. God is giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and some mockers will be his: a Roman centurion, watching him die, confessed him as the Son of God (Mark 15:39). When you hear Christ mocked, grieve, speak up with grace where you can, and pray for the mocker. He may yet kneel.

In everyday life. Watch for the Pilate in yourself: the wish to be seen as fair while doing the unjust thing. If you have harmed someone and are asking others to admire your reasonableness, stop, and put it right. The King who took those blows has borne that sin too, so you can own it without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate shows the beaten Jesus to the crowd hoping for pity, but the sight of the true man, crowned with the curse, draws only a howl for his death. In this one man we see both God’s verdict on human sin and God’s answer to it.

Behold the man! In Latin, Ecce homo, one of the most often painted scenes in the Gospels. Pilate means it cynically: look at the state of him; this is your dangerous rebel. He is betting the sight will end their demand for his death. But suffering does not reliably produce pity, and here it produces a howl.

The true man. John hears more: here is the true human being, the second Adam, the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13), and perhaps an echo of Zechariah’s “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch” (Zechariah 6:12), crowned as a priest on his throne. He is the human race’s representative, whose obedience counts for others: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). The curse that fell on the first Adam sits on the second’s head in the form of thorns.

Crucify him, crucify him! The chief priests and officers lead the shout, and we should not distance ourselves from it too quickly. This is what happened when God became visible and stood before a crowd at close range without power: not indifference or confusion, but a demand that he be removed. Anyone who wonders why God does not simply show himself finds part of an answer here, and it is not comfortable. Here is everything humanity was meant to be, beaten and robed in mockery, and everything humanity has become, howling for his death. Pilate’s reply is his third declaration of innocence, and a taunt: he knows they cannot legally crucify.

Would I have shouted with the crowd? In one sense, yes: not because you were in Jerusalem that morning, but because the same heart is in all of us by nature, the heart that wants God out of the way when he comes too close (Romans 8:7). The cross was done for our sins, and in that sense by us. But the gospel does not leave you in the crowd. The man they rejected prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34, words missing from some early manuscripts but printed in most Bibles), and about three thousand people in that same city were baptised seven weeks later (Acts 2:23, 36–41). The shout of “Crucify him” is answered by the cry “It is finished.”

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real charge against Jesus was always that he claimed to be the Son of God, and because the claim is true, even a Roman governor is afraid.

We have a law. The law against blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), which a Roman court had no business enforcing. All morning they had dressed a religious charge up as a political one, a rival king, because that was the only kind Rome would hear. Now, frustrated, they fall back on the real charge, and hand Pilate a question he is not competent to judge.

The Son of God. This is what the council had actually condemned him for (5:18; 10:33), and they had understood him exactly (8:59; 10:31). The only question is whether it is true. The eternal Son stood in a governor’s court accused of being exactly who he was.

Even more afraid. Something about this prisoner has unsettled Pilate since the first interview. Matthew says his wife sent him a warning that day, after a dream: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matthew 27:19). Romans believed in sons of gods (Augustus was officially son of the deified Julius), and every Roman knew stories of gods walking about in disguise and of what befell those who mistreated them unrecognised. What if this man really was one?

Did Jesus really claim to be God? Yes, and his enemies understood it better than many modern readers. He called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (5:18). He said, “before Abraham was, I am” (8:58), and “I and the Father are one,” and they took up stones because “you, being a man, make yourself God” (10:30–33). He accepted Thomas’s “My Lord and my God!” (20:28). He did not die for claiming to be a good teacher, but for claiming to be the Son of God. As C. S. Lewis argued, a man who said these things would be deluded, a deceiver, or the Lord he claimed to be. The resurrection settled which.

In everyday life. If he is the Son of God, everything he says has the authority of God, including what he says about your money, your marriage, your fears and your sins. Bring the area where you have treated his words as optional under his claim today, trusting the Spirit he has given you to work in you both the will and the doing (Philippians 2:13).

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frightened, Pilate asks the right question at last, “Where are you from?”, but Jesus, who has already told him the truth, is silent, and Pilate falls back on his power. The reader knows the answer: he is from the Father.

Where are you from? Not his hometown, which Pilate knows (Luke 23:6–7), but: who are you, really? It is the great question of this Gospel, raised by the crowd who thought they knew where he came from (7:27) and by the Pharisees who said they did not (9:29). Now a frightened Roman asks it in a private room, and it is the right question at last.

No answer. After a night of speaking, the one question that goes to the centre is met with silence. This is Isaiah’s Servant: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). And Pilate had already been told the truth (18:37), asked “What is truth?” and walked out without waiting (18:38). A man who leaves before the answer to one question does not get an answer to the next.

Do you not know that I have authority? Just frightened, Pilate reaches for his rank, as small men in authority do when ignored. He thinks he holds Jesus’ life in his hands. Power has seldom been so mistaken about itself.

The answer John has already given. The reader has had it since the first verse: he is the Word who was with God and was God (1:1), come from the Father into the world (16:28). The prisoner in the purple robe is the one through whom Pilate, Rome and the pavement under their feet were made (1:3), and he has come from the Father’s side to take sinners back there with him (14:3).

Silent before his judge. Christ was silent before his judge, so that we might have something to say before ours: he died for me. And the one who would not answer Pilate answers every sinner who comes to him: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (6:37).

What if God is silent when I ask him something? Some have asked God something real, not idly, and received not a refusal but silence, and are tempted to conclude that nobody is there, or that the asking was somehow disqualified. This verse shows that God’s silence is not always what it appears. Jesus’ silence was not indifference: the man before Pilate was on his way to die for sinners, and the nearest thing to an answer Pilate would ever get stood there in a purple robe with his hands tied. That does not explain any particular silence. It establishes something narrower and worth having: a silent Christ and an absent Christ are not the same thing. Keep praying, keep reading his word, and remember that he has already given his clearest answer at the cross.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells Pilate that his power is lent by God and that the one who handed Jesus over bears the greater guilt; Pilate tries to free him, until the threat that he is no friend of Caesar settles it.

From above. Anōthen, the word that baffled Nicodemus (3:3), where it can mean “again” or “from above”. Here it plainly means from God, and the claim is enormous. All human authority is delegated by God (Romans 13:1), and God had ordained this hour (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Pilate holds real power, but it is on loan. The Father had given Pilate his authority, the Son had given himself into his hands, and that terrible morning was moving according to a purpose formed before the world began.

The greater sin. The one who handed him over, most probably Caiaphas (see the box below), had the Scriptures, the office and full knowledge; Pilate, a Gentile administrator out of his depth, is guilty, but less so. There are degrees of sin (Luke 12:47–48), and Scripture measures guilt by how much a person knew, which is uncomfortable for the well-taught and merciful toward the ignorant.

Not Caesar’s friend. This sentence ends the trial. Friend of Caesar was an honorary title for loyal officials, and the emperor Tiberius was suspicious and quick to punish disloyalty. Pilate’s record was poor: he had provoked riots with the emperor’s image in Jerusalem, had probably been overruled by Tiberius after the Jewish leaders complained over his head, and within a few years would be sent to Rome to answer for a massacre in Samaria. The men making the threat know it. The acquittals, the fear and the attempts at release all collapse the moment his career is threatened.

Comfort under bad authority. Here is comfort for anyone under an authority behaving badly, and it must not become a defence of tyranny: somebody has the greater sin, so sin is being committed and measured. What it says is that the power being abused is borrowed and bounded, and that the man wielding it will answer for how he used what he was lent.

If God is in control, was Pilate really to blame? Yes. God’s sovereignty never excuses human sin. Pilate’s authority came from above, but his decision to condemn an innocent man to save his position came from his own heart, and Jesus calls it sin. Peter holds both together in one sentence: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). That is not a puzzle to be solved by dropping one half. It is the believer’s comfort that even the worst human choices cannot escape God’s purpose.

Must I obey authorities who act unjustly? In general, yes, in everything lawful, because their authority is from God (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), including rulers we did not vote for and employers we do not admire. But when a ruler commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Christians may also resist injustice by lawful means: appeal, protest, the ballot, the courts. And abuse in a home or a church is never to be submitted to; get help and get safe.

Uncertain wording. “He who delivered me over to you” is singular, and Jesus does not say whom he means. Most probably it is Caiaphas, who had urged that one man should die for the people and sent Jesus on to Pilate (11:49–53; 18:24, 28); some think Judas, others the leaders as a group, spoken of as one. On any reading the one who handed him over knew more, and sinned more, than Pilate.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate takes the judge’s seat to sentence the true Judge, and in Passover week he presents the thorn-crowned Jesus to his people as their King. From here the chapter carries two threads to their end: the King enthroned on a cross, and the Lamb sacrificed in Passover week.

The judgment seat. The raised platform (bēma) from which a Roman official gave formal sentence, at the Stone Pavement, in Aramaic Gabbatha: an eyewitness detail. The irony is that Jesus is the true Judge (5:22, 27). Pilate sits in judgment over the one before whose judgment seat he himself will one day stand (2 Corinthians 5:10).

The day of Preparation. The regular term for Friday (v. 31; Mark 15:42): here the Friday of Passover week (see the box below), and John wants us to see the Passover Lamb (1:29). Some note that the lambs were slaughtered from about midday, the hour John seems to name, but if John is using Roman hours that match disappears, so hold it lightly. His symbolism rests on the day, not the clock: Jesus was killed on the day of Preparation, in the week the Passover lambs were sacrificed.

It was about the sixth hour. About noon by Jewish reckoning (see hours of the day). Mark says he was crucified at the third hour, about 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25), and the trial cannot run three hours after the crucifixion. Two reasonable answers are offered. John may be counting hours the Roman civil way, from midnight, making his sixth hour about six in the morning. Or, since people divided the day into rough quarters (third, sixth, ninth hour), each writer named the marker nearest an event that fell between two. John writes “about the sixth hour”; nobody in that courtyard had a watch.

Behold your King! Pilate mocks the Jews, and speaks the truth. Crowned with thorns and robed in purple, Jesus shows what God’s promised King looks like: enthroned in suffering, crowned with the curse. The trial has turned on one question since Pilate first asked, “Are you the King of the Jews?” (18:33), and here it reaches its climax.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of the Aramaic name Gabbatha is not known for sure (perhaps “a raised place”). More important is “the day of Preparation of the Passover”. Matthew, Mark and Luke say the Last Supper was a Passover meal (Mark 14:12–16), while John seems to put the Passover a day later (13:1; 18:28). Some think different groups followed different calendars that year, or that Jesus held the meal early. The more likely answer is that the phrase means the Friday of Passover week, the day of preparation for the Sabbath (compare 19:31; Mark 15:42), and that “the Passover” in 18:28 means the meals of the festival week; then the Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus died on the Friday of Passover. It is not the only careful answer, and believers who hold every word of the Gospels true still weigh these options.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion; times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
To be rid of Jesus, the chief priests renounce both their promised King and God’s own kingship, and Pilate hands him over to be crucified.

Away with him! Total rejection, and Pilate twists the knife: “Shall I crucify your King?”

We have no king but Caesar. Said not by the crowd or a hothead but by the chief priests, whose office existed to represent Israel before God. Israel was founded on the conviction that its true King was God: when the people first asked Samuel for a king, the LORD said they had rejected him from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7), and Gideon refused a crown because “the LORD will rule over you” (Judges 8:23). Israel longed for the Messiah, David’s son, to rule under God. Now, at Passover, which celebrated deliverance from a pagan king, a few hundred yards from the temple, the priesthood declares loyalty to the emperor of the occupying army to secure the execution of its own Messiah. In rejecting Jesus they reject God. Some forty years later Caesar’s soldiers burned the temple to the ground.

Delivered him over. “To them” means to do what they wanted; Roman soldiers carried it out (v. 23). The verb carries weight in this Gospel: Judas delivered him to the priests, the priests to Pilate, and Pilate delivers him to be crucified. Behind them all stands another delivering: the Father “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

Caesar’s throne is dust. His own priests disowned the King, and he did not disown them. Within weeks thousands in the same city bowed to him as Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36), and before long “a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith” (Acts 6:7). Caesar’s throne is dust. Christ’s stands, and its gates are still open to those who once cried, “Away with him.”

There is always a Caesar. When the true King is inconvenient, something can always be appealed to as the real authority: career, safety, respectability, a group’s approval. The chief priests did not stop believing in God that morning. Under pressure, they named somebody else as the one whose displeasure they could not risk.

In everyday life. Finish this sentence honestly: the thing I could not bear to lose, even for Christ, is… Whatever fills the gap is the Caesar you are tempted to bow to. Bring it to him today, and say aloud that he is your King.

Does this mean God has rejected the Jewish people? No. This verse has been badly misused, so the safeguard must be stated. It is a sentence spoken by a group of officials in one courtyard on one morning, not a verdict on a people. The Gospel’s author, its subject, Jesus’ mother and all his apostles were Jews, and Paul says plainly that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Christians differ on what Romans 11 promises for Israel’s future (see the note on vv. 37–38), but no view gives any ground for contempt. The verse is a warning about religious leadership, and it lands nearest those most like the men who said it: people who know the Scriptures, hold religious office, and find the real King inconvenient.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes out of the city carrying his own cross and is crucified at Golgotha between two criminals: the Lamb carrying the wood, the Servant numbered with the transgressors.

Bearing his own cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution, where the upright usually stood already. The other Gospels say Simon of Cyrene was made to carry it behind Jesus (Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26), and the accounts fit: after a night of blows and a Roman flogging Jesus could not finish the walk, as often happened. John, whose whole account insists that nothing was taken from Jesus and everything was given, records that he went out carrying it himself.

Golgotha. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution; “Calvary” comes from the Latin calvaria, skull. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre probably marks the site, then just outside the city wall and beside a road, because public execution was meant to be seen.

There they crucified him. None of the Gospels describes the process; every first-century reader knew what the words covered. Crucifixion was the cruellest and most shameful death Rome inflicted, reserved for slaves and rebels. Nails were driven through his hands and, it seems, his feet (20:25; Luke 24:39; the word for hand can include the wrist), and the victim died slowly, of exhaustion, shock and laboured breathing, often over days. Cicero said the very word “cross” should be far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts. The evangelists want us to see not the gore but the meaning.

Jesus between them. Isaiah had said the Servant would be “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), and a Roman work detail carried out that line with no idea what they were doing. The Lord of glory hung in the middle, where sinners are, so that sinners could be brought to where he is.

Isaac and the wood. John may be recalling Isaac carrying the wood up Mount Moriah for his own sacrifice (Genesis 22:6). Abraham said God would provide the lamb; here the Father provides the Lamb, and the Lamb carries the wood. There was no ram in the thicket to take his place, because he was the provision.

Outside the camp. He went outside the city, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). So Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood, cleansing sinners and setting them apart as God’s own, and we are to go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:12–13).

What does it mean for me to take up my cross? Not to carry his cross; that was his alone, and no one shares the work of atonement. But Jesus said that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow (Luke 9:23). To carry your cross is to accept, for his sake, the cost of belonging to him: lost approval, the death of your own way, the hardships obedience brings. It is not every misfortune, a bad back or a difficult neighbour, though he helps with those too. And it is always carried following him, so it leads, as his did, through death to resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate’s notice over the cross, meant as mockery and warning, proclaims to the whole world in three languages that the crucified Jesus is the King.

An inscription. The charge was usually written on a board (titulus), carried before the condemned man or hung round his neck, then nailed to the cross, to tell the crowd what crime was being punished. Matthew calls this one the charge against him (Matthew 27:37), yet it names no deed, only a person and a title. The only crime it can point to is being who he is, and Pilate had three times found no guilt in him.

The King of the Jews. Meant to mock him and warn would-be kings, it proclaims the truth: on the cross Jesus is enthroned as King. The Latin initials INRI (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum) appear on many crucifixes.

In Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek. Aramaic (literally Hebrew, as older translations have it), the language of home and street; Latin, of the army and the law; Greek, the common language of trade and learning. So the first public proclamation of Jesus’ kingship was in three languages, official, posted over his head beside a main road at the busiest time of the Jewish year, and paid for by the Roman government. It has never been taken down.

Is Jesus King now, or only when he returns? Now. He was enthroned at the cross and the resurrection, and he is seated at the Father’s right hand, reigning until all his enemies are put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25; Ephesians 1:20–22), with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). His reign is hidden now, exercised through his word and Spirit as he gathers his people from every nation, and it will be visible to all when he returns. So the church can be confident in every age and place. The board over the cross was not a joke that came true later. It was true when it was nailed up.

In everyday life. Pray today for Bible translators, for missionaries learning a hard language, for a church whose language you do not speak. The cross was first proclaimed in three languages; it will finally be praised in all of them.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests want the title turned into a mere claim, but Pilate refuses to change it, so the truth about Jesus stands written over his cross.

Do not write The King of the Jews. The sign says that the Jews’ king has been crucified, and the chief priests are humiliated. They want it turned into a report, “This man said, I am King of the Jews”: the claim of a dead pretender. It is an old way of getting rid of a truth without denying it outright.

What I have written I have written. Pilate, who has conceded everything all morning, refuses. In Greek both verbs describe something done and still in force: it stands written, and will go on standing. It is probably not conscience but a man pushed around all morning finding one thing he can refuse: a small, safe, spiteful assertion of the authority he failed to use when it mattered. His Latin words, Quod scripsi, scripsi, became a proverb for standing firm. They were about a notice, after the nails were in.

God served by a governor’s irritation. Like Caiaphas (11:51), Pilate testified to the truth without meaning to. God’s purposes at Calvary were served by a governor’s petty irritation, as by soldiers gambling and a priest’s political calculation. The only official document we know of from the crucifixion, a legal notice in three languages over his head, never withdrawn, says that he is the King.

How do people today turn the truth into a quotation? Whenever Jesus’ claims are reported only as what he said, or what his followers believed, so that nobody has to reckon with whether they are true: “Christians believe that Jesus is Lord”, rather than “Jesus is Lord”. In the right setting that is honest description. But watch for it in your own heart: the habit of holding Christ’s words at arm’s length as interesting claims, rather than receiving them as the truth about the world. Scripture does not say he said he was King. It says he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King dies as the Passover Lamb, finishing the work his Father gave him, and he truly dies. Four times in a few verses John notes that Scripture was fulfilled: the garments divided (vv. 23–24), the thirst (v. 28), the bones unbroken and the side pierced (vv. 36–37). Between them Jesus gives his mother a home with the disciple he loved (vv. 25–27) and cries “It is finished” before handing over his life (vv. 28–30). The spear and the eyewitness’s testimony establish his death so that we may believe (vv. 31–37), and two secret disciples come into the open to give him a king’s burial in a new tomb in a garden (vv. 38–42).
verseByVerse.theology: “It is finished” stands at the centre of John’s account (see the note on v. 30). Salvation is received, not achieved.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross with the women is a model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost was highest. On his testimony to the blood and water, see the notes on vv. 34–35.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers share out Jesus’ clothes and gamble for his seamless tunic, fulfilling Psalm 22 to the letter without knowing it. The trial has shown human beings doing what they chose; the cross shows God doing what he had said.

Four parts. Four shares suggest a squad of four; the clothes of the condemned were the executioners’ perk, perhaps the outer cloak, belt, sandals and head covering, with one item left over. Jesus was probably crucified naked, as the condemned usually were, the final humiliation.

The tunic was seamless. The inner garment (see tunic and cloak). According to Josephus the high priest’s robe was woven in one piece (compare Exodus 28:32), and readers since the early centuries have seen the priest’s garment kept whole on the body of the Priest, or a picture of the church’s unity. It is a possible echo, not something to build on; John does not explain, but points to the fulfilment of Scripture.

To fulfil the Scripture. Psalm 22:18, written about a thousand years earlier, centuries before crucifixion is known to have been practised, contains a line with no obvious application: “they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” It reads like Hebrew poetry saying one thing twice. At Golgotha it turns out to be two things: they shared out the other clothes, and cast lots for the tunic, because a garment woven in one piece would be ruined by tearing.

So the soldiers did these things. Four men gambling at the foot of a cross, entirely of their own free choice, fulfilled to the letter a poem they had never read. It is the first of four fulfilments John notes in a few verses: the garments, the thirst (v. 28), the unbroken bones (v. 36) and the pierced side (v. 37).

Psalm 22 read whole. It opens with the cry Jesus quotes from the cross; it has mocking men wagging their heads, hands and feet pierced, bones out of joint, a tongue stuck to the jaw; and it ends, unaccountably, with all the families of the nations worshipping and a people yet unborn told that he has done it. Christians from the first have found it very hard to read as coincidence.

The naked King clothes sinners. The soldiers gambled for his last possession while he was purchasing an inheritance for his people, and the King stripped on the cross clothes sinners with “the garments of salvation” and “the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10).

Did the Gospel writers simply make the story fit the psalm? The answer lies in what they could not have invented. Dividing a prisoner’s clothes was routine for Roman execution squads, done in public, and John says he stood at the cross himself (19:26, 35). More than that, nobody inventing a Messiah would have given him a cross: a crucified Christ was “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1:23). The first Christians told the story because it happened, and then found, to their astonishment, that God had written it down a thousand years before.

Was Psalm 22 really about Jesus, or about David? Both, in their proper order. David wrote out of his own suffering, and the psalm makes sense in his life. But it goes far beyond anything David endured: the piercing, the stripping, the casting of lots, and above all the ending, where the sufferer’s deliverance brings the ends of the earth to worship God. David was a prophet who knew that God had promised a greater Son (Acts 2:30–31), and the Spirit who moved him was speaking of the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Peter 1:11). So Jesus could take its first line as his own, and John could see its details fulfilled at the cross. The psalm was always his.

Textual note. In Psalm 22:16 the Hebrew of the line about hands and feet is uncertain: most Hebrew manuscripts read “like a lion”, while the ancient Greek translation and some Hebrew evidence point to “pierced”, which the ESV follows.
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even while bearing the sins of the world, Jesus cares for his mother, giving her a son and a home in the disciple he loved.

Standing by the cross. Probably four women: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene, from whom Jesus had cast seven demons (Luke 8:2). The men who had sworn the night before to die with him are absent, except one, and those near enough for him to see are women with no power to do anything at all.

Woman, behold, your son! “Woman” is not cold but respectful, and John sets it at both ends of the ministry: at Cana, where his hour had not yet come (2:4), and at Golgotha, where it has. The disciple whom he loved is the only male follower John places at the cross. In his agony Jesus provides for his mother as the eldest son should, since his brothers did not yet believe (7:5).

A sword through her soul. Simeon’s prophecy is fulfilled: “a sword will pierce through your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). She has had some thirty years to wonder what he meant, and she is finding out. And the son she watches die is dying for her too. She had rejoiced in God her Saviour when she first carried him (Luke 1:47); now she stands beneath the cross as one of those he is saving, and in the hour he bears her sins he provides for her body.

The heart of our Saviour. The Son of God, bearing the sins of the world, turned his eyes from the weight of the cross to his mother’s face and made sure she would have a home. He is never so taken up with saving the world that he forgets the one standing in front of him. And even on the cross he kept the fifth commandment, perfectly and in your place, where your own honouring of your parents has fallen short.

Being there. What these women could do was be there, close enough for him to see them, and John records their names. If you have stood beside a suffering you could not fix, a child’s illness or a son’s or daughter’s grave, you are not alone at that place: the mother of the Lord stood there, and her Son saw her.

What if my own family does not believe? Jesus knows; his brothers did not believe in him at the time (7:5), and he still loved and provided for his own. Keep loving them, honour your parents, and pray patiently, without making them feel they are a project. The brothers who doubted came to faith after the resurrection: James became a leader of the Jerusalem church, and both he and Jude wrote letters in the New Testament (Acts 1:14; 15:13). Meanwhile the church becomes family to you, as the beloved disciple became a son to Mary.

In everyday life. Look after your parents gladly, especially in their need. And when someone you love is suffering and you cannot fix it, do not stay away for fear of being useless. Be there.

Where Christians differ: Mary at the cross. Roman Catholic teaching sees here Mary made the spiritual mother of all believers, and sometimes speaks of her as co-redemptrix, sharing in Christ’s saving work. Many Roman Catholic friends honour Mary out of real love for her Son, and that love deserves respect even where we must differ. This commentary’s view: the plain meaning is that a loving son provides a home for his widowed mother. Christ alone is the Redeemer, and his sacrifice needs no human partner (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 10:14). Mary is honoured as a believer and the mother of our Lord, but she is not a mediator. The scene also suggests that Mary had no other sons who believed at that time, but it does not prove she had no other sons at all (Mark 6:3).

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the cross Jesus forms a new family, giving his mother to the disciple, and then, knowing his work is complete, says “I thirst” to fulfil the Scripture.

Behold, your mother! He had brothers, and ordinarily the eldest son’s responsibility would pass to the next son. He passes it instead to a disciple: the new family is not founded on blood, for whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35).

To his own home. Tradition says she later lived with him in Ephesus. It is the first act of the church, performed while its Lord was still dying, and it consists of somebody taking a widow in (James 1:27).

Knowing that all was now finished. The word is the same as in v. 30: everything the Father gave him to do was complete, except his final words and death. On a cross every breath was a labour, and he had spent that breath settling who would look after his mother.

I thirst. The Scriptures are Psalm 69:21 and Psalm 22:15. The thirst was real: he had been flogged and had lost blood for hours, and dehydration is one of the ways crucifixion kills. John means that Jesus knew what he was doing when he said it aloud: in his last minutes he names the one prophecy still unfulfilled.

The fountain thirsts. The giver of living water (4:14; 7:37), who promised a woman at a well that she would never thirst again, died thirsty. Every drink of grace we have ever taken was paid for by that thirst. And because he thirsted there, a multitude no one can number will never thirst again: the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, guiding them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 7:16–17).

What being his family looks like. This family was made at the cross, by the blood of the one dying on it, and that is why it can bear weight. It is not a club of like-minded people but brothers and sisters adopted by the same Father at the same price (Galatians 4:4–7), and it shows in ordinary things. Know who is alone. Learn the names of the widows, the single, the elderly and the newcomers in your church, and notice when one is missing. Open your home. Have someone to Sunday lunch or Christmas dinner who would otherwise eat alone. Share real needs. Help with a lift, a repair or a bill, as family does, without keeping score (Acts 2:44–45). Stay. Families do not dissolve when someone becomes difficult or dull; bear with one another as he bears with you. Whoever you take in, you are doing what the dying Lord asked of the disciple he loved.

Did Jesus suffer as God or as man? As the one person who is both. God in his divine nature cannot suffer or die, and the eternal Son did not cease to uphold the universe on the cross. But the Son took a true human nature, body and soul, and in it he truly thirsted, bled and died; so Scripture can say that God obtained the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). The thirst on the cross was not play-acting by a divine being in a costume, but the real thirst of a real man who was also God.

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With hyssop at his lips, Jesus declares the work his Father gave him complete and freely hands over his life: “It is finished.” The debt is paid, the sacrifice offered once for all, and nothing remains to be added.

Sour wine. Cheap, vinegary wine (oxos), the soldiers’ drink; not the drugged wine he refused earlier (Mark 15:23).

On a hyssop branch. Hyssop was used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22), and in purification (Psalm 51:7). It is not an obvious thing to hold a soaked sponge up with, and John very likely names it because he knew what it was for: as the true Passover Lamb is dying, a stalk of it is lifted to his mouth. John records it and says nothing, which is his habit.

It is finished. One word in Greek, tetelestai: finished, and remaining finished. The verb turns up in business papyri for a tax or debt paid, and it is often said that receipts were marked with it to mean “paid in full”; however that may be, the New Testament uses it for paying a tax (Matthew 17:24; Romans 13:6). Not “I am finished”, which is what a dying man says, but “It is finished”: the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4). The sacrifice for sin is complete, the debt paid, the prophecies fulfilled. The whole Gospel has been moving toward this word: John opened the upper room by saying that Jesus loved his own to the end (13:1), and the word for end belongs to the same family.

He bowed his head. A dying man’s head falls when he dies. John has him bow it first, as one lying down to rest, and then give up his spirit, a verb of handing something into another’s keeping. The Good Shepherd had said, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (10:18), and here he does it, with the words Luke records: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). The clothes were taken from him that afternoon, and the freedom, the reputation and the blood. His life he handed over, at a moment of his choosing, having first said that the account was settled.

One sacrifice, and he said so. Glory to the Lamb who did not die defeated. No Old Testament priest ever finished his work: they offered day after day the same sacrifices, “which can never take away sins” (Hebrews 10:11). He offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, and said so, with hyssop at his lips; and he lives to make sure that not one of those he paid for is ever charged again.

What this word rules out. If the work is finished, nothing can be added to it: not penance, not devotion, not a lifetime of good behaviour, nothing done on our worst day or our best. The commonest form of Christian misery is the suspicion that something is still outstanding. This word was cried from a cross to settle it.

A culture that is never finished. We live with lists that never end: the inbox refills overnight, and the body, the career and the children could always have more. The philosopher Byung-Chul Han, in The Burnout Society, argued that modern people are driven less by masters outside them than by an inner command to achieve, so that we exploit ourselves, call it freedom, and wear out: the old religion of earning one’s place, with God taken out and the anxiety left in. The moralist says, keep trying and God may accept you; the achiever says, keep trying and you may finally be someone. Both wait for a word neither can ever say: done. On the cross the only person who ever had nothing left to prove said it on our behalf. Those who rest in his finished work can work hard without working for their worth, because the verdict on them was settled that afternoon outside Jerusalem.

In everyday life. Name what you are still trying to add: the extra effort to feel forgiven, the penance of self-punishment, the sense that God is waiting for you to make it up to him. Then say the word aloud, receive the forgiveness, and serve him out of gratitude, not to pay a cancelled debt.

Was Jesus really forsaken by the Father? Yes, in the sense Scripture means, and it was the deepest part of his suffering: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). The Father did not stop loving his Son, who was never more pleasing to him than in this obedience. But as the sin-bearer Christ endured the Father’s judgment on sin and the withdrawal of the felt comfort of his presence, the experience of the condemned. The union of the Trinity was not broken. He bore the forsakenness our sins deserved, so that we would never be forsaken (Hebrews 13:5). John records the end of it: when the wrath was exhausted, he cried, “It is finished,” and committed his spirit to his Father.

If it is finished, why do I still struggle with sin and suffering? Because what was finished is the payment, not yet the whole renewal. The work that saves you is complete: your guilt paid, your standing with God secure, your future certain. Nothing you suffer is punishment for sins Christ has paid for; it is a Father’s training (Hebrews 12:5–11). But the application of that work goes on: the Spirit is making you holy, and creation still groans until Christ returns (Romans 8:18–23). You fight sin not to finish what he left undone, but because he has finished it, and his victory guarantees yours.

Where Christians differ: what happened at the cross? Some say Christ’s death was mainly an example of love, or a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore God’s punishment for our sin. This commentary’s view: Christ’s death was a victory and an example, but at its heart it was penal substitution: he bore the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). That is why “It is finished” can mean “paid in full.” Nor does the Mass repeat or re-present the sacrifice; it was offered once for all, finished (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To keep the high Sabbath undefiled, the leaders ask for the crucified men’s legs to be broken and their bodies taken down, not knowing that the man in the middle is bearing the very curse their law speaks of.

Not on the Sabbath. The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and the coming Sabbath made it urgent. The Romans often left bodies on crosses for days as a warning, but in Judea they seem generally to have respected Jewish custom.

A high day. The weekly Sabbath falling within the festival, especially solemn: hence the pressure to have the bodies down, and the speed of the burial. The Lord of the Sabbath died on its eve, so that his body rested in the tomb on the day God rested from his works.

That their legs might be broken. Breaking the legs (crurifragium) with a heavy mallet sped death: a crucified man could breathe, it is commonly thought, only by pushing himself up on his feet, so with his legs broken he soon suffocated. It is the irony of the governor’s door that morning again (18:28): men who would not enter a Gentile house in case it barred them from a meal arrange that afternoon for living men’s legs to be shattered so that the evening’s observance is not spoiled.

The curse taken down before nightfall. The law they invoke says why: “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23). They do not know that the man on the middle cross is bearing that very curse, not for any crime of his own but for his people’s sins, becoming a curse for us to redeem us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13). The law wanted the curse removed by nightfall, and by nightfall he had borne it to the end (2 Corinthians 5:21).

What about the thief who believed? Luke tells us that one of these two men asked Jesus to remember him when he came into his kingdom, and Jesus answered, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). So one of the men whose legs were broken that afternoon died soon after and went straight into the presence of Christ, with no baptism, no record of good works, no time to make amends. He was saved by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and his broken legs could not keep him from paradise. There is no purgatory in that promise, only “today” and “with me”.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers find Jesus already dead, and the spear that makes sure of it brings out blood and water: proof that he truly died, and a sign of the cleansing his death opens.

Already dead. Jesus died quickly, after some hours on the cross (about six, on Mark’s timing), and Pilate was surprised (Mark 15:44). The suggestion that he merely fainted and revived in the cool of the tomb founders here. These men were a professional execution squad, and a soldier who let a condemned man off a cross alive would have faced severe punishment. They looked at him and did not bother breaking his legs: the judgment of experts.

Blood and water. The soldier meant to make sure, and what came out settled it. Medical explanations vary and none commands agreement; for John the point is that this man was dead.

Why John insists on it. By the time he wrote, teachers were already saying that the Christ could not really have suffered: that the divine had departed before the death, or that the body was only an appearance (the error later called docetism, from the Greek for “seem”). John’s letters go after exactly that: “every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God” (1 John 4:2–3). The blood and water are his answer: a witness giving evidence about a body.

The sign in the wound. John also sees a sign: the blood of atonement and the water of cleansing and life (7:38–39; 1 John 5:6–8). Many church fathers saw here the gospel’s two great gifts, forgiveness and the Spirit, and pictures of the Supper and baptism. John does write on more than one level, but the primary meaning is the plainer and harder one, the evidence of death. Zechariah promised a fountain opened “to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness” (Zechariah 13:1). The spear meant to confirm his death opened the fountain the prophet had promised, and it has never been closed.

Does it matter whether Jesus really died? Everything depends on it. If he did not die, he did not bear the penalty of sin, which is death (Romans 6:23), and there was no resurrection, only a recovery; and “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). His real death also means he has gone through what we will go through. He has tasted death for everyone who is his (Hebrews 2:9), and he knows the way out. When you stand at a deathbed, you are standing where he has been.

Textual note. In 1 John 5:7–8 the KJV adds words about three that bear record in heaven; they appear only in late manuscripts, so modern Bibles leave them out.

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eyewitness solemnly vouches for what he saw so that we may believe, and the unbroken bones show Jesus to be the true Passover Lamb.

He who saw it has borne witness. The author steps forward: apart from one phrase in the prologue (1:14), he has not once stopped to vouch for himself. The beloved disciple, who stood at the cross (19:26), insists that he saw it (21:24). That is how a witness talks under oath, and the Christian faith rests on historical events, seen and reported.

That you also may believe. The purpose of the whole Gospel (20:31). He records the spear-thrust not because it is moving but because the reader’s faith depends on the man having actually died, and he was there.

Not one of his bones will be broken. The fulfilment this Gospel has built toward since John the Baptist called him the Lamb of God (1:29). The Passover lamb was to be eaten in one house, and not a bone of it broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12); Psalm 34:20 says the same of the righteous sufferer. For fourteen hundred years the lambs were handled as the law required, and not one of them could take away sin. Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood shelters his people from judgment.

How the rule was kept. Not by anyone’s intention. A Roman work detail hurrying to finish before sunset left one body intact because nothing was gained by damaging it, and so handled the Lamb of God exactly as the law required.

Can I trust testimony written down decades later? Yes, for good reasons. John was there, says so with unusual force, and wrote while others who were there could still contradict him. The Gospels were written within the lifetime of eyewitnesses: Luke drew on “those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses” (Luke 1:1–4), and Paul could appeal to more than five hundred who had seen the risen Christ, most still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6). These witnesses gained nothing by their testimony but hardship and, for many, death. And the Spirit who inspired the writing bears witness in the reader’s heart that it is true (1 John 5:6).

Uncertain wording. In “he knows that he is telling the truth”, the first “he” is emphatic, literally “that one knows”. Most take it as the witness speaking of himself in the third person, as he does whenever he calls himself the disciple whom Jesus loved; some think “that one” is Christ, or God, called on to vouch for him. Either way it is a solemn guarantee that the testimony is true.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture said that people would look on the one they pierced, and among the first to look and come into the open is Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple who now asks for Jesus’ body.

Him whom they have pierced. In Zechariah 12:10 it is the Lord himself who speaks of being pierced, and the people mourn as for an only child. John quotes it over a body with a spear-wound in its side: at Golgotha God the Son was pierced in the flesh he had taken. Some looked in mockery; many will look in repentance and faith (Revelation 1:7).

From looking to mourning to a fountain. In Zechariah the looking leads to a whole land mourning, and the mourning to the fountain for sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1; see the note on vv. 33–34). That is the way every sinner comes to Christ: he looks at the one he pierced, grieves, and is washed.

Joseph of Arimathea. Joseph, from Arimathea, a town of Judea, was a member of the council who had not agreed to its decision (Luke 23:50–51), and a rich man (Matthew 27:57). His secrecy came from the same fear that silenced the blind man’s parents and the authorities who believed and would not say so (9:22; 12:42). The fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25), and Joseph had been caught in it, perhaps for years.

He asked for the body. Mark says he took courage (Mark 15:43). Not during the trial, but when the movement seemed finished, he goes to a Roman governor to ask for the body of an executed rebel.

Courage at the costliest moment. This Gospel does not excuse Joseph’s years of silence, but he came into the open when it cost most and profited least. Jesus had said that when he was lifted up he would draw all people to himself (12:32). The cross scattered the Twelve, and among the first drawn to him after he died were two members of the council who had been too afraid to come while he lived. The pierced Christ makes cowards brave and mourners clean.

I have kept my faith quiet for years. Is it too late? No. When Joseph finally came out, Christ received his gift; the Lord who welcomed Nicodemus by night accepted Joseph’s tomb by day. But do not wait for the moment that costs most. Tell one person this week that you belong to Christ, ask to be baptised if you have not been, and join a church. Secret discipleship may begin in fear; it is not meant to stay there, and the cross is what draws it into the open.

Will Israel one day look on him and mourn? Christians differ here, and the views should be stated fairly. Some believe Zechariah and Romans 11:25–27 point to a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when they will look on the one they pierced and mourn. Others understand “all Israel” as the whole number of God’s elect from Jews and Gentiles, gathered through the age, and see the mourning fulfilled whenever Jews and Gentiles come to faith, from Pentecost onward (Acts 2:37). Both agree that John sees the prophecy beginning at the cross, that its full completion comes when every eye sees him at his return (Revelation 1:7), and that there is one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: looking in faith to the pierced Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who first came to Jesus by night, now comes openly, and the king’s burial he and Joseph give Jesus, at real cost to themselves, confesses the crucified one as King.

Nicodemus also. The man who came in the dark (3:2), cautiously, with a compliment and a question, later raised a careful procedural point in the council and was slapped down for it (7:50–51). Now Nicodemus is here in daylight, in public, with a great weight of spices and his hands on a dead body.

Myrrh and aloes. Myrrh was a fragrant resin; aloes, a fragrant wood powder. The weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds (ESV note), about 34 kilograms: enough for a king’s burial (2 Chronicles 16:14), where ordinary burials used a fraction of it. They did not embalm the body, but surrounded it with spices to honour it and mask the smell of decay.

Linen cloths with the spices. Strips of linen were wound around the body with spices between, as with Lazarus (11:44): the burial custom John mentions. It cost them more than spices. Handling a corpse made a Jew ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), so on the eve of the high Sabbath both men shut themselves out of the rest of the festival to bury him. They lost nothing: the true Passover Lamb had already been sacrificed.

What Nicodemus had been told. On that first night Jesus spoke of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness (3:14–15), and Nicodemus could not follow. This afternoon he has seen it. The teacher of Israel who stumbled over talk of new birth now handles the body whose death makes that new birth possible, and the king’s burial he brings is his confession that the one lifted up is the King.

No love spent on Christ is wasted. A fortune was poured out on a corpse. Nicodemus thought he was honouring a dead king; he was wrapping a body that would leave the linen behind on the third day. No love spent on Christ is wasted, even when it seems to come too late, because the one it is spent on does not stay dead.

A slow conversion. Comfort for anyone who has waited long for somebody to come to Christ: it took Nicodemus years, and the visible steps were a private conversation, one cautious question in a hostile room, and then everything at once.

In everyday life. Give him your best: not your leftovers of time and money, but something costly, given when it looks as though it will gain you nothing.

Does it matter how Christians bury their dead? Scripture lays down no law about burial or cremation, and the resurrection does not depend on what happens to the body; God who made it from dust can raise it from ashes or the sea (Revelation 20:13). But burial has long been the Christian custom, following the burial of Christ and the patriarchs, because it honours the body as belonging to the Lord and destined to be raised (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Whatever your family chooses, do it with reverence and hope, not as disposal. The body you lay to rest is a seed, not rubbish.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the weight is literally a hundred Roman pounds, a quantity fit for a royal burial. Myrrh and aloes were aromatic spices laid with the linen wrappings.

parallels.desc: King Asa laid on a bier filled with spices
myrrh at his birth

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, truly dead, is laid in a rich man’s new tomb in a garden near the cross, as Isaiah had foretold.

A garden. John ends this part of the story as he began it (18:1): a garden where he was taken, and a garden where he is laid. Eden was lost in a garden; the King is buried in one; and in this garden he will rise, and Mary will think him the gardener (20:15). The new creation begins in a garden.

A new tomb. Matthew says it was Joseph’s own tomb, cut in the rock (Matthew 27:60). Two details matter as evidence. It was new, with no other body in it, which rules out confusion about whose body was missing on Sunday. And it was Joseph’s: a wealthy man gave away the grave he had probably cut for himself and his family.

Close at hand. The last clause is very flat: they chose it because it was near and the light was going. Two men who had been afraid of being seen with him work quickly against a deadline, put a body in a borrowed grave, and go home. There the chapter stops, at a closed tomb on a Friday evening, exactly where everybody who loved him was left.

With a rich man in his death. Isaiah had said of the Servant, “they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death” (Isaiah 53:9). Both halves came true within hours, by opposite means: the state numbered him with criminals and meant him to lie with them, and a private citizen put him in a rich man’s tomb.

Every Christian grave a garden plot. “He was buried” is part of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:4): it proves he truly died. The one who had said, “I am the resurrection and the life,” lay silent in a borrowed grave, but he had gone into it as a conqueror goes into an enemy’s fortress, and for us. He has lain where we will lie, and has come out. Every Christian grave since has been a garden plot, because his was first: the grain of wheat fell into the ground and died (12:24), and on the third day it came up as the firstfruits of all who sleep in him.

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in Joseph’s tomb; his human soul went to his Father. He had told the thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). He did not sleep unconscious, nor go to a place of further suffering; his suffering was finished on the cross. When the Apostles’ Creed says he descended into hell, Reformed Christians have understood it of the hellish agonies he endured on the cross (Heidelberg Catechism, question 44) and of his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Westminster Larger Catechism, question 50). So it is for believers: at death the body rests in the grave, while the soul goes at once to be with Christ, awaiting the resurrection (Philippians 1:23; Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death

Pilate said to them, “Behold the man!”<sup>6</sup>When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him.”<sup>7</sup>The Jews answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God.”<sup>8</sup>When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.<sup>9</sup>He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.<sup>10</sup>So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”<sup>11</sup>Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin.”<sup>12</sup>From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend.
