Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”<sup>13</sup>So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha.<sup>14</sup>Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold your King!”<sup>15</sup>They cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”<sup>16</sup>So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,<sup>17</sup>and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.<sup>18</sup>There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.<sup>19</sup>Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”<sup>20</sup>Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.<sup>21</sup>So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ’The King of the Jews,’ but rather, ’This man said, I am King of the Jews.’”<sup>22</sup>Pilate answered, “What I have written I have written.”<sup>23</sup>When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom,<sup>24</sup>so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be.” This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So the soldiers did these things,<sup>25</sup>but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.<sup>26</sup>When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.<sup>28</sup>After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), “I thirst.”<sup>29</sup>A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth.<sup>30</sup>When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.<sup>31</sup>Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.<sup>32</sup>So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.<sup>33</sup>But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.<sup>34</sup>But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.<sup>35</sup>He who saw it has borne witness— his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth— that you also may believe.<sup>36</sup>For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “Not one of his bones will be broken.”<sup>37</sup>And again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they have pierced.”<sup>38</sup>After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.<sup>39</sup>Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.<sup>40</sup>So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.<sup>41</sup>Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.<sup>42</sup>So because of the Jewish day of Preparation, since the tomb was close at hand, they laid Jesus there.
19.overview:
Where we are. The trial before Pilate, begun at 18:28, reaches its end. Pilate has found no guilt in Jesus, only to hear the crowd choose Barabbas (18:38–40). Now the hour this Gospel has been moving toward since Cana arrives.

The message. The man condemned, mocked and crucified is the King, and the cross is where he takes his throne and finishes his work. No one takes his life from him: Pilate’s power is lent, soldiers and priests fulfil Scriptures they have never read, and Jesus lays his life down with the words “It is finished.” He dies as the true Passover Lamb, truly dead, so that all who look on him whom they pierced may believe and have life.

Why it was said. John’s readers lived under Rome’s power, some put out of the synagogue for confessing Jesus, among teachers who said the Christ had not truly suffered in the flesh (see the introduction). They needed an eyewitness’s word that he really died, that the shame of the cross was his glory, and that secret faith is meant to come into the open.

How the chapter makes its case. Pilate’s attempts to release Jesus fail one by one: the flogging and mock coronation (vv. 1–6), the charge that he made himself the Son of God (vv. 7–11), until the threat about Caesar settles it and the chief priests declare that they have no king but Caesar (vv. 12–16). Jesus is crucified under a title in three languages that Pilate refuses to change (vv. 17–22). At the cross Scripture is fulfilled four times (vv. 24, 28, 36, 37), and between the fulfilments he gives his mother a home (vv. 25–27) and cries “It is finished” (vv. 28–30). The spear and the eyewitness establish that he died (vv. 31–37), and two secret disciples give him a king’s burial in a garden tomb (vv. 38–42).

Where it leads. Here the Gospel reaches its centre, and the chapter does not so much point to Christ as show him. Every thread is pulled tight: the Lamb of God (1:29), the Son of Man lifted up (3:14), the good shepherd laying down his life (10:18), the hour of glory (12:23). Crowned with the curse’s thorns, proclaimed King to the nations, numbered with the transgressors and buried with a rich man, he is everything the Scriptures said. And the tomb is in a garden, where chapter 20 begins.

For us. Because it is finished, nothing remains for us to add: the debt is paid, and the Father’s welcome is secure. Because every Pilate’s power is lent, no human authority has the last word. And because Joseph and Nicodemus came into the open at the costliest moment, the cross calls every timid believer to stand publicly with the crucified King.

keyVerse.quote: When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished,” and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
keyVerse.note: Everything in this chapter, and in the whole Gospel, has been moving toward this one word. The work the Father gave the Son is complete and the sacrifice for sin offered once for all, so nothing remains for us to add. And the King who said it was not overpowered: he bowed his head and handed over his life of his own accord (10:18).

19.reflection:
Pilate knew Jesus was innocent but gave way the moment his position was threatened (vv. 12–16), and the chief priests chose Caesar rather than lose what they had. What is the “Caesar” you are most tempted to fear or please more than Christ, and what would it look like to name Jesus as your King there this week?

Jesus told Pilate that his authority had been “given you from above” (v. 11), yet he still held him and others guilty. How does it help you to know that God rules over unjust people and events, and why does that never excuse those who do wrong?

“It is finished” (v. 30) means that nothing can be added to Christ’s work. Where are you still trying to add something of your own, through effort, penance or feeling bad enough? How would resting in his finished work change the way you live and serve?

Jesus gave his mother a home from the cross (vv. 25–27), and Joseph and Nicodemus, who had kept their faith quiet, came into the open at the costliest moment (vv. 38–42). Who around you needs to be taken in as family, and where might your own faith need to come out into the open?

20.title: The Resurrection

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Empty Tomb and Mary's Encounter with the Risen Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Easter morning moves from an empty tomb to a living voice, and the first witness is the one who could not leave. Mary finds the stone taken away and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that the body has been stolen (vv. 1–2). The two race to the tomb and find the grave clothes lying in place, and the beloved disciple sees and believes, though none of them yet understands the Scripture (vv. 3–10). Mary stays weeping, sees angels where the body had lain, and does not know Jesus until he speaks her name (vv. 11–16). He sends her to his brothers with the news that his Father is now theirs, and she announces, “I have seen the Lord” (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The resurrection appearances in John turn on recognition. The beloved disciple believes from the linen cloths; Mary knows Jesus when he calls her name, as the sheep know the Good Shepherd’s voice (10:3); Thomas knows him when invited to touch the wounds. Each meeting is suited to the person, and in each the same risen Jesus comes to the disciple where he or she is.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary Magdalene, weeping at a tomb, heard her name from the one she thought was dead, and was sent with the first resurrection message: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before dawn on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple that the body has been taken. The greatest event in history has already happened, unseen.

Now on the first day of the week. Literally day one of the week: the ordinary way of saying Sunday, but it echoes Genesis, as John’s opening words, “In the beginning”, did. After a Friday on which Jesus said “It is finished” and a Sabbath on which his body lay at rest in the tomb, comes day one again. The Son who finished his work on the sixth day, as God finished the heavens and the earth, opens the new creation on its first morning. His risen body is the first piece of the world God will make new (1 Corinthians 15:20), and everyone joined to him by faith already belongs to it (2 Corinthians 5:17). The day he rose became the day his people gather, the Lord’s day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

Early, while it was still dark. Darkness outside, and in her heart. Mark has “when the sun had risen” (Mark 16:2): she left in the dark and arrived as it was getting light.

The stone taken away. Not rolled away so that Jesus could get out (that evening he will stand in a room with the doors locked, v. 19), but so that the witnesses could get in. He had already taken up again the life he laid down, as he said he had authority to do (10:18). The greatest event in history had no human spectator, only evidence, left for those who loved him to find.

They have taken the Lord. Grave robbers, or the authorities: resurrection does not cross her mind. It is the sensible interpretation, and it is wrong. The witnesses did not expect resurrection, which makes their testimony more believable: they did not see what they wanted to see.

The “we” left standing. John names only Mary Magdalene; the other Gospels name other women with her. Yet she says “we do not know”. He has written the scene around one woman and left the plural in her speech, as happens when somebody reports a conversation without tidying it.

She ran to Peter. She goes to the man who denied him, whom the others might reasonably have written off, and treats him as one of the people to be told. Nobody in the account has excluded Peter from anything.

Risen while it was still dark. On the first day God said, let there be light, and on this first day the Light of the world had risen before anyone came looking. The Lord of life needed no witness to rise and no hand to help with the stone. Every first day since has dawned in the light of his morning.

Where Christians differ: is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), regard the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath, the fourth commandment’s weekly day of rest and worship moved to the day of resurrection. Others read the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), and Sunday gathering as a glad privilege rather than a sabbath law. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest, and the first day is set apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment transferred to Sunday; no one may bind another believer’s conscience over it (Romans 14:5). The Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree that Christians should gather with the church each Lord’s Day, and rest in Christ’s finished work.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and the beloved disciple run to the tomb, the younger arriving first: a detail only an eyewitness would bother with, and a sign that the Shepherd has kept even the sheep who denied him.

Outran Peter. Two grown men sprinting through Jerusalem at first light after a stolen body, and the detail is mentioned twice (here and in v. 8); the usual guess is that the other disciple, traditionally John, was the younger man.

The pair. These two appear together again and again (13:23–24; 18:15–16; 21:7; Acts 3:1): the one who sees and the one who acts. The beloved disciple arrives first; bold Peter goes in first. The church has always needed both: the young and the old, the quick and the slow, the one who loved and the one who failed, all running toward the place where death had been undone.

Of those you gave me I have lost not one. Why does Peter run at all? Only days earlier he had sworn beside a fire that he did not know the man. In the garden Jesus stepped forward to be arrested so that his disciples could go free, that the word he had spoken might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one” (18:8–9). Peter’s denial had not cancelled that word. The man running through the streets is held by a grip stronger than his own: the Shepherd who laid down his life has kept every sheep the Father gave him, including the one who disowned him.

In everyday life. Run to Christ, whatever your past failures. If you have been avoiding church, prayer or a Christian friend because of something you are ashamed of, go today; his welcome does not wait on your record.

Why would the Gospel record such small details? Because they are what eyewitnesses remember and inventors have little reason to include. Who ran faster, who stooped, how the cloths lay: none obviously serves a theological purpose, and some do the disciples no credit. Vivid detail cannot prove a report on its own, since a skilled storyteller can invent it too; but it fits what this Gospel claims to be, the testimony of a man who was there (21:24). A man constructing a legend would not have had two men arrive, look and go home (on a woman as the first witness, see vv. 17–18). Such unpolished details are part of why many historians, not only believers, take the Gospels seriously as testimony.

parallels.desc: Peter runs to the tomb

verseByVerse.quote: And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beloved disciple looks in from the doorway, Peter goes straight in, and both see the linen cloths lying in place: not the scene a robbery leaves behind.

Stooping to look in. Tomb entrances were low, which fits the rock-cut tombs of the period. He saw the linen cloths lying (keimena): lying flat, in place, not scattered. But he did not go in, perhaps from awe, or reluctance to make himself ritually unclean by entering a tomb.

Peter went in. Peter, characteristically, goes straight in. Neither is criticised, and John records the hesitation as his own.

He saw the linen cloths lying there. Saw (theōrei): looked carefully, studied. John describes the seeing in stages (vv. 5, 6, 8): a glance, then a study, then an understanding, told by a man who was there.

What they were looking at. The position of the cloths is what matters. Grave robbers would hardly stop to undress a body and leave the valuable linen and spices. John uses two words: the othonia, the linen strips that bound the body, and the soudarion of the next verse, the cloth that covered the face and was tied round the head. Their positions were different, and that is the point.

Linen for a king. Nicodemus had given him a king’s burial (19:39–40), and now the king’s burial clothes lie empty. The honour his friends gave him was real and loving, and he has no further use for it. No one took his life from him, and no one could keep his body.

In everyday life. Faith is not a refusal to look; it is a willingness to look carefully. If you have doubts, read the four accounts side by side, or a careful book on the resurrection, and ask what best explains them.

verseByVerse.quote: and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The face cloth lies apart, as if the body had simply passed out of its wrappings, and the beloved disciple, seeing it, believes.

The face cloth. Robbers would still less have folded the face cloth (on the linen, see vv. 5–6). It lay apart, undisturbed (on “folded up”, see the end of this note).

He saw and believed. In John’s account he is the first to believe in the resurrection, and John writes it about himself, in the third person, without elaboration. No angel had spoken, he had not seen the risen Lord, and he did not yet understand the Scripture (v. 9). He had an empty tomb and the way the linen lay, and that was enough.

Lazarus came out bound. Lazarus came out with his hands and feet bound and his face wrapped in a cloth, and had to be unbound (11:44). He came back to a life that would end again. Jesus came out of death for ever and left the wrappings behind, because nothing of the grave clings to him any more. At Bethany he had said, I am the resurrection and the life (11:25). Lazarus received resurrection; Jesus is it.

Where every believer stands. Every believer since has stood in that empty tomb by faith: looking at a grave that could not keep the Lord of life, and knowing that it will not keep us either. “Blessed are those who have not seen” (v. 29).

A story to set aside. A widely told sermon illustration says that a Jewish servant would leave a napkin crumpled if the meal was over and fold it if his master meant to return, so the folded face cloth is Jesus saying “I am coming back”. No ancient source knows any such custom, and the word is a burial face cloth, not table linen. The verse is strong enough without it.

What about the other explanations? Each runs into a known difficulty. If the disciples stole the body, they suffered, and some died, for what they knew was a lie, and would hardly have left the grave clothes. If the authorities moved it, they would have produced it when the apostles began preaching in Jerusalem weeks later. If the women went to the wrong tomb, the authorities had only to show the right one. If Jesus only fainted, Roman soldiers who knew death were fooled, and a half-dead man somehow convinced his friends he had conquered death. If the disciples hallucinated, a whole group shared a normally private experience again and again over weeks, and hallucinations do not empty tombs. The explanation that best fits the empty tomb, the appearances and the transformation of frightened men into bold witnesses is the one they gave: he is risen. No argument can force faith; but believers are not choosing against the evidence when they say it.

Uncertain wording. “Folded up” (entetuligmenon) means wrapped or rolled together, and “in a place by itself” is literally “into one place”. It is not certain whether the cloth had been folded and laid aside, or still lay rolled in the shape it had round the head. Either way it had not been thrown down in a hurry, and nothing suggests that anyone carried the body off.
verseByVerse.note: Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

verseByVerse.quote: for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples believed what they saw before they understood that Scripture had said he must rise, and then they simply went home.

They did not understand the Scripture. Jesus had told them plainly that he would rise on the third day; only later did they see that the Old Testament foretold it (Luke 24:25–27, 44–46). Must (dei): it was necessary, written into the Father’s plan before the cross was raised.

Which Scriptures? The apostles later point to Psalm 16, “you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption” (Psalm 16:10), the text of Peter’s Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:25–31). Paul says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4). Hosea has a third day (Hosea 6:2), Jonah has three days, and Isaiah 53 has a servant who is cut off and then shall see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10). It had been there for centuries, and none of them had put it together: one of them admits it here, decades later.

Back to their homes. The most matter-of-fact verse in the story: one of them has just believed, and there is no announcement, no gathering, which is unlike a legend and exactly like people. And it means that the first to meet the risen Christ is the one who stayed.

The Amen to every promise. The God who promised that his Holy One would not see corruption kept his word to the letter on the third day. He had been writing toward this morning since the first promise in Eden (Genesis 3:15), and the Son walked out of the tomb as the Amen to every one of those promises (2 Corinthians 1:20). His slow, forgetful disciples discovered, too late to have helped and just in time to believe, that every word had been true.

How should I read the Old Testament, then? With Christ at the centre, as Jesus taught. On the road to Emmaus he began with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). Not every verse is a hidden riddle about Jesus, but the whole story is moving toward him: the promises to Abraham, the sacrifices, the kings, the psalms of suffering and vindication, the prophets’ hope. Ask what a passage shows of the God who would send his Son, what problem is crying out for Christ to solve, and where its promise lands in him.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary stays weeping at the tomb after the men have gone home, and finds two angels sitting where the body had lain. The one who could not leave is about to be the first to meet him.

Mary stood weeping. Mary stays outside a tomb everyone else has finished with. As far as she knows the body has been stolen, and with it the last service left to her. She simply cannot leave. The risen Christ appears first not to the one who reasoned correctly from the evidence, nor the one who went in first, nor the eleven, but to the one who could not go home.

She stooped to look into the tomb. The verb of verse 5: a second look at a space two men have already searched. Grief checks again, and this time there is something there.

Two angels in white. Mary does not seem to realise they are angels. She answers them as though they were attendants, and turns away: her grief is so large that two angels do not register.

The mercy seat. One at the head and one at the feet, with an empty space between them where a body had lain, like the two cherubim of gold at either end of the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22), where the blood of atonement was sprinkled and where God said he would meet with his people. John does not draw the picture, but it is hard to miss. Jesus is the true mercy seat: Paul calls him a propitiation, using the Greek Bible’s word for the mercy seat (Romans 3:25), an offering that bears God’s holy anger against sin and so puts it away. The ark pictured that once a year, behind a curtain, on the Day of Atonement; at the cross it happened once for all, the curtain torn (Matthew 27:51), and the empty place where his body lay is the proof. The place where wrath has been turned away is the place where mourners are met.

In everyday life. Look around your church for the one still grieving after everyone else has moved on: the widow a year later, the parents after a miscarriage, the friend whose loss nobody mentions now. Sit with them, and say the name of the one they lost.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve so deeply? No. Mary wept at the tomb, Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (11:35), and nobody in this scene tells her to stop (see vv. 13–14). Paul does not forbid Christians to grieve; we do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christian grief is real grief, sometimes long and heavy, held in the hands of a risen Lord. If your sorrow has outlasted other people’s patience, do not be ashamed of it; bring it to him. He came first to the one who could not stop weeping.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping?" She said to them, "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him." Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels ask Mary why she is weeping, and she, still sure the body has been stolen, turns and sees Jesus without knowing him. She is weeping over the absence of a body that is standing behind her, alive.

Woman, why are you weeping? A gentle question, which Jesus will ask a moment later, and not an accusation in either mouth: it lets somebody say aloud what is wrong. Two angels and the risen Son of God, and not one of them tells her she should not be upset. And the next to ask it is the one who wept at the grave of Lazarus (11:35) and is himself the answer to her tears.

They have taken away my Lord. In verse 2 she said “the Lord”; here she says “my Lord”. The public title has become a personal one, though she still thinks of a dead body.

She did not know that it was Jesus. The risen Jesus was not always recognised at first (Luke 24:16; John 21:4). His resurrection body was the same body, with its wounds (v. 20), but transformed. And her eyes were full of tears: grief had already decided what she might find, and a living Jesus was not among the possibilities. Nothing blameworthy in that.

Will we recognise one another in the resurrection? Yes. Mary knew his voice, the disciples his wounds, the Emmaus pair the breaking of bread. Paul expects to see his converts in the presence of Christ as his crown and joy (1 Thessalonians 2:19), and comforts the bereaved with the promise that we shall be with them and with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). We will know as we are known (1 Corinthians 13:12), and the faces we loved will be there, made new.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Aramaic, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks one word, her name, and Mary knows him at once: the Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice.

Whom are you seeking? He has asked this at the moments that matter in this book: of the first two disciples, “What are you seeking?” (1:38), and twice of the arresting party in the garden, “Whom do you seek?” (18:4, 7). Now, in another garden, he asks it of a weeping woman. It always searches the heart of the one who answers: what, and whom, do you really want?

Supposing him to be the gardener. An understandable mistake, and yet she is more right than she knows. The first Adam was put in a garden to keep it, and lost it. Jesus, the second Adam, stands in a garden (19:41), the gardener of the new creation.

I will take him away. Love that does not calculate: she proposes to carry off a grown man’s body, wrapped in spices, by herself, with no plan for where to put it.

Mary. One word, her name: not an explanation, not a rebuke, and she is turned round in an instant. He had said that the shepherd calls his own sheep by name and they know his voice (10:3–4), and this is that sentence happening.

Rabboni. Aramaic for “my teacher”, a warm and respectful form of rabbi. She uses the name she always used, because he is the same man, and she has no words yet for what has happened.

His first risen words: her name. Death could not make the Shepherd forget one of his sheep. The Word who calls the stars by name spent his first risen words on a single woman’s name, and that one word turned a mourner into a witness. The same voice will sound over every grave of his people (5:28–29), and each will hear their own name, turn, and know him.

Does the risen Jesus really know me personally? Yes. He knows his sheep by name (10:3, 14): your history, your sins, your griefs, the things you have never told anyone. The Father gave you to him by name before the world began (17:6), and he laid down his life for you by name. He calls you now through his word, and the Spirit makes that call personal, so that you know the voice is for you (10:27). You may feel forgotten in a crowd of eight billion. You are not forgotten by him.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabboni” is Aramaic for “my teacher,” a warm and respectful address.

parallels.desc: he calls his own sheep by name

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" — and that he had said these things to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells Mary to stop holding on to him and sends her to his brothers with the news that his Father is now their Father, and she becomes the first to announce the resurrection.

Do not cling to me. Not “do not touch me” (the old translation), but stop holding on to me. The Latin Noli me tangere has produced many paintings of a recoiling Christ, but this form of the Greek command usually means stop doing what you are already doing. She has hold of him, as if never to let go (Matthew records the other women taking hold of his feet, Matthew 28:9). A week later Jesus invites Thomas to put his finger in the nail marks (v. 27), so this is no ban on touching. He is telling her: you cannot keep me here; I have not come back to the old life in Galilee.

Not yet ascended. He is on his way to the Father, and from there he will be with all his people at once, nearer than an embrace, by the Spirit (16:7). Since 13:1 this Gospel has spoken of his going to the Father: the cross, the resurrection, and the ascension forty days later (Acts 1:3, 9). He goes so that his Father may be theirs, and so that the Spirit may come, the Spirit he will breathe on them in verse 22. Meanwhile Mary has a task.

My brothers. For the first time in this Gospel, Jesus calls his disciples brothers. At supper he had raised them from servants to friends (15:15). Now, after every one of them has run away and one has denied him three times, he calls them his brothers, children of his Father (Hebrews 2:11–12).

My Father and your Father. Not “our Father”. His sonship is unique and eternal; theirs is by adoption, through him. Yet he shares his Father with them, because the cross has made it possible. Nowhere in the Gospels does he include himself with the disciples in a single “our Father”.

I have seen the Lord. The first witness to the risen Christ was a woman, at a time when women’s testimony was not readily accepted in Jewish courts. Nobody fabricating an account would have picked her. Her message is the simplest and fullest resurrection proclamation there is.

What does it mean that God is my Father because he is Christ’s Father? Your standing with God is not a lesser copy of a relationship but a share in the real one. By nature the Son alone is the Father’s child; by adoption, through faith in Christ, the Father receives you as his son or daughter, with the Spirit in your heart crying Abba (Galatians 4:4–7). You come not as a servant hoping for wages but as a child at home. He knows what you need before you ask (Matthew 6:8), disciplines you because he loves you (Hebrews 12:6), and has made you an heir with his Son (Romans 8:17). The risen Christ came out of the tomb and called the Father yours.

In everyday life. When you pray today, begin with the word the risen Son himself put in your mouth: Father.

Does Mary’s witness mean women should be pastors? Christ himself honoured her witness, and every Christian, man or woman, is called to say what she said: I have seen the Lord, and this is what he told me. Women prayed, prophesied and laboured in the gospel throughout the New Testament (Acts 1:14; Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:2–3). But Mary was sent with a message to the apostles, not appointed one of them, and the New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). That is no judgment on women’s gifts or worth: Christ entrusted the greatest news ever told to a woman first. It is the pattern of ordered service he gave his church, grounded by Paul in creation, not local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), which is why this commentary holds it (the view often called complementarian: equal worth, different callings). Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and recognise women as pastors, and they deserve to be heard as brothers and sisters who love the same Lord.

Uncertain wording. The reason Jesus gives, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father”, is one of the harder sentences in this Gospel: it is not obvious why his not yet having ascended is a reason for Mary to let go. The likeliest sense is the one taken above: his going to the Father is not complete, so this is not yet the lasting reunion, and meanwhile there is a message to carry. Other suggestions reach the same point: the old way of having him is over, and a better one is coming.
verseByVerse.note: “Do not cling to me” means the old relationship cannot simply resume; he is going to the Father.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — Appearances to the Disciples and to Thomas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Jesus comes to his frightened disciples with peace, makes them his witnesses, and brings even the doubter to the highest confession of faith. On Easter evening he shows them his wounds, sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them the Holy Spirit and entrusts them with the announcement of forgiveness (vv. 19–23). Thomas, who was absent, refuses to believe without seeing the wounds (vv. 24–25); a week later Jesus comes again for him, and he confesses, “My Lord and my God!” (vv. 26–28). Jesus blesses all who will believe without seeing, and John states why he has written: that we may believe and have life in his name (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: “Peace be with you” (vv. 19, 21, 26): Jesus says it three times. The peace he brings is not first the end of the disciples’ fear but his own presence among them. And he shows them his hands and his side: the wounds are carried into the resurrection body (see vv. 19–20 and 25–26).
verseByVerse.examples: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (v. 29): this is the blessing on every Christian since the first generation (see the note on vv. 29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, "Peace be with you." When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On Easter evening the risen Jesus comes through locked doors to the frightened men who had deserted him, speaks peace and shows them his wounds, and their fear turns to joy.

The doors being locked. On Easter evening the church is in a bolted room, expecting arrest, with men who have heard Mary’s news and done nothing with it (Luke 24:11). “The Jews” here, as often in John, means the Jerusalem authorities who had just had Jesus put to death, not the Jewish people: every man in that room was a Jew. The fear was reasonable: rulers who had struck the shepherd might well come for the sheep. Their boldness in the coming months is the measure of what the risen Christ and his Spirit will do with them.

Jesus came and stood among them. Locked doors do not stop him. His resurrection body is real and physical, but not limited as ours are (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). John does not explain it, and neither should anyone else.

Peace be with you. The ordinary greeting, shalom, but from the risen Lord to the men who deserted him it is far more: the peace he promised (14:27; 16:33), now won by the cross (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14–17). He does not begin with a rebuke; he greets them. Peace with God is more than a calm feeling: the war between a holy God and rebel sinners is over, because the Son took the hostility on himself (Romans 5:10), and the men who ran from him are welcome at his side.

He showed them his hands and his side. Proof that this is the Jesus who was crucified. The marks were kept on purpose: the one thing he carried out of the grave from the old world into the new creation is the evidence of what our salvation cost. His wounds remain in his glorified body, the eternal marks of his love (Revelation 5:6).

They were glad. Three nights earlier he had promised it: your sorrow will turn into joy; I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you (16:20–22). The sorrow arrived exactly as described, and so did the joy.

In everyday life. Behind which locked door are you hiding: fear of a diagnosis, of a person, of the future, of being found out? The risen Christ comes through locked doors with peace, and his wounds prove that you are safe with him. Tell a trusted friend what you are afraid of, and pray together.

What will our resurrection bodies be like? Like his (Philippians 3:21; 1 John 3:2). His risen body was truly physical: he could be touched, he ate fish (Luke 24:42–43), he bore the marks of his history. Yet it was no longer subject to weakness, decay or death. It is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–44): the same you, made whole and glorious, with nothing lost that was truly yours and nothing left that sin had spoiled.
verseByVerse.note: “Peace be with you” was the ordinary Hebrew greeting, shalom, now full of meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus sends his disciples into the world as the Father sent him, and breathes on them the Holy Spirit, the breath of a new creation.

As the Father has sent me. Peace again, now for their mission: this is John’s Great Commission. The Son’s mission becomes the church’s (17:18): to make the Father known, to serve, to suffer, and to bring people to God. “As” means more than in a similar spirit: the Son was sent all the way into our world, at his own cost, and stayed within reach of people who did not want him. So are they sent, and he says it while showing them the marks.

He breathed on them. The verb (emphysaō) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it is used of God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), and of the breath that comes upon the slain in Ezekiel’s valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). Creation, and new life breathed into a field of corpses: in a locked room, on the first day of the week, a new creation begins. Something real was given, not a mere symbol, for no one is sent on that errand without the Spirit.

Receive the Holy Spirit. The word for spirit is the word for breath in both Hebrew and Greek: he breathes, and says, receive the Breath.

In the flow. Verses 19–23 keep, one after another, the promises of the upper room: peace (14:27), joy (16:22), the sending (17:18) and the Spirit (14:16–17; 16:7). Peace comes first, because men not at peace with God cannot be sent; then the commission; then the Spirit; and in verse 23 the message itself, forgiveness of sins.

Only God can give the Spirit of God. The Son who received the Spirit without measure now breathes him out on his friends: he is not only the one on whom the Spirit rests but the one who gives him. On the first day of the new creation the breath of life came from the mouth of a man with nail marks in his hands, and he is the Lord God. Every Christian alive is a person the risen Lord has breathed on.

In everyday life. You are sent as Christ was sent. Pick the place this week where you are most like a missionary: the office, the school gate, the club, the family table. Ask the Spirit for courage there, and do one concrete thing for one person in his name.

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit after conversion? No. The apostles stood at a unique turning point between the resurrection and Pentecost, and received the Spirit in stages because redemption itself was unfolding in stages. Since Pentecost every believer receives the Spirit at conversion: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), and in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). What you need is not a second blessing but a daily filling, keeping in step with the Spirit you already have (Galatians 5:25; Ephesians 5:18) through the word, prayer and obedience. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers, often marked by deep love for Christ, teach a later baptism in the Spirit; we differ because the letters written to ordinary churches never tell believers to seek one, but we differ as brothers.

Where Christians differ: this gift and Pentecost. Some see this as John’s version of Pentecost; others as a separate, partial gift. This commentary’s view: this is a real gift, but also an acted promise, preparing the disciples for the full outpouring at Pentecost about seven weeks later, when Jesus had ascended (7:39; 16:7; Acts 1:4–5, 8). The Spirit was given to them here, and poured out in power there. Both show that the Spirit comes from the risen Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam.

parallels.desc: the breath of life
come, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld." Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord entrusts his church with the announcement of forgiveness: through the gospel it declares forgiven those whom God forgives, and unforgiven those who refuse him. And Thomas was not there to hear it.

If you forgive the sins of any. In the best manuscripts both verbs are in a Greek tense that describes something already done: they have already been forgiven, they have already been withheld. The disciples do not create forgiveness; they announce what God has done (Acts 2:38; 13:38–39). It is the construction Jesus used of binding and loosing, where what the church binds on earth will already have been bound in heaven (Matthew 16:19; 18:18). Grammar alone cannot settle a doctrine, but it points one way: heaven does not ratify the church’s verdict; the church announces heaven’s.

The reading that deserves an answer. A great many Christians hold the Roman reading: the apostles, and the bishops and priests who succeed them, are given power to absolve sins in the confessional, and the Council of Trent cited this text for it. The words plainly commit something about sins to these men, so it deserves an answer. Nowhere in the New Testament does an apostle hear a private confession and pronounce a man absolved. Peter does not absolve Simon the magician but sends him to God: “Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you” (Acts 8:22). And John, who wrote this verse down, tells us in his letter where a sinner is to take his sins: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Confession there is to God, and the promise rests on his faithfulness, not on a mediator’s word.

What the verse does mean. Christ has entrusted his church with the announcement that decides where people stand: the keys of the kingdom, as Matthew calls them. When the gospel is preached, forgiveness is really offered and really withheld. To the one who repents and believes, the church may say with full authority, your sins are forgiven; to the one who will not, it must say with equal authority that they are not. Every gospel sermon is the risen Lord announcing from heaven what he accomplished on the cross. The Reformers kept the declaration of pardon in public worship, and Luther valued private confession to a pastor for a conscience too troubled to believe a general promise. What they refused was the idea that forgiveness waits on the minister. He is a herald carrying a message, not a judge holding a power, and the best thing he can do for a frightened soul is tell him what God has already said.

Thomas was not with them. John does not say why Thomas was absent, and does not blame him; his story follows (vv. 25–28).

Should I ever confess my sins to another Christian? Yes, sometimes, though not to receive absolution. Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed (James 5:16). Confessing a secret sin to a mature believer or a pastor can break its power, bring accountability, and let you hear the gospel’s promises spoken to you by name. Where you have sinned against someone, confess to them and make it right (Matthew 5:23–24). But the forgiveness itself comes from God alone, through Christ alone, the moment you confess to him. Every sin is first of all against God (Psalm 51:4), and only the one who has been wronged can release the debt: a brother can remind you that you are forgiven; only God can forgive you.

Where Christians differ: who forgives sins? Roman Catholic teaching sees here the institution of the sacrament of penance, giving priests power to absolve sins in confession. This commentary’s view: only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). The words are given to the disciples as a group, and their exercise in Acts is the preaching of the gospel: forgiveness is proclaimed to all who repent and believe. Every Christian who declares the gospel speaks with this authority, and church discipline also applies it (1 Corinthians 5:4–5; 2 Corinthians 2:7–10). There is no special priestly power to absolve.

verseByVerse.quote: So the other disciples told him, "We have seen the Lord." But he said to them, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thomas will not believe the others’ word unless he sees and touches the wounds, and a week later the risen Lord comes again, through locked doors, for him.

Unless I see. The ten give Thomas the testimony Mary gave them, “We have seen the Lord”, and he answers with a condition. “Doubting Thomas” has become a byword, but the text does not support the caricature. The others were glad only when Jesus showed them his hands and his side (v. 20), and they had not believed Mary’s word either (Luke 24:11). Thomas is asking for exactly what they were given: not more evidence than his friends had, but no less.

I will never believe. “Never” is the strongest “no” Greek has (ou mē). He is not a cynic but a realist who will not accept something so great on hearsay, and his doubt, recorded honestly, shows the disciples were not gullible. This is the man who, when the others argued against returning to Judea, said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (11:16). Yet his words carry a warning: the heart loves to set God its terms and tell him what proof it will accept. Jesus met Thomas’s terms in mercy, but he is not bound to meet ours, and he has already given the evidence he means us to weigh (vv. 30–31).

The week he spent. For eight days ten friends told him the same impossible thing, and he alone stood outside it, unable to believe and unwilling to pretend. Yet he stayed, and on the following Sunday he was in the room. The risen Lord, who could have left Thomas to catch up from the others’ reports, came again for one man and spoke the same peace to him. The Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine for the one, and comes through locked doors to find him.

The marks he insisted on. Thomas’s test is more theological than he knows. He asks not for a sign in the sky but for the nail marks and the spear wound: the only risen Lord he will believe in is the crucified one, and he is right. A Christ without wounds would be some other figure, a ghost or a hero, and could save no one. The resurrection is not the cross undone but the cross shown to be accepted by God: the body that bore our sins is the body God raised, and the scars prove that the sacrifice and the victory belong to the same person.

What should I do when I struggle to believe? Do what Thomas did: stay where the others are, and keep turning up. Thomas did not reason his way out; he was in the room when Jesus came back. Do not withdraw from the church because you are struggling. Tell a trusted believer honestly what you are finding hard. Keep reading the Gospels, and pray even if it feels like talking to the ceiling: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Distinguish doubt from unbelief: doubt is a faith that is struggling, unbelief a refusal. Jesus was patient with the first, and he came back for Thomas.
verseByVerse.note: Nails were driven through the hands (or wrists) and feet.

parallels.desc: they have pierced my hands and feet

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe." Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus offers Thomas the very proof he demanded, and Thomas answers with the highest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!”

Put your finger here. Jesus gives Thomas back his own words from eight days earlier, almost exactly, though he was not visibly there when they were said, and there is no rebuke in the offer (see vv. 25–26).

Do not disbelieve, but believe. Literally “do not become unbelieving, but believing”: addressed to the whole direction of Thomas’s heart, not only to the moment.

My Lord and my God! The climax of John’s Gospel. We are not told that Thomas touched him: the offer itself seems to have been enough. A devout Jew, whose creed was “the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), stands in front of a man he knew had died and calls him God, and Jesus, who had corrected people about far less, does not correct him. Not “the Lord” but “my Lord”: not a formula, but a man handing himself over.

The frame of the book. John has framed the whole account between two statements that Christ is God: his own, “the Word was God” (1:1), and Thomas’s, spoken by the most reluctant man in the group, to a face, with the wounds visible. It also answers the claim that the church made Jesus God centuries later, at the Council of Nicaea (AD 325): here the confession stands in a first-century Gospel, on the lips of an eyewitness, and Paul’s letters, earlier still, already worship him as Lord (Philippians 2:6–11).

Our lord and god. If this Gospel was written in the nineties, as many think (see the introduction), it appeared under the emperor Domitian, who is reported to have liked being styled “our lord and god”. John hands Christians a sentence in which those words are addressed to somebody else.

The hands through which all things were made. The wounds Thomas demanded to see are the wounds of God. The Lord of glory was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), and the hands held out to the doubter are the hands through which all things were made. He is my Lord, because he bought me with those wounds. He is my God, because no one less could have paid that price.

In everyday life. If he is your Lord, what instruction of his are you resisting? If he is your God, what are you trusting instead of him? To say “my Lord” and “my God” is to hand over the whole of life, and none of us does it completely; but the wounded Lord obeyed the Father perfectly in our place, and his Spirit goes on making the confession true.

Why did Jesus not correct Thomas, when worship was refused elsewhere? Because the confession was true. When people tried to worship Paul and Barnabas, or when John fell at an angel’s feet, they were rebuked at once: worship God (Acts 14:14–15; Revelation 19:10). Jesus receives worship throughout the Gospels without protest (Matthew 14:33; 28:9, 17), and here the highest title there is. If he were not God, accepting it would be the very blasphemy he was crucified for. He accepts it, and blesses those who will say it after Thomas.

Where Christians differ: what Thomas meant. Some, such as Jehovah’s Witnesses, suggest Thomas was exclaiming in surprise, like an oath, or addressing the Father. This commentary’s view: the Greek says Thomas answered “him”, Jesus, and a devout Jew would hardly use God’s name as an exclamation (the third commandment). It is a confession, addressed to Jesus, and Jesus commends it in the next verse. Jesus is God.

parallels.desc: my God and my Lord

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces a blessing on everyone who will believe without seeing, and John explains that he has chosen his signs from many others for that very purpose.

Have you believed because you have seen me? Not a rebuke but a statement: Thomas stands there having just confessed Jesus as his God.

Blessed are those who have not seen. The last beatitude (a saying that begins “Blessed are”) of the Gospels, and it is for us. Every believer since the apostles has believed without seeing (1 Peter 1:8), resting on the testimony of those who saw (v. 31; 1 John 1:1–3), and Jesus calls us blessed, not second-class. He was looking past the room at people he had prayed for on the night before he died: “I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (17:20). The beatitude is that prayer answered, and one day the blessed who did not see will see him face to face.

Not blind faith. Not seeing carries a blessing of its own, but the beatitude is not “blessed are those who believe without evidence”. John has just spent twenty chapters supplying evidence, and says in the next verse that he selected it on purpose.

Almost everything we know, we were told. Many people today feel that Thomas had the right instinct: believe only what you can check for yourself. It sounds like honesty, but nobody lives that way. Augustine noticed, in his Confessions, how many things he believed without having seen them: the events of history, cities he had never visited, even who his own parents were, which he knew only because others told him. You have not checked that the earth goes round the sun, that your medicine contains what the label says, or that you were born on the date on your birth certificate. We live by testimony, and the real question is never whether to trust witnesses but which ones. So this beatitude is not a blessing on gullibility. It blesses people who receive a reliable report rather than insisting on judging every fact in person. And the deepest things in any life are known this way. Nobody can prove under a microscope that they love you; you take their word and watch how they keep it. The Gospels are that kind of word, from a God who kept his, and showed the wounds to prove it.

Many other signs. John has been selective (21:25), the mark of an honest writer: seven signs, as they are usually counted, out of many; a handful of days out of three years. He says so, and explains what his selection was for.

In the flow. The whole chapter has been a ladder of believing: the linen (v. 8), the name (v. 16), the hands and side (v. 20), the offered wounds (v. 28). Verse 29 adds the last rung, and it is ours: believing through the word of those who saw.

Why does Jesus not appear to people today to settle their doubts? Because he has already given what is needed, and more sight would not change hearts that will not believe. In Jesus’ parable, Abraham tells the rich man that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). The risen Christ appeared to chosen witnesses (Acts 10:40–41), whose testimony is written so that all may believe. Now he speaks through that word, and the Spirit opens blind eyes to see his glory in it (2 Corinthians 4:6). When he appears again, it will not be to invite faith but to judge and to save (Hebrews 9:28). None of this makes honest questions wrong: Jesus was patient with Thomas, and the witnesses wrote precisely so that questioners could weigh what they saw.

parallels.desc: though you do not now see him, you believe in him

verseByVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John states why he wrote: so that his readers may believe that Jesus is the promised Christ and the Son of God, and by believing share his own life. Every sign and every meeting in the book has served this one sentence.

So that you may believe. The purpose of the whole Gospel, and the last sentence of the book as John first ended it; chapter 21 reads as an epilogue. Twenty chapters arranged around one outcome, stated in a single sentence.

That Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The content of faith: Jesus of Nazareth is the promised Messiah of Israel, and the Son of God, sharing the Father’s nature. Martha confessed it (11:27); Thomas confessed it in its fullest form (v. 28). Both titles have been fought over in this book: the crowds argued over the Christ, and the Son of God is what they picked up stones over and Pilate was afraid of.

Life in his name. Eternal life, now and for ever (3:16; 17:3), through who he is and what he has done. The book began there: in him was life, and the life was the light of men (1:4). Everything since, from the water made wine to the name spoken in a garden, has served that one word, and it is offered at the end to whoever is holding the book.

He would not keep his life to himself. The Son of God did not leave his glory to rumour. He chose the witnesses and had it written down, so that people he would never meet in the flesh could hear his voice on a page and live. The faith the book asks for is his gift, and the life it promises is his own. Glory to Jesus, the Christ, the Son of God, the Life who would not keep his life to himself.

In everyday life. Give a copy of John’s Gospel to someone this month, and offer to read it with them.

How do I know whether I have this life? Do you believe that he is the Christ, the Son of God, who died for sinners and rose again, and are you relying on him, not your record, for your acceptance with God? Then you have life now, because he has said so: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life (3:36), and John wrote his letter so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). The evidence of that life will grow, in love for God’s people, hatred of sin and a desire to obey him, but it rests on his promise, not on your feelings. If you are not sure, believe him now. That is what the book was written for.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.” One reading suggests “that you may come to believe”, making the book evangelistic, for outsiders; the other “that you may go on believing”, making it a book for the church. The manuscripts are divided and the question has never been settled. It is a happy dispute, because the book plainly does both: it has brought sceptics to Christ and held Christians steady for twenty centuries.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “may continue to believe.”

20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.<sup>2</sup>So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>3</sup>So Peter went out with the other disciple, and they were going toward the tomb.<sup>4</sup>Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.<sup>5</sup>And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.<sup>6</sup>Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,<sup>7</sup>and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself.<sup>8</sup>Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;<sup>9</sup>for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.<sup>10</sup>Then the disciples went back to their homes.<sup>11</sup>But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb.<sup>12</sup>And she saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet.<sup>13</sup>They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”<sup>14</sup>Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>15</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher).<sup>17</sup>Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ’I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”<sup>18</sup>Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord”—and that he had said these things to her.<sup>19</sup>On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the doors being locked where the disciples were for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”<sup>20</sup>When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord.<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”<sup>22</sup>And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.<sup>23</sup>If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld.”<sup>24</sup>Now Thomas, one of the twelve, called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.<sup>25</sup>So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe.”<sup>26</sup>Eight days later, his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”<sup>27</sup>Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.”<sup>28</sup>Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”<sup>29</sup>Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;<sup>31</sup>but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
20.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 19 ended in a garden, with the body of Jesus laid in a new tomb as the Sabbath began. Now the first day of the week dawns, in the last chapter of the Gospel as John first ended it (v. 31); chapter 21 follows as an epilogue.

The message. The Jesus who was crucified is risen in the body, still bearing his wounds, and he comes to his own one by one to turn grief, fear and doubt into faith. Every meeting leads to one confession, that Jesus is Lord and God, and the blessing reaches beyond the room: those who believe the witnesses without seeing are blessed, and have life in his name.

Why it was said. John’s readers lived decades later, without the sight Thomas was given, some paying a price for confessing Jesus (see the introduction). They needed an eyewitness account of an empty tomb and a wounded, risen body, and the assurance that believing without seeing is not second best.

How the chapter makes its case. A ladder of believing. Mary finds the tomb open and supposes the body stolen (vv. 1–2); the beloved disciple sees the grave clothes lying in place and believes (vv. 3–10). Mary, weeping, knows Jesus when he calls her name and is sent to his brothers as the first witness (vv. 11–18). That evening he gives the frightened disciples peace, shows his wounds, sends them as the Father sent him, and breathes on them the Holy Spirit with the message of forgiveness (vv. 19–23). Thomas will not believe without the wounds; a week later Jesus offers them, and Thomas confesses, “My Lord and my God!” (vv. 24–29). John closes by stating the purpose of his book (vv. 30–31).

Where it leads. The chapter does not point to Christ from a distance; it shows him risen. The first day of the week becomes the first day of a new creation. The Good Shepherd calls his sheep by name (10:3). The one who said “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25) walks out of the grave and leaves the wrappings behind. The Son breathes the Spirit as God breathed life into Adam, and the Word who “was God” (1:1) is confessed as God by a doubter with the nail marks in front of him.

For us. The risen Christ still comes to grieving, frightened and doubting people through the testimony written in this book, and he speaks peace before he gives any task. You have not seen him, and you are not second-class: believe the witnesses, confess him as your Lord and your God, and carry his peace to the people around you.

keyVerse.quote: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
keyVerse.note: This verse states the purpose of the whole Gospel, and the chapter before it is that purpose acted out: Mary, the beloved disciple, the ten and Thomas each move from grief, fear or doubt to faith in the risen Jesus. Those who come after them and have not seen (v. 29) are given the witnesses’ written word, and by believing it they share his life.

20.reflection:
Mary did not know Jesus until he spoke her name (v. 16), and he spoke peace to the disciples who had deserted him before he gave them any task (vv. 19–21). What does the way the risen Jesus meets each person show you about how he deals with you in your grief, fear or failure?

Jesus says, “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (v. 21), and gives his disciples the Spirit and the message of forgiveness (vv. 22–23). Where are you sent this week, and how could you speak of the forgiveness Christ offers to someone there?

Thomas would not believe on the others’ word, yet he stayed with them and was in the room a week later (vv. 24–28). How should a church treat those who struggle to believe, and what has helped you when your own faith was weak?

Jesus calls those who believe without seeing “blessed” (v. 29), and John wrote “so that you may believe” (v. 31). Why is trusting the testimony of eyewitnesses reasonable rather than blind, and what would it mean for you this week to call Jesus “my Lord and my God”?

21.title: The Restoration of Peter and the Beloved Disciple

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Breakfast on the Shore: Restoration and Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last chapter shows the risen Christ providing for, restoring and sending his disciples. At his word an empty net is filled, and at his fire the men who had deserted him are fed (vv. 1–14). Beside that fire, the same kind as the one where Peter denied him, three questions answer three denials and three commissions give the failed disciple the flock to shepherd; Peter is told how he will glorify God by his death and is called again to follow (vv. 15–19). When he asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus tells him to mind his own road (vv. 20–23). The beloved disciple signs his witness as true, and the book closes on the countless deeds of Jesus that no library could hold (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration of Peter is one of the most pastoral scenes in the Gospels. Three questions match three denials, and three commissions answer three failures. The charcoal fire (18:18; see vv. 9–10) brings back the scene of the denial, and the failure is healed there, not passed over (see vv. 17–18). His answer to failure is not silence but a renewed commission: the shepherd who fell is restored to shepherd the flock.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple is the witness who wrote these things (v. 24): the account of one who stood at the cross, ran to the empty tomb and ate breakfast on this shore. And it ends not with a doctrine but with a person (see v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the Gospel’s first ending, the risen Jesus takes the initiative again and shows himself to seven of his disciples, not in the temple or on a mountain but by the lake where they earned their living. Without this chapter, Peter’s denial would still be lying where chapter 18 left it, beside a charcoal fire, unhealed.

By the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Galilee, named after the city Herod Antipas built on its shore; the place is full of memories for them. Jesus had told them he would meet them in Galilee (Mark 16:7). “Revealed himself” (ephanerōsen): made himself known. The initiative is entirely his: they went to work, and he showed himself to them (compare 1:43).

Seven disciples. Simon Peter is listed first: the denier who will be restored is the centre of this final scene. Thomas is here, the last we see of him, a man who stayed. Nathanael is given a home town for the only time: Cana, where Jesus did his first sign (2:1–11). The sons of Zebedee, James and John, are mentioned only here in this Gospel, John as usual keeping himself out of view, and two are left unnamed, an odd choice for a writer inventing a scene.

Does Jesus still reveal himself today? Yes, though not by appearing in a body on the shore. Those appearances were given to chosen witnesses for a limited time (Acts 1:3; 1 Corinthians 15:5–8), and they ended with his ascension, apart from the unique appearance to Paul, last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8). Now he makes himself known through his word, preached and read, by his Spirit, who takes what is Christ’s and declares it to us (16:14). He is present when his people gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), and, as here, he often makes himself known in ordinary places, at work and at home. Do not wait for a vision. Open the book where he has already revealed himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee. Nathanael came from Cana; the sons of Zebedee are James and John.

parallels.desc: he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to them, "I am going fishing." They said to him, "We will go with you." They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they wait in Galilee as they were told, the disciples go back to their boat and toil all night for nothing, and at daybreak Jesus is standing on the shore, unrecognised.

I am going fishing. This is often preached as Peter giving up his calling and going back to his old trade. The text does not support that. The risen Jesus had sent word: “tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me” (Matthew 28:10; Mark 16:7). They are waiting where they were told to wait, with no date given, and men who are waiting have to eat; six go with him, including the disciple whom Jesus loved. What is true, and sadder, is how aimless it is: not rebellion, but a man who has seen the risen Lord twice, and denied him three times, filling the hours while waiting for something he cannot arrange.

That night they caught nothing. Fishing on the lake was often done at night. A wasted night for professional fishermen on their own water, as at their first calling (Luke 5:5). It is the second time John has put them on that lake in the dark with nothing going right (6:16–21), and both times the story ends with somebody standing where they did not expect him.

They did not know that it was Jesus. As with Mary (20:14) and the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:16), they do not recognise him until he makes himself known.

As day was breaking. At dawn, as at the tomb, just when the night’s failure is confirmed. He stands on the shore, already through his own night of death, watching theirs end: that is where the risen Christ is for his church, not absent from the dark, but ahead of it, on the far side of death, where the morning has already come.

What should I do while I wait for God to show me the way? Do the next ordinary, faithful thing. The disciples had been told to go to Galilee and wait, and they waited by working. Waiting on God is neither idleness nor anxious sign-hunting. Keep doing what is in front of you: your job, your family duties, your place in the church, your prayers. Obey what he has made clear, and trust him for the rest. Guidance usually comes as it did here, to people already at their nets, not to people standing on the shore refusing to move until the heavens open.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night.

parallels.desc: we toiled all night and took nothing

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" They answered him, "No." He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a stranger’s word the empty net is suddenly too full to haul: without him they catch nothing, and with him more than they can hold (15:5).

Children, do you have any fish? “Children” (paidia) was a friendly way of addressing men, like “lads”: not the tender “little children” of the upper room (13:33) but the word a man uses hailing a boat. And what he asks about is not fish in general but the bit of fish you eat with your bread. It is the question a buyer shouts from the beach at dawn: caught anything? The Greek form expects the answer no, and they give it in one bare word. So the risen Son of God opens the conversation of Peter’s restoration by asking about breakfast.

Cast the net on the right side. A strange instruction to experienced fishermen from a stranger, and they obey. The Word through whom all things were made (1:3) is Lord of the shoal under the boat as well, and he knows where it is.

Not able to haul it in. The miracle recalls their first calling, when Jesus said they would be fishers of men (Luke 5:4–10). Then too there was a wasted night, an instruction, nets so full they began to break, and Peter on his knees saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.” This time Peter does not ask him to go away; he goes into the water to get to him. John does not mention Luke’s story, but the men in the boat had lived it, and when the nets went heavy a second time one of them knew at once who was on the beach.

Called and recalled with a full net. He called them with a full net and he recalled them with a full net, and between the two he went to the cross. Everything between those two catches was his doing, and the harvest of the nations still comes up in nets that he fills.

If I obey God, will he always give me success? Not always success as we would measure it, but always fruit as he measures it.
