Obedience is not a technique for guaranteed results: Jeremiah preached faithfully for forty years and was rejected. The promise is that whoever abides in Christ bears much fruit (15:5), and that your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). The size and timing of the catch are his. So work hard, obey his word, and leave the results in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: “Children” was a friendly way of addressing men.

parallels.desc: the first great catch

verseByVerse.quote: That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beloved disciple recognises the Lord in the full net, and Peter, true to form, cannot wait for the boat. One sees; the other jumps, exactly as they have all the way through (compare 20:4–8).

It is the Lord! Since the empty tomb this Gospel has given Jesus one title above all. Mary says “I have seen the Lord”, the ten say “We have seen the Lord”, Thomas says “My Lord and my God!”, and now the beloved disciple, peering at a figure on a beach, says “It is the Lord!” Kyrios is the word the Greek Old Testament used to render the name of God himself, so this is more than recognising a friend: that Jesus is Lord is the confession the church has made ever since (Romans 10:9).

He put on his outer garment. Fishermen worked in a loincloth or a short tunic. Oddly, he dresses before he swims, most likely because a Jew would not greet a person of standing improperly clothed; so he tucks up his garment and goes over the side in it.

Threw himself into the sea. He could have waited perhaps three minutes for the boat. That is Peter all over: the same impulse that drew a sword in the garden and swore he would die first. Nothing about Peter’s temperament has been corrected by his failure, and Jesus is about to give him a job without asking him to become somebody else.

About a hundred yards off. Literally two hundred cubits, about 90 metres; meanwhile the others drag the net ashore. Small measurements like this run all through this Gospel (2:6; 6:19; 19:39) and add nothing to the teaching. They are the kind of thing a man includes when he is describing something he watched; they cannot prove the account on their own, but they fit its claim to come from one who was there (v. 24).

Does Jesus want me to change my personality? He wants to make it holy, not erase it. Peter was still impulsive after the resurrection, and John still quietly perceptive; Christ used both. Grace does not make every Christian the same; it purges the sin that clings to our temperament: Peter’s boasting was broken, but his eagerness was turned toward Christ. So do not envy another believer’s temperament or despise your own. Ask the Lord to cut away what is sinful in it and to use what is left for his glory. The church needs those who see first, those who jump first, and those who quietly bring in the boat.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally two hundred cubits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread. Jesus said to them, "Bring some of the fish that you have just caught."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has breakfast cooking on a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire as the one where Peter denied him: grace is ready before the failure is even mentioned.

A charcoal fire. The word for a charcoal fire occurs exactly twice in the New Testament: here, and in the courtyard on the night Peter said “I am not” (18:18). John uses it again without explanation, and it is deliberate. Few things call back a memory like the smell of a fire. Peter denied his Lord beside one charcoal fire; he will be restored beside another.

Breakfast already cooking. Coals take time to make. While seven men spent the night failing on the water, he spent part of it making a fire.

Bring some of the fish. He does not need their fish; he has his own. But he asks for theirs and puts them on the fire beside his own, which is very nearly all there is to say about Christian work. He does not need anything we bring. He asks for it anyway, and he uses it alongside his own.

Between the two fires stood the cross. Peter had warmed himself at one fire while his Lord was being struck; now his Lord has lit another and waits at it with bread. Between the two fires stood the cross, where the Shepherd took the blows the sheep deserved. The one who tends this second fire has already dealt with the failure it recalls.

What if the memory of my failure keeps coming back? Look at what Jesus did with Peter’s memory. He did not pretend the courtyard had not happened, and he did not leave Peter alone with it. He lit the same kind of fire and made breakfast beside it, so that the smell of failure would from then on be mixed with the smell of grace. When an old sin comes back, do not bury it or let it accuse you. Bring it to Christ and look at it in the light of the cross: it was real, it was forgiven, and he has given you work to do since. The Lord does not erase our history; he redeems it, until the worst memory becomes a place where we learned how much he loves us.
verseByVerse.note: John mentions a charcoal fire only here and at Peter’s denial.

verseByVerse.quote: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn. Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter hauls the great catch ashore, unbroken, and Jesus invites the men who deserted him to breakfast; they know it is the Lord, and none of them dares to say a word.

153 of them. The number has attracted more ingenuity than any other detail in the Gospel. Jerome said there were 153 kinds of fish, standing for all nations; Augustine noticed that 153 is the sum of every number from 1 to 17. None of it commands agreement, and most of it could be done for almost any number. The plainest point is that fishermen counted their catch to share it out, and decades later an old man still remembered the figure: the memory of an eyewitness (see the note on vv. 7–8).

The net was not torn. In Luke 5:6 the nets began to break; here they hold. Some see a picture of the church: gathering all kinds of people, and not torn apart.

Come and have breakfast. As plain an invitation as there is, and the Lord of life speaks it. He does not explain himself or ease the awkwardness; he feeds them. The guest who supplied the wine at a wedding in Cana is the host now, and the first thing he does with men too awed to speak is give them a place at his fire.

None of the disciples dared ask him, Who are you? Something about him was different, and yet they knew it was the Lord: awe and certainty together. Seven men stand round a fire in a silence too large to break: not doubt, and not fear exactly, but the strangeness of standing beside someone you abandoned, who died, and who is cooking your breakfast.

In the flow. Chapter 21 shows what the sending of 20:21 will be like: at his word the nets overflow (vv. 3–11); in verses 15–17 the fishermen are made shepherds, because those who gather people in must also feed them; and the breakfast between says that the one who sends them goes on feeding them himself.

What does the full net say about the church’s mission? That the gathering of people is Christ’s work, that it is great, and that his net holds. The church is gathered from every nation and kind, and the strain often looks as though it must tear it. It will not. Christ will bring in all whom the Father has given him (6:37), and not one will slip through. So pray for missionaries, support the work of the gospel, and cast your own net, knowing that the outcome is in his hands.

In everyday life. Come and have breakfast with Jesus. Before the phone, the news and the day’s demands, give the first minutes to him: a psalm, a Gospel passage, a prayer. He has already prepared the meal.
verseByVerse.note: Many symbolic meanings have been proposed for 153; the plainest point is that someone counted: a detail from an eyewitness.

parallels.desc: their nets were breaking

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish. This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Lord serves his friends with his own hands, as he did before he died: his third appearance to the disciples is a real meal, and he is still the one who serves.

He took the bread and gave it. The verbs of the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake (6:11). Then the crowd wanted to make him king and walked away when he explained what it meant; now there is no crowd and no argument, just seven men eating breakfast with him. Luke tells us the risen Jesus also ate (Luke 24:42–43): his body was real.

He serves them. The risen Lord of glory, with the marks still in his hands, hands bread to seven fishermen who have been up all night. He had told them that he was among them as the one who serves (Luke 22:27), and he had knelt with a towel to prove it. The one who washed their feet before he died is cooking their breakfast after.

The third time. The third appearance to the group of disciples in John (20:19, 26); there were others (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The first two were indoors, behind locked doors; this one is outdoors at dawn, over a meal, under the open sky, with the whole world before them.

Not promoted out of serving. The bread of life (6:35) has not been promoted out of serving: exalted to the right hand of God, he still feeds his people by his word and at his table, and he has promised that when he returns the master himself will dress for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The fire on the beach was a foretaste of that table.

Is this a picture of the Lord’s Supper? Not directly; it is a real breakfast on a real beach, and John does not call it a sacrament. But it echoes the meals that point to his table, the feeding of the five thousand and the upper room, where the same Lord fed his people with his own hands. The Lord’s Supper is a memorial of his death and a means by which he nourishes your faith; you are not merely remembering an absent Christ. You are being fed by the risen one, spiritually present by his Spirit, who still takes bread and gives it to his disciples.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He said to him a second time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Tend my sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After breakfast Jesus asks Peter, by his old name, whether he loves him, and answers each “Yes, Lord” by entrusting to him his own flock: the restoration of the denier is also his commission.

Simon, son of John. Not Peter, the rock, but his old name, as at his first meeting with Jesus (1:42), when he was told, “You shall be called Cephas”, which means rock. Peter has not been a rock. Using the old name is not cruel; it is honest. A man who has failed badly cannot be repaired by being told the failure did not matter. Jesus takes him back to Simon son of John, and starts again from there.

The question nobody would predict. Not “Are you sorry?” or “Will you promise?” Peter is never asked to explain himself or to remake the vow he broke. “Do you love me?” That is the whole examination for restoration to apostolic ministry, and it is about love rather than performance. Religion left to itself offers a way back by penance: prove you are sorry, earn your place again, and perhaps you will be trusted. Jesus offers no such scheme, because Peter’s debt was paid at the cross; what he asks for is not repayment but love.

Two words for love. Jesus asks with agapaō the first two times; Peter answers with phileō each time; the third time Jesus uses phileō. Some see Jesus asking for the highest love, Peter offering only friendship love, and Jesus coming down to Peter’s level. But John uses the two words interchangeably elsewhere (both are used of the Father’s love for the Son, 3:35; 5:20), and in these three verses he varies four pairs of words (love, feed and tend, lambs and sheep, knowing), very likely just for variety. That does not settle it, and the older reading remains moving: Jesus meeting a chastened Peter where he is. Either way the meaning stands: three questions answering three denials, and a full restoration.

Feed my lambs. The flock is “my lambs”: they belong to Christ, not to Peter. Peter had disowned the Shepherd; now the Good Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep (10:11) puts the sheep into his hands. The shepherd must feed them, with the word of God, and tend them (poimaine): shepherd, care for, guide, protect.

In the flow. Peter’s story runs in three scenes: the boast at the supper (13:37–38), the denials beside a charcoal fire (18:17, 25–27), and this scene beside another fire, where verses 18–19 take up the old boast: Peter will indeed lay down his life, not by his own resolve this time, but because the Lord who restored him will keep him.

Does Feed my sheep make Peter the head of the church and the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching reads it so. On why this commentary reads it as the restoration of a fallen apostle, see the box “Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy” at the end of the note on vv. 17–18. The commission is for every faithful pastor.

What if I do not feel much love for Jesus? Then do what Peter did: take your love, such as it is, to the one who knows everything. Love for Christ is measured not by the intensity of your feelings on a given day but by whether you want him, trust him, grieve when you fail him, and want to obey him. Weak love is still love. And love grows by looking at his love for you: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Read the passion narrative slowly, and this chapter, then ask him to increase your love. It is a prayer he delights to answer.

In everyday life. Love for Christ shows itself in care for his people. Think of one lamb in your church, a new believer, a child, a struggling member, and do one thing to feed them this week.

Uncertain wording. “More than these” is compressed in the Greek and can mean more than these men love me, more than you love these men, or more than you love these things, the boats, nets and fish. The grammar allows all three. The first is most likely: Peter had boasted that even if all fell away, he would not (Mark 14:29; Matthew 26:33). Jesus gently probes that pride, raising Peter’s own comparison once and never again.
verseByVerse.note: “More than these” probably means more than the other disciples love me: Peter had claimed he would never fall away.

parallels.desc: shepherd the flock of God

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" and he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep. Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third question matches the third denial; Peter, grieved, rests his case on Jesus’ knowledge, receives the flock again, and is told that he will one day follow his Lord to a cross. Jesus does not pretend the denials did not happen; he heals them, as precisely as they were committed: a charcoal fire for a charcoal fire, three questions for three denials.

Peter was grieved. A strong verb: distressed, pained, and it was the third asking that did it. He knew what the third time pointed back to.

You know everything. Peter cannot prove his love by his record, so he throws himself on Jesus’ knowledge. He has run out of evidence about himself, and promises had proved worthless; he has only “you know everything”. And he is saying something about Jesus as well as himself. Only God knows the human heart (1 Kings 8:39; John 2:24–25), and the disciples had already confessed, “Now we know that you know all things” (16:30). Peter stakes everything on a knowledge that belongs to God alone. Jesus accepts it, requires no more, and at once hands over the sheep. Failure is not the end of service.

When you were young. “Stretch out your hands” was an ancient way of describing crucifixion, and the next verse says outright that it refers to his death. Early tradition says he was crucified in Rome under Nero, around AD 64–68, and a later tradition adds that he asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord did. Peter had said he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37); now Jesus says he will. He is told quietly, over breakfast, that he will die for his Lord and will not want to go. The Lord does not pretend the road is easy, and he does not withhold the commission because the man will suffer for it.

He spoke to Peter’s love, not his denials. The Lord who knows everything chose to speak to Peter’s love rather than his denials, because the denials had already been carried to the cross and paid for in the wounds he bore. The fisherman who once could not admit to a servant girl that he knew Jesus died owning him before the world, and the grace that did that has not grown weaker since.

Why do we fear being carried more than dying? Jesus describes Peter’s youth in words that could serve as the creed of our age: you dressed yourself and walked wherever you wanted. What modern people dread about old age is often less the pain than the dependence; in the American states that keep records of assisted deaths, the concern most often reported is not pain but losing autonomy. Jesus neither flatters that ideal nor despises Peter’s fear; he tells him the truth. The young man who walked wherever he wanted walked straight into a courtyard and denied his Lord; the old man who will be bound and led will glorify God. The freedom that was all self-direction failed him, and the dependence he dreads will be the making of him. Nor will he be carried anywhere his Lord has not gone first. Jesus was bound and led away (18:12, 24), and stretched out his hands on a cross, so that for his people the road ends not in the loss of the self but with the one who says, “Follow me.”

Can a pastor who has fallen be restored to ministry? Every repentant sinner can be restored to Christ and to the fellowship of the church, fully and gladly. Restoration to the office of pastor is a different question. Peter was restored by the Lord himself, in person, to an apostleship that only Christ could give. Today the church must apply the qualifications Christ has set: an elder must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled and well thought of (1 Timothy 3:1–7). Some sins, especially abuse of the flock, betray a trust so deeply that the person should never again hold the office, however real his repentance; protecting the sheep comes first. Other failures may allow a careful return after time, accountability and proven change. Forgiveness is always offered. Office is a trust, not a right.

In everyday life. Confessed and forgiven failure does not disqualify you from Christ’s service. If you have been sitting on the sidelines of the church because of something in your past that has been confessed and forgiven, ask your pastor this week how you can serve.

Where Christians differ: Peter and the papacy. Roman Catholic teaching sees this passage, with Matthew 16:18, as Christ giving Peter primacy over the whole church, passed on to the bishops of Rome. This commentary’s view: this is the restoration of a fallen apostle, not the founding of an office. Peter calls himself a “fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1) and tells all elders to shepherd the flock (1 Peter 5:2). Paul opposed him to his face (Galatians 2:11). The New Testament says nothing of Peter’s successors. All pastors are under-shepherds of the one Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4).
verseByVerse.note: Three questions mirror Peter’s three denials. “Stretch out your hands” was an expression used of crucifixion; early Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God. And after saying this he said to him, "Follow me." Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, "Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter’s death will glorify God, and the command that began his discipleship now renews it: “Follow me.” As he turns, the beloved disciple is already following.

By what kind of death. By the time John wrote, Peter had died, and John has used this form of words once before, about Jesus (12:33). Peter’s death will not atone for sin, which only Christ’s death could do, but it will glorify God. A martyr’s death is not a defeat: a man who goes to a cross rather than deny Christ tells the watching world, with the last thing he has, that Christ is worth more than life (Philippians 1:20–21).

Follow me. Where it began (1:43; Mark 1:17), it ends. They are the words he said to Peter beside this very lake, with a net in his hands (Matthew 4:19). Everything has happened in between, the sinking in the waves, the sword in the garden, the courtyard and the rooster, and the instruction has not changed by a syllable. There was no new arrangement for a man who had failed: no reduced role, no probation. Jesus had not lowered the terms; he had paid for the failure and renewed the call. And it is not a single decision but a way of going on, all the way, even to a cross.

The disciple whom Jesus loved following them. John identifies him by the supper, where he leaned back against Jesus and asked who the betrayer was (13:23–25): the one closest to Jesus that night is quietly doing what Peter has just been told to do.

The end of the road. Peter died glorifying God because the one he followed had died first, and risen, and was waiting at the end of the road.

What does following Christ look like day by day? It means going where he leads, at his pace, by his word: listening to him in Scripture; taking his commands as your instructions for the day; choosing his way when it costs you; confessing quickly when you stray and getting back behind him. It means being with his people, because he is leading a flock, not a set of individuals. And it means accepting the road he chooses, for Peter a cross and for John a long old age. Following is not admiring him from a distance but walking behind him.

In everyday life. “Follow me” is not only a word for the great crossroads. It is spoken over the commute, the inbox and the hard conversation you would rather avoid, and answered there, one ordinary step behind him. You will follow unevenly, as Peter did; the one ahead of you did the Father’s will without a misstep, in your place, and your standing rests on his obedience, not yours.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, "Lord, what about this man?" Jesus said to him, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter asks what will become of the beloved disciple, and Jesus declines to answer: each disciple’s road is the Lord’s to appoint, and the business of each is to follow.

Lord, what about this man? Very human, and the timing is what makes it so useful. Peter has just been restored, commissioned and told how he will die. Within a sentence he has turned round, spotted the beloved disciple behind them, and asked about him. It is not malice but the instinct that arrives the moment a person is given something hard: to find out what the other man is getting. Peter has just been handed a cross, and his first move is to check whether crosses are being handed out evenly.

If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? A blunt word. Jesus does not tell Peter what John’s road will be, or justify the difference, or soften it; he declines the question. “You follow me!”: “you” is emphatic in the Greek. Mind your own call.

Until I come. Inside the “if” sits a certainty. Jesus does not say whether this disciple will live to see it, but he speaks of his coming as fixed, the point towards which every disciple’s road runs. Peter’s cross and John’s old age both run toward the return of the same Lord, who holds both lives in his hand (14:3). The question for a disciple is never how long he has, but who is coming.

The comparison that corrodes. Every Christian eventually notices that another believer’s marriage, health, children or work looks easier. The comparison corrodes both ways, breeding resentment when we come off worse and complacency when we come off better. Jesus’ answer to it is “what is that to you?” He calls each disciple for himself, not by comparison with anyone else. By early tradition Peter’s road ended on a cross in Rome and John’s in extreme old age in Ephesus, and neither was owed the other’s.

Is it wrong to ask God why my life is harder than someone else’s? It is not wrong to bring your grief honestly to God; the psalmists did it constantly. Asaph envied the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary of God and saw their end (Psalm 73). What is wrong is to keep the comparison as a grievance, as though God owed you another person’s road. Bring the question to him, and then let him answer as he answered Peter: your road is mine to choose; follow me on it. He chose it in love, he walks it with you, and every road his people walk ends in the same place, with him.

How do I keep my eyes on my own road? Comparison arrives, as it did for Peter, as a quick glance over the shoulder. Some ordinary ways to answer it: Catch the question. When you find yourself asking “what about him?”, say it to the Lord in so many words instead of letting it run on underneath. Hear his answer. Your road is not a share of a fixed amount that someone else got more of; it is his particular call to you. Look at the one who chose it. It was chosen by a Shepherd who walked a harder road first, all the way to a cross, for you, and who has already given you what no comparison can touch: himself (Romans 8:32). Take the next step. Ask what obedience he is asking of you today, and do that. Turn the glance into prayer. When the other person comes to mind, pray for them by name, and thank God for one specific mercy in your own lot.

verseByVerse.quote: So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John corrects a rumour by quoting Jesus’ exact words, “if” and all, and then signs his Gospel: the beloved disciple is the witness who wrote these things, and his testimony is true.

The saying spread abroad. The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age; tradition says John lived in Ephesus until the reign of Trajan, around AD 98, the last of the apostles (see the introduction). A sentence beginning “if” gets repeated, the “if” falls off, and within a generation it is a promise. If the beloved disciple was by then very old, or had died, believers might conclude that Jesus’ word had failed; John shows that Jesus never said it.

Jesus did not say. John corrects the rumour without indignation or embarrassment: he quotes the sentence back exactly, with the “if” restored, and points out the difference. The Spirit who brought Christ’s words to the apostles’ remembrance (14:26) has kept those words for us, exact, “if” and all.

The disciple who is bearing witness. The author identifies himself as the beloved disciple: the Gospel is eyewitness testimony. Witness is the thread through the whole book (1:7; 5:36–37), and here the promise that the Spirit and the disciples would bear witness about Jesus (15:26–27) is kept. The man who leaned against him at the supper has borne his witness, and it is all about one person. He never names himself; he names Jesus on every page.

How do I guard against misreading Scripture as the rumour did? Do what John did: go back to the exact words. Read the whole sentence in its context; notice the small words, the ifs and buts and therefores; compare Scripture with Scripture, since the Bible is its own best interpreter. Be suspicious of teaching that rests on a single verse in isolation, especially one that promises what Jesus did not clearly say, and read with the church, past and present.

Was chapter 21 added later? Some scholars argue that this whole chapter was added after John’s death by the church that preserved his teaching. The case is not silly: 20:30–31 reads like the end of a book, and here at the close someone other than the author appears to vouch for him.

Why it belongs to the book. Two things weigh heavily the other way. First, no surviving manuscript of this Gospel that preserves its ending lacks chapter 21, as far as is known, in any language. That is quite unlike the woman caught in adultery or the long ending of Mark, where the copies genuinely divide and your Bible carries a footnote saying so: there is no evidence that this book ever circulated without these verses. Second, the “we” needs no editor to explain it (see “Uncertain wording” below): a document can carry the endorsement of the elders who published it without ceasing to be the author’s own, much as a preface signed by others does not make a book someone else’s.

No ascension scene. Luke tells the ascension twice because he is writing the sequel; John simply stops. Once his purpose (20:31) is done he does not need a departure scene (on the Gospel’s last picture, see v. 25).

Uncertain wording. Who are the “we” of “we know that his testimony is true”? John does not say. Most likely they are the elders of the church at Ephesus, or the circle around John, who knew him and vouch for his Gospel. Some think it is the author himself speaking with the shared apostolic witness, as in “we have seen his glory” (1:14). Either way the sense is plain: this testimony is attested as true.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour may have spread because the beloved disciple lived to a great age. Verse 24 identifies him as the author of the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John ends by admitting that his book is a selection: Jesus did far more than any library could hold, and what is written is enough to believe and have life. A reader could close the book thinking he now has Jesus complete, between two covers; John’s last act is to say that what is not here would swamp the world.

The world could not contain the books. A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of saying countless, flagged with “I suppose”: a man who has finished writing about someone he loves and finds it absurdly inadequate. Yet it is true that the person and work of Jesus are inexhaustible. If the Word through whom all things were made (1:3) became flesh, then the world itself is too small to hold the full account of him. The book is finished. The subject is not.

More than every library on earth. The Lord whose deeds would overflow every library on earth stooped into a single human life, three years, one week, a cross and a garden, and then let an old disciple choose a handful of days to show us who he is. The book closes and its subject goes on, and the whole of eternity will be his people discovering that the half was not told them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that we need other sources, traditions or revelations to know Jesus truly. What is written is enough to believe and have life (20:31). The Scriptures are sufficient, though not exhaustive: everything we need to know Christ, be saved and live for God is there (2 Timothy 3:15–17).

The last picture. The Gospel ends not with a doctrine or an ascension but on a beach in Galilee, with a charcoal fire burning down and a man who had failed being told to keep walking. Not a throne or a cloud, but a meal cooking, a question that is not “Are you sorry?” but “Do you love me?”, and two words that never change.

Will we keep learning about Jesus in heaven? Yes, for ever. Knowing him is eternal life (17:3), and an infinite person cannot be exhausted by finite creatures in any number of ages. Paul prays that we may comprehend the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:18–19), and the coming ages will show the immeasurable riches of his grace (Ephesians 2:7). We will know truly and without distortion (1 Corinthians 13:12), but never completely, because he is God. Heaven will be the beginning of discovery, without sin to blur the view, and every new sight of him will be cause for fresh worship.

In everyday life. If you have read this Gospel through, do not put it away as finished. Begin it again, and ask for one new sight of Christ in every chapter.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.<sup>2</sup>Simon Peter, Thomas (called the Twin), Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.<sup>3</sup>Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We will go with you.” They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.<sup>4</sup>Just as day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.<sup>5</sup>Jesus said to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answered him, “No.”<sup>6</sup>He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.<sup>7</sup>That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.<sup>8</sup>The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land, but about a hundred yards off.<sup>9</sup>When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.”<sup>11</sup>So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net ashore, full of large fish, 153 of them. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.<sup>12</sup>Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” Now none of the disciples dared ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and so with the fish.<sup>14</sup>This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after he was raised from the dead.<sup>15</sup>When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”<sup>16</sup>He said to him a second time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”<sup>17</sup>He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.<sup>18</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go.”<sup>19</sup>(This he said to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God.) And after saying this he said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>20</sup>Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who also had leaned back against him during the supper and had said, “Lord, who is it that is going to betray you?”<sup>21</sup>When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”<sup>22</sup>Jesus said to him, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”<sup>23</sup>So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die; yet Jesus did not say to him that he was not to die, but, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?”<sup>24</sup>This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true.<sup>25</sup>Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
21.overview:
Where we are. John 20 closed with the purpose of the book (20:30–31), and chapter 21 follows as an epilogue. The scene moves to the Sea of Galilee. Peter has seen the Lord risen, but his threefold denial beside a charcoal fire (18:15–27) still lies where chapter 18 left it, unhealed.

The message. The risen Jesus goes on caring for his own: he fills their empty nets, cooks their breakfast and restores the one who failed him. He does not restore Peter by pretending the denials never happened, nor by penance, but by asking for love and giving him the flock to shepherd. Each disciple has his own road, appointed by the Lord, and the one command for all of them is “Follow me.”

Why it was said. By the time John wrote, Peter had died a martyr’s death and the beloved disciple was very old (see the introduction). The churches needed to know that Peter’s fall had been healed and his shepherding was Christ’s gift, that the rumour of John living until Christ came was never Jesus’ promise, and that their Gospel came from a true eyewitness.

How the chapter makes its case. After a fruitless night a stranger’s word fills the net; the beloved disciple knows the Lord, and Peter throws himself into the sea (vv. 1–8). Jesus feeds them at a charcoal fire (vv. 9–14). Three times he asks Peter, “Do you love me?”, three times commissions him to feed his sheep, then tells him the death by which he will glorify God and calls him again: “Follow me” (vv. 15–19). Peter asks about the beloved disciple and is told to mind his own call, and John corrects the rumour that grew from it (vv. 20–23), signs his testimony and closes with the countless things Jesus did (vv. 24–25).

Where it leads. Here the risen Christ does what he promised as the Good Shepherd (10:11–16, 27–29): he keeps the sheep the Father gave him, even the one who disowned him. Between the two charcoal fires stood the cross, so the question “Do you love me?” rests on a debt already paid, and a failed shepherd can be sent back to the flock. The Gospel that began with the Word through whom all things were made ends with that Word handing bread to fishermen.

For us. No failure confessed to Christ is beyond his restoring, and he restores us not to the sidelines but to service. He asks us what he asked Peter: not whether we are sorry enough, but whether we love him. And when we glance at someone else’s road, he says to us what he said to Peter: “You follow me!”

keyVerse.quote: He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this moment. Three questions answer three denials, Peter rests his love on the Lord’s knowledge rather than on his own record, and the disciple who failed is sent at once to shepherd Christ’s flock. It shows how the risen Lord restores sinners: not by pretending and not by penance, but by love and a renewed call.

21.reflection:
Jesus restored Peter beside a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire where Peter had denied him, and asked him not whether he was sorry but “Do you love me?” (vv. 9, 15–17). What does this show about the way Christ deals with our failures, and is there a memory you need to bring to him?

The disciples caught nothing all night, and at Jesus’ word the net was full; then he asked them to bring some of their fish to his fire (vv. 3–10). How should this shape the way we think about our work, in the church and outside it?

Peter’s love for Christ was to show itself in feeding Christ’s lambs and sheep (vv. 15–17). Who in your church is one of those lambs, and what could you do to care for them this month?

Told of his own hard road, Peter at once asked, “Lord, what about this man?” (v. 21). Where are you tempted to compare your lot with another believer’s, and how does Jesus’ answer, “You follow me!”, help you?
